This split — intrinsics for primitive numeric operators and class-typed equality, declared methods for user-defined and string-concatenation operators — keeps the std lib's record-syntax primitive declarations short (they exist mainly to host static methods like `Parse` and `MaxValue`, not to enumerate every operator) while preserving the regular operator-overload mechanism for user types.

<a id="sec-derived-type-properties"></a>
### 3.6 Derived type properties

Several rules in this specification classify types by a predicate computed from the type's *structure* — its declaration and, for a generic type, its type arguments — rather than by anything the programmer declares. Such a predicate is a **derived type property**. This section defines the mechanism once; the individual properties are defined where their subject matter lives and obey the common rules below.

The derived type properties of this revision:

| Property | Defined in | Classifies |
|---|---|---|
| **trivial-dispose** | [§28.9](#sec-runtime-managed-types) | classes whose disposal provably runs no user code and releases only memory: no destructor, no `owned` fields of non-trivial-dispose type, no owning-inline-array fields, trivial-dispose base |
| **borrow-bearing** | [§9.7](#sec-records-and-disposal) | records (and inline arrays, [§15.1](#sec-inline-arrays)) carrying at least one borrow of a non-runtime-managed reference type; for choices the [§35.4](#sec-choice-classification) rule-2 classification |
| **choice classification** | [§35.4](#sec-choice-classification) | every choice type, as value-like, borrow-bearing, or owning — the classification on which a choice's copyability, move/dispose semantics, and disposal obligation depend |
| **holds-borrows** | [§35.4](#sec-choice-classification) | every choice type: whether any case has a *borrow-carrying* payload field ([§9.7](#sec-records-and-disposal)'s field-level predicate), reading **this** property at a nested choice payload — the condition on which the [§9.7](#sec-records-and-disposal) borrow-lifetime obligations key for choices; an owning choice can hold borrows beside its owned payloads |
| **auto-hashable** | [§9.2](#sec-body-records) | records and value-like choices for which `=`, `GetHashCode`, and `ToString` are synthesized ([§35.7](#sec-choice-equality)); membership is computed after `equality skip` exclusions ([§9.2](#sec-equality-skip)) |
| **serialization-eligible** | [§9.8](#sec-serialization-synthesis) | records, enums, and value-like choices for which `Serialize`/`Deserialize` are synthesized ([§35.7](#sec-choice-equality)) |
| **hashable** | [§8.3](#sec-equals-and-gethashcode), [§9.2](#sec-body-records) | types usable where consistent `Equals`/`GetHashCode` are required (hash-container keys/elements): every type except (a) a record that is neither auto-hashable nor declares user equality, (b) a choice that is neither value-like auto-hashable nor declares user equality ([§35.7](#sec-choice-equality) — owning and borrow-bearing choices are not hashable; a value-like choice outside auto-hashable **only** because it carries a homogeneous `=`/`<>` overload is hashable on the strength of the `Equals(T)`/`GetHashCode` [§25.2](#sec-operator-overloading-restrictions)'s co-declaration rule obliges beside it), and (c) a nullable type `T?`, or an inline array of any [§15.1](#sec-inline-arrays) form whose element type is `T` or `T?`, where `T` is itself not hashable — such a type's `Equals` and `GetHashCode` are `T`'s, through [§8.4](#sec-=-and)'s null-safe wrapper or [§15.1.2](#sec-inline-array-members)'s element-wise equality; *declaring user equality* means (`operator =`/`<>` with `Equals(T)`/`GetHashCode` per the [§25.2](#sec-operator-overloading-restrictions) co-declaration rule) |
| **element category** | [§28.11](#sec-collection-element-ownership), stdlib [§4.14](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-owned-buffers-and-spans) | every type, as collection-element: value, runtime-managed reference, class/interface, or move-only value — the classification on which collection and buffer slot semantics dispatch |
| **sendable** | [§30.14](#sec-sendable-types) | types whose values may cross an execution-domain boundary (spawn arguments and results, channel elements) |
| **C-compatible** | [§32.13](#sec-c-compatible-records) | records passable across the FFI boundary by address: fixed field order, fields drawn from the FFI-compatible scalars, inline arrays of them, and nested C-compatible records, target-C-ABI layout |
| **defaultable** | [§17.11](#sec-the-default-operator) | types for which `default(T)` is defined: every nullable type `T?`; and every non-nullable value type whose components are recursively defaultable — the primitives, the unit type, an enum **declaring a zero-valued constant**, a record all of whose declared fields are defaultable and which is not constructor-only ([§9.9](#sec-constructor-only-records)), an inline array whose element type is defaultable (the owning forms `[N owned]T?` included). Not defaultable: non-nullable reference types; **every choice type** ([§35.10](#sec-choice-default-with)); an enum with no zero-valued constant; a constructor-only record ([§9.9](#sec-constructor-only-records)); and any record or inline array with a non-defaultable component |
| **constructor-only** | [§9.9](#sec-constructor-only-records) | records declaring a constructor carrying a contract clause ([§22.16](#sec-contract-clauses)): such a record is not defaultable and admits no `with` ([§9.5](#sec-non-destructive-update-with)) — a claim about a value's provenance, not about its validity |

Common rules, normative for every derived type property:

1. **Computed, never declared.** A derived type property cannot be asserted, opted into, or waived by annotation. It follows from structure; the only way to change it is to change the structure.
2. **Per-instantiation evaluation for generics.** For a generic type or member, the property is evaluated at each instantiation, after substituting the type arguments. A generic body type-checks under the weakest assumption its constraints establish; an instantiation that violates a property-dependent requirement is rejected *at the instantiation site*, with a diagnostic naming the property, the offending type argument, and the structural reason ([§28.5](#sec-owned-fields)'s generic-owned-field check and the owning-collection element restriction of [§14.4](#sec-owned-as-a-generic-argument) follow this pattern). A requirement carried by a body's use of a type parameter — an interior use whose admissibility is read at the substitution, such as [§7.10](#sec-generics-and-nullability)'s copy demand or [§9.2](#sec-equality-through-a-type-parameter)'s equality use — belongs to the declaration that declares the parameter and is checked at that declaration's instantiations ([§14.1](#sec-generic-declarations) *Instantiation and its site*). A use of a generic **type's** parameter, in any member body, accessor, constructor, initializer or destructor the program declares for the type, is therefore a requirement of the constructed type, checked at every site that names it whether or not the program reaches that member; a use of a generic **method's** own parameter is checked at each instantiation of the method, a call at explicit or inferred type arguments among them. A requirement reaches a declaration through a substitution the same way: where a user declaration forms an instantiation at a type argument that is or contains a type parameter in scope — a field `Bag<T>` in `class Outer<T>`, a call `Eq<U>(a, b)` in the body of `F<U>` — a requirement of that instantiation — an interior use's, or an instantiation-site rule's such as [§14.4](#sec-owned-as-a-generic-argument)'s, [§15.1.1](#sec-owning-inline-arrays)'s or [§28.5](#sec-owned-fields)'s — which the parameter's constraints do not establish ([§14.2](#sec-constraints)) is decided not at that site but at the instantiations the declaration's own instantiations form by substitution ([§14.1](#sec-generic-declarations) *Instantiation and its site*): `Outer<R>` is rejected wherever it is named where `Bag<R>` would be, whether or not the member forming it is reached, and `F<R>` at each call where `Eq<R>` would be, through any chain of such declarations, the diagnostic landing at the first site whose argument decides the requirement and naming the chain. A declared constraint is not a requirement of this kind: its satisfaction at such an argument is decided by [§14.2](#sec-constraints). The requirement is read from user declarations only: a standard-library generic type's members' bodies, the span records' Bezel realization included (stdlib [§4.14](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-owned-buffers-and-spans), [§4.15](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-arrayspant-readonlyarrayspant)), contribute no requirement of this kind, so such a type is rejected at an instantiation only by its declared constraints and the instantiation-site rules stated for it ([§14.4](#sec-owned-as-a-generic-argument)'s class-only restriction among them). A member that should demand of the type's arguments more than the type does is written as a generic method over a parameter of its own, or in a constrained extension block ([§26.4](#sec-generic-extensions)), the form [§14.2](#sec-conditionally-admitted-members) names as user-writable for a member present at some instantiations only; a user declaration carries no member-level condition (Appendix [C.1](#sec-appendix-c-type-system)). A member neither form can carry — among them an override, an interface implementation, an operator, an indexer, a constructor, a destructor, a field initializer and a settable property ([§26.3](#sec-extension-blocks-restrictions)) — makes its use a requirement of the type, stated in the signature by a constraint on the type's parameter.
3. **Part of the public contract.** A declaration change that flips a derived type property of a public type — adding a destructor flips trivial-dispose; adding a computed property in the wrong form flips auto-hashable; adding or removing a contract clause on a record's constructor flips constructor-only ([§9.9](#sec-constructor-only-records)); adding or removing `equality skip` on a member ([§9.2](#sec-equality-skip)) flips comparison results and hash values for clients and can flip auto-hashable/hashable — is a breaking change for clients relying on it, exactly as a signature change is (the artifact interface carries the clause as it carries `serialized` clauses, [§2.8.2](#sec-artifact-interface)). Library documentation should state the properties a type's clients are expected to rely on. An edit that adds a requirement under rule 2 to a public generic declaration — to a member body, a field, or a declaration it reaches — is breaking in the same sense, for the instantiations it newly rejects ([§2.8.6](#sec-interface-delta-classification)'s requirement-summary rows).
4. **Named in diagnostics.** A diagnostic produced by a property-dependent rule names the property in the words of the table above, so the reader can find the defining section.

Dispatch of *behavior* (not merely admissibility) on a derived type property — as the element category does for buffer and collection slot semantics ([§28.11](#sec-collection-element-ownership), stdlib [§4.14](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-owned-buffers-and-spans)) — is reserved to compiler-known standard-library types; it is not a user-available mechanism in this revision; two scoped exceptions are recorded. The **C-compatible** classification ([§32.13](#sec-c-compatible-records)) — whose consequence is a static representation guarantee, compile-time-visible and constant, never behavior dispatch — was ratified with the FFI's structured-data design (rationale §16.5). The **choice classification** ([§35.4](#sec-choice-classification)) does flip per-instantiation behavior (copy vs. move on assignment, disposal vs. none at scope end), and is admitted because the dispatch is performed by the language on a language construct — derived from structure, identical for every user, with no user-programmable hook — the recorded generalization path of the compiler-known specializations (rationale §5.15); users still cannot write code conditioned on a type parameter's category. The reservation bounds the **user-facing surface** — what user code may condition on — not an implementation's realization strategy for generics, which [§11.8](#sec-static-interface-members) leaves open so long as the observable binding is unchanged. Conditioning a member's **admissibility** — as distinct from its behavior — on the enclosing type's arguments is a separate mechanism with its own register and its own reservation, defined at [§14.2](#sec-conditionally-admitted-members); its conditions are not confined to the properties of this section.

New rules added to this specification that need a structural classification of types must define it as a derived type property under the rules of this section, rather than introducing a parallel mechanism.

---

<a id="sec-built-in-types"></a>
## 4. Built-in Types

<a id="sec-bool"></a>
### 4.1 `bool`

Two values: `true` and `false`. No implicit conversion to or from any other type. Conditions of `if`/`elif` and `while`, and a `case`/`catch` arm's `when` guard ([§19.4](#sec-guards)), require `bool`.

<a id="sec-integer-types"></a>
### 4.2 Integer types

| Type | Width | Range |
|---|---|---|
| `byte` | 8, unsigned | 0 to 255 |
| `sbyte` | 8, signed | −128 to 127 |
| `short` | 16, signed | −32 768 to 32 767 |
| `ushort` | 16, unsigned | 0 to 65 535 |
| `int` | 32, signed | −2 147 483 648 to 2 147 483 647 |
| `uint` | 32, unsigned | 0 to 4 294 967 295 |
| `long` | 64, signed | −2⁶³ to 2⁶³ − 1 |
| `ulong` | 64, unsigned | 0 to 2⁶⁴ − 1 |

An integer literal without a suffix has type `int` if it fits in `int`'s range; otherwise it is a **target-typed integer constant** (below) and needs a written integer target or a suffix. Suffixes are case-insensitive: `L` (long), `U` (uint), `UL` or `LU` (ulong — both orderings accepted). A **suffixed** integer literal whose value does not fit the suffix's type is a **compile error** (`5000000000U` exceeds `uint`'s range — write `5000000000UL`), except as the boundary carve-out below admits: literal formation is range-checked, uniformly with the target-typed constant's check against its declared target.

**Boundary carve-out.** The decimal literal of magnitude 2³¹ (unsuffixed) or 2⁶³ (`L`-suffixed) is admitted **only** as the immediate operand of unary `-`, denoting `int.MinValue` / `long.MinValue` respectively (`-2147483648`, `-9223372036854775808L`); anywhere else those magnitudes remain errors. Without this carve-out the most negative values would be unwritable as literals (the magnitude alone overflows before the `-` applies). **Immediate** means the operand of that unary `-` after grouping: parentheses group and introduce no expression of their own ([§17.14](#sec-constant-expressions) admits a parenthesized constant expression as the same expression), so `-(2147483648)` is the carve-out's form and denotes `int.MinValue` exactly as `-2147483648` does. An intervening **operation** is not: `-(2147483647 + 1)` is an overflowing constant expression and a compile error there ([§17.14](#sec-constant-expressions)), and `int.MinValue` / `long.MinValue` (stdlib [§1](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-primitive-type-members)) name the values with no literal at all.

**Target-typed integer constants.** An unsuffixed integer literal (decimal, hexadecimal, or binary spelling alike) whose value exceeds `int`'s range has **no standalone type**: it is an integer compile-time constant ([§17.14](#sec-constant-expressions)) admitted exactly where [§5.1](#sec-implicit-conversions)'s constant narrowing admits one — at a declared integer target whose range contains it, taking that target's type, including every [written-declared-type position](#sec-written-declared-type-positions) ([§17.7](#sec-the-new-operator)) whose written type is an integer type (`var x: long := 3_000_000_000;`) and the two component-typed sites beside the family that §5.1 names, a collection-literal element and an enum constant value ([§10.2](#sec-explicit-values)) — and it participates in overload-resolution applicability on the same terms ([§22.6](#sec-overloading)): `f(3_000_000_000)` against `f(long)` and `f(double)` selects `f(long)`, the `double` candidate being inapplicable because the constant is admitted at integer targets only. The suffix discipline's purpose (no *accidental* width) is preserved: the wider type is taken only from a written integer target, and the value is range-checked against it. In an **untyped** context (`var x := 3_000_000_000;`), and at a non-integer target (`var d: double := 3_000_000_000;`), the literal is a compile error directing to a suffix (`3_000_000_000L`, which then converts by §5.1).

<a id="sec-floating-point-types"></a>
### 4.3 Floating-point types

| Type | Width | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `float` | 32 | IEEE 754 single-precision |
| `double` | 64 | IEEE 754 double-precision |

A floating-point literal (one with a decimal point or exponent) has type `double` by default. The `f` suffix produces `float`. IEEE 754 values `Infinity`, `-Infinity`, and `NaN` are valid; floating-point division by zero produces one of these rather than raising an exception. A floating-point literal denotes the nearest representable value of its type: its value rounded as IEEE 754 rounds to nearest, a tie to the even significand. A literal whose value, so rounded, is not finite is a **compile error**: its magnitude is at least its type's largest finite value plus half a unit in that value's last place, the tie itself rounding up since that value's significand is odd. So `1.7976931348623158e308` is `double.MaxValue`, and `3.4028235e38f`, the digits `float.MaxValue.ToString()` prints, is `float.MaxValue`, while `1.7976931348623159e308`, `1e999` and `1e40f` are out of range. Literal formation is range-checked like the integer literals of [§4.2](#sec-integer-types), and a literal never denotes `±Infinity` ([§6.3](#sec-floating-point-arithmetic)'s overflow-to-infinity governs arithmetic operations, not literals; spell an infinity explicitly via `double.PositiveInfinity`). A `decimal` literal out of `decimal`'s range is likewise a compile error; [§4.4](#sec-decimal) states that range with the literal's rounding: a `decimal` literal is out of range when its value, so rounded, does not fit at scale 0 ([§6.4](#sec-decimal-arithmetic)).

<a id="sec-equality-semantics-for-floating-point-types"></a>
### 4.3.1 Equality semantics for floating-point types

The equality operators `=` and `<>` ([§17.3](#sec-the-=-and-operators)) follow reflexive-equality semantics rather than IEEE 754:

- `NaN = NaN` is **true**. Any non-NaN value compared with NaN by `=` is **false**.
- `-0.0 = +0.0` is **true**.
- For all other pairs, `=` agrees with IEEE 754 equality.

The relational operators `<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=` follow IEEE 754: any comparison involving `NaN` is false, including `NaN < NaN`, `NaN > NaN`, `NaN <= NaN`, and `NaN >= NaN`.

The IEEE self-inequality test does not carry over: `x <> x` is `false` for every `x`, NaN included, and a NaN test is written `Double.IsNaN(x)` (`Float.IsNaN(x)`). (Rationale [§7.4](Bezel_Design_Rationale.md#sec-float-equality-is-reflexive).)

For strict IEEE comparison (where `NaN` is unequal to itself), use `Double.IeeeEquals(a, b)` and `Float.IeeeEquals(a, b)` from the standard library. For bitwise comparison (which distinguishes the bit patterns of `+0.0` and `-0.0` and of distinct NaN payloads), use `Double.BitwiseEquals`/`Float.BitwiseEquals`.

`decimal` has no `Infinity`, `NaN`, or signed zero, so the question does not arise: `=` on `decimal` is straightforward value equality.

<a id="sec-decimal"></a>
### 4.4 `decimal`

High-precision decimal floating-point. 28–29 significant decimal digits. Exact representation of finite decimal fractions: the values are exactly ±*m* × 10^−*s* for integers 0 ≤ *m* ≤ 2^96 − 1 and 0 ≤ *s* ≤ 28 (`MaxValue`, stdlib [§9.3](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-decimal), is 2^96 − 1); neither the scale *s* nor the sign of a zero is part of the value. A `decimal` literal, a string parsed as `decimal` (stdlib [§9.3](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-decimal)), and the shortest round-trip form a `decimal(x)` conversion reads ([§5.2](#sec-explicit-conversions)), whose value is not in this set denote that value rounded as [§6.4](#sec-decimal-arithmetic) rounds an inexact result (`39614081257132168796771975166.5m` is `39614081257132168796771975166`), and are out of `decimal`'s range ([§4.3](#sec-floating-point-types)) exactly when that rounding does not fit at scale 0, as [§6.4](#sec-decimal-arithmetic)'s overflow is: `79228162514264337593543950335.4m` is `MaxValue`, while `79228162514264337593543950335.5m`, a tie rounding to the even 2^96, is out of range. The `m` suffix produces a `decimal` literal: `1.50m`. Division by zero raises `DivideByZeroException`. `decimal` has no `Infinity` or `NaN`.

<a id="sec-char"></a>
### 4.5 `char`

A single Unicode scalar value, 32 bits wide. Surrogate code points (U+D800 to U+DFFF) are not valid `char` values.

Character literals: `'a'`, `'\n'`, `'\u0041'`, `'\U0001F600'`. Character values compare by code-point value: `'A' < 'B'`.

<a id="sec-string"></a>
### 4.6 `string`

An immutable sequence of `char` (Unicode scalar values). A reference type with content-based equality. `string` implements `IEnumerable<char>`, so strings may be iterated with `for`:

```bezel
for var c in "hello" do Console.WriteLine(c); end;
```

Operations:

- `s.Length` returns the number of code points in `s`. O(1).
- `s[i]` returns the `char` at code-point position `i`, zero-indexed. O(1). Out-of-range raises `IndexOutOfRangeException`.
- `s[r]` for a `Range<int>` value `r` returns the substring spanning `r`. O(k) for a result of length `k`. Endpoints follow the standard rules for `Range<int>` over `s`'s indices: a closed `s[a..b]` includes both ends, a half-open `s[a..<b]` excludes the upper, and the open-ended forms (`s[..b]`, `s[a..]`, `s[..]`) extend to the start or end of the string. Out-of-range endpoints raise `IndexOutOfRangeException`; an empty range produces the empty string. The result is a fresh `string`; mutating one does not affect the other (strings are immutable, so this is observably true regardless of representation).
- `s = t` and `s <> t` compare by code-point sequence. O(min(|s|, |t|)).
- `s < t`, `s > t`, `s <= t`, `s >= t` perform ordinal lexicographic comparison of the code-point sequence. Locale-aware comparison is provided by standard library methods. Ordering requires **non-nullable** operands: an operand of static type `string?` is a compile error — [§7.11](#sec-lifted-operators)'s rule read at `string` (narrow first, [§7.4](#sec-member-access-on-nullable-values)); equality stays null-safe per [§8.4](#sec-=-and).
- `s + t` concatenates two strings. The compiler does not implicitly convert other types to `string`; use interpolation or `.ToString()`.
- `c in s` tests whether the character `c` appears in `s` (equivalent to `s.Contains(c)`, [§17.5](#sec-the-in-operator)).

The user-visible model is "a sequence of code points indexed in O(1)." The internal representation is implementation-defined: an implementation is expected to choose a per-string storage width — typically 1, 2, or 4 bytes per code point, selected at construction based on the largest code point in the value — to keep the common case (predominantly-ASCII text) compact while preserving O(1) indexing for every string. The choice of width is invisible at the language level; programs observe only the `char` sequence and its length.

A pure-ASCII string (every code point in U+0000–U+007F) is identical in memory layout to a UTF-8 byte sequence. Implementations expose this through the runtime predicate `s.IsAscii: bool` (standard library [§9.6](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-string)). Byte access to a string's contents goes through `Encoding.UTF8.GetBytes` (standard library [§3.2](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-encoding)) in one of two forms: `GetBytes(s)` produces a fresh owned `Array<byte>` — `O(n)` and always correct — and the span-destination form `GetBytes(s, destination: Span<byte>)`, paired with `GetByteCount(s)`, encodes into a caller-reused buffer — the allocation-conscious path for repeated encoding: zero per-call allocation, for every string, not only ASCII ones. (`ReadOnlyAsciiByteSpan` is retired, stdlib §3.4.)

`string` is **runtime-managed**: its memory is reclaimed automatically. `Dispose()` on a string is a no-op. String fields cannot be marked `owned`. See [§28.9](#sec-runtime-managed-types).

Whether the runtime interns strings (shares storage for identical string values) is implementation-defined. String literals appearing in source code may be interned at compile time. The `=` operator on strings always performs content comparison ([§4.6](#sec-string) above); implementations may short-circuit via reference equality when both operands refer to the same object, but this optimization is invisible to programs.

<a id="sec-the-unit-type"></a>
### 4.7 The unit type

`()` is the type with exactly one value, also written `()`. It is the return type of methods declared without an explicit return type.

Wrapping the unit type with `?` (yielding `()?`) is permitted by the grammar and produces an optional with two values, `null` and `()`. It is rarely useful; the natural representation of "presence or absence" for a procedure-shaped result is `bool`.

The unit type is a value type and can in principle be boxed via the `Object` derivation chain ([§8.6](#sec-boxing)) — `var o: Object := ();` is grammatically valid and produces a boxed `()`. The result is rarely meaningful; treat the unit value as a sentinel, not as a value to store in `Object`-typed variables. The interface-substitution description in [§3.1](#sec-type-kinds) omits boxed unit for the same reason.

<a id="sec-ffi-only-primitive-types"></a>
### 4.8 FFI-only primitive types

The standard library defines `IntPtr`, `UIntPtr`, `CString`, `WString`, and `RawBytes` for use at the FFI boundary. `IntPtr` and `UIntPtr` are compiler intrinsics. The `CString`, `WString`, and `RawBytes` APIs are documented in standard library [§10](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-ffi-boundary-types). See [§32](#sec-foreign-function-interface) for FFI-side usage. These types live in the auto-imported `System` module ([§2.3](#sec-always-available-names)). The typed foreign-memory family — `Ptr<T>` and the `Interop` intrinsics — lives in the explicitly-imported `System.Interop` module (stdlib [§10.5](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-system-interop-ptr)–[§10.6](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-system-interop-interop); language rules in [§32.12](#sec-foreign-memory)).

---

<a id="sec-type-conversions"></a>
## 5. Type Conversions

<a id="sec-implicit-conversions"></a>
### 5.1 Implicit conversions

A value of one type implicitly converts to another when no programmer-visible information is lost — or, for the floating-point cases noted below, when the operation is universally safe enough that explicit casts would create unjustified noise.

| From | Implicitly converts to |
|---|---|
| `sbyte` | `short`, `int`, `long`, `float`, `double`, `decimal` |
| `byte` | `short`, `ushort`, `int`, `uint`, `long`, `ulong`, `float`, `double`, `decimal` |
| `short` | `int`, `long`, `float`, `double`, `decimal` |
| `ushort` | `int`, `uint`, `long`, `ulong`, `float`, `double`, `decimal` |
| `int` | `long`, `float`, `double`, `decimal` |
| `uint` | `long`, `ulong`, `float`, `double`, `decimal` |
| `long` | `float`, `double`, `decimal` |
| `ulong` | `float`, `double`, `decimal` |
| `float` | `double` |
| `char` | `int`, `uint`, `long`, `ulong`, `float`, `double`, `decimal` |

Implicit conversions to `float` from integers wider than 24 bits, and to `double` from integers wider than 53 bits, may lose precision but never overflow.

The following are **never implicit**:

- Between signed and unsigned types of the same or narrower width (e.g. `int → uint`, `uint → int`, `short → ushort`). Widening from unsigned to a strictly larger signed type (e.g. `byte → short`, `ushort → int`) is permitted because no value is lost. This bullet governs **non-constant** expressions; an integer compile-time constant ([§17.14](#sec-constant-expressions)) converts by value under constant narrowing (below), which may cross signedness — `var b: byte := 50;` is exactly such a conversion.
- Between `decimal` and binary floats (`float`, `double`).
- Between an enum and its underlying integer.
- Between integers and `bool`.

**Constant narrowing.** An expression of integer type that is a **compile-time constant** ([§17.14](#sec-constant-expressions)) implicitly converts to any integer type whose range contains its value: `var b: byte := 50;`, `Set(level: byte)` called as `Set(3)`, and enum constants of the underlying type ([§10.2](#sec-explicit-values)) are all well-typed by this rule. The rule is **value-based, not type-based**: the source may be a compile-time constant of **any** integer type — not only `int` — and the target any integer type whose range contains the value, **across signedness** (`const N: long := 8; var b: byte := N;` is well-typed; a `uint`-typed constant `7` is admissible where `int` is expected); for non-constant expressions the conversion table and the never-implicit list above govern unchanged. A constant whose value does not fit the target's range is a **compile error** at the conversion site — never a silent truncation. The rule applies to constants only; a run-time `int` value still requires the explicit `byte(x)` narrowing of [§5.2](#sec-explicit-conversions). Constant narrowing applies at **every** position where this section's implicit conversions apply — there is no position carve-out: initializers, assignments, call arguments (`Set(3)`), returns, record positional arguments, collection-literal elements ([§15.4](#sec-collection-literals)), and default arguments — the list is illustrative, not closed: it covers every [written-declared-type position](#sec-written-declared-type-positions) ([§17.7](#sec-the-new-operator)) and the two component-typed sites beside that family (a collection-literal element, an enum constant value), and applies equally wherever else this section's conversions apply — and it participates in overload-resolution applicability ([§22.6](#sec-overloading)) and in the nullable lifting below. An unsuffixed literal beyond `int`'s range — [§4.2](#sec-integer-types)'s target-typed integer constant — is admitted by this rule wherever it applies; what it additionally requires is a **written** integer target, so an untyped context (`var x := …`) and a non-integer target remain the §4.2 error.

**Nullable conversions.** For any type `T`, `T` implicitly converts to `T?`: for a reference type, the same reference viewed as nullable ([§7.1](#sec-non-nullable-and-nullable-types)); for a value type, the present-value wrapping ([§7.2](#sec-nullable-value-types)). Each implicit conversion of this section also **lifts** to the nullable forms: `S?` implicitly converts to `T?` whenever `S` implicitly converts to `T` — a present value converts by the underlying conversion, `null` converts to `null` (`int?` → `long?`); constant narrowing (above) participates for a present constant value. The two rules compose through at most one `?` on each side ([§7.10](#sec-generics-and-nullability): `?` is idempotent): `S` converts to `T?` via `S → T → T?`, so an `int` is admissible where a `long?` is expected.

<a id="sec-reference-conversions"></a>
**Reference conversions.** The following conversions are implicit, and the term *implicit conversion* throughout this document — including every citation of "the §5.1 conversions" — includes them:

- **identity**: every type converts to itself;
- **class to base class**, transitively, up to `Object`;
- **any type to `Object`**: reference types (classes including the heap
  arrays, interfaces, `string`, function types) directly; value types
  (primitives, records, enums, choices, non-owning inline arrays, the unit type) by
  boxing ([§8.6](#sec-boxing)) — move-only owning inline arrays excluded,
  since they cannot be boxed ([§8.6](#sec-boxing)), and so are owning choices ([§35.8](#sec-choice-boxing));
- **a type to an interface it implements or conforms to**: classes by
  declaration or inheritance ([§11.2](#sec-interface-declaration), including
  the compiler-generated `IDisposable`, [§28.2](#sec-the-idisposable-contract));
  records and enums by declaration ([§9.6](#sec-records-and-inheritance),
  [§10.5](#sec-restrictions)), boxing; primitives by the compiler-provided
  conformances ([§11.8](#sec-static-interface-members)), boxing;
- **interface to extended interface**, directly or transitively;
- **a type parameter to an interface or class its constraints guarantee
  conformance to** ([§14.2](#sec-constraints) — a type-bound constraint
  `where T: IFoo`/`where T: SomeClass`, directly or through a `where T: U`
  chain): inside the generic body a `T`-typed value converts to the bound;
  the conversion is realized at instantiation by the substituted type's own
  conversion of this section, boxing where the substitution is a value type;
- the **variance-induced conversions** of [§12.9](#sec-variance):
  `I<S…> → I<T…>` per the declared `in`/`out` markers, for reference-typed
  arguments only.

(Function-typed *values* additionally convert under the identity-preserving variance rule of [§27.1.1](#sec-function-type-assignability), and method-reference *formation* may bridge any conversion of this section by synthesizing an adapter, [§27.6](#sec-method-references) — both stated there.)

A reference conversion of a reference-typed value is representation-preserving — the same reference viewed at a wider static type; the boxing rows allocate the box but preserve the value ([§8.6](#sec-boxing) — subject to §8.6's borrow-lifetime constraints for borrow-bearing records and reference-element inline arrays). The **ownership state of the source expression carries through unchanged**: upcasting an owned value yields an owned value of the wider type (the usual transfer rules apply at the receiving position, [§28.8](#sec-ownership-transfer)), and upcasting a borrow yields a borrow with the same source — a reference conversion never transfers, discharges, or creates a disposal obligation. The nullable lifting above composes: `Dog?` converts to `Animal?` (a present reference by the underlying conversion, `null` to `null`). Constant narrowing is unrelated to this subsection. For overload resolution, reference conversions rank **co-equal** with the other implicit conversions ([§22.6](#sec-implicit-conversion-ranking)): given `M(a: Animal)` and `M(o: Object)`, the call `M(dog)` is ambiguous — upcast explicitly. No finer ranking among implicit conversions applies (rationale [§14.5](Bezel_Design_Rationale.md#sec-no-implicit-conversion-operators)).

<a id="sec-explicit-conversions"></a>
### 5.2 Explicit conversions

Explicit conversion uses function-call syntax: the target type's name applied to the source value.

```bezel
var y: short := short(x);
var i: int := int(d);             // truncates toward zero
var c: char := char(n);           // n must be a valid code point
var f: double := double(m);       // decimal to double
```

Integer narrowing raises `OverflowException` if the value does not fit. **Constant operands are decided at compile time:** where the operand of an explicit conversion is a compile-time constant ([§17.14](#sec-constant-expressions)) whose value would raise `OverflowException` under any rule of this section — integer narrowing, the same-width signedness change, the integer-to-`char` code-point range, and the floating-point and `decimal` conversions below — the conversion is a **compile error at the conversion site**, never a deferred runtime fault: `uint(-1)`, `byte(300)`, `char(0xD800)`, and `int(1e30)` are rejected where they are written. This is the posture of [§5.1](#sec-implicit-conversions)'s constant-narrowing range error, [§5.4](#sec-enum-casts)'s constant enum cast, and [§17.14](#sec-constant-expressions)'s constant-evaluation faults; a **non-constant** operand raises `OverflowException` at run time as stated throughout this section. Two bounds: the rule reads the **operand**, and does not make a conversion expression a constant expression ([§17.14](#sec-constant-expressions)'s inductive set is unchanged — `const K := byte(1);` is still not a compile-time `const`); and a conversion that **saturates** rather than raises is unaffected, so `float(1e300)` is `Infinity` and `float(0.0 / 0.0)` is `NaN` at a constant operand exactly as at a runtime one. Floating-point and `decimal` to integer truncate toward zero; `NaN`, `±Infinity`, and a value whose truncation is outside the destination type's range raise `OverflowException`: `uint(x)` is `0` where `x` is `-0.5` or `-0.5m`, `sbyte(x)` is `-128` where `x` is `-128.9`, and a non-constant `x` of `-1.0` or `-1.0m` makes `uint(x)` raise. Integer to floating-point never overflows; precision may be lost.

**`bool` to integer.** An explicit conversion from `bool` to any integer type is admitted: `int(b)` yields `0` for `false` and `1` for `true` (total, never fails). The idiom turns a comparison into a number — `return int(r = null);`, branchless counting `sum := sum + int(x > 0);`. The directions are deliberately **asymmetric**: `bool(n)` remains an error in both the implicit and explicit forms ([§5.1](#sec-implicit-conversions)) — a numeric-to-`bool` reading is partial and truthiness-shaped (which value is `true`? what of `2`?), exactly the ambiguity the no-truthiness rule ([§4.1](#sec-bool), rationale §17.1) exists to exclude; write the comparison (`n <> 0`) instead. A `bool` source likewise does not convert to `float`/`double`/`decimal` (no privileged numeric reading) or `char` (a code point, not a number).

A conversion between a signed and an unsigned integer type of the *same width* (`int` ↔ `uint`, `long` ↔ `ulong`, `short` ↔ `ushort`, `byte` ↔ `sbyte`) is likewise a checked narrowing: it raises `OverflowException` when the value is not representable in the destination type — a negative value cast to an unsigned type, or an unsigned value greater than the destination type's signed maximum. Such a cast is a *value* conversion, not a reinterpretation of bits: it preserves the numeric value or fails. To view the bit pattern of a same-width integer under the other signedness *without* a range check — reading a `uint` as the `int` with the identical representation — use [`BitConverter.Reinterpret<T>`](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-bitconverter), the standard library's bit-reinterpretation surface ([stdlib §2.12](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-bitconverter)).

Casting an integer to `char` requires the integer to fall in U+0000–U+10FFFF excluding the surrogate range; otherwise `OverflowException`. A `float`, `double`, or `decimal` source does not convert to `char` — a code point, not a number, as for `bool` above (nor is `char` an arithmetic operand, [§3.5](#sec-operators-on-primitive-types)) — so `char(x)` over one is a compile error; `char(int(x))` writes the truncation toward zero and the code-point check as the two conversions they are.

**Floating-point, `decimal`, and `char` conversion semantics.** `double(m)` and `float(m)` for `decimal` `m` round to the nearest representable binary value and never fail (`float`'s and `double`'s finite ranges exceed `decimal`'s). `decimal(x)` for binary-float `x` yields the value of `x`'s **shortest round-trip form** — the digits `x`'s no-format `ToString()` produces, the shortest decimal string that parses back to `x` in `x`'s own type and, of several such, the one nearest `x` (stdlib [§2.18](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-iformattable)) — rounded as [§4.4](#sec-decimal) states where that value is not in `decimal`'s set: `decimal(0.1)` is `0.1`, `decimal(0.1 + 0.2)` is `0.30000000000000004`, `decimal(0.1f)` is `0.1`, and `decimal(2.5e-28)` is `0.0000000000000000000000000002`, the form's tie at scale 28 going to the even digit. `NaN`, `±Infinity`, and a value out of `decimal`'s range as [§4.4](#sec-decimal) states it raise `OverflowException` (mirroring float-to-integer above — `decimal` has no non-finite values, [§6.4](#sec-decimal-arithmetic)). `float(d)` for `double` `d` rounds `d`'s value to the nearest `float`, a tie to the even significand; a value whose rounding is not finite, its magnitude at least `float.MaxValue` plus half a unit in its last place, yields `±Infinity` and never raises (so `float(3.4028235e38)` is `float.MaxValue`) — floating-point narrowing follows floating-point arithmetic's own overflow behavior ([§6.3](#sec-floating-point-arithmetic): overflow produces `±Infinity`), exactly as integer narrowing's `OverflowException` follows checked integer arithmetic ([§6.1](#sec-integer-arithmetic)); `NaN` converts to `NaN`. The throw-vs-saturate split is therefore principled per target family, not an asymmetry. `I(c)` for `char` `c` and any integer type `I` converts the code-point value under the integer rules: the widening directions of [§5.1](#sec-implicit-conversions) always succeed, and narrower targets (`byte(c)`, `sbyte(c)`, `short(c)`) are checked narrowings raising `OverflowException` when the code point does not fit.

<a id="sec-nullable-casts"></a>
### 5.3 Nullable casts

```bezel
var y: long? := long?(x);             // nullable to nullable; null stays null
var m: int := int(n);                 // raises NullReferenceException if n is null
```

Casting a nullable to its non-nullable form requires the value to be non-null at runtime. The safer forms are `n!` (assert non-null then cast, [§7.8](#sec-null-forgiving)) and `n ?? default` (substitute a default).

**The general rule.** For a target type `T`, the nullable cast form `T?(x)` is admitted exactly when the corresponding non-nullable conversion `T(v)` is admitted from the non-nullable form of `x`'s type ([§5.2](#sec-explicit-conversions), [§5.4](#sec-enum-casts)). A `null` operand yields `null`; a present value `v` converts by `T(v)` under that conversion's own semantics, including its runtime checks (`OverflowException` on a non-fitting present value — for an enum target, [§5.4](#sec-enum-casts)'s declared-constant check included — and so on) and its constant-operand compile error ([§5.2](#sec-explicit-conversions), [§5.4](#sec-enum-casts)). The non-nullable form `T(x)` applied to a nullable operand first requires the value to be present — `null` raises `NullReferenceException`, as above — and then converts identically.

<a id="sec-enum-casts"></a>
### 5.4 Enum casts

Enums require explicit casts to and from their underlying integer type:

```bezel
var p: Priority := Priority(1);       // int to enum
var n: int := int(p);                 // enum to int
```

<a id="sec-out-of-range-integer-to-enum-casts"></a>
An integer-to-enum cast `E(n)` is **checked against the declared constants**: it succeeds exactly when `n` equals the underlying value of some declared constant of `E`, and yields that value. When `n` is a compile-time constant ([§17.14](#sec-constant-expressions)) equal to no declared constant, the cast is a **compile error at the cast site** — the same posture as [§5.1](#sec-implicit-conversions)'s constant-narrowing range error. When `n` is not a constant, a value equal to no declared constant raises `OverflowException` at runtime, the diagnostic naming the enum type and the value. In-range-vs-out-of-range is not a user-visible distinction: an `n` outside the underlying type's range is, a fortiori, equal to no declared constant, so the single rule subsumes the former range check — the same compile error for constants, the same `OverflowException` at runtime. **There is no value of an enum type that is not equal to a declared constant.** (Under duplicate constant values, [§10.2](#sec-explicit-values), the declared-value set is the set of distinct values: `E(1)` where `Legacy := 1, Current := 1` yields that one value.)

The checked cast is the assert-shaped tier — an undeclared value is a bug at its call sites. Boundary code for which an undeclared value is an expected input branches instead of catching: every enum carries a compiler-provided static member `E.FromUnderlyingOrNull(value: U): E?` ([§10.4](#sec-methods-properties-static-members)), which returns `null` where the cast would fault.

<a id="sec-non-int-underlying-types"></a>
#### Non-`int` underlying types

For an enum `E` with underlying type `U` ([§10.3](#sec-underlying-type)) and any integer type `I` ([§4.2](#sec-integer-types)), the cast `I(e)` converts `e` to `U` and then applies [§5.2](#sec-explicit-conversions)'s integer conversion `I(u)`: a widening always succeeds, a narrowing or a signedness change is checked by value (`OverflowException`, [§6.1](#sec-integer-arithmetic)), and §5.2's constant-operand rule, with both its bounds, applies to the second step — a reference to a declared constant of `E` is a compile-time constant ([§17.14](#sec-constant-expressions)). So for `long`-backed `HttpStatus`, `int(HttpStatus.Huge)` at `Huge := 5000000000` is a **compile error at the cast site**, while `int(s)` over a local `s` holding that value raises `OverflowException` at run time. `U(e)` makes the second step the identity and is the round-trip-safe spelling.

---

<a id="sec-arithmetic-and-overflow"></a>
## 6. Arithmetic and Overflow

<a id="sec-integer-arithmetic"></a>
### 6.1 Integer arithmetic

Operators `+`, `-`, `*`, `/`, `mod`, unary `-`, `++`, and `--` on integer types are checked for overflow. An operation whose mathematical result is not representable in the result type raises `OverflowException`.

```bezel
var a: int := 2_000_000_000;
var b: int := 2_000_000_000;
var c := a + b;                       // OverflowException
```

`++` and `--` are postfix-only and statement-only; they do not produce a value. See [§17.6](#sec-the-increment-and-decrement-operators).

Division `/` between two integers truncates toward zero. `mod` follows the dividend's sign:

```bezel
var q := -7 / 3;                      // -2
var r := -7 mod 3;                    // -1
```

Division and `mod` raise `DivideByZeroException` when the right operand is zero.

`mod` is defined on integer types and on `decimal` (where it follows the same dividend-sign rule and raises `DivideByZeroException` when the divisor is zero). It is **not** defined on `float` or `double`; an expression of the form `x mod y` where either operand has a binary floating-point type is a compile error. The reason is that `mod` carries no floating-point semantics in this spec — the natural choice (IEEE 754 remainder, or C `fmod`) is a deliberate decision rather than a syntactic afterthought, and naming it explicitly avoids the ambiguity. The standard library exposes `Math.Fmod(x: double, y: double): double` for the C-compatible same-sign-as-dividend remainder, and `Math.IEEERemainder(x: double, y: double): double` for the IEEE 754 nearest-even form.

<a id="sec-mixed-type-arithmetic"></a>
### 6.2 Mixed-type arithmetic

When operands have different types, the smaller-range operand is implicitly promoted to the larger type using [§5.1](#sec-implicit-conversions). The result has the larger type. If no implicit conversion exists between the operand types (e.g. `double` and `decimal`), the operation is a compile error and an explicit cast is required.

<a id="sec-floating-point-arithmetic"></a>
### 6.3 Floating-point arithmetic

`float` and `double` arithmetic follows IEEE 754. Overflow produces `±Infinity`. Operations involving `NaN` propagate `NaN`. Division by zero produces `±Infinity` or `NaN`. No exception is raised.

Modulo on floating-point values is intentionally not provided as an operator. Use `Math.Fmod` (C-style same-sign-as-dividend) or `Math.IEEERemainder` (IEEE 754 nearest-even) instead; see [§6.1](#sec-integer-arithmetic).

<a id="sec-decimal-arithmetic"></a>
### 6.4 Decimal arithmetic

`decimal` arithmetic raises `OverflowException` on overflow and `DivideByZeroException` on division by zero. There is no `Infinity` or `NaN` for `decimal`.

The result of `+`, `-`, `*`, and `/` is the exact result when [§4.4](#sec-decimal) can represent it. Otherwise it is the exact result rounded at the largest scale *s* ≤ 28 whose rounded mantissa is at most 2^96 − 1 — to nearest, a tie to the even last digit, the rounding `Decimal.Round` and the format specifiers use (stdlib [§9.3](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-decimal), [§2.18](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-iformattable)). **Overflow** is a result that does not fit at scale 0; a nonzero result that rounds to zero is zero (`-1e-28m / 3m` is `0`). So `1m / 3m` is `0.3333333333333333333333333333`, `2m / 3m` is `0.6666666666666666666666666667`, `100m / 7m` is `14.285714285714285714285714286`, and `decimal.MaxValue / 10m` is `7922816251426433759354395033.5`.

<a id="sec-bitwise-operations"></a>
### 6.5 Bitwise operations

Operators `&` (AND), `|` (OR), `^` (XOR), `<<` (left shift), `>>` (right shift), and unary `~` (complement) operate on the binary representation of integer values. They are not valid on `bool`, `char`, or floating-point types.

`~x` is the bitwise complement; for signed types, `~x = -(x + 1)`. The keyword `not` is boolean negation, valid only on `bool`. `not` is not user-overloadable; types wanting domain-specific inversion provide a named method (e.g. `.Negate()`) or overload `~` if a bitwise reading applies. `~` and `not` are not interchangeable.

A shift's result type is the type of its **left** operand. The right operand supplies only the shift count: it does **not** participate in the mixed-type promotion of [§6.2](#sec-mixed-type-arithmetic), so a narrower left operand is *not* widened to match a wider count (`byte << int` yields `byte`, not `int`). Left shift fills with zeros on the right. Right shift fills with the sign bit on signed types, zero on unsigned.

The shift count's **domain** is `0` through `width−1`, where width is the bit width of the **left (shifted) operand's type** — `0..7` for `byte`/`sbyte`, `0..15` for `short`/`ushort`, `0..31` for the 32-bit types (`int`/`uint`), `0..63` for the 64-bit types (`long`/`ulong`). A count outside the domain — negative, or ≥ width — is a fault: a **compile error** when the count is a compile-time constant ([§17.14](#sec-constant-expressions)), and `OverflowException` at runtime otherwise. Within the domain, bits shifted beyond the left operand's width are discarded silently — that is the operation, exactly as `&` discards bits — and the result never faults. Code that wants the modular count deliberately writes it: `v << (k & 31)` (`& 63` for 64-bit left operands) — the mask is then in the source, visible and in-domain by construction. ([§17.2](#sec-notes-on-operators)'s mandatory-parenthesization rules do not cover shift-with-bitwise mixes, but `&` binds looser than `<<`, so the parentheses around `k & 31` are required by precedence — the spelling is unambiguous.) The constant-count diagnostic for a negative count notes the direction confusion: a negative count does not reverse the shift's direction — use the opposite operator, or mask deliberately with `& 31`.

Compound assignments: `&=`, `|=`, `^=`, `<<=`, `>>=`. There is no `~=` (unary operators have no compound form).

<a id="sec-compound-assignments"></a>
### 6.6 Compound assignments

The compound assignment operators are `+=`, `-=`, `*=`, `/=`, `mod=`, `&=`, `|=`, `^=`, `<<=`, `>>=`, and `??=`. Unary operators have no compound forms ([§6.5](#sec-bitwise-operations)).

**Desugaring.** For every operator above except `??=`, the statement `x op= e` is equivalent to `x := x op e` with the target evaluated **once**:

- every constituent of the left-hand side's lvalue chain (grammar A.6
  `LValue`) is evaluated exactly once, left to right: the base identifier or
  `this`, each mid-chain member hop (a property hop's getter is invoked once
  as part of locating the target), and every index expression in the chain;
- when the final segment is accessor-mediated (a property or an indexer), its
  getter and setter are each invoked exactly once — the getter produces the
  left operand, the setter stores the result;
- the order is: the LHS chain's constituent expressions, then the final
  segment's getter (where applicable), then `e`, then the operation, then the
  store.

[§17.6](#sec-increment-decrement-on-indexer-slots)'s indexer desugaring is the indexer instance of this rule. A.6's lvalue shape applies unchanged: a method-call result cannot base the chain — extract it to a local first. The store is an ordinary assignment: for an owned target, [§28.7](#sec-reassigning-owned-fields)'s drop-on-overwrite applies, and an assignment that may drop a live value is a throwable expression for [§28.8.1](#sec-the-move-expression)'s restoration analysis.

**Typing; the narrow-integer write-back.** Let T be the left-hand side's type and R the type of `x op e` under the rules of this chapter ([§6.2](#sec-mixed-type-arithmetic) promotion, [§6.5](#sec-bitwise-operations) shifts and bitwise, [§25.2](#sec-operator-overloading-restrictions) overloads). If R is T, or R implicitly converts to T ([§5.1](#sec-implicit-conversions)), the result is stored directly. Otherwise, when **T is an integer type or `char` and R is an integer type**, the result is converted back to T by the corresponding [§5.2](#sec-explicit-conversions) **checked** narrowing: `b += 10` on `b: byte` is `b := byte(b + 10)` — the addition runs in `int` per §6.2, and a result outside `byte`'s range raises `OverflowException` ([§6.1](#sec-integer-arithmetic)'s checked posture; never a silent truncation). A `char` operand is not arithmetic ([§3.5](#sec-operators-on-primitive-types)), so a `char` target admits only `+=` and `-=` — the code-point advance [§17.6](#sec-the-increment-and-decrement-operators)'s `c++` and `c--` desugar to — with R the type of `int(x) op e`, and the write-back applies the §5.2 code-point rules: `c += 1` is `c := char(int(c) + 1)`. The right operand is typed as in `int op e` under §6.2 — `sbyte`, `byte`, `short`, `ushort`, `int` or `long`, or an integer constant under [§5.1](#sec-implicit-conversions)'s constant narrowing; a `char` right operand is not arithmetic either (`c -= d` over `d: char` is rejected — write `c := char(int(c) - int(d))`), and a non-constant `uint` or `ulong` operand has no §6.2 promotion with `int` and is a compile error. `c *= 2`, `c /= 2` and `c mod= n` are compile errors — `char` is not an arithmetic type, so a code point is advanced, never scaled — and a bitwise or shift form on a `char` target has no R ([§6.5](#sec-bitwise-operations)). In every other case the compound form is a **compile error** naming the explicit remedy — notably a binary-float or `decimal` result against a different LHS type (`b += 1.5`; `f += 2.5` where `f: float` promotes to `double`): the §5.2 float narrowings round or truncate *silently*, which is precisely the information loss [§5.1](#sec-implicit-conversions)'s admission line exists to exclude; write `f := float(f + 2.5);` when that loss is intended. The write-back is scoped to the compound form only: plain `b := b + 10` remains the §6.2/§5.1 compile error it has always been, so the no-implicit-narrowing rule is undisturbed everywhere else. The shift forms never need it: a shift's result already has the left operand's type ([§6.5](#sec-bitwise-operations)). `x <<= k` and `x >>= k` inherit [§6.5](#sec-bitwise-operations)'s count-domain rule through the desugaring: an out-of-domain count is the same fault — compile error for a constant count, `OverflowException` at runtime otherwise.

**Nullable targets and operands.** A read-modify-write compound assignment — `+=`, `-=`, `*=`, `/=`, `mod=`, `&=`, `|=`, `^=`, `<<=`, `>>=` — takes the verdict its expansion `x op e` has on a nullable operand ([§7.11](#sec-lifted-operators)): a target or right operand whose static type, read after [§7.4](#sec-member-access-on-nullable-values)'s narrowing, is nullable — a nullable reference-typed target included — is a **compile error** naming §7.11's remedies (`b := (b ?? 0) + 1;`, `b := b! + 1;`, or a narrowing check), and one §7.4 has narrowed non-null is a non-nullable operand, the store leaving the narrowing in place. The narrow-integer write-back above is a typing rule and is unreached on a nullable operand. `??=` is unaffected: it is not a read-modify-write (below). The `++`/`--` forms take the same reading ([§17.6](#sec-the-increment-and-decrement-operators)).

**`??=`** is not a read-modify-write: `x ??= e` assigns `e` only when `x`'s current value is null, with the typing and ownership rules of [§7.7](#sec-null-coalescing-and-=). The LHS chain is evaluated once as above, the getter once; `e` is evaluated — and the setter invoked — only when the assignment actually occurs.

**Events.** `+=`/`-=` whose left operand's static type is `EventSource<T>`, `AsyncEventSource<T>`, or `SharedEventSource<T>` are the fixed subscription desugaring of [§17.2](#sec-notes-on-operators), selected by that operand type before this section applies; they are not compound assignments ([§25.1](#sec-overloadable-operators)).

**Operator overloads.** For an operand type overloading the underlying binary operator, the desugaring applies with `x op e` resolved per [§25.2](#sec-operator-overloading-restrictions); the compound form is well-typed exactly when the overload's result stores back under the typing rule above (in practice: the result type implicitly converts to T). This makes [§25.1](#sec-overloadable-operators)'s "desugar mechanically to read-modify-write" precise.

```bezel
var b: byte := 250;
b += 4;                    // b := byte(b + 4) — 254, in range
b += 10;                   // byte(264) → OverflowException at runtime, never a wraparound
var checksum: byte := 0;
checksum ^= b;             // byte ^ byte : byte — R = T, no write-back involved
var n: int := 2;
var acc: byte := 40;
acc += n;                  // admitted: R = int; checked write-back at runtime (42)
n mod= 3;                  // n := n mod 3 — 2; a zero divisor raises DivideByZeroException (§6.1)
var s: short := 1;
s <<= 2;                   // R = short (§6.5) — 4, no write-back involved
var c: char := 'a';
c += 1;                    // c := char(int(c) + 1) — 'b'; §5.2's code-point check applies
var m: int? := 0;
m += 1;                    // admitted: the initializer narrowed m non-null (§7.4) — 1
m := null;                 // reassigned from null, a nullable-typed expression: the narrowing ends (§7.4)
// m += 1;                 // compile error: `+` is not defined on a nullable operand
//                         //   (§7.11) — write m := (m ?? 0) + 1; or narrow first
// m++;                    // compile error: the same rule through §17.6's desugaring
counts[category] += 1;     // §17.6's indexer instance: collection, index, getter, setter — once each
// var f: float := 1.0f;
// f += 2.5;               // compile error: R = double does not return to float implicitly —
//                         //   write f += 2.5f; (float promotion stays in-family) or
//                         //   f := float(f + 2.5); if the double-rounding is intended
```

---

<a id="sec-nullability-2"></a>
## 7. Nullability

<a id="sec-non-nullable-and-nullable-types"></a>
### 7.1 Non-nullable and nullable types

A plain reference type is non-nullable; a `?` suffix produces its nullable form:

```bezel
var name: string := "Alice";        // non-nullable
var middle: string? := null;        // nullable
```

`string` and `string?` are distinct types. The compiler enforces the distinction at every assignment, parameter pass, and return.

A non-nullable reference type implicitly converts to its nullable form. The reverse requires a null check or `!`.

<a id="sec-nullable-value-types"></a>
### 7.2 Nullable value types

A value type wrapped in `?` is an optional: it either holds a value or `null`. `int?`, `Priority?`, and `DateTime?` are optional value types.

<a id="sec-assigning-null"></a>
### 7.3 Assigning null

Assigning `null` to a non-nullable target is a compile error.

<a id="sec-member-access-on-nullable-values"></a>
### 7.4 Member access on nullable values

Member access, method calls, and indexing on a nullable value are compile errors unless the compiler has narrowed it to non-null:

```bezel
var user: User? := GetUser();
if user <> null then
  Console.WriteLine(user.Name);     // narrowed to User here
end;
```

(A hole's *implicit `ToString` dispatch* on its operand inside an interpolated string is not a member access for this rule — [§18.5](#sec-interpolated-strings)'s null-rendering case defines it. Expressions *written inside* the hole remain governed by this section: `$"{user.Name}"` over `user: User?` is still a compile error.)

Narrowing also applies after early return, after `is not null`, inside the controlled block of a successful `is` test ([§12.7](#sec-type-tests-is-is-not-as)), and — for an `out` recipient — in the region where a call's `bool` result is known to equal the callee's declared nullability postcondition ([§22.4](#sec-out-nullability-postcondition)).

**How narrowing is established.** Narrowing is flow-sensitive: at each program point the compiler tracks, per local variable and per parameter other than a `ref` parameter (*Narrowing applies to locals — and `readonly` fields — only*, below), whether its value is known non-null. The knowledge is established by:

- a null test in either spelling — `x <> null` or `x is not null` (narrowing the true branch), `x = null` or `x is null` (narrowing the *false* branch) — or a successful `is`/typed-pattern test ([§12.7](#sec-type-tests-is-is-not-as), [§19.3](#sec-patterns)) — in an `if`/`elif` condition (of the statement or of the [§20](#sec-the-if-expression) conditional atom, each condition narrowing its own branches), a `while` condition, or a `when` guard ([§19.4](#sec-guards), narrowing that arm's body);
- boolean composition of tests: in `A and B`, `B` (and the true branch) is checked under `A`'s true-facts; in `A or B`, `B` (and the false branch) sees `A`'s false-facts; `not` swaps the fact sets — the standard three-outcome flow analysis, so `x <> null and x.Length > 0` is well-typed. The `not`-swap applies to **null facts**; a *type-classification* fact is established only by the `is`/`is not` operators and typed patterns directly, never by `not`-composition — `not (x is T)` has the same truth value as `x is not T` but narrows neither branch ([§17.4](#sec-the-is-is-not-and-as-operators));
- an early exit: after `if x = null then return; end;` or `if x is null then return; end;` (or `throw`, `break`, `continue` in that branch), the surviving path is narrowed;
- assignment: after `x := expr;` where `expr`'s static type is non-nullable — or `expr` is itself narrowed non-null at that point — `x` is narrowed until invalidated; likewise after `x ??= expr;` with such an `expr` (on every path `x` then holds a non-null value, [§7.7](#sec-null-coalescing-and-=)), and from a declaration whose initializer is such an `expr` — `var x: T? := expr;` or `const x: T? := expr;` ([§21.1](#sec-variable-declarations)) — which is the declaration's assignment, its narrowing invalidated by exactly the forms below;
- a call to a method declaring a `when true`/`when false` nullability postcondition on an `out` recipient ([§22.4](#sec-out-nullability-postcondition)): in any region where the call's `bool` result is statically known to equal the stated constant, the recipient is narrowed non-null, composing through boolean operators and early exits like any other fact.

**How narrowing is invalidated.** The narrowing of a variable is invalidated when, within the controlled block:

- the variable is reassigned from a nullable-typed expression; or
- the variable is passed as a `ref` **or `out`** argument (the callee may — for `out`, must ([§22.3](#sec-parameter-modifiers)) — reassign it. The invalidation is deliberately **uniform over the parameter's declared nullability**: even a non-nullable `out T` parameter — whose mandatory assignment could soundly *re-establish* the fact — invalidates, one predictable rule rather than a nullability-dependent one; the sound non-nullable-`out` refinement is recorded liftable, not implementation-optional — narrowing must not vary between conforming implementations); or
- the variable is **mutably captured** — assigned, or passed as `ref`/`out`, anywhere inside any lambda of the enclosing function body ([§27.5](#sec-closures)) — and the block performs *any* operation that can transfer control to user code: a method, constructor, accessor, or user-defined-operator call, an invocation of a function value, or an `await` (across which another continuation of the domain may run the closure, [§30.13](#sec-runtime-model)). A mutably-captured local has exactly the unseen writer the field paragraph below names — "a closure invoked in between" — so after the first such operation the narrowing is gone; re-test, or copy to an uncaptured local (the same remedy as for fields). The rule is deliberately syntactic and conservative: any lambda in the body counts, whether or not it escapes, so the check needs no escape analysis. Straight-line check-then-use of a captured local (`if x <> null then x.M(); end;` — no call *between* the test and the use) remains accepted.

The compiler does not attempt deeper analysis of which methods could reassign which variables transitively; beyond the forms above, nothing invalidates a local's narrowing. A `const` local's narrowing ([§21.1](#sec-variable-declarations)), once established, is **never invalidated**: no invalidating form can apply to it — it cannot be reassigned, cannot be passed as `ref` or `out`, and cannot be mutably captured (assignment to a `const` is a compile error everywhere, lambda bodies included). A null test on a `const` local therefore narrows it for the remainder of its scope, across calls and `await`s; the field-copy idiom of this section is airtight when the copy is `const`.

<a id="sec-stable-locals"></a>
**Stable locals.** A **stable local** of a body, over a stated region of it, is a local variable or parameter of that body that is not mutably captured (above), is not named by a `ref` or `out` argument in the region, and is not a parameter that binds the caller's storage: a `ref` parameter, written or inferred ([§27.1](#sec-lambda-parameter-modifiers)), or a move-only operator operand or `Equals(T)` parameter ([§25.2](#sec-operator-overloading-restrictions)). Two rules are built on the term, and each states its region and what it adds or excludes. [§9.4](#sec-value-receivers-are-borrows)'s in-place pass of a fixed receiver takes the region of one call, adds storage inside the enclosing activation's own fixed receiver, and admits no field. [§19.3](#sec-patterns)'s provably unwritten sources take the region of the whole construct, exclude a binding a borrowing match introduces as a root, add a `readonly` field outside its construction window, and never count `this` in a value-kind member body.

**Storage inside a narrowed nullable value.** Over a local or non-`ref` parameter `n` of nullable value type narrowed non-null (`n: Pt?` for a record `Pt`), a member or index chain from `n` whose store would land in `n`'s own storage (no hop leaves the value through a class- or interface-typed member, [§9.4](#sec-value-receivers-are-borrows)'s key) names storage inside `n`'s value. It is an assignable location wherever the same chain is one on a local of type `Pt` ([§17.6](#sec-the-increment-and-decrement-operators)'s categories): `n.X := 5` stores into `n`'s value, and `n` stays non-null. The location exists only while `n` holds a value, so a store to it requires `n` narrowed **at the store**, under the forms above. An assignment stores after its right operand is evaluated, and a compound assignment after its target is located and its right operand evaluated ([§6.6](#sec-compound-assignments)), so a right operand that invalidates the narrowing makes the store a compile error: `n.X += F()` with `n` mutably captured, or `n.X := G(ref n)`. A `ref` argument, and an inline-array argument at an `extern` parameter ([§32.5](#sec-ffi-compatible-types)/[§15.1.3](#sec-inline-array-ffi)), can store at any point of the call; an `out` argument stores at its copy-out on normal return, and an accessor target at its write-back ([§22.3](#sec-ref-and-out-argument-locations)), in each case after the callee's code has run. The forms above state what holds between operations, not during a call, and during it a closure that captured `n`, or another argument naming `n` in the same call, can set `n := null` before that store. Such a chain at those positions is therefore a compile error (`ref n.X`, `out n.Y`), and the diagnostic names the copy-out spelling `var p: Pt := n; Inc(ref p.X); n := p;`. A member call on the narrowed `n` is unaffected by a writer during the call: it runs over the fixed receiver value ([§9.4](#sec-value-receivers-are-borrows)), so `n := null` from a closure the member invokes changes nothing the member reads; a move-only `n` is borrowed in place instead ([§9.4](#sec-value-receivers-are-borrows) *Move-only receivers*). A chain that leaves `n`'s value through a class- or interface-typed member (`ref n.Owner.Name`) names storage in that object, a borrow ([§9.7](#sec-records-and-disposal)) that a later store to `n` does not affect, and is admitted. A `ref` parameter is never narrowed (*Narrowing applies to locals — and `readonly` fields — only*, below), so no chain from one of nullable value type names storage inside its value: copy it to a local, narrow and store into the copy, and write the whole value back — `var c := n; if c <> null then c.X := 5; n := c; end;` — the store `n := c` being an ordinary store to the parameter, which lands in the caller's location whatever that location held meanwhile.

<a id="sec-narrowing-applies-to-locals-only"></a>
#### Narrowing applies to locals — and `readonly` fields — only

The compiler narrows local variables, parameters other than `ref` parameters, and `readonly` fields in the tracked shape below; these are the **narrowing carriers**. It never narrows mutable fields, properties, or `ref` parameters. A field may be reassigned to `null` between a null check and a subsequent use by paths the compiler cannot see: a method call whose body (directly, or through another reference to the same object) writes the field, a closure invoked in between, re-entrant code reached from the checked expression itself, or — across an `await` — another continuation of the same domain interleaving at the suspension point ([§30.13](#sec-runtime-model)); foreign threads introduced through the FFI ([§32](#sec-foreign-function-interface), [§30.12](#sec-thread-synchronization)) are the residual concurrent case. Narrowing a field would therefore manufacture TOCTOU (time-of-check / time-of-use) bugs the compiler cannot prevent.

The standard pattern is to copy a nullable field to a local before narrowing:

```bezel
var u := _user;
if u <> null then
  u.DoStuff();          // u is narrowed; safe regardless of _user changes
end;
```

Local-variable narrowing applies to the copy, which no other thread can observe. Accessing a nullable *mutable* field without first copying it to a local is a compile error when the access requires non-null.

**`readonly` fields narrow.** A nullable **`readonly`** field — instance or `static` — participates in flow narrowing, because the blanket refusal's premise (unseen writers) does not exist for it: outside its construction window ([§22.8](#sec-field-initializers)'s single-assignment rule) a `readonly` field has no writer on any path, through any alias, so no call, `await`, or closure can invalidate a fact about its value. The tracked shape is exactly **one field off an admitted root** — `this._f`, `TypeName._s`, or `v._f` where `v` is a local variable or non-`ref` parameter that is itself narrowing-tracked; a fact rides its root (reassigning `v` drops it), and **any non-final field segment makes a path non-trackable** (`a.b._f` establishes nothing — `a.b` is a mutable read). The rule does not apply inside the declaring type's constructors, field initializers, static constructor, or static field initializers (the assignment window); elsewhere it composes with construction's [§22.7](#sec-observing-this-during-construction) `this`-escape residual exactly as stated there: a during-construction narrowing test observes either the null watermark (establishing nothing) or the field's single assigned value, final by §22.8 — the residual is §22.7's, inherited, not enlarged. Mutable fields and properties are unchanged: copy to a local first (rationale [§6.1](Bezel_Design_Rationale.md#sec-field-narrowing-is-not-safe-across-threads)).

**`ref` parameters do not narrow.** A `ref` parameter ([§22.3](#sec-parameter-modifiers)) — of a method, constructor, or lambda ([§27.3](#sec-lambda-expressions)), its `ref` written or inferred from the target type ([§27.1](#sec-lambda-parameter-modifiers)) — aliases a location the caller chose, and the caller's other names for that location stay live for the whole call: among them a closure the caller passed as another argument, a second `ref` argument naming the same storage (`G(ref m, ref m)`), and a field the callee can reach through another argument, its receiver, or static state (`G(ref h.F, h)`, `h.G(ref h.F)`). A write through any of them is a write to the parameter that none of the invalidating forms above names, and the last two need no call: in `G(ref a: Animal?, ref b: Animal?)` called as `G(ref m, ref m)` the store `b := null` writes `a`, and so does `h.F := null` in `G(ref a: Animal?, h: Holder)` called as `G(ref h.F, h)`. The compiler therefore establishes **no** narrowing fact about a `ref` parameter. A null test, type test ([§12.7](#sec-type-tests-is-is-not-as)), assignment, `??=`, early exit, or `out`-recipient postcondition ([§22.4](#sec-out-nullability-postcondition)) on it narrows nothing — in an `if`, `elif` or `while` condition, a `when` guard, a conditional atom, or a `case` alike — and a `readonly`-field path rooted at it (`a._f`) is not trackable, since its root is not. A pattern binding over it is unaffected: `case a of var d: Dog => d.Bark(), …` binds a fresh local ([§19.3](#sec-patterns)) holding the matched value, which no caller alias reaches, and `d` is typed and narrowed as any local is; `as` likewise. A `ref` parameter is read at its **declared** type at every position, exactly as a mutable field is: member access, indexing and calls on a nullable one, and [§7.11](#sec-lifted-operators)'s operators over a nullable one, are compile errors, and the remedies are `?.`, `??`, `!`, or the copy. The standard pattern is the field pattern — copy to a local and narrow the copy:

```bezel
public static method Greet(ref a: Animal?, f: () -> ()): string
  var c := a;                 // a borrow of the same object; `c` has one name
  if c <> null then
    f();                      // may store null through the caller's alias of `a`
    return c.Speak();         // `c` still holds the object; narrowing is sound
  end;
  return "none";
end Greet;
```

Where the caller should observe a change, write back with an ordinary store, `a := c;`, which lands in the caller's location whatever that location held meanwhile, as any store through an alias does. The diagnostic at a rejected use names this remedy. Every other parameter kind is the callee's own storage and narrows under the forms above: a plain, `owned`, or `scoped` parameter holds the callee's copy of the argument, and an `out` parameter denotes a callee-local slot that no caller alias names before its copy-out on normal return ([§22.3](#sec-parameter-modifiers)) — which is what lets [§22.4](#sec-out-nullability-postcondition)'s postcondition be discharged inside the declaring body.

<a id="sec-null-conditional-access"></a>
### 7.5 Null-conditional access (`?.`)

`x?.M` returns null if `x` is null; otherwise it performs the access. The result type is always nullable:

```bezel
var name: string? := user?.Name;
var length: int? := user?.Name?.Length;
user?.Log("Accessed");
```

**Evaluation.** `?.` short-circuits. The receiver is evaluated first; if it is null the access does not occur and **nothing to its right in the chain is evaluated** — no member is read, no call is performed, and the argument and index expressions of the skipped suffixes are not evaluated either. If any segment of a chain is null, the remainder of the chain is skipped on the same terms and the whole chain's result is `null`: `user?.Log(Render(x))` calls neither `Log` nor `Render` when `user` is null.

<a id="sec-null-conditional-call-args"></a>
### 7.6 Null-conditional call (`?(args)`)

A function value of nullable function type may be invoked with `?(...)`:

```bezel
var handler: ((int) -> ())? := null;
handler?(42);                       // no-op when null
```

The result type is nullable (or `()` for procedure-typed values). **Evaluation** is [§7.5](#sec-null-conditional-access)'s: the function-valued operand is evaluated first, and when it is null the invocation does not occur and **the argument expressions are not evaluated** — `handler?(Next())` does not call `Next` when `handler` is null.

<a id="sec-null-coalescing-and-="></a>
### 7.7 Null-coalescing (`??` and `??=`)

`a ?? b` returns `a` if non-null, else `b`. **Typing:** for a left operand of type `T?`, the right operand must be implicitly convertible ([§5.1](#sec-implicit-conversions)) to `T` or to `T?`; the result type is `T` when the right operand is non-nullable and `T?` when it is nullable — `user?.Name ?? "Anonymous"` is `string`, while `primary ?? fallback` over two `string?` values is `string?`; a right-associative chain stays nullable until a non-nullable operand terminates it (`a ?? b ?? ""` is `string`). When the operands are owned (or owned-nullable), `??` is a two-branch *expression* and its result ownership follows the same meet rule as an `if`/`else` join — see the producer table in [§28.3](#sec-local-variables-ownership-and-borrows): `owned ?? owned` is owned (the chosen value is discharged once), and an owned arm mixed with a borrowed arm is rejected.

**Evaluation.** `??` is conditional. The left operand is evaluated **exactly once**, and the **right operand is evaluated only when the left operand's value is `null`** — when the left is non-null the right operand expression does not run at all, and none of its calls, allocations, side effects, or faults occur; this is what makes `LoadConfig() ?? throw new InvalidOperationException("no config")` ([§17.12](#sec-the-throw-expression)) a fallback rather than an unconditional raise. The rule governs the operand expression as a whole and so composes through the right-associative chain ([§17.2](#sec-notes-on-operators)): in `a ?? b ?? c` a non-null `a` skips both `b` and `c`. `??` is therefore a control-flow join ([K7](#sec-kernel-k7)) rather than a two-operand operation, and **no operand's value is ever produced and then discarded**: the left is discarded only in the case where it is `null`, which owns nothing, and the right is evaluated only where it is selected. The ownership meet above needs no rule about unselected producers for that reason — an owned right operand that is not selected was never produced.
