Where `??` appears as an argument, [§22.5](#sec-optional-parameters-and-named-arguments)'s call-site textual order is undisturbed: that rule fixes the order of a call's argument expressions relative to one another and never makes the operands *within* one of them unconditional. The compound form `??=` evaluates its right-hand side, and invokes the setter, only when the assignment occurs ([§6.6](#sec-compound-assignments)).

```bezel
var displayName: string := user?.Name ?? "Anonymous";
// with `private owned _cache: Cache?;` — a fresh `new` requires an `owned` field (§28.6)
_cache ??= new Cache();             // assign only if currently null
```

<a id="sec-null-forgiving"></a>
### 7.8 Null-forgiving (`!`)

`x!` asserts non-nullness. If `x` is null at runtime, `NullReferenceException` is raised. The result is the non-nullable form of the expression. `!` is the only postfix `!` operator in the language; there is no prefix `!`.

<a id="sec-definite-assignment-for-non-nullable-fields"></a>
### 7.9 Definite assignment for non-nullable fields

Every non-nullable field must be either:
- assigned a value in every constructor before the constructor returns, or
- given a field initializer at its declaration.

Definite-assignment analysis applies the same rule to locals, keyed on the same property: a local of **non-defaultable** type ([§17.11](#sec-the-default-operator)) must be assigned before it is read (in a lambda body that captures it, as [§27.5](#sec-closures) reads the body from the lambda's formation), and a local of **defaultable** type declared without an initializer holds that type's default from its declaration (*Default initialization* below).

The guarantee this rule exists to provide is operational: **no non-nullable field is ever observed unset**. For ordinary (hand-written) construction the constructor-scoped rule above delivers that guarantee together with the construction-time observation rules of [§22.7](#sec-observing-this-during-construction): code that can observe the object mid-construction — an instance call on `this`, an escape of `this`, a virtual dispatch — is admitted only where the observable fields are assigned, virtual dispatch from non-sealed constructor bodies is rejected, and the recorded residual routes (dispatch reached through helpers, escapes, or construction-time closure invocations, [§22.7](#sec-observing-this-during-construction)) are bounded by the null watermark and checked-mode `NullReferenceException` defined there. Synthesized deserialization is bound by the same rule with no exception: an owning-tree component and a plain borrowing back-edge are supplied as constructor arguments (bound before the constructor body runs), and a cycle-closing reference is a nullable `Weak<T>?` field — discharged by its null initializer at construction and wired afterward by ordinary mutation. No synthesized construction mode escapes the constructor-scoped rule; definite assignment holds for synthesized and hand-written construction alike (serialization synthesis, [§9.8](#sec-serialization-synthesis); rationale [§5.22](Bezel_Design_Rationale.md#sec-type-driven-serialization)).

<a id="sec-default-initialization"></a>
#### Default initialization

A field whose type is **defaultable** ([§17.11](#sec-the-default-operator) — every nullable type, whose default is `null`, and every value type the property admits) satisfies the must-initialize rule vacuously and is implicitly initialized to that default ([§17.11](#sec-the-default-operator)'s per-kind values); an explicit initializer is permitted and overrides it. A field whose type is **not** defaultable — a non-nullable reference type, a choice, or a value type with a non-defaultable component — requires an explicit initializer: a field initializer, or assignment in every constructor (for instance fields) or in the static constructor (for static fields). The compiler emits a definite-assignment error if neither path supplies a value.

**Inline-array fields take this rule through their element type.** An inline-array field is defaultable exactly when its element type is ([§17.11](#sec-the-default-operator)), the owning forms included: a field of type `[N]T?`, `[N owned]T?`, or `[N]T` at a defaultable `T` satisfies the must-initialize rule vacuously and is implicitly initialized per slot — all-`null` at a nullable element type, the element's zero value otherwise — so no constructor need assign it. A field of `[N]T` at a non-defaultable element type (a non-nullable class type is the common case), and `[N owned]T` in every form, requires an explicit initializer or assignment in every constructor like any other non-defaultable field. (A record may declare no `[N owned]…` field at all, [§9.7](#sec-records-and-disposal).)

The same split applies in the standard `var`-declaration case: a local of defaultable type can be declared without an initializer (it gets the type's default — `0` for `var n: int;`, `null` for a nullable local, and per-slot for an inline array, [§15.1](#sec-inline-arrays)); a local of non-defaultable type must be assigned before it is read.

<a id="sec-generics-and-nullability"></a>
### 7.10 Generics and nullability

Inside an unconstrained generic body, `T` is treated conservatively as possibly nullable. Storage of type `T` should be declared `T?`.

`where T: notnull` restricts T to non-nullable types. Inside the body, `T` is non-nullable.

`where T: class` restricts T to non-nullable reference types — classes (including `Array<T>`, `OwningArray<T>`), interfaces, `string`, function types.

`where T: value` restricts T to non-nullable value types — records, enums, choices ([§35](#sec-choices)), primitives, inline arrays (all forms, including `[N owned]…` owning forms), and the unit type. A nullable value type (e.g. `int?`) does not satisfy the constraint ([§14.2](#sec-constraints)); inside the body, T is the non-nullable value type and `T?` is its nullable companion. Inside the body, operations that copy T (assignment, parameter passing by value, returning by value) are checked at instantiation: for move-only inline arrays ([§15.3](#sec-move-only-value-types)), copy operations are replaced by moves, and any operation the generic body uses that requires copy semantics (e.g., reading T twice without an intervening assignment) is rejected at instantiation with a message naming the move-only type.

`where T: SomeClass` and `where T: IFoo` are *type-bound* constraints. They restrict T to non-nullable types conforming to the named type:
- `where T: SomeClass` admits SomeClass and its subclasses. Interfaces do not extend classes in Bezel, so this constraint admits class types only.
- `where T: IFoo` admits any non-nullable type that conforms to `IFoo`: classes that implement it (directly, by inheritance, or implicitly — `IDisposable`, [§28.2](#sec-the-idisposable-contract)), records and enums that implement it, interfaces that extend it (directly or transitively), and primitives conforming through their standard-library declarations or the compiler-provided conformances of [§11.8](#sec-static-interface-members). See [§14.2](#sec-constraints) for the conformance rule and worked examples.

Inside the generic body, T is non-nullable under any type-bound constraint.

`T?` always means "the nullable form of T," regardless of constraint. Under `where T: notnull`, `T` is the non-nullable form and `T?` is the nullable companion.

**`?` is idempotent under substitution.** When an unconstrained `T` is instantiated with a nullable type `U?`, the substituted `T?` denotes `U?` itself — there is no two-level optional, consistent with the grammar (Appendix A: `Type ::= TypeNoNullable "?"?`, at most one `?`) and with [§8.6](#sec-boxing)'s single-wrapper boxing. Consequently an API whose result type is `T?` (e.g. the stdlib `FirstOrNull` family) cannot distinguish "no value" from "a present `null`" when instantiated at a nullable `T`; callers who need the distinction use the shape that carries it (`Count`/index checks, or the `Try` pattern). A field or local of **bare** type `T` under an unconstrained parameter follows [§7.9](#sec-definite-assignment-for-non-nullable-fields)'s non-nullable-reference rules (must-initialize, no vacuous `null` default), since T may be instantiated non-nullable; *reads* remain conservatively possibly-null per this section.

<a id="sec-lifted-operators"></a>
### 7.11 Operators over nullable operands

No operator **lifts** to a nullable type. For a nullable value type `T?`, the operators [§3.5](#sec-operators-on-primitive-types) defines on the underlying type `T` are not defined on `T?`: an operand whose static type is a nullable value type is a **compile error** at every arithmetic, bitwise, shift, and relational operator — on either side, and in the mixed `T?`/`T` pairing alike — with the diagnostic naming the remedies the language uses at every other position where a nullable value meets a non-nullable one: a [§7.4](#sec-member-access-on-nullable-values) narrowing check, `??` ([§7.7](#sec-null-coalescing-and-=)), or `!` ([§7.8](#sec-null-forgiving)). The rule reads the operand's **static** type, so an operand that [§7.4](#sec-member-access-on-nullable-values) has narrowed non-null is a non-nullable operand and the ordinary operator applies to it unchanged; no separate rule is needed for that case. Nullable **reference** operands take the same answer at their own types ([§4.6](#sec-string) for `string`). What propagates absence in this language is marked: `?.` ([§7.5](#sec-null-conditional-access)), `?(args)` ([§7.6](#sec-null-conditional-call-args)), `??` and `??=` ([§7.7](#sec-null-coalescing-and-=)) each carry the `?` that announces it. Equality is total over an absent operand and is unaffected by this section ([§8.4](#sec-=-and): `null = null` is `true`, `null = nonNull` is `false`). (Rationale [§6.4](Bezel_Design_Rationale.md#sec-operators-do-not-lift).)

**The rejected operators.** The binary `+`, `-`, `*`, `/`, `mod`, `&`, `|`, `^`, `<<`, `>>`; the unary `+`, `-`, `~`; and the relational `<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=`. Their compound-assignment forms are rejected with them ([§6.6](#sec-compound-assignments)), as are `++` and `--`, whose desugaring is §6.6's ([§17.6](#sec-the-increment-and-decrement-operators)) — `??=` excepted, which is not a read-modify-write ([§6.6](#sec-compound-assignments)). The runtime checks these operators carry are unchanged and unmoved: `OverflowException` on integer overflow ([§6.1](#sec-integer-arithmetic)), `DivideByZeroException` on integer or `decimal` division or `mod` by zero ([§6.1](#sec-integer-arithmetic)), and the shift-count domain ([§6.5](#sec-bitwise-operations)) are checks of the operation on present operands, reached after the operands are narrowed. This section introduces no fault of its own and no new throwable expression ([§28.8.1](#sec-the-move-expression)): an absent operand is diagnosed at compile time, and the remedies that assert presence rather than test it (`!`, [§7.8](#sec-null-forgiving)) carry their own already-defined fault.

**Ordering, specifically.** `<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=` reject a nullable operand rather than answer for it: an absent participant is not less than, equal to, or greater than a value. This is [§4.6](#sec-string)'s rule for `string?` read at every other type. An order over possibly-absent values is written where the reader can see the choice: `(a ?? 0) < b` names a sentinel, `a! < b` asserts presence, and a [§7.4](#sec-member-access-on-nullable-values) check ranks the absent case in a branch of its own. Pattern position takes the same rule: a relational or range pattern requires a non-nullable scrutinee ([§19.3](#sec-patterns), [§16.6](#sec-empty-ranges-and-equal-bound-ranges)).

**No three-valued logic.** There are no `bool?` logical operators. `and`, `or`, `not` ([§17.2](#sec-notes-on-operators)) operate only on `bool`; a `bool?` operand is a compile error, and code combining `bool?` values handles the absent case explicitly (`??` ([§7.7](#sec-null-coalescing-and-=)), or a narrowing check). This is not a separate rule but this section's rule at the boolean operators: the language carries no third truth value, and it does not collapse one into `false` at an operator either.

**User-defined operators.** The rule does not turn on where an operator is declared. A user-declared `operator` on a record or class type ([§25](#sec-operator-overloading)) is likewise not defined on a nullable operand: such an operand at a user-defined-operator position is the same compile error, naming the same remedies. `=` and `<>` are excepted, as this section's opening states: an overloaded equality operator is reached through [§8.4](#sec-=-and)'s null-safe wrapper, which decides an absent operand before the overload runs.

---

<a id="sec-the-object-class"></a>
## 8. The Object Class

<a id="sec-definition"></a>
### 8.1 Definition

```bezel
public class Object
  public method GetType(): Type;
  public virtual method Equals(other: Object?): bool;
  public virtual method GetHashCode(): int;
  public virtual method ToString(): string;
  public static method ReferenceEquals(a: Object?, b: Object?): bool;
end Object;
```

`Object` is a compiler intrinsic; method bodies are provided by the runtime. The declaration above defines the public surface. Its module is `System` ([§2.3](#sec-always-available-names)), as `Type`'s is, so `System.Object` is its qualified name: [§2.7](#sec-name-resolution-order) rule 2 reaches it, and stdlib [§2.13](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-the-type-class)'s `FullName` renders it `"System.Object"`. User code cannot redeclare or replace `Object`. The ban is on a user module-level type declaration — a class, record, enum, interface, choice or type alias — named `Object` with no type parameters, in any user module and at any visibility. Every other declaration of the name is ordinary: a generic `Object<T>` is a different name ([§2.2](#sec-imports)); a nested type or a type parameter named `Object` shadows the root under [§2.7](#sec-name-resolution-order) as any declaration shadows an always-available name, and `System.Object` still reaches it; and a method-local type may not take the name ([§21.10](#sec-local-type-declarations)). Wherever this specification names `Object`, it means the root.

`Object` is the universal root. Every type derives from it: classes (including heap-array classes `Array<T>` and `OwningArray<T>`) directly through the inheritance chain, with `string`, interfaces, and function types reaching `Object` similarly via their reference-type heap representation; records, enums, choices, primitives, inline arrays, and the unit type derive via boxing ([§8.6](#sec-boxing)) when used in `Object`-typed positions (subject to the move-only boxing rules: [§8.6](#sec-boxing-of-inline-arrays) for inline arrays, [§35.8](#sec-choice-boxing) for choices).

<a id="sec-gettype"></a>
### 8.2 `GetType`

`v.GetType()` returns the `Type` value for the runtime type of `v`. For a value-typed `v` the answer is always the static type — value types have no derivation, so runtime and static type coincide — and the call is answered from the static type with no observable boxing (move-only inline arrays, [§15.3](#sec-move-only-value-types), cannot be boxed ([§8.6](#sec-boxing-of-inline-arrays)) but may be asked their type — the receiver is borrowed, not copied). An implementation remains free to box internally where the type admits it; the result is identical either way.

`GetType` is non-virtual; runtime type identity is fixed at allocation and cannot be overridden.

`GetType` complements the `typeof(T)` expression ([§17.10](#sec-the-typeof-operator)), which produces the `Type` for a statically named type.

<a id="sec-equals-and-gethashcode"></a>
### 8.3 `Equals` and `GetHashCode`

`Equals` defines value-level equality. The compiler generates a default appropriate to each type kind:

| Type kind | Default `Equals` | Default `GetHashCode` |
|---|---|---|
| Class | Reference equality | Identity-based |
| Positional record | Field-by-field value equality (admissible component fields only, [§9.3](#sec-combined-form); otherwise no default and comparison is a compile error) | Hash of all positional fields |
| Body-only record | Auto-hashable ([§9.2](#sec-body-records)): property-by-property value equality; otherwise no default — `=`/`<>`/`.Equals`/`.GetHashCode` use is a compile error | Same |
| Enum | Underlying integer equality | Hash of integer value |
| Primitive | Value comparison | Value-based |
| Inline array `[N]T`, `[N]T?` | Element-by-element value equality ([§15.1.2](#sec-inline-array-members)) | Hash combining element hashes in slot order |
| Inline array `[N owned]T`, `[N owned]T?` | Element-by-element equality via borrow ([§15.3](#sec-move-only-value-types)) | Hash combining element hashes in slot order |

`GetHashCode` must satisfy: if `a.Equals(b)` then `a.GetHashCode() = b.GetHashCode()`. Hash collisions on non-equal values are permitted. The auto-generated `GetHashCode` for positional records combines per-field hashes in declaration order; the combining function **must be order-sensitive** (a commutative combiner such as plain XOR does not satisfy this): the hash of a sequence of component hashes must depend on their order, not only on their multiset, so `Pair(1, 2)` and `Pair(2, 1)` are not *systematically* hash-equal (incidental collisions remain permitted, as for any hash). The choice of combining algorithm is otherwise implementation-defined, subject to the hash-equality invariant and this order-sensitivity requirement.

A type that overrides `Equals` must also override `GetHashCode`. The compiler enforces this. On an enum or a choice, whose `Object`-slot `Equals` takes its own type and is declared `override` or plain, the two spellings declaring one member ([§10.5](#sec-restrictions), [§35.2](#sec-choice-members)), the rule reads both spellings of both members: a plain `Equals` obliges `GetHashCode`, and a plain `GetHashCode` discharges the obligation. A choice that no boxing reaches, one owning at every instantiation ([§35.4](#sec-choice-classification), [§35.11](#sec-choice-generics)), has no slot to fill, so its declared `Equals` carries no such obligation ([§35.7](#sec-choice-equality)).

<a id="sec-identity-hash-assignment"></a>
**Identity hashes are assigned, not derived.** The identity-based default `GetHashCode` for classes is **assigned on first request**, not derived from the object's storage address: the runtime draws the value from a per-domain deterministic sequence (objects first hashed outside any domain draw from the startup/shutdown thread's sequence, [§30.13](#sec-runtime-model)) and stores it with the object thereafter. Identity hash codes are therefore a function of the order in which objects' hashes are first requested — deterministic under [§30.13](#sec-determinism) — and never expose addresses. Programs must continue to treat identity hashes as opaque per-run values; only their stability within a run and their address-independence are promised.

<a id="sec-=-and"></a>
### 8.4 `=` and `<>`

`a = b` invokes `a.Equals(b)`, with a null-safe wrapper: `null = null` is `true`; `null = nonNull` and `nonNull = null` are `false`. `<>` is the negation. The wrapper belongs to the equality operators, not to `Equals`: over a nullable operand, `a = b` and `a <> b` decide the absent cases first, as above, and only when both operands are present dispatch to the overloaded operator where one is declared ([§25.2](#sec-operator-overloading-restrictions)), or to `Equals` otherwise. [§7.11](#sec-lifted-operators)'s rejection of a nullable operand at a user-defined operator therefore does not reach `=` and `<>`.

For classes, `=` always invokes `Equals`. Operator overloading of `=` and `<>` is not permitted on classes; classes customize equality by overriding `Equals`. Records, enums, and choices may overload `=` and `<>` ([§25](#sec-operator-overloading); [§35.2](#sec-choice-members) admits of a choice body exactly what an enum body admits, operator overloads included).

`Object.ReferenceEquals(a, b)` compares object identity, ignoring any `Equals` override. It is an ordinary static method with `Object?` parameters, so value-typed arguments are **boxed before the comparison** and the result is the identity of the boxes ([§8.6](#sec-boxing)): a non-null value-typed argument produces a fresh box and compares unequal to every other argument — except boxed `()`, which an implementation may intern ([§8.6](#sec-boxing-of-the-unit-value)), making that comparison unspecified — while a **null** nullable-value argument boxes to the null reference ([§8.6](#sec-nullable-value-type-boxing)), so `ReferenceEquals(x, null)` is `true` for a null `int?` `x`. The compiler warns on any value-typed argument: the question being answered is box identity, which is almost never what the caller means.

<a id="sec-tostring"></a>
### 8.5 `ToString`

`ToString` is invoked implicitly inside string interpolation ([§18.5](#sec-interpolated-strings)) via virtual dispatch — for present values; a `null` value of a nullable-typed hole renders as the text `null` with no dispatch ([§18.5](#sec-interpolated-strings)). The compiler-generated default returns:

- For classes: the type's **qualified name** — the module-path-qualified rendering stdlib [§2.13](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-the-type-class) defines for `Type.FullName` (`"BankingApp.BankAccount"`, and `"System.Object"` for `new Object()`, [§8.1](#sec-definition); a nested class carries its enclosing-type path — `"BankingApp.Ledger.Entry"` for `Entry` declared inside `Ledger`, [§11.6](#sec-nested-types); a generic instantiation renders per stdlib §2.13 rule 3, type arguments recursing). The default and `FullName` are one rendering contract, not two.
- For positional records: a representation of fields, e.g. `"Point(X: 10, Y: 20)"`.
- For body records that satisfy the auto-equality conditions ([§9.2](#sec-body-records) — only auto-properties, no manually-declared `Equals` or `GetHashCode`, and no homogeneous `=`/`<>` overload): a representation of auto-properties, formatted as `"TypeName(Prop1: value1, Prop2: value2)"`. Auto-`ToString` accompanies the auto-equality members, with one asymmetry: an `override ToString` replaces only the formatting — the record keeps auto-`Equals`/`GetHashCode`/`=` — while an `Equals`/`GetHashCode` override — or a homogeneous `=`/`<>` overload — disqualifies the whole package ([§9.2](#sec-body-records)), auto-`ToString` included: such a **body** record renders by the next bullet's qualified-name default, and neither [§25.2](#sec-operator-overloading-restrictions)'s co-declaration rule nor anything else restores the property-listing form, so a record that wants it declares its own `ToString`. A **positional** record is unaffected — this bullet's split is by declaration form, and §9.1's positional head keeps its field listing whatever equality members the body adds. This matches the analogous design in C# records and lets `Console.WriteLine(person)` produce useful output for auto-equality records without ceremony.
- For body records that do not satisfy auto-equality conditions, and for enums: the type's qualified name (the stdlib [§2.13](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-the-type-class) `FullName` rendering, as for classes). An enum may replace its default by declaring a `ToString(): string` member, `override` or plain ([§10.5](#sec-restrictions)); the replacement is used by every consumer, including interpolation and boxed dispatch. The constant's identifier is `E.NameOf(value)` ([§10.4](#sec-methods-properties-static-members)); an enum whose rendering should be that name declares `ToString` to return it.
- For **choices** that are value-like and **auto-hashable** ([§35.7](#sec-choice-equality)): the case-shaped representation §35.7 fixes — `"TypeName.CaseName(field1: value1, …)"`, and `"TypeName.CaseName"` for a payload-free case — with the head **unqualified**, on the same asymmetry the record heads take below: the rendering already identifies itself by shape (`"Status.Active(code: 7)"`, not `"Conf.Status.Active(code: 7)"`). Each payload renders as its own `ToString` renders it, by this section's component rule. The generated `ToString` is part of §35.7's auto-hashable package exactly as auto-`ToString` is part of §9.2's auto-equality package, and a declared `ToString(): string` member ([§35.2](#sec-choice-members)) replaces it for every consumer, interpolation and boxed dispatch included.
- For every **other** choice — borrow-bearing, owning, or value-like with an inadmissible payload ([§35.7](#sec-choice-equality)'s non-auto-hashable set): **no default is generated**. A `ToString()` call on such a value at a statically-known receiver type — a direct call, or an interpolation hole (whose hole expression carries such a type, whatever the opening paragraph calls the dispatch) — is §35.7's **use-site compile error**, which the author removes by declaring the member ([§35.2](#sec-choice-members), [§10.5](#sec-restrictions)'s plain-member replacement model). No case-shaped default is synthesized in its place, for the reason the inline-array bullet below declines element listing: such a choice's payloads may be owned or borrowed class values whose formatting is not the container's business. Where the receiver is **boxed** — a dispatched call through `Object` or an interface, which no static rejection can reach — the rendering is the qualified-name default the body-record-and-enum bullet above gives (an *owning* choice is not boxable at all, [§35.8](#sec-choice-boxing)). The same qualified name is the rendering, and nothing is rejected, where no `ToString()` call is written at the choice's own static type, in two further ways: a `T`-typed operand — a receiver or interpolation hole whose static type is a type parameter, instantiated at such a choice, an owning one included (its receiver is borrowed, not boxed) — and a component of a generated rendering, such as a positional record's field (the component rule below). The same holds where the receiver or hole is typed by a generic choice whose type arguments are or contain a type parameter in scope — `r.ToString()` or `$"{r}"` for `r: Result<T, E>` in a generic body: the choice's classification, and so whether it has a generated `ToString`, is decided per instantiation ([§35.11](#sec-choice-generics)), so at an instantiation where it is not auto-hashable and declares none the rendering is the instantiated type's qualified name (its `FullName` rendering, type arguments recursing, as the class bullet above gives it) and the instantiation is not rejected, while a choice type containing no type parameter (`Result<Widget, string>`) is a statically-known receiver type in a generic body as anywhere else and keeps the use-site error. No constraint states a `ToString` requirement, and the qualified name does not depend on how an implementation realizes generics ([§11.8](#sec-static-interface-members)).
- For inline arrays (all forms, including move-only `[N owned]…` arrays, whose receiver is borrowed for the call) and for the unit type: the type's name — `"[3]int"`-style for an inline array, `"()"` for unit (element-listing output is deliberately not synthesized — an inline array's elements may be class-typed borrows whose formatting is not the container's business).

The record heads' unqualified spelling is a deliberate asymmetry: positional-record and auto-equality formatting keeps the **unqualified** head (`"Point(X: 10, Y: 20)"`, [§9.1](#sec-positional-records)) — a record rendering already identifies itself by shape, while a bare class or enum default is *only* a name and therefore carries the module path.

The defaults above are generated for **every** type of the applicable kind, wherever declared — user modules and the standard library alike. The standard library's positional records (`Span<T>`, `ReadOnlySpan<T>`, `ArraySpan<T>`, `ReadOnlyArraySpan<T>`, …) carry the positional-record default like any other record (stdlib [§4.14](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-owned-buffers-and-spans): the span records are purely user-level Bezel, standard language features throughout); `Range<T>` (a compiler-intrinsic body record, stdlib [§9.8](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-ranget)) carries the auto-equality body-record default of the bullet above, rendering the **declared** auto-property surface — all six of stdlib §9.8's properties, the intrinsically-derived pair recomputed, equality indifferent to the count: the ruling at [#3131](https://github.com/s8lap/bezel-lang/issues/3131); record: rationale [§9.3](Bezel_Design_Rationale.md#sec-auto-equality-on-body-only-records)) resolved for the declared surface, and [§9.2](#sec-body-records)'s declaration-surface rule is its normative statement, read here — so the rendered `IsOpenEnded`/`IsEmpty` and the member reads cannot disagree (an open-ended range renders `IsEmpty: False`, agreeing with `r.IsEmpty`, [§16.3](#sec-range-operations)). Each component renders as its own `ToString` renders it (virtual dispatch — a class-typed component with no override renders its class default, the qualified name per the bullet above); a `null`-valued nullable component renders as the text `null` ([§18.5](#sec-interpolated-strings)'s rule). Rendering is a call-bounded borrow of the receiver and its components: the default's own execution neither retains, consumes, nor extends any borrow ([§9.7](#sec-records-and-disposal) is unaffected). A **boxed** receiver's rendering borrows the box's payload for the call, exactly as an unboxed receiver's borrows the value — the uniform value-receiver borrow of [§9.4](#sec-value-receivers-are-borrows) ([#3124](https://github.com/s8lap/bezel-lang/issues/3124)).

<a id="sec-boxing"></a>
### 8.6 Boxing

When a value type is used where `Object` (or an interface implemented by the value type) is expected, the value is **boxed**: a heap-allocated wrapper holds the value. A type-test operand ([§12.7](#sec-type-tests-is-is-not-as)) and a pattern scrutinee ([§19.3](#sec-patterns)) are not such positions. Boxed values are runtime-managed ([§28.9](#sec-runtime-managed-types)). The wrapper's payload is **fixed at boxing**: a value enters a box by being copied in and leaves it by being read out — a narrowed read ([§12.7](#sec-type-tests-is-is-not-as)), an unboxing `as` ([§17.4](#sec-the-is-is-not-and-as-operators)), or a typed-pattern binding over a boxed scrutinee ([§19.3](#sec-patterns)); a member call on the box reads nothing out — it **borrows** the payload for the call's duration ([§9.4](#sec-value-receivers-are-borrows)'s value-receiver rule; [§8.5](#sec-tostring)'s rendering case) — and **no operation writes it**. The payload a member call borrows stays alive for the call ([§9.4](#sec-value-receivers-are-borrows)'s fixed receiver, [K8.4](#sec-kernel-k8)): releasing the last reference to the box during the call does not end the borrow. The shapes that could appear to are compile errors at their own sites: a write through a [§12.7](#sec-type-tests-is-is-not-as) value-narrowed binding at an `Object` or interface location, in any of the positions §12.7 enumerates, and a member-body store landing in the receiver's own storage in a value kind — including the settable-member interface conformance that would dispatch one — under [§9.4](#sec-value-receivers-are-borrows) ([#3124](https://github.com/s8lap/bezel-lang/issues/3124)).

<a id="sec-boxing-of-the-unit-value"></a>
#### Boxing of the unit value

The unit type `()` has exactly one value, so all boxings of `()` may share a single heap object. Implementations are permitted (but not required) to intern boxed `()` such that every boxing produces the same reference. Programs should not rely on boxed unit values being either reference-equal or reference-distinct; both interpretations are conforming. The only guarantee is the standard one: a boxed `()` value, when unboxed, yields `()`.

<a id="sec-nullable-value-type-boxing"></a>
#### Nullable value-type boxing

When a nullable value type `T?` is boxed:

- If the value is `null`, the result is a null `Object` reference.
- If the value is non-null, the result is a boxed `T` (the non-nullable form). The nullable wrapper is stripped during boxing.

Unboxing reverses the process: a null `Object` reference unboxes to `null` of the target nullable type; a non-null boxed `T` unboxes to a non-null `T?`.

<a id="sec-boxing-of-borrow-bearing-records"></a>
#### Boxing of borrow-bearing records

Boxing a borrow-bearing record ([§9.7](#sec-records-and-disposal)) is subject to the same borrow-lifetime constraints as any other operation on a borrow-bearing value. The boxed copy on the heap holds the same borrowed references as the source record; it does not extend their lifetimes. The compiler enforces: a boxed borrow-bearing record value may not be stored in a location that could outlive the source of any borrow the record contains. In practice, this means a borrow-bearing record may be boxed for a short-lived interface call (e.g. passing to a method accepting `Object`) provided the boxed value does not escape the borrow's source scope. Storing a boxed borrow-bearing record in a field, returning it from a method, or capturing it in a closure that escapes the source scope is rejected by the same rules as the unboxed form ([§9.7](#sec-records-and-disposal), [§28.3](#sec-local-variables-ownership-and-borrows)). The canonical sanctioned use is passing a span to a parameter of type `IReadOnlySpan<TElement>` (stdlib [§4.16](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-ireadonlyspan)): the box is bounded by the call frame, the interface surface is escape-free by construction (no `GetEnumerator`, no `Slice`, no operation returning a borrow-retaining handle), and the source outlives the call in the common synchronous case. The same bound applies to the **receiver** of an extension-block call whose head is an interface ([§26.2](#sec-what-can-be-extended), [§26.5](#sec-resolution) rule 2): the receiver boxes for the call's duration on identical terms. The contrasting *forbidden* case is the `IEnumerable<T>` enumerator path: `GetEnumerator()` returns a heap object that would hold the span's borrow across its own, unbounded lifetime, which the borrow tracker cannot bound — which is why spans do not implement `IEnumerable<T?>` ([§29.2](#sec-desugaring-of-for)). The distinction is escaping (an enumerator/field/return/escaping-closure) versus call-bounded, not boxing per se. A borrow-bearing **choice** ([§35.4](#sec-choice-classification)) boxes under exactly these rules.

<a id="sec-boxing-of-inline-arrays"></a>
#### Boxing of inline arrays

Non-owning inline arrays (`[N]T` and `[N]T?`) are ordinary value types and box per the general rule. When the array is borrow-bearing ([§15.1.2](#sec-inline-array-members)), the boxed array carries borrows; the same borrow-lifetime constraints apply as for boxed borrow-bearing records (above).

Move-only value types — owning inline arrays (`[N owned]T` and `[N owned]T?`) and owning-classified choices ([§35.4](#sec-choice-classification)) — cannot be boxed. Boxing a value type copies the value into a heap wrapper, but move-only types forbid copying ([§15.3](#sec-move-only-value-types)). A program that needs the contents of an owning inline array to cross a boxed-value boundary must explicitly transfer ownership — typically by draining the inline array into a heap collection (`OwningArray<T>`), which is itself a class type and is passed by reference rather than boxed.

<a id="sec-dispose-is-not-on-object"></a>
### 8.7 `Dispose` is not on `Object`

`Dispose()` is class-only. The compiler generates `IDisposable` on every non-static class. Static classes, records, enums, choices, primitives, and inline arrays do not implement `IDisposable`.


---

<a id="sec-records"></a>
## 9. Records

A record is a value type. Records are stack-allocated or stored inline in their containing object. Records have value semantics: assignment copies the value.

<a id="sec-positional-records"></a>
### 9.1 Positional records

A record may declare positional fields in parentheses after its name:

```bezel
record Point(X: int, Y: int);
record Person(Name: string, Age: int);
```

For each positional record, the compiler generates:

- A primary constructor whose parameters are the positional fields, in declaration order.
- Public read-only properties, one per positional field, with the same names — auto-properties in [§23.1](#sec-auto-properties)'s sense, assignable in a constructor of the declaring record under that section's context.
- Value equality (`=`, `<>`) based on all positional fields (those marked `equality skip` excepted — [§9.2](#sec-equality-skip)) — generated only when every participating positional field is of an admissible component type ([§9.3](#sec-combined-form)); a positional record with an inadmissible field declares fine, but comparing it is a compile error rather than silent reference equality.
- `Equals(Object?)` and `Equals(T)` over the same participating positional fields, agreeing with the generated `=` ([§8.3](#sec-equals-and-gethashcode)); the synthesized `Equals(T)` is what satisfies a declared `IEquatable<T>` conformance ([§14.2](#sec-constraints)).
- `GetHashCode` based on the same participating positional fields.
- `ToString` formatted as `"TypeName(Field1: value1, Field2: value2)"`.

Positional field names are PascalCase by convention; the compiler does not transform them.

A positional-only record ends with `;`:

```bezel
record Point(X: int, Y: int);
```

<a id="sec-body-records"></a>
### 9.2 Body records

A body record declares members in a block. The body may contain auto-properties, methods, expression-bodied properties, constructors, and operator overloads — the member set this section's auto-equality package is defined over, not an exhaustive account of what a record body admits. A member outside it, an explicit field declaration among them, suppresses the auto-generated equality members and leaves the declaration itself legal ([§9.3](#sec-combined-form)):

```bezel
record Rectangle
  public readonly property Width: decimal;
  public readonly property Height: decimal;

  public constructor(width: decimal, height: decimal)
    Width := width;
    Height := height;
  end constructor;

  public method Area(): decimal => Width * Height;
end Rectangle;
```

<a id="sec-record-dispatch-modifiers"></a>
#### Dispatch modifiers on value kinds

A member of a value kind — a record, an enum ([§10](#sec-enums)) or a choice ([§35](#sec-choices)) — may not be declared `virtual`, `abstract`, or `sealed override`; `override` is admitted only on the `Object`-virtual members `Equals`, `GetHashCode` and `ToString` ([§8.1](#sec-definition)), and is rejected on every other member, whatever its kind: method, property, or indexer ([§23.4](#sec-indexers): indexers participate in the dispatch modifiers like methods — here, not at all). Each kind's admitted spellings are stated with the kind. A record's `Equals` is the `Equals(Object?)` spelling, which replaces §8.1's `Object`-virtual member, and the co-declared `Equals(T)` of [§25.2](#sec-operator-overloading-restrictions), admitted with the same spelling; an enum's are [§10.5](#sec-restrictions)'s, and a choice's [§35.2](#sec-choice-members)'s. The value kinds are implicitly sealed (for records, [§9.6](#sec-records-and-inheritance)) and have no virtual-dispatch surface of their own, so the dispatch modifiers carry no meaning on their members; such members are always dispatched statically, and an `override` names the `Object` slot the member fills and implies no chain. The rejection is at the declaration: an inert modifier is not admitted and ignored, for the reason [§9.8](#sec-serialization-synthesis)'s inert-annotation rule gives — a modifier that reads as load-bearing and is not would mislead every reader of the declaration. (Bare `sealed` on any member is already [§12.4](#sec-sealing)'s error; this subsection adds `sealed override`.)

<a id="sec-auto-generated-equality"></a>
#### Auto-generated equality

A body-only record receives auto-generated `=`, `<>`, `Equals(Object?)`, `Equals(T)`, `GetHashCode`, and `ToString` over its **auto-properties** (and only its auto-properties) when every **instance** member of the record **not marked `equality skip`** ([the clause below](#sec-equality-skip)) is one of:

- An auto-property whose type is an **admissible component type** (below) — or an auto-property marked `equality skip` regardless of its type (the clause removes it from the computation; [the `equality skip` clause](#sec-equality-skip) below).
- A method or expression-bodied (computed) property — these contribute no storage and do not participate in equality. What their bodies compute is irrelevant to eligibility — equality, hashing, and `ToString` are defined over storage only, so no behavior of a computed member can affect their correctness.
- An overload of any operator **other than a homogeneous `=`/`<>`** — that is, other than an `=`/`<>` overload both of whose operands are the declaring type ([§25.2](#sec-operator-overloading-restrictions)). A **heterogeneous**-operand `=`/`<>` overload (`T = U`) defines a comparison the synthesis never provided and takes over nothing: it neither qualifies nor disqualifies, exactly as [§25.2](#sec-operator-overloading-restrictions) frees it from the co-declaration obligation. A **homogeneous** one is the third disqualifier below.
- A constructor — regardless of what its body does (see the eligibility note below).

**Static members are ignored**: `const` declarations, `static readonly` fields, and static methods and properties contribute no instance storage and neither qualify nor disqualify the record — a record may carry `Origin`-style constants and static factories without losing `=`. The same static-member exemption applies wherever this membership rule is reused ([§9.8](#sec-serialization-synthesis)).

**Admissible component types** (one recursive rule, applied per storage component):

- a primitive type, an enum, or `string`;
- another record that is itself auto-hashable (recursively, this same rule);
- `T?` where `T` is admissible — the comparison is the null-safe `=` of [§8.4](#sec-=-and);
- a non-owning inline array `[N]T` or `[N]T?` whose element type is admissible — the comparison is element-by-element per [§8.3](#sec-equals-and-gethashcode)'s inline-array rows;
- a **value-like choice** that is itself auto-hashable ([§35.7](#sec-choice-equality) — recursively, this same list applied to every case's payload fields).

Such a record is said to be **auto-hashable** — a derived type property ([§3.6](#sec-derived-type-properties)). The generated `=` compares each auto-property by its declared type's `=`; the generated `GetHashCode` combines per-property hashes; the generated `ToString` produces `"TypeName(Prop1: value1, Prop2: value2)"` over the auto-properties in declaration order (matching the positional-record form in [§8.5](#sec-tostring)). Computed (expression-bodied) properties are not part of the equality comparison or the ToString output even when they are visible on the public surface — equality and the auto-formatted representation are always over storage, never over derived values. That storage-vs-derived rule is a statement about the **declaration surface** ([#3131](https://github.com/s8lap/bezel-lang/issues/3131)): for a user-authored record the two coincide — storage is the auto-properties, and the derived tier is exactly the expression-bodied spelling, the only computed form this section admits. For a **compiler-intrinsic** body record, whose implementation may store fewer slots than its declaration states, the plain-declared properties *are* the auto-property surface whatever the intrinsic's layout: stdlib [§9.8](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-ranget)'s `Range<T>` declares six, and its generated `ToString` renders all six ([§8.5](#sec-tostring)), the intrinsically-derived pair recomputed by the same [§16.3](#sec-range-operations) rules its member reads use — with equality indifferent to the distinction, the derived pair being a function of the stored components, so the storage reading and the declared-surface reading of the generated `=` coincide.

A body record is **not** auto-hashable — and `=` on it without an explicit overload is a compile error — when it contains:

- An explicit field declaration (storage that is not an auto-property) — **unless the field is marked `equality skip`** (the clause below), which removes it from the membership computation entirely: a skipped member cannot disqualify the record.
- An `override` of `Equals` or `GetHashCode`. Declaring either means the author has taken over equality, and the synthesized structural `=` would silently ignore the override; the record is therefore not auto-hashable, and `=`/`<>` are a compile error unless the author also declares the `operator =`/`<>` overloads; the direct `.Equals`/`.GetHashCode` calls are governed per member by the use-site rule below, each answered by the record's own declaration of that member where one exists. (An `override` of `ToString` alone suppresses only the auto-`ToString`; auto-`Equals`/auto-`GetHashCode`/`=` remain — the author took over formatting, not equality.)
- A **homogeneous** `operator =`/`<>` overload — one whose operands are both the declaring type ([§25.2](#sec-operator-overloading-restrictions)). Declaring it takes over the record's own equality: `a = b` invokes the overload directly and does not delegate to `Equals` ([§25.2](#sec-operator-overloading-restrictions)), so a synthesized `Equals`/`GetHashCode` computed by a different rule would be exactly the silent three-surface divergence [§25.2](#sec-operator-overloading-restrictions)'s co-declaration rule exists to prevent — `a = b` true while a `Set<T>` treats them as distinct. The record is therefore not auto-hashable, and it is [§25.2](#sec-operator-overloading-restrictions)'s co-declaration rule, not synthesis, that supplies `Equals(T)` and `override GetHashCode`; by that rule the two disqualifiers always fire together, so this bullet decides nothing on its own for a conforming record and is stated so that neither list can be read alone and be wrong. It is not conditioned on the record's component count: a zero-auto-property record is the *maximal* case of the divergence (every pair equal, one hash value), not an exception to it. A **heterogeneous**-operand `=`/`<>` overload (`T = U`) does **not** disqualify — see the membership list above.

A validating or normalizing constructor is fully compatible with auto-equality. `with` bypasses constructors ([§9.5](#sec-non-destructive-update-with)); the synthesized `Deserialize` runs a matching declared constructor ([§9.8](#sec-serialization-synthesis)).

Authors who want explicit equality on a record outside the auto-hashable set declare `=` and `<>` overloads in the body, along with `Equals(Object?)`, `Equals(T)`, and `GetHashCode` overrides as needed.

The compile error applies to the `=` and `<>` operators **and to direct calls of `.Equals(Object?)` and `.GetHashCode()`** on the record. Calling `someRecord.Equals(other)` or `someRecord.GetHashCode()` on a non-auto-hashable record without a user-defined declaration of that member — the `override` spelling or the plain one — is a compile error pointing to the same fix as the `=` error: declare custom equality, or simplify the record to an auto-hashable form. The error covers `Equals(Object?)`, `Equals(T)` (when the record implements `IEquatable<T>`), and `GetHashCode` (rationale [§9.3](Bezel_Design_Rationale.md#sec-auto-equality-on-body-only-records)).

The error is at the call site, not the declaration site; declaring a non-auto-hashable record is fine on its own. The error fires when user code attempts to invoke equality on it. Calls through a **boxed** receiver, `Object`- or interface-typed ([§8.6](#sec-boxing)) as in `var o: Object := someRecord; o.Equals(...)`, bypass the static-type check. On a record that is **not** auto-hashable, such a call reaches, member by member, the record's own declaration of `Equals(Object?)` or `GetHashCode` where it declares one ([§9.2](#sec-record-dispatch-modifiers)'s `Object` slot), and otherwise the inherited `Object` member. The inherited `Equals` is reference equality of the two boxes, and that covers a record whose only `Equals` is `Equals(T)` ([§25.2](#sec-operator-overloading-restrictions)). The inherited `GetHashCode` is the box's identity hash, assigned as for a class instance ([§8.3](#sec-identity-hash-assignment)). No structural comparison or hash is synthesized for the boxed path, over the admissible components or the inadmissible ones. Two distinct boxes holding equal-looking values therefore compare unequal unless the record declares `Equals(Object?)`. The rule is the same for positional and combined forms ([§9.3](#sec-combined-form)). (An auto-hashable record's box dispatches the generated `Equals(Object?)` and `GetHashCode` above.) The static-type-erasure escape hatch is unavoidable but is rare in practice.

<a id="sec-equality-through-a-type-parameter"></a>
**Through a type parameter.** In a generic body, a call of `Equals` or `GetHashCode` on a `T`-typed operand that binds `Object`'s member ([§8.1](#sec-definition)), no constraint of `T` supplying one, type-checks once against that surface, and so do `=` and `<>` over `T`-typed operands, which are [§8.4](#sec-=-and)'s `Equals` ([§25.2](#sec-operator-overloading-restrictions)). The body's check fixes each such use as one of three **kinds**: `Equals` with a `T`-typed argument, `=` and `<>` included; `Equals` with an argument of any other type; and `GetHashCode`. At each instantiation the use's kind, not the body, is read against the substituted type S, nullability stripped ([§3.6](#sec-derived-type-properties) rule 2; [§35.11](#sec-choice-generics) lists equality among the admissibility rules enforced there), and reaches S's own member for that kind. At a record, an enum or a choice S, the first kind reaches a record's declared `Equals(T)` where it declares one, and otherwise its declared `Equals(Object?)` or its generated members, and an enum's or a choice's declared `Equals` or its generated one; the second kind reaches S's declared or generated `Equals(Object?)`, and where S has none but has a member for the first kind, an argument that is a boxed S compares by that member on the box's payload, and any other argument, `null` included, compares unequal; and `GetHashCode` reaches S's declared or generated `GetHashCode`. At every other S, each kind reaches the member the same use on an S-typed operand binds, an inherited `Object` member included; at an S that is a type parameter in scope no constraint of which supplies a member for the use's kind (`Bag<T>` named in an unconstrained `Outer<T>`'s declaration), that use is a use through S, read in turn at S's substitutions ([§3.6](#sec-derived-type-properties) rule 2). Where S has no member for the use's kind (for the first kind and `GetHashCode`, exactly where the same use on an S-typed operand draws the use-site error above, [§35.7](#sec-choice-equality)'s or [§15.1.2](#sec-inline-array-members)'s; for the second, where S has neither `Equals(Object?)` nor a first-kind member), the instantiation is rejected at its site, the diagnostic naming the use, the type argument, the missing member and the `hashable` remedy. The boxed path's identity default is not reached through a type parameter: box identity is a property of boxes, a `T`-typed operand of a value substitution is a value, and identity would make `x.Equals(x)` turn on how an implementation realizes generics, which [§11.8](#sec-static-interface-members) leaves open. No structural comparison or hash is synthesized for this path either. Every **hashable** S ([§3.6](#sec-derived-type-properties)) has a member for all three kinds, so a `where T: hashable` constraint ([§14.2](#sec-derived-property-constraints)) states the requirement in the signature, and the constraint failure at the instantiation site replaces the interior diagnostic.

A body-only record with zero auto-properties (and no other storage) is auto-hashable by the membership rule above. The generated `=` returns `true` for every pair of values; the generated `GetHashCode` returns a fixed implementation-defined constant; the generated `ToString` produces `"TypeName()"` — the type name followed by empty parens, the natural specialization of the property-listing format for zero properties. Such a record represents a singleton-by-value: every instance is equal to every other. The `with` expression on such a record is a compile error (no fields to replace), and `default(T)` produces the (single) value.

`with` ([§9.5](#sec-non-destructive-update-with)) and `default` ([§17.11](#sec-the-default-operator)) are independent of equality; they apply to any record that satisfies their own rules.

<a id="sec-equality-skip"></a>
#### The `equality skip` clause

A storage component may carry the clause **`equality skip`** (`EqualityClause ::= "equality" "skip"`, Appendix [A.3](#sec-type-declarations)/[A.4](#sec-members); `equality` is a contextual keyword, Appendix [B.2](#sec-contextual-keywords) — exactly `serialized`'s row). The clause attaches to a positional field, an auto-property, an **explicit field declaration**, or a choice payload field ([§35.7](#sec-choice-equality)), mirroring `serialized skip`'s ([§9.8](#sec-serialization-synthesis)) grammar, placement, and discipline; only the `skip` form exists — rename and `optional` have no equality analogue, so the vocabulary is one word, closed.

A storage component marked `equality skip` is **removed from the auto-equality membership computation**: it does not participate in the generated `=`/`<>`, `Equals(T)`/`Equals(Object?)`, or `GetHashCode`, and it is exempt from the admissible-component-type requirement — a member whose type is inadmissible, including an explicit field declaration, does not disqualify the record when marked `equality skip`. Every other role of the member is untouched: an equality-skipped component is still storage, still a `with` target ([§9.5](#sec-non-destructive-update-with) — the copy carries its value; a copied cache is at worst stale, the cache author's existing contract), still rendered by the generated `ToString` (one clause, one effect — renderings are not contracts), and still a serialized component when the type opts into [§9.8](#sec-serialization-synthesis). The membership computation is one computation with per-package clauses; wherever it is reused — [§9.8](#sec-serialization-synthesis)'s body-record eligibility, [§35.7](#sec-choice-equality)'s choice equality (which adds a value-like gate of its own), [§3.6](#sec-derived-type-properties)'s auto-hashable property — the table below is the normative statement of what each package's readings see, and the other sites cite it:

| **The two-package skip model** | Equality package (`equality skip`, this section) | Serialization package (`serialized skip`, [§9.8](#sec-serialization-synthesis)) |
|---|---|---|
| **Participation** — the component set the package's generated members compute over | Own clause only: a skipped component leaves `=`/`<>`/`Equals`/`GetHashCode`; every other role, the wire form included, is untouched | Own clause only: a skipped component leaves the wire; what `=` compares is unchanged |
| **Eligibility gate** — the skips read when deciding whether the package runs on the type at all | `equality skip` **only** — gate and participation are the same set within the package, so a `serialized skip` never rescues an equality-inadmissible component | **Both** packages' skips — a component skipped by either clause is structurally absent from [§9.8](#sec-serialization-synthesis)'s eligibility gate |

Participation never crosses packages; the eligibility gate is the one shared reading, and it runs in one direction only ([§9.8](#sec-serialization-synthesis)'s). One reach of the clause is worth naming where it meets [§3.6](#sec-derived-type-properties): the borrow-bearing property ([§9.7](#sec-records-and-disposal)) is untouched by the skip, so an equality-skipped class-typed field leaves a borrow-bearing **record** auto-hashable — and hashable ([§3.6](#sec-derived-type-properties)'s hashable row), a reach previously available only through [§25.2](#sec-operator-overloading-restrictions)'s five-member user-equality route — while a borrow-bearing **choice** stays non-hashable whatever its skips ([§35.7](#sec-choice-equality)'s value-like gate has no record analogue).

```bezel
record Interval
  public readonly property Lo: int;
  public readonly property Hi: int;
  private equality skip _cachedLen: int;    // excluded from =, Equals, GetHashCode —
                                            //   and the package survives the field
  public constructor(lo: int, hi: int)
    Lo := lo;
    Hi := hi;
    _cachedLen := hi - lo;
  end constructor;
end Interval;
// new Interval(1, 5) = new Interval(1, 5) is true whatever the cache states.
```

The worked consequences:

- **The rescue reaches the disqualifier list's first bullet only.** The *second* and *third* disqualifiers — an `override` of `Equals`/`GetHashCode`, and a homogeneous `=`/`<>` overload — are untouched and unrescuable: the author who takes over equality has taken over all of it; `equality skip` composes with the *generated* members only. A record with both an equality-skipped member and an `Equals` override is not auto-hashable (the override governs) — and the skip clause on it is **not** an error: it is meaningful to a reader and future-proof against the override's removal. (Contrast [§9.8](#sec-serialization-synthesis)'s inert-annotation error, which fires when the *type* is outside synthesis entirely; here the type is a record and the package is merely suppressed.)
- **Hashing coherence cannot break ([§8.3](#sec-equals-and-gethashcode)).** The generated `=` and the generated `GetHashCode` are computed over the *same* reduced member set: if `a = b`, every participating member compares equal, and the hash combines exactly those members' hashes in declaration order ([§8.3](#sec-equals-and-gethashcode)'s order-sensitive combiner, unchanged) — so `a.GetHashCode() = b.GetHashCode()` holds by construction. No configuration exists in which a member is hashed but not compared, or compared but not hashed.
- **All members skipped.** A record whose every storage component is equality-skipped has an empty participating set and takes the zero-auto-property **equality and hashing** semantics above (`with` and `ToString` are unaffected — the storage is present): every pair of values equal, a fixed implementation-defined hash, `ToString` rendering the auto-properties, skipped or not. Defined, no diagnostic — the zero-property record draws none, and an all-skipped record is the same value semantically.
- **The recursive admissibility rule is unchanged in shape.** "Another record that is itself auto-hashable" evaluates the inner record *with its own skips applied* — the same reuse discipline, not a new rule: the property is [§3.6](#sec-derived-type-properties)-derived, computed per type from its declaration, and the outer record consumes the inner's verdict. An inner record rescued by `equality skip` is admissible as a component exactly as any auto-hashable record is.
- **What the skip is not.** Not custom equality logic — skip only *excludes*; a record needing projection equality still declares the operators under [§25.2](#sec-operator-overloading-restrictions)'s co-declaration rule, the sanctioned route for logic. Not a mutability license — [§9.4](#sec-mutability)'s advice stands; a skipped *mutable* member is the expected use (a cache mutated behind `readonly` structure), but skipping does not make mutating *participating* members any safer. Not available to classes — classes have no auto-equality ([§8.3](#sec-equals-and-gethashcode): reference equality); nothing to skip.

The clause is admitted on storage components only. On a computed (expression-bodied) property, a method, a static member, an enum constant, or a choice *case* (the case is the discriminant — skipping it is incoherent), `equality skip` is a **compile error**, mirroring [§9.8](#sec-serialization-synthesis)'s inert-annotation rule: such members never participate in equality, and silently ignoring the clause would be the inert-looking-but-load-bearing annotation rationale [§18](Bezel_Design_Rationale.md#sec-things-deferred) warns against. Adding or removing `equality skip` on a public type's member is a **breaking change** ([§3.6](#sec-derived-type-properties) rule 3): it flips comparison results and hash values for clients, and can flip the auto-hashable/hashable derived properties; the artifact interface ([§2.8.2](#sec-artifact-interface)) carries the clause exactly as it carries `serialized` clauses.

<a id="sec-combined-form"></a>
### 9.3 Combined form

A record may have both positional fields and a body:

```bezel
record Vector2(X: double, Y: double)
  public method Length(): double => Math.Sqrt(X * X + Y * Y);

  public static method operator +(a: Vector2, b: Vector2): Vector2 =>
    new Vector2(a.X + b.X, a.Y + b.Y);
end Vector2;
```

The auto-generated members are present and the body adds further members. Conflicts:

- The body may not declare a constructor with the same parameter list as the auto-generated primary constructor, in [§11.3](#sec-member-body)'s clash sense ([§22.6](#sec-overloading)'s overload identity): parameter names and defaults do not distinguish, so `constructor(x: int, y: int)` beside `record Point(X: int, Y: int)` is rejected. A body constructor with a **different** parameter list is **not** required to chain to the primary — [§22.10](#sec-methods-and-constructors-primary-constructors)'s convenience-constructor rule is a class rule, and its two grounds (one base call, one capture point) are vacuous for a record, which has no base ([§9.6](#sec-records-and-inheritance)) and no capture fields. Such a constructor initializes the positional storage by **assigning the auto-generated read-only properties**, which [§9.1](#sec-positional-records) makes auto-properties in [§23.1](#sec-auto-properties)'s sense, in its body, under that section's constructor-assignable context — the spelling [§9.2](#sec-body-records)'s own example uses — and owes [§7.9](#sec-definite-assignment-for-non-nullable-fields)'s obligation on each: a non-defaultable positional field must be assigned on every path, a defaultable one may be left to its default ([§7.9](#sec-default-initialization)). Chaining with `this(...)` to the primary remains available and is governed by [§12.8](#sec-constructor-chaining) unchanged. The auto-generated primary assigns the positional storage only, and [§7.9](#sec-definite-assignment-for-non-nullable-fields)'s obligation is per constructor, so a non-defaultable body field or auto-property is satisfied only by a field initializer ([§22.8](#sec-field-initializers)); a body constructor, of any parameter list, does not assign it for the primary.
- The body may not declare a property with the same name as a positional field's auto-generated property.
- The body may not declare a constructor carrying a contract clause ([§22.16](#sec-contract-clauses)) — the auto-generated primary constructor can carry none, so no record declaring positional fields is **constructor-only** ([§9.9](#sec-constructor-only-records), which states the rule and names its two remedies).

**Eligibility of the combined form.** The [§9.2](#sec-body-records) membership and disqualifier rules apply to the combined form with the positional fields counted as storage components alongside the body's auto-properties: every storage component must be of an admissible component type, and a disqualifying body member (an `Equals`/`GetHashCode` override, a homogeneous `=`/`<>` overload, or any other member outside the §9.2 list) suppresses the auto-generated equality members — the declaration itself stays legal, and any *use* of `=`/`<>` on the type, or a `.Equals`/`.GetHashCode` call naming a member the type does **not** declare itself, gets §9.2's existing per-member use-site error. The same use-site-error discipline applies to a **purely positional** record whose fields fall outside the admissible-component rule: it declares fine, but comparing it is a compile error rather than silent reference-shaped equality. A positional field may carry **`equality skip`** ([§9.2](#sec-equality-skip); grammar A.3 `PositionalField`): the field is excluded from equality but present, constructed, and rendered, and — as everywhere — a skipped field's inadmissible type does not disqualify the record.

<a id="sec-mutability"></a>
### 9.4 Mutability

Properties auto-generated from positional fields are read-only. A record declared only with positional fields is immutable.

In the body form, properties may be declared with any mutability. Mutable records are permitted but are inadvisable: value-equality and hashing rely on the value being stable.

<a id="sec-value-receivers-are-borrows"></a>
#### Value receivers are borrows

In every instance member body of a **value kind** ([#3124](https://github.com/s8lap/bezel-lang/issues/3124)) — a record method or accessor body here; choice methods ([§35.2](#sec-choice-members)), enum members ([§10.4](#sec-methods-properties-static-members)), and extension members over a value-kind receiver ([§26.7](#sec-ownership-in-extensions)) read identically; inline arrays have no member bodies: their fixed surface is compiler-provided ([§15.1.2](#sec-members-and-operations)) and admits no extension ([§26.2](#sec-what-can-be-extended)) — `this` binds a **borrow of the receiver value**. This is the reading the language's receiver and binding positions already state piecewise — [§35.2](#sec-choice-members) for choices, [§26.7](#sec-ownership-in-extensions) for extension receivers, [§19.3](#sec-patterns)'s move-only scrutinee bindings, [§28.9](#sec-runtime-managed-types)'s move-only closure captures, and [§28.3](#sec-producers)'s producers table, whose `this` row classifies the receiver as borrowed — stated here once, generally. The subsection is homed in the Records chapter because records are the one value kind whose member bodies have receiver storage to target, but it governs all four value kinds and extension receivers alike.

Consequently a store that would land in the **receiver's own storage** is a **compile error at the member body**: a borrow admits no store, and no receiver-position reading of such a store is sound. The receiver's own storage is what an lvalue chain rooted at `this` reaches without leaving the value — an explicit `this.X := e`, a bare `X := e` resolving to the receiver's storage or settable property, or an inline-array-field chain `this._arr[i] := e` (a `[N]T` field is stored inline in the record, [§15](#sec-inline-arrays)). Through a directly-held receiver such a store would mutate, invisibly at the call site, what every other receiver position treats as read-only; through a **boxed** receiver — reached by ordinary interface dispatch ([§8.6](#sec-boxing)), with no type test anywhere, or by a [§12.7](#sec-type-tests-is-is-not-as) narrowing — an aliasing write would mutate the shared box — the aliased mutation of a value that [§12.7](#sec-type-tests-is-is-not-as)'s write rule exists to exclude — and a copy-bound write would be silently discarded. The diagnostic names the record update idiom: return the updated value, built with `with` ([§9.5](#sec-non-destructive-update-with)) — or, for a **constructor-only** record ([§9.9](#sec-constructor-only-records)), where `with` is itself rejected, returned from a named method whose body constructs the result. The rule keys on **where the store would land** — never on the chain's root or the statement's form — [§12.7](#sec-type-tests-is-is-not-as)'s position families applied at the `this` root, in each spelling: a compound assignment or `++`/`--` classifies through its [§6.6](#sec-compound-assignments)/[§17.6](#sec-the-increment-and-decrement-operators) desugaring; a `this`-rooted chain reaching the receiver's own storage passed as a `ref`/`out` argument ([§22.3](#sec-parameter-modifiers)), or a `this`-rooted inline-array chain at a by-address `extern` parameter ([§32.5](#sec-ffi-compatible-types)/[§15.1.3](#sec-inline-array-ffi)), is the same store by other syntax. By the same key, a chain that hops **through a class- or interface-typed member leaves the receiver**: a record's reference-typed fields are borrows ([§9.7](#sec-records-and-disposal)), so a store beyond such a hop lands in the borrowed heap object, not in the receiver, and is **legal** — the sound **mediating** shape, and the answer to what a record accessor body can do. It is the shape of stdlib [§4.14](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-owned-buffers-and-spans)'s span records: `Span<T>`'s indexer setter stores `Buffer[Start + i] := value` into the `OwningBuffer<T>` (a class) that the `Buffer` field borrows, and `ArraySpan<T>`'s ([§4.15](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-arrayspant-readonlyarrayspant)) stores `Source[Start + i] := value` into the borrowed `Array<T>` — chains rooted at `this` whose stores mutate the viewed buffer and never the span value itself. Because the rejection is at the declaration side, every call site is safe by construction: no mutating-member classification exists or is needed, a member call on a boxed receiver is admissible exactly as any other, and the box payload's immutability ([§8.6](#sec-boxing)/[§28.9](#sec-runtime-managed-types)) holds with no member-shaped carve.

Two boundaries. **Constructor bodies are not receiver positions**: a record constructor initializes the value under construction — `Width := width;` is [§9.2](#sec-body-records)'s own canonical form, governed by [§22.8](#sec-field-initializers)'s once-only and [§7.9](#sec-definite-assignment-for-non-nullable-fields)'s definite-assignment machinery — so its stores to the record's own storage are the initialization the form exists for, not stores through a borrowed receiver. **Settable properties keep their purpose**: an external store through a named binding's lvalue chain — `r.X := 5` on a settable auto-property — remains legal, the store landing in `r`'s storage, announced by the assignment itself. What runs there is the **synthesized** auto-property setter, a receiver-writing member body invoked as an accessor ([§6.6](#sec-compound-assignments)'s accounting invokes getter and setter each exactly once; [§22.15](#sec-pure-members) classifies the auto-property setter as never pure; [§22.16](#sec-contract-clauses) instruments auto-property setters alike; [§9.5](#sec-non-destructive-update-with)'s never-invokes-setters contrast is a contrast precisely because assignment does invoke them) — and it is legal because this rule governs **author-written** bodies: the synthesized setter's store is the external assignment's own store, directed at the named binding's storage and announced at the call site. What retires is the author-written store into the receiver's own storage: a record may still declare a block-form property or indexer (a member outside [§9.2](#sec-body-records)'s list merely suppresses auto-equality, [§9.3](#sec-combined-form)) — including a setter in the mediating shape above, every store landing beyond a class- or interface-typed hop — but a *setter body* whose store lands in the receiver's own storage is rejected like any other member body. And a value kind cannot **conform to an interface that declares a settable property or indexer member** at all: the conformance is rejected at the declaration ([§9.6](#sec-records-and-inheritance)), exactly as for a missing member — a **blanket** rejection, not keyed on where the supplied accessor's stores would land (the deliberate simplification and its recorded cost: rationale [§9.13](Bezel_Design_Rationale.md#sec-value-receivers-are-borrows-rationale)). That conformance rejection — not any vacuity — is what closes the **boxed** case: receiver-writing members do exist on value kinds, the synthesized auto-property setter being one, but a box's dispatch faces are `Object` and the conformed interfaces ([§8.6](#sec-boxing)), `Object` declares no settable member ([§8.1](#sec-definition)), and no conformable interface may — so no member reachable through a box writes any receiver, and `i.X := 42` through an interface view of a boxed record has no settable member to name.

**The receiver value is fixed at the call.** A member call on a **copyable** value-kind receiver — a record, enum or primitive receiver, a copyable choice or inline-array receiver ([§15.3](#sec-move-only-value-types)), directly held, narrowed non-null ([§7.4](#sec-member-access-on-nullable-values)), or boxed ([§8.6](#sec-boxing)); a declared member or an extension member ([§26.7](#sec-ownership-in-extensions)) alike — runs over **the value its receiver expression denoted when that expression was evaluated** — for a boxed receiver, the payload of the box it denoted. For the whole activation `this` denotes that value — its own bytes, the references it holds included, though not the objects those references name: no store that runs during the call — to the storage the receiver expression named, through any alias of it, or to anything else — changes what `this` denotes, and the activation's completion stores nothing back. The receiver value is a **full-expression temporary** of the call ([K8](#sec-kernel-k8)), and the borrow `this` is bounded by it ([K8.4](#sec-kernel-k8)); a borrow-bearing receiver value carries into the call exactly the borrows the receiver expression's value carried, checked at the call site by [§9.7](#sec-records-and-disposal)'s rules as every other read of that value is. A member whose activation outlives the call — an `async` member ([§30.1](#sec-async-methods)) or an iterator member ([§29.3](#sec-iterator-methods)) — holds the fixed receiver value in its frame, as the frame holds a plain value argument ([§29.4](#sec-lazy-evaluation)), the value's borrows becoming carried sources of the frame ([K6](#sec-kernel-k6)). The rule governs what the member **reads**, and an author-written accessor that an assignment or compound assignment invokes ([§6.6](#sec-compound-assignments)) is a member call like any other. The **synthesized** auto-property setter alone runs no author-written body: it stores where the assignment itself stores — the named location — and that store is the assignment's (the boundary above).

Whether the implementation realizes the fixed value as a **copy** or passes the source storage **in place** is unobservable for a copyable value kind and is the implementation's choice, under one obligation. Storage is passed in place only to a member whose activation ends before the call returns, and only where **no code reachable during the call can write or release it**: a [stable local](#sec-stable-locals) of the calling body over the call ([§7.4](#sec-member-access-on-nullable-values)); storage inside such a local's value, reached without leaving the value (the key above); or storage inside the enclosing activation's own fixed receiver, reached the same way. Everywhere else it is copied. For a **move-only** receiver ([§15.3](#sec-move-only-value-types)) the choice is not free: see *Move-only receivers* below.

**Move-only receivers.** A move-only value ([§15.3](#sec-move-only-value-types): an owning inline array, an owning-classified choice) cannot be copied, so the fixed-value semantic above does not reach it. A call to a **bodied** member — a declared method or property of an owning choice ([§35.2](#sec-choice-members)); neither move-only kind can be extended ([§26.2](#sec-what-can-be-extended)) — on a move-only receiver passes the receiver's **storage in place, at every source**, and for the activation `this` is a borrow of that storage, **bounded by the call** as a copyable receiver's fixed value is ([K8.4](#sec-kernel-k8)), and is a borrow as a class receiver's `this` is a borrow of its object. A whole-value overwrite of the storage that runs during the call, through an alias of its holder ([§28.7](#sec-reassigning-owned-fields)), is visible through `this` afterwards, whole, tag and payload together, and every payload object the store displaces is disposed by it and flag-backstopped ([K4.1](#sec-kernel-k4)). That is the posture every borrow of a field's or slot's current value already has ([§28.3](#sec-consume-site-freeze) *Scope*). A move-only value disposed in place **with no replacement** — the nullable location holding it set to null ([§35.9](#sec-choice-nullable)), or its holder destroyed ([§28.4](#sec-the-destructor)) — is left in a **disposed state**. In checked disposal mode a read of the value in that state, through an in-place `this` or through a borrowing-match binding of it, faults as `DisposedAccessException` ([§28.2](#sec-checked-disposal)): the state stands as the value's disposed flag, readable under the deferred reclamation the flag test already relies on, and unchecked mode elides the test. What such a store must never do is leave a borrow addressing bytes it has rewritten. Two borrows could. One is a payload binding of a borrowing match over `this`. The other is a `this` that addresses payload bytes inside another value, because the receiver expression was such a binding. [§19.3](#sec-patterns)'s rule *Move-only payload bindings across a write point* rejects both: `this`'s source is the caller's, which no member body sees, so it is never provably unwritten, and a binding used as a receiver is live across the call. A member whose activation outlives the call — an `async` ([§30.1](#sec-async-methods)) or iterator ([§29.3](#sec-iterator-methods)) member — **cannot be called on a move-only receiver**: the frame could hold the value only by consuming it, which a method invocation never does ([§35.2](#sec-choice-members)), and in place its storage would outlive nothing the frame can see ([K6.4](#sec-kernel-k6)); the call is a **compile error at the call site**, at every source — for a generic choice, at the instantiation whose classification is owning ([§3.6](#sec-derived-type-properties) rule 2) — the diagnostic naming a static member that takes the payloads it needs after a match. The compiler-provided operations of an inline array ([§15.1.2](#sec-members-and-operations): `Length`, indexing, `GetType`, `ToString`, equality, `Contains`) run no author-written body and are slot reads under [§28.11](#sec-element-slot-policy)'s posture, not member calls for this rule. The decision record, with the alternatives declined, is rationale [§9.15](Bezel_Design_Rationale.md#sec-value-receivers-fixed-at-the-call-rationale).

<a id="sec-non-destructive-update-with"></a>
### 9.5 Non-destructive update: `with`

A `with` expression produces a new record value with named fields replaced:

```bezel
var p1 := new Point(1, 2);
var p2 := p1 with(Y := 99);             // Point(1, 99)
var p3 := p2 with(X := 0, Y := 0);      // Point(0, 0)
```

Syntax: `recordExpr with(Name := value, ...)`. The parentheses are part of the suffix — the assignment list reads as a named-argument list ([§22.5](#sec-optional-parameters-and-named-arguments)) — and the suffix carries no `end`. A trailing comma after the last assignment is permitted. The source expression must be **record-typed**; `with` produces a copy with the named fields replaced — the original record value is unchanged.
