A `with` expression whose source is class-typed is a **compile error naming this rule** (the retired object-initializer reading, [§22.11](#sec-object-initializer-blocks)); the diagnostic names both remedies: named/optional constructor arguments ([§22.5](#sec-optional-parameters-and-named-arguments)), which run the constructor and respect its invariants, or binding the instance to a named local and assigning its members as statements. The discriminator is the source expression's **type kind**, never the presence of `new`: `new Point(1, 2) with(Y := 9)` has a record-typed source and is an ordinary record `with` applied to the freshly-constructed value; the same spelling on a class-typed `new` expression is rejected.

The named fields must be auto-generated positional-field properties (regardless of their read-only status), auto-properties declared in the record body, or public fields. A `with` target must be **accessible at the use site under the member's own declared accessibility** ([§13](#sec-visibility)): a `private` auto-property is a valid target only inside the declaring record. Because `with` copies storage directly and never invokes setters (below), **accessor-level** visibility is irrelevant — a `private set` does not restrict `with`, by the same logic that lets read-only positional-field properties, which have no setter at all, be targets. For body-only records, `with` targets any auto-property that has backing storage; expression-bodied (computed) properties are not valid targets. All other fields keep their values from the source record. The result has the same static type as the source. The `with` operation constructs the copy directly from the source's storage; it does not invoke setters, so read-only positional-field properties are valid targets even though they have no setter.

`with` copies field values directly; it does not invoke the record's constructor. A constructor that validates cross-field invariants (e.g. `Width > 0 and Height > 0`) is not re-run during `with`. If a record enforces invariants that may be violated by independent field replacement, the record should provide a named method for constrained updates rather than relying on `with`.

A `with` expression whose source expression's static type is a **constructor-only** record ([§9.9](#sec-constructor-only-records)) is a **compile error** at the `with` expression, naming the property and the source type. Such a record's values are produced by its declared constructors; `with` invokes none, so the copy it produces would be a value of the type with no constructor behind it. The diagnostic names the remedy the paragraph above already recommends: a named method for constrained updates, whose body constructs the result. The rejection is unconditional and independent of [§13](#sec-visibility) accessibility — it reaches the declaring record's own code, where every target is accessible.

The `with` keyword has two uses across the language: record non-destructive update (this section) and cancellation in `await for ... with token` ([§30.7](#sec-asynchronous-programming-async-iterators)). The two are syntactically distinguished by grammar position and shape: record `with(...)` is a parenthesized primary suffix following the source expression; `await for`'s `with` (no parenthesized assignment list — its content is a single `CancellationToken` expression) follows the iteration source and precedes `do`. In an `await for` header, `with` followed by `(` and `Identifier :=` is the record-update suffix binding to the source expression; any other `with` opens the cancellation clause.

<a id="sec-records-and-inheritance"></a>
### 9.6 Records and inheritance

A record cannot derive from another record or from a class (other than the implicit `Object` root). A record may implement any number of interfaces that declare no **settable** property or indexer member — a conformance naming an interface with one is rejected at the declaration ([§9.4](#sec-value-receivers-are-borrows): a value kind supplies no receiver-storing accessor), the rule shared by every value kind ([§11.2](#sec-interface-declaration), [§35.8](#sec-choice-boxing)):

```bezel
record Point(X: int, Y: int): IComparable<Point>
  public method CompareTo(other: Point): int =>
    (if X <> other.X then (if X < other.X then -1 else 1)
     elif Y <> other.Y then (if Y < other.Y then -1 else 1)
     else 0);
end Point;
```

Records are implicitly sealed — and, having no virtual-dispatch surface, admit no dispatch modifier on their members ([§9.2](#sec-record-dispatch-modifiers), *Dispatch modifiers on value kinds*). A record may implement one or more interfaces (subject to the no-settable-member exclusion above); the interface names appear after a colon following the record name or positional fields.

<a id="sec-records-and-disposal"></a>
### 9.7 Records and disposal

Records cannot have destructors, `owned` fields, or implement `IDisposable`. Records also cannot have inline-array fields whose slots carry the `owned` marker (`[N owned]T?` or `[N owned]T`); such fields are move-only value types ([§15.3](#sec-move-only-value-types)), and records support only copy semantics. Reference-typed fields in records are always borrows; the record does not own what they point to. See [§28](#sec-resource-management).

A record type is a **borrow-bearing record** — a derived type property ([§3.6](#sec-derived-type-properties)) — if it holds at least one *borrow-carrying* field of a non-runtime-managed type. A field is borrow-carrying when:

- Its type is a reference type (class or interface, nullable or not, including the `T?` forms).
- Its type is a borrow-bearing inline array ([§15.1.2](#sec-inline-array-members)): one without the `owned` marker whose element type, nullability stripped, is a reference type (`[N]C`, `[N]C?` for class-or-interface C) or a borrow-bearing record or a choice that holds borrows (`[N]Pair` for a borrow-bearing record `Pair`).
- Its type is another borrow-bearing record, or a borrow-bearing choice ([§35.4](#sec-choice-classification)) (transitivity).

The predicate reads **declared field types** — here as in every bullet above: a field is classified by the type its declaration gives it, after substitution at the instantiation ([§3.6](#sec-derived-type-properties) rule 2), never by what its values hold at run time. Reference-typed fields whose **declared** types are runtime-managed (`string`, function types) do not make the record borrow-bearing because runtime-managed values have unbounded lifetime by construction; the same is true of inline-array fields whose element type is a runtime-managed reference type. A field declared `Object` or an interface type — nullable or not — is **borrow-carrying** under the first bullet: neither is a runtime-managed type, and **no declared type is a boxed value type**, which [§28.9](#sec-runtime-managed-types) defines as a category of runtime *value*, produced when a value type is used where `Object` or an interface is expected ([§8.6](#sec-boxing)). That such a field may at run time hold a box is a property of the values it admits, not of its declaration, and does not lift the classification; the contrary reading would classify a record by its contents, which [§3.6](#sec-derived-type-properties) rule 1 forbids and [§2.8.2](#sec-artifact-interface)'s computed verdicts cannot carry ([#3281](https://github.com/s8lap/bezel-lang/issues/3281)). **Choices that hold borrows** ([§35.4](#sec-choice-classification)'s holds-borrows property — every borrow-bearing choice, and any owning choice with a borrow-carrying payload beside its owned ones) are subject to this section's **borrow-lifetime rules** — the bullet list below, its null-source forms included — with "record" read as "record or choice" throughout; the first paragraph's record restrictions (no `owned` fields, no owning-inline-array fields, no ownership of what reference fields point to) are record rules and do not travel — an owning choice's `owned` and move-only payloads are exactly what it owns ([§35.1](#sec-choice-declaration), [§35.4](#sec-choice-classification) rule 1). (For records the label/property split cannot arise: a move-only value may not be a field of a record ([§15.3](#sec-move-only-value-types)), and the first paragraph bars owning-inline-array fields, so no record can contain an owning choice that holds borrows — a record that carries borrows *is* a borrow-bearing record.) Values of a borrow-bearing record are subject to the borrow lifetime rules of [§28.3](#sec-local-variables-ownership-and-borrows). In particular:

- A borrow-bearing record value may not outlive the source of any borrow it contains. For inline-array-field borrows, this applies element-wise: every slot's source must outlive the record.
- A borrow-bearing record may not be **constructed from a temporary** bound to one of its borrow-carrying fields. A construction argument that is a temporary — a collection or array literal, or a fresh call result that is not bound to a named location — has a lifetime that ends at the construction expression, so the record would immediately outlive that borrow's source (a dangling borrow). For example, `new Bag([10, 20, 30])` where `record Bag(Items: Array<int>)` borrows the array literal is rejected; bind the source to a named local (`var xs: Array<int> := [10, 20, 30]; var b := new Bag(xs);` — the annotation is required, a collection literal having no standalone type, [§15.4](#sec-collection-literals)) whose scope outlives `b`, and pass that. The same no-temporary-source rejection applies to a fresh producer passed to a class- or interface-typed `scoped` parameter ([§28.14](#sec-scoped-callback-parameters) — `new StreamReader(scoped new FileStream(...))` is rejected; bind the stream first).
- A borrow-bearing record value may not be stored in an **instance field of a class** (this specializes the umbrella rule into an explicit escape bullet, the same pattern as the closure bullet below). A class instance's lifetime is not bounded by any borrow source's scope, and a record-carried borrow — unlike a **direct** class-typed borrow field, whose every use is a member access through the reference and therefore hits the disposed-flag check ([§28.3](#sec-local-variables-ownership-and-borrows)'s field-store rule, which is unchanged) — may be consumed through access paths with **no per-access disposed-flag check** (a span's buffer window is the canonical case). The checked-mode trust regime is therefore unavailable and the store is **rejected statically**. For a record whose every access *does* pass through a tracked reference (`CancellationToken`), the rejection is for **regime uniformity** — one rule for record-carried borrows, not a per-record judgment of access paths — rather than a missing backstop. Stores of the **null-source** form are admitted, on the definition the static-field bullet below gives — every reference-typed field, and every reference-typed slot of every inline-array field, `null`, through nested record and choice components. This specification defines the form **once**, there, and refers to it everywhere else rather than restating it; a store whose record carries a non-null reference-typed field is rejected here for the same reason it is rejected as a static, whether or not that field is borrow-carrying ([#3291](https://github.com/s8lap/bezel-lang/issues/3291)). The remedy is to store the *source* — an `owned` field of the underlying class (e.g. an `owned CancellationTokenSource` rather than a `CancellationToken`) or a direct class-typed borrow field — and re-derive the record view at the use site.
- A borrow-bearing record may not be stored in a static field of any type, *except* when every reference-typed field (and every reference-typed slot of every inline-array field) of the value is `null` (the **null-source** form). The form reads value-typed components at any depth: a value is null-source only where every record or choice value among its fields and inline-array slots is null-source too, so a `[2]Pair` field qualifies only where both slots hold a null-source `Pair`. A choice value's fields are its active case's payload fields: a value of a payload-free case is null-source, a value of a case with payloads is null-source exactly where those payloads meet this definition, and the payloads of the choice's other cases take no part. The quantifier is over **reference-typed** fields, not over borrow-carrying fields alone: a field whose declared type is reference-typed but **not** borrow-carrying — a `string`, a function type ([§28.9](#sec-runtime-managed-types)'s runtime-managed set) — must be `null` too, so a null-source value holds no reference of any kind. `record Tok(Src: Object?, Name: string)` initialized `new Tok(null, "missing")` is therefore **rejected**; at `Name: string?`, `new Tok(null, null)` is admitted. The stricter quantifier is the rule, and the reason is the one [§22.12](#sec-static-members) rule 4's note (f) states in a line — *a null-source value references nothing* — which the borrow-only reading would falsify: it would let process-global storage hold a function value whose captured variables are a heap-allocated mutable cell reachable and writable from every domain ([§27.5](#sec-closures)) with **no** rule-4 warning, through a route that rule warns about at every other declaration, and it would make that waiver switchable by adding an unrelated null `Object`-typed field. A static field of borrow-bearing record type may therefore hold only a value every one of whose reference-typed components is null; the type's accessors must handle this state explicitly. ([#3291](https://github.com/s8lap/bezel-lang/issues/3291); the two phrasings became decidable at [#3281](https://github.com/s8lap/bezel-lang/issues/3281), which settled *reference-typed but not borrow-carrying* as a category.) This exception exists to allow standard library "sentinel" values like `CancellationToken.None`, whose semantics are defined by the absence of a source rather than by holding one. It is available only to a type that *declares* a nullable source: a record whose backing reference field is non-nullable has no null-source value, so neither this exception nor the instance-field bullet's identical admission is reachable for it. The buffer- and array-backed spans are that case — `Span<T>`, `ReadOnlySpan<T>`, `ArraySpan<T>`, `ReadOnlyArraySpan<T>` each declare a non-nullable `Buffer`/`Source` (stdlib [§4.14](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-owned-buffers-and-spans), [§4.15](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-arrayspant-readonlyarrayspant)) — so no span is storable in a static field or in a class instance field at all. (`ReadOnlyStringSpan` is not a borrow-bearing record and is outside this rule entirely, its only reference-typed field being a runtime-managed `string`.)
- A borrow-bearing record may be **returned** only when every borrow it carries has a source the **caller re-establishes at the call site** ([K2.4](#sec-kernel-k2)); a return carrying any other borrow is rejected at the return site. The sufficiency this bullet demands is read not off the return *type* — a value-typed return is the [announcement table](#sec-announcement-table)'s **row 7**, which announces no ownership classification at any callee kind — but off the **source** each carried borrow has in the returning body, exactly as [§28.3](#sec-borrow-lifetime-rules)'s callee-side list decides a reference return. Rejected at the return site, therefore: a borrow of a scope-bound local, of a `using var`, of an `owned` parameter, of an unbound temporary (the no-temporary-source bullet above), and — the case that separates a record return from a deferred-activation frame return ([§28.3](#sec-returning-a-deferred-activation-frame)) — of a **plain parameter** of the returning method: a frame's declared type is mint-announcing and its signature re-establishes the carried sources against each caller's own actuals ([K2.4](#sec-kernel-k2)), where a record type announces no source set at all, so a caller has nothing but the receiver to re-establish and a parameter-sourced record return would hand back a borrow no call site could bound — the asymmetry item 4 of [§28.3](#sec-borrow-lifetime-rules)'s callee-side list rejects for reference returns, in its value-carried form. This plain-parameter rejection does not reach a return that [§28.3](#sec-bare-type-parameter-returns)'s *Bare-type-parameter returns* classifies, at a substitution that is a borrow-bearing record or inline array, or a choice that holds borrows: that signature announces its source parameters (the [announcement table](#sec-announcement-table)'s row 5), the rule's callee-side clause 1 bounds what such a return carries, and its callers count it (caller-side clause 3). The rejection is per **return expression**, never at the declaration: a borrow-bearing record return *type* stays admissible at every member kind, a `static` method included — it is what the admitted forms below are returned through. Those forms are:
  1. **Receiver-sourced** — a borrow of `this`, of a bare read of one of the receiver's own fields (an `owned` field included: the lending bare read of [§28.6](#sec-leak-prevention)), or of anything reached through the receiver's fields and indexers, returned from an instance method, property getter, or indexer getter; for an extension member, the receiver parameter ([§26.7](#sec-ownership-in-extensions)). This is the **span shape**: `public method ScanLine(y: int): Span<Pixel> => new Span<Pixel>(_pixels, y * _width, _width);` over a `private owned _pixels: OwningBuffer<Pixel>` field is admitted (stdlib [§4.14](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-owned-buffers-and-spans)'s *Construction patterns*, whose `FrameBuffer` is the worked case), and at the call site the returned value carries a borrow whose **source is the receiver expression** — the source set [§28.3](#sec-consume-site-freeze)'s consume-site freeze already reads off `var s := buf.AsSpan();`, and against which every rule of this bullet list is then re-established caller-side.
  2. **Static-storage-sourced** — a record carrying a borrow of a `static` field admissible as the static-storage-sourced return of [§28.3](#sec-borrow-lifetime-rules)'s callee-side list (item 2), returned from a **static property getter** only, on that item's terms; its source is [K2](#sec-kernel-k2)'s always-live source, as in §28.3's *Static field access `T.f`* producers row.
  3. The **null-source** form (the static-field bullet above), which carries no borrow at all and is returnable from any member, a `static` method included — `public static method None(): Handle => new Handle(null);`.
- A borrow-bearing record may not be captured by a closure that escapes its source's scope.
- A borrow-bearing record value may be **copied into a collection** only when every carried borrow's source provably outlives the collection's own binding scope: a store into a collection that is a field, is reachable from one, escapes the method, or whose binding's scope strictly encloses a carried source's scope is rejected at the store site ([§28.11](#sec-element-slot-policy)'s copy slots carry this obligation). The check is the same structural scope comparison as [§28.3](#sec-local-variables-ownership-and-borrows)'s borrow rules; there is **no trust residual for record-carried borrows** (same reasoning as the instance-field bullet above). A collection of `CancellationToken`s whose source is declared before the collection remains expressible.

For typical short-lived uses — a record passed by value to a synchronous call frame, a `CancellationToken` ([§30.8](#sec-cancellation)) handed to an async call that completes before the source is disposed — these rules are automatic and require no annotation. (Asynchronous state-machine frames are the non-automatic case: borrow-bearing records are forbidden as `async` parameters and results, and constrained as locals across `await` — [§30.1](#sec-async-methods) — with `CancellationToken` as the single stdlib-certified exception, [§30.8](#sec-cancellation).)

As noted above, a record whose only reference-typed fields are of **declared** runtime-managed types (`string`, function types) is **not** a borrow-bearing record; runtime-managed values have unbounded lifetime by construction, so no borrow-lifetime rules apply. A component whose declared type is a function type admits only a capture-free function value, at construction and in `with` ([§28.3](#sec-borrow-lifetime-rules)'s *record components of function type*). A field declared `Object` or an interface type is not such a field — it is borrow-carrying, and a record holding one *is* borrow-bearing (the declared-field-types paragraph above).

<a id="sec-serialization-synthesis"></a>
### 9.8 Serialization synthesis

A record or enum that declares conformance to `ISerializable` and/or `IDeserializable` (standard library [§2.14](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-serialization-vocabulary)) and satisfies the **synthesis-eligibility rule** below has the corresponding member bodies generated by the compiler. This is the same kind of opt-in-by-conformance, structural compile-time generation as auto-equality ([§9.2](#sec-body-records)); the eligibility rule, the recursive component check, and the compile-error discipline deliberately mirror it. Declaring the conformance is the opt-in; the synthesis is automatic when eligible and a compile error at the conformance declaration when not.

<a id="sec-synthesis-eligibility"></a>
#### Synthesis-eligibility

A type is **serialization-eligible** — a derived type property ([§3.6](#sec-derived-type-properties)) — when it is a record or an enum and every serialized component is itself serializable:

- **Enums** are always serialization-eligible. The synthesized form writes the member's serialized name as a string (via `WriteString`) — its `serialized "<name>"` rename where one is declared, its identifier otherwise ([field-name customization](#sec-field-name-customization)) — and reads it back by matching against the declared members' serialized names; that table is the encoded form only — [§10.4](#sec-methods-properties-static-members)'s `E.NameOf`/`E.FromNameOrNull`, [§17.9](#sec-the-nameof-operator)'s `nameof` and stdlib [§2.13](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-the-type-class)'s `EnumNames` read the declared identifiers, so a rename changes the encoded form and nothing else; an encoded name matching no declared member raises `SerializationException` on read (on write no failing case exists — every enum value is a declared value, [§5.4](#sec-enum-casts)). When several constants share one underlying value ([§10.2](#sec-explicit-values)), the synthesized form writes the **first-declared** constant's name for that value and accepts every declared name on read (all denote the same value, so the round trip is stable). Writing the name rather than the underlying integer makes the encoded form stable against reordering or renumbering of members and self-describing in text formats; programs that need the integer form serialize `int(e)` (or the underlying-typed cast) explicitly through a hand-written `Serialize`.
- **Positional records** ([§9.1](#sec-positional-records)) are serialization-eligible when every positional field's type is **admissible as a serialized component** and **record-admissible** (the record clause below — heap collections and other class-typed components are class components only). The synthesized form is an object whose field names are the positional-field names in declaration order.
- **Body records** ([§9.2](#sec-body-records)) are serialization-eligible under exactly the auto-equality membership conditions of [§9.2](#sec-body-records) — the §9.2 member list and admissible-component rule are the single normative statement, applied here unchanged, evaluated with **both packages' skips applied** ([§9.2](#sec-equality-skip)'s skip-model table — this eligibility gate reads both clauses, so a member marked `serialized skip` *or* `equality skip` is structurally absent from the membership conditions for this check), **with the equality package's operator clause read out in both of its statements**: [§9.2](#sec-body-records)'s homogeneous-`=`/`<>` disqualifier *and* the matching exclusion in [§9.2](#sec-body-records)'s membership list belong to the *equality* package and are **not** read here — for this check a homogeneous `=`/`<>` overload is an admitted member exactly as any other operator overload is — an overloaded `=` states how two values compare and says nothing about which components serialize, so a record that overloads `=` stays serialization-eligible on the strength of its components alone. The `override Equals`/`GetHashCode` disqualifier is read out for the same reason and always was, being the same author-takes-over-equality fact stated at the member — *and* additionally every auto-property's type is admissible as a serialized component. The serialized components are the auto-properties in declaration order; computed (expression-bodied) properties are not serialized, exactly as they do not participate in equality or `ToString`. With the record clause below, positional and body records agree: a heap-collection component makes either form ineligible, with the same remedy.
- A component type is **admissible as a serialized component** when it is: a primitive (`bool`, the integer types, `float`, `double`, `decimal`, `char`); `string`; an enum; another serialization-eligible record that itself declares `ISerializable`/`IDeserializable`; a value-like serialization-eligible choice that itself declares `ISerializable`/`IDeserializable` ([the choice subsection](#sec-choice-serialization)); a serialization-eligible **synthesized class** (a class that declares `ISerializable`/`IDeserializable` and whose serialized components are each admissible as serialized components, below); a `Shared<T>` or `Weak<T>` whose `T` is a serialization-eligible class; a nullable `T?` whose `T` is admissible as a serialized component (encoded as the value or `WriteNull`/`TryReadNull`); or a standard sequence collection (`Array<T>`, `OwningArray<T>`, `LinkedList<T>`, etc., and inline arrays `[N]T`) whose element type is admissible as a serialized component (encoded with `BeginArray`/`EndArray`). A standard dictionary (`Dictionary<K, V>`, `OwningDictionary<K, V>`) is admissible as a serialized component when both `K` and `V` are (encoded as an array of key/value pairs to admit non-string keys uniformly). Of these, the class-typed rows — synthesized classes, `Shared<T>`/`Weak<T>`, and the heap collections (sequence and dictionary alike, which are class types, [§3.1](#sec-type-kinds)) — are admissible in **class** components only; for records see the record clause below. The conformance requirement on the record, choice, and class rows is what makes the component encodable: the synthesized members reach a nested value's own `Serialize`/`Deserialize` ([synthesized `Serialize`](#sec-synthesized-serialize), [synthesized `Deserialize`](#sec-synthesized-deserialize)), which the conformance is the sole source of, so a record or choice that is shaped eligibly and declares neither interface is not an admissible component and naming one is the conformance-declaration error below. Enums need no conformance of their own: they are always eligible and are encoded as a name string rather than by calling a member.

A type that declares `: ISerializable` or `: IDeserializable` but is **not** serialization-eligible is a **compile error at the conformance declaration**, naming the first offending member and the reason (mirroring the auto-equality non-membership error of [§9.2](#sec-body-records), but reported at the declaration rather than the use site, because the conformance declaration is the explicit opt-in and the obstruction should be reported where the promise is made). The error names the remedy: remove the conformance, make the offending component serializable, or hand-write `Serialize`/`Deserialize` (which suppresses synthesis — see below), the last not for a direction a base class synthesizes (*Inherited components* below).

<a id="sec-tree-shaped-class-synthesis"></a>
##### Class serialization synthesis

A class opts into serialization synthesis by declaring `: ISerializable` and/or `: IDeserializable`; it needs no header shape clause, because the **serialized shape is read from the field types** — exactly as the owning-tree/back-edge partition has always been read from the `owned`/borrow annotations the language already requires. A field's type states its serialized role: an `owned` (or value-typed) field is an **owning edge**, written inline; a `Shared<T>` field is an **identity participant**, written once and referenced by identity at each alias; a `Weak<T>` field, and a plain borrowing field, are **back-references**. The graph a class serializes is a tree, a directed acyclic graph, or a cyclic graph as a consequence of those types — a class with no back-references serializes as a tree; one with borrowing or `Shared<T>` fields may alias; one with `Weak<T>` fields (or a `Shared<T>` that reaches an ancestor, the documented Shared-cycle leak, [§28.13](#sec-shared-ownership)) may cycle — and the deserializer reconstructs whichever shape the field types and the wire identity tags describe, with no header assertion to declare or to police. (`sealed` is irrelevant to serialization: a sealed class follows the same eligibility rules and wire form as any other class.)

A class is serialization-eligible when every serialized component's type is admissible as a serialized component (recursively admitting other conforming classes, `Shared<T>`/`Weak<T>` of an eligible class `T`, and owned collections of eligible elements).

A **record** cannot hold a class-typed component in its serialized set at all: a record's reference-typed fields are always borrows, and a borrow has no position in an owning spanning tree — there is no owner for an inline write to reconstruct against, and the synthesized `Deserialize` could not construct the record without binding a freshly-produced component to a borrowing field, which [§9.7](#sec-records-and-disposal)'s no-temporary-source rule rejects. The same holds for `Shared<T>`, `Weak<T>`, interface-typed, **and standard heap-collection** components (the heap collections are class types, [§3.1](#sec-type-kinds), and the Deserialize argument above applies to them verbatim — a freshly-reconstructed `Array<T>` bound to a borrowing record field is exactly the shape §9.7 rejects, and no named-local workaround survives the record's return from `Deserialize`; the collection would have no owner). A record's serialized components must therefore be **record-admissible**: a primitive, `string`, an enum, another serialization-eligible record, **a value-like serialization-eligible choice ([the choice subsection below](#sec-choice-serialization) — matching [§9.2](#sec-body-records)'s admission of value-like choices as equality components)**, `T?` of a record-admissible `T`, or a non-owning inline array `[N]T`/`[N]T?` of record-admissible element type — value-shaped storage throughout. A record with a class-, interface-, `Shared<T>`-, `Weak<T>`-, or heap-collection-typed serialized component is not serialization-eligible — a compile error at the conformance declaration, naming the field. The remedy is an owning **class** envelope (a sealed class with an `owned` field serializes the same shape, above); `serialized skip` on the offending component where its type admits one (skip reconstructs with `default(T)`, a compile error for a non-nullable reference type, [§17.11](#sec-the-default-operator) — a non-nullable collection component must become nullable first, or use the envelope); or a hand-written `Serialize`/`Deserialize`. (A write-only admission — `ISerializable` without `IDeserializable` over collection components, which the read direction's argument does not reach — was considered and declined for uniformity: eligibility would become direction-dependent for exactly one component kind; recorded liftable.)

The serialized components of a class are its `owned` and value-typed fields and auto-properties, its `Shared<T>` and `Weak<T>` fields, and its plain **borrowing** reference fields, in declaration order. The `owned`/value edges form the **owning spanning tree**; a `Shared<T>` field is an **identity participant** (an owned share of a value reachable elsewhere by another handle); `Weak<T>` fields and plain borrowing fields are **back-edges** into the graph. This partition is read directly from the field types the language already requires — it is not inferred and not guessed.

**Inherited components.** A derived class's serialized components include those it inherits: the components of its base-class chain come first, from the root of the chain down, each class's in its own declaration order, under its own [field-name customization](#sec-field-name-customization) and at the type the derived class's base clause instantiates it to, followed by the class's own. The serialized-name uniqueness rule runs over the whole set, so an inherited `private` field or primary-constructor capture ([§22.10](#sec-methods-and-constructors-primary-constructors)) and an own component sharing a serialized name — a pair [§12.2](#sec-hiding-is-not-allowed) admits — are a compile error at the conformance declaration naming both. Each class in the chain that declares a serialized component of its own must itself declare `ISerializable` or `IDeserializable` and hand-write neither `Serialize` nor `Deserialize`; a base that does not is a compile error at the derived class's conformance declaration, naming the base. A base that declares no component of its own, such as the abstract `Shape` of the [`polymorphic` registry](#sec-polymorphic-dispatch-synthesis) example, contributes nothing and needs no conformance. The derived class's synthesized `Serialize` and `Deserialize` belong to its own conformance and are not hiding declarations under [§12.2](#sec-hiding-is-not-allowed), as a registered derived type's are not. A `Serialize` or `Deserialize` the derived class hand-writes where a base's member of that name is synthesized is a hiding declaration under §12.2, as any other member of a base member's name is, so for a direction a base synthesizes the derived class's own member is its synthesized one. The synthesized `Deserialize` constructs the derived instance, base subobject included, by the ordinary constructor call below, whose base-constructor call ([§12.8](#sec-constructor-chaining), [§22.10](#sec-methods-and-constructors-primary-constructors)) constructs the base as at any `new`. *Constructor selection* (below) treats inherited components exactly as own ones: the selected constructor's parameters bind the inherited owning-tree and plain borrowing components by name, and inherited `Shared<T>` and `Weak<T>?` components are bound after construction. So `class Derived(v: int, extra: int): Base(v)` capturing `extra`, over a `class Base(v: int)` capturing `v`, both declaring the two interfaces, round-trips `v` and `extra`, while `class Derived(): Base(999)` has no constructor binding `v` and is *Constructor selection*'s compile error. Name lookup selects between a base's synthesized members and a derived class's by the receiver's static type, as between the distinct members of [§12.2](#sec-hiding-is-not-allowed), a receiver of type-parameter type selecting as one of its type argument: `b.Serialize(s)` on a `Base`-typed `b` runs `Base`'s `Serialize` whatever `b`'s run-time type, and the class *Synthesized `Serialize`* paragraph below states what it writes for a derived instance; a call through an `ISerializable`-typed receiver runs the member the run-time class conforms through ([§14.2](#sec-interface-conformance) clause 1), which is its own where its inheritance clause lists the interface. A class is a synthesized class, and admissible as a component under that row of the eligibility rule, only for a serialization interface its own inheritance clause lists. A class that conforms to `ISerializable` only through a base whose `Serialize` is synthesized inherits that member, which raises `SerializationException` for an instance of the class — by the run-time type check of the class *Synthesized `Serialize`* paragraph below, or by the base's registry, whose registered types each declare the interface themselves — so a component the class declares is never silently left out of a form; the class serializes in its own form by declaring `ISerializable` itself.

**Synthesized `Serialize`.** The serializer assigns an identity tag the first time it reaches an object through an owning edge, and writes the object's components there. A `Shared<T>` field participates by identity: the tag is keyed on the **underlying value** the handle's `Get()` borrows (object-reference identity, [§8](#sec-the-object-class)) — so two independently `Clone()`d handles to one value collapse to one tag — written once at first occurrence and as a `$ref` at every later occurrence. A `Weak<T>` field and a plain borrowing field are never written inline; each is written as a `$ref` to the tag of the object it references (for a plain borrow the target is necessarily present in the owning tree, because a borrow's lifetime is bounded by an owner that outlives it; for a `Weak<T>` the target must be strongly reached elsewhere in the graph, enforced at read, below). No header assertion is made about aliasing or cycles: the field types fix which components alias and which are back-references, and the identity-tag mechanism records the actual sharing in the data. The synthesized `Serialize` of a class `C` with no `polymorphic` registry of its own writes `C`'s form, and raises `SerializationException` when the receiver's run-time type is a class derived from `C`, because that form omits the derived class's own components and reads back as a `C`. This is the registry's closed-set rule with `C` as the set's one member. It holds however the member is reached: as a component's `Serialize`, through a `C`-typed receiver, or as the member a derived class inherits. A `Weak<T>` or plain borrowing back-edge does not reach it, being written as a `$ref`, and a derived class's own synthesized `Serialize` writes its inherited components itself (*Inherited components* above) without reaching it. A class with a registry writes the run-time type through the registry ([polymorphic dispatch](#sec-polymorphic-dispatch-synthesis)).

**Synthesized `Deserialize`.** The synthesized factory reconstructs the owning spanning tree first, in **owner-before-borrower order**: each owned object is constructed by an ordinary call to its constructor. A `Shared<T>` component is reconstructed at its first (tagged) occurrence and registered in the tag→object table; each later `$ref` to that tag is bound by `Clone()`ing the registered handle (identity preserved, the shared count incremented). A plain borrowing field is supplied **as a constructor argument** resolved against the tag→object table — a directed acyclic graph admits an owner-before-borrower order, so the target precedes the borrower and [§7.9](#sec-definite-assignment-for-non-nullable-fields) is satisfied **unmodified**, with no observable intermediate state. A `Weak<T>` `$ref` is bound by `Downgrade()` from the reconstructed `Shared<T>` its tag resolves to; because a cycle-closing `Weak<T>` field is **nullable** (its target may be released), it is assigned after construction as ordinary mutation, so a cycle needs no two-phase window and [§7.9](#sec-definite-assignment-for-non-nullable-fields) is again satisfied — the null initializer discharges it, the later wiring is ordinary assignment. The class return shape is [§2.14](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-serialization-vocabulary)'s: `owned C` for a class that *holds* shared/weak components, and `owned Shared<C>` when the class *is* a shared node (the co-owned entry); the choice is locally decidable from the entry type.

**Constructor selection.** When the class declares more than one constructor, the synthesized `Deserialize` uses the *unique* constructor whose parameter list binds exactly the owning-tree components and plain borrowing fields, matched by name (order-insensitive and compared case-insensitively, so the conventional camelCase constructor parameter matches its PascalCase component; `serialized "<name>"` renames do not affect the parameter-name match, which uses the declared identifiers). `Shared<T>` aliases and nullable `Weak<T>?` back-edges are bound after construction (identity-table `Clone()`/`Downgrade()`), so they are not part of the constructor parameter match. If no constructor matches, or more than one does, the conformance declaration is a compile error naming the candidate constructors — the same compile-error discipline as the eligibility rule, reported where the opt-in is declared.

The synthesized deserializer preserves identity and enforces the one property the field types cannot decide:

- **Identity is preserved, never duplicated.** A `$ref` whose target has already been reconstructed binds to that object: a `Shared<T>` alias `Clone()`s the registered handle, a `Weak<T>` reference `Downgrade()`s it, and a plain borrow takes the resolved reference. The reference-unaware-serializer failure mode — distinct objects where the input shared one — cannot occur.
- **Weak-reachability is checked at read.** A `Weak<T>` `$ref` whose target is never strongly reached anywhere in the graph (no `Shared<T>` occurrence ever registered that tag) raises `SerializationException` — strong-reachability is a per-value property the field types cannot decide. A cheap static lint additionally flags, at the conformance declaration, a `Weak<T>` field in a class that serializes no `Shared<T>` of a matching `T`; the lint is a necessary-not-sufficient early check, not a replacement for the dynamic guarantee.

The serialized shape is **type-scoped** — read from the type's own field types, intrinsic to the type and identical for every caller, format, and call site — in contrast to the deserializer's *operation*-scoped unknown-field policy (stdlib [§2.15](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-concrete-serialization-formats)), a property of a particular read; the placement criterion is rationale [§5.22](Bezel_Design_Rationale.md#sec-type-driven-serialization).

A component holding an instance of a class derived from its static type — **polymorphic dispatch** — is covered by the explicit `polymorphic` registry below. Without a registry the component is written in its static type's form, and the run-time type check of the class *Synthesized `Serialize`* paragraph above raises `SerializationException` for a derived instance. Whether a class has derived classes is not a static fact: any class not `sealed` may be derived from, in its own module or in a downstream one ([§2.8](#sec-module-identity)), so no component is rejected for its static type having, or being able to have, derived classes. An `abstract` or `closed` class ([§11.7](#sec-static-classes)) with no registry of its own has no instance of its own type to write and no concrete type for `Deserialize` to construct ([§12.5](#sec-abstract-classes-and-members)). Where such a class's `Serialize` is synthesized, a serialized component whose type is that class, directly or as the underlying type of `T?`, the argument of `Shared<T>`, or a collection's element, key or value type, is a compile error at the conformance declaration; a `Weak<T>` or plain borrowing back-edge of that type is admitted, being written as a `$ref` that never calls the member. The class's own `IDeserializable` conformance with no hand-written `Deserialize` is likewise a compile error there. The remedy for either is a registry or a hand-written member.

A serialized **cycle** closes through a `Weak<T>` back-edge on a `Shared<T>` spine, both ordinary owned handles, so the cyclic graph is constructed in ownership-valid Bezel and round-trips through the ownership checker. The wire form is the identity/`$ref` mechanism the owning-tree synthesis already establishes: the `Shared<T>` value carries an identity tag at its first occurrence, and the `Weak<T>` back-edge is written as a `$ref` to that tag. There is no two-phase construction and no self-contained-constructor restriction: a cycle-closing `Weak<T>?` field is nullable, so on deserialization it is bound after the spine is reconstructed by `Downgrade()`ing the `Shared<T>` its tag resolves to — ordinary post-construction mutation, with definite assignment ([§7.9](#sec-definite-assignment-for-non-nullable-fields)) discharged by the null initializer (rationale [§5.22](Bezel_Design_Rationale.md#sec-type-driven-serialization)).

<a id="sec-polymorphic-dispatch-synthesis"></a>
##### Polymorphic dispatch

A base class whose serialized components may, at run time, hold instances of registered derived classes declares a `polymorphic` registry as a member of its body:

```text
public abstract class Shape: ISerializable, IDeserializable
  polymorphic ("circle": Circle, "square": Square);
  // ... other members ...
end Shape;
```

The registry is a closed, explicitly written map from a **wire discriminator string** to a **permitted concrete derived type**. There is no reflective discovery of subtypes: the only types the synthesized deserializer will ever construct for this hierarchy are those the registry names. This is the [§5.18](Bezel_Design_Rationale.md#sec-type-identity-not-reflection) explicit-registration-never-reflection principle applied directly — it is the reason a serialized type discriminator cannot be turned into an arbitrary-type construction primitive (the defect that made reflective `$type` binders a remote-code-execution vector elsewhere).

Each registry entry's discriminator must be a non-empty string literal, unique within the registry. Each named type must be assignable to the declaring class and must itself be type-driven serialization-eligible (declare `: ISerializable`/`: IDeserializable` with serialization-eligible components); a registered type that is not is a compile error at the registry. The registry is a member of a class that declares `: ISerializable`/`: IDeserializable` and has no dependence on any header clause — the registry governs which concrete type is chosen, and that type's own field types govern how its edges reconstruct. The declaring base class may be concrete (it registers a discriminator for itself like any other case) or abstract (it registers none for itself; an input discriminator naming the base is then a `SerializationException`).

**Synthesized `Serialize`.** When writing a component whose static type is a polymorphic base, the synthesized serializer writes the discriminator of the value's concrete run-time type as a distinguished leading field (the discriminator field name is `$type`, reserved within an object written for a polymorphic base; it precedes all component fields), followed by that concrete type's own synthesized form. A run-time type not present in the registry is a `SerializationException` at serialization — the closed set is enforced on both directions, never silently widened.

**Interaction with the identity/`$ref` mechanism.** When a polymorphic object is also a shared or cyclic reference target (the graph aliases or cycles through it), the discriminator and the identity tag coexist by a single rule: the object's **first** occurrence carries its identity tag and, because it is polymorphic, its `$type` discriminator, then its body; every **subsequent** occurrence is a pure `$ref` to that identity tag and carries **no** `$type` and no body. The concrete type is fixed at the first occurrence; a back-reference neither repeats nor may contradict it. On read, a `$ref` is resolved against the identity table (a `Shared<T>` alias by `Clone()`, a `Weak<T>` back-edge by `Downgrade()`) with no further dispatch — dispatch happened once, at the referent's first occurrence. This makes the wire form unambiguous for independent implementations regardless of how polymorphism, aliasing, and cycles combine.

**Synthesized `Deserialize`.** The discriminator is read **first**, before any component of the object, and consumed by dispatch — it is not bound as an ordinary component and is never subject to field-name customization, `serialized optional`, or the unknown-field policy (it is structural, not a data field). The deserializer looks the discriminator up in the registry, selects the concrete type's synthesized `Deserialize`, and delegates the remainder of the object to it (returning `owned Base`, the derived instance transferred as the base type, [§28.8](#sec-ownership-transfer)). A discriminator string absent from the registry raises `SerializationException` — the closed-set assertion enforced dynamically, the same assert-and-enforce discipline as graph shape. Because the discriminator is consumed before component binding, it has no interaction with back-edge binding (whether the constructor-argument binding of a plain borrow or the `Clone()`/`Downgrade()` identity resolution of a `Shared<T>`/`Weak<T>` component): dispatch selects *which* concrete type's reconstruction path runs; that path is then exactly the type-driven reconstruction already specified for that concrete type.

The `polymorphic` registry is **type-scoped** for the same reason the serialized shape is: the permitted-subtype set is an intrinsic property of the base type's serialization contract — the hierarchy serializes against the same registry for every caller, format, and call site — the placement criterion of rationale [§5.22](Bezel_Design_Rationale.md#sec-type-driven-serialization). Polymorphic dispatch **composes uniformly with the type-driven model**: a registered type is reconstructed under whatever shape its own field types describe, including a cyclic shape closed by a `Weak<T>` back-edge. Dispatch selecting a concrete type does not interact with that type's identity or back-edge binding — the discriminator is consumed before any component or back-edge binding, so polymorphism is fully orthogonal to aliasing and cycles.

Classes that declare neither `ISerializable` nor `IDeserializable` remain outside synthesis entirely and participate only by hand-writing `Serialize` and a recognized static `Deserialize` ([§2.14](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-serialization-vocabulary) of the standard library), exactly as before. Declaring the conformance is the only route into synthesis; the field types then fix the serialized shape — the owning-tree/identity/back-edge partition is read from the `owned`/`Shared<T>`/`Weak<T>`/borrow annotations, with no further assertion required.

<a id="sec-synthesized-serialize"></a>
#### Synthesized `Serialize`

For an eligible record, the synthesized `Serialize(s: ISerializer)` body is:

1. `s.BeginObject(n)` where `n` is the number of serialized components.
2. For each component in declaration order: `s.WriteFieldName("<name>")` followed by the component's encoding — `s.WriteInt`/`WriteString`/etc. for a primitive or `string`; the nested value's `Serialize(s)` for a serializable record; the enum-name string for an enum; `BeginArray`/per-element encoding/`EndArray` for a collection; `WriteNull` for a null nullable.
3. `s.EndObject()`.

For an eligible enum, the synthesized `Serialize` is `s.WriteString("<member-name>")` (no surrounding object) — no failing case exists ([§5.4](#sec-enum-casts)).

<a id="sec-synthesized-deserialize"></a>
#### Synthesized `Deserialize`

The synthesized recognized static factory has the value-type return shape of [§2.14](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-serialization-vocabulary) — `Deserialize(d: IDeserializer): T` for a record or enum `T` (plain by-value; no `owned`, records and enums being value types). Its body:

1. `d.BeginObject()`; then repeatedly `d.ReadFieldName()` and dispatch on the name, reading each recognized component with the mirror operation (`d.ReadInt`, the nested type's `Deserialize`, etc.) into a local. Wherever a synthesized `Deserialize` reads a `float` value (a component, a nullable component's value, an element, a dictionary's key or value), it reads `d.ReadFloat()` and converts the `double` as [§5.2](#sec-explicit-conversions)'s `float(x)`; a finite value whose conversion is not finite raises `SerializationException`, the component being unable to hold the number the input carries (a JSON `3.5e38` read into a `float` component raises). Wherever it reads a value of an integer type narrower than 64 bits, a dictionary's key or value included, it reads `d.ReadInt()` for `sbyte`, `short` and `int` and `d.ReadUInt()` for `byte`, `ushort` and `uint`; a value outside the type's range raises `SerializationException` for the same reason, and is never truncated to the type's width (a JSON `5000000000` read into an `int` component, or `300` into a `byte` component, raises). When a read field name matches no declared component, the synthesized code calls `d.SkipValue()` ([§2.14](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-serialization-vocabulary)) — it does not itself decide whether an unknown field is an error. Whether reaching an unknown field is permitted is the *deserializer's* configured policy: a strict deserializer (the default) raises `SerializationException` from `ReadFieldName`/`SkipValue` on an unrecognized field; a deserializer configured to tolerate unknown fields skips the value and continues. Then `d.EndObject()`.
2. Construct the result. If the record declares one or more **explicit constructors**, the synthesized `Deserialize` calls the *unique* explicit constructor — or, when no explicit constructor matches, the auto-generated primary of a record declaring positional fields ([§9.3](#sec-combined-form)) — whose parameter list binds exactly the record's components — the serialized components together with every `serialized skip` component, which binds its `default(T)` ([field-name customization](#sec-field-name-customization)) — matched by name — compared **case-insensitively**, so the conventional camelCase parameter matches its PascalCase component (`constructor(width: decimal, height: decimal)` binds `Width`/`Height`); `serialized "<name>"` renames do not affect the match, which uses declared identifiers. If explicit constructors exist but none matches and the primary does not match either, more than one explicit constructor matches, or the case-insensitive comparison leaves a parameter ambiguous between two components, the conformance declaration is a compile error naming the candidates — the same discipline as the class rule above, whose matching this rule shares. A record that declares **no** explicit constructor is constructed directly from the read components at the storage level — the same constructor-bypassing construction that `with` ([§9.5](#sec-non-destructive-update-with)) and `default(T)` ([§17.11](#sec-the-default-operator)) already perform; for a purely positional record this coincides with calling the auto-generated primary constructor in positional order. For an enum, read the name string and map it to the declared constant (under duplicate constant values, every declared name maps to its value — [§10.2](#sec-explicit-values)).

Field order in the input need not match declaration order — dispatch is by field name. A **missing** required component (one neither present nor `serialized optional`), a **duplicate** field name, a type mismatch, or a name not matching any enum constant raises `SerializationException` unconditionally — these are structural faults in the input regardless of policy. An **unknown** field (present in the input, matching no declared component) is the one case governed by *operation* policy rather than the synthesized code: it is an error by default and is skipped when the deserializer is configured to ignore unknown fields (stdlib [§2.15](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-concrete-serialization-formats)). This policy is deliberately a property of the deserialization operation, not an annotation on the type — the same type may be read strictly in one context and leniently in another, a decision that belongs to the caller with the input, not to the type's contract (rationale [§5.19](Bezel_Design_Rationale.md#sec-serialization-without-reflection)). The synthesized code is identical regardless of policy: it always skips an unrecognized field via the deserializer; strictness lives entirely in the deserializer. A contract clause evaluating `false` during the construction step — a `requires` or `ensures` clause of the selected constructor ([§22.16](#sec-contract-clauses)) — raises `SerializationException` from the synthesized code, by the same implementation-internal route as the missing-, duplicate-, and mismatched-component faults above, with the `ContractViolationException` recorded in the raised exception's `CauseChain` in [§31.4](#sec-standard-exception-types)'s snapshot form. The input is data, not a caller's broken promise: a decoded value that fails the type's own validation is a structural fault in the input, classified with the faults above. A clause that **faults** rather than evaluating `false` is not covered by this rule and propagates as itself ([§22.16](#sec-contract-clauses)). The construction is an ordinary constructor call at a static program point, so a record's field types, nullability, and definite-assignment rules are checked normally; this is the structural reason synthesis is sound where reflection was not ([§5.18](Bezel_Design_Rationale.md#sec-type-identity-not-reflection)).

<a id="sec-field-name-customization"></a>
#### Field-name customization

By default the synthesized form uses each component's declared name as its serialized field name (and each enum member's declared name as its serialized value). A `serialized` clause on a positional field, an auto-property, an enum constant, a choice case, or a choice payload field ([the choice subsection below](#sec-choice-serialization)) customizes this. The clause vocabulary is closed (no user-defined forms, no parameters interpreted by external machinery, no runtime introspection — this is a compiler-recognized declaration modifier in the sense of [§18](Bezel_Design_Rationale.md#sec-things-deferred)'s narrow-modifier escape hatch, deliberately *not* an attribute system). It expresses three independent effects — rename, exclude, tolerate — where rename and tolerate may combine and exclude is mutually exclusive with both:

- **`serialized "<name>"`** — the component is serialized and deserialized under `<name>` instead of its declared identifier. The string must be a non-empty literal and must be unique among the **serialized names** of the type's components — for a choice, among the payload fields of the **same case**, two cases' payload fields never sharing a wire object — **and, alike, unique among an enum's constants, and among a choice's cases**; a member's serialized name is its rename where one is declared and its declared identifier otherwise, so a rename equal to another member's identifier collides too. Names are compared **ordinally** — the wire's own comparison, not the case-insensitive comparison this section's constructor matching uses. A collision is a compile error at the conformance declaration, mirroring the eligibility-error discipline. The clause reaches enum constants and choice cases because its purpose does: two constants — or two cases — encoded under one name make the read direction ambiguous, and no reading of the wire can recover which was written. It is not relaxed for same-valued constants ([§10.2](#sec-explicit-values)): the write direction already uses the first-declared name for a shared value, so a second constant's duplicate rename could never be written — it would be exactly the inert-looking annotation this section's clause-on-an-unsynthesized-type rule rejects below. On an enum constant, the constant is encoded as `<name>` rather than its identifier.
- **`serialized optional`** — read/write tolerance for that component. On write, if the component is a nullable `T?` whose value is null, the field is omitted (rather than written as `WriteNull`); otherwise it is written normally. On read, a missing field yields `default(T)` instead of raising `SerializationException`; a present field is read normally. A `serialized optional` component whose type is not defaultable ([§17.11](#sec-the-default-operator)) is a compile error at the conformance declaration (a missing field would have no value to supply), exactly as for `serialized skip` below; the same holds for a choice payload field marked `serialized optional`. The remedy is the nullable form. This is the per-field, *missing*-field tolerant-mode opt-in; it is orthogonal to the *unknown*-field policy, which is a property of the deserialization operation (the deserializer's configuration, stdlib [§2.15](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-concrete-serialization-formats)) rather than of the member or the type — the two leniencies compose freely. Not admitted on enum constants.
- **`serialized "<name>" optional`** — both of the above on the same component: renamed *and* tolerant. This is the common real-world case (an externally-named field that may be absent), so the grammar admits the combination directly rather than forcing a choice.
- **`serialized skip`** — the component is excluded from both directions entirely. The synthesized `Serialize` does not write it; the synthesized `Deserialize` does not read it and supplies the component's `default(T)` ([§17.11](#sec-the-default-operator)) to the constructor. A `serialized skip` component whose type is not defaultable ([§17.11](#sec-the-default-operator)) is a compile error at the conformance declaration (the synthesized `Deserialize` would have no value to construct with). `skip` is mutually exclusive with a name or `optional` (excluding a field and renaming/tolerating it are contradictory; the grammar does not admit the combination). Not admitted on enum constants ([Appendix A](#sec-appendix-a) grammar note): an enum value is a single member, not an omittable field.

The clause attaches to the member it affects and is total: a component with no `serialized` clause is coded under its own name, always. There is no separate exhaustive key list to keep synchronized, so adding a component never silently drops it from serialization — the failure mode of an all-or-nothing customization list (rationale [§5.19](Bezel_Design_Rationale.md#sec-serialization-without-reflection)) does not arise. A `serialized` clause on a member of a type that declares no serialization conformance, or on a member of a type whose serialization is hand-written (synthesis suppressed — see below), is a compile error: the clause only has meaning as an input to synthesis, and silently ignoring it would be the kind of inert-looking-but-load-bearing annotation [§18](Bezel_Design_Rationale.md#sec-things-deferred) warns against.

`serialized skip` interacts with the eligibility rule by *removing* its component from consideration: a field that would otherwise make the type ineligible (a non-serializable component type) but is marked `serialized skip` does not disqualify the type, because it is no longer a serialized component. This is the supported way to make an otherwise-eligible record serializable when one field is of a non-serializable type and is not needed in the encoded form.

<a id="sec-choice-serialization"></a>
#### Choice serialization

A choice ([§35](#sec-choices)) opts in by declaring `: ISerializable` / `: IDeserializable`, exactly as records and enums do. A choice is **serialization-eligible** when it is value-like ([§35.4](#sec-choice-classification)) and every payload field's type is admissible as a serialized component and record-admissible (value-shaped storage throughout; the borrow-bearing and owning classifications are never eligible — the same `Deserialize`-has-no-owner argument as for class-typed record fields). An ineligible conformance declaration is the compile error above, naming the first offending payload.

**Wire shape.** The synthesized `Serialize` writes an object whose distinguished leading field is the **case discriminator** `"$case"` — the case's declared name, or its `serialized "<name>"` rename — followed by the active case's payload fields by name, in declaration order, each encoded per its component rule; a payload-free case writes the object with only the discriminator. The `$case` field name joins the `$`-reserved set of stdlib [§2.15](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-concrete-serialization-formats)'s JSON mapping; a payload rename beginning with `$` is a compile error. The synthesized `Deserialize` reads the discriminator **first**, consumed by case dispatch before any component binding — it is structural, not a data field, and is never subject to `serialized optional` or the unknown-field policy, exactly the polymorphic-registry discipline above; an undeclared discriminator string raises `SerializationException`, as does an object that does not lead with the discriminator (dispatch must select the case before component binding can begin); the selected case's payloads then read under the standard missing/duplicate/unknown rules, and the value is constructed by the case's own construction form. The `serialized` clause on a **case** admits the rename form only (a case is not omittable — the enum-constant rule); on a **payload field** the full vocabulary applies (`skip` requiring a **defaultable** ([§17.11](#sec-the-default-operator)) payload type). A choice all of whose cases are payload-free still writes the object form (uniformity; such a type should usually be an enum).

<a id="sec-suppression-and-interaction"></a>
#### Suppression and interaction

Hand-writing `Serialize` (respectively a recognized static `Deserialize`) **suppresses** synthesis of that direction, exactly as a manually declared `Equals`/`GetHashCode` suppresses auto-equality. The two directions are independent: a type may synthesize one and hand-write the other. Declaring `: ISerializable` without an eligible structure and without a hand-written `Serialize` is the compile error above; declaring it *with* a hand-written `Serialize` is always valid regardless of eligibility (the hand-written body is the contract).

Synthesis composes with auto-equality and `ToString`: a body record may be simultaneously auto-hashable and serialization-eligible; the feature sets are independent packages over the same auto-properties, each scoping the shared [§9.2](#sec-body-records) membership computation with its own clause. What each clause reads and reaches is [§9.2](#sec-equality-skip)'s **skip-model table**: participation never crosses packages, and the one shared reading is this section's eligibility gate, which reads both clauses — which is what keeps a record with an equality-skipped explicit cache field serialization-eligible with no second clause (explicit fields were never serialized components, so the one clause suffices). The `serialized` clause is a single closed grammar production ([Appendix A](#sec-appendix-a)); apart from it, `: ISerializable, IDeserializable` is ordinary interface-conformance syntax ([§11](#sec-classes-and-interfaces)) and the normative content is the eligibility rule, the generated-body semantics, and the customization semantics defined here. The wire shapes are normative so that independent implementations agree; the rationale for the specific choices (names not integers for enums, declaration order, key/value-pair dictionaries) and for the modifier-not-attribute design is in [§5.19](Bezel_Design_Rationale.md#sec-serialization-without-reflection).

<a id="sec-constructor-only-records"></a>
### 9.9 Constructor-only records

A record type is **constructor-only** — a derived type property ([§3.6](#sec-derived-type-properties)) — when it declares a constructor carrying a contract clause ([§22.16](#sec-contract-clauses)): a `requires` clause, an `ensures` clause, or both, on any constructor of the record, of any visibility, in any recorded tier (the clause's own `static` proven-tier qualifier included, [§22.16](#sec-contract-clauses)). The property reads the declaration and nothing else — never what a clause says, whether every constructor declares one, or which tier a clause occupies — and is never annotated ([§3.6](#sec-derived-type-properties) rule 1). It is constant across the instantiations of a generic record: no substitution adds or removes a clause.

What the property claims is **provenance**: every value of a constructor-only record is produced by a call to one of that record's declared constructors, or is a copy of such a value. It is not a claim about validity. The property does not assert that any predicate holds of any value at any instant, and a clause's truth at construction is not carried forward. In particular it does not prevent a constructor from producing a value its own clauses do not describe; it does not restrict what a constructor writes into the value it is constructing ([§22.8](#sec-field-initializers)'s and [§23.1](#sec-auto-properties)'s `readonly` assignable context reaches that instance's own storage, and no other value's); it does not decide which constructor [§9.8](#sec-serialization-synthesis) selects for a record declaring more than one; and it does not reach values produced or altered outside the language ([§32.10](#sec-boundary-contract)).

Two consequences follow. Both are static, and both hold in every build mode:

- A constructor-only record is **not defaultable** ([§17.11](#sec-the-default-operator)). So `default(R)`, `new T()` at such a substitution ([§14.2](#sec-constraints)), default initialization of `R`-typed storage ([§7.9](#sec-definite-assignment-for-non-nullable-fields), [§15.1](#sec-inline-arrays)), a `default(R)` default-value expression ([§22.5](#sec-optional-parameters-and-named-arguments)), and every other site that supplies a `default(T)` are rejected. The remedy is a constructor or factory call — or, where a zero value is genuinely wanted, `R?` and `default(R?)`.
- A `with` expression over such a record is a **compile error** ([§9.5](#sec-non-destructive-update-with)).

A record declaring **positional fields** ([§9.1](#sec-positional-records), [§9.3](#sec-combined-form)) may not declare such a constructor: a compile error at the record declaration. The auto-generated primary constructor carries no clause — `RecordDecl` admits none (Appendix [A.3](#sec-type-declarations)), exactly as `ClassDecl` admits none on a class primary constructor — so the combination would leave the door `new R(…)` most naturally reaches outside every gate the declared constructor states, while flipping a property clients depend on. The diagnostic names two remedies: declare the storage as auto-properties in a body record ([§9.2](#sec-body-records)), so that every constructor is declared; or state the condition on a **static factory method** ([§22.16](#sec-contract-scope) admits clauses on static methods), where the type is not meant to be constructor-only.

The clauses themselves keep their ordinary meaning and their ordinary evaluation ([§22.16](#sec-contract-clauses)), and the two kinds differ in when they run: a `requires` constrains the arguments and is evaluated on every invocation in every build mode, while an unproven `ensures` constrains the constructed value at body completion and is evaluated under checked-contracts mode only. An author wanting an always-on gate writes `requires`; one wanting to state what the constructed value is writes `ensures` and takes the mode with it.

```bezel
public record Port
  public readonly property Value: int;

  public constructor(value: int)
    requires(value >= 0 and value <= 65535)
    ensures(Value >= 0 and Value <= 65535)

    Value := value;
  end constructor;
end Port;
```

`Port` is constructor-only. `default(Port)`, **default initialization of `Port`-typed storage** ([§7.9](#sec-definite-assignment-for-non-nullable-fields): a `Port`-typed field that neither carries an initializer nor is assigned in every constructor), an `[8]Port` declaration relying on default slots, `Port` at a `where T: new()` substitution, and `p with(Value := -1)` are compile errors, each diagnostic naming the property ([§3.6](#sec-derived-type-properties) rule 4). A `Port`-typed **local** is not among them: it is governed by [§7.9](#sec-definite-assignment-for-non-nullable-fields)'s definite-assignment rule like any other local of non-defaultable type — `var p: Port;` is not itself an error, and reading `p` before it is assigned is. The declaration site is the right site for a **field**, which has no flow to analyse; a local has one, and the two-step declare-then-assign shape stays writable for every constructor-only record. In every other respect `Port` is an ordinary record: a constructor is a member [§9.2](#sec-body-records) admits regardless of what its body does, so `Port` remains auto-hashable, hashable, and serialization-eligible, and no other classification reads this property ([§9.7](#sec-records-and-disposal), [§28.11](#sec-collection-element-ownership), [§30.14](#sec-sendable-types), [§32.13](#sec-c-compatible-records) are unaffected).

Adding or removing a constructor clause on a public record flips this property, which [§3.6](#sec-derived-type-properties) rule 3 makes part of the public contract and [§2.8.6](#sec-interface-delta-classification) classifies as a breaking delta in both directions. A record that should carry a validating condition without carrying the property states that condition on a static factory method instead.

---

<a id="sec-enums"></a>
## 10. Enums

An enum is a value type whose values are drawn from a fixed, named set of constants. Each value is backed by an integer at runtime. An enum is not implicitly convertible to or from its underlying integer type.

<a id="sec-basic-syntax"></a>
### 10.1 Basic syntax

```bezel
enum Priority
  Low, Medium, High;
end Priority;
```

This declares constants `Priority.Low`, `Priority.Medium`, `Priority.High` of type `Priority`. The default underlying values are 0, 1, 2 — assigned in declaration order from zero.

<a id="sec-explicit-values"></a>
### 10.2 Explicit values

```bezel
enum HttpStatus
  Ok := 200,
  Created := 201,
  NotFound := 404,
  ServerError := 500;
end HttpStatus;
```

Values must be compile-time constants ([§17.14](#sec-constant-expressions)) of the underlying type. Unspecified values continue from the previous explicit value, incrementing by 1.

**Sibling constants in value initializers.** Within the enum's own value initializers, a reference to one of the enum's constants, bare (`A`) or qualified (`E.A`), denotes that constant's underlying value at the underlying type, not a value of the enum. So `enum E A := 10, B, C := A + 100; end E;` gives `C` the value 110 under [§17.14](#sec-constant-expressions)'s primitive arithmetic, and `Current := Legacy` declares an alias of `Legacy`. The referenced constant must be declared earlier in the list: a reference to the constant being declared, or to one declared after it, is a compile error. For [§2.7](#sec-name-resolution-order)'s lookup a value initializer is inside the enum's body, so a bare name finds the enum's constants at the enclosing-type-member rank, ahead of module declarations: a bare `A` naming a later constant is that error, not a reference to an outer `A`. Everywhere else, member bodies included, an enum constant is a value of the enum type, and an operator over it resolves under [§25.2](#sec-operator-overloading-restrictions) ([§10.5](#sec-restrictions), *Ordering*).

**Duplicate constant values.** Two or more constants of one enum may share an underlying value, whether written explicitly (`Legacy := 1, Current := 1`) or produced by auto-increment continuation. Aliasing is legal and draws no diagnostic; but since an enum value *is* its underlying integer ([§10.3](#sec-underlying-type)), same-valued constants denote **one value**: `Legacy = Current` is `true`, and no construct can distinguish them at run time. Three consequences follow from that identity: in a `case` over the enum, two arms — or two `|` alternatives — naming same-valued constants are a **compile error**, the later one being unreachable; exhaustiveness ([§19.6](#sec-exhaustiveness)) is over the set of distinct declared *values*, so an arm naming either alias covers both; and serialization synthesis ([§9.8](#sec-serialization-synthesis)) writes the **first-declared** constant's name for a shared value and accepts every declared name on read.

<a id="sec-underlying-type"></a>
### 10.3 Underlying type

The default underlying type is `int`. A different integer type may be specified with a colon:

```bezel
enum HttpStatus: short
  Ok := 200,
  NotFound := 404;
end HttpStatus;
```

The underlying type must be one of `byte`, `sbyte`, `short`, `ushort`, `int`, `uint`, `long`, `ulong`, spelled by the keyword or by its reserved PascalCase alias ([§3.4](#sec-keyword-aliases-for-built-in-types)) — `enum E: Int16` and `enum E: short` declare the same type. The colon list is one list (grammar A.3 `EnumInheritance`): if its first item resolves to one of these eight types, that item is the underlying type and the rest name interfaces ([§10.5](#sec-restrictions)); otherwise the underlying type is `int` and every item names an interface. Where the *otherwise* branch then fails because the **first** item names a type that is not an interface — `enum Ratio: double` — the diagnostic should name the **underlying-type** fact: that the type is not one of the eight admissible underlying types, listing them. (Diagnostic identity remains implementation-defined, Appendix [D](#appendix-d-conformance-levels); what this clause fixes is which fact is most useful to surface, not any wording.) All declared values must fit in the underlying type's range.

<a id="sec-methods-properties-static-members"></a>
### 10.4 Methods, properties, static members

An enum may declare **exactly** the following members, and no others: instance methods, expression-bodied read-only instance properties, static methods, `static readonly` fields (including `static owned readonly`, initialized or not), `const` members, and operator overloads ([§25](#sec-operator-overloading)). The grammar admits the full member production on an enum body (A.3 `EnumDecl`, A.4 `Member`); this list and [§10.5](#sec-restrictions) are what reject the rest:

```bezel
enum Priority
  Low, Medium, High;

  public method IsUrgent(): bool => this = High;

  public property Name: string => (case this of
    Low => "Low",
    Medium => "Medium",
    High => "High");

  public static owned readonly All: FrozenArray<Priority> :=
      FrozenArray<Priority>.From([Low, Medium, High]);

  public static method Parse(text: string): Priority =>
      Priority.FromNameOrNull(text)
      ?? throw new ArgumentException($"unknown priority {text}", "text");
end Priority;
```

Inside an instance method, `this` refers to the current enum value.

The `Name` property's `case` lists only the declared constants, and that coverage is total: every value of `Priority` is a declared constant ([§5.4](#sec-enum-casts)), so the case expression is statically exhaustive over the whole value space and cannot raise `MatchFailureException` ([§19.6](#sec-exhaustiveness)). No defensive `_` arm is needed — or wanted: a `_` arm would silence the missing-arm diagnostic when a constant is added. (For this particular table — each constant to its own identifier — the compiler-provided `Priority.NameOf(this)` below already is the answer; the hand-written `case` is here for the exhaustiveness rule it illustrates.)
