Static readonly fields on enums are initialized lazily on first use, following the same rules as class static fields ([§22.13](#sec-static-initialization-order)). Enum constants are compile-time values and are available before any static readonly initializer runs; a static readonly field initializer on an enum may freely reference the enum's declared constants.

The statics an enum may declare — `const` members, static methods, and `static readonly` fields — carry the class rules for those forms; a mutable static field, a `static` property, and a static constructor are not among them (the list above). A `const` member (grammar A.4 `ConstDecl`) follows [§22.12](#sec-static-members)'s class-level `const` rules: implicitly static, compile-time-constant initializer, primitive or `string` type. A static readonly field of class type may be marked `owned` — `public static owned readonly Cache: ConnectionPool := new ConnectionPool();` — enrolling it in [§22.13](#sec-static-initialization-order)'s program-exit disposal; without `owned`, [§22.13](#sec-static-initialization-order)'s resource-bearing-static warning and its add-`owned` remedy apply on enums exactly as on classes. (Appendix A.4 `FieldDecl` carries the `owned` slot.) The example's `All` field shows the sanctioned spelling for a shared constant collection: `FrozenArray<Priority>` declares the **immutable** statics-and-sharing fact (stdlib §1, §4.19), placing it in [§22.12](#sec-static-members) rule 4's warning-suppression set — a `static owned readonly` of it is a warning-free, every-domain-readable singleton, where the same field at `Array<Priority>` (a mutable class type outside the set) would draw rule 4's declaration-site sharing warning.

**The compiler-provided tier.** Every enum `E` with underlying type `U` ([§10.3](#sec-underlying-type)) carries three **compiler-provided** static members — no declaration is written, and no user declaration — a member or a declared constant — may override or overload any of them (they join the type's surface the way [§11.8](#sec-static-interface-members)'s compiler-provided conformances join the primitives):

```bezel
public static method FromUnderlyingOrNull(value: U): E?;
public static method FromNameOrNull(name: string): E?;
public static method NameOf(value: E): string;
```

`FromUnderlyingOrNull` returns the declared constant whose underlying value equals `value`, or `null` when there is none. It is **total** — it never raises. Under duplicate constant values ([§10.2](#sec-explicit-values)) the result is the shared value (all aliases denote it). The parameter type is the underlying type `U` exactly: a wider integer in hand is narrowed explicitly first ([§5.2](#sec-explicit-conversions), checked), keeping the two failure modes — out of `U`'s range vs. not a declared value — separately visible. The member is the branch-shaped tier beside the checked cast (stdlib §1's `*OrNull` tier): `E(n)` treats an undeclared value as a bug at the call site ([§5.4](#sec-enum-casts)); `E.FromUnderlyingOrNull(n)` lets boundary code state its policy in one line:

```bezel
// A parser validating a wire-read value (wire, trusted: int; ProtocolException
// stands for a user exception class):
var p := Priority.FromUnderlyingOrNull(wire)
         ?? throw new ProtocolException($"bad priority {wire}");    // reject
var p2 := Priority.FromUnderlyingOrNull(wire) ?? Priority.Low;      // tolerate with a default
var p3 := Priority(trusted);   // the checked cast is the assert: failure is a bug (§5.4)
```

**The name pair.** `FromNameOrNull` and `NameOf` are the two directions of one table, the enum's **declared-identifier table**: each constant's own identifier — the bare name as written, never a qualified `E.A` spelling — the table [§17.9](#sec-the-nameof-operator)'s `nameof` reads at compile time and stdlib [§2.13](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-the-type-class)'s `Type.EnumNames` lists. `FromNameOrNull(name)` returns the declared constant whose identifier equals `name`, or `null` when there is none; the comparison is exact — ordinal code-point equality (stdlib [§9.6](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-string)), case-sensitive, nothing trimmed — and a digit string names no constant, since no identifier begins with a digit ([§1](#1-lexical-structure)); the underlying-value direction is `FromUnderlyingOrNull`, and a boundary that accepts both spellings composes the two. It is **total** — it never raises. `NameOf(value)` returns the identifier of the constant `value` denotes; it is total because every value of an enum type is a declared value ([§5.4](#sec-enum-casts)), and for a written constant `E.NameOf(E.A) = nameof(E.A)` — `NameOf` extends the compile-time operator to a runtime value over the same table. Under duplicate constant values ([§10.2](#sec-explicit-values)) `NameOf` yields the **first-declared** constant's identifier for a shared value and `FromNameOrNull` accepts every declared identifier (all denote the one value), so the pair round-trips **up to aliasing**: `E.FromNameOrNull(E.NameOf(v)) = v` for every `v: E`, and `E.NameOf(E.FromNameOrNull(s)!) = s` for every `s` that is the first-declared identifier of its value — for an alias's identifier it returns the first-declared one. A `serialized "<name>"` clause ([§9.8](#sec-field-name-customization)) changes the constant's **encoded** form only: the synthesized `Serialize`/`Deserialize` read the serialized-name table, and `NameOf`/`FromNameOrNull` — like `nameof` and `EnumNames` — never see a rename; a boundary that wants the wire spelling goes through [§9.8](#sec-serialization-synthesis)'s serializers. The table is a compile-time constant of the declaration, consulted for a constant of a statically known type — not an enumeration of members (rationale [§5.18](Bezel_Design_Rationale.md#sec-type-identity-not-reflection)). `NameOf` does not change `ToString` ([§8.5](#sec-tostring) renders an enum by its qualified type name) — an enum that wants its constants' names in interpolation declares `ToString` to return them (`public override method ToString(): string => Priority.NameOf(this);` on the example above).

```bezel
// Configuration text (text: string; ConfigException stands for a user
// exception class):
var level := Priority.FromNameOrNull(text)                // "High" → High; "high" → null
             ?? throw new ConfigException($"unknown priority {text}");
var label := Priority.NameOf(level);                      // "High" — nameof(Priority.High)
```

<a id="sec-restrictions"></a>
### 10.5 Restrictions

An enum may not declare:

- Instance fields (the runtime representation is the underlying integer).
- Constructors.
- Block-form properties or properties with backing storage.
- Nested types.
- Indexers.
- Inheritance from another type.

Enum members take the value kinds' dispatch-modifier rule ([§9.2](#sec-record-dispatch-modifiers), *Dispatch modifiers on value kinds*) and are always dispatched statically; `override` is admitted only on the `Object`-virtual members the next paragraph names — `Equals`, `GetHashCode`, `ToString` — with the same admission a record body has for them ([§8.1](#sec-definition), [§9.2](#sec-body-records)).

Static dispatch does not orphan the `Object`-virtual surface. An enum may declare — spelled `override` or plain, the two spellings declaring the same member — `Equals` taking the enum's own type (as [§25.2](#sec-operator-overloading-restrictions)'s co-declaration rule already requires alongside an `=` overload), `GetHashCode(): int`, and `ToString(): string`. Each **replaces the compiler-generated default for every consumer**: direct calls, hash containers (`Set<E>` and `Dictionary<E, V>` reach the user's `Equals`/`GetHashCode`), string interpolation ([§8.5](#sec-tostring)), and virtual dispatch through a boxed reference ([§8.6](#sec-boxing)) — the compiler populates the enum's box vtable with these members, a static wiring that is well-defined because enums are sealed. There is no override chain and no `base` access — `override` here names the `Object` slot the member fills, as it does on a record, and implies no chain; the user member *is* the enum's implementation of that surface.

An enum may implement one or more interfaces. The interface names appear after the underlying type (if any) following a colon. The enum must provide matching public members for every interface member:

```bezel
enum Priority: IComparable<Priority>
  Low, Medium, High;

  public method CompareTo(other: Priority): int =>
    (if int(this) < int(other) then -1
     elif int(this) > int(other) then 1
     else 0);
end Priority;
```

When both an underlying type and interfaces are specified, the underlying type comes first: `enum Priority: int, IComparable<Priority>`.

**Ordering.** An enum has no intrinsic ordering. Its values compare for equality under [§8.4](#sec-=-and), by underlying integer ([§8.3](#sec-equals-and-gethashcode)), but `<`, `<=`, `>` and `>=` are not intrinsic on an enum — [§3.5](#sec-operators-on-primitive-types) defines them on the primitives and `string`, and an enum is neither — so on enum operands they resolve only to `operator` overloads the operand types declare ([§25.2](#sec-operator-overloading-restrictions)), and where none applies `a < b` is a compile error. [§10.2](#sec-explicit-values)'s identity of a value with its underlying integer decides equality and aliasing; it supplies no operator. An enum that wants an order states it: at the use, by comparing the underlying values explicitly (`int(a) < int(b)`); on the type, by declaring the four-operator group, whose bodies are the order; or, for interface-constrained generics such as `Sort` and `OrderBy`, by implementing `IComparable<E>` as above. A relational or range pattern over an enum scrutinee is a compile error whether or not the enum declares the group ([§19.3](#sec-patterns)).

<a id="sec-case-matching"></a>
### 10.6 Case matching

Inside a `case` whose scrutinee is an enum, the enum prefix may be omitted:

```bezel
case p of
  Low => Console.WriteLine("low"),
  Medium | High => Console.WriteLine("medium or high")
end;
```

---

<a id="sec-classes-and-interfaces"></a>
## 11. Classes and Interfaces

<a id="sec-class-declaration"></a>
### 11.1 Class declaration

A class is a reference type with optional inheritance, optional interfaces, and a member body:

```bezel
public class BankAccount: IBankAccount
  // members
end BankAccount;
```

A class may declare at most one base class and any number of interfaces. The base class, if any, is listed first, followed by interfaces, all comma-separated. There is no semicolon after the inheritance list.

A generic interface may be listed at **two or more instantiations** (`class D: IComparable<int>, IComparable<string>`), directly or through a base class. The class still declares **one** member set, and [§11.2](#sec-interface-declaration)'s matching rule is applied once per obligation, each under its own instantiation's substitution; there is no explicit-implementation form. So the class is well-formed exactly when one member set satisfies every obligation — which it does where the obligations' members are distinguishable as overloads ([§22.6](#sec-overloading)), and does not where they differ only in return type, in which case the declarations clash at [§11.3](#sec-member-body). This is the case [§14.5](#sec-type-argument-inference)'s non-unique-instantiation clause governs at a call.

If no base class is specified, the implicit base is `Object`.

<a id="sec-primary-constructors"></a>
#### Primary constructors

A class may declare parameters in parentheses after its name, analogous to a record's positional fields:

```bezel
public class BankAccount(name: string, initialBalance: decimal): IBankAccount
  private _name: string := name;
  private _balance: decimal := initialBalance;
end BankAccount;
```

The compiler generates a primary constructor whose parameter list matches the parenthesized declaration. The primary constructor's parameters are in scope throughout the class body — including field initializers, property initializers, the inheritance clause's base call, and the bodies of methods, properties, constructors, and destructors. Parameters referenced only in initializers do not generate backing fields; parameters referenced in method, property, constructor, or destructor bodies are captured into compiler-generated private fields. The capture is invisible at the source level — the parameter name resolves to the parameter in initializer positions and to the captured field in body positions, and the two reads observe the same value.

For each primary-constructor parameter, the compiler does **not** generate an auto-property (unlike records). The parameters are initialization-time values, optionally captured for body use; the class author decides which fields or properties to declare publicly. This keeps the class's public API explicit.

If the class has a base class that requires constructor arguments, the base's arguments appear in parentheses after the base class name in the inheritance list:

```bezel
public class SavingsAccount(name: string, balance: decimal, rate: decimal): BankAccount(name, balance)
  private _rate: decimal := rate;
end SavingsAccount;
```

This desugars to a primary constructor that chains to `base(name, balance)` before executing field initializers.

A class with a primary constructor may also declare additional constructors in its body using the `constructor` keyword; such constructors must chain to the primary constructor via `this(...)`:

```bezel
public class BankAccount(name: string, initialBalance: decimal)
  private _name: string := name;
  private _balance: decimal := initialBalance;

  public constructor(name: string)
    this(name, 0m);
  end constructor;
end BankAccount;
```

The primary constructor's visibility follows the class's visibility. The body may not redeclare a constructor with the same parameter list as the primary constructor, in [§11.3](#sec-member-body)'s clash sense ([§22.6](#sec-overloading)'s overload identity; parameter names and defaults do not distinguish).

Primary constructors interact with `owned` parameters: a primary-constructor parameter may be declared `owned`, and the same ownership-transfer rules as regular constructor parameters apply:

```bezel
public class ResourceHolder(owned resource: Stream)
  private owned _resource: Stream := resource;
end ResourceHolder;
```

An `owned` primary-constructor parameter referenced in a *body* position is captured as an `owned` field and disposed with the object; combining a body reference with an initializer that consumes the parameter is a compile error ([§22.10](#sec-capture-rule-and-layout-stability)).

<a id="sec-interface-declaration"></a>
### 11.2 Interface declaration

*(A class member implementing a `pure` interface member is declared `pure` — [§22.15](#sec-pure-dispatch). Interface members may carry contract clauses, inherited by implementations and never restated; multi-root contracts combine per [§22.16](#sec-contract-inheritance).)*

```bezel
interface IBankAccount
  method Deposit(amount: decimal);
  method Withdraw(amount: decimal);
  property Balance: decimal;
  readonly property AccountNumber: string;
  readonly property BalanceChanged: IEvent<BalanceChangedEvent>;
end IBankAccount;
```

Interface members are implicitly public, have no body, and end with `;`. A class implements an interface implicitly: by declaring matching public members. (A **value kind** — record, choice, or enum — cannot conform to an interface that declares a *settable* property or indexer member: the conformance is rejected at the declaration, [§9.4](#sec-value-receivers-are-borrows)/[§9.6](#sec-records-and-inheritance).)

A member **matches** an interface member when it is declared `public`, has the same name, the same arity (parameter count), the same number of type parameters of its own (*Generic members* below), the same parameter modifiers (`ref`, `out`, `owned`, `scoped`), parameter types that are exactly equal under the interface's substitution, and a return type that is exactly equal under the interface's substitution — and, for a generic method, a constraint set equivalent to the interface method's ([§14.2](#sec-constraints-on-overrides)). One narrow widening is permitted on parameter types:

1. **Nullability widening on parameters.** An implementation may declare a parameter as `T?` where the interface requires `T` (the implementation accepts more inputs than the interface promises to pass). The reverse — interface `T?`, implementation `T` — is rejected, because the implementation would refuse a `null` the interface promised to accept.
2. **No widening elsewhere.** Parameter types other than the nullability case must match exactly. Return types must match exactly (no covariance in this version). Parameter modifiers must match exactly: an interface declaring `out T` requires the implementation to declare `out T`, and the same applies to `ref`, `owned`, and `scoped`.

The asymmetry on nullability mirrors the standard contravariant-parameter / covariant-return reasoning: implementations may accept more than they were asked to. Bezel admits the parameter-nullability case because it is the common one (most concrete `Equals` implementations want to accept `null` cleanly), and because the type system can verify it without further machinery. The same allowance extends to `override` declarations ([§12.1](#sec-members-are-non-virtual-by-default)).

**Generic members.** A member's own type parameters take part in the match by number and position, not by name. The interface's substitution maps each of the interface's type parameters to the implementing type's argument, and each of the interface member's own type parameters to the candidate's type parameter **at the same position**; parameter types, the return type and the constraints ([§14.2](#sec-constraints-on-overrides)) are compared after that mapping. So `public method Show<U>(x: U): string` matches `method Show<T>(x: T): string;`, while `public method Pair<T, U>(a: U, b: T): int` does not match `method Pair<T, U>(a: T, b: U): int;`. A candidate declaring a different number of type parameters of its own does not match: neither `Show<T, U>(x: T): string` nor, on a `class C<T>`, a non-generic `Show(x: T): string` whose `T` is the class's. Under a different count there is no positional correspondence to compare under, and a call through the interface supplies or infers exactly the interface member's type arguments ([§14.5](#sec-type-argument-inference)): an extra type parameter of the candidate's would have nothing to bind it, and the non-generic `Show(x: T)` would be reached through the interface with any type argument while its `T` is fixed by the instantiation of `C<T>`.

<a id="sec-owned-in-interface-signatures"></a>
#### `owned` in interface signatures

The "must match exactly" rule above applies to every position where `owned` may appear, compared — like the parameter and return types — **under the interface's substitution**: for a slot whose declared type is a bare type parameter of the interface, the marker is read from the substituted signature, so at a value or runtime-managed implementing type a declared `owned` marker is erased by the substitution ([§28.1](#sec-where-the-owned-modifier-can-appear)) and the implementation is spelled without the marker (which the concrete type would reject). For concretely-typed slots, an implementing method's signature and the interface method's signature must agree on:

- **`owned` as a parameter modifier** (e.g. `M(owned t: T)`). Interface declaring `M(owned t: T)` requires implementation to declare `M(owned t: T)`. Either both have `owned` or neither does.
- **`owned` on an `out` parameter** (e.g. `M(out owned t: T)`). Interface declaring `M(out owned t: T)` requires implementation to declare `M(out owned t: T)`; interface declaring `M(out t: T)` requires implementation to declare `M(out t: T)`.
- **Use of an owning generic type** (e.g. `M(): OwningTask<T>`). Interface declaring `M(): OwningTask<T>` requires implementation to declare `M(): OwningTask<T>`; interface declaring `M(): Task<T>` requires implementation to declare `M(): Task<T>`. (Per [§14.4](#sec-owned-as-a-generic-argument), `OwningTask<T>` and `Task<T>` are distinct named types with no implicit conversion; the same applies to `OwningArray<T>` vs `Array<T>` and the other owning/borrowing collection pairs.)
- **`owned` inside function-type parameters or return types** (e.g. `M(callback: (owned T) -> ())`). Same rule — exact match.
- **`owned` on a **mint-announcing** return type — not compared.** Where the return type, nullability stripped, is mint-announcing — a `Task`-family or iterable-family type — the [announcement table](#sec-announcement-table)'s rows 2 and 3 are identical on both the caller and the callee side, so the marker announces nothing the declared type has not already announced: **either spelling matches, in either direction.** `public method GetEnumerator(): IEnumerator<T>` and `public method GetEnumerator(): owned IEnumerator<T>` both implement `method GetEnumerator(): owned IEnumerator<T>;` ([§29.1](#sec-iterator-protocol)). This is the same reasoning as the substitution-erasure clause above: the comparison is dropped exactly where the marker can carry no content, and is unweakened everywhere it can.

A mismatch in any position is a compile error at the implementing class. Two reasons for the strict rule:

1. **Loosening `owned` off a return type would leak ownership.** If the interface declares `Acquire(): owned Connection` and the implementation declares `Acquire(): Connection`, callers calling through the interface classify the call at the interface's declaration — the [announcement table](#sec-announcement-table)'s row 1 — and take ownership, while the body is admitted under row 4 to return a receiver-sourced borrow: the caller would dispose a value the receiver still owns. (`OwningTask<T>` versus `Task<T>` is a different case — distinct named types, caught by the return-type equality rule above and stated in the owning-generic-type bullet.)

2. **Tightening from `T` to `owned T` in a parameter would create undischarged ownership.** If the interface declares `Send(payload: T)` and the implementation declares `Send(owned payload: T)`, callers calling through the interface pass a borrow per the interface contract, but the implementation expects ownership transfer. The implementation would attempt to take ownership of a value the caller intended to retain, leaving the value's original owner with a dangling reference.

Bezel's stance is uniform: `owned` is part of the type-and-modifier signature, and signatures match exactly. There is no `owned`-direction variance.

**`scoped` in interface signatures.** The same exact-match rule covers the `scoped` modifier, in both directions, for the same reason there is no `owned`-direction variance: a `scoped`/unscoped mismatch changes the *caller's* contract. An implementation adding `scoped` to a parameter the interface declares plain would retain a callback — or store a class-typed borrow — that callers through the interface admitted under a call-bounded, non-retaining contract ([§28.14](#sec-scoped-callback-parameters), [§22.3](#sec-parameter-modifiers)): their captures were never checked against a bound, and a class-typed argument was never marked or frozen — a use-after-free shape. An implementation *dropping* the interface's `scoped` is the safe direction semantically (the callee retains less than announced), but it is rejected all the same: `scoped` is part of a function type's identity ([§27.1](#sec-function-types)) and never distinguishes overloads ([§22.6](#sec-overloading)), so the matching rule that keeps signatures exact elsewhere keeps it exact here — any variance would be a third, position-local rule with no compensating capability. (This governs the **top-level** parameter modifier; `scoped` *inside* a function-typed parameter's type was always caught by the exact-type-equality clause above.)

An observable contract on an interface is an ordinary get-only property of type `IEvent<T>` (or `IAsyncEvent<T>`) — the interface face of the stdlib [§6.5](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-events-ievent-eventsource) event pattern, as `BalanceChanged` above (interface `event` members are retired with the member kind, [§24](#sec-events)). The implementing class satisfies it with the pattern's borrowing property; consumers reach only `Subscribe`.

An interface may extend other interfaces:

```bezel
interface IList<T>: IReadOnlyList<T>, ICollection<T>
  property [i: int]: T;
end IList;
```

Multiple-interface inheritance is permitted. Diamond resolution: a single implementation in the implementing class satisfies all interface methods with the same signature. A read-write member satisfies a read-only interface member of the same name and type: if `IReadOnlyList<T>` declares `readonly property [i: int]: T` and `IList<T>` declares `property [i: int]: T`, a single read-write indexer in the implementing class satisfies both. `Add`, `Clear`, `Remove`, and the rest of the mutating surface in the example above are inherited from `ICollection<T>`. `Count` reaches `IList<T>` through two inheritance paths — through `IReadOnlyList<T>` via `IReadOnlyCollection<T>`, and through `ICollection<T>` via `IReadOnlyCollection<T>` again — but both paths substitute to the same property declared on `IReadOnlyCollection<T>`, so the implementing class satisfies both inherited declarations with a single property.

<a id="sec-member-body"></a>
### 11.3 Member body

A class body may contain fields, methods, properties, indexers, constructors, a destructor, operator overloads, nested types, and class-level constants.

Every class member must declare its visibility explicitly ([§13](#sec-visibility)). Interface members do not declare visibility (they are always public).

A type may not declare two members that are not distinguishable from each other. Two members **clash** when they have the same name and the type system cannot tell them apart: two fields, properties, or nested types with the same name; or two methods, constructors, or operator overloads with the same name that are not distinguishable as overloads ([§22.6](#sec-overloading)) — that is, that do not differ in number of parameters, number of type parameters of their own, parameter types, the `ref`/`out` modifiers in a participating position, or — where [§22.6](#sec-overloading)'s declaration guard admits the pair — `owned` on an ordinary parameter (a pair differing only by ordinary `owned` at a position that fails the guard clashes under this rule; `owned` on an `out` parameter and `scoped` never distinguish overloads, [§22.6](#sec-overloading)). A non-overloadable member — a field, property, or nested type — additionally clashes with **any** other member of the type that shares its name, regardless of kind: within a type a given name belongs either to exactly one non-overloadable member or to a single overload family of methods, constructors, or operators. A clash is a compile error at the second declaration, reported at the type, and names the conflicting members. Legal overloads — members of the same name that *are* distinguishable per [§22.6](#sec-overloading) — are unaffected; this rule rejects only the duplicates that overloading does not admit. The same rule applies to interface members within an interface declaration.

**Generic methods.** Two methods declaring the same number of type parameters of their own compare their parameter types with those type parameters corresponding by position, not by name, as in [§11.2](#sec-interface-declaration)'s *Generic members*. So `M<T>(x: T)` and `M<U>(x: U)` clash. `M<T, U>(a: T, b: U)` and `M<T, U>(a: U, b: T)` do not: an explicit type-argument list naming two different types gives them different signatures ([§14.5](#sec-type-argument-inference)), and a call that leaves them to inference is ambiguous ([§22.6](#sec-overloading)). Two methods declaring different numbers of type parameters of their own never clash, whatever their parameters: `M<T>(x: T)` beside `M<T, U>(x: T)`, or `FromException<T>(owned exception: Exception)` beside the non-generic `FromException(owned exception: Exception)` ([§30.10](#sec-standard-library-task-helpers), stdlib [§6.7](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-task-static-helpers)). An explicit list selects by its length, and without one a candidate whose type parameter no argument or target binds fails inference and is inapplicable ([§14.5](#sec-type-argument-inference)). Neither type-parameter names nor `where` constraints distinguish members; constraints matter only where [§22.6](#sec-overloading)'s declaration guard reads them, each member's separately, to decide whether an ordinary-`owned` difference does.

<a id="sec-block-endings"></a>
### 11.4 Block endings

A class ends with `end ClassName;`. Members may end with `end MemberName;` or `end;`; the named form is recommended. Control structures inside method bodies may end with plain `end;` or repeat their introducing keyword ([§1.6](#sec-statements-and-termination)).

<a id="sec-modifier-order"></a>
### 11.5 Modifier order

When a member declaration carries multiple modifiers, they appear in this order:

```text
visibility static (async | pure) (abstract | virtual | override | sealed override) (owned | scoped) readonly member-kind Name ...
```

`abstract`, `virtual`, `override`, and `sealed override` are mutually exclusive — at most one may appear. A non-virtual member carries none of them. `sealed override` seals a previously-virtual member against further overriding. `sealed` alone is a class-level modifier that prevents inheritance ([§12.4](#sec-sealing)); [A.4](#sec-appendix-a)'s `VirtualKind` admits it on a member only as `sealed override`, and a declaration carrying `sealed` without `override` is a compile error ([§12.4](#sec-sealing)).

`owned` ([§28.5](#sec-owned-fields)) — or, on function-typed fields, `scoped` ([§28.14](#sec-scoped-callback-parameters)), which occupies the same slot and is mutually exclusive with it — appears between the virtual-modifier slot and `readonly`. It applies only to fields; methods, properties, and other members do not carry `owned`. The combination `static owned readonly` is the canonical form for a static field that owns a long-lived resource ([§22.13](#sec-static-initialization-order)).

The compiler rejects out-of-order modifiers.

<a id="sec-nested-types"></a>
### 11.6 Nested types

A class body may declare nested classes, records, enums, and interfaces. Nested types may be `public`, `internal`, `protected`, or `private`, and the visibility keyword is **required**: a nested type is a class member ([§11.3](#sec-member-body)), and [§13.3](#sec-class-members)'s explicit-visibility rule applies with no exception for nested types — omitting the keyword is a compile error, not a default. (The `Visibility?` in the reused type-declaration grammar productions serves [§13.2](#sec-top-level-types)'s default-`internal` rule for *top-level* declarations only; Appendix A.4 `NestedTypeDecl`.) A nested type's effective visibility is the more restrictive of its declared visibility and its enclosing class's visibility.

```bezel
public class Parser
  public record Token(Kind: TokenKind, Text: string, Line: int);

  public enum TokenKind
    Identifier, Number, Operator, EndOfFile;
  end TokenKind;
end Parser;
```

A nested type none of whose enclosing types is generic is referenced from outside as `Outer.Nested` (a generic enclosing type is below), and the enclosing path is part of its qualified name wherever one is rendered: `Type.FullName` and [§8.5](#sec-tostring)'s default `ToString` render `"M.Outer.Nested"` for a nested type declared in module `M`, and `"M.Outer<_>.Nested"` when `Outer` is generic, while `Type.Name` renders `"Nested"` (stdlib [§2.13](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-the-type-class)). A nested class has access to all members (including `private`) of its enclosing class when it holds an instance of the enclosing class. The enclosing class similarly has full access to its nested types' members.

Nested types may themselves contain nested types. Nested types in records are permitted but uncommon.

**Nested types of a generic type.** A nested type is one type, whatever the instantiation of its enclosing type: [§2.8.3](#sec-transitive-closure-and-type-identity) rule 3 identifies it by its declaring module, its qualified name with the enclosing-type path, and its own generic arity, with no component for the enclosing type's type arguments. The enclosing type's type parameters are therefore **not in scope** in a nested type's declaration — its base list, `where` clauses, fields, member signatures and bodies, and those of the types nested in it. A reference to one is a compile error naming this rule (the name is not in scope there, but the rule is stated so the diagnostic is the named one); the remedy is a type parameter of the nested type's own, which the enclosing type's members supply (`public class Node<U>` inside `class Tree<T>`, used there as `Node<T>`). Because the name is not in scope, a nested type, or a method of one, may declare a type parameter spelled like an enclosing type's ([§14.1](#sec-generic-declarations)). A chain head that supplies the enclosing type's arguments ([§2.7](#sec-name-resolution-order) rule 1, `Tree<int>.Node<int>.Create()`) reaches that one type whatever the arguments, and its static members have one cell each ([§22.12](#sec-static-members)), not one per enclosing instantiation. A bare enclosing segment fixes arity 0 ([§2.2](#sec-imports), [§14.1](#sec-generic-declarations)), so `Tree.Node<int>` at a generic-only `Tree` is [Appendix C.1](#sec-appendix-c-type-system)'s arity error, and [A.5](#sec-types)'s `TypeNoNullable` admits type arguments after the last segment only. In a type position, therefore, no name passes through a generic enclosing type: a type nested in a generic type, at any depth, is named only where [§2.7](#sec-name-resolution-order)'s enclosing-type lookup reaches it, or reaches a non-generic type enclosing it below the generic one (`Node<int>` in `Tree`'s own declaration or in the body of a type deriving from `Tree`; `Inner.Leaf` there for a `Leaf` nested in a non-generic `Inner`). Elsewhere a chain head reaches its static members, and a local declared without a type annotation holds a value of it (`var n := tree.Root();`). Rendered, an enclosing generic type shows one `_` per type parameter, since the nested type has no enclosing arguments: `"M.Tree<_>.Node<int>"` (stdlib [§2.13](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-the-type-class) rule 1). That form is a rendering, not a type expression.

A nested type is a *member* and lives in a type body; it is distinct from a **method-local** `record`/`enum` ([§21.10](#sec-local-type-declarations)), which is a body-scoped *statement* with no access surface. The visibility rules are deliberately opposite: a nested type **requires** the keyword (above), a local type **forbids** it — a member has an access surface to declare, a local does not. A local record's own body may itself contain §11.6 nested member types, which follow their own rules.

<a id="sec-static-classes"></a>
### 11.7 Static classes

A class declared `static` may contain only static members:

```bezel
public static class Utils
  public static method Max(a: int, b: int): int => (if a > b then a else b);
end Utils;
```

A static class may not be instantiated: `new` on a static class is a compile error. A static class may not have instance fields, instance methods, instance properties, indexers, constructors (other than a static constructor), or destructors. **Static `owned` fields are permitted:** `static owned readonly` fields and static owning-inline-array fields participate in [§22.13](#sec-static-initialization-order)'s program-exit disposal exactly as on any other type — that mechanism is runtime-driven and independent of instance `Dispose()`. A static class may not be inherited from and does not implement interfaces.

Because a static class cannot be instantiated, it does not implement `IDisposable` — the compiler-generated `Dispose()` rule ([§8.7](#sec-dispose-is-not-on-object), [§28](#sec-resource-management)) applies only to non-static classes. The `abstract` and `static` modifiers are mutually exclusive, and `sealed` and `static` are mutually exclusive; combining either pair is a compile error. A class declared with the **`closed`** modifier is a **closed abstract class**: a class that cannot be instantiated directly and cannot be inherited from outside the declaring module. Classes derived from a `closed` base must be declared in the same module; the compiler rejects subclasses in other modules. A `closed` class may declare abstract members ([§12.5](#sec-abstract-classes-and-members)) without carrying the `abstract` modifier — `closed` subsumes it — and combining `closed` with `abstract`, `sealed`, or `static` is a compile error; the modifier pair `sealed abstract` is rejected too, the diagnostic naming `closed`. The `closed` modifier is the recommended way to define a closed hierarchy for exhaustive `case` matching ([§19.6](#sec-exhaustiveness)):

```bezel
public closed class Shape
  public abstract method Area(): double;
end Shape;

public sealed class Circle(radius: double): Shape
  public readonly property Radius: double := radius;
  public override method Area(): double => Math.Pi * Radius * Radius;
end Circle;

public sealed class Square(side: double): Shape
  public readonly property Side: double := side;
  public override method Area(): double => Side * Side;
end Square;

public sealed class Triangle(baseLength: double, height: double): Shape
  public readonly property Base: double := baseLength;
  public readonly property Height: double := height;
  public override method Area(): double => 0.5 * Base * Height;
end Triangle;
```

Because `Shape` is `closed`, no class outside the declaring module may extend it. The compiler can therefore prove exhaustiveness of `case` matches over `Shape` without requiring a `_` arm, even across module boundaries.

<a id="sec-static-interface-members"></a>
### 11.8 Static interface members

An interface member may be declared `static`: a contract the conforming **type** — not an instance — must satisfy. Static interface members are **abstract-only** (no default bodies; the same diamond-avoidance posture as the declined default interface methods, rationale §17.4) and may be **methods** or **operators**; static constants and properties are deferred (spell a constant as a nullary method: `Zero()`).

```bezel
interface INumber<T> where T: INumber<T>
  static method Zero(): owned T;
  static operator +(a: T, b: T): owned T;
  static operator *(a: T, b: T): owned T;
end INumber;
```

**The recurrence constraint.** The self-referential form `where T: INumber<T>` is the ordinary generic-constraint machinery — no new syntax, no `Self` keyword (deliberately declined for v1: the recurrence is explicit and already expressible). A conforming type declares `class Meters: INumber<Meters>` and supplies the static members with exact signatures (the §11.2 matching rule, applied to statics) — exact against the **substituted** signature: at a value or runtime-managed conforming type a declared `owned` return or `out owned` slot is erased by the substitution ([§28.1](#sec-where-the-owned-modifier-can-appear)), so the witness is spelled without the marker (which would be a compile error on the concrete type); a class or interface conformer spells the marker exactly, and its witness bodies are checked under the ordinary transfer rules — a fresh value on every return path ([§28.8](#sec-ownership-transfer)).

**Dispatch through the type parameter.** In a generic body whose parameter `T` carries a static-interface constraint, `T.Member(...)` calls the conforming type's static member, and an operator applied to `T`-typed operands resolves through the constraint's static operators. Resolution happens **at instantiation** — a statement about *semantics*, not implementation strategy: the binding of `T.Member(...)`, and of constraint-sourced operators ([§25.2](#sec-operator-overloading-restrictions)), is fixed per concrete type argument, exactly as if each instantiation were compiled separately. An implementation may realize this by per-instantiation specialization or by shared code carrying a per-instantiation dispatch table — rationale §10's recorded strategy does both, specializing value-type substitutions and sharing reference-type ones — so long as the observable binding is the conforming type's member:

```bezel
public static method Sum<T>(items: Array<T>): owned T where T: INumber<T>
  var total := T.Zero();                          // owned at class/interface T; a plain value otherwise
  for var x in items do total := total + x; end;  // fresh result in; displaced total disposed (§28.7)
  return total;                                   // transfers; a by-value return at value T
end Sum;
```

At a class or interface substitution of `T`, `total` is an owned local: `T.Zero()` and each operator result transfer per stdlib §2.19's `owned` producer signatures, the loop's reassignment disposes the displaced previous total by drop-on-overwrite ([§28.7](#sec-reassigning-owned-fields)), and the `return` transfers to the caller. At value and runtime-managed substitutions the markers are erased and every step is a plain copy ([§28.1](#sec-where-the-owned-modifier-can-appear), [§28.9](#sec-runtime-managed-types)).

**Static-member interfaces as ordinary types.** Declaring static members does not remove an interface from the ordinary type grammar: it remains usable as a variable, field, parameter, or return type, as a boxing target, and as an `is`/`is not`/`as` operand ([§12.7](#sec-type-tests-is-is-not-as)) — the tests behave as for any interface, since a runtime type conforms only by declaring the full member set, statics included, so there is no partial-conformance state to probe. Two consequences are normative. (1) Static interface members contribute **nothing to the instance surface**: through an interface-typed *value* only instance members are reachable, and calling a static member on the interface *name* (`INumber<int>.Zero()`) is a compile error — the interface declares no bodies to run. `T.Member(...)` dispatch requires a generic type **parameter** constrained by the interface: a value's static type names no single conforming type, so "static dispatch through a value" would be hidden dynamic dispatch, which Bezel declines. (2) An interface that declares static members may not mark its type parameters variant (`in`/`out`, [§12.9](#sec-variance)) — a compile error at the declaration: variance is defined by instance-reference assignability, the position rules have no recorded reading for static signatures, and invariance keeps the question closed until a use case arrives (recorded v1 bound, liftable).

**Primitive conformances (compiler-provided).** The primitive numeric tower (`byte`…`ulong`, `float`, `double`, `decimal`) conforms to the standard-library `INumber<T>`/`ISteppable<T>`/`IParsable<T>` interfaces, and `char` to `ISteppable<char>`/`IParsable<char>` (stdlib §2.19), **without declaring them**: primitive operators are compiler intrinsics (§3.5), so the compiler bridges the intrinsic/declared split by treating each primitive as conforming with its intrinsic operations as the member bodies. User code observes no difference from a declared conformance. The bridge covers not only the intrinsic/declared operator split but also the `IParsable<T>.TryParse` **out-nullability** shape: the per-type witnesses declare `out result: T` (a concrete value type), while the interface declares `out owned value: T?` — the nullability required for user class conformers, for which `default(T)` is a compile error ([§17.11](#sec-the-default-operator)). A call through the constraint observes the declared slot under the class assumption, erased at value substitutions; a direct call observes `out result: T`. The stdlib §2.19 producer markers themselves (`owned` returns; the `out owned` slot) ask nothing extra of the bridge: at every primitive conformer they are erased by the substitution ([§28.1](#sec-where-the-owned-modifier-can-appear)), so the intrinsic value operations witness the erased — unmarked — signatures directly.

---

<a id="sec-inheritance-and-dispatch"></a>
## 12. Inheritance and Dispatch

<a id="sec-members-are-non-virtual-by-default"></a>
### 12.1 Members are non-virtual by default

*(Purity at override boundaries: an `override` of a `pure` member restates `pure` — omission is a compile error; an override may add `pure` where the base is not (usable through the derived static type only); purity never narrows down a chain — [§22.15](#sec-pure-dispatch). Contract clauses at override boundaries: inherited verbatim, never restated; an override may add `ensures` and may not declare `requires` — [§22.16](#sec-contract-inheritance).)*

A method, property, or indexer is non-virtual unless marked `virtual`. To override a virtual member in a derived class, mark the matching member `override`. Visibility, return type, parameter types, and parameter modifiers must match the base member exactly, with one allowance: an override may declare a parameter as `T?` where the overridden member declares `T` — the same contravariant nullability widening [§11.2](#sec-interface-declaration) grants interface implementations, admitted here for the same recorded reason (the override accepts more inputs than the virtual slot promises to pass; the reasoning applies verbatim). Widening is **monotone down the chain**: an override matches against the *nearest* overridden declaration, so once a parameter is `T?` a further override must keep it `T?` — narrowing back would let a `null` admitted through an intermediate static type reach a non-nullable parameter. The reverse direction (overridden `T?`, override `T`) is rejected, as in §11.2. Return types must still match exactly (no covariance in this version). An override declares exactly as many type parameters of its own as the overridden member (none where that member declares none), the two lists corresponding by position as in [§11.2](#sec-interface-declaration)'s *Generic members*: `public override method Echo<U>(x: U): string` overrides `public virtual method Echo<T>(x: T): string`, and `Echo<T, U>(x: T): string` matches no virtual member of that name.

Parameter modifiers that must match: `ref`, `out`, `owned`, `scoped` (a `scoped`/unscoped mismatch changes the caller's capture/freeze contract in both directions, [§11.2](#sec-interface-declaration)). The `when true`/`when false` postcondition clause on an `out` parameter ([§22.4](#sec-out-nullability-postcondition)) must match exactly as well — an override may neither add nor drop it. Return modifiers that must match: `owned`. A mismatch — for example, a base method declaring `Foo(owned x: T)` and the override declaring `Foo(x: T)` — is a compile error. The compiler does not infer or relax these modifiers across the override boundary, because they affect the method's contract rather than its implementation.

Fields, constructors, destructors, and static members may not be virtual.

<a id="sec-hiding-is-not-allowed"></a>
### 12.2 Hiding is not allowed

Declaring a member in a derived class with the same name as **any** inherited member **visible at the derived class's declaration site** is a compile error, unless the declaration is an `override` of a virtual member with a matching signature per [§12.1](#sec-members-are-non-virtual-by-default) — exact, except for the parameter-nullability widening (`T` → `T?`) that §12.1 admits. This holds even when the signatures differ: a derived class cannot add an overload to an inherited method's name, and an inherited overload set does not extend across the inheritance boundary (Appendix C.1). To override a virtual base member, use `override`. To add a new member, choose a different name. A `Serialize` or `Deserialize` synthesized for a derived class's own serialization conformance is not a hiding declaration ([§9.8](#sec-serialization-synthesis) *Inherited components*); one the derived class hand-writes over a base's synthesized member is.

**The blocked-name set.** `public` and `protected` base members always block; an `internal` base member blocks exactly when it is visible at the derived declaration site ([§13.4](#sec-modules-and-internal) — the base class is in the same module); a `private` base member never blocks — two same-named `private` fields in base and derived are distinct members and legal, and a base class adding a `private` member is never a source-breaking change for subclasses that cannot see it — except that a derived class nested inside the base class ([§11.6](#sec-nested-types)) sees the base's `private` members and is blocked by them. The rule's recorded motivation is shadowing a member the author *could see* (rationale [§8.1](Bezel_Design_Rationale.md#sec-member-hiding-is-forbidden)); an invisible member confuses no reader and no dispatch. When a base member was invisible at the derived declaration site, the derived declaration creates a **distinct member**: no override relationship and no shared overload family exist between the two. Name lookup — which already filters by visibility — *selects* a member by the receiver's static type ([§12.1](#sec-members-are-non-virtual-by-default)); the selected member then dispatches per its own §12.1 virtual-ness (an `internal virtual` base member keeps its own override chain). An access through the derived type's surface reaches the derived member; an access through a base-typed receiver reaches the base member — for every caller, including one that can see both. This residual is the deliberate scope of the no-shadow guarantee across module boundaries: a cross-module `internal` name collision is invisible at authoring time, and guarding against it would make a module's non-public member names a compatibility contract.

The rule is not limited to instance members. A static member's name is likewise unavailable for redeclaration in a derived class — static members cannot be virtual ([§12.1](#sec-members-are-non-virtual-by-default)), so no `override` escape exists for them. Operator declarations are covered **per operator token**: a derived class may not declare an `operator <op>` overload when any base class declares an overload of the same token, whatever the parameter types. This is what keeps [§25.2](#sec-operator-overloading-restrictions)'s inherited-operator candidate set duplicate-free within a single inheritance chain — a chain contributes at most one declaring type per operator token, so derived-operand resolution never faces a base-vs-derived intra-chain ambiguity.

<a id="sec-base-member"></a>
### 12.3 `base.Member`

Inside a derived member, `base.Name(...)` calls the base class's implementation, bypassing virtual dispatch. `base` is legal only inside instance members of a derived class.

<a id="sec-sealing"></a>
### 12.4 Sealing

`sealed` on an override prevents further overriding. `sealed` on a class prevents inheritance from that class:

```bezel
public sealed override method Speak(): string => "Woof!";

public sealed class Bulldog: Dog
  // ...
end Bulldog;
```

On a member, `sealed` appears only as the compound `sealed override` ([§11.5](#sec-modifier-order)): a member declaration carrying `sealed` without `override` is a compile error, whatever the member's kind and whatever other dispatch modifier it carries. A `sealed override` names a virtual member to override, under [§12.1](#sec-members-are-non-virtual-by-default)'s override-matching rule, like any other `override`.

A member of a `sealed` class may not be declared `virtual`: the class admits no subclass, so a new virtual slot on it can never be filled, and an inert modifier that reads as load-bearing misleads every reader of the declaration — the rule [§9.2](#sec-record-dispatch-modifiers) states for the implicitly sealed value kinds, read here for the explicitly sealed class. `override` and `sealed override` are unaffected: they fill a slot an ancestor declared, which is what the `sealed override` example above and the sealed-derived-class idiom do. `abstract` on a member is already excluded — it requires an `abstract` class ([§12.5](#sec-abstract-classes-and-members)), and `abstract` and `sealed` are mutually exclusive class modifiers ([§11.7](#sec-static-classes)).

<a id="sec-abstract-classes-and-members"></a>
### 12.5 Abstract classes and members

`abstract` on a class permits abstract members and forbids direct instantiation. `abstract` on a member declares it without a body; every concrete subclass must override it.

```bezel
public abstract class Shape
  public abstract method Area(): decimal;
  public abstract property Name: string;

  public method Describe(): string => $"A {Name} with area {Area()}";
end Shape;
```

An abstract member ends with `;` and has no `end`. Abstract members are implicitly virtual; the `virtual` keyword is not written.

A class containing one or more abstract members must itself be `abstract` (or `closed`, [§11.7](#sec-static-classes)). An abstract class need not override every abstract member of its base.

`new` on an abstract or `closed` class is a compile error.

A call to an `abstract` (or any virtual-family) member on `this` from a constructor body is governed by [§22.7](#sec-observing-this-during-construction): rejected outside sealed, non-abstract classes.

<a id="sec-async-and-abstract"></a>
### 12.6 `async` and `abstract`

`async abstract` is a compile error. An abstract method whose implementations are expected to be asynchronous declares a `Task` or `Task<T>` return type without `async`:

```bezel
public abstract class DataSource
  public abstract method LoadAsync(): Task<string>;
  public abstract method SaveAsync(data: string): Task;
end DataSource;

public class FileSource: DataSource
  public async override method LoadAsync(): Task<string>
    return await File.ReadAllTextAsync(_path);
  end LoadAsync;

  public async override method SaveAsync(data: string): Task
    await File.WriteAllTextAsync(_path, data);
  end SaveAsync;
end FileSource;
```

The same rule applies to interface members.

<a id="sec-type-tests-is-is-not-as"></a>
### 12.7 Type tests: `is`, `is not`, `as`

`is T` tests whether a value is an instance of `T` and produces `bool`. When the test succeeds and the tested expression is one of [§7.4](#sec-narrowing-applies-to-locals-only)'s narrowing carriers, the carrier is **flow-narrowed** to `T` within the controlled block:

```bezel
if animal is Dog then
  animal.Bark();        // animal narrowed to Dog
end;
```

Narrowing applies to the original carrier. A `readonly`-field carrier is tracked as §7.4 tracks it: no call, `await` or closure invalidates the fact, reassigning its root drops it, and the rule does not apply in the declaring type's construction window — `if this._f is Dog then this._f.Bark(); end;` over `readonly _f: Animal` narrows `this._f`. A `ref` parameter is never type-narrowed, for the reason [§7.4](#sec-narrowing-applies-to-locals-only) gives for its nullability: inside `if a is Dog then … end;` over `ref a: Animal`, `a` is an `Animal` throughout the block, and the value is reached through a copy (`var c := a; if c is Dog then c.Bark(); end;`) or bound with `as` (`var d := a as Dog;`). Reassignment within the controlled block invalidates the type narrowing, whatever the right-hand side's type (the assignment may still establish [§7.4](#sec-member-access-on-nullable-values)'s non-null fact), and so do §7.4's other invalidating forms: passing the variable as a `ref` or `out` argument and, for a mutably captured variable, the first operation that can transfer control to user code.

`is null` tests whether the value is null. `is not null` tests whether it is non-null and narrows to the non-nullable form.

`is not T` (for a non-null type T) does not narrow in the true branch (the value could be many non-T types).

In `else` branches: for `is null` and `is not null`, narrowing applies (the variable is known-null or non-null respectively); for `is T`, no narrowing in the else branch (the variable could be many non-T types); for `is not T`, the variable is narrowed to `T` in the else branch.

When two `is` tests are joined with `and`, both narrowings are in effect throughout the combined true branch.

**Narrowing at an `Object` or interface location.** When the narrowed carrier's *declared* type is `Object`, an interface, or the nullable form of either (`Object?`, `I?`) and the tested type `T` is a **value type**, that carrier's storage is a [§8.6](#sec-boxing) box, and the two directions differ. The carriers are [§7.4](#sec-narrowing-applies-to-locals-only)'s narrowing carriers throughout. **Reads** through the narrowed binding read the box's payload: after `var a: [3]int := [4, 5, 6]; var o: Object := a;`, inside `if o is [3]int then … end;` the read `o[0]` reads the payload's element, and `var b: [3]int := o;` copies the payload out under [§3.2](#sec-reference-vs-value-types)'s value-copy rule — in neither case the `a` it was copied from.

**A write whose store would land in the box is a compile error**, in each of the three positions that can produce one: **(i)** an assignment, compound assignment, or `++`/`--` whose target is an lvalue chain (grammar [A.6](#sec-appendix-a-statements) `LValue`) extending the binding with a `.` or `[…]` hop — `o[0] := 9`, `o.X := 5`, `o[0] += 1`, `o.X++`; **(ii)** such a chain passed as a **`ref` or `out` argument**, which [§22.3](#sec-ref-and-out-argument-locations)'s assignable-storage-location categories admit (`ref o[0]`, `out o.X`) and through which the callee's write reaches the payload alike whether the argument aliases the caller's location directly or is written back through the accessor bracket — `Swap(ref o[0], ref o[1])` is the shape; and **(iii)** the binding, or such a chain, passed as an **inline-array argument at an `extern` parameter**, where the by-address rule of [§32.5](#sec-ffi-compatible-types)/[§15.1.3](#sec-inline-array-ffi) passes the address of that storage and native writes land in the payload exactly as a Bezel write would. What is *not* rejected is the **bare-binding** compound and `++`/`--` form: `o += 1` and `o++` are equivalent to `o := o + 1` ([§6.6](#sec-compound-assignments), [§17.6](#sec-the-increment-and-decrement-operators)), and that store targets the *declared* `Object`/interface location — it reads through the narrowing, boxes the result afresh under [§5.1](#sec-implicit-conversions), and invalidates the narrowing, exactly as the spelled-out `o := o + 1` does; only the chain-rooted forms of (i) store into the box. The diagnostic names [§8.6](#sec-boxing) — boxing copied the value; the box is shared — and the explicit copy-out/mutate/re-box spelling, `var b: [3]int := o; b[0] := 9; o := b;`. That final `o := b` is not a write through the narrowing: it stores to the declared `Object`/interface location, boxing its right-hand side under [§5.1](#sec-implicit-conversions) into a **fresh** box — boxed `()`, which an implementation may intern ([§8.6](#sec-boxing-of-the-unit-value)), is the one licensed exception — that leaves every other reference to the old one untouched, and — being a reassignment of the narrowed variable — it invalidates the narrowing for the remainder of the controlled block (above). Narrowing to a *reference* type is unaffected: no box is involved, and writes through the narrowed binding are ordinary reference-type writes. (Rationale [§11.6](Bezel_Design_Rationale.md#sec-is-does-not-bind).)

**Value-typed operands.** An operand whose static type is a value type or the nullable form of one — a primitive, record, enum, choice, inline array, or the unit type; for a carrier **type**-narrowed by this section, its *declared* type, so a narrowed `Object` or interface carrier stays a boxed reference operand ([§7.4](#sec-member-access-on-nullable-values)'s nullability narrowing changes no operand's value or reference kind) — tested by `is`, `is not`, or `as` against a **reference** target (a class, an interface — including one the value type implements — `string`, or `Object`) is a **compile error**, as the [§19.3](#sec-patterns) type pattern is: the test could not discriminate at runtime, and answering it would need an implicit boxing conversion, which a type-test operand never performs. Box explicitly and test the box — `var o: Object := p;` then `o is IShape`, or `(var o: Object := p; o is IShape)` ([§17.15](#sec-the-binding-atom)). A test in which a **type parameter** stands on either side — a carrier `v: T` or `v: T?`, or a target `T` — is decided **per instantiation** ([§3.6](#sec-derived-type-properties) rule 2), and the rejection above is not re-applied through a substitution: where the operand's type at the instantiation is a reference type the test is the ordinary runtime test; where it is a value type — a carrier's value substitution, or a concrete value operand — `is` and `is not` against a reference target `R`, written or a target's substitution (a nullable substitution counting as its underlying type), take, allocating nothing, the answer the boxed value would give (for a move-only value, which is never boxed, the answer its type's conformance gives) — `v is R` is true exactly when `v` is non-null and `R` is `Object` or an interface to which the boxed value converts ([§14.2](#sec-interface-conformance) conformance, with [§12.9](#sec-variance) variance) — and `as` against a reference target is rejected at the instantiation site whatever the answer, since a true answer would be the implicit box, the diagnostic naming the explicit box and, for a carrier, `where T: class`: `p is T` with `p: int` is `true` at `T = Object` and `false` at `T = string`, and `p as T` is rejected at both. Against a value type other than its own or its own nullable form that is not a type parameter, a concrete value-typed operand is likewise a compile error, as the [§19.3](#sec-patterns) pattern naming another type is: its runtime type is its static type ([§8.2](#sec-gettype)), so `i is long` over an `int`, `a is [4]int` over a `[3]int` and `p as Q` over a record `Pt` could never succeed — `is` tests the type, never whether the value would convert ([§5.2](#sec-explicit-conversions)). A test naming the operand's own type is admitted: statically true (for `as`, the value wrapped as `T?`), or, over the nullable form, the null test. Where a type parameter stands on either side (above) and at an instantiation both the operand's type and the target are value types, the test is likewise decided per instantiation, allocating nothing and never rejected for its answer: `true` when the substituted types are identical, a nullable substitution of the target counting as its underlying type (over the nullable form, the null test; for `as`, the value wrapped as `T?`), `false` otherwise (`as`: `null`) — `v is long` with `v: T` is `false` at `T = int`, and `p is T` with `p: int` is `true` at `T = int` and `false` at `T = long`. An inline-array or unit `as` target is rejected at the instantiation site whatever the answer ([§17.4](#sec-the-is-is-not-and-as-operators)).

`is` does not bind. There is no `is T name` syntax. To bind, use `as` (a recorded decline-with-reasons — rationale [§11.6](Bezel_Design_Rationale.md#sec-is-does-not-bind)):

```bezel
var dog: Dog? := animal as Dog;
if dog <> null then
  Console.WriteLine(dog.Name);
end;
```

`as` returns the value cast to the target type, or `null` if the cast fails. Its result is always nullable.

**Ownership.** Both `is` and `as` are non-destructive on their operand — the operand retains its ownership state, the narrowing above and the borrow `as` produces transfer nothing, and transferring across a type test takes an explicit move from the original variable after narrowing: the rule, with the borrowed-result rationale and the explicit-move remedy, is [§17.4](#sec-the-is-is-not-and-as-operators)'s (*Type tests and ownership*).

<a id="sec-constructor-chaining"></a>
### 12.8 Constructor chaining

A derived class's constructor may chain to a base constructor:

```bezel
public constructor(name: string, balance: decimal, rate: decimal)
  base(name, balance);
  _rate := rate;
end constructor;
```

A `base(...)` call, if present, appears before the constructor body — it is syntactically distinct from the body's statements (see grammar A.4, `CtorChain`). If neither `base(...)` nor `this(...)` is written, the compiler inserts an implicit `base()` call (which requires the base class to have a parameterless constructor; otherwise the chain must be explicit).

`this(...)` chains to another constructor in the same type, and the chain must end: following each constructor's `this(...)` to the constructor it resolves to ([§22.6](#sec-overloading)) — resolved at the declaration, not per instantiation — must reach a constructor that does not chain with `this(...)`. A constructor that reaches itself — directly or through other constructors of the type — is a compile error at its declaration, reported naming the participating constructors, as for an inheritance cycle ([§12.10](#sec-inheritance-cycles)). At most one of `base(...)` or `this(...)` may appear, and only in the chaining position before the body. The chaining position is outside the body: the only reads a `base(...)`/`this(...)` argument may make are of the constructor's own parameters, constants, and statics; it may **not** read a field or auto-property of the object under construction — nor, in a class with a primary constructor, a primary-constructor parameter ([§22.10](#sec-methods-and-constructors-primary-constructors); the field half is [§22.7](#sec-observing-this-during-construction)'s ground: nothing of `this` is assigned yet).

A constructor in an abstract class is permitted; it runs only via `base(...)` from a concrete subclass.

<a id="sec-variance"></a>
### 12.9 Variance

Generic interface type parameters may be marked `out` (covariant) or `in` (contravariant):

```bezel
interface IEnumerable<out T>
  method GetEnumerator(): owned IEnumerator<T>;
end IEnumerable;

interface IComparer<in T>            // illustrative: the standard library declares no
  method Compare(a: T, b: T): int;   //   contravariant interface (`IEqualityComparer<T>`
end IComparer;                       //   is invariant)
```

`out` requires T to appear only in output positions (return types, read-only property types, `out` parameters). `in` requires T to appear only in input positions. The compiler enforces position constraints.

Position is composed across nested type constructors. A type parameter inside another generic type inherits position from that wrapper's variance: T inside `IEnumerator<T>` (where `IEnumerator` is `out T'`) has the same position the wrapper itself sits in. Function types are themselves variant (covariant in return, contravariant in parameter, see below), and the same composition rule applies. The practical consequence — relevant for event interfaces — is that T appearing inside the *parameter* of a function type that is itself the *parameter* of a method ends up in covariant position, because contravariant-of-contravariant is covariant. A concrete worked example: in `IEvent<out T>` (stdlib [§6.5](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-events-ievent-eventsource)), the method `Subscribe(scoped handler: (T) -> ())` places T inside `(T) -> ()` (contravariant in T) which is itself a parameter of `Subscribe` (an input, contravariant), giving T a covariant position overall — `out T` is sound.

Type parameters without `out` or `in` are invariant. Classes, records, and concrete generic types are always invariant — and the variance markers are **interface-only syntax**: `in`/`out` on a generic parameter of a class, record, method, or type alias ([§27.8](#sec-type-aliases)) is a **compile error** (makes the rejection explicit; the shared `GenericParam` grammar admits the marker everywhere and outside interface declarations it is rejected semantically, Appendix A.4). A marker the language cannot honor must not parse as decoration — `class Box<out T>` silently accepted-and-ignored would promise an assignability the type does not have. Additionally, an interface declaring **static members** may not mark its parameters variant ([§11.8](#sec-static-interface-members)).

Variance applies only when the type argument is a reference type. `IEnumerable<int>` is a perfectly valid type and is used pervasively; what is rejected is the *variant assignment* of `IEnumerable<int>` to `IEnumerable<Object>`, which would require per-element boxing at every access. For value-typed T, the only legal assignment of `IEnumerable<T>` is to `IEnumerable<T>` itself or to `Object`. Reference-typed T admits the full covariant chain — `IEnumerable<Dog>` is assignable to `IEnumerable<Animal>` and to `IEnumerable<Object>` because the underlying references compose without conversion.

Function types are automatically variant — covariant in return type, contravariant in parameter types (subject to [§27.1.1](#sec-function-type-assignability)'s announcement-bearing return slots, which admit no conversion across a family boundary — composed positions included).

<a id="sec-variance-and-interface-inheritance"></a>
#### Variance and interface inheritance

A generic interface may extend a generic base whose variance is different from its own. The most common case in the standard library: `IList<T>` is invariant in T (it has mutating methods) and extends `IReadOnlyList<out T>` (which is covariant in T):

```bezel
public interface IReadOnlyCollection<out T>: IEnumerable<T>
  pure readonly property Count: int;
end IReadOnlyCollection;

public interface IReadOnlyList<out T>: IReadOnlyCollection<T>
  readonly property [i: int]: T;
end IReadOnlyList;

public interface IList<T>: IReadOnlyList<T>, ICollection<T>
  property [i: int]: T;
end IList;
```

The extending interface instantiates the base's variant parameter with its own type parameter, holding the deriving interface's variance. The substitution is `IReadOnlyList<T>` where the bound T is whatever T the deriving interface has; if `IList<T>` has T invariant, then the inherited `IReadOnlyList<T>` is also invariant in T from `IList<T>`'s perspective. The base's covariance is *available* when accessed through the base type — `IReadOnlyList<Dog>` is assignable to `IReadOnlyList<Animal>` — but accessing the same instance through `IList<Dog>` does not admit the covariant assignment, because `IList<T>` is invariant.

This means an instance whose runtime type implements `IList<Dog>` is assignable to:
- `IList<Dog>` (exact match)
- `IReadOnlyList<Dog>`, `IReadOnlyList<Animal>`, `IReadOnlyList<Object>` (covariant chain via the read-only view)
- `IReadOnlyCollection<Dog>`, `IReadOnlyCollection<Animal>`, `IReadOnlyCollection<Object>` (covariant chain via the read-only-collection view)
- `ICollection<Dog>`, `IEnumerable<Dog>`, `IEnumerable<Animal>`, `IEnumerable<Object>` (other inherited interfaces, with their own variance)

It is *not* assignable to `IList<Animal>` — the variance of the base interface does not propagate through the deriving interface's signature.

The position-composition rules above continue to apply within each interface in isolation. The compiler enforces position constraints on each interface declaration independently: `IReadOnlyList<out T>` is checked with T in covariant position throughout its body; `IList<T>` is checked with T in any position throughout its body. The inheritance relation only fixes the type argument substituted into the base — it does not alter what positions T may legally appear in within the derived interface.

<a id="sec-inheritance-cycles"></a>
### 12.10 Inheritance cycles

An inheritance cycle is a compile error. A type may not, directly or transitively, list itself among its base types — neither as the base class of a class, nor as an extended interface of an interface. The relation followed is the union of base-class edges ([§11.1](#sec-class-declaration)) and extended-interface edges ([§11.2](#sec-interface-declaration)); a cycle is any sequence of types where each lists the next as a base type and the sequence returns to its start. The simplest case is a type naming itself (`class C: C`); the general case is a chain (`class A: B`, `class B: C`, `class C: A`), or the same shape among interfaces (`interface I: J`, `interface J: I`). **Every cycle lies wholly within one edge kind:** an interface may extend only other interfaces ([§11.2](#sec-interface-declaration)), so no edge ever returns from an interface to a class, and a class's conformance edge to an interface is a one-way exit from the class-extension relation — there are no mixed class/interface cycles for the check to find. (The grammar does not produce one either: `Inheritance` is shared between `ClassDecl` and `InterfaceDecl` (Appendix A.3), so an interface naming a class *parses*, but [§11.2](#sec-interface-declaration) rejects it before any cycle check reaches it.) The compiler detects the cycle and reports an error naming the participating types; the cycle is never silently broken or otherwise tolerated.

---

<a id="sec-visibility"></a>
## 13. Visibility

<a id="sec-levels"></a>
### 13.1 Levels

Four levels:

| Level | Visible to |
|---|---|
| `public` | Anyone who can see the enclosing context |
| `internal` | Code in the same module |
| `protected` | The declaring class and all classes derived from it |
| `private` | The declaring class only |

`internal` and `protected` are incomparable: a derived class in a different module sees `protected` but not `internal`; an unrelated class in the same module sees `internal` but not `protected`.

<a id="sec-top-level-types"></a>
### 13.2 Top-level types

Top-level types may be `public` or `internal`. They may not be `protected` (no enclosing class) or `private` (no file-scope concept). The default is `internal`:

```bezel
public class BankAccount
  // ...
end BankAccount;

class Helper           // implicitly internal
  // ...
end Helper;
```

<a id="sec-class-members"></a>
### 13.3 Class members

Every class member must declare its visibility explicitly, except a member kind user code can never invoke or name at a use site — for such a member no visibility choice exists to spell, and it carries no visibility keyword. Currently four kinds qualify: a `static constructor` (the runtime is the only caller; [§22.7](#sec-constructors)); a `polymorphic` registry (a compiler-consumed serialization map, not a callable member; [§9.8](#sec-serialization-synthesis), Appendix A.3); a `destructor` (an implementation hook called by the compiler-generated `Dispose()`, never directly callable — the customization point is `destructor`, the public surface is `Dispose()`; [§28.4](#sec-the-destructor)); and an `invariant` member (a predicate the compiler instruments at the class's public boundary; grammar A.4 `InvariantDecl`, [§22.16](#sec-class-invariants)). On every other member, omitting the visibility keyword is a compile error. (The asymmetry with [§13.2](#sec-top-level-types)'s file-scope default is deliberate: file scope has one safe default — module-internal — while a member's four-way choice has none, so explicitness is demanded.)

Interface members do not declare visibility; they are implicitly public.

<a id="sec-modules-and-internal"></a>
### 13.4 Modules and `internal`

A module is the set of all source files declaring the same `module Name.Path;` **presented to the module's one compilation ([§2.8.1](#sec-module-identity-and-closure))**; `internal` access is closed by that compilation — no later source file joins a module by declaring its name, and within an SCC unit each member module's internals remain invisible to the other members. The dotted form is a single name; files in `Foo` get no special access to files in `Foo.Bar`.

A file declares exactly one module.

<a id="sec-no-combined-visibilities"></a>
### 13.5 No combined visibilities

Bezel does not provide combined forms (no `protected internal`, no `private protected`).

<a id="sec-accessor-visibility"></a>
### 13.6 Accessor visibility

A property or indexer's `get` or `set` may carry its own visibility, which must not be *less* restrictive than the property's overall visibility (equal visibility is permitted, though redundant; the useful form is a more restrictive accessor):

```bezel
public property Name: string
  get => _name;
  private set => _name := value;
end Name;
```

An accessor without explicit visibility inherits the property's overall visibility. An accessor visibility *less* restrictive than the property is a compile error.

The auto-property shorthand `public property Name: string private set;` is equivalent to the block form.

<a id="sec-visibility-and-inheritance"></a>
### 13.7 Visibility and inheritance

- An override must declare the same visibility as the base member.
- **Every type appearing in a member's signature must be at least as visible as the member.** The rule covers: field types, parameter types, return types, property types, indexer parameter and result types, and types named in `where` clauses on a public/protected member. The rule applies at every visibility level — a `public` member's signature types must be `public` (or more permissive); an `internal` member's signature types must be `internal` (or more); a `protected` member's must be at least `protected`; a `private` member is unconstrained (since `private` is the most restrictive level).
- A class's base class and implemented interfaces must be at least as visible as the class.

The signature-type-visibility rule applies to a member's *declared* signature. Generic-method type parameters whose substitution at the call site could narrow visibility are not constrained — the caller's substitution is the caller's choice, not the declarer's.

```bezel
public class Outer
  private class NestedPrivate
    // ...
  end NestedPrivate;
  
  // ERROR: _x is internal, but NestedPrivate is private — the field's
  //        type is not as visible as the field.
  internal _x: NestedPrivate;

  // OK: also private, matches NestedPrivate's visibility.
  private _y: NestedPrivate;
end Outer;
```

---

<a id="sec-generics"></a>
## 14. Generics

<a id="sec-generic-declarations"></a>
### 14.1 Generic declarations

Classes, interfaces, records, and methods may be generic:

```bezel
class MyArray<T>
  // ...
end MyArray;

interface IComparable<T>
  method CompareTo(other: T): int;
end IComparable;

record Pair<TFirst, TSecond>(First: TFirst, Second: TSecond);

static class Utils
  public static method Swap<T>(ref a: T, ref b: T)
    var temp := a;
    a := b;
    b := temp;
  end Swap;
end Utils;
```

Type parameters use angle brackets. Multiple parameters are comma-separated.

**Type-parameter names.** The names in one type-parameter list are distinct, and a generic method's type parameter may not reuse the name of a type parameter in scope at the method's declaration, including its enclosing type's and its generic extension block's ([§26.4](#sec-generic-extensions)), but not, at a method of a local type, an enclosing method's or type's, which is not in scope in a local type's declaration ([§21.10](#sec-local-type-declarations)'s no-reference restriction), as an enclosing type's is not in a nested type's ([§11.6](#sec-nested-types)). Either is a compile error at the offending type-parameter list naming this rule; the remedy is renaming one of the two.
