A type parameter has no qualified spelling, so a method parameter reusing an enclosing one's name would leave the enclosing parameter unnameable in the method's signature, `where` clauses and body while the members it types stay in reach: a field typed by the class's `T` beside a parameter typed by the method's `T`, two types spelled alike in one body. Type parameters of declarations that do not nest share no scope: a `Go<T>` calling a static `Id<T>` is admitted, and the call substitutes the callee's own parameter ([§14.5](#sec-type-argument-inference)). The rename is always available to an override or an interface implementation, because a method's type parameters match the overridden or implemented declaration's by number and position, not by name ([§11.2](#sec-interface-declaration)'s *Generic members*, [§12.1](#sec-members-are-non-virtual-by-default)): inside `class Sh<X>: Base`, `Base`'s `virtual method VB<X>(b: Box<X>): int` is overridden as `override method VB<Y>(b: Box<Y>): int`. The rule compares type parameters with type parameters only; it does not reach a type parameter named like an ordinary type ([§2.3](#sec-always-available-names)'s `Object` row).

**Instantiation and its site.** An **instantiation** of a generic declaration is the constructed type or constructed member obtained by substituting type arguments for its type parameters; its **site** is the program point at which the program forms one. A generic type is instantiated by being **named**, not only by being constructed: a constructed type in a field, local, parameter, or return type annotation, in a base clause or interface list, in a `where` bound, in a choice payload or inline-array element type, in a type alias ([§27.8](#sec-type-aliases)), or as a type argument of another constructed type is an instantiation site, as are a `new` expression, a `typeof` or `default` operand, and a call to a generic member at explicit or inferred type arguments. `var b: Box<string>;` forms `Box<string>` exactly as `new Box<string>(…)` does, and the nullable form `G<A>?` forms `G<A>`. **Every such reference supplies exactly the declared number of type arguments**. Bezel has no raw and no open generic type reference: `Box` bare and `Box<int, string>` are equally compile errors at a `class Box<T>`, each naming the declared arity, and the same holds for a generic type alias ([§27.8](#sec-type-aliases)) — an alias reference has no arity to fall back on, its body being a substitution rather than a type. The rule holds inside a generic type's own declaration — its member bodies, field initializers and member signatures: there, too, the bare `Box` fixes arity 0 ([§2.2](#sec-imports)), and the current instantiation is spelled with the type's own parameters, `Box<T>`, or a member of it is reached by its bare name through [§2.7](#sec-name-resolution-order)'s enclosing-type lookup. This is what makes a type's program-wide identity, which [§2.8.3](#sec-transitive-closure-and-type-identity) keys on arity, well defined at every naming site. Arity is not inferred at a *type* reference: [§14.5](#sec-type-argument-inference)'s omit-or-supply-in-full rule is about a call to a generic **member**, which has arguments to infer from, and a type reference has none. Wherever a rule of this specification fires *at the instantiation site* — [§3.6](#sec-derived-type-properties) rule 2's per-instantiation property evaluation, this section's constraint checks ([§14.2](#sec-constraints)), the owning-element restriction of [§14.4](#sec-owned-as-a-generic-argument), the owning-inline-array element check of [§15.1.1](#sec-owning-inline-arrays), and the generic-owned-field check of [§28.5](#sec-owned-fields) — it fires at every such site. A site in a user declaration whose type arguments are or contain a type parameter in scope forms, at each instantiation of the declaration that declares the parameter (the innermost such declaration, where the arguments contain parameters of nested declarations), the instantiation its arguments substitute to, and that instantiation's site is then an instantiation site of the formed one: the site of `Outer<R>` forms the `Bag<R>` of `Outer<T>`'s field `Bag<T>`, and a call `F<R>(…)` forms the `Eq<R>` of the call `Eq<U>(a, b)` in `F<U>`'s body ([§3.6](#sec-derived-type-properties) rule 2 states what this carries). The instantiation-request graph of [§14.6](#sec-recursive-instantiation) reads the same forms.

<a id="sec-constraints"></a>
### 14.2 Constraints

The `where` clause restricts the substitutions a type parameter accepts:

| Constraint | Accepts |
|---|---|
| *(none)* | Any type, nullable or not. T is treated conservatively as possibly nullable. |
| `where T: notnull` | Non-nullable types only (value or reference). A nullable type, value or reference, is excluded. |
| `where T: class` | Non-nullable reference types only — classes (including `Array<T>`, `OwningArray<T>`, and other heap collection types), interfaces, `string`, function types. |
| `where T: value` | Non-nullable value types — records, enums, choices ([§35](#sec-choices)), primitives, inline arrays (all forms), the unit type. A nullable value type (e.g. `int?`) does **not** satisfy `value`. Generic body must use only move-compatible operations on T if T may be a move-only value — a move-only inline array or an owning-classified choice instantiation ([§15.3](#sec-move-only-value-types), [§35.4](#sec-choice-classification)); the demand is checked at each instantiation ([§7.10](#sec-generics-and-nullability), [§3.6](#sec-derived-type-properties) rule 2). |
| `where T: SomeClass` | Non-nullable subtypes of `SomeClass` (the class itself and its descendants). Class types only; interfaces do not extend classes in Bezel. |
| `where T: IFoo` | Non-nullable types conforming to `IFoo`: classes implementing it, records and enums implementing it, interfaces extending it, and primitives conforming through their standard-library declarations or the compiler-provided conformances of [§11.8](#sec-static-interface-members) (clause 5 below). See "Interface conformance" below. |
| `where T: U` (U a type parameter) | Non-nullable types assignable to the substitution for `U`. See "Type-parameter bounds" below. |
| `where T: new()` | Class types with a `public` parameterless constructor, `abstract` and `closed` classes excluded ([§12.5](#sec-abstract-classes-and-members)); **defaultable** value types ([§17.11](#sec-the-default-operator)), every nullable value type among them. A nullable reference type is excluded. |
| `where T: sendable` | Types whose **sendable** derived type property ([§3.6](#sec-derived-type-properties), [§30.14](#sec-sendable-types)) holds, decided by the §30.14 computation unchanged ("Derived-property constraints" below). Composes with the other forms (`where T: sendable, class` admits sendable class types). |
| `where T: hashable` | Types whose **hashable** derived type property ([§3.6](#sec-derived-type-properties)) holds — consistent `Equals`/`GetHashCode`, usable as hash-container keys and elements — decided per instantiation by §3.6's computation. States in the signature what `Dictionary<K, V>`/`Set<T>` keys structurally require, so the diagnostic lands at the instantiation of the *user's* generic rather than deep inside the stdlib type. |

Constraints may be combined: `where T: class, IDisposable, new()` requires a non-nullable reference type that implements `IDisposable` and has a public parameterless constructor.

For `where T: new()`: a **class** substitution satisfies the constraint exactly when the class declares a parameterless constructor that is `public` — not merely accessible from some scope — or declares no instance constructor at all, in which case [§22.7](#sec-constructors)'s implicit parameterless constructor, which is `public`, satisfies it on the same terms (a standard-library builtin declaring no constructor satisfies nothing here, [§17.7](#sec-the-new-operator)). Constraint satisfaction is a property of the type alone, checked wherever an instantiation occurs; keying it to accessibility would let the same substitution satisfy the constraint in one module and fail it in another. A **value-type** substitution satisfies the constraint exactly when it is **defaultable** ([§17.11](#sec-the-default-operator)). A nullable value type (`int?`, `Priority?`, the nullable form of any record, enum or choice) is such a substitution and is always defaultable, so it satisfies the constraint, and `new T()` there is `null`. A **nullable reference type** (`Widget?`, `IFoo?`, `string?`) satisfies neither arm: it is not a class type, so it names no constructor for `new T()` to call, and it is not a value type. Inside the generic body, `new T()` for a value substitution is equivalent to `default(T)`: for records this is the zero-valued record (admitting `record Point(X: int, Y: int)` while rejecting records with non-nullable reference fields); for enums it is the zero value — an enum with no declared zero-valued constant is not defaultable ([§17.11](#sec-the-default-operator)) and does not satisfy the constraint. For a class substitution, `new T()` produces an owned reference via the class's parameterless constructor under the standard ownership-discharge rules of [§28.3](#sec-local-variables-ownership-and-borrows). Interface substitutions never satisfy `new()` — no constructor exists. **Nor does an `abstract` or `closed` class**, whether it declares a `public` parameterless constructor or takes [§22.7](#sec-constructors)'s implicit one: [§12.5](#sec-abstract-classes-and-members) makes `new` on such a class a compile error, so admitting the substitution would satisfy a constraint whose sole purpose — `new T()` in the generic body — the language forbids on the very type being substituted. The diagnostic is at the **instantiation site**, naming the class and the constraint, on the same footing as the interface exclusion: it names the type the author wrote rather than a `new T()` in a body they may not own. [§22.7](#sec-constructors)'s implicit constructor is unaffected — an abstract or `closed` base needs it as [§12.8](#sec-constructor-chaining)'s inserted `base()` target, and this exclusion is about the constraint, not about the constructor's existence. **Choices never satisfy the value-type arm** — a consequence of the property: no choice is defaultable ([§17.11](#sec-the-default-operator), [§35.10](#sec-choice-default-with)). A nullable choice `C?` is a nullable value type and satisfies it, as above.

A type-bound constraint — naming a class or interface — implies non-null T. The reasoning is that nullable types `MyClass?` and `IFoo?` are distinct from their non-nullable forms ([§7.1](#sec-non-nullable-and-nullable-types)) and do not themselves implement the interfaces of their non-nullable counterparts: a `null` value satisfies no interface contract. Constraining on a class or interface name therefore admits only non-nullable substitutions, the same way `where T: class` does. Inside the generic body, T is non-nullable; `T?` is its nullable companion.

**`value` requires a non-nullable value type.** A nullable value type — `int?`, `Priority?`, `DateTime?`, and the nullable form of any record or enum — does *not* satisfy `where T: value`. The `value` constraint admits only the non-nullable value type itself; `where T: value` then makes `T?` the nullable companion inside the body. The reasoning matches the type-bound case above: a nullable value type is a distinct type from its non-nullable form ([§7.1](#sec-non-nullable-and-nullable-types)), and its representation differs (it carries the additional `null` state). `where T: notnull` likewise excludes every nullable type — value or reference — for the same reason. To accept a nullable value type, write the constraint against the underlying value type and use `T?` in the body.

`T?` always denotes the nullable form of T. `default(T)` produces the zero/null value of T ([§17.11](#sec-the-default-operator)).

Contradictory constraint combinations (e.g. `class, value`) are compile errors.

**Type-parameter bounds (`where T: U`).** A constraint whose bound is another type parameter — of the same declaration, or of the enclosing type — is grammatical and has subtype semantics: a substitution S for `T` satisfies `where T: U` exactly when S is non-nullable and is *assignable to* the substitution for `U` — identical to it, a subclass of a class substitution ([§12](#sec-inheritance-and-dispatch)), or a type conforming to an interface substitution (the conformance rule below). The check runs at instantiation, after both parameters are substituted. Inside the body, a `T`-typed value is usable in any `U`-typed position, and `T` conforms to every interface that `U`'s own constraints guarantee; an unconstrained `U` contributes only `Object`'s surface. Like every type-bound constraint, `where T: U` implies non-null `T` (`T?` is the nullable companion). A self-referential bound (`where T: T`) or a cycle among type-parameter bounds (`where T: U` together with `where U: T`) is a compile error at the declaration.

**A type parameter as the type argument.** At an instantiation site ([§14.1](#sec-generic-declarations)) whose type argument for a constrained parameter is itself a type parameter `P` in scope — a field `C<W>` in `class Box<W>`, a call `G<U>(…)` at written or inferred type arguments in the body of `F<U>` — the constraint is decided **at that site, by `P`'s own constraints**, the assumption under which the enclosing declaration is checked ([§3.6](#sec-derived-type-properties) rule 2); for a method type parameter of an override or interface implementation, they are its constraint set as *Constraints on overrides and interface implementations* below defines it. `P` satisfies the constraint exactly when its constraints guarantee it at every substitution they admit, as a matter of language rule, which is how [§22.6](#sec-owned-and-overload-resolution)'s declaration guard reads this section's conformance computation: an ordinary interface's conforming set is open, so an interface bound excludes only what a language rule excludes. So for `class C<T> where T: new()`, `C<W>` is admitted in `class Box<W> where W: new()` and rejected in an unconstrained `class Box<W>`. `class` is guaranteed, for instance, by `where W: class`, by a class bound, and by a bound naming `IDisposable` or an interface extending it, whose conforming set holds classes and interfaces only (*Worked example: `where T: IDisposable`* below). A type bound guarantees `where T: IFoo` by *Interface conformance* rule 6 below, and `where T: SomeClass` when it names `SomeClass` or a class derived from it, directly or through a `where W: V` chain. A derived-property constraint is guaranteed only by `P`'s carrying the same constraint, since nothing is inferred (*Derived-property constraints* below). An unsatisfied constraint is a compile error at that site, naming the constraint and `P`; the remedy is stating the constraint on `P`, where it binds the declaration's own instantiations instead. The instantiations the site forms at those instantiations ([§14.1](#sec-generic-declarations) *Instantiation and its site*) then satisfy the constraint by construction. **An argument that contains a type parameter.** The same holds wherever a constraint's satisfaction turns on a type parameter in scope though the argument for the constrained parameter is not one: an argument that contains one (`C<Pair<W>>`, `C<Array<W>>`, `C<W?>`), or, under `where T: U`, an argument for `T` whose bound's argument is or contains one (`C<Widget, X>` in `class Box<X>`, for `class C<T, U> where T: U`). The constraint is decided at that site, and holds exactly when it holds at every substitution of those parameters that their constraints admit, as a matter of language rule; for a derived-property constraint, a parameter the argument contains counts as having the property only where it carries the same constraint. So `C<Array<W>>` satisfies `class` and fails `value` whatever `W`'s constraints; `C<W?>` fails `notnull`, `class`, `value` and every type bound, and satisfies `hashable` exactly where `W` carries `hashable` ([§3.6](#sec-derived-type-properties)'s hashable row, clause (c)) and `new()` exactly where `W`'s constraints guarantee a value type (as `where W: value` does, `W?` then being a nullable value type); and `C<Widget, X>` is rejected in an unconstrained `Box<X>`, which admits `X = int`. An unsatisfied constraint is a compile error at that site, naming the constraint, the argument and the parameter it turns on; nothing of it is carried to the naming declaration's instantiations. The remedy is a constraint on the parameter that guarantees it (`where W: hashable` for `C<W?>`), or an argument whose satisfaction does not turn on the parameter.

<a id="sec-derived-property-constraints"></a>
#### Derived-property constraints

A `where` clause may name a derived type property ([§3.6](#sec-derived-type-properties)) from the **admitted set** below. Satisfaction is decided per instantiation, after substitution, by the property's defining computation — the same evaluation §3.6 rule 2 already performs; the constraint adds no second definition of the property and can therefore never disagree with the property itself. Nothing is inferred and nothing propagates: a generic declaration that requires the property of a parameter writes the constraint; an unconstrained parameter never acquires it; a generic *type's own* properties remain computed from its structure at each instantiation (§3.6 rule 1 — the constraint is an admission filter on substitutions, never a declaration of the property). Inside the body, `T` counts as having the property wherever a rule of this specification demands it — the per-instantiation re-check for those interior uses is subsumed by the constraint, and one diagnostic (the constraint failure, at the instantiation site) replaces the interior one. Overrides and interface implementations inherit the constraint under the unchanged inheritance rule above. The admitted set grows only by recorded ruling — one property, one decision; there is no negated form and no user-extensible mechanism.

Admitted set of this revision: **`sendable`** ([§30.14](#sec-sendable-types)) and **`hashable`** (the §3.6 property of the same name).

A failed derived-property constraint is diagnosed at the instantiation site naming the constraint, the offending type argument, and the structural reason **as a component path** — §3.6 rule 4, sharpened: for `sendable`, the failing §30.14 rule and the field/element chain that violates it.

<a id="sec-conditionally-admitted-members"></a>
#### Conditionally-admitted members

A **conditionally-admitted member** is a member of a generic type whose *admissibility* — whether it exists on a given receiver at all — is decided per instantiation from the enclosing type's type arguments, rather than from the member's own signature. The enclosing type is well-formed at every admitted substitution; only the member is absent where the condition fails.

Five rules govern every such member:

1. **Compiler-known standard-library types only.** A conditionally-admitted member may be declared only on a type this specification's standard-library companion declares, and only where a row of the register below names it. **A user declaration cannot be conditioned on the enclosing type's arguments**, and a `where` clause on a member naming a type parameter of the *enclosing* declaration is a compile error naming this subsection (a clause naming the *member's own* type parameter is the ordinary constraint form of this section and is unaffected, including where its bound names an enclosing parameter).
2. **Decided after substitution, at the use site.** The condition is evaluated after substitution, on the receiver's instantiated type arguments — the per-instantiation *shape* of [§3.6](#sec-derived-type-properties) rule 2, applied to conditions that need not be derived type properties at all (this register's first two rows are interface conformance and membership of an enumerated set; [§3.6](#sec-derived-type-properties)'s closing sentence). A call at a non-satisfying instantiation is rejected **at the call**, never at the declaration or at the enclosing type's instantiation. **In a generic body**, where the receiver's type arguments, or those of a result instantiation the condition reads, are or contain a type parameter in scope, the condition is read as the section defining it reads a type parameter, under that parameter's constraints. An interface-conformance condition is decided at the call by *Interface conformance* below (rule 6 at a bare type parameter): `Array<T>.Sort()` is rejected in a body whose `T` is unconstrained and admitted under `where T: IComparable<T>`, as `x.CompareTo(y)` on a `T`-typed `x` would be. A condition its defining section decides at each instantiation, where the parameters' constraints do not establish it, makes the call that body's own interior use: the choice classification ([§35.11](#sec-choice-generics)), membership of the FFI-pointee set ([§32.12](#sec-foreign-memory)), and [§9.2](#sec-equality-through-a-type-parameter)'s first kind where no constraint supplies the member. Such a call is not a call at a non-satisfying instantiation: it is read at the instantiations of the declaration that declares the parameter exactly as the condition would be at the substituted arguments ([§3.6](#sec-derived-type-properties) rule 2, [§14.1](#sec-generic-declarations) *Instantiation and its site*), and an equality search exactly as the same `Equals` written on its element type would be.
3. **The diagnostic.** The rejection names (a) the member and the receiver type as instantiated, with the offending type argument spelled out; (b) the condition, in the words of the section that defines it; (c) the structural reason the argument fails it — as a component path where the condition is a derived type property ([§3.6](#sec-derived-type-properties) rule 4); and (d) the remedy the register row states.
4. **An ordinary call otherwise.** Where the member is admitted, the call is an ordinary call: overload resolution ([§22.6](#sec-overloading)), argument evaluation order ([§22.5](#sec-optional-parameters-and-named-arguments)), purity, and ownership all apply unchanged. Conditional admissibility grants no exemption from any of them.
5. **Part of the public contract.** A change to a member's condition is a breaking change for clients relying on it, exactly as [§3.6](#sec-derived-type-properties) rule 3 makes a derived-property flip one.

**The register.** The set is closed and grows **only by recorded ruling** — one member family, one decision; there is no negated form and no user-extensible mechanism.

| Member(s) | Condition on the enclosing type argument | Condition defined in | Remedy the diagnostic states |
|---|---|---|---|
| `Array<T>.Sort()`, `Array<T>.Sorted()`, `OwningArray<T>.Sort()` | `T` conforms to `IComparable<T>` (this section's *Interface conformance*) | this section | the comparer-taking overload |
| `OwningBuffer<T>.DangerousPointer()` | `T` is in the FFI-pointee set (value-typed presentation only) | [§32.12](#sec-foreign-memory), [§32.13](#sec-c-compatible-records) | `OwningBuffer<IntPtr>` for pointer elements |
| `Result<T, E>.Map`, `.MapError`, `.AndThen`, `.UnwrapOr` | receiver **and** result instantiation both value-like | [§35.4](#sec-choice-classification) rule 3; member-specific clauses at [§35.2](#sec-choice-members) | the owning match ([§35.5](#sec-choice-matching)) |
| `ICollection<T>.Contains`/`.Remove(item)` and their `Array<T>` and `LinkedList<T>` implementations; `Stack<T>.Contains`, `Queue<T>.Contains`; `Array<T>.IndexOf`/`.LastIndexOf`; `LinkedList<T>.Find`; the span family's `IndexOf`, `Contains`, `SequenceEqual` | the element type, nullability stripped, has a member for [§9.2](#sec-equality-through-a-type-parameter)'s first kind (`Equals` with an argument of that type) | [§9.2](#sec-equality-through-a-type-parameter) *Through a type parameter* | declaring equality on the element type, which makes it **hashable**; or testing a key the element exposes, by a predicate (stdlib §5's `Any`) or a loop |

**No row of this register is a standing grant.** Each carries a recorded disposition off it, and the register is expected to empty rather than to grow:

- **`Array<T>`/`OwningArray<T>` sorting** is here because [§26.5](#sec-resolution) rule 1 commits instance resolution by *name*: the receiver declares `Sort`, so a constrained extension ([§26.4](#sec-generic-extensions)) spelled `Sort` is never consulted, whatever its clause. Two ways out are open and neither is decided here — give the natural-order form a name the receiver does not declare, or admit a member-level condition (declined at this revision, [Appendix C.1](#sec-appendix-c-type-system)). The row lapses when one is taken.
- **`DangerousPointer()`** is **not implemented** — no admissibility arm and no lowering — and is tracked as a specification-ahead-of-implementation delta ([#1717](https://github.com/s8lap/bezel-lang/issues/1717)); its unimplemented state is not a ground for removal. The row lapses with the sorting row's second way out, as the equality search's does: a member-level condition, once admitted, is the member's declared form. Its row records that status on its face; a row whose member the compiler does not implement, or whose condition it does not enforce, is an ordinary specification-ahead-of-implementation delta and is tracked as one.
- **`Result<T, E>`'s combinators** are here because [§26.2](#sec-what-can-be-extended) closes the extendable list against the choice kind, and closes it *for this reason*: no constraint of this section names the classification a payload-generic extension surface would need. Admitting such a constraint, and opening [§26.2](#sec-what-can-be-extended) with it, would make these four an ordinary constrained extension and retire the row; that is a separate ruling, not assumed here.
- **The equality search** (stdlib [§4](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-collection-equality-search) lists its members) is here because they compare by `Equals` on an unconstrained element type, as the borrowing collections' and spans' signatures declare it, and no signature states the condition: the interface members among them (`ICollection<T>`'s, `IReadOnlySpan<TElement>`'s) cannot move to a constrained extension ([§26.4](#sec-generic-extensions)), which is never consulted for a name the receiver declares ([§26.5](#sec-resolution) rule 1) and cannot carry an interface implementation ([§26.3](#sec-extension-blocks-restrictions)); no admitted constraint states the condition exactly, **hashable** also demanding a `GetHashCode` the comparison never calls; and a `hashable` constraint on the type would refuse `Array<R>` itself. The row lapses with the sorting row's second way out: a member-level condition, once admitted, is these members' declared form.

(Two exclusions, so the closure is checkable. The standard library's `hashable`-requiring sequence operators are **not** in this register: their requirement is an ordinary constraint of this section on a [§26.4](#sec-generic-extensions) extension block, and the standard library spells it there. Nor is a **two-presentation declaration** — a compiler-known standard-library type declared twice by its argument's category, each presentation carrying its own member list (`OwningBuffer<T>`, `Span<T>`, `ReadOnlySpan<T>`; stdlib [§4.14](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-owned-buffers-and-spans)). That is a whole-declaration split under [§3.6](#sec-derived-type-properties)'s behavior-dispatch reservation, which names it by example; this register counts only a member conditioned **within** one presentation — which is why `DangerousPointer()`'s row reads *value-typed presentation only* and is still a row.)

**This is not the `where` clause.** A `where` clause filters the substitutions a type parameter accepts, decided when that parameter's own declaration is instantiated (this section's *Type-parameter bounds*: *"The check runs at instantiation, after both parameters are substituted"*). A conditional member's condition decides nothing about substitutions: `Array<Widget>` is a well-formed type for a `Widget` with no ordering, and only `Array<Widget>.Sort()` is not a call. **The user-writable form of a conditional member is the constrained extension block** ([§26.4](#sec-generic-extensions)), whose `where` clause *"constrains which instantiations of the extended type the extension applies to"* — available for any member name the receiver's type does not itself declare ([§26.5](#sec-resolution) rule 1).

<a id="sec-interface-conformance"></a>
#### Interface conformance

For an interface I and a candidate type T, T **conforms to** I exactly when one of the following holds:

1. **T is a class** that lists I (or any interface extending I) in its inheritance clause, that inherits from a class which conforms to I, or that conforms **implicitly** — every class conforms to `IDisposable` without listing it ([§28.2](#sec-the-idisposable-contract)). Implementation may be direct (the class declares the matching members), inherited (a base class declares them), or compiler-generated (the implicit `Dispose`).
2. **T is a record** that lists I (or any interface extending I) in its inheritance clause and declares matching members — auto-generated members count: the synthesized `Equals(T)` satisfies `IEquatable<T>` (stdlib §2.9's recorded convention — "Records implement this implicitly") whether the record lists `IEquatable<T>` itself or an interface extending it, and satisfies no `IEquatable<U>` at a `U` other than the record type itself at its own type parameters (so `record Pair<T>(A: T): IEquatable<Pair<int>>` still needs a written `Equals`). Records are sealed ([§9.6](#sec-records-and-inheritance)), so conformance is always direct, never inherited from a base type.
3. **T is an interface** that has I in its extension chain — either I is named directly in T's inheritance clause, or T extends an interface that itself conforms to I.
4. **T is an enum** that lists I (or any interface extending I) in its inheritance clause and declares the matching public members ([§10.5](#sec-restrictions)): `enum Priority: IComparable<Priority>` satisfies `where T: IComparable<T>` exactly as a record would — enum interface conformance exists precisely to make enums visible to interface-constrained generics (rationale §9.4).
5. **T is a primitive.** A primitive conforms to the interfaces its standard-library declaration lists: the keyword and PascalCase forms name one type ([§3.4](#sec-keyword-aliases-for-built-in-types)), and stdlib §9 declares that type in record syntax, so `int` conforms to `IComparable<int>`/`IEquatable<int>` through the `Int32` declaration exactly as clause 2 reads for records. A primitive additionally carries the **compiler-provided conformances** of [§11.8](#sec-static-interface-members): the numeric tower conforms to the stdlib §2.19 `INumber<T>`/`ISteppable<T>`/`IParsable<T>` interfaces, and `char` to `ISteppable<char>`/`IParsable<char>`, with no declaration listing them — the intrinsic operations serve as the member witnesses. (The primitive kind remains distinct from the record kind, [§3.1](#sec-type-kinds); this clause, not clause 2, is a primitive's conformance source.)
6. **T is a type parameter** whose constraints guarantee conformance to I ("Type-parameter bounds" above): a type-bound constraint naming I or an interface extending I, directly or through a `where T: U` chain.
7. **T is a choice** ([§35](#sec-choices)) that lists I (or any interface extending I) in its inheritance clause and declares the matching public members ([§35.8](#sec-choice-boxing)) — the enum model. Choices are sealed, so conformance is always direct. For an owning-classified instantiation, conformance admits constraint satisfaction and generic dispatch but not the boxing *conversion* ([§35.8](#sec-choice-boxing)).

`where T: IFoo` admits exactly the substitutions for which T conforms to `IFoo` per the rule above. Inside the generic body, T's surface includes IFoo's members, regardless of which conformance category T belongs to; the body cannot tell whether T was satisfied by a class, a record, an enum, an interface, a primitive, or another type parameter, and does not need to.

<a id="sec-worked-example-where-t-idisposable"></a>
#### Worked example: `where T: IDisposable`

Every class implicitly implements `IDisposable` ([§28.2](#sec-the-idisposable-contract)), and records cannot implement `IDisposable` ([§9.7](#sec-records-and-disposal)). Applying the conformance rule:

- Every non-nullable class type conforms (rule 1).
- No record type conforms (rule 2 fails because records cannot implement `IDisposable`).
- Interface types conform when they extend `IDisposable` (rule 3): `IAsyncDisposable`, `IEnumerator<T>`, `IAsyncEnumerator<T>`, and any user-defined interface that lists `IDisposable` in its extension clause.

So `where T: IDisposable` admits the same *class* substitutions as `where T: class` (every class qualifies under both) but a strictly smaller set of *interface* substitutions (only `IDisposable`-extending interfaces, versus all interfaces under `where T: class`). The difference rarely matters in practice — programmers usually write `where T: IDisposable` when the body calls `Dispose()`, and that's exactly when admitting only `IDisposable`-conforming interfaces is what was wanted.

<a id="sec-worked-example-where-t-icomparableint"></a>
#### Worked example: `where T: IComparable<int>`

`IComparable<int>` is implemented by `int` itself — its standard-library declaration lists it (stdlib [§9.1](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-integer-types)), and `Int32` names the same type ([§3.4](#sec-keyword-aliases-for-built-in-types)) — and by user-defined records and classes that implement it. Applying the conformance rule:

- `int` (rule 5): conforms — its standard-library declaration lists `IComparable<int>`. `Int32` names the same type ([§3.4](#sec-keyword-aliases-for-built-in-types)), not a separate conformer.
- Any user record listing `IComparable<int>` in its inheritance clause **and declaring the matching member** (rule 2 — `CompareTo` is not auto-generated; only the equality members are, [§9.2](#sec-body-records)): conforms. For example, `record Wrapper(value: int): IComparable<int>` with a declared `CompareTo(other: int): int`.
- Any user class implementing `IComparable<int>` (rule 1): conforms.
- An interface `IIntComparable: IComparable<int>` (rule 3): conforms.

`where T: IComparable<int>` therefore admits a mix of primitive, class, record, and interface substitutions — illustrating that interface constraints are not class-only, unlike the class-bound constraint `where T: SomeClass`.

<a id="sec-constraints-on-overrides"></a>
#### Constraints on overrides and interface implementations

An `override` of a generic method, and a method implementing a generic interface method (an interface member declaring type parameters of its own, whose `where` clauses sit where a class method's do: Appendix A.4 `IfaceMethod`, `IfaceStaticMethod`), **inherits the overridden or implemented declaration's constraints**. Omitting the `where` clauses is the recommended spelling and means exactly the inherited set; the clauses may instead be restated in an equivalent form — the same constraint set per type parameter, compared **order-insensitively and after type-alias resolution** ([§27.8](#sec-type-aliases)): `where T: IFoo` and `where T: AliasOfIFoo` restate the same set — for readability. A **differing** clause — added, removed, narrowed, or widened relative to the inherited set — is a compile error naming the inherited constraints: dispatch flows through the base or interface signature, so its constraints are the only ones call sites are ever checked against — an *added* constraint on the override would go unenforced at every virtual call (unsound), and a *weakened* one would advertise admissions the dispatch surface never grants. The two declarations' method-level type parameters, equal in number, correspond by position ([§11.2](#sec-interface-declaration)'s *Generic members*), and the inherited set is read under the implemented interface's or overridden base's substitution, its method type parameters renamed positionally: `method M<S>(x: S) where S: U;` on `interface I<U>` is inherited as `where T: IFoo` by `method M<T>(x: T)` in a class conforming to `I<IFoo>`. In every comparison this paragraph makes, a method's **constraint set** is its stated clauses or, where it omits them, the set it inherits here. Two further rules follow. A method that a class **inherits from a base class** and that satisfies an interface method of the class inherits nothing from the interface: it matches ([§11.2](#sec-interface-declaration)) only when its constraint set is equivalent to the interface method's. A stronger set is unsound, because calls through the interface are checked against the interface's set and reach that body; a weaker one is rejected as it is for a declared implementation, since the match is one relation wherever the witness is declared. And a method that implements or overrides two or more generic declarations (two interfaces, two instantiations of one interface, or a base virtual member and an interface) whose constraint sets are not equivalent has no inherited set: it is a compile error at the implementing type, naming both sets, whether the method's clauses are omitted or restated.

<a id="sec-generics-variance"></a>
### 14.3 Variance

See [§12.9](#sec-variance).

<a id="sec-owned-and-generic-type-arguments"></a>
<a id="sec-owned-as-a-generic-argument"></a>
<a id="sec-substitution-of-owned-bearing-type-arguments"></a>
<a id="sec-merged-declarations-and-form-dependent-members"></a>
<a id="sec-conditioning-method-existence-on-ts-modifier"></a>
### 14.4 `owned` and generic type arguments

**`owned` does not propagate through generic type arguments.** A generic argument's type is whatever class, value, or interface type is supplied; the `owned` modifier — which expresses an ownership-tracking obligation at a declaration position — does not attach to type arguments.

So `Array<owned T>` is not a type. The owning forms are separate named types with their own declarations, members, and inheritance (stdlib [§4](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-system-collections-generic), [§6](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-system-threading)): `OwningArray<T>` beside `Array<T>`, `OwningDictionary<K, V>` beside `Dictionary<K, V>`, `OwningTask<T>` beside `Task<T>`, `IOwningEnumerable<T>` beside `IEnumerable<T>`, and so on — an owning collection's `Add` takes ownership of the element where a borrowing collection's `Add` takes a borrow (rationale [§5.3](Bezel_Design_Rationale.md#sec-collections-do-not-own-their-elements)).

The admissible positions for `owned` are enumerated in [§28.1](#sec-where-the-owned-modifier-can-appear); types and positions that do not admit `owned` (record fields, inline-array element types, generic type arguments) reject the modifier at the position itself, not through any substitution rule.

<a id="sec-generic-constraints-and-class-types"></a>
#### Generic constraints and class types

Generic methods and types can constrain their parameters to class types via `where T: class` ([§14.2](#sec-constraints)). A class type C satisfies `where T: class`. A generic method with a `where T: class` constraint may be called with T = C; the call site supplies a value of type C (whether the value is owned or a borrow at that site is determined by the declaration position of the parameter the call argument flows into, not by T's identity; a call *result* whose declared return type is a bare type parameter is likewise classified by declaration shape — [§28.3](#sec-bare-type-parameter-returns)'s bare-type-parameter rule — not by T's substitution).

Generic types that store class-typed values do not, by themselves, become "owning" by having a class type argument. `Array<MyClass>` stores borrows of `MyClass` — references whose ownership remains with whoever passed them in. To get an owning collection, the user reaches for `OwningArray<MyClass>` — a different class with different semantics.

**Class-only restriction on owning generics.** Most standard-library owning types (`OwningArray<T>`, `OwningLinkedList<T>`, `OwningSet<T>`, `OwningStack<T>`, `OwningQueue<T>`, `OwningDictionary<K, V>`, `OwningTask<T>`, `IOwningEnumerable<T>`, `IOwningEnumerator<T>`, `IOwningAsyncEnumerable<T>`, `IOwningAsyncEnumerator<T>`, `IOwningCollection<T>`, `IOwningList<T>`) restrict their element type T to **class and interface types**. Value types are rejected at the instantiation site. The `where T: class` constraint in their declarations is a slight imprecision — per [§14.2](#sec-constraints) `where T: class` admits all non-nullable reference types (classes, interfaces, `string`, function types) — but the standard-library owning types are compiler-enforced to reject the runtime-managed reference types (`string`, function values). The reason: those types are runtime-managed ([§28.9](#sec-runtime-managed-types)) and have no disposal obligation; owning them is degenerate. The error message at instantiation names the rejected type and points the reader to the relevant stdlib section.

`OwningBuffer<T>`, `Span<T>`, and `ReadOnlySpan<T>` (stdlib [§4.14](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-owned-buffers-and-spans)) are exceptions to this restriction. They admit T to be either class-typed (with ownership semantics as above) or value-typed (with plain value semantics — no per-slot ownership, no Dispose cascade, no `move` admission). They still reject the runtime-managed reference types (`string`, function values) and move-only value types — both kinds of [§15.3](#sec-move-only-value-types): the owning inline arrays `[N owned]T` and `[N owned]T?`, and the owning-classified choice ([§35.4](#sec-choice-classification)). Value-like and borrow-bearing choices are copyable value types ([§15.3](#sec-move-only-value-types)) and are admitted as value-typed T, as stdlib [§4.14](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-owned-buffers-and-spans) sets out.

**Nullable class types and interfaces are admitted.** The owning-type instantiation rule checks the *underlying* type, not the nullable-wrapper. `OwningTask<Lock?>` (a Pattern B task whose result is `owned Lock | null`) is admitted because `Lock` is a class type; the nullability of the result is independent of the disposal obligation. The same applies to interface types: `OwningArray<IConnection>` is admitted because `IConnection` may be implemented by class types with real disposal obligations; iteration produces borrows of `IConnection`, and `Add(owned)` takes ownership of an `IConnection` reference whose runtime dispatch resolves to a real class's `Dispose()` at disposal time.

A user-defined generic type that needs to own its elements composes over `OwningArray<T>` (or another `Owned…` collection type):

```bezel
public class OwningCache<T> where T: class
  private owned _items: OwningArray<T>;

  public constructor() _items := new(); end;

  public method Add(owned item: T)
    _items.Add(move item);
  end Add;

  public method Drain(): owned IOwningEnumerable<T>
    return _items.Drain();
  end Drain;
end OwningCache;
```

This composition pattern works under the existing field-ownership and generic-type rules; no special mechanism is required. User-defined generic types with class-typed parameters that do not store anything owned (read-only views, transformations) just declare their members in the normal way.

<a id="sec-historical-references"></a>
#### Historical references

This section's anchors are kept so that the changelog's links to earlier forms of the rule resolve; the changelog carries that history.

<a id="sec-type-argument-inference"></a>
### 14.5 Type-argument inference for generic methods

A call to a generic method may omit the type-argument list; the compiler then infers the method-level type arguments from the call.

**Scope.** Inference covers **method-level** type parameters only. Class-, record-, and interface-level type arguments are never inferred from constructor arguments: `new Pair(1, "x")` against `record Pair<TF, TS>(First: TF, Second: TS)` is a compile error directing to explicit arguments (`new Pair<int, string>(1, "x")`) or, where a target type exists, the `new()` shorthand ([§17.7](#sec-the-new-operator)). Extension-block-level parameters are inferred from the receiver first ([§26.5](#sec-resolution) step 2, this section's unification applied to the extension head); the resulting substitution is in force while the method-level parameters are inferred below.

**Explicit lists are all-or-nothing.** An explicit type-argument list (`obj.Method<int>(args)`, [§22.12](#sec-static-members)/A.7) binds the declared type parameters in declaration order and must supply exactly as many arguments as the method declares type parameters. A shorter or a longer list is a compile error; there are no partial lists. When a full explicit list is supplied, no inference runs. Where the name is overloaded, the list's length selects first: only candidates declaring exactly that many type parameters of their own take part in resolution (a non-generic candidate takes no list), and the error above is reported only when no candidate declares that many (`Task.FromException<int>(ex)` reaches the generic member, `Task.FromException(ex)` the non-generic one whatever the target, by [§22.6](#sec-overloading)'s non-generic preference; [§11.3](#sec-member-body)).

**Inputs and phases.** Inference runs after arity filtering and named-argument binding ([§22.5](#sec-optional-parameters-and-named-arguments)) fix the argument-to-parameter correspondence; omitted optional parameters contribute nothing. It proceeds in three phases; every phase binds type parameters under one **agreement rule** stated after them.

1. **Argument-driven unification.** Each argument whose type is
   self-determined — every non-function-typed argument, a function-typed
   *value*, and a lambda's **annotated** parameter types — is unified
   structurally against its parameter type (a bare `null` literal argument is
   not self-determined and contributes no binding):

   - a parameter type that is a bare type parameter `X` binds `X` to the
     argument's static type;
   - `X?` binds through the nullable wrapping: an argument of type `U?` binds
     `X` to `U`; a non-nullable argument of type `A` binds `X` to `A` (the
     present-value wrapping of [§5.1](#sec-implicit-conversions)). This bullet
     is about the **parameter position's** own `?`, and it does not compose
     into the nested case: a bare `X` reached through a constructed
     parameter type binds by the bullet above it — to the argument's static
     type at that position, nullable or not — so `b: Box<Box<X>>` against a
     `Box<Box<int?>>` argument binds `X` to `int?`, not to `int`. Nullability
     is therefore part of a binding, and *Agreement* below polices it: an `X`
     bound `int` at one position and `int?` at another is an inference
     failure, not a widening;
   - a constructed parameter type `G<P1, …, Pn>` unifies component-wise and
     **invariantly** against an argument of the same generic type, or against
     the unique instantiation of `G` that the argument's type implements or
     extends (an `Array<int>` argument against `xs: IEnumerable<T>` binds
     `T` to `int`); an argument whose type reaches no instantiation of `G`
     makes the candidate inapplicable, and so does one whose type reaches
     **more than one** (a type implementing both `I<int>` and `I<string>`,
     against `p: I<X>`) — a non-unique instantiation is never resolved by
     choice (*Agreement* below); cast the argument to the intended
     instantiation or supply explicit type arguments;
   - a function-typed parameter unifies component-wise — each parameter
     slot against the argument's slot in order, the return slot against the
     return slot — and only against a function type of the **same parameter
     count**: an argument whose function type has a different number of
     parameter slots reaches no unification, and the candidate is
     **inapplicable** — an inference failure that drops it out (*Interaction
     with overloading* below), never an error reported at that candidate
     (the same at every function-typed position —
     [§22.6](#sec-overloading)'s *Parameter count at a function-typed
     position*); modifier slots (`owned`/`ref`/`out`/`out owned`/`scoped`)
     must match exactly ([§27.1](#sec-function-types));
   - a `ref` or `out` parameter position unifies **exactly**: the parameter
     aliases the caller's location, so no conversion is admitted at the
     binding or later at the applicability check
     ([§22.3](#sec-ref-and-out-argument-locations));
   - a parameter type containing no type parameters contributes no bindings.

   Unification is over **static types, exactly**: no [§5.1](#sec-implicit-conversions)
   conversion, no constant narrowing, and no variance step participates in
   *binding*. Conversions get their say afterward, argument by argument, at the
   [§22.6](#sec-overloading) applicability check against the substituted
   signature — which is why `var o: Object := Util.Id(5);` infers `T` as `int`
   from the argument and then converts the `int` result to `Object` as an
   ordinary assignment conversion.

2. **Function-typed arguments, left to right.** For each lambda-literal
   argument in argument order: the bindings established so far are substituted
   into its parameter's function type; if every parameter position of the
   lambda is then closed, the lambda's parameters take those types
   ([§27.4](#sec-parameter-type-inference) — a destructuring head acts as its
   annotation) and the body is typed ([§27.3](#sec-lambda-expressions)); the
   lambda's inferred return type then unifies against the function type's
   return position, binding type parameters still free. When the substituted
   return position contains **no** free type parameter, the lambda's inferred
   return type must equal it or implicitly convert to it
   ([§5.1](#sec-implicit-conversions)); otherwise the candidate is
   inapplicable — this is the general admission rule for lambda-literal
   arguments, stated with its ranking consequences in
   [§22.6](#sec-overloading). A later function-typed argument may use
   bindings an earlier one produced. A method-reference argument resolves
   against the substituted target per [§27.6](#sec-method-references); type
   parameters free in that target are bound by the winning candidate's
   signature under the exact-preferred ranking of
   [§27.6](#sec-method-references-to-overloaded-methods) — and the formed
   reference then ranks among the *callee's* candidates as
   [§22.6](#sec-overloading)'s *Method-reference arguments* states.
   If a lambda's parameter positions are still open after this phase, inference
   fails: annotate the lambda's parameters or supply explicit type arguments.
   Two shapes contribute **no return binding**. A lambda whose
   body — its expression body, or a `return` operand — is a **collection
   literal** has no self-determined return type, the literal having no
   standalone type ([§15.4](#sec-collection-literals)): the literal is typed
   against the substituted return position, which must be **closed** at the
   lambda's turn in this phase and must admit a literal (a
   collection-interface position such as `IEnumerable<U>` admits none) —
   otherwise the lambda is a compile error at the body, the literal having
   no target. The remedy is a block body binding the literal to an
   explicitly typed local; a type parameter such a position would have
   bound must come from an earlier argument or an explicit list. At an
   overloaded call the position ranks as [§22.6](#sec-overloading)'s
   *Lambda-literal arguments* states. A lambda **nested** in a lambda body
   is an expression of that body: it is typed by
   [§27.3](#sec-lambda-expressions)/[§27.4](#sec-parameter-type-inference)
   against the target its own position supplies (the enclosing lambda's
   substituted return position when it is the body's result, a call's
   parameter type, a typed local) and never re-enters this phase — its
   parameter positions bind nothing of the enclosing call's type
   parameters, and what it contributes is the enclosing lambda's inferred
   return type, unified as above.

3. **Target-typed completion.** A type parameter still unbound is bound from
   the call's **target type**, where the call site has one, by unifying the
   method's declared return type — current bindings applied — against the
   target; this unification may bind through the return type's base-class or
   implemented-interface positions (`Util.Empty<T>(): owned Array<T>` against a
   target `IEnumerable<int>` binds `T` to `int`) and through the nullable
   wrapping. The **target contexts** are: the initializer of a typed
   declaration (field or local), an assignment to a typed location, a `return`
   statement against a declared return type, a default parameter value, and an
   argument position whose parameter type is closed once the enclosing call's
   own phase-1 bindings are applied — [§17.7](#sec-the-new-operator)'s
   `new()`-shorthand contexts, extended by typed assignments and determined
   argument positions — groups (i), (ii), (iii), (iv), (vi) and the `return e;`
   statement of (v) of the
   [written-declared-type family](#sec-written-declared-type-positions)
   (this list is §14.5's own). The target never overrides an
   argument-derived binding;
   it only completes. A type parameter that remains unbound — it appears in no
   self-determined argument position and no target context supplies it — is a
   compile error naming the parameter: supply explicit type arguments, or give
   the call a target (assign to a typed local, or return it from a method with
   a declared return type).

**Agreement.** All bindings a type parameter receives — across arguments, lambda returns, and the target — must be the **same type**. Two different bindings are an inference failure: a compile error naming the type parameter and both types, remedied with explicit type arguments or an explicit cast. The compiler computes no common supertype and no widened join — `Util.Pick<T>(a: T, b: T)` called as `Pick(1, 2L)` or as `Pick(dog, animal)` is an error, not `long` or `Animal` (the same declined-unification stance as lambda return types, [§27.3](#sec-lambda-expressions), and the `if` expression's two-way rule, [§20](#sec-the-if-expression)). Constant expressions contribute their static types (`Pick(b, 250)` for `b: byte` is an error — `250` is an `int`); [§5.1](#sec-implicit-conversions)'s constant narrowing is a conversion-site rule and never participates in a join. With an explicit list — `Pick<byte>(b, 250)` — the parameter type is `byte` and the literal constant-narrows at the argument conversion site as usual.

**Constraints.** [§14.2](#sec-constraints) constraint satisfaction is checked after inference completes, on the full substitution, exactly as for a written type-argument list. Constraints do not act as inference sources in this version (recorded liftable). Nor do a generic method's own `where` constraints take part in resolving a call to it (also recorded liftable): they are checked on the candidate [§22.6](#sec-overloading) selects, after resolution, whether its type arguments were inferred or written. An unsatisfied constraint is not an inference failure and does not make a candidate inapplicable. The candidate stays in the set, and if resolution selects it the call is a compile error naming the constraint; resolution never falls back to another overload. So with `M(o: Object)` beside `M<T>(x: T) where T: class`, the call `M(5)` infers `T = int`, the generic candidate wins as the exact match, and the call is rejected for `where T: class`. An extension block's `where` clause is a different fact: it decides whether the block applies to the receiver at all ([§26.4](#sec-generic-extensions)).

**Interaction with overloading.** Inference is **per candidate** and precedes applicability: each generic candidate infers against the call independently; a candidate whose inference fails is inapplicable and drops out (the call then resolves among the remaining candidates as usual). Surviving candidates enter [§22.6](#sec-overloading) with their substituted signatures. A non-generic candidate otherwise tied with a generic one wins ([§22.6](#sec-overloading) — the last comparison before ambiguity, after the defaulted-arity tie-break).

**Failure diagnostics.** The two failure shapes carry distinct diagnostics, both naming the type parameter: *unbindable* ("cannot infer the type argument of `Empty`'s call from its arguments; it appears only in the return type, so a target type is required — assign the result to a typed local or return it from a method with a declared return type") and *conflicting* ("type parameter `T` cannot be bound to both `int` and `long` — all arguments for a type parameter must agree; write explicit type arguments"). Neither ever resolves by silent choice.

```bezel
var xs: Array<int> := [1, 2, 3];

var doubled := xs.Select(lambda(x) => x * 2);      // block T = int from the receiver (§26.5);
                                             //   phase 2: lambda param x : int, body int ⇒ U = int
var byKey := xs.OrderBy(lambda(x) => x mod 3);     // TKey = int (phase 2); the §14.2 constraint
                                             //   check (IComparable<int>) runs after inference
var total := xs.Aggregate(0L, lambda(acc, x) => acc + x);
                                             // TAccum = long from the seed (phase 1);
                                             //   lambda checks as (long, int) -> long (phase 2)
var empty: Array<string> := Util.Empty();    // T = string from the target (phase 3)
var n := Util.CountOf(xs);                   // CountOf<T>(xs: IEnumerable<T>): int —
                                             //   Array<int> vs IEnumerable<T> ⇒ T = int (phase 1)
// var bad := Util.Pick(1, 2L);              // error: T bound to both int and long — agree, or
                                             //        Pick<long>(1, 2L)
// var loose := Util.Empty();                // error: T appears only in the return type —
                                             //        target or explicit argument required
```

<a id="sec-recursive-instantiation"></a>
### 14.6 Recursive instantiation

Generic declarations request instantiations of one another — through generic calls, generic-type instantiations, base-clause references, and field, choice-payload, and signature types — and such requests may form cycles. The **instantiation-request graph** makes the shape checkable at declarations. Its nodes are the program's generic types and generic members: **each generic type is a node, and each generic member is its own node**, wherever declared; a **non-generic** member's edges attach to its **declaring type's node**. Each edge runs from the node whose declaration requests the instantiation to the requested generic, labeled with the substitution the request applies; a type's node carries an edge to one of its own generic members **only at a requested instantiation site** — a request naming that member at specific arguments — never implicitly for all its members. An override's body contributes its edges to the overridden or implemented member's node, since dispatch reaches it ([§14.2](#sec-constraints-on-overrides)).

**Bounded instantiation closure.** Within each strongly-connected component of the instantiation-request graph, every edge must substitute each type parameter of its target with either a **bare type parameter in scope at the source declaration** — the source's own, or an enclosing declaration's — or a **closed type** (a type containing no type parameter). Any other substitution on an in-SCC edge — an argument containing an in-scope type parameter other than as the bare argument itself, the nullable form `T?` included — is a **compile error at the declaration holding the edge** — the declaration-site shape of [§14.2](#sec-constraints)'s bound-cycle rule and [§27.8](#sec-type-aliases)'s alias rule — with a diagnostic naming the cycle and the growing argument.

Consequences. Recursion at the same arguments stays legal: `F<T>` calling `F<T>` is an ordinary edge substituting the bare in-scope parameter, a cycle whose edges permute or repeat bare parameters (`F<T, U>` calling `F<U, T>`) is equally within the rule, and so is a generic member's edge to its enclosing type at the enclosing parameters. What the rule rejects is the expanding shape, on either route it can take: a call `F<Pair<T, T>>` inside `F<T>`'s body, and equally a field of type `Node<Pair<T, T>>?` inside `Node<T>` — each such edge nests an in-scope parameter inside a larger argument, so the component's instantiation closure has no bound. The condition is **per-edge over the component**, deliberately stronger than boundedness of the closure: an in-SCC edge that fails it is rejected even where another edge of the cycle would in fact bound the closure. The rejection is likewise independent of dynamic reachability: what the rule bounds is the set of instantiations a program's declarations request ([§2.8.2](#sec-artifact-interface)'s instantiation obligation), not the set an execution reaches. It is likewise independent of which parameters are *fixed* across the component: an in-SCC edge whose argument is constructed over an **enclosing declaration's** parameter — `M<Pair<X, X>>` in the body of a generic member `M<T>` of `Holder<X>` — is rejected although `X` is fixed for the whole instantiation and the edge cannot expand, because `Pair<X, X>` is neither a bare parameter nor closed and the rule reads the argument's shape alone, never which parameters are fixed relative to which component; hoist the argument to a closed type, or pass the parameter bare. Cycles spanning modules are checked over the compilation closure [§2.8.3](#sec-transitive-closure-and-type-identity) rule 1 supplies.

<a id="sec-arrays"></a>
## 15. Arrays

Bezel provides two array kinds:

- **Inline arrays** `[N]T` — value-typed, fixed size set at compile time, stored inline in their enclosing context (stack frame, class storage, or record layout). No heap allocation, no `Dispose`.
- **Heap arrays** `Array<T>` and `OwningArray<T>` — class types from the standard library, allocated with `new`, require disposal. May be used at fixed size (by not calling resize methods) or resizably (the natural use).

The two kinds serve different purposes. Inline arrays are a value-type storage primitive: they live in the place that holds them, copy by value (when copyable), and have no allocation cost. Heap arrays are the general-purpose container family: they grow and shrink, support iteration protocols, and carry the ownership obligations associated with their allocated storage.

<a id="sec-inline-arrays"></a>
<a id="sec-fixed-size-arrays"></a>
### 15.1 Inline arrays

The type `[N]T` is an inline array of N elements of type T. N is a compile-time integer constant; T is any type subject to the element-type rules below.

```bezel
var pixels: [16]byte;                    // 16 default-initialized (zero) bytes
var matrix: [9]float;                    // 9 default-initialized (zero) floats
var rgb:    [3]byte := [255, 128, 64];   // explicit initialization
```

**Size.** N must be a constant expression of integer type ([§17.14](#sec-constant-expressions)): integer literals, `const` references, and arithmetic on these (e.g., `[BufferSize * 2]byte`) are the common forms. N must be greater than zero; `[0]T` is a compile error.

The size N is part of the type. `[3]int` and `[4]int` are distinct types that do not interconvert.

**Element type.** The element type T may be:

- A value type other than an inline array — a primitive, a record, an enum or a choice, nullable or not, or the unit type ([§3.2](#sec-reference-vs-value-types)): the array stores the values directly, inline. The element type is never a **move-only** value type ([§15.3](#sec-move-only-value-types)): an inline array without the `owned` marker is copyable, a copy would duplicate what such an element owns, and the `owned` marker admits class and interface elements only ([§15.1.1](#sec-owning-inline-arrays)). An owning choice ([§35.4](#sec-choice-classification)), or its nullable form, as `T` is therefore a compile error, and so is a type parameter `T` substituted by one, at the instantiation site ([§3.6](#sec-derived-type-properties) rule 2). An owning inline array is excluded by the one-dimensional rule below.
- A class or interface type (`C` or `C?`): the array stores references inline; the referenced objects live on the heap as usual.
- A runtime-managed reference type (`string`, `Type`, function values; [§28.9](#sec-runtime-managed-types)): the array stores references inline; the underlying memory is managed by the runtime. A slot of function type, a local array's included, admits only a capture-free function value ([§28.3](#sec-borrow-lifetime-rules)'s *choice payloads and inline-array slots of function type*).

Inline arrays may not be elements of inline arrays in the form `[N][M]T` — multi-dimensional inline arrays are deferred to a future revision. The current spec admits only one-dimensional inline arrays, wherever the nested form arises: a type parameter `T` of `[N]T` substituted by an inline array is a compile error at the instantiation site ([§3.6](#sec-derived-type-properties) rule 2), and so is a generic type alias reference whose expansion forms one ([§27.8](#sec-generic-type-aliases)).

**No nullable inline-array types.** Inline arrays themselves do not have a nullable form: `([3]int)?` is not admitted. The element type may be nullable (`[3]int?` is well-formed and denotes an inline array of nullable int), but the array as a whole always has a value. The grammar parses `[3]int?` greedily as "inline array of `int?`," not as "nullable inline array of `int`." The motivation: inline arrays are stored inline in their host, so a "null" inline array would have no natural representation (every slot would have to indicate "the whole array is absent"), and the use cases for a sentinel "no array yet" value are well-served by either a nullable wrapping record or a nullable class-typed reference to a heap array. Consequently an inline array is not an admissible `as` target ([§17.4](#sec-the-is-is-not-and-as-operators)).

**Initialization.** When the element type T is **defaultable** ([§17.11](#sec-the-default-operator) — any nullable type T? included; an enum is defaultable only when it declares a zero-valued constant) — an inline array declaration without an explicit initializer is filled with that element default per slot:

```bezel
var counts: [10]int;             // 10 zeros
var maybe:  [5]Connection?;       // 5 nulls
var verts:  [3]Vertex;            // 3 default-initialized Vertex records (if Vertex is defaultable)
```

When the element type is not defaultable — a non-nullable class type is the common case — the array has no default slots and is initialized explicitly under [§7.9](#sec-definite-assignment-for-non-nullable-fields)'s rules: a local before its first use, at its declaration or by a later assignment of the whole array, and a field by a field initializer or an assignment in every constructor. The array is one variable: an element store `a[i] := v` does not assign it, and on a local not yet assigned it is a use of the unassigned local, rejected like a read. The initializer is a comma-separated list of N expressions in brackets:

```bezel
var rgb: [3]byte       := [255, 128, 64];
var pt:  [2]Point      := [new Point(0, 0), new Point(1, 1)];   // value-typed Point record
```

For non-nullable class-typed elements (`[N]C` without the `owned` slot marker), the elements stored in the array are *borrows* — the initializer expressions must be borrows of class instances already owned elsewhere, and those owners must outlive the inline array. To construct an inline array that *owns* its non-null class-typed slots, use the `[N owned]T` form ([§15.1.1](#sec-owning-inline-arrays)) with an initializer of owned expressions; ownership transfers from each expression into the array.

The list must contain exactly N elements; mismatch is a compile error.

<a id="sec-owning-inline-arrays"></a>
#### 15.1.1 Owning inline arrays

The form `[N owned]T` (or `[N owned]T?`) denotes an inline array whose slots own their (non-null) class-typed contents. T must be a class or interface type; value types and runtime-managed reference types are not admitted with the `owned` marker. When T is a generic type parameter, the class-or-interface restriction is checked at *instantiation* — a generic constraint `where T: class` admits broader types (including runtime-managed reference types) per [§14.2](#sec-constraints), so instantiating an inline array `[N owned]T?` with T = `string` or another non-class-or-interface type is a compile error at the instantiation site, paralleling the generic-class-fields rule of [§28.5](#sec-owned-fields).

```bezel
// Non-null owned slots; no default slots, so initialized explicitly (§7.9)
var fixed: [3 owned]Connection := [
  Connect("primary"), Connect("secondary"), Connect("tertiary")
];

// Nullable owned slots; defaults to all null
var pool: [16 owned]Connection?;
```

An owning inline array is a *move-only* value type ([§15.3](#sec-move-only-value-types)). Assignment transfers ownership rather than copying. Copying is forbidden, since copying would duplicate ownership of each slot's contents.

When an owning inline array's lifetime ends, the array's auto-dispose pass disposes each non-null slot, **in reverse slot order** — the same order, and the same multi-value-cleanup discipline ([§28.4](#sec-the-destructor): a throwing slot disposer does not stop the pass), as the whole-value-reassignment pass of [§15.3](#sec-move-only-value-types), so one pass definition governs all four of this paragraph's endings. A slot of interface type holding a boxed value type ([§8.6](#sec-boxing)) holds a runtime-managed value ([§28.9](#sec-runtime-managed-types)): the pass runs no user code for it, the box's `Dispose()` being §28.9's no-op. For locals, this happens at scope end via the standard owned-local discharge ([§28.3](#sec-local-variables-ownership-and-borrows)); for instance fields, the enclosing class's compiler-generated `Dispose()` disposes each non-null slot ([§28.4](#sec-the-destructor) step 2), and no user-written `destructor` is required ([§28.5](#sec-owned-fields)). A third ending is **whole-value reassignment**: overwriting an owning-inline-array local or instance field disposes each live slot of the displaced value before the store — [§15.3](#sec-move-only-value-types)'s per-slot drop-on-overwrite, the same pass run at the overwrite point. A fourth is **program exit**, for a static field of owning-inline-array type: the exit pass disposes each non-null slot of each such field, in this paragraph's reverse slot order, taking the fields themselves in reverse order of static initialization ([§22.13](#sec-disposal-of-static-owned-fields)).

The `move arr[i]` form is admitted on both `[N owned]T?` and `[N owned]T` slots ([§28.11](#sec-collections-do-not-own-elements)). For nullable slots, the field-restoration rule is satisfied by assigning `null` to the slot. For non-nullable slots, restoration requires assigning a fresh owned T (e.g., a constructor call, another moved value, or a borrow promoted to ownership via a factory) — the same rule as for non-nullable `OwningArray<T>` slots ([§4.5](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-ownedarrayt) of the standard library). Code that needs "leave the slot empty after take" requires the nullable form; non-nullable slots must always hold a value at every observable point.

<a id="sec-inline-array-members"></a>
<a id="sec-members-and-operations"></a>
#### 15.1.2 Members and operations

Every inline array `[N]T` (with any modifier combination) exposes:

- `arr.Length: int` — compile-time constant N.
- Indexer `arr[i]` for read and write. Bounds checking applies; a constant index proven in-range at compile time elides the check.
- `arr.ToArray(): owned Array<T>` — a fresh heap array of the N slots: value-typed slots copied; class-typed slots stored as borrows. For `[N owned]…` arrays the result borrows the slots — the inline array retains ownership, matching the iteration/equality borrow rule below.
- `arr.Contains(item: T): bool` — a linear search comparing `item` with each element by the element type's `Equals` ([§9.2](#sec-equality-through-a-type-parameter)'s first kind). Through [§17.5](#sec-the-in-operator)'s structural `Contains` lookup this makes `x in arr` well-formed with no grammar change.

Iteration over an inline array uses the standard `for var x in arr do … end` form. The compiler emits a direct indexed loop without involving the `IEnumerable<T>` protocol: inline arrays are not class types and do not implement interfaces. For value-typed T, each iteration variable `x` is a copy of the slot's value; for class-typed T, each `x` is a borrow of the slot's reference. For `[N owned]…` arrays, iteration produces borrows into the owned slots (the iteration variable is a borrow; the slot retains ownership); to consume slot contents, use explicit `move arr[i]` followed by restoration (assignment of `null` on `[N owned]T?` arrays, or assignment of a fresh owned T on `[N owned]T` arrays). Passing an inline array to a method expecting `IEnumerable<T>` is rejected: inline arrays declare no interface conformances (unlike records, which may implement interfaces), so the value does not satisfy the interface contract. Callers who need to forward the contents to an IEnumerable-taking method call `arr.ToArray()` (above) and pass the fresh heap array.

Two inline-array values of the same type are equal iff their elements are pairwise equal under the element type's equality. Inline arrays follow record-equality discipline: structural equality grounded in element equality, with no special cases. Owning inline arrays (`[N owned]…`) admit equality only via element borrow; the comparison reads each slot without taking ownership. An inline array whose element type, nullability stripped, is not **hashable** ([§3.6](#sec-derived-type-properties)) has no equality: `=`, `<>`, `Equals` and `GetHashCode` on it are a compile error at the use site naming the element type, with the remedies [§9.2](#sec-body-records) or [§35.7](#sec-choice-equality) gives for that type, and no element-wise comparison or hash is synthesized in their place. `Contains` (and so `in`) compares elements and never hashes, so it is keyed on the comparison: it is a compile error at the use site, naming the element type and its remedies, exactly where the element type, nullability stripped, has no member for [§9.2](#sec-equality-through-a-type-parameter)'s first kind, as the standard library's equality search is ([§14.2](#sec-conditionally-admitted-members)'s register), and it is admitted at an element type that is not hashable but declares an `Equals` of its own. Where the element type is or contains a type parameter (`[N]T`, `[N]T?`, `[N]Pair<T>`), the check is made at each instantiation, which is rejected where the substituted element type is not hashable (for `Contains`, where it has no first-kind member) ([§3.6](#sec-derived-type-properties) rule 2); `where T: hashable` ([§14.2](#sec-derived-property-constraints)) states the requirement in the signature.

**Lifetime of inline arrays carrying borrows.** An inline array without the `owned` marker is **borrow-bearing** ([§3.6](#sec-derived-type-properties)) exactly when its element type, nullability stripped, is a class or interface type that is not runtime-managed ([§28.9](#sec-runtime-managed-types)), a borrow-bearing record ([§9.7](#sec-records-and-disposal)), or a choice that holds borrows ([§35.4](#sec-choice-classification)). `[N]C` or `[N]C?` over a class or interface `C` carries N (potentially null) borrows in its slots; `[2]Pair`, for `record Pair(A: Item, B: Item)` over a class `Item`, carries the borrows each slot's record carries. When such an array is passed by value, returned from a method, stored as a field, or captured by a closure, the same borrow-lifetime rules apply that govern borrow-bearing records ([§9.7](#sec-records-and-disposal), [§28.3](#sec-local-variables-ownership-and-borrows)): the array value may not outlive the source of any borrow in any of its slots. So that conforming implementations agree on which programs compile, the check reads one **source set** per array value ([K2](#sec-kernel-k2)), for a class, interface, record or choice element alike: the union of the source sets of the borrows its slots carry, a record or choice element contributing every borrow it carries. A whole-value assignment `xs := e` gives the array `e`'s set, as an assignment to any local does. A slot store `xs[i] := e`, at a constant index or a computed one, adds `e`'s set to the array's and is checked as an assignment to the array's holder: at a local array it is rejected where the local's scope strictly encloses a source's scope ([§28.3](#sec-borrow-lifetime-rules)'s local-scope bullet). Sets join at control-flow merges ([K7](#sec-kernel-k7)). A slot read carries the array's whole set, a class- or interface-typed slot's borrow and a record or choice value copied out of a slot alike: the array is a transit point for the borrows it holds, as a borrowing collection is ([§28.11](#sec-borrowing-collections)). Every escape of the array value is checked against that set, and a live local of the array counts, for the consume-site freeze, as a live local borrow of every source in it ([§28.3](#sec-consume-site-freeze)). A slot store narrows no slot: a source stays in the set after every slot that carried its borrow is overwritten. The over-approximation is deliberate and recorded liftable. Borrows a slot carries through a record or choice element are under [§9.7](#sec-records-and-disposal)'s bullet list exactly as that record or choice is: a `[2]Pair` value is stored in a class instance field, in a static field, or in a longer-lived collection only where a `Pair` value would be, and is under [§30.1](#sec-async-methods)'s `async` ban as `Pair` is. Inline arrays of value-typed elements that carry no borrows (primitives, enums, the unit type, records that are not borrow-bearing, value-like choices), of runtime-managed reference-typed elements (`string`, `Type`, function values), or that carry only owned slots (`[N owned]…`) are not borrow-bearing.

<a id="sec-inline-array-ffi"></a>
<a id="sec-ffi"></a>
#### 15.1.3 FFI

Inline arrays of FFI-compatible scalar elements (`[N]byte`, `[N]int`, `[N]float`, `[N]IntPtr`, `[N]Ptr<T>`, and similar — the element set of [§32.5](#sec-ffi-compatible-types): the integer types, `float`, `double`, and `bool`, plus the pointer-sized scalars) have C-equivalent storage layout: N elements packed contiguously, no header.
