Such arrays may appear as `extern` method **parameters** under [§32.5](#sec-ffi-compatible-types)'s by-address rule: the argument must be an assignable storage location, the call passes the address of that storage (C's array-to-pointer convention), and native reads and writes are visible to the caller after the call. `[N]T` is **not** admitted as an extern **return** type — C functions do not return arrays ([§32.5](#sec-ffi-compatible-types)).

Inline arrays of class-typed, interface-typed, record-typed, or runtime-managed-reference-typed elements do not have C-equivalent layout and are not admitted in extern signatures (as fields of C-compatible records, [§32.13](#sec-c-compatible-records) restates the same scalar element set; inline arrays of C-compatible record elements are a recorded liftable bound, [§32.14](#sec-deferred-ffi-surface)). Owning inline arrays are not admitted. Multi-dimensional inline arrays remain deferred and not admitted at FFI boundaries.

<a id="sec-arrayt"></a>
<a id="sec-heap-arrays"></a>
### 15.2 Heap arrays

`Array<T>` and `OwningArray<T>` are the heap-allocated array types, documented in standard library [§4.4](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-arrayt) and [§4.5](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-ownedarrayt) respectively. They are class types allocated with `new` and requiring disposal via `using var`, owned field, or explicit `.Dispose()`.

Both support resizing operations. Users who want fixed-size discipline do not call resizing methods; the array's `Count` matches its construction-time capacity throughout its lifetime. The language does not provide a separate "fixed-size heap array" type; the discipline of not resizing is sufficient.

```bezel
// General use — resizable
using var data := new Array<int>();
data.Add(1); data.Add(2); data.Add(3);

// Fixed-size discipline — pre-allocate via literal, don't resize
using var snapshot: Array<int> := [1, 2, 3];
// snapshot.Count = 3 throughout its lifetime; no Add calls

// Owning heap array
using var pool: OwningArray<Connection> := [
  Connect("a"), Connect("b"), Connect("c")
];
```

<a id="sec-move-only-value-types"></a>
### 15.3 Move-only value types

A move-only value type is a value type whose instances cannot be duplicated. Assignment transfers the value from source to destination, leaving the source in moved-from state. Reading from a moved-from location is a compile error.

The move-only value type kinds in this specification are two: the owning inline array (`[N owned]T` or `[N owned]T?`, see [§15.1.1](#sec-owning-inline-arrays)) and the owning-classified choice ([§35.4](#sec-choice-classification)), its nullable wrapper `C?` included ([§35.9](#sec-choice-nullable)). Other value types — primitives, records, value-like and borrow-bearing choices, and inline arrays without the `owned` modifier — remain copyable. Move-only membership follows from *structure*, never from a declaration form: an inline array is move-only exactly when its slots carry the `owned` marker, and a choice, or its nullable wrapper, exactly when the choice's classification is owning. Both kinds take [§28.7](#sec-reassigning-owned-fields)'s automatic drop-on-overwrite at whole-value reassignment (for the owning inline array — per slot, the *Whole-value reassignment* rule below; the owning choice has it as well, [§35.4](#sec-choice-classification)).

**Rules.** Where an ordinary value type V supports an operation, a move-only V substitutes a moved variant or rejects the operation:

- **Local-to-local assignment** `var y := x;`: copies for an ordinary value type; moves for a move-only value type. After the move, `x` is in moved-from state and may not be read until reassigned. *(scope note: the binding/assignment transfer marker of [§28.3](#sec-local-variables-ownership-and-borrows) applies to **class-typed** owned bindings, where an unmarked binding is ambiguous between borrow and transfer and defaults to borrow. A move-only value binding has no borrow reading to disambiguate — copies are forbidden, so the plain binding can only move — and therefore stays unmarked, as this rule has always defined. The consume-site freeze applies regardless: moving a move-only local while a live borrow of it exists — e.g. a closure capture, [§28.9](#sec-runtime-managed-types) — is a compile error.)*
- **Whole-value reassignment** `arr := newValue;` on a move-only local or instance field is [§28.7](#sec-reassigning-owned-fields)'s drop-on-overwrite, applied **per slot** (retiring axiom A13's plain-store carve): the RHS is evaluated first ([K9.5](#sec-kernel-k9)); then each slot of the displaced value that is **live** — non-null and not moved-from, §28.7's liveness test — is disposed, **in reverse slot order**; then the new value is stored. The reassignment is a **consume of the displaced value**, governed by the consume table ([§28.3](#sec-consume-table)) and [§28.7](#sec-reassigning-owned-fields) like any other overwrite — at a local, frozen while a live local borrow of the displaced value exists, a borrow of any **slot's object** included, since the pass disposes it (`var s := arr[0]; arr := other;` with `s` live afterwards is a compile error naming the borrow); at an instance field, §28.7's owned-field overwrite regime, as for every field overwrite. No manual emptying is required or useful: the displaced value is torn down by the store itself, so the displaced value's outstanding slot-restoration obligations are **discharged by the kill** ([K9.3](#sec-kernel-k9)'s ground — teardown leaves no future read), exactly as a destructor body's are; a slot already moved-from contributes nothing to the pass (its object's obligation left with the `move` that emptied it), and at the non-nullable form `[N owned]T` the liveness test's null half is vacuous, so every non-moved-from slot is disposed. The new value arrives with its own per-slot states — `a := b;` where `b` (a whole-value move) carries moved-from slots leaves `a` carrying them, with `b`'s restoration obligations transferred to `a`. **A reassignment whose RHS consumes the LHS** — self-assignment `arr := arr;`, `arr := f(arr)` (a by-value-move parameter, this section's *Parameter passing* bullet), any RHS whose evaluation whole-value-moves the location — is well-defined: the RHS move leaves the location moved-from **before** the pass runs, so the pass disposes nothing ([§28.7](#sec-reassigning-owned-fields)'s *Moved-from and null*), and self-assignment is therefore a no-op. This rule holds at locals and instance fields — §28.7's own scope; a **static** owning-inline-array field's whole-field reassignment is the one location that keeps the plain store, on [§22.13](#sec-static-initialization-order)'s static-overwrite posture, not on any per-kind carve, and the reassignment warning survives at exactly that form ([§22.12](#sec-static-members) form (iv) states both).
- **Parameter passing**: a parameter declared `(x: V)` for an ordinary V is by value (copy); for a move-only V, it is by value-move (transfer ownership). The caller's argument expression is in moved-from state after the call. (Operator operands and the comparison surface's `Equals(T)` parameter are not plain parameters in this sense: they bind borrows — [§25.2](#sec-operator-overloading-restrictions).) A parameter declared `(owned x: V)` is identical to plain `(x: V)` for a move-only V; the modifier is admitted for documentation but is redundant. The redundancy reaches the **call site**: at either parameter spelling the argument is written **unmarked** — `Take(arr)`, not `Take(move arr)` — including where it is a named binding the call leaves moved-from. The position is [K3.12](#sec-kernel-k3)'s marker-free store into an owning location, not [K3.3](#sec-kernel-k3)'s marked `owned` argument: [§22.3](#sec-parameter-modifiers)'s marker disambiguates borrow from transfer, and a move-only value has no borrow reading to disambiguate ([K3.13](#sec-kernel-k3)'s marker economy), so `move` at such an argument is rejected as at any marker-free position ([§28.8.1](#sec-the-move-expression)). The one position at which a move-only operand *is* marked is the owning-match scrutinee `case move c of …`, where the marker selects the owning match rather than announcing the transfer ([§35.5](#sec-owning-match), [K3.4](#sec-kernel-k3)).
- **Return**: returning a move-only value transfers it to the caller. The callee's local is moved-from after the return.
- **Field placement**: a move-only value carrying no borrows may be a field of a class; the class's destructor disposes the field's owned slots. The borrow-free condition has exactly one non-vacuous case: an **owning choice that holds borrows** ([§35.4](#sec-choice-classification)'s holds-borrows property) may not be a class field, since a class instance's lifetime is not bounded by any borrow source's scope ([§9.7](#sec-records-and-disposal)'s instance-field bullet, which the property applies to it); an owning inline array never holds borrows (its slots are `owned`, [§15.1.1](#sec-owning-inline-arrays)) and is unaffected. A move-only value may also be a **case-payload field of a choice**: the containing choice becomes owning ([§35.4](#sec-choice-classification) rule 1), the `owned` marker on such a field is admitted-but-redundant ([§35.1](#sec-choice-declaration), [§28.1](#sec-where-the-owned-modifier-can-appear)), and binding semantics in matches are [§35.5](#sec-choice-matching)'s. A move-only value may not be a field of a record (records support only copy semantics, not move semantics). At **static** fields the two move-only kinds part: an owning inline array may be one and is disposed by [§22.13](#sec-static-initialization-order)'s program-exit pass, while an **owning choice** may not: the declaration is a compile error ([§22.12](#sec-static-members) rule 4's note (g)), no rule enrolling it in that pass.
- **Local lifetime**: a move-only local's owned slots are auto-disposed at scope end by the compiler, in reverse slot order ([§15.1.1](#sec-owning-inline-arrays)). Unlike owned class-typed locals ([§28.3](#sec-local-variables-ownership-and-borrows)), the array as a whole does not require an explicit discharge call (no `Dispose()` to invoke; the array is not a class). However, the field-restoration rule still applies to individual slots: any slot moved-from via `move arr[i]` must be reassigned before any exit edge, because auto-dispose on a moved-from slot is not defined. A **whole-value** move — a plain binding, a plain argument, a return — creates no such obligation on a **local**: it leaves the local holding no value rather than a hole, so no pass walks it ([K1](#sec-kernel-k1)'s moved-from state: "discharge machinery skips it"; [§28.3](#sec-owned-local-discharge-requirement)'s auto-drop runs only on a local "not in moved-from state"), and a read before reassignment is already an error. A whole-value `move` out of a **field** is [K9.2](#sec-kernel-k9)'s restoration rule unchanged. The standard restoration mechanisms apply: assign a fresh owned value, or for `[N owned]T?` arrays, assign `null` to mark the slot empty. **No must-use warning attaches to this auto-drop at an owning inline array** ([§28.3](#sec-owned-local-discharge-requirement)'s lint, [K3.14](#sec-kernel-k3)): the slot pass is unconditional and runs identically under plain `var` and under `using var`, so the two spellings differ in nothing the lint could announce — `using var`'s only observable consequence at this kind is the reassignment lock (the paragraph below). (A **static** owning-inline-array *field* is a different site with its own declaration-site warning, [§22.12](#sec-static-members) form (iv) and note 4(h).) The **owning choice**, the other move-only kind, *does* draw the lint at its local's auto-drop: that drop is the implicit drop of one owned value in the position an owned class-typed local occupies, with that position's ordinary alternatives — transfer it, discard it, or declare it `using var` — and [§35.4](#sec-choice-classification) states both the warning and its `using var` suppression.
- **Exception-path discharge**: on exception edges, the slots are auto-disposed by the implicit `try`/`finally` rule ([§28.3](#sec-local-variables-ownership-and-borrows)). The same mechanism that handles owned class-typed locals on exception paths handles move-only inline-array locals.
- **Equality**: move-only values support equality via borrowing comparison (reads each slot without moving), provided their element types support equality.
- **Pattern binding**: a `case` binding over a move-only scrutinee is a **borrow** of the value; consuming operations through the binding (`move s[i]`) are rejected ([§19.3](#sec-patterns)). In an **owning match** over an owning choice ([§35.5](#sec-owning-match)), a case-payload of move-only value type matched by a **positional slot or a marked named slot** instead **transfers into its binding at arm selection**, exactly as an `owned` payload does; an **unmarked named slot** keeps the borrow ([§19.3](#sec-patterns)); the transferred binding is then a move-only owned local of the arm body's scope under this section's rules. A borrowing-match binding of a move-only payload may not be live at a write point of the construct unless the scrutinee's source is provably unwritten ([§19.3](#sec-patterns)).
- **Member calls**: a bodied member call on a move-only receiver passes the receiver's storage in place at every source, `this` a borrow of that storage for the activation; an `async` or iterator member cannot be called on a move-only receiver ([§9.4](#sec-value-receivers-are-borrows) *Move-only receivers*).

`using var` is admitted for move-only inline arrays per the general rule of [§28.10](#sec-using-var) (which admits `using var` for any value-type or runtime-managed RHS). For a move-only inline-array local, `using var` has no disposal effect (scope-end auto-dispose runs whether or not `using var` is applied), and its only observable consequence is preventing reassignment; an unmarked move-only initializer is **adopted**, not pinned ([§28.10](#sec-using-var)). Programs that want to express "this owning inline-array binding is fixed at construction and may not be rebound" may use `using var arr: [16 owned]Connection?;`; programs that do not need the reassignment lock use plain `var`. Both are admitted; both produce identical runtime behavior at scope end, and neither draws a diagnostic — the must-use lint does not attach at this kind (*Local lifetime* above).

**Move-only is determined by structure, not by declaration.** Move-only is not a user-declarable property. The language determines whether a value type is move-only by inspecting its structure:

- Inline arrays with the `owned` modifier (`[N owned]T?` or `[N owned]T`), and owning-classified choices ([§35.4](#sec-choice-classification)), are move-only.
- All other value types — primitives, records, enums, value-like and borrow-bearing choices, inline arrays without `owned` (whose element type is never move-only, [§15.1](#sec-inline-arrays)) — are copyable.

A user-defined value-type-with-move-only-semantics is not provided in this revision. The move-only property exists to support owning inline arrays and owning-classified choices and may be extended in a future revision if a real use case for user-defined move-only types emerges.

<a id="sec-collection-literals"></a>
### 15.4 Collection literals

A collection literal is a comma-separated list of expressions in square brackets:

```bezel
[1, 2, 3]
[Connect("a"), Connect("b")]
[]                                // empty literal
```

A collection literal has no standalone type. It is well-typed only in a context that provides the target type: a **type annotation**, or the **parameter type of a method call**. The annotation is any declared location's, not a local's alone — a local declaration ([§21.1](#sec-variable-declarations)), a **field declaration's initializer**, instance or `static` (`private _rgb: [3]byte := [255, 128, 64];`), an assignment to any such location (`xs := [3, 4];`, resolution 4 below), and a `return` whose enclosing method's return type supplies it (the paragraph below). Supplying the target type is all the context does: whether the literal's *production* may then be stored there is the ordinary business of the ownership rules — a reference-typed collection literal is a fresh owned production, so it reaches an `owned` field as a marker-free transfer ([K3.1](#sec-kernel-k3)) and a non-`owned` class-typed field not at all ([§28.6](#sec-leak-prevention)'s fresh-store error), and a `static` field of either form carries [§22.12](#sec-static-members) rule 4's declaration-site warnings.

```bezel
var a: [3]int := [1, 2, 3];                       // inline array
using var b: Array<int> := [1, 2, 3];             // heap array
using var c: OwningArray<Connection> := [          // owning heap array
  Connect("a"), Connect("b"), Connect("c")
];

ProcessBuffer([1, 2, 3]);                          // type from parameter
```

A collection literal in a position where no target type is determinable is a compile error:

```bezel
var x := [1, 2, 3];        // ERROR: cannot infer target type
```

`return [1, 2, 3]` is admitted when the enclosing method's return type determines the target type — and, for the heap-collection targets, only when the return announces the transfer (a marker-free position, [K3.13](#sec-kernel-k3)): an `owned` return type ([§28.8](#sec-ownership-transfer); the constructed collection's obligation — and, under the literal-tree rule below, its fresh nodes' aggregate — follows the container through the transfer, [K3](#sec-kernel-k3)). A fresh literal returned through a non-`owned` **instance** return is rejected exactly as any freshly-produced owned value is ([§28.6](#sec-leak-prevention)); a static callee's admissible signature already spells the type announcement (the static-return rule, [§28.3](#sec-factory-methods-and-sourceless-returns)). Inline-array targets are value types and are outside this requirement.

The target types that admit collection literals are:

- Inline arrays `[N]T`, `[N]T?`, `[N owned]T`, `[N owned]T?` (the literal must have exactly N elements; for owning targets, each element expression must produce an owned value).
- `Array<T>` (heap-borrowing) and `OwningArray<T>` (heap-owning).
- `Set<T>` and `OwningSet<T>` (sets).
- `LinkedList<T>` and `OwningLinkedList<T>` (doubly-linked lists).
- `Stack<T>` and `OwningStack<T>` (LIFO stacks).
- `Queue<T>` and `OwningQueue<T>` (FIFO queues).
- `Dictionary<K, V>` and `OwningDictionary<K, V>` (dictionaries; key-value pair syntax `[k: v, ...]`).
- Any class that is a sequence-literal target under [§15.4.1](#sec-the-user-defined-sequence-literal-protocol) — one conforming to `ICollectionLiteralTarget<TSelf, T>` or `IOwningCollectionLiteralTarget<TSelf, T>` (stdlib [§2.19](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-static-abstractions)) at `TSelf` = itself. The built-in **sequence** collections above are exactly such classes: each declares the conformance in its standard-library declaration (stdlib §4.3), so the bullets above restate those declarations rather than defining the set; sequence-literal form only.

The **sequence literal** form `[e1, e2, ...]` (bare expressions) targets every sequence-shaped type above — inline arrays, `Array<T>`/`OwningArray<T>`, `Set<T>`/`OwningSet<T>`, `LinkedList<T>`/`OwningLinkedList<T>`, `Stack<T>`/`OwningStack<T>`, `Queue<T>`/`OwningQueue<T>`, and every other sequence-literal target per [§15.4.1](#sec-the-user-defined-sequence-literal-protocol). The **dictionary literal** form `[k1: v1, k2: v2, ...]` (colon-separated pairs) targets only the built-in `Dictionary<K, V>` and `OwningDictionary<K, V>`. The two forms are syntactically distinguished by whether the elements contain a top-level colon; a literal cannot mix bare expressions and colon pairs (doing so is a compile error).

**Element-order semantics by target.** The literal's textual element order maps to the target's natural construction order:

- Inline arrays, `Array<T>`, `OwningArray<T>`, `LinkedList<T>`, `OwningLinkedList<T>`: elements are stored in textual order; index 0 (or the list head) is the first literal element.
- `Queue<T>`, `OwningQueue<T>`: the first literal element is at the front of the queue (the next to be dequeued); the last literal element is at the back. `[1, 2, 3]` dequeues `1`, then `2`, then `3`.
- `Stack<T>`, `OwningStack<T>`: the first literal element is pushed first and ends up at the bottom; the last literal element is on top (the next to be popped). `[1, 2, 3]` pops `3`, then `2`, then `1`. This matches the reading "the literal lists elements bottom-to-top."
- `Set<T>`, `OwningSet<T>`: duplicates are collapsed (see below). For `Set<T>` the resulting iteration order **is** the literal's textual order of first occurrences — insertion order, which stdlib [§4.10](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-sett-and-ownedsett) guarantees; `OwningSet<T>` makes no iteration-order guarantee (same section).
- `Dictionary<K, V>`, `OwningDictionary<K, V>`: insertion order follows textual order; this matters because dictionary iteration is insertion-ordered (stdlib [§4.8](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-dictionaryk-v)).

For owning targets, the literal's element expressions must produce owned values; ownership transfers from each expression into the constructed collection. This applies uniformly to `OwningArray<T>`, `OwningLinkedList<T>`, `OwningStack<T>`, `OwningQueue<T>`, `OwningSet<T>`, and `OwningDictionary<K, V>` (value position; its key position is a borrowing position, which the fresh-store warning below reaches — the literal-site rejection of this paragraph is deliberately not extended to it). (For fresh trivial-dispose nodes transferred into owning element slots, the literal-tree ownership rule below assigns each node's aggregate to its owning slot.)

For **borrowing-family** targets (every borrowing-form target under [§15.4.1](#sec-the-user-defined-sequence-literal-protocol) — `Array<T>`, `Set<T>`, `LinkedList<T>`, `Stack<T>`, `Queue<T>`, and any user class that is one — and the key and value positions of `Dictionary<K, V>`), each element expression of **non-trivial-dispose class type** ([§28.9](#sec-runtime-managed-types)) must be a **borrow** whose source satisfies the store rule of [§28.11](#sec-borrowing-collections); an element expression that is a **fresh producer** of such a type — an unbound owned temporary ([§28.3](#sec-unbound-owned-temporaries)): a `new` expression, a nested collection literal targeting a non-trivial-dispose collection type (built-in, or any sequence-literal target under [§15.4.1](#sec-the-user-defined-sequence-literal-protocol) — the factory result is `owned TSelf`), or an `owned`-returning call — is rejected at the literal site. The temporary would be disposed at the end of the declaration statement, leaving the constructed collection holding a dangling borrow from birth — the statically-certain dangle of [§9.7](#sec-records-and-disposal)'s no-temporary-source rule, and an escape of a fresh owned value into a non-owning location ([§28.6](#sec-leak-prevention)). The remedy names the source first — `using var c := new Connection("a"); var conns: Array<Connection> := [c];` — or uses the owning family (`OwningArray<Connection>`), which takes ownership.

A fresh element of **trivial-dispose** class type ([§28.9](#sec-runtime-managed-types)) is admitted — not as a borrow, and not as an unbound temporary of its own, but as a **fresh node of the literal tree**, owned and freed under the **literal-tree ownership rule**:

> **The fresh nodes of a collection literal — nested literal nodes, fresh producer elements (`new` expressions and `owned`-returning calls in element position), and any element expression whose arm-meet classification is owned (a conditional element such as `[(if c then new Box<int>(1) else new Box<int>(2))]` joins the aggregate) — form an aggregate per maximal borrowing-family subtree. Each aggregate is owned by whatever owns its subtree's root: the receiving binding, the [K8](#sec-kernel-k8) temporary, an owning collection's element slot, an `owned` parameter or return through which the container transfers, an `owned` field (the aggregate freed in the containing object's teardown cascade — [§28.5](#sec-owned-fields), [§28.9](#sec-runtime-managed-types)), or static storage (process exit). The compiler frees the aggregate — all nodes, one obligation — at that owner's release point. Aggregate membership is fixed at construction; borrowed elements (`cached` in `["a": [1], "b": cached]`) are never members and are never freed with it.**

This is what keeps this section's own nested-literal examples well-formed: in the `groups` and `config` examples below, the nested `Array<int>` and `Dictionary<string, int>` values are fresh nodes of their literals' trees, aggregate-owned by the receiving `using var` bindings and freed when those bindings' scopes end. Resolutions at the rule's edges:

1. **Literal as a call argument** (`ProcessBuffer([1, 2, 3]);` above; the [§22.14](#sec-no-params-no-ref-returns) variadic idiom `Log(["hello", "world"]);`): the aggregate's owner is the [K8](#sec-kernel-k8) temporary, freed at its K8 boundary — statement end in the common case, per **evaluation** in conditions and guards ([K8.2](#sec-kernel-k8), so loop iterations never accumulate aggregates), and the binding atom's or `case` construct's boundary where [K8.5](#sec-kernel-k8)/[K8.3](#sec-kernel-k8) apply; the callee's plain parameter borrows it call-bounded. Callee retention is the standard unbound-temporary residual ([§28.3](#sec-unbound-owned-temporaries)) — no new trust category. An `owned` parameter takes the aggregate by transfer instead.
2. **Returned literal** (`return [1, 2, 3];`): legal through an `owned` return — the aggregate follows the container's obligation wherever [K3](#sec-kernel-k3) sends it (the stdlib's own `Build(): owned OwningArray<Connection>` example, stdlib [§4.5](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-ownedarrayt), has this shape). Through a non-`owned` instance return: rejected ([§28.6](#sec-leak-prevention)'s fresh-value rule; the sentence above).
3. **Owning-family boundaries**: an element consumed by an owned ingress position inside the literal leaves the aggregate at construction — the owning collection's cascade owns it. This is why the rule is per *maximal borrowing subtree*, not per outermost literal: in an `OwningArray<Array<int>>` literal `[[1, 2], [3]]` the inner fresh nodes belong to the owning slots, and there is no double owner.
4. **Reassignment of the receiving binding** (`xs := [3, 4];`): drop-on-overwrite ([§28.7](#sec-reassigning-owned-fields)) frees the whole displaced aggregate after RHS evaluation. The consume-site freeze ([§28.3](#sec-consume-site-freeze)) applies if any borrow of any node of the displaced tree is live; the granularity is **per-aggregate conservative** — a borrow of an interior node (`var inner := groups["primes"];`) freezes the whole aggregate. (Recorded widening path: per-node freeze tracking would only *admit more* programs, so the granularity may be refined by a later revision without breaking any accepted program.)
5. **`Add` after construction is not a literal position** (the store paragraph below). Aggregate membership never grows.
6. **Field initializers**: a fresh class-typed literal tree in a field initializer ([§22.8](#sec-field-initializers)) requires an `owned` field — [§28.6](#sec-leak-prevention)'s fresh-store rule, applied uniformly at trivial-dispose types — and the aggregate is then freed in the containing object's teardown cascade. An `owned` field of trivial-dispose type does not flip the containing class's classification ([§28.9](#sec-runtime-managed-types)).

The rejection of non-trivial fresh producers is deliberately **literal-only** (recorded): `Add`, `Insert`, and the indexer-set on a borrowing collection remain governed by [§28.3](#sec-unbound-owned-temporaries)'s unbound-temporary admission and [§28.11](#sec-borrowing-collections)'s residual-trust store rule — an opaque callee's signature type-announces no retention — so `coll.Add(new Connection("a"))` stays admissible and stays the borrow-lifetime hazard that checked disposal mode backstops. A literal is a language construct whose storage semantics the compiler fully knows; it does not hide behind signature-level trust. The same admission covers a **fresh trivial-dispose argument** — `groups.Add("odds", [1, 3, 5]);` — as the same hazard: the argument is an unbound owned temporary (or a K8-temporary-owned aggregate, per resolution 1) freed at its K8 boundary, so the collection retains a reference to a freed instance, backstopped by checked disposal mode ([§28.2](#sec-checked-disposal)). Because the retention is statically certain to outlive the value, the compiler **must warn** when a store-position argument in a **borrowing position** — `Add`/`Insert` and the indexer-set on a borrowing-family collection, key and value positions alike, and the **key** position of `OwningDictionary<K, V>`, which owns its values and not its keys (stdlib [§4.9](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-owneddictionaryk-v)), so a class-typed key is held as a borrow exactly as `Dictionary<K, V>`'s is — is a **fresh unbound owned temporary of class type** ([§28.3](#sec-unbound-owned-temporaries)): a `new` expression, a collection literal, an `owned`-returning call result, a `move` result, or a **`Task`-family call result** (calls mint, [§28.3](#sec-producers)) — the trivial-dispose shape above and the full non-trivial set alike (the taken #1813 follow-on; rationale [§5.28](Bezel_Design_Rationale.md#sec-silent-tracking)). The warning names the [K8](#sec-kernel-k8) boundary at which the argument dies and the remedies — bind the source to a named holder first (`var odds: Array<int> := [1, 3, 5]; groups.Add("odds", odds);` — the annotation supplies the literal's target type, and the store rule's ordinary residual then attaches to `odds`), or use the owning family, whose store positions take ownership (`OwningDictionary<string, Array<int>>`, whose `Add` takes the value `owned` — for an owning map's *key* only the first remedy applies, `using var k := new K(); od[k] := v;`, and only where [§28.11](#sec-borrowing-collections)'s store rule admits the bound key, the collection not outliving `k`'s scope; for dynamic task fan-in, `OwningArray<OwningTask<T>>` with the owning `Task.WhenAll` overload, stdlib [§6.7](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-task-static-helpers)). The stated hazard splits by family: for a **trivial-dispose** argument the boundary event is the compiler's free and the hazard is the retained dangling reference (checked-mode `DisposedAccessException` on later use, [§28.2](#sec-checked-disposal)); for a **`Task`-family** argument the boundary event is the task's disposal — the operation is *abandoned*: it runs to its terminal state unsupervised and its result, if owned, is disposed on arrival ([§30.5](#sec-result-lifetime-and-task-disposal)) — and the slot dangles besides; for any other non-trivial-dispose class the boundary event is the value's disposal and the hazard is the dangling slot. The warning does not narrow the admission: the program remains accepted, no `using var` is demanded, and the recorded literal-only-rejection asymmetry above stands unchanged.

For `Set<T>`, the literal elements must have type `T`. Duplicate elements (per `T`'s equality contract) are silently collapsed; the first occurrence in textual order is retained. For `OwningSet<T>`, duplicates are silently collapsed and each later duplicate's owned element is disposed at construction (the set retains only the first instance per equality class).

The set and dictionary literal rules are deliberately asymmetric, twice. A statically-detectable duplicate dictionary key is an *error* while a duplicate set element *collapses*, because a duplicate key silently discards a value expression the literal supplies — almost certainly a bug — while a duplicate set element discards nothing: collapsing is what a set means. And sets retain the **first** occurrence while dictionaries take the **last** value, because first-retention is what makes the `Set<T>` insertion-order guarantee above coherent (the first occurrence claims the position), while a dictionary literal reads as a sequence of insertions, whose repeated-key semantics is the indexer's last-write-wins upsert (stdlib [§4.8](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-dictionaryk-v)).

For `Dictionary<K, V>` and `OwningDictionary<K, V>`, each element in the literal uses `key: value` syntax: the sub-expression left of the colon is the key (type `K`), the sub-expression right of the colon is the value (type `V`). Duplicate keys are a compile error when all duplicate keys are compile-time constants; when duplicates are not statically detectable, the last value in textual order wins, and for `OwningDictionary` the displaced earlier value is disposed at construction. The key-value pair syntax is recognized only when the target type is `Dictionary<K, V>` or `OwningDictionary<K, V>`; in any other target context a colon inside a literal element is a compile error. For `Dictionary<K, V>`, an entry's **key** sub-expression is an element expression for the rules of this section: the borrowing-family admission above applies to it, and a fresh trivial-dispose key (a nested literal, a `new` expression, or an `owned`-returning call) joins the literal tree as a fresh node exactly as a value-position node does. A class-typed key's equality contract is [§8.3](#sec-equals-and-gethashcode)'s default — identity — unless the key type declares otherwise.

**Examples.**

```bezel
// Sequence literals targeting different sequence types
using var list:  LinkedList<int> := [10, 20, 30];
using var stack: Stack<int>      := [1, 2, 3];        // 3 is on top
using var queue: Queue<int>      := [1, 2, 3];        // 1 is at the front
using var set:   Set<string>     := ["a", "b", "a"];  // collapses to {"a", "b"}

// Dictionary literal
using var ages: Dictionary<string, int> := [
  "alice": 30,
  "bob":   25,
  "carol": 41
];

// Nested: dictionary of arrays
using var groups: Dictionary<string, Array<int>> := [
  "primes": [2, 3, 5, 7],
  "evens":  [2, 4, 6, 8]
];

// Nested: dictionary of dictionaries
using var config: Dictionary<string, Dictionary<string, int>> := [
  "server": ["port": 8080, "timeout": 30],
  "client": ["retries": 3]
];

// Record-typed keys (no tuples in this version; use a named record)
record Point(X: int, Y: int);
using var labels: Dictionary<Point, string> := [
  new Point(0, 0): "origin",
  new Point(1, 0): "east"
];

// Owning collections — element expressions must produce owned values
using var conns: OwningArray<Connection> := [Connect("a"), Connect("b")];
using var pool:  OwningDictionary<string, Connection> := [
  "primary": Connect("p"),
  "backup":  Connect("b")
];
```

**Trailing comma.** A trailing comma after the last element or dictionary entry is permitted.

**Empty literals.** The empty literal `[]` is admitted for every collection target listed above (every collection type has a well-defined empty value) but is always rejected for inline arrays (a literal must supply exactly N ≥ 1 elements, [§15.1](#sec-inline-arrays)), and is rejected when no target type is determinable. The empty dictionary literal is also `[]` (there is no `[:]`-style disambiguator) — the target type determines whether `[]` constructs an empty sequence collection or an empty dictionary. An empty literal in a non-collection or undeterminable context is the usual "cannot infer target type" compile error.

Rationale [§5.16](Bezel_Design_Rationale.md#sec-collection-literals-for-complex-collections) records why the dictionary form is spelled `[k: v, ...]`.

User-defined collection types opt into sequence-literal construction via the protocol of [§15.4.1](#sec-the-user-defined-sequence-literal-protocol). The dictionary-literal form `[k: v, ...]` remains restricted to the built-in `Dictionary<K, V>` and `OwningDictionary<K, V>`; a user-extensible dictionary-literal protocol is deferred (rationale [§18](Bezel_Design_Rationale.md#sec-things-deferred)).

<a id="sec-user-defined-collection-literal-protocol"></a>
<a id="sec-the-user-defined-sequence-literal-protocol"></a>
#### 15.4.1 The user-defined sequence-literal protocol

A **class** opts into sequence-literal construction by conforming ([§12.7](#sec-interface-conformance)) to one of two static interfaces (stdlib [§2.19](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-static-abstractions), [§11.8](#sec-static-interface-members)) — `ICollectionLiteralTarget<TSelf, T>`, which makes it a **borrowing-form target**, or `IOwningCollectionLiteralTarget<TSelf, T>`, which makes it an **owning-form target** — with `TSelf` the conforming class itself at its own instantiation, and supplying the one static member each declares, `FromCollectionLiteral`, under [§11.2](#sec-interface-declaration)'s exact-signature matching. A class `C` is a **sequence-literal target** exactly when it conforms to one of the two interfaces at `TSelf = C`; a conformance at any other `TSelf` is an ordinary conformance and not a target. A generic type parameter whose constraints guarantee that conformance at `TSelf` = the parameter ([§12.7](#sec-interface-conformance)) is likewise a sequence-literal target within the body that declares it; the lowering below then dispatches through the constraint ([§11.8](#sec-static-interface-members)). An interface type is never a sequence-literal target, whatever it extends ([§11.8](#sec-static-interface-members): the interface name declares no body to run). Being a sequence-literal target is derived from a type's declared conformances, not from its structure — it is not a [§3.6](#sec-derived-type-properties) derived type property. The built-in sequence collections declare the conformance in their standard-library declarations (stdlib §4.3). A sequence literal in a context targeting a type that is not a sequence-literal target is the usual "cannot infer target type" / "no applicable target" compile error.

**Borrowing form.** For a class `C<T>` whose elements are borrows (the type does not own its elements), the conformance is `ICollectionLiteralTarget<C<T>, T>` and the witness — stdlib §2.19's member at `TSelf = C<T>` — is:

```bezel
public static method FromCollectionLiteral(elements: ReadOnlyArraySpan<T>): owned C<T>;
```

The carrier is the **borrowing family's** read-only view (stdlib [§4.15](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-arrayspant-readonlyarrayspant)), whose source `Array<T>` borrows its class-`T` slots — matching this form's own definition. The owning family's `ReadOnlySpan<T>` is not a carrier for either form: its source `OwningBuffer<T>` owns those slots (stdlib [§4.14](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-owned-buffers-and-spans)), and the two span families are not interchangeable.

**Owning form.** For a class `C<T>` that owns its elements (`where T: class`), the conformance is `IOwningCollectionLiteralTarget<C<T>, T>` and the witness is:

```bezel
public static method FromCollectionLiteral(owned elements: OwningArray<T>): owned C<T>;
```

A class declares, on itself, at most one of the two conformances at `TSelf` = itself, at one element type: declaring both interfaces, or one of them at two element types, is a compile error at the declaration (the literal's element-expression ownership would not unambiguously select a target). A conformance inherited from a base class is at `TSelf` = the base and neither counts against this rule nor makes the derived class a target; a derived class that wants to be one declares its own conformance. An extension block cannot declare conformance ([§26](#sec-extension-blocks)). A value kind — record, choice, or enum — may not conform to either interface: the literal's result is a fresh owned heap value ([§15.4](#sec-collection-literals)'s literal-tree rule; *Result ownership* below), and the [§11.8](#sec-static-interface-members) erasure of the member's `owned` return at a value kind does not make one a target (a compile error at the declaration; recorded liftable, proposals `DECLINED.md`). That erasure also fixes how such a witness is **spelled**: at a value kind a declared `owned` return is erased by the substitution, so the attempted `FromCollectionLiteral` is declared — and remains — **unmarked** ([§11.8](#sec-static-interface-members), stdlib [§2.19](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-static-abstractions)); the marked spelling is independently inadmissible over a record, choice, or enum ([§28.1](#sec-where-the-owned-modifier-can-appear)). The rejection above is the verdict at that unmarked spelling: the conformance is rejected for being a value kind's, not for a marker. The element type is the conformance's `T` — read from the declaration, not inferred — and is the type against which every literal element expression is checked. A class that declares a `public static` method named `FromCollectionLiteral` whose signature matches either interface's member at `TSelf` = the class, but that conforms to neither interface, is a compile error at that declaration naming the missing conformance and its remedy (add `: ICollectionLiteralTarget<C, T>` or `: IOwningCollectionLiteralTarget<C, T>` to the class header).

**Lowering.** For the built-in sequence collections (stdlib §4.3) the literal is constructed directly under [§15.4](#sec-collection-literals)'s element-order rules; their listed `FromCollectionLiteral` is the intrinsic factory that produces the same value, and the lowering below governs every other sequence-literal target. For a sequence literal `[e1, e2, ..., en]` with determined target type `C<U>` that is such a target (a conforming user class, or a type parameter constrained to conform):

- *Borrowing form.* The compiler materializes a temporary `Array<U>` holding the n element values and a `ReadOnlyArraySpan<U>` over it (the backing array is compiler-owned and named by no binding; its lifetime encloses only the `FromCollectionLiteral` call) and emits `C<U>.FromCollectionLiteral(thatSpan)`. Each `ei` is type-checked against `U`, must be implicitly convertible to it, and — for class-typed `U` — is subject to [§15.4](#sec-collection-literals)'s borrowing-family element rule. The temporary span and its backing array are released after the call returns; the factory must not retain the span beyond its own execution (the span is a borrow-bearing value subject to [§28.6](#sec-leak-prevention) — storing it in the constructed collection's field is a borrow-lifetime violation, diagnosed in the factory body, not at the literal site).
- *Owning form.* The compiler materializes a temporary `owned OwningArray<U>`, evaluates each `ei` (which must produce an owned `U`) and transfers it into the temporary in textual order, then emits `C<U>.FromCollectionLiteral(thatArray)` transferring ownership of the temporary array into the call. The factory drains the array (typically via the array's `move`-based element extraction) and is responsible for the array's discharge per the standard owned-parameter rules ([§28.3](#sec-local-variables-ownership-and-borrows)). If element evaluation throws partway, the already-evaluated owned elements and the partially-filled temporary array are disposed by the standard exception-path discharge ([§28.3](#sec-local-variables-ownership-and-borrows)), exactly as for an `OwningArray<U>` literal.

The empty literal `[]` targeting such a type is admitted: the borrowing form receives an empty `ReadOnlyArraySpan<U>`; the owning form receives an empty `OwningArray<U>`. The factory is responsible for handling the empty case (it always must, since an empty collection is a valid general input).

**Result ownership.** `FromCollectionLiteral` returns `owned C<U>`; the literal expression therefore produces an owned value, subject to the standard owned-result discharge rules ([§28.3](#sec-local-variables-ownership-and-borrows)) — identical to the ownership treatment of a built-in `Array<U>` / `OwningArray<U>` literal.

**Recognition category.** This is interface-based recognition, like the iteration protocol ([§29.1](#sec-the-protocol)) and unlike the single structural-dispatch rule for `Contains` / `in` ([§17.5](#sec-the-in-operator)). The dictionary-literal form is *not* covered by this protocol; only the bare sequence-literal form `[e1, ..., en]` participates. Because the built-in sequence collections declare the conformance and list the factory (stdlib [§4.3](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-how-the-borrowing-and-owning-hierarchies-relate)), a generic body constrained by either interface may construct any target through `TSelf.FromCollectionLiteral(…)` or through a literal, and a direct static call on a built-in's listed factory produces exactly what the literal produces. Rationale [§5.16](Bezel_Design_Rationale.md#sec-collection-literals-for-complex-collections) explains the choice of mechanism and the contrast with C#'s `[CollectionBuilder]` attribute.

**Example.**

```bezel
public class RingBuffer<T>: ICollectionLiteralTarget<RingBuffer<T>, T>
  private owned _slots: Array<T>;
  private _head: int;

  public constructor(capacity: int)
    _slots := new Array<T>(capacity);
    _head := 0;
  end;

  public method Push(item: T) ... end;

  public static method FromCollectionLiteral(elements: ReadOnlyArraySpan<T>): owned RingBuffer<T>
    var rb := new RingBuffer<T>(elements.Length);
    for var i in 0..<elements.Length do
      rb.Push(elements[i]);
    end;
    return rb;
  end FromCollectionLiteral;
end RingBuffer;

// Usage — identical syntax to built-in collections:
using var rb: RingBuffer<int> := [1, 2, 3, 4];
using var empty: RingBuffer<int> := [];
```

<a id="sec-length-vs-count"></a>
<a id="sec-length-and-count"></a>
### 15.5 Length and Count

One rule assigns the member name: **fixed extent ⇒ `.Length`; resizable ⇒ `.Count`**. The table is its case list:

| Member | Used by | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `.Length` | `[N]T` (inline), `string`, and the fixed-extent buffer/span family (`OwningBuffer<T>`, `Span<T>`/`ReadOnlySpan<T>`, `ArraySpan<T>`/`ReadOnlyArraySpan<T>`) | Size, compile-time constant for inline arrays |
| `.Count` | `Array<T>`, `OwningArray<T>`, and other resizable collections | Current size; may change for resizable collections |

Heap arrays expose `.Count`. A heap array used in fixed-size discipline still has `.Count`, equal to its capacity, throughout its lifetime; the language does not enforce immutability of `.Count`, only the user's discipline.

<a id="sec-slicing"></a>
### 15.6 Slicing

Range slicing `arr[a..b]`, `arr[..b]`, `arr[a..]`, `arr[..]` is supported on `Array<T>`. Slicing produces a new `Array<T>` containing copies of the references (or values) in the range; mutating the slice does not affect the original. The produced array is **owned** by the caller (the slice is a fresh container, exactly like `ToArray()` — stdlib §4.4 documents the form as the compiler-recognized equivalent of `Slice(r: Range<int>): owned Array<T>`): the standard discharge rules of [§28.3](#sec-local-variables-ownership-and-borrows) apply — bind it, transfer it, or let an unbound slice temporary be disposed at the end of the full expression. Element ownership is untouched: for class-typed `T` the fresh array holds copies of the element *borrows*, so disposing the slice never disposes elements.

Out-of-bounds endpoints raise `IndexOutOfRangeException`. An empty range produces an empty array.

Slicing is not supported on inline arrays in this version. A copy-returning slice would need the range bounds to be compile-time constants (the result type `[K]T` encodes its length in the type), and a borrowing slice would need a span type over inline-array storage — but no inline-array span type exists (`Span<T>` and `ReadOnlySpan<T>` view `OwningBuffer<T>`; `ArraySpan<T>` views heap `Array<T>`; none views `[N]T`). A span over inline arrays is deferred indefinitely (rationale [§5.15](Bezel_Design_Rationale.md#sec-owned-buffers-and-spans), [§18](Bezel_Design_Rationale.md#sec-things-deferred)). Users who want a sub-range of an inline array iterate the index range explicitly:

```bezel
for var i in 2..5 do Process(arr[i]); end;
```

Slicing is not admitted on `OwningArray<T>`. The copy-returning semantics would manufacture a second owner for each owned element, violating the ownership contract. Users who want a range-bounded ownership transfer use `Drain()` plus filtering, or a sequence of `PopAt` calls. Users who want a borrowing view of a sub-range iterate the index range explicitly — the indexer-get produces a borrow, which respects ownership without taking it.

Multi-dimensional arrays are deferred to a future revision. The current spec does not provide `T[,]` or `[N, M]T`-style multi-dimensional inline arrays.

The copy-returning semantics for `Array<T>` slicing are stable. Callers wanting a non-allocating sub-range view of an `Array<T>` use `arr.AsSpan(start, length)` to obtain an `ArraySpan<T>` (standard library [§4.15](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-arrayspant-readonlyarrayspant)) — a record carrying a borrow of the array, no allocation. Slicing (`arr[start..end]`) and span-view construction (`arr.AsSpan(start, length)`) coexist as complementary operations; the first manufactures a fresh independent array, the second produces a borrowing view.

---

<a id="sec-range-expressions"></a>
## 16. Range Expressions

A range is a value representing a contiguous span of an ordered type. Ranges are first-class: they may be stored, passed, and returned.

<a id="sec-construction"></a>
### 16.1 Construction

```bezel
var r := 1..10;                       // inclusive: 1 through 10
var h := 0..<10;                      // half-open: 0 through 9
```

`a..b` is inclusive on both ends; `a..<b` is inclusive on the lower bound, exclusive on the upper.

<a id="sec-open-ended-ranges"></a>
### 16.2 Open-ended ranges

A range may omit one endpoint, producing an open-ended range used for slicing and pattern matching:

```bezel
arr[2..5]            // elements 2 through 5 inclusive
arr[..5]             // from start through 5
arr[10..]            // from 10 through last
arr[..]              // all
```

In a pattern, `..<0` matches "any value less than 0" and `31..` matches "any value at or above 31."

The fully open `..` is an ordinary range expression (grammar [A.7](#sec-expressions) `RangeExpr`), not an index-position-only spelling: both endpoints are `null`, so `IsOpenEnded` is `true`, `IsEmpty` is `false`, and `Contains` holds of every value ([§16.3](#sec-range-operations)). Because neither endpoint supplies `T`, the form has **no standalone type** and is admitted only where a written type supplies one — a declared `Range<T>` location (`var all: Range<int> := ..;`), an index position, or an argument position whose parameter type is a `Range<T>` — and is a compile error in an untyped context (`var r := ..;`), the diagnostic directing to an ascription; this is the same admission [§4.2](#sec-integer-types) gives its target-typed integer constants. Like every open-ended range it is not iterable ([§16.5](#sec-iteration-open-ended-ranges)).

<a id="sec-the-ranget-type"></a>
### 16.3 The `Range<T>` type

A range over `T` has type `Range<T>`. `T` is restricted by the compiler to the integer types (`byte`, `sbyte`, `short`, `ushort`, `int`, `uint`, `long`, `ulong`) and `char`. Other substitutions are rejected — at the range expression or the `Range<T>` annotation; a bare type parameter is checked at its substitution. The nine admitted types are compiler-provided `ISteppable<T>` conformers (stdlib §2.19, [§11.8](#sec-static-interface-members)), and conformance to `ISteppable<T>` is **necessary but not sufficient**: `float`, `double`, and `decimal` conform and are not admitted, and a user `ISteppable<T>` conformer is not admitted. The restriction is therefore a compiler-intrinsic rule and not a spelling of a `where T: ISteppable<T>` clause — that clause would admit every conformer, a widening recorded as a deferred design change (`docs/proposals/DECLINED.md`, *`Range<T>` element widening*), not as a follow-up.

`Range<T>` is a compiler-intrinsic record that implements `IEnumerable<T>`:

```bezel
/// Compiler-intrinsic; T restricted to integer types and char.
public record Range<T>: IEnumerable<T>
  public readonly property Start: T?;
  public readonly property End: T?;
  public readonly property Step: long;
  public readonly property IsEndInclusive: bool;
  public pure readonly property IsOpenEnded: bool;
  public pure readonly property IsEmpty: bool;

  public pure method Contains(value: T): bool;
  public method GetEnumerator(): owned IEnumerator<T>;
end Range;
```

`Start` and `End` are nullable; a `null` endpoint indicates the range is open-ended on that side. For closed ranges (both endpoints present), both are non-null.

`Step` is a signed 64-bit integer, to support descending iteration over both signed and unsigned `T`; the default step is 1, and for `T = ulong` its magnitude is at most `long.MaxValue` (`2^63 - 1`). `Step` is independent of `T`'s range, so a step beyond that range is **accepted at construction** (`0..10 step 256` over `T = byte` constructs without error). Iteration stops silently, raising no `OverflowException`, before the first value that would pass the range's endpoint or fall outside `T`'s representable range, whichever comes first: over `byte`, `0..10 step 256` yields only `0`, `0..255 step 128` yields `0` and `128`, and `200..255 step 100` yields `200`. Code computing a step at runtime validates it against `T`'s range where a stricter check is wanted.

<a id="sec-range-operations"></a>
#### Range operations

`IsOpenEnded` is `true` when `Start` is `null` or `End` is `null`.

`IsEmpty` is `true` when **iteration of the range yields no values** (the lower bound exceeds the upper bound in the direction of iteration, or both endpoints are present and equal with an exclusive upper bound). An **open-ended** range is never empty: `IsEmpty` is `false` whenever `Start` or `End` is `null` (emptiness is a property of the range's extent, and a missing endpoint imposes no bound, as the membership formula below already states; that open-ended ranges are not *iterable* is a separate fact). `IsEmpty` and `Contains` agree: an empty range contains nothing. (No operation needs a zero-step case: a `Range<T>` value with a zero step cannot exist, [§16.4](#sec-stride).)

`Contains` is the operation invoked by `in` ([§17.5](#sec-the-in-operator)). **Normative formula:** `Contains(v)` is `true` iff the range is **nonempty under iteration** (`IsEmpty` is `false`) **and** `min(Start, End) <= v <= max(Start, End)`, with `v = End` additionally excluded when `IsEndInclusive` is `false`; a `null` endpoint (open-ended form) imposes no bound on its side and never makes the range empty. `Step` affects membership only through emptiness/direction — `0..10 step 2` contains `3`. Consequently an iteration-empty range contains nothing: `50 in 100..0` is `false` (matching Rust and Python), while `(100..0 step -1).Contains(50)` is `true` (descending and nonempty). A caller who wants *unordered-interval* membership over possibly-inverted endpoints writes it explicitly: `Math.Min(a,b) <= v and v <= Math.Max(a,b)`.

`GetEnumerator` produces an enumerator that yields values from `Start` to `End` (inclusive or exclusive per `IsEndInclusive`), incrementing by `Step`. Calling `GetEnumerator` on an open-ended range raises `InvalidOperationException`. The compiler warns when an open-ended range literal appears directly in a `for` statement or other iteration context.

<a id="sec-iteration-over-rangechar"></a>
#### Iteration over `Range<char>`

For `T = char`, the validity of `T`'s range is itself non-contiguous: code points U+D800 through U+DFFF are surrogate code points and not valid `char` values ([§4.5](#sec-char)). Iteration **steps across the gap**: the successor of U+D7FF is U+E000 and the predecessor of U+E000 is U+D7FF; the surrogate block is not part of `char`'s value sequence.

Concretely: `'\u0000'..'\U0010FFFF'` yields every valid `char` — U+0000 through U+D7FF, then U+E000 through U+10FFFF; a descending range yields the same values in reverse. A stride of k is defined as k applications of the successor (or, descending, the predecessor) function, so a stepped range continues across the gap instead of stopping at it: `'\uD7F0'..'\uE010' step 4` yields U+D7F0, U+D7F4, U+D7F8, U+D7FC, then U+E000 (the fourth successor of U+D7FC), then U+E004, U+E008, U+E00C, U+E010. No surrogate is ever yielded and no exception is raised. Overflow of `char`'s outer bounds (below U+0000, above U+10FFFF) remains the silent termination condition, exactly as for the integer types.

Surrogate code points themselves cannot be written as `char` literals — `'\uD800'` and similar escapes are compile errors per [§18.3](#sec-character-literals) and [§18.8](#sec-escape-sequences-non-verbatim), and `char(0xD800)` is a compile error at the conversion site, its operand being a compile-time constant ([§5.2](#sec-explicit-conversions)); a non-constant integer expression evaluating to a surrogate code point raises `OverflowException` at run time. Range endpoints, however, are integer-valued at construction; a `Range<char>` constructed from the integer endpoints by other means (e.g. by deserialization from a saved value) is bounded by `char`'s validity contract regardless of how the endpoints were spelled. The `Contains` operation uses the normative membership formula of [§16.3](#sec-range-operations) (above) and does not exclude surrogates from the within-extent test of a nonempty range — for a range `r` whose integer extent covers U+D800, the integer-level membership test for U+D800 returns `true`, though iteration of `r` never yields it — U+D800 is not a `char` value. With gap-skipping iteration the asymmetry is confined to the surrogate block itself: iteration yields exactly the valid `char` values within the extent that `Contains` describes.

<a id="sec-stride"></a>
<a id="sec-step"></a>
### 16.4 Stride

A range may include a `step` modifier. The step is part of the range value:

```bezel
var evens := 0..100 step 2;          // 0, 2, 4, …, 100
var down := 100..0 step -1;          // 100, 99, …, 0
var fives := 0..<50 step 5;          // 0, 5, 10, …, 45
```

Rules:

- Step's sign must agree with the range's direction. A range whose direction disagrees with its step's sign produces an empty iteration.
- When the compiler can prove at compile time that a range's direction and step sign disagree (both endpoints and step are constants or constant after folding), it emits a warning: *"this range produces an empty iteration."* The warning is not produced for runtime-computed steps, where sign mismatches may be intentional.
- A step of zero is rejected **at construction**: a literal (or constant-folded) step of zero is a compile error at the range expression, and evaluating a range expression whose computed step is zero raises `OverflowException` at the expression. Range expressions are the sole producer of `Range<T>` values (the record is compiler-intrinsic and declares no constructor, [§16.3](#sec-the-ranget-type); [§17.7](#sec-the-new-operator)'s closed-constructor-surface rule; the deserialization path [§16.3](#sec-the-ranget-type) mentions for `Range<char>` validates identically, raising `SerializationException` per [§9.8](#sec-serialization-synthesis)'s deserialization contract — the bad input arrived on the wire, §9.8's posture, while the in-language expression fault stays `OverflowException`), so no `Range<T>` value with a zero step can exist.
- `step` may not be applied to open-ended ranges.
- `step` is not legal in `case` patterns (patterns test the written bounds; stride has no meaning). The grammar forecloses it — Appendix [A.7](#sec-expressions)'s `RangePattern` carries no step clause — so the diagnostic is a **syntax error**; this bullet is stated for the reader (Appendix [A](#sec-appendix-a)'s foreclosed-prohibition index).

<a id="sec-iteration"></a>
### 16.5 Iteration

A range may be iterated with `for` ([§21.4](#sec-the-for-statement)):

```bezel
for var i in 1..10 do Console.WriteLine(i); end;
for var i in 0..<n do Process(i); end;
for var i in 0..100 step 2 do Console.WriteLine(i); end;
```

`..` produces inclusive iteration; `..<` excludes the upper bound.

Because `Range<T>` implements `IEnumerable<T>`, ranges compose with all IEnumerable-based APIs:

```bezel
var evenSquares := (1..20).Where(lambda(x) => x mod 2 = 0).Select(lambda(x) => x * x);
```

<a id="sec-compiler-optimization"></a>
#### Compiler optimization

The compiler may optimize `for var i in rangeExpr do ... end` into a counted loop that bypasses the `IEnumerable` protocol, provided the observable behavior is identical. For range literals with constant endpoints, this produces tight loop code with no heap allocation. For range variables, the compiler may still optimize when it can prove the range is closed.

<a id="sec-iteration-open-ended-ranges"></a>
#### Open-ended ranges

Iterating an open-ended range raises `InvalidOperationException` at the call to `GetEnumerator`, before any iteration occurs. The compiler emits a warning when an open-ended range literal appears in an iteration context:

```bezel
for var i in 10.. do ... end;     // WARNING: open-ended range cannot be iterated
```

For ranges stored in variables, the check is deferred to runtime:

```bezel
var r: Range<int> := (if someCondition then 1..10 else 10..);
for var i in r do ... end;        // InvalidOperationException if r is open-ended
```

Open-ended ranges are designed for slicing ([§15.6](#sec-slicing)) and pattern matching ([§19.3](#sec-patterns)), not iteration.

<a id="sec-empty-ranges-and-equal-bound-ranges"></a>
### 16.6 Empty ranges and equal-bound ranges

A range whose lower bound exceeds its upper bound (in the direction of iteration) is empty. Iterating an empty range is a no-op. Construction is not an error. **Range patterns:** a range pattern `lo..hi` / `lo..<hi` (necessarily stepless, [§16.4](#sec-step)) matches `v` iff `lo <= v <= hi` (resp. `< hi`) read directionally as written. A range pattern is admitted only over a scrutinee whose type is one [§16.3](#sec-the-ranget-type) admits as `T` — the integer types and `char` ([§19.3](#sec-patterns), *Ordered scrutinee types*). With the `Contains` rule this **agrees exactly with `in`** on the stepless forms — a reversed pattern like `100..0` matches nothing, and `50 in 100..0` is likewise `false`; there is no pattern-vs-`Contains` asymmetry. The agreement extends to absent values: a range pattern rejects a nullable scrutinee — keyed on the pattern's **kind**, the open-ended and fully open forms with the closed ones, never on which bounds are written ([§19.3](#sec-patterns)'s rule) — and `v in r` over a nullable `v` is rejected alike ([§17.5](#sec-the-in-operator)), both for one reason: range membership is an ordering test ([§16.3](#sec-range-operations)), and ordering admits no absent participant ([§7.11](#sec-lifted-operators)). The two rejections are reached by different rules and their diagnostics differ; what agrees is the verdict. Because a *constant* reversed range pattern can never match, the compiler emits a **warning** at the pattern ("this pattern never matches — bounds are reversed"), the same constant-fold discipline as [§16.4](#sec-step)'s step diagnostics.

A range whose bounds are equal is a special case where direction is undefined:

- An **inclusive** equal-bounds range (`5..5`, `5..5 step 1`, `5..5 step -1`) yields exactly one value — the bound itself. The step's sign does not matter; the iteration produces the start, the next computed value (start ± step) is past the inclusive end, and iteration terminates.
- A **half-open** equal-bounds range (`5..<5`, `5..<5 step n`) is empty for any step. The lower bound equals the upper bound and the upper bound is excluded, so no value is in range.

---

<a id="sec-expressions-and-operators"></a>
## 17. Expressions and Operators

<a id="sec-precedence"></a>
### 17.1 Precedence

Operators are evaluated according to the following table, from highest to lowest precedence.

| Level | Category | Operators | Associativity |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Primary | `.` `?.` `[ ]` `( )` `?( )` `new` `!` (postfix) | left-to-right |
| 2 | Unary | `+` `-` `not` `~` (prefix), `await` | right-to-left |
| 3 | Multiplicative | `*` `/` `mod` | left-to-right |
| 4 | Additive | `+` `-` | left-to-right |
| 5 | Shift | `<<` `>>` | left-to-right |
| 6 | Range | `..` `..<` (with optional `step`) | non-associative |
| 7 | Bitwise AND | `&` | left-to-right |
| 8 | Bitwise XOR | `^` | left-to-right |
| 9 | Bitwise OR | `\|` | left-to-right |
| 10 | Relational | `<` `>` `<=` `>=` `in` `is` `is not` `as` | left-to-right |
| 11 | Equality | `=` `<>` | left-to-right |
| 12 | Null-coalescing | `??` | right-to-left |
| 13 | Logical AND | `and` | left-to-right |
| 14 | Logical OR | `or` | left-to-right |
| 15 | Throw | `throw expr` | right-to-left |
| 16 | Assignment | `:=` `+=` `-=` `*=` `/=` `mod=` `&=` `\|=` `^=` `<<=` `>>=` `??=` | right-to-left |

<a id="sec-notes-on-operators"></a>
### 17.2 Notes on operators

- `and` and `or` short-circuit: the right operand is not evaluated if the result is determined by the left.
- `??` is right-associative: `a ?? b ?? c` means `a ?? (b ?? c)`. `??` binds tighter than `and`/`or`, so `a ?? b or c` parses as `(a ?? b) or c`. `??` also short-circuits: its right operand is evaluated only when the left is `null` ([§7.7](#sec-null-coalescing-and-=)), as do `?.` and `?(…)` ([§7.5](#sec-null-conditional-access), [§7.6](#sec-null-conditional-call-args)).
- `?.`, `?(...)`, and `!` (postfix) are primary-level. They bind as tightly as `.` and `[ ]`.
- The `(if …)` and `(case …)` expression atoms, and the `(var …)` binding atom ([§17.15](#sec-the-binding-atom)), do not appear in the table: each is self-delimited and parses as a **primary atom** (grammar A.7 `PrimaryAtom`), composable in any operand position without further parenthesization. `throw expr` genuinely belongs at level 15: its operand is a full `Expression`, so it extends maximally to the right; inside an atom, a branch or arm derives a full expression, so a bare `throw` branch needs no parenthesization ([§20](#sec-the-if-expression)).
- Assignments and compound assignments are statements, not expressions; they produce no value.
- **Event-subscription forms `+=`/`-=`.** When the static type of the left operand of `+=` or `-=` is `EventSource<T>`, `AsyncEventSource<T>`, or `SharedEventSource<T>` (stdlib [§6.5](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-events-ievent-eventsource)), the statement is a fixed, language-defined desugaring: `lhs += h` rewrites to `lhs.Add(h)` and `lhs -= h` to `lhs.Remove(h)`, selected by that operand type before the compound-assignment rules of [§6.6](#sec-compound-assignments) apply. Grammatically the form is an `AssignmentStmt` (A.6) reinterpreted by the LHS's static type; the forms are not compound assignments, not user-overloadable ([§25.1](#sec-overloadable-operators)), and `lhs += h` **evaluates `lhs` only as the receiver of the desugared call** — it performs no read-modify-write of the location and never assigns to it. The desugaring is recognized **before** `readonly`-assignability checking, so the forms are available on a `readonly` field — the recommended declaration of stdlib §6.5's event pattern (`private owned readonly _clicked: EventSource<T> := new();` … `_clicked += OnClicked;`). `Add` is a `scoped` (storing) position: [§28.14](#sec-scoped-callback-parameters)'s storage-bounded admission applies to the desugared call (for the pattern's spelling the receiver chain roots at `this` through an `owned` field — form 4); on `SharedEventSource<T>` the handler position admits only **capture-free** handlers ([§28.14](#sec-scoped-callback-parameters)'s stdlib-stated capture-free register). `Remove` is call-bounded — it only compares its argument, by function-value equality ([§27.7.1](#sec-equality-of-function-values)); when no handler matches, `-=` is a no-op.
- `++` and `--` are statement-only ([§17.6](#sec-the-increment-and-decrement-operators)) and do not appear in the precedence table. They are not expression operators; they cannot be combined with other operators.
- Range operators `..` and `..<` bind looser than arithmetic and shift, but tighter than the bitwise, relational, equality, logical, and conditional operators. Worked examples:
  - `0..n+1` parses as `0..(n+1)` — Range looser than Additive.
  - `a..b*2 step 2` parses as `a..(b*2) step 2` — Range looser than Multiplicative, and `step`'s operand binds at the same level as the range bounds.
  - `1<<2..1<<10` parses as `(1<<2)..(1<<10)` — Range looser than Shift.
  - `score in 60..100` parses as `score in (60..100)` — Range tighter than Relational.
  - `r = 0..10` parses as `r = (0..10)` — Range tighter than Equality.
  - `(if cond then 0..10 else 20..30)` — the conditional atom's branches are full expressions, so range branches need no grouping.
- Range sits in the bitwise band (level 6), so arithmetic in bounds (`0..n+1`) and `in`-with-range (`x in a..b`) parse without parentheses; bitwise-with-range mixes are rejected by the mandatory-parenthesization rules below (rationale [§14.2](Bezel_Design_Rationale.md#sec-mandatory-parentheses-on-mixed-precedence)).
- `await` is a unary-precedence prefix operator (level 2). Worked examples:
  - `await x.y` parses as `await (x.y)` — primary access binds tighter than unary `await`.
  - `await x + 1` parses as `(await x) + 1` — `await` is unary-level, additive `+` is looser, so the additive operator combines the awaited result with `1`. To await the *sum*, write `await (x + 1)`.
  - `await -x` parses as `await (-x)` — both `await` and unary `-` are at level 2, and the level is right-recursive in the grammar, so `await` wraps a unary expression that itself begins with `-`.
  - `(await x) + 1` is the explicit form for "first await, then add."
  - `await await x` is permitted (rare but valid: awaiting a `Task<Task<T>>` gives a `Task<T>`, which is then awaited again).
- Parentheses `( )` always override precedence.

<a id="sec-mandatory-parenthesization"></a>
#### Mandatory parenthesization

The following operator pairs are **non-associative across categories** and require explicit parenthesization when mixed in the same expression. The compiler rejects unparenthesized mixes with a syntax error suggesting where to place parentheses.

- Bitwise (`&`, `|`, `^`) with equality (`=`, `<>`) or relational (`<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=`).
  *Example:* `a & 1 = 0` is a compile error; write `(a & 1) = 0`.
- Bitwise with logical (`and`, `or`).
  *Example:* `flags & MASK and ready` is a compile error; write `(flags & MASK) <> 0 and ready`.
- Shift (`<<`, `>>`) with arithmetic (`+`, `-`).
  *Example:* `a << 2 + 1` is a compile error; write `a << (2 + 1)` or `(a << 2) + 1`.
- Range (`..`, `..<`) with bitwise (`&`, `|`, `^`).
  *Example:* `mask & 0..n` is a compile error; write `(mask & 0)..n` to disambiguate. (In practice, bitwise-with-range mixes are almost certainly bugs, and the explicit parentheses make the intent visible.)

These mandatory-parenthesization rules cost nothing on programs that mean what they say and catch the precedence pitfalls C inherited (notably the `a & MASK = 0` bug). They apply only across the listed categories; within a single category the table's associativity governs as usual. The rule is **syntactic**: it reads the operators' categories and whether an operand is parenthesized, never the operands' types, so a listed mix is rejected whether or not some grouping of it would type-check. A parenthesization above therefore restores a *parse*; the resulting expression is then subject to the ordinary operand rules ([§3.5](#sec-operators-on-primitive-types), [§6.5](#sec-bitwise-operations), [§25.2](#sec-operator-overloading-restrictions)) like any other. The bitwise-with-logical remedy shows the shape: `(flags & MASK) <> 0 and ready` supplies the `bool` operand `and` requires, because the intrinsic `&` yields an integer ([§3.5](#sec-operators-on-primitive-types)) and no regrouping of `flags & MASK and ready` would.

<a id="sec-the-=-and-operators"></a>
### 17.3 The `=` and `<>` operators

`=` and `<>` invoke `Equals` with a null-safe wrapper ([§8.4](#sec-=-and)). For classes, `=` cannot be overloaded; for records and enums, it can. For inline arrays, `=` cannot be overloaded (inline arrays are neither classes, records, nor enums, and the [§26.2](#sec-what-can-be-extended) extension rules forbid extending them); the default structural equality of [§8.3](#sec-equals-and-gethashcode) is used.

<a id="sec-the-is-is-not-and-as-operators"></a>
### 17.4 The `is`, `is not`, and `as` operators

Type tests and narrowing are described in [§12.7](#sec-type-tests-is-is-not-as). Two operator-level details are worth noting here.

**Precedence.** `is`, `is not`, and `as` bind at the relational precedence level (level 10, [§17.1](#sec-precedence)). `is not` is a single operator with two-token spelling — the parser does not accept `not is`, and `not (x is T)` is a different expression (a boolean negation of a relational test) with the same truth value but no narrowing in the negated branch.

**`as` on value types.** When the target type is a value type, `x as T` produces `T?`: the boxed `Object`-or-interface input is unboxed to the value type if compatible, and the result is `null` otherwise. So `someObj as int` has type `int?`. The result type of `as` is always nullable, independent of whether the target is a value or reference type.

**Degenerate value-type targets.** `as` requires its result type `T?` to exist and to be informative. An **inline-array target** (any form — `[N]T`, `[N]T?`, and the owning forms, which cannot even be boxed, [§8.6](#sec-boxing-of-inline-arrays)) is a **compile error naming this rule**: [§15.1](#sec-inline-arrays) admits no nullable inline-array form, so the operator's contract is unsatisfiable. The remedy is the `is` test, whose [§12.7](#sec-type-tests-is-is-not-as) narrowing admits copying the value out: `if o is [3]int then var a: [3]int := o; end;`. The **unit type** is likewise a compile error as an `as` target: `()` has exactly one value, so the operation could never carry more information than `x is ()` ([§12.7](#sec-type-tests-is-is-not-as)), which the diagnostic names as the remedy — `()?` remains a well-formed type ([§4.7](#sec-the-unit-type)); the rejection is of the operator form, not of the type. When the target is a generic type parameter, the check applies **per instantiation** ([§3.6](#sec-derived-type-properties) rule 2): `x as T` at an inline-array or unit substitution is rejected at the instantiation site.

**Type tests and ownership.** `is`, `is not`, and `as` are **non-destructive on their operand**: each reads the operand and inspects its runtime type without moving from it, so after `if x is T then … end` — and after `var r := x as T` — `x` retains whatever ownership state it had before the test, and the narrowing `is` enables ([§12.7](#sec-type-tests-is-is-not-as)) transfers nothing. For `as`, the result is additionally a *borrow* of `x` (more precisely, a borrow with the same source as `x`), regardless of whether `x` is owned or borrowed.

The result is borrowed even when the operand is owned because the result type is nullable, and `null` cannot carry ownership. The ground is particular to `as`: the null-forgiving `x!`, whose result is non-nullable, keeps `x`'s own classification ([§17.8](#sec-the-null-forgiving-operator)). A successful cast yields a non-null borrow narrowable to the target type; a failed cast yields `null`. In both cases, the original `x` retains its ownership state — the cast neither transfers ownership out of `x` nor disposes `x`'s value. Code that needs the result to be owned must move from `x` explicitly into a target-typed owned location after narrowing:

```bezel
using var thing: Animal := Acquire();          // owned
var maybeDog := thing as Dog;                  // borrow; thing still owned
if maybeDog <> null then
  // maybeDog is a borrowed Dog reference; thing remains the owner.
  // To transfer ownership, the standard owned-local rules of §28.3 apply
  // to `thing`, not to the result of `as`.
end;
```

See the producer table in [§28.3](#sec-local-variables-ownership-and-borrows).

<a id="sec-the-in-operator"></a>
### 17.5 The `in` operator

`x in collection` evaluates to `true` if `collection.Contains(x)` is true. The right operand must expose a `Contains(T): bool` method (instance or extension):

```bezel
var found := 42 in numbers;
var inRange := score in 60..100;
var hasChar := 'a' in "abcdef";
```

`in` produces `bool`. `in` cannot be overloaded directly; types customize membership by providing `Contains`.

**A nullable left operand.** `in` states no nullability rule of its own: `x in c` *is* the call `c.Contains(x)`, so the left operand is admitted exactly when it is admissible as that call's argument under the ordinary conversion rules ([§5.1](#sec-implicit-conversions)) — which is what "compatible type" means in the structural-lookup paragraph below. Where the selected `Contains` declares a **non-nullable** parameter, a nullable left operand is a **compile error** (`T?` does not implicitly convert to `T`, [§5.1](#sec-implicit-conversions)), the diagnostic naming the language's standing remedies — a [§7.4](#sec-member-access-on-nullable-values) narrowing check, `??` ([§7.7](#sec-null-coalescing-and-=)), or `!` ([§7.8](#sec-null-forgiving)). This covers **every range test**: stdlib [§9.8](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-ranget) declares `Contains(value: T)` over the non-nullable `T` of [§16.3](#sec-the-ranget-type), and range membership is an ordering test, which admits no absent participant ([§16.3](#sec-range-operations), [§7.11](#sec-lifted-operators)) — so `n in 1..5` over an `int?` is rejected. Where the selected `Contains` parameter is **itself** nullable — `Array<int?>`'s `Contains(item: int?)`, or `Span<T>`/`ReadOnlySpan<T>` at class-typed `T`, whose parameter stdlib [§4.14](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-owned-buffers-and-spans) declares `value: T?` — a nullable left operand is **admitted**: the test performed is the null-safe equality of [§8.4](#sec-=-and), total over an absent operand and unaffected by [§7.11](#sec-lifted-operators).

Negated membership is written `not (x in c)` — the parentheses are required because unary `not` binds tighter than the relational `in` ([§17.1](#sec-precedence)), so `not x in c` parses as `(not x) in c`, a type error for a non-`bool` `x`. A two-token `not in` operator paralleling `is not` is **deliberately not provided**: `in` desugars to a plain `bool`-returning `Contains` call, so negation composes with nothing lost but one pair of parentheses, and admitting `x not in c` would only half-serve the habit it targets — `not x in c` would still parse the other way. `is not` earns its two-token spelling as the negation of a type-classifying operator with narrowing semantics of its own ([§12.7](#sec-type-tests-is-is-not-as)); membership has no such semantics to protect.

The `Contains` lookup is structural rather than interface-based: any accessible method named `Contains` taking one parameter of compatible type and returning `bool` qualifies, whether it is an instance member or an extension method ([§26](#sec-extension-blocks)). This is the only structural-dispatch rule in Bezel's expression surface (the iteration protocol of [§29.1](#sec-the-protocol) and the collection-literal protocol of [§15.4.1](#sec-the-user-defined-sequence-literal-protocol) are interface-based by contrast).
