(Rationale [§5.16](Bezel_Design_Rationale.md#sec-collection-literals-for-complex-collections), *One opt-in path, not two*.)

Inline arrays expose an intrinsic `Contains` ([§15.1.2](#sec-inline-array-members)), so `x in inlineArr` is admitted through this section's structural lookup like any other collection — no special case.

<a id="sec-the-increment-and-decrement-operators"></a>
### 17.6 The increment and decrement operators

`++` and `--` are postfix-only. They are statements, not expressions:

```bezel
var c := 5;
c++;            // c is 6
c--;            // c is 5
```

`x := y++` is a compile error; `++c` is a parse error. There is no prefix form.

The operand must be an assignable lvalue (a local variable, a parameter, a writable field, an indexer slot, or a property with a setter — the same storage categories [§22.3](#sec-ref-and-out-argument-locations)'s `ref`/`out` arguments reuse). Read-only locations cannot be incremented. The operand's type is one [§6.6](#sec-compound-assignments)'s compound form admits for `+= 1` — an integer type, a floating-point type, `decimal`, or `char` — and `x++` is equivalent to `x := x + 1` (and likewise `x--` to `x := x - 1`) under exactly §6.6's rules: the same overflow semantics as `+` and `-` ([§6.1](#sec-integer-arithmetic)), §6.6's checked narrowing for a narrow integer target, and for a `char` target the [§5.2](#sec-explicit-conversions) code-point rules (`c++` is `c := char(int(c) + 1)`). An operand whose static type is a nullable type is a **compile error**: `x++` takes the verdict `x += 1` has on a nullable operand ([§6.6](#sec-compound-assignments), [§7.11](#sec-lifted-operators)) — write `x := (x ?? 0) + 1;`, `x := x! + 1;`, or narrow first. On an operand of any other type the statement is a **compile error** on a separate ground: `++`/`--` are not user-overloadable ([§25.1](#sec-overloadable-operators)), so a type spells advancement as `x := x + 1` under its own `operator +`, or as a named method. The static type is read as §6.6 and §7.11 read it, after [§7.4](#sec-member-access-on-nullable-values)'s narrowing: a local `n: int?` that §7.4 has narrowed non-null admits `n++` exactly as it admits `n := n + 1`, and stays narrowed after it.

<a id="sec-increment-decrement-on-indexer-slots"></a>
#### Increment/decrement on indexer slots

For an indexer slot `expr[i]` (or `expr[i, j, ...]` for a multi-dim indexer), `expr[i]++` desugars to a read-modify-write through the indexer:

```bezel
// Source:                         // Desugars to:
counts[category]++;                do
                                     var __coll := counts;
                                     var __idx := category;
                                     __coll[__idx] := __coll[__idx] + 1;
                                   end;
```

The full desugaring is:

```bezel
do
  var __coll := expr;
  var __idx := i;
  __coll[__idx] := __coll[__idx] + 1;
end;
```

Each subexpression in the LHS — the collection expression and every index expression — is evaluated exactly once. The indexer's getter and setter are each called once.

Implementations may not deduplicate the getter+setter pair: every `arr[i]++` performs one logical read followed by one logical write through the indexer — on a `Dictionary<K, int>`, two hash lookups. The two-access cost is **inherent** to indexer-mediated read-modify-write: the language has no ref-returning indexers (a recorded deferral, [rationale §18](Bezel_Design_Rationale.md#sec-things-deferred)), so no rewrite of the statement changes it — spelling the read and write as separate statements performs the same getter and setter calls, and re-evaluates the collection and index expressions besides. For **tallying** specifically, the standard library's `Counter<K>` ([stdlib §4.20](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-counterk)) is the dedicated single-operation form (`tally.Increment(key);`, with absent keys created at the delta); for general accumulation the indexer read-modify-write, in either spelling, is the supported idiom (stdlib [§4.8](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-dictionaryk-v)).

The same desugaring applies to `--`. For `+=`, `-=`, and the other compound assignments on indexer slots, the same desugaring applies with the operator changed accordingly; it is the indexer instance of the general compound-assignment rule of [§6.6](#sec-compound-assignments), which also fixes the result's typing — including the checked narrow-integer write-back — for every target kind.

<a id="sec-the-new-operator"></a>
### 17.7 The `new` operator

`new T(args)` constructs an instance of T. For classes, `new` produces an owned reference ([§28](#sec-resource-management)). For records, `new` produces a value. An allocation the runtime cannot satisfy terminates the program — allocation failure is a fatal runtime error, not a catchable exception ([§31.4](#sec-standard-exception-types)). (One exception, deliberate: the [§31.2](#sec-try-catch-finally) supersession-snapshot append is best-effort and drops its entry rather than terminating — diagnostic data, never a correctness surface.)

`new` is not used to construct inline arrays. Inline arrays (`[N]T`, [§15.1](#sec-inline-arrays)) are constructed by collection literals (`[expr, expr, ...]`, contextually typed to the array's declared type, [§15.4](#sec-collection-literals)) or by the implicit zero/null fill at declaration when the element type is defaultable ([§17.11](#sec-the-default-operator)). `new [3]int(0, 1, 2)` is rejected by the type checker — inline arrays do not declare constructors, and the `new` syntax has no meaning on them.

**Standard-library builtins have a closed constructor surface.** For a standard-library builtin type — any type the standard-library document declares — the constructor surface is exactly what that document declares — `new T(...)` resolves only against a declared constructor, never against a compiler-supplied fallback. A builtin declaring **no** constructor — `Guid` (stdlib [§2.6](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-guid)), `IntPtr`/`UIntPtr` (stdlib [§10.0](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-intptr-and-uintptr)) — admits no `new T(...)` at any argument list; the diagnostic names the declared producers — for `Guid`: `Guid.Empty`, `Guid.NewGuid()`, or `default(Guid)` ([§17.11](#sec-the-default-operator)); for `IntPtr`: `IntPtr.Zero` or `default(IntPtr)`. For a builtin record whose only declared constructor is its positional primary constructor (`ExceptionInfo`, [§31.4](#sec-standard-exception-types); `ReadOnlyStringSpan`, stdlib [§3.3](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-readonlystringspan)), the undeclared parameterless form `new T()` is rejected the same way — exactly as for an identically-shaped user record. [§14.2](#sec-constraints)'s generic-body equivalence (`new T()` ≡ `default(T)` for a value substitution under `where T: new()`) is unaffected: `Guid` satisfies `new()` — `Guid` is defaultable — so generic factories still mint empty Guids.

A field initializer or typed local declaration may use the `new()` shorthand when the type is unambiguous:

```bezel
private owned _items: Array<int> := new();          // class-typed field taking a fresh
private owned _config: Config := new(verbose := true);   //   value is `owned` (§28.6)
var xs: Array<int> := new();
```

<a id="sec-written-declared-type-positions"></a>
**The written-declared-type positions.** Several rules let a *written* declared type flow inward into the expression at a position; each names its own subset of one family, defined here once. The **written-declared-type positions** are: (i) a **typed field initializer**; (ii) a **typed local initializer** — a `var`/`const` declaration with a written type, and each ascribed clause of a binding atom ([§17.15](#sec-the-binding-atom)); (iii) a **default parameter value**; (iv) a **typed assignment target**; (v) the **declared-result positions** of [§35.3](#sec-choice-construction), as that section defines them — a `return e;` operand under a declared return type, a member's or accessor's expression body checked against a declared type ([§22.2](#sec-expression-bodied-methods), [§23.2](#sec-expression-bodied-read-only-properties), [§23.3](#sec-block-form-properties), [§23.4](#sec-indexers)), and a `return` operand or expression body checked against a lambda's return-type ascription ([§27.3](#sec-lambda-expressions)); in an `async` body the written type at the position is the declared `Task<T>`'s result type, per §35.3; and (vi) an **argument at a determined parameter type** — a non-generic candidate's declared parameter type, or a generic candidate's once [§14.5](#sec-type-argument-inference)'s bindings are substituted (a record positional argument is one). A lambda whose return type arrives only by target inference, a `var` initializer without a written type, and a subexpression of any of these positions are outside the family. The subsets, each stated at its own rule: the `new()` shorthand below takes (i), (ii), (iii) and the `return e;` statement of (v); [§35.3](#sec-choice-construction)'s case reading takes (v) alone; [§4.2](#sec-integer-types)'s target-typed integer constant reaches every position of the family whose written type is an integer type, among the sites [§5.1](#sec-implicit-conversions) governs; [§14.5](#sec-type-argument-inference)'s target contexts are (i), (ii), (iii), (iv), (vi) and the `return e;` statement of (v) — its own list, kept there.

The shorthand is permitted at the written-declared-type positions (i), (ii), (iii) and the `return e;` statement of (v) above: field initializers, typed local-variable declarations, default parameter values, and return statements (when the method has a declared return type). It is **not** permitted at an expression body or at a lambda's ascribed return (the family's other declared-result members — the case reading of [§35.3](#sec-choice-construction) takes all three, this shorthand takes only the statement), nor at a typed assignment target (`xs := new();` — [§14.5](#sec-type-argument-inference)'s target contexts include assignments; this shorthand does not), nor in general expression contexts where the type would have to be inferred from broader context (overload resolution, `var` without annotation).

<a id="sec-the-null-forgiving-operator"></a>
### 17.8 The null-forgiving operator `!`

`x!` asserts that `x` is non-null. The result type is the non-nullable form of the expression's type. If `x` is null at runtime, `NullReferenceException` is raised.

The null-forgiving operator preserves ownership: if `x` has ownership state *owned* (a moved-from-after-this read pattern applies to the result, just as for a plain owned read), `x!` is owned; if `x` is borrowed, `x!` is borrowed with the same source. The operator is purely a type-system assertion (with a runtime null check); it does not move, copy, or borrow beyond what reading `x` already does.

Over a named owned binding, `x!` is therefore classified by its position exactly as the bare read `x` is ([§28.3](#sec-producers)). At a **marker-free** position of the [consume table](#sec-consume-table) — for example a store into an `owned` field, an owning-collection slot or a `set(owned)` accessor, an `owned` or mint-announcing `return`, `throw`, the discard, an owning iterator's `yield return`, the operand of a Pattern B `await` — `sink._f := x!;` consumes `x` exactly as `sink._f := x;` does. At a **marked** position — an `owned` argument, a local binding or assignment ([K3.3](#sec-kernel-k3), [K3.4](#sec-kernel-k3)) — the transfer is spelled `move x!`, the `!` being transparent to the marker ([§28.8.1](#sec-the-move-expression), Appendix A.7), and an unmarked `x!` is read as an unmarked `x` is. `move x!` at a marker-free position is the redundant marker [§28.3](#sec-move-semantics-for-owned-locals) rejects. [§17.4](#sec-the-is-is-not-and-as-operators)'s borrowed result for `as` does not extend to `!`: its ground is a nullable result, and `x!` is never `null`.

`!` is the only postfix `!` operator. There is no prefix `!`; boolean negation is `not`.

<a id="sec-the-nameof-operator"></a>
### 17.9 The `nameof` operator

`nameof(expr)` returns the source-level name of an identifier as a compile-time `string` constant.

```bezel
nameof(amount)              // "amount"
nameof(_balance)            // "_balance"
nameof(BankAccount)         // "BankAccount"
nameof(BankAccount.Deposit) // "Deposit"
nameof(System.Console)      // "Console"
```

Rules:

- For a dotted expression, the result is the rightmost identifier.
- For a type parameter `T`, `nameof(T)` returns the source-level name as written in the declaration: `"T"`, `"TElement"`, etc. It does not return the substituted runtime type's name.
- Method calls, indexings, arithmetic, and literals are compile errors: `nameof(Foo())`, `nameof(a + b)`, `nameof(arr[0])`, `nameof(42)`.

For an enum constant held as a runtime value rather than written, `E.NameOf(value)` ([§10.4](#sec-methods-properties-static-members)) returns the identifier `nameof` would — `E.NameOf(E.A) = nameof(E.A)` — and `E.FromNameOrNull` is its inverse; the three read one table. For the fully-qualified name of a type, use `typeof(T).FullName` ([§17.10](#sec-the-typeof-operator)). `nameof` deliberately returns only the rightmost identifier; programmers wanting the namespace path go through `typeof`.

The result is a compile-time constant ([§17.14](#sec-constant-expressions)): usable in `const` initializers and every other constant context, and in default parameter values ([§22.5](#sec-optional-parameters-and-named-arguments), which admit more than constants). There is no runtime cost.

<a id="sec-the-typeof-operator"></a>
### 17.10 The `typeof` operator

`typeof(TypeName)` returns the `Type` value for a statically named type:

```bezel
var t: Type := typeof(BankAccount);
Console.WriteLine(t.Name);        // "BankAccount"
Console.WriteLine(t.FullName);    // "BankingApp.BankAccount"
```

`Type` is a sealed class. Its full surface is defined in the standard library ([§2.13](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-the-type-class)); the members most commonly used are:

```bezel
public sealed class Type
  public readonly property Name: string;            // "BankAccount"
  public readonly property FullName: string;        // "BankingApp.BankAccount"

  // Kind predicates — see stdlib §2.13 for the full set and the exact mapping
  // to the §3.1 type kinds.
  public readonly property IsClass: bool;
  public readonly property IsInterface: bool;
  public readonly property IsRecord: bool;
  public readonly property IsEnum: bool;
  public readonly property IsChoice: bool;
  public readonly property IsValueType: bool;

  // Lattice queries.
  public readonly property BaseType: Type?;
  public method IsAssignableFrom(other: Type): bool;

  // Enum metadata (valid only when IsEnum; otherwise raises
  // InvalidOperationException).
  public readonly property EnumNames: IReadOnlyList<string>;
  public readonly property EnumValues: IReadOnlyList<long>;
end Type;
```

The `Type` surface is deliberately confined to type *identity* and *lattice metadata*. There is no member enumeration, field/method access by name, attribute reading, or dynamic construction: Bezel provides type identity, not member-access reflection. The reasoning — the ownership system has no static site to carry the contract for a reflectively-accessed `owned` member, and member reflection is the maximal violation of the no-hidden-magic principle — is given in rationale [§5.18](Bezel_Design_Rationale.md#sec-type-identity-not-reflection).

The runtime guarantees a single `Type` instance per type, so `=` and `Object.ReferenceEquals` agree on `Type` values. `Type` is therefore **runtime-managed** ([§28.9](#sec-runtime-managed-types)): `typeof` is not an owned production, a `Type` value carries no ownership classification and no borrow source, `Dispose()` on one is a no-op, and `owned Type` is inadmissible. For generic instantiations, each substitution **distinct up to top-level nullability** produces a distinct `Type`: `typeof(Array<int>)` and `typeof(Array<string>)` are different `Type` values, but `typeof(Array<int>)` evaluated at two different call sites produces the same instance. **Top-level nullability is erased at reification**: no `Type` value exists for a nullable form, so inside a generic body `typeof(T)` returns the `Type` of the substituted type argument *with its top-level nullability erased* — at a substitution `T = U?` it returns `typeof(U)`, and the substitutions `T = int` and `T = int?` yield the **same** `Type` — while nullability **inside** a composite is part of that instantiation's identity, so `typeof(Array<int>)` and `typeof(Array<int?>)` remain distinct `Type` values (stdlib [§2.13](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-the-type-class)'s rendering-and-reification contract). Consequence, recorded: generic code that keys a registry or diagnostic on bare `typeof(T)` conflates `T = U` with `T = U?`; keys on composite `Type`s do not.

`typeof` accepts:

- Primitive types: `typeof(int)`, `typeof(string)`.
- User-defined types: `typeof(BankAccount)`, `typeof(Priority)`.
- Generic instantiations: `typeof(Array<int>)`, `typeof(Dictionary<string, int>)`.
- Inline-array types: `typeof([3]int)`, `typeof([16 owned]Connection?)` ([§15.1](#sec-inline-arrays)). Each `[N]T` combination produces a distinct `Type` value; `typeof([3]int)` and `typeof([4]int)` are different.
- Type parameters inside a generic body: `typeof(T)` returns the runtime substituted type, top-level nullability erased (above).

Nullable forms are not accepted (`typeof(int?)` is a compile error); a nullable substitution of `T` reifies to the underlying type's `Type` (above; stdlib [§2.13](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-the-type-class)).

`typeof` does not accept variables, method names, or literals — those are compile errors. For the runtime type of a *value*, use `value.GetType()` ([§8.2](#sec-gettype)).

`typeof(this)` and `typeof(base)` are compile errors. `this` and `base` are values, not type names. To obtain the runtime type of the receiver, use `this.GetType()`. To obtain the static type of the enclosing class, write the class name explicitly: `typeof(BankAccount)`.

<a id="sec-the-default-operator"></a>
### 17.11 The `default` operator

`default(T)` produces the zero value of type T. The types for which `default(T)` is defined are exactly the **defaultable** types — a derived type property ([§3.6](#sec-derived-type-properties)): every nullable type `T?`, and every non-nullable value type whose components are recursively defaultable. The per-kind values:

- Numeric types: `0`, `0.0`, `0m`, etc.
- `bool`: `false`.
- `char`: `'\0'`.
- Enums: the value with underlying integer 0 — necessarily a declared constant, per the compile error below.
- Reference types: `null` if the location is nullable.
- Records all of whose declared fields are defaultable and which are not **constructor-only** ([§9.9](#sec-constructor-only-records)): the record value with each field at its zero value. For positional records, the positional fields are considered. For body-only records, the backing storage of all auto-properties is considered. Expression-bodied (computed) properties have no backing storage and do not affect `default` eligibility.
- Inline arrays whose element type is defaultable: the array with each slot at the element's zero value. `default([3]int)` is `[0, 0, 0]`; `default([5]Connection?)` is five `null`s. Owning inline-array forms (`[N owned]T?`) are admitted: `default([16 owned]Connection?)` produces 16 null slots and is a valid (move-only) value.
- **Choices: no choice type is defaultable — `default(C)` is a compile error for every choice type** ([§35.10](#sec-choice-default-with)) — a sum yields no distinguished zero case, and electing one would make program meaning depend on declaration order. `default(C?)` is the valid null (for an owning `C`, move-only) value, as for owning inline arrays.
- The unit type: `()`. The unit **type** is written `()` wherever a type is written — Appendix [A.5](#sec-types)'s `TypeNoNullable` carries the row, and [§4.7](#sec-the-unit-type)'s `()?` and `var o: Object := ();` are written on it — so this row is reached by writing `default(())`, and is not confined to the `default(T)` the compiler supplies internally ([§7.9](#sec-definite-assignment-for-non-nullable-fields) default initialization, [§9.8](#sec-serialization-synthesis)'s `serialized skip`). `var u: () := default(());` and `var u: () := ();` bind the same value.

`default(T)` is a compile error for the non-defaultable types:

- An enum type with no declared constant of underlying value 0. Every producer of an enum value yields a declared value ([§5.4](#sec-enum-casts), [§9.8](#sec-serialization-synthesis)), and `default` is no exception: for such an enum, `default(E)`, `new T()` at such a substitution ([§14.2](#sec-constraints)), default initialization of enum-typed storage ([§7.9](#sec-definite-assignment-for-non-nullable-fields), [§15.1](#sec-inline-arrays)), and any other site that supplies a `default(T)` (e.g. [§9.8](#sec-serialization-synthesis)'s `serialized skip`) are rejected. The remedy is declaring a zero-valued constant.
- A non-nullable reference type.
- Every choice type ([§35.10](#sec-choice-default-with)) — the bullet above; `default(C?)` remains the valid null value.
- A record any of whose declared fields is not defaultable — a non-nullable reference type, a choice, an enum with no zero-valued constant, or (recursively) a record or inline array with a non-defaultable component.
- A **constructor-only** record ([§9.9](#sec-constructor-only-records)) — a record declaring a constructor carrying a contract clause ([§22.16](#sec-contract-clauses)). Every value of such a record is produced by a call to one of its declared constructors, and `default(T)` calls none; a fabricated zero value would be a value of the type with no constructor behind it. For such a record, `default(R)`, `new T()` at such a substitution ([§14.2](#sec-constraints)), default initialization of `R`-typed storage ([§7.9](#sec-definite-assignment-for-non-nullable-fields), [§15.1](#sec-inline-arrays)), a default-value expression spelled `default(R)` ([§22.5](#sec-optional-parameters-and-named-arguments)), and any other site that supplies a `default(T)` (e.g. [§9.8](#sec-serialization-synthesis)'s `serialized skip` and `serialized optional`) are rejected. The remedy is a constructor or factory call — or, where a zero value is genuinely wanted, `R?` and `default(R?)`. The property claims provenance, not validity ([§9.9](#sec-constructor-only-records)).
- An inline array whose element type is not defaultable. `default([3]Connection)` (non-nullable Connection elements) is a compile error; the user must supply explicit initializers. Owning inline arrays `[N owned]T` (non-nullable owning) are likewise an error for the same reason.

In a generic body:

- For unconstrained `T`, `default(T)` is permitted but its result is treated as possibly null and cannot be assigned to a non-nullable T-typed location.
- Under `where T: notnull` with value-type substitutions, `default(T)` is non-null.
- Under `where T: value`, `default(T)` is always non-null.
- Under `where T: class` (or any type-bound constraint that implies non-null T per [§14.2](#sec-constraints)), `default(T)` is a compile error — the constraint guarantees T is non-nullable, and the null value `default(T)` would produce does not fit T's contract. To express the nullable counterpart, write `default(T?)`, which produces `null` of type `T?`.

A substitution that is not **defaultable** — an enum with no zero-valued constant included — is rejected at the instantiation site ([§3.6](#sec-derived-type-properties) rule 2's per-instantiation evaluation; the diagnostic names the property per rule 4).

<a id="sec-the-throw-expression"></a>
### 17.12 The `throw` expression

`throw` is an expression. Its operand is optional:

- `throw expr` raises the supplied exception — an owned instance of an `Exception`-derived class type (the operand rule is [§31.1](#sec-throwing)'s). Valid in any expression position.
- `throw` (no operand) re-raises the currently-handled exception with its stack trace preserved. Valid only as an expression appearing inside a catch arm body ([§31.2.4](#sec-bare-re-raise)).

Both forms have the bottom type — assignable to any expected type — because control transfers to the matching handler before any value is produced.

```bezel
public property [i: int]: double => (case i of
  0 => X,
  1 => Y,
  2 => Z,
  _ => throw new IndexOutOfRangeException());

var name := (if user <> null then user.Name
             else throw new InvalidOperationException("user is null"));

using var config := LoadConfig() ?? throw new InvalidOperationException("no config");

try
  DoWork();
catch
  var ex: TransientException => Retry(ex),
  var ex: Exception => throw          // bare throw: re-raises the current exception
end;
```

The statement form `throw;` (with the trailing semicolon, [§21.8](#sec-throw)) continues to work and is equivalent to the bare expression form followed by a semicolon. The two forms are interchangeable inside a catch arm body; the expression form is shorter and is preferred when the re-raise is the entire body of an arm.

Bare `throw` outside a catch arm body is a compile error, with the same diagnostic as the statement form `throw;` outside a catch context.

<a id="sec-the-discard-_"></a>
### 17.13 The discard `_`

The bare token `_` is **reserved** ([§1.3](#sec-identifiers), Appendix [B.1](#sec-reserved-keywords)): it is never an identifier — never declarable, never readable as a name. It is a *discard* — a sink that consumes or ignores a value without binding it. Every position in which `_` can appear is one of the sanctioned forms of this section — a discard or wildcard, an ignore, or the anonymous owning binding — or a compile error whose diagnostic names the sanctioned forms (the rejected positions are listed below). A discard is valid exactly where receiving-and-ignoring a value is coherent, and an error everywhere else. Identifiers merely *containing* underscores (`_camelCase`, `_f`) are ordinary identifiers and unaffected by this section.

**Pattern position.** Inside a `case` arm or destructuring pattern, `_` matches any value without binding.

```bezel
case shape of
  Circle(_) => "circle",
  Rectangle(_, _) => "rectangle",
  _ => "other"
end;
```

**Out-argument position.** As a positional argument with the `out` modifier, `_` discards the out-parameter result.

```bezel
if dict.TryGetValue(key, out _) then    // we only care that it was present
  // ...
end;
```

`out _` does not introduce a variable; the receiving slot is internal to the compiler and is not observable. The argument is type-inferred from the parameter's declared type. A type annotation on `out _` is not permitted (`out _: int` is a syntax error), mirroring the rule for `out var name` ([§22.4](#sec-inline-out-declarations)) — **a bare ignore takes its type from context, never an annotation**, one rule uniform across every ignore form of this section (`out _`, lambda-parameter `_`, `for var _`). The discard composes with `out` only: **`ref _` is a compile error** — a `ref` argument reads its operand, which a discard cannot supply; pass a named location ([§22.3](#sec-ref-and-out-argument-locations)). (An `out` parameter is pure output, so "receive and ignore" is coherent.) `out var _` is likewise a compile error — it would declare nothing; write `out _`, which already means exactly this ([§22.4](#sec-inline-out-declarations)).

**Discard statement.** The form `_ := expression;` evaluates `expression` and discards its value. The discard statement is syntactically distinct from assignment: `_` is not an lvalue, and the form is recognized lexically by the leading `_` token.

The discard statement's legality is one rule keyed on the result's ownership classification ([§28.3](#sec-local-variables-ownership-and-borrows)), plus one exception; in every permitted form the discard also suppresses the [§21.9](#sec-statement-form-of-expressions) *unused result* warning where the undiscarded expression statement would draw one:

- **An owned result is disposed at the end of the discard statement.** If the result is an owned value — a class instance, an interface-typed value, or a move-only value ([§15.3](#sec-move-only-value-types), [§35.4](#sec-choice-classification)) — it is an *unbound owned temporary* ([§28.3](#sec-unbound-owned-temporaries)): `_ := expression;` evaluates `expression` and discharges the disposal obligation once the statement completes. For a **non-trivial-dispose class** the discharge runs `Dispose()` — the explicit "I want this owned result disposed now" form, useful when an `owned`-returning method's result is not needed (`_ := OpenLog();` — for an illustrative `OpenLog(): owned FileStream` — closes the fresh stream at end of statement). For an **interface-typed value** disposal calls `Dispose()` on the *runtime* type (disposal is virtual), so whatever conforming implementation the reference binds — a future one in another module with a non-trivial destructor included — is disposed correctly; there is no cross-module hazard. For a **trivial-dispose class** ([§28.9](#sec-runtime-managed-types)) the value is **freed** at the end of the discard statement, and the free runs no user code (the class has none to run, [§28.9](#sec-runtime-managed-types)): the discard runs no cleanup the language would not already run — an undiscarded trivial-dispose result is freed at the same boundary, and neither form draws the ownership-discharge warning (the ceremony exemption). For a **move-only value** (an owning inline array `[N owned]T?`/`[N owned]T`, or an owning-classified choice) its owned slots — for a choice, the active case's owned payloads — are disposed in the usual order. In every arm the difference from `using var _ := expression;` (below) is **disposal timing**, not legality: `_ := …` disposes at end of *statement*; `using var _ := …` disposes at end of *scope*. (Auto-drop, [§28.3](#sec-owned-local-discharge-requirement), makes the obligation always satisfiable; the discard names the immediate-disposal point. An operand in **borrow state** carries no obligation to discharge — the borrow carve-out below.)
- **Any other result makes the discard purely cosmetic.** For value types, `string`, primitives, and the other runtime-managed types ([§28.9](#sec-runtime-managed-types)) — inline arrays without owned slots (`[N]T`, `[N]T?`) included — no disposal is required, so the discard does nothing beyond the warning suppression above.
- **Exception: a `Task`-family result may not be discarded.** The `Task` family — `Task`, `Task<T>`, and `OwningTask<T>` ([§30.3](#sec-the-task-taskt-and-ownedtaskt-types)) — has a destructor that handles continuation cleanup and exception propagation, and for `OwningTask<T>` disposes any unconsumed owned result, and disposing a task abandons a running operation — a semantic, not a leak, concern. The discard is a compile error — and so is the anonymous binding `using var _ := expression;` (and `await using var _ := …;`, below) over a `Task`-family value: nothing can await an unnamed binding, so it is the same abandonment one scope later. Use `Task.FireAndForget(expression)` for supervised fire-and-forget, or a **named** `using var t := expression;` for the unsupervised scope-end drop ([§30.10](#sec-standard-library-task-helpers)). Both diagnostics name `Task.FireAndForget` specifically. **The keying strips nullability**, exactly as the [announcement table](#sec-announcement-table)'s Keying rule does for its own rows: a `Task?`, `Task<T>?` or `OwningTask<T>?` operand is a `Task`-family value here, and discarding it is the same compile error. The rule exists to prevent abandonment of a running operation, and a non-null `Task?` abandons exactly the one a `Task` does; a nullable static type changes what may be absent, not what is abandoned when it is present. Where the operand may be null, the supervised spelling takes the null check with it — `if t <> null then Task.FireAndForget(t); end;`.

```bezel
_ := ComputeChecksum();                     // int: cosmetic — suppresses the unused-result warning
_ := someStringBuilder.ToString();          // string: runtime-managed; cosmetic
_ := new Random();                          // trivial-dispose (§28.9): freed at end of statement; no user code runs
_ := items.ToArray();                       // trivial-dispose: same
_ := new FileStream(path, FileMode.Open);   // non-trivial-dispose: opened, then disposed at end of statement

_ := DoTelemetryAsync();                 // ERROR: a Task may not be discarded — disposing
                                         //   a task abandons a running operation
Task.FireAndForget(DoTelemetryAsync());  // OK — supervised

using var _ := new FileStream(path, FileMode.Open);     // OK — disposed at scope end
```

**Discard of a named owned binding.** `_ := x;` where `x` is a named owned binding — an owned local or an `owned` parameter — is a **marker-free consume**: the value is disposed at the end of the discard statement, and `x` is thereafter treated exactly as explicitly disposed ([§28.3](#sec-owned-local-discharge-requirement) — the scope-end pass skips it; a later read falls under the use-after-dispose regime of [§28.2](#sec-checked-disposal), and a join with a still-owned path yields maybe-consumed). No transfer marker is required and `_ := move x;` is not a form: the discard sink is itself the source-visible announcement — the same no-marker logic as `throw x` ([§31.1](#sec-the-throw-operand)) and `owned` returns. For the same reason the consume-site freeze does not apply ([K5.3](#sec-kernel-k5)'s site-announced kills — the disposed flag is the runtime backstop). The type-keyed legality list above is unchanged: a named `Task`-family binding may not be discarded (above). By contrast, a discard whose operand is in **borrow state** — `_ := b;` on a borrowed local or parameter, `_ := obj.Field;`, a discarded borrow-returning call result — disposes nothing: the discard is purely cosmetic (it silences the [§21.9](#sec-statement-form-of-expressions) unused-result warning where one would fire), and the value's owner keeps the obligation.

The discard form acknowledges a deliberately-unused value *and* discharges its disposal obligation: for an owned class or move-only value, `_ := …` disposes it at end of statement. The disposal contract remains universal — a class instance with a non-trivial `Dispose()` reaches an owned location, becomes the operand of `using var`, is explicitly disposed, is discarded with `_ := …`, or is auto-dropped at scope end ([§28.3](#sec-owned-local-discharge-requirement)) — but no path leaks. The only discards that remain errors are those of a `Task`-family value (above). The rule keys on the **discarded expression's** declared type, so `_ := t;` over an `OwningTask<T>` binding is this error while `_ := await t;` is not: the latter discards the awaited **result**, an owned value in an owned-consuming position ([§30.5](#sec-result-lifetime-and-task-disposal)'s Pattern B list), and the task is consumed by the `await`, not abandoned.

**Ignore forms.** Two binding positions admit `_` as a **true ignore** — accepted, binding nothing: a **lambda parameter** ([§27.3](#sec-lambda-expressions)) — the ignored slot still contributes to the function type, and because nothing is named several ignores may coexist (`lambda(_, _) => 0` is legal) — and a **`for` loop variable** ([§21.4](#sec-the-for-statement)) — `for var _ in xs do … end;` iterates for effects with the element unbound, [§29.2](#sec-desugaring-of-for)'s semantics unchanged (in an owning iteration the unbound element is disposed per iteration exactly as a bound-but-unused one is). No parameter modifier and no type annotation composes with a bare ignore.

**Rejected positions.** Everything else is a compile error whose diagnostic names the sanctioned forms: `var _ := e;` and `const _ := e;` (`_` is a discard, not a declarable name — the diagnostic names both remedies, `_ := e;` for end-of-statement release or `using var _ := e;` for the anonymous scope-end hold; [§21.1](#sec-variable-declarations)); `out var _` and `ref _` (above); every declaration named `_` — a method or constructor parameter (parameter names are call-site-addressable API surface, [§22.5](#sec-optional-parameters-and-named-arguments), carried by the artifact interface, [§2.8.2](#sec-artifact-interface) — choose a name), a field, property, method, type, module, enum constant, choice case, loop label ([§21.5](#sec-break-and-continue)), or alias; the binding spellings of `_` — a pattern binding (`case x of var _ =>`, [§19.3](#sec-patterns)) and a catch-arm binding (`catch var _: E =>`, [§31.2](#sec-try-catch-finally)), where the bare wildcard already means match-without-binding (write `_`, or the bindingless `catch E =>`), and a binding-atom clause (`(var _ := E; body)`, [§17.15](#sec-the-binding-atom)), whose remedy is naming the binding or restructuring the expression — the statement remedies above are not spellable inside the atom; and a bare `_` in expression position (`_` is not a value — nothing binds it, so no such read can resolve).

<a id="sec-recap-of-the-difference-between-discard-and-using-var-_"></a>
<a id="sec-the-anonymous-owning-binding"></a>
#### The anonymous owning binding `using var _`

`using var _ := expression;` (and `await using var _ := …;` in async contexts, [§28.12](#sec-asynchronous-disposal)) is the **one `_` form that owns storage**: it binds the value to an unnamed scope-bound local — scope-end disposal, non-reassignability, and every other [§28.10](#sec-using-var) rule of a named `using var`, the borrow-pin case included — and binds **no name**: `_` is not in scope after the declaration, and nothing can read the value. The ordinary `using var` ascription is retained (`using var _: Stream := …;`): the no-annotation rule governs the bare ignores of this section, not this binding. It is the scope-end counterpart of the discard statement; the choice between the two is one of **disposal timing**, not legality: `_ := e;` disposes at end of statement, `using var _ := e;` at end of scope, and a `Task`-family value takes neither (above). Use `_ := …` to dispose an owned result you do not need *now*; use `using var _ := …` when the value must outlive the statement and needs no name.

<a id="sec-constant-expressions"></a>
### 17.14 Constant expressions

Several rules key on an expression being a **compile-time constant**: `const` initializers (class-level, [§22.12](#sec-static-members); local, grammar A.6), enum member values ([§10.2](#sec-explicit-values)), constant narrowing ([§5.1](#sec-implicit-conversions)), inline-array sizes ([§15.1](#sec-inline-arrays)), and static duplicate-key detection in dictionary literals ([§15.4](#sec-collection-literals)). This section defines the term; grammar A.8's `ConstExpr` (and A.5's `ConstIntExpr`) refer here.

A **constant expression** is built from exactly these forms:

- a literal, excluding interpolated strings: integer, floating-point, and
  character literals, string literals, `true`, `false`, `null` (A.8);
- a reference to a `const` member — class-level, local, or the
  compiler-provided constants of the primitive wrapper types
  (`int.MaxValue`, stdlib §1) — or to an enum constant (inside its own enum's value
  initializers, an underlying-type value, [§10.2](#sec-explicit-values));
- `nameof(…)` ([§17.9](#sec-the-nameof-operator));
- the unary operators `-`, `+`, `~`, and `not` applied to a constant operand;
- the binary arithmetic (`+`, `-`, `*`, `/`, `mod`), bitwise and shift (`&`,
  `|`, `^`, `<<`, `>>`), comparison (`<`, `>`, `<=`, `>=`, `=`, `<>`), and
  boolean (`and`, `or`) operators applied to constant operands of primitive
  or `string` type — including `+` as constant `string` concatenation, which
  folds;
- the `if` expression `(if c then a else b)` ([§20](#sec-the-if-expression)) whose
  condition and both branches are constant expressions;
- a parenthesized constant expression.

Nothing else is constant. In particular: explicit conversions (`byte(x)` — constant narrowing at the use site covers the useful direction; casts in constants are recorded liftable), `default(T)` (declined-liftable: for primitives it folds trivially, but the sublanguage is literal-rooted and `0`/`false`/`0.0` already spell those values), `typeof` (a `Type` is a runtime object), `new`, collection literals, interpolated strings, and calls of any kind (including operator overloads — the operators above are the built-in primitive/string operators only) are not constant expressions.

**Evaluation.** A constant expression is evaluated at compile time under the *same semantics* the expression has at run time — [§6.1](#sec-integer-arithmetic) checked integer arithmetic, [§6.3](#sec-floating-point-arithmetic) IEEE 754 (overflow to `±Infinity` and `NaN` propagation are *values*, not faults), [§6.4](#sec-decimal-arithmetic) decimal, [§6.5](#sec-bitwise-operations) bitwise and shift semantics, [§20](#sec-the-if-expression)'s and the boolean operators' short-circuiting (an operand that would not be evaluated at run time is not evaluated at compile time and contributes no fault). An evaluation **fault** — integer or `decimal` overflow, division or `mod` by zero, a shift count outside the [§6.5](#sec-bitwise-operations) domain — is a **compile error at the constant expression**, never a deferred runtime fault: `const B := 2147483647 + 1;`, `const D := 5 / 0;`, and `const F := 1 << 64;` are rejected where they are written, the same posture as [§5.1](#sec-implicit-conversions)'s constant-narrowing range error.

**Type restriction on `const`.** The two conditions — a constant-expression initializer *and* a declared or inferred type that is a primitive value type or `string` — define the **compile-time classification** of a `const` declaration ([§22.12](#sec-static-members)) and remain mandatory for class-level and `static const` declarations. A *local* `const` failing either condition is a **runtime const** ([§21.1](#sec-variable-declarations)) rather than an error; a reference to a local `const` is a constant expression only when the declaration is compile-time-classified. A **faulting** initializer fails neither condition — membership in the sublanguage is decided by the forms above, not by whether evaluation succeeds — so the three rejected examples under *Evaluation* are compile errors at **local** scope exactly as at class level, and a faulting constant expression is never reclassified as a runtime const ([§21.1](#sec-runtime-const-locals) states the same rule from the declaration side).

`case`-pattern constants are the narrower syntactic form `Constant` of grammar A.8 — a possibly-negated literal, an enum constant, or a named `const` reference — not the full sublanguage; [§19.3](#sec-patterns) is unchanged.

```bezel
const H := int.MaxValue / 2;              // 1073741823 : int
const Flags: long := (1 << 10) | (1 << 3); // folds under §6.5 semantics (parens for clarity;
                                           //   shift-with-bitwise is not a §17.2 mandatory mix)
const Greeting := "Hello, " + "world";    // constant string concatenation
const Who := nameof(Greeting);            // "Greeting"
const Cap := (if Flags > 0 then 64 else 32);     // constant conditional
// const B := 2147483647 + 1;             // compile error: constant evaluation overflows (§6.1)
// const F := 1 << 64;                    // compile error: shift count outside 0..31, the int
//                                        //   left operand's domain (§6.5)
// const S := $"v{H}";                    // compile error: interpolated strings are not constant
```

<a id="sec-the-binding-atom"></a>
### 17.15 The binding atom

The binding atom names a subexpression within expression position (grammar A.7 `BindExpr`, the PrimaryAtom family):

```text
(var name := initializer; body)
(var a := E1; var b := E2; body)
```

The parentheses are part of the form: in atom-start position, `(` followed by the reserved `var` — which begins no other expression — commits the reading at the second token, exactly as the `(if …)` and `(case …)` atoms commit ([§20](#sec-the-if-expression)); in call- and index-argument position the atom supplies its own pair. Each **clause** — `var x := E;` or `var x: T := E;` — introduces one binding and is terminated by `;` (no expression contains a top-level `;`, so the clause's extent is unambiguous); at least one clause is required; clauses chain; the **body** is one full expression, and the atom's value, type, and ownership classification are the body's. The atom takes no precedence-table entry ([§17.1](#sec-precedence)): it is self-delimited and composes in any operand position, exactly as the other paren atoms do.

```bezel
var area := (var w := bounds.Width(); w * w);
var label := (var n := items.Count; (if n = 1 then "one item" else $"{n} items"));
```

**It is binding, not assignment-in-expression.** Each binding is initialized exactly once, at its clause, by ordinary evaluation in textual order — clauses first, body last, every clause on every evaluation. Like a runtime `const` ([§21.1](#sec-runtime-const-locals)), a binding is **not an assignable location**: assignment, compound assignment, `++`/`--`, and binding to a `ref` or `out` parameter are compile errors naming this rule (assignment forms are statements and cannot be spelled *inside* the atom at all; the location rule additionally covers a `do`-bodied lambda within the atom that captures the binding). A lambda may capture a binding by read, under the ordinary capture rules ([§27](#sec-lambdas-and-function-types)).

**Scope and typing.** A binding is in scope from the end of its own clause: the subsequent clauses' initializers and the body see it; its own initializer does not; nothing outside the atom ever does. The atom's bindings are one scope, nested in the scope in which the atom appears: a binding reusing the name of an earlier binding of the same atom, or of a local or parameter in scope where the atom appears, is a compile error under [§21.1](#sec-variable-declarations)'s *Local names* rule. Each clause types exactly as the [§21.1](#sec-variable-declarations) declaration statement it is spelled as: the type is ascribed (a written integer target admitting [§4.2](#sec-integer-types)'s target-typed integer constant, [§5.1](#sec-implicit-conversions)) or inferred from the initializer; a bare `null` initializer requires a nullable ascription (`var x: T? := null;` — the binding is then permanently null, [§28.3](#sec-local-variables-ownership-and-borrows)'s dead-null warning applying, since no later assignment exists). The atom is **not** a constant expression ([§17.14](#sec-constant-expressions)'s inductive set is unchanged; admission of all-constant atoms is recorded liftable). In statement position the atom is an ordinary expression statement — [§21.9](#sec-statement-form-of-expressions)'s discard regime applies to the body's value — but at statement level the declaration statements it abbreviates are the idiomatic spelling.

**Ownership rides the kernel** ([§28.3](#sec-local-variables-ownership-and-borrows)); the atom adds no new ownership rules. A clause is a *binding form*: a borrow initializer makes its binding a borrow carrying the initializer's source set ([K2](#sec-kernel-k2)); a marked transfer `var y := move x;` is [K3.4](#sec-kernel-k3)'s binding transfer, consuming the outer binding on the atom's straight-line evaluation; an owned production makes its binding a **named unbound owned temporary whose boundary is the atom itself** ([K8.5](#sec-kernel-k8), this revision): if still undischarged when the atom completes, it is disposed there — after the body's evaluation, in reverse clause order, exception edges discharging by the unwinding pass ([K3.15](#sec-kernel-k3)) — with no must-use warning (a temporary's disposal is the language's job, not an unclaimed obligation). Within the atom such a binding is an ordinary named owned binding: [K3](#sec-kernel-k3)'s consuming positions (an `owned` argument, an explicit `Dispose()`) discharge it and the atom-boundary disposal then does not run. A borrow whose source is an atom binding may not escape the atom — in the body's value or any other holder — per [K8.4](#sec-kernel-k8): rejected, never lifetime-extended; bind at statement level (`using var`, [§28.10](#sec-using-var)) when the value must outlive the expression. The body is **not** among [K3.4](#sec-kernel-k3)'s marked-transfer positions in this revision (no `move x` body; an atom cannot transfer its own binding out as its result; recorded liftable with the other A.7 positional bounds).

**In contract clauses** ([§22.16](#sec-contract-clauses)) the atom is admitted — it is the form's motivating position: clauses are expression-only and pure, so without the atom a clause using a subresult twice would have to recompute it. Clause initializers and the body are checked under the clause rules expression-wise ([§22.16](#sec-clause-typing)); owned productions cannot arise there (the pure fragment's records-only allocation, [§22.15](#sec-pure-body-rules)), so clause atoms never carry disposals.

---

<a id="sec-literals-and-strings"></a>
## 18. Literals and Strings

<a id="sec-numeric-literals"></a>
### 18.1 Numeric literals

Integer literals:
```bezel
42                  // int
0xFF                // hex
0b10101010          // binary
1_234_567           // digit separators allowed except at start/end
42L                 // long
42U                 // uint
42UL                // ulong
```

Floating-point and decimal literals:
```bezel
3.14                // double
3.14f               // float
-1.23e-4            // scientific notation, double
1.23456789m         // decimal
1.23e2m             // scientific notation, decimal
```

Suffixes are case-insensitive: `L`/`l`, `U`/`u`, `F`/`f`, `M`/`m`. The compiler does not silently promote integer literals: in an untyped context `3_000_000_000` is a compile error without an `L` suffix. (At a written integer target whose range contains it the literal is admitted at the target type — [§4.2](#sec-integer-types)'s target-typed integer constant.)

<a id="sec-boolean-and-null-literals"></a>
### 18.2 Boolean and null literals

`true`, `false`, `null`.

<a id="sec-character-literals"></a>
### 18.3 Character literals

```bezel
'a'         '\n'      '\t'      '\r'      '\\'      '\''
'\u0041'              // 4 hex digits, BMP
'\U0001F600'          // 8 hex digits, full code point range
```

Escape sequences resolving to U+D800–U+DFFF are compile errors.

<a id="sec-string-literals"></a>
### 18.4 String literals

```bezel
"Hello, Bezel!"
"Line 1\nLine 2"      // escapes processed
```

<a id="sec-interpolated-strings"></a>
### 18.5 Interpolated strings

A `$` prefix introduces interpolation. Any expression may appear inside `{}`:

```bezel
var greeting := $"Hello, {name}!";
var msg := $"({point.X}, {point.Y}) - area = {point.Area()}";
```

An interpolation may include alignment and a format specifier:

```text
{expression}
{expression,alignment}
{expression:format}
{expression,alignment:format}
```

- Alignment is an integer, optionally negated; positive right-aligns in a field of that width, negative left-aligns. Wider results overflow the field.
- Format is a type-specific string passed to the value's formatter — see the dispatch rule below.

```bezel
$"{amount:F2}"           // "1234.50"
$"{ratio:P1}"            // "85.0%"
$"{value:X}"             // "FF"
$"{date:yyyy-MM-dd}"
$"|{name,20}|"           // right-aligned in 20-character field
$"{amount,12:F2}"
```

**Format dispatch.** A hole *without* a format spec formats via the value's ordinary `ToString()` ([§8.5](#sec-tostring)). A hole *with* a format spec dispatches to `ToString(format: string)`: the primitive and temporal types provide it intrinsically (the specifier vocabulary and its invariant-culture semantics are normative in stdlib [§2.18](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-iformattable)); a **user** type opts in by implementing the auto-imported interface `IFormattable` (stdlib [§2.18](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-iformattable)). A format spec on an operand whose type is neither intrinsically formattable nor `IFormattable` is a **compile error** naming this rule. An unrecognized specifier at runtime raises `FormatException` (the defined-fault rule, stdlib §2.18).

**Nullable holes.** A hole expression may have a nullable type; no narrowing is required. When the value is `null` at render time, the hole renders as the four-character text `null`, and no `ToString()` or `ToString(format)` dispatch occurs — [§8.5](#sec-tostring)'s implicit invocation is defined for present values. A format spec on a nullable-typed hole is checked at compile time against the **non-nullable form** of the operand's type under the dispatch rule above (the type-formattability check; specifier recognition remains the runtime rule above), and the spec is not invoked when the value is null. The alignment applies to the rendered text `null` exactly as to any other rendered text (it participates in field padding). The hole is not a [§7.4](#sec-member-access-on-nullable-values) member access: the dispatch is performed by the language with a defined null case, the same posture as the null-safe `=`/`<>` of [§8.4](#sec-=-and) — and unlike the ordering rules ([§4.6](#sec-string), [§7.11](#sec-lifted-operators)), where a null participant has no defensible result, rendering one does: making it *visible*. Rendering `null` rather than the empty string keeps absent values diagnosable in output.

```bezel
var name: string? := null;
Console.WriteLine($"user={name}");     // prints: user=null
var x: double? := null;
Console.WriteLine($"[{x,8:F2}]");      // prints: [    null] — the type-formattability check
                                       //   applies to double; F2 is not invoked on null;
                                       //   the alignment pads the text
x := 3.0;
Console.WriteLine($"[{x,8:F2}]");      // prints: [    3.00] — present value: ordinary dispatch
```

**Hole delimitation (normative).** Inside `{…}` the lexer tracks nesting of `(` `)` `[` `]` `{` `}` and skips nested string/char literals (recognized by their own opening quote and parsed as complete literals; they do not terminate the outer string). The alignment `,` and the format-spec `:` are recognized only at the **top nesting level** of the hole; the first top-level `,` begins the alignment, the first top-level `:` begins the format spec. Consequently `{d[k]:F2}` needs no parenthesization tricks (`[…]` nests its colon) and `{(if c then a else b),8}` aligns the conditional. The tracked pairs are exactly `()`, `[]`, `{}` — balanced `<…>` is **deliberately not tracked**: the generic-arguments reading of `<` is a parser-level commitment ([§22.12](#sec-static-members)'s balanced-scan-plus-continuation rule), and this boundary rule stays implementable without a parser; a lexer-level `<`-balance test would also re-cut legal holes like `{x < y,8}`, a comparison with an alignment. A **multi-argument** generic-arguments list at the hole's top level is therefore cut at its comma — `{Cache<int, string>.Default}` is a compile error at the mis-cut fragment — and the remedy is the same parenthesization as for the conditional above: `{(Cache<int, string>.Default)}`. Single-argument forms (`{Cache<string>.Default}`) contain no top-level `,` and need nothing. The format spec runs from its `:` to the hole's closing `}`; braces do not appear inside a format spec (a `{` there is a compile error).

**Literal braces.** In interpolated strings (`$"…"` and `$@"…"`), a doubled brace denotes a literal brace: `{{` produces `{`, `}}` produces `}`. An unescaped `}` that does not close a hole is a compile error; write `}}` for a literal closing brace. Non-interpolated strings are unaffected (braces are ordinary characters there).

<a id="sec-verbatim-strings"></a>
### 18.6 Verbatim strings

A `@` prefix suppresses escape processing. Verbatim strings may span multiple lines; line breaks become part of the string value.

```bezel
var path := @"C:\Users\Bezel\Program.bzl";
var sql := @"SELECT name, age
FROM users
WHERE active = 1";
```

Inside a verbatim string, `""` produces a single `"`.

<a id="sec-interpolated-verbatim-strings"></a>
### 18.7 Interpolated verbatim strings

`$@` combines both:

```bezel
var documentPath := $@"C:\Users\{user}\Documents\report.pdf";
```

<a id="sec-escape-sequences-non-verbatim"></a>
### 18.8 Escape sequences (non-verbatim)

| Escape | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `\n` | Newline (LF) |
| `\r` | Carriage return |
| `\t` | Horizontal tab |
| `\\` | Backslash |
| `\"` | Double quote |
| `\'` | Single quote |
| `\0` | Null character |
| `\a` | Alert (bell) |
| `\b` | Backspace |
| `\f` | Form feed |
| `\v` | Vertical tab |
| `\uXXXX` | Unicode scalar value, BMP only |
| `\UXXXXXXXX` | Unicode scalar value, full range |

The table is closed: a backslash followed by any character it does not list is a compile error.

Surrogate escapes (U+D800–U+DFFF) are compile errors.

---

<a id="sec-the-case-construct"></a>
## 19. The `case` Construct

`case` is multi-way pattern matching against a scrutinee: a single construct that produces a value; in statement position, the value is discarded per the [§21.9](#sec-statement-form-of-expressions) rules (applied per arm — see below). **Expression-position type:** the construct's type is the left-fold of its arm-body types under the [§20](#sec-the-if-expression) common-type rule (`throw` arms are bottom-typed and impose no constraint). Only the selected arm's body is evaluated. The arm bodies are those of [§19.2](#sec-arms), and the construct appears in either position, with the closer keyed to the position: in expression position it is a parenthesized, self-delimited **atom** — `(case … of …)`, expression-bodied arms only — and in statement position an `end`-terminated **statement** (`case … of … end case?;`, grammar A.6 `CaseStmt`) whose arms may also be single statements or `do … end` blocks. Multi-way selection over *conditions* rather than over one scrutinee is the `if`/`elif` chain — the [§21.2](#sec-the-if-statement) statement and the [§20](#sec-the-if-expression) atom.

<a id="sec-forms"></a>
### 19.1 Forms

**`case` (scrutinee form)** — `case expression of` followed by arms. The scrutinee is evaluated once and matched against each pattern in order. Wherever [§19](#sec-the-case-construct) reads the scrutinee's nullability — [§19.3](#sec-patterns)'s pattern rules and [§19.6](#sec-exhaustiveness)'s proofs — it reads the scrutinee's static type after [§7.4](#sec-member-access-on-nullable-values) narrowing at the `case`, as [§7.11](#sec-lifted-operators) reads an operand's: a scrutinee §7.4 has narrowed non-null there is a non-nullable scrutinee. The fact read is the null fact alone (a [§12.7](#sec-type-tests-is-is-not-as) type narrowing leaves the scrutinee's declared type in place), and it is established before the `case`: no pattern establishes one for a later arm. `case` **always** takes a scrutinee; a `case` written with no scrutinee expression is a syntax error — a ladder of conditions is an `if`/`elif` chain ([§20](#sec-the-if-expression)).

**The `of` delimiter.** The keyword `of` terminates the scrutinee and introduces the arms — the Pascal-heritage spelling (`case x of`). Because the boundary is explicit, the scrutinee is a **full Expression** with no precedence restriction and no parenthesization rule: `case x - 1 of`, `case flags & mask of`, and `case lo..hi of` are all direct. A first pattern may begin with any pattern token — a negative range bound in particular — with no possibility of the scrutinee absorbing it:

```bezel
case delta of
  -10..-6 => "strongly down",
  ..<0    => "down",
  0       => "flat",
  _       => "up"
end;
```

A missing `of` is a syntax error at the first arm token; the diagnostic names the delimiter ("expected `of` after the case scrutinee").

```bezel
var grade := (case score of
  90..100 => "A",
  80..89 => "B",
  70..<80 => "C",
  _ => "F");
```

<a id="sec-arms"></a>
### 19.2 Arms

Each arm has the form `pattern => body`. An arm body has three possible shapes:

- **An expression** (any Bezel expression — literal, method call, another `case`, etc.). Valid in both positions, and the **only** form an expression-position `case` admits (where the whole `case` produces a value).
- **A single statement** (e.g. `=> _x := y;`, `=> return;`, `=> throw new ArgumentException("nope");`). Valid in *statement-position* `case` only. The statement's terminating `;` ends the arm body, and the arm separator `,` follows. This is the convenient form for the common one-line arm body that is a statement rather than an expression.
- **A `do … end` block** of statements. Has type `()` and produces no value, so it is valid in statement-position `case` only. Use this when the arm body needs multiple statements.

In an expression-position `case`, an arm result may be the **marked transfer** `move x` ([§28.3](#sec-producers), K3.4): the named binding is consumed on the path where that arm is selected, and is per-path consumed after the construct ([K7.4](#sec-kernel-k7)). An arm result marking the *scrutinee's own binding* is always rejected by the consume-site freeze — the scrutinee borrow is live through the selected arm's completion ([K8.3](#sec-kernel-k8), [§28.3](#sec-consume-site-freeze)); transfer after the construct instead.

Multi-statement logic in *expression-position* arms is extracted into a helper method or local lambda — both produce values, and the extraction makes the arm's intent visible at its declaration site:

```bezel
var description := (case score of
  > 90 => "excellent",
  > 70 => "good",
  > 50 => "passing",
  _    => Classify(score));          // helper for the multi-step case

private static method Classify(score: int): string
  Log("low score: " + score.ToString());
  return (if score < 0 then "invalid" else "failing");
end Classify;
```

Calls to a helper are zero-overhead in the common case (the compiler is permitted to inline them) and keep the arm body to a single expression. The extraction also gives the per-arm logic a name a reader can use, and localizes any side effects the arm performs — both of which are valuable independent of the syntactic question. Rationale [§5.13](Bezel_Design_Rationale.md#sec-no-block-expressions) discusses why Bezel does not provide a value-returning `do ... end` form.

`return` inside an arm exits the enclosing callable, not the arm. `case` cannot be exited "early" via `return`; restructure into helper methods.

Arms are comma-separated. A trailing comma after the last arm is optional. In expression position, the ownership of the `case` result follows the arm-meet rule of [§28.3](#sec-producers)'s producers table — identical to `??` and the `if` expression ([§20](#sec-the-if-expression)).

<a id="sec-patterns"></a>
### 19.3 Patterns

**Constants:** `1`, `42`, `-7`, `"hello"`, `Priority.High`. A leading `-` on a numeric literal is part of the constant pattern (grammar A.8).

**Alternatives:** `2 | 3 | 4 | 5` matches any of these. The alternative separator is `|` (grammar: `AltPattern`); the comma means exactly one thing in pattern context — the separator of arms and of positional slots — so no `=>` lookahead is needed to tell them apart. In `1 | 2 => "low", 3 => "high"`, the first arm matches 1 or 2; the second arm matches 3.

In an alternative list, every member must be **binding-free**: a constant (a literal, an enum constant, or a named `const`), a **payload-free choice case name** ([§35.5](#sec-choice-matching) — nullary, binding-free, and countable toward exhaustiveness like an enum constant), a **range pattern**, or a **relational pattern** — ranges and relationals admitted; like constants they bind nothing and contribute pure membership tests, so `1..5 | 10 => …` and `< 0 | > 100 => …` are single arms. A member that resolves to a *type* is a compile error in a `case` pattern — grouped type tests are written as separate arms; types alter exhaustiveness and binding analysis, which is exactly what the recorded constants-only reasoning targeted (rationale §3.8). Range and relational alternative members do not contribute to static exhaustiveness proofs ([§19.6](#sec-exhaustiveness) counts declared constants, not extents), and an alternative list binds nothing regardless of member kind. (`catch` arms, whose members are exclusively types, use the same `|` spelling for their multi-type alternatives — [§31.2](#sec-try-catch-finally).)

Because the alternative separator `|` is distinct from the slot separator `,`, alternatives are available **per slot** inside a positional destructuring pattern: `TwoColor(Color.Red | Color.Blue, var x)` is a two-slot pattern whose first position matches either color. Alternative members are binding-free per the rule above, so a binding (`var c`) cannot appear inside an alternative list (constants, ranges, and relationals can).

**No collision with bitwise-or (normative note).** `|` is the bitwise-or operator in expressions, but the expression positions embedded in patterns — a relational pattern's operand and a range pattern's bounds — are `Shift` productions (grammar A.7, `PatternBound`), *below* `|`, so a `|` at pattern level is always the alternative separator. A scrutinee-level `|` belongs to the scrutinee expression (delimited by `of`, [§19.1](#sec-forms)); the [§17.2](#sec-mandatory-parenthesization) mandatory-parenthesization discipline covers any residual mixed reading.

**Inclusive and exclusive ranges:** `90..100`, `0..<60`. Open-ended forms allowed: `..<0` (less than 0), `31..` (at least 31), and the **fully open** `..` (grammar A.7), which states no bound on either side and therefore matches every value of the scrutinee's type — an absent endpoint imposes no bound and never makes the range empty ([§16.3](#sec-range-operations)'s membership formula), so with both absent the test is vacuous. `_` is the idiomatic spelling of an arm that matches everything ([§19.6](#sec-exhaustiveness) counts `_` and an untyped `var x`, not `..`, toward a static exhaustiveness proof).

**Relational:** `> 70`, `< 50`, `<= 100`, `>= 0`. Compares the scrutinee against the right-hand operand, under the **intrinsic** ordering of the scrutinee's type ([§3.5](#sec-operators-on-primitive-types)); the scrutinee types that have one are stated under *Ordered scrutinee types* below. A **nullable** scrutinee — value or reference — is a compile error at a relational pattern, and at a range pattern ([§16.6](#sec-empty-ranges-and-equal-bound-ranges)) alike: ordering admits no absent participant ([§7.11](#sec-lifted-operators)), and pattern position performs no narrowing of its own. A scrutinee [§7.4](#sec-member-access-on-nullable-values) has narrowed non-null at the `case` is non-nullable ([§19.1](#sec-forms)), and a relational or range pattern over it is admitted, as `v in r` over it is ([§17.5](#sec-the-in-operator), [§16.6](#sec-empty-ranges-and-equal-bound-ranges)). The rejection is keyed on the **kind** of pattern, not on which bounds are written, so it reaches the open-ended forms and the fully open `..` with the closed ones — a rule that counted bounds would give a range pattern and another range pattern of the same extent opposite verdicts, and the fully open form's reading over a nullable scrutinee ("any present value") already has its own spelling in the type pattern `int` ([§19.5](#sec-type-pattern-matching-never-matches-null)), with `null` and `_` for the absent case. The absent case is separated first and the ordering interrogated on the bound value — `case n of null => …, var m: int when m > 70 => …, _ => … end` ([§19.5](#sec-type-pattern-matching-never-matches-null): a typed binding pattern matches only non-null values). Constant patterns over a nullable scrutinee are unaffected: a constant pattern is the equality test of [§8.4](#sec-=-and), which is total on `null` and does not equal a constant.

**Ordered scrutinee types.** A relational pattern is admitted over a scrutinee whose type has an intrinsic ordering: the integer types, `float`, `double`, `decimal` and `char` ([§3.5](#sec-operators-on-primitive-types) orders every primitive except `bool`), and `string` (ordinal, [§4.6](#sec-string)). A range pattern is admitted over a scrutinee whose type [§16.3](#sec-the-ranget-type) admits as a range's `T` — the integer types and `char` — because its test is that range's membership ([§16.6](#sec-empty-ranges-and-equal-bound-ranges)). Over `float`, `double`, `decimal` and `string`, therefore, `>= lo` is admitted and `lo..` is not, and a test bounded on both sides is written as a guard. Over `float` and `double` the comparison is [§4.3.1](#sec-equality-semantics-for-floating-point-types)'s IEEE one, so a `NaN` scrutinee satisfies no relational pattern. Over every other scrutinee type either pattern is a compile error naming the type: `bool`, the unit type, an inline array, a record, an enum, a choice, a class, an interface, `Object`, a function type, and a type parameter, whatever its constraints, in the generic body. The verdict is keyed on the type, never on whether a declaration supplies ordering operators for it: an `operator <` group that a record, enum, choice or class declares ([§25](#sec-operator-overloading)) is a set of methods that `a < b` resolves to in an expression, not the ordering a pattern reads, and the `<` a constraint grants a type parameter ([§25.2](#sec-operator-overloading-restrictions)) is a static-interface member bound at the instantiation, likewise not intrinsic. Such a test is written as a guard over a binding, where the operator resolves as in any expression: `case w of var x when x < limit => …` ([§19.4](#sec-guards)). The rule holds at every position the two patterns take — an arm, an alternative member, and a destructuring slot, whose tested type is the slot's type under the scrutinee's type arguments — and, as with the nullable rule above, a scrutinee [§7.4](#sec-member-access-on-nullable-values) has narrowed non-null is tested at its non-nullable type.

**Type patterns without binding:** `string`, `int`, `Dog`. Subtypes match: a `Dog` value matches an `Animal` pattern. Subtype matching is a property of *reference-typed* scrutinees. Over an **unboxed value-typed scrutinee** (a primitive, record, enum, choice, inline array, or the unit type — [§12.7](#sec-type-tests-is-is-not-as)'s operand kinds; a choice's case patterns, a case name or a case destructuring, are not type patterns, [§35.5](#sec-case-patterns)), a type pattern is a **static** test — the value's runtime and static type coincide ([§8.2](#sec-gettype)) — so over a non-nullable value scrutinee a type pattern naming its exact type always matches (over a *nullable* value scrutinee `T?` — one [§7.4](#sec-member-access-on-nullable-values) has not narrowed non-null at the `case` ([§19.1](#sec-forms)) — the `T` pattern remains the null-rejecting refutable test of [§19.5](#sec-type-pattern-matching-never-matches-null)), and a pattern naming any *reference* type (a class, an interface — including one the value type implements — `string`, or `Object`) is a compile error: the pattern could never discriminate at runtime, and matching it would require an implicit boxing conversion, which pattern position never performs ([§8.6](#sec-boxing) boxing is a conversion at value-use sites; a pattern naming any *other* type is likewise rejected under this section's pattern/scrutinee compatibility rules). To test a value against an interface it implements, box explicitly via an `Object`-ascribed binding and match the boxed scrutinee: `var o: Object := p;` then `case o of var q: IShape => …` (a move-only value — an owning choice or owning inline array — cannot be boxed, [§8.6](#sec-boxing); its conformance is static and needs no test). The same applies to type patterns with binding (`var q: IShape`). Against a reference type `R` (a class, an interface, `string` or `Object`) — written, or a pattern type parameter's substitution (*Type parameters as pattern types* below), a nullable substitution counting as its underlying type — a **type-parameter** scrutinee `v: T` or `v: T?`, and a value scrutinee against such a substituted `R`, is decided **per instantiation** ([§3.6](#sec-derived-type-properties) rule 2), as [§12.7](#sec-type-tests-is-is-not-as) decides `is` and `as` over such a carrier or target: where the scrutinee's type at the instantiation is a reference type it is the ordinary runtime test; where it is a value type — a value substitution, or the scrutinee's own value type — a type pattern without binding, and a named destructuring's class head (its slot bindings are member reads and are not rejected; at a value substitution the head never matches), takes, allocating nothing, the answer [§12.7](#sec-type-tests-is-is-not-as) gives the same `is R` test there, so an arm that can never match is admitted and never selected, while a type pattern with binding is rejected at the instantiation site whatever the static answer, as `as` is; against a value-type pattern, see *Type parameters as pattern types* below. Such an answer neither supplies nor removes a [§19.6](#sec-exhaustiveness) static proof, which is a verdict about the generic body.

**Type patterns with binding:** `var n: int`, `var d: Dog`. The bound name is in scope in that arm's `when` guard and body (matching the `catch`-arm rule, [§31.2](#sec-try-catch-finally)).

**Type parameters as pattern types:** in a generic body, a type parameter may be used as a pattern type — `var x: T` and bare `T` test against the **substituted** type argument, per instantiation, the same rule as catch arms ([§31.2.1](#sec-arm-patterns)); all type-pattern rules then apply to the substituted type, including the null rule ([§19.5](#sec-type-pattern-matching-never-matches-null)), save the two rejections of a pattern over a value scrutinee (above), which a substitution never re-applies: an instantiation-site rejection tracks the box, not the answer, so only a binding to a reference type, which would form the box, is rejected there. Where a value scrutinee meets a reference type at the instantiation — whichever side the type parameter stands on, `case v of IShape` or `var x: IShape` over `v: T` at `T = int`, `case p of T` or `var x: T` over `p: int` at `T = Object`, `case v of U` over `v: T` at `T = int` and `U = IShape` — the pattern takes the per-instantiation answer above: `case p of T` over `p: int` matches at `T = Object` and never matches at `T = string`, and `var x: T` is rejected at the instantiation site at both, since a true answer would bind a reference over a value no box holds. Where a pattern and scrutinee are both value types at the instantiation — `case v of int` or `var x: int` over `v: T`, `case p of T` or `var x: T` over `p: int` — no box is ever formed, and the rejection of a pattern naming another value type is not re-applied. The pattern is decided **per instantiation** ([§3.6](#sec-derived-type-properties) rule 2), allocating nothing: it matches exactly when the two substituted types are identical, a nullable substitution of a pattern type parameter counting as its underlying type (over a nullable scrutinee, its non-null values), with or without binding, and otherwise never matches, the arm being admitted and never selected. As for a reference pattern, such an answer neither supplies nor removes a [§19.6](#sec-exhaustiveness) static proof.

**Record destructuring:** `Point(x, y)`, `MyRecord(a, b, c)`. The type name followed by parenthesized bindings matches the type and binds positional fields by position. The number of bindings must match the record's positional-field count. Individual positions may be discarded with `_`: `Point(_, y)`. Destructuring patterns compose with `when` guards and with subtype matching.

**Positional** destructuring applies to records and choice cases ([§35.5](#sec-choice-matching)) — the positional binding is over a record's positional fields ([§9.1](#sec-positional-records)) or a choice case's payload fields. Classes do not have a positional-destructuring surface, even when they declare a primary constructor ([§22.10](#sec-methods-and-constructors-primary-constructors)): primary-constructor parameters are not auto-promoted to public properties, and the positional shape is not part of the class's pattern-match surface. **The restriction is on the positional surface only.** The *Named destructuring* form below **is** admitted over a class-typed pattern head, its slots naming the class's public readable properties — the by-name match surface a class does have, reading which transfers nothing. To match a class hierarchy, use a type-test pattern (`Dog`, `var d: Dog`) and access fields through the bound name, or a named destructuring whose head names the class (`Dog(Name = var n)`). The [§19.6](#sec-exhaustiveness) exhaustive-match example over a `closed` class hierarchy uses the type-test form.

Inside a positional destructuring pattern, a naked identifier is interpreted as a binding for that position — `Point(x, y)` binds `x` and `y` (it does not type-test the positions against types named `x` and `y`). The naked-identifier form is the common shorthand; the explicit `Point(var x, var y)` is also accepted and means the same thing. The naked-identifier form is *not* available outside positional destructuring: at the top level of a pattern, an identifier alone is parsed as a type test, so a binding requires the explicit `var` form (`var x` or `var x: T`). Nested patterns inside a destructuring (e.g. `Outer(Inner(x))`) follow the same rule recursively.

**Named destructuring:** `Rect(Width = var w, Height = var h)`, `Header(Version = 1, Body = var b)`. A destructuring pattern's parenthesized slot list may be written **by name** instead of by position: each named slot is `Identifier "=" Pattern` (grammar A.7 `NamedSlot`), where the `Identifier` names a member of the pattern's type and the pattern after `=` interrogates that member. A slot list is **either** positional **or** named, never mixed in one pattern (v1); mixing (`Rect(3, Height = var h)`) is a compile error naming the rule. At least one slot is required, as for the positional form. A named slot may carry the transfer marker on its source — `move N = var x` (grammar A.7) — admitted only in an owning match ([§35.5](#sec-owning-match)); the *Named-slot bindings and ownership* paragraph below gives the rule.

The `=` is the interrogation reading of [§8.4](#sec-=-and), not an assignment: a call site *constructs* by name with `:=` (`new Rect(Width := 3)`, [§22.5](#sec-optional-parameters-and-named-arguments)), while a pattern *asks* whether a member holds a value (`Rect(Width = 3)` — "is `Width` 3?"), which is exactly what `=` means. No new token is introduced and no collision arises: `=` is not a pattern relational operator (grammar A.7 admits only `<` `>` `<=` `>=`, and a bare constant already means equals), and a pattern-embedded expression is a `Shift` production (grammar A.7, `PatternBound`), below equality, so none can absorb a slot's `=`.

A named slot's `Identifier` resolves against the pattern's type, by kind:

- **Record** — a positional field's auto-generated property ([§9.1](#sec-positional-records)), a body auto-property ([§9.2](#sec-body-records)), or a **public explicit field** ([§9.2](#sec-body-records); the slot read is the same storage read the other two perform, and the *Named-slot bindings and ownership* paragraph below applies to it verbatim).
