Computed (expression-bodied) record properties are not named-slot targets in v1 — the storage set, the same targets `with` takes ([§9.5](#sec-non-destructive-update-with)).
- **Choice case** — a payload field name of the case the pattern's head names ([§35.1](#sec-choice-declaration), [§35.5](#sec-case-patterns), with the [§19.8](#sec-inside-enum-scrutinees)/[§35.5](#sec-choice-matching) prefix-omission rule); the head names the case, not the choice type.
- **Class** — a **public readable instance property**, stored or computed, declared or inherited ([§23](#sec-properties-and-indexers)). **A class-typed pattern head is admitted in the named form**: positional destructuring deliberately gives classes no pattern surface (above), while the named form is the by-name match surface a class's public readable properties are, and reading one transfers nothing. The head's type test is the ordinary subtype-matching one (below), so `T(N = p)` over a class-typed scrutinee matches a derived instance and never matches `null` ([§19.5](#sec-type-pattern-matching-never-matches-null)), and an all-slots-irrefutable arm over a sealed-hierarchy leaf counts toward exhaustiveness exactly as that leaf's bare type pattern does ([§19.6](#sec-exhaustiveness)).

An unknown name, a duplicate name in one slot list, a write-only property ([§23.3](#sec-block-form-properties)), an indexer ([§23.4](#sec-indexers)), a static member, a record **method** or non-`public` explicit field, or — on a class — a field or method rather than a property, is a compile error at the pattern, each naming its rule. Enums and primitives have no named-destructure form (they have no slot surface). An interface-typed pattern head is not admitted in v1. Resolution honours ordinary member visibility ([§13](#sec-visibility)); v1 fixes the class set to *public* readable properties.

Matching `T(N1 = p1, …, Nk = pk)` proceeds like the positional form: the **type test comes first** (subtype matching for a class hierarchy, the case-tag test for a choice case; a named pattern therefore never matches `null`, [§19.5](#sec-type-pattern-matching-never-matches-null), and no slot is read on a failed type test), then the named members are read in **textual order**, short-circuiting on the first refuted slot. Each read is the ordinary member read — a record field copy/borrow, a choice payload read, or a **class property getter invocation** — and a getter *runs* during matching: [§19.4](#sec-guards)'s first-match arm order makes the getter-evaluation order deterministic and observable, and a getter that throws propagates out of the `case` construct from the arm being tried (`pure` and contract-bearing getters keep their [§22.15](#sec-pure-members)/[§22.16](#sec-contract-clauses) semantics; matching adds no purity requirement). Each slot's right-hand side is a **full pattern** (grammar A.7 `AltPattern`): a binding (`var w`), `_`, a constant, `null`, a range, a relational, a per-slot `|` alternative among binding-free members (§19.3, unchanged), a type test, or a nested destructuring — named or positional — recursively. A **constant slot is the equality test** `scrutinee.N = c` under the slot's declared type's `=` ([§8.4](#sec-=-and), null-safe over a nullable slot); a constant slot whose declared type does not bear `=` (e.g. a record that is neither auto-hashable nor declares user equality, [§9.2](#sec-body-records) — the two are not the same thing: a record outside auto-hashable *because* it overloads homogeneous `=` does bear `=` — its own) is a compile error at the pattern — the same use-site discipline as writing the comparison out.

A naked identifier on a named slot's right-hand side is **not** a binding. Directly after `=` — the interrogation operator — it resolves as at the top level of a pattern: a constant reference or a type test by name resolution, so `Rect(Width = w)` is an equality test when `w` names a `const`. The positional naked-binding shorthand (above) is scoped to positional slots, where there is no `=` to misread; a binding in a named slot is spelled `var w`.

**Named-slot bindings and ownership.** [§19.3](#sec-patterns)'s pattern-binding ownership rule applies verbatim to every **unmarked** named slot: the binding is a **borrow**, non-destructive on the scrutinee — for a class property, a borrow whose source is the scrutinee ([§28.3](#sec-local-variables-ownership-and-borrows) producers, the instance-getter row); for a copyable value-typed record/choice payload, a copy; for a payload of **move-only value type**, a borrow ([§15.3](#sec-move-only-value-types) — copies are forbidden, and an unmarked slot never transfers); for `string`/runtime-managed, a shared reference. An **unmarked** named slot never transfers: a getter may not return a fresh owned value ([§28.6](#sec-leak-prevention)), so no slot read can mint an obligation, and in an **owning match** ([§35.5](#sec-owning-match)) an owned or move-only value payload matched by an unmarked named slot is borrowed during the arm and disposed at construct completion by the standard [§35.5](#sec-owning-match-traces) machinery, exactly as a discarded slot.

A named slot may instead carry the transfer marker on its **source**: `move N = var x`. The marked slot is admitted exactly when **(i)** the match is an **owning match** ([§35.5](#sec-owning-match) — either trigger), **(ii)** `N` names an **`owned`-marked payload field or a payload field of move-only value type** of the matched case ([§35.1](#sec-choice-declaration), [§15.3](#sec-move-only-value-types); [§28.1](#sec-where-the-owned-modifier-can-appear)'s marker is admitted-but-redundant on a move-only value field, so the marked and unmarked field spellings satisfy the condition alike), and **(iii)** the slot's pattern is a top-level binding (`var x`; v1). Any number of slots in one list may be marked: the admission conditions and the transfer semantics are per-slot and compose — the positional form already transfers *every* obligation-bearing slot at once, so multiple named transfers spell a subset of what the construct already does. On arm selection each marked payload transfers into its binding exactly as the corresponding positional slot would: `x` is an owned local of the arm body's scope under [§35.5](#sec-owning-match)'s standard arm-binding rules, and unmarked named slots in the same list keep the borrow reading above. The marker's operand is the payload field — the location being emptied — the same left-to-right reading as the field take-out `move x.f` ([§28.8.1](#sec-the-move-expression)).

The marker anywhere else is a compile error naming the failed condition: on a slot of a **borrowing match** (the scrutinee retains ownership, so no slot can mint an obligation from it — the diagnostic names both routes: mark the scrutinee, `case move x of`, or match the temporary); on a **copyable value, `string`, or runtime-managed payload** (no obligation to transfer — a payload of *move-only* value type carries one and is admitted under condition (ii)); on a **plain (unmarked) class- or interface-typed payload field** of an owning case (the slot is a borrow, not an obligation — the case's owning classification comes from a sibling field, [§35.4](#sec-choice-classification), and an unmarked field routes nothing to transfer; the remedy is to mark the field `owned` at the declaration if the case is meant to own it, [§35.1](#sec-choice-declaration)); and on a **record or class** pattern head — by derivation, not fiat: no obligation-bearing slot can exist there (records carry no `owned` fields, [§28.5](#sec-owned-fields), and a class getter may not mint an owned value, [§28.6](#sec-leak-prevention)), so marked slots are choice-case-only. A **`_` right-hand side** (`move N = _`) is already inadmissible under condition (iii) — `_` is no binding — and its diagnostic names the sanctioned forms and the remedy per [§17.13](#sec-the-discard-_)'s discipline: *"a discarded payload is already disposed at construct completion — drop the marker, or bind with `var x` to transfer."* A program that wants an owned or move-only value payload transferred writes the positional destructure, or the marked named slot.

```bezel
case client.Fetch(url) of                            // owning match (§35.5 trigger 1)
  Fetched(move response = var r)                     // marked slot: r is owned Response
    => RenderOwned(move r),                          //   in the arm, per §35.5's arm rules
  NotModified          => RenderCached(),
  Failed(var s, var m) => ShowError(s, m)
end;
```

One parse note, mirrored in grammar A.7: the marked reading commits at the three tokens `move Identifier "="` — no pattern-embedded expression can absorb the `=` (above) — and the `move`-rooted *positional* forms the grammar admits (a range bound rooted at `move x`) were already semantically rejected by [§28.8.1](#sec-the-move-expression)'s positional-admission list, so the marked slot pre-empts only parse-then-reject forms.

**Var patterns:** `var t`. Matches any value, binds it. Almost always combined with a `when` guard.

**Discard `_`:** Matches any value, binds nothing. When used as a top-level pattern (a catch-all arm), it must be the last arm (see [§19.6](#sec-exhaustiveness)); inside destructuring patterns (`Point(_, y)`), `_` may appear in any position with no last-arm restriction.

**Pattern binding and ownership.** A pattern binding (`var d: Dog`, the naked identifier `x` in `Point(x, y)`, or the unconstrained `var t`) is **non-destructive on the scrutinee**: the scrutinee retains whatever ownership state it had, and the bound name is a borrow whose source is the scrutinee's source. This matches the `as` operator's behavior ([§17.4](#sec-the-is-is-not-and-as-operators)). When the scrutinee is an owned local of class type and the user wants to transfer ownership through a pattern match, the user moves from the original scrutinee variable after the case construct selects an arm — the case construct itself never moves from the scrutinee. For value-type scrutinees, the binding is a copy by the standard value-type rules; for runtime-managed scrutinees (`string`, function values), the binding is a shared reference. For a scrutinee of **move-only value type** ([§15.3](#sec-move-only-value-types) — an owning inline array; for an owning *choice* scrutinee, the borrowing/owning match split of [§35.5](#sec-choice-matching) governs), the binding is a **borrow** of the value: a copy is forbidden and the case construct never moves from the scrutinee, so the borrow form is the only consistent option — the same reasoning as closure capture of a move-only local ([§28.9](#sec-runtime-managed-types)). Slot reads through the binding are admitted; `move s[i]` through the binding is rejected (the binding does not own the array). The narrowing produced by the case arm is purely informational about the type tag; it does not change the ownership state of the scrutinee.

**Move-only payload bindings across a write point.** A borrowing-match binding of a payload of **move-only value type**, at any depth of the pattern ([§35.5](#sec-choice-borrowing-match); an owning inline array, or a nested owning choice), borrows the payload **in place**. It addresses storage inside the scrutinee's source, and a store to that source while the binding is live would leave it addressing another case's bytes, a confusion no disposed flag backstops ([K4.1](#sec-kernel-k4)). A binding of the whole scrutinee is such a binding too when the scrutinee is itself one (`case inner of var z => …`): it addresses the same payload storage. Such a binding may therefore not be **live at a write point** of the construct, **unless the scrutinee's source is provably unwritten during the construct**. *Live* has [K5.5](#sec-kernel-k5)'s meaning: some later use on a normal or exceptional path, a live closure that captured the binding included. A use of the binding as the **receiver** of a call, as an operand or `Equals(T)` argument of an operator ([§25.2](#sec-operator-overloading-restrictions)), or as the operand of a compiler-provided operation that invokes the element type's members (an inline array's equality, `Contains` and so `in`, `ToString` or `GetHashCode`) is live **across** that call, because the callee holds the borrow for its activation; so is a closure that captured the binding, at a call that invokes it or takes it as an argument. A **write point** is a point of the construct, in evaluation order ([§22.5](#sec-optional-parameters-and-named-arguments), [K9.5](#sec-kernel-k9)), in the pattern after the case test that selected the binding's payload, in the guard, or in the arm, at which one of the following happens:

- a call in any spelling whose statically resolved declaration is not `pure` ([§22.15](#sec-pure-members)) — a method, function value, constructor, operator, accessor or extension member, including one a construct invokes implicitly: a named slot's getter or a constant slot's `=` during matching (*Named destructuring* above), a disposal at scope end, at a full expression's end ([K8](#sec-kernel-k8)) or by a discard, an interpolation's `ToString`, or such a compiler-provided operation;
- a store of a move-only value to, or a `move` out of, storage other than a local of the body ([K9.2](#sec-kernel-k9));
- a store that disposes a displaced value ([§28.7](#sec-reassigning-owned-fields));
- an `await` or a `yield return`.

Each arm's case test reads the source as it stands when that arm is tried ([§19.4](#sec-guards)), so a write point in a declined arm's guard is not a write point for a later arm's bindings. The scrutinee's source is **provably unwritten** in exactly these cases:

- a [stable local](#sec-stable-locals) of the body over the construct ([§7.4](#sec-member-access-on-nullable-values)), other than a binding a borrowing match introduces (the last case below). An owning match's transferred binding ([§35.5](#sec-owning-match)) is such a local.
- storage inside such a local's value, reached from it without leaving the value ([§9.4](#sec-value-receivers-are-borrows)'s key: no hop through a class- or interface-typed member).
- a `readonly` field outside its construction window, in [§7.4](#sec-narrowing-applies-to-locals-only)'s tracked shape.
- a borrowing-match binding whose own scrutinee's source is provably unwritten. A pattern binding's source is its scrutinee's source, so a binding is never a source in its own right.

`this` in a value-kind member body is never such a source ([§9.4](#sec-value-receivers-are-borrows) *Move-only receivers*); neither is any other field, an element, a static, or a property or indexer read. The violation is a compile error at the use, naming the binding, the write point and the remedies: read what the arm needs **before** the point; or match the value where the construct owns it — the owning match over the take, `case move h.C of …` ([§35.5](#sec-owning-match); [K9.2](#sec-kernel-k9)'s restoration applies). For a payload typed by a **type parameter** the binding's kind is read at the substitution ([§3.6](#sec-derived-type-properties) rule 2): the use is admitted at a copyable or class substitution. At a move-only substitution it is a requirement of the constructed type, rejected at every site that names that type, as [§7.10](#sec-generics-and-nullability)'s copy demand is.

<a id="sec-guards"></a>
### 19.4 Guards

A `when` clause adds a runtime guard:

```bezel
case temperature of
  var t when t > 30 => Console.WriteLine($"Hot: {t}"),
  var t when t < 0 => Console.WriteLine($"Freezing: {t}"),
  var t => Console.WriteLine($"Mild: {t}")
end;
```

Arms are evaluated in textual order. The first arm whose pattern matches *and* whose guard is true is selected.

<a id="sec-type-pattern-matching-never-matches-null"></a>
### 19.5 Type-pattern matching never matches `null`

A bare type pattern `T` matches only non-null values. A typed binding pattern `var n: T` also matches only non-null values — the type annotation makes it a type-constrained binding, not an unconditional binding. `null` is matched only by the explicit `null` pattern, by untyped `var x` patterns (which bind any value including null), or by `_`.

<a id="sec-exhaustiveness"></a>
### 19.6 Exhaustiveness

If `_` appears, it must be the last arm; placing it earlier is a compile error.

A `case` with no `_` arm is permitted. In statement position, an unmatched value falls through with no action — except for a statement-`case` that [§21.7](#sec-the-return-statement) grants totality, whose no-match edge is statically dead and is lowered as a defined trap rather than a fall-through. In expression position, an unmatched value raises `MatchFailureException` at runtime; the compiler warns when it cannot prove exhaustiveness statically.

The compiler proves exhaustiveness statically in the following cases:

- **Any scrutinee — irrefutable arm:** some arm is irrefutable — an unguarded `_`, or an unguarded untyped `var x` pattern (which binds any value, including `null`, [§19.5](#sec-type-pattern-matching-never-matches-null)).
- **Enum scrutinee:** every declared constant has a matching pattern — a constant pattern ([§19.3](#sec-patterns)) naming it directly or as a member of a `|` alternative list, a `var` binding, or `_`. Coverage is by **value**: under duplicate constant values ([§10.2](#sec-explicit-values)), an arm naming either alias covers both. Because every producer of an enum value yields a declared value ([§5.4](#sec-enum-casts), [§9.8](#sec-serialization-synthesis), [§17.11](#sec-the-default-operator)), a statically exhaustive enum `case` cannot raise `MatchFailureException`.
- **Choice scrutinee:** every declared case is covered by an unguarded arm — a payload-free case by a constant-style pattern naming it, directly or as a member of a `|` alternative list; a payload-carrying case by a positional destructuring pattern for it whose every slot is **irrefutable** (a binding or `_`). Guarded arms contribute nothing (the rule), and an arm whose slot patterns are refutable (a constant, range, relational, alternative, or nested destructuring slot) covers only part of its case's value space and likewise contributes nothing; coverage is counted per case name, one level deep ([§35.6](#sec-choice-exhaustiveness)). When every case is covered, no `_` arm is required — including across module boundaries: the case set is closed by the declaration, so the cross-module rule below applies with "leaf type" read as "declared case", and adding a case to a published choice is a source-breaking change for consumers exactly as adding a sealed leaf is. Generic choice scrutinees need no per-instantiation analysis: coverage is by case name, not by type.
- **Bool scrutinee:** both `true` and `false` are covered.
- **Record scrutinee:** the scrutinee's static type is a **non-nullable record type** and some unguarded arm matches every value of it — a positional or named destructuring pattern whose head names that type and **every** of whose slots is irrefutable (a binding or `_`), or a type pattern naming that exact type ([§19.3](#sec-patterns): over a non-nullable value scrutinee a type pattern naming its exact type always matches). A record has exactly one shape and is implicitly sealed ([§9.6](#sec-records-and-inheritance)), so covering that shape covers every value; no `_` arm is required. Coverage is one level deep with **no per-slot value-space analysis** — a refutable slot (a constant, `null`, range, relational, alternative list, type test, or nested destructuring) makes the arm contribute nothing, exactly as a refutable choice-case slot does. A **nullable** record scrutinee takes the nullable bullet below.
- **Sealed class hierarchy scrutinee:** when the scrutinee's static type is a `closed` class, or an `abstract` class whose only direct subclasses are themselves `sealed` or recursively form a closed set, and every leaf type in the closed hierarchy is matched by a type pattern (with or without binding), no `_` arm is required. A **leaf type** is every **concrete** (neither `abstract` nor `closed`) class in the closed set — including a concrete class that itself has subclasses: its exact-runtime-class instances exist, so the childless-only reading would claim a proof while such a value matches no arm. Abstract and `closed` members of the set have no instances ([§11.7](#sec-static-classes), [§12.5](#sec-abstract-classes-and-members)) and need no arm. A leaf is **covered** when some unguarded type pattern it is assignable to matches it — subtype matching, [§19.3](#sec-patterns) — so an arm for a concrete intermediate also covers its concrete descendants; to discriminate, place the descendant's arm first ([§19.4](#sec-guards) first-match order). This is the runtime test's static image (for non-generic hierarchies; see the *Generic hierarchies* subsection): every non-null value's runtime class is some concrete member of the closed set, so covering each concrete member covers every value. The leaves may be matched in any order; the analysis is purely on type coverage. When the root or any leaf is generic, leaf coverage is **not attempted** and the match is completable only by an irrefutable arm (the *Generic hierarchies* subsection below). Class leaves are matched by type-test patterns (`var c: Circle => ...`) and — equivalently for coverage — by **named** destructuring patterns whose head names the leaf (`Circle(Radius = var r) => ...`, the *Named-destructure arms* paragraph below); it is **positional** destructuring ([§19.3](#sec-patterns)) that applies to record leaves and not to class leaves. A `closed` class ([§11.7](#sec-static-classes)) provides the strongest guarantee: no subclass outside the declaring module can exist, so exhaustiveness holds across module boundaries.
- **Nullable scrutinee:** under the rules above plus an explicit `null` pattern. A scrutinee [§7.4](#sec-member-access-on-nullable-values) has narrowed non-null at the `case` is not nullable here ([§19.1](#sec-forms)): the rules above prove it with no `null` arm. A `null` arm over a scrutinee that cannot hold `null` — non-nullable by its declared type (a type parameter only under a constraint that implies non-null, [§14.2](#sec-constraints)) or narrowed non-null — is admitted and never selected.

Every proof in the list above is a **closed-value-space** proof, on the ground its bullet states: an irrefutable arm absorbs any value; a choice's case set, a record's single shape (sealed, [§9.6](#sec-records-and-inheritance)) and a closed hierarchy's concrete-class set ([§11.7](#sec-static-classes) — across artifacts under [§2.8](#sec-module-identity)'s compilation-closure view, the *Exhaustiveness across module boundaries* subsection below) are closed by declaration; an enum's value set is closed by its declaration and by its producers ([§5.4](#sec-enum-casts), [§9.8](#sec-serialization-synthesis), [§17.11](#sec-the-default-operator)), so a statically exhaustive enum match's no-match edge is unreachable; no conversion manufactures a third `bool` value ([§4.1](#sec-bool)); and the nullable bullet closes the added `null` with its explicit arm. [§21.7](#sec-the-return-statement)'s statement-`case` totality grant is keyed to exactly this property, and this list is its registry; a warning-only reading over an *open* value space (an open hierarchy) is not a static proof and grants nothing there.

An arm carrying a `when` guard contributes **nothing** to static exhaustiveness (the compiler does not evaluate guards): the analysis considers only unguarded patterns. A match whose every arm is guarded is therefore never statically exhaustive — in expression position it draws the warning and raises `MatchFailureException` if every guard declines at run time.

**Named-destructure arms.** An unguarded arm whose pattern is a named destructuring `T(N1 = p1, …, Nk = pk)` ([§19.3](#sec-patterns)) contributes to static exhaustiveness **exactly where an unguarded arm covering `T` by the rules above would** — a type pattern for a sealed-hierarchy leaf, or, for a choice case or a record scrutinee, where the all-slots-irrefutable positional destructure would (the choice bullet above) — **if and only if every named slot is irrefutable** (a binding or `_`; a marked slot `move N = var x` ([§19.3](#sec-patterns)) is an irrefutable binding — its right-hand side is a binding by admission — and contributes exactly as `N = var x` does). Any refutable slot (a constant, `null`, range, relational, alternative list, type test, or nested destructuring) makes the arm contribute nothing, exactly as a refutable positional slot does: coverage is counted per type or case name, one level deep, with **no per-property value-space analysis** in v1 (`Rect(Width = 1..100)` arms never sum to coverage of `Rect`, whatever the property's type). Consequently a sealed hierarchy is matched exhaustively with no `_` arm by named-destructure arms whose slots are all irrefutable, exactly as by bare type patterns.

```bezel
public closed class Shape ... end Shape;
public sealed class Circle: Shape ... end Circle;
public sealed class Square: Shape ... end Square;
public sealed class Triangle: Shape ... end Triangle;

var area := (case shape of
  var c: Circle => Math.Pi * c.Radius * c.Radius,
  var s: Square => s.Side * s.Side,
  var t: Triangle => 0.5 * t.Base * t.Height);                       // exhaustive: every leaf covered, no _ needed
```

When the hierarchy is open (the base is neither `closed` nor an abstract class whose transitive subclass set is closed per the rule above), exhaustiveness cannot be proven statically and the warning is emitted unless the user supplies `_`.

<a id="sec-exhaustiveness-generic-leaves"></a>
#### Generic hierarchies: leaf coverage is not attempted

When the closed hierarchy's root or any leaf is generic, leaf coverage is **not attempted**: type patterns name single instantiations, and the compiler attempts no leaf-inhabitation analysis against the scrutinee type, so no arrangement of type-pattern arms is a static proof — including the sub-case in which every leaf is non-generic and all are named (rationale [§8.2](Bezel_Design_Rationale.md#sec-class-hierarchy-exhaustiveness-in-case) records the earlier determination rule). Such a `case` is completable only by an **irrefutable arm** — an unguarded `_` or an unguarded untyped `var` — and draws the non-exhaustiveness warning without one; the warning names the generic hierarchy and prescribes the `_` arm and, for value-shaped sums, a `choice` ([§35](#sec-choices)), whose exhaustiveness is counted by case name ([§35.6](#sec-choice-exhaustiveness)) and needs no `_`. This applies across module boundaries exactly as within one: the analysis is not attempted at any scrutinee type. (If evidence for `_`-free generic-leaf matching ever arrives, the recorded reopening shape is the **existential pattern** — a type pattern matching a generic leaf at *any* instantiation, with its attendant binding-surface questions — which would make such coverage expressible with no per-leaf computation; it is a language extension needing its own RFC, not a reading of this rule. Rationale §8.2 carries the record.)

<a id="sec-exhaustiveness-across-module-boundaries"></a>
#### Exhaustiveness across module boundaries

Exhaustiveness is established at compile time against the visible set of leaf types. When a `case` matches over a sealed hierarchy declared in another module, the closed set is computed from that module's source as it appeared at compile time. If a downstream version of the declaring module adds a new sealed leaf, existing exhaustive matches in dependent modules become non-exhaustive — recompiling against the new version will emit the missing-arm warning, and at runtime an unmatched value raises `MatchFailureException`.

The recommended discipline is treating any addition of a leaf type to a sealed hierarchy as a source-breaking change for consumers. Alternatively, a producer who anticipates extension points can leave the base class non-sealed; consumers will then be required to supply a `_` arm, which handles future leaves automatically.

<a id="sec-termination"></a>
### 19.7 Termination

The closer is keyed to the position. In expression position the construct is a parenthesized atom — it opens with `(case` and its closing parenthesis is the terminator; there is no `end`. In statement position it is an `end`-terminated statement, with the statement's `;` following the `end`:

```bezel
var grade := (case score of
  90..100 => "A",
  _ => "F");             // the atom's ')' closes the case; ';' ends the declaration

case month of
  1 => Console.WriteLine("Jan"),
  _ => Console.WriteLine("Other")
end;                    // statement position: 'end' closes the case; ';' the statement
```

The atom is self-delimited and composes inside any expression position, including inside string interpolations and as another arm's body. In call- and index-argument position its parentheses are its own — the argument list's do not substitute: `f((case x of 1 => a, 2 => b), y)`.

<a id="sec-inside-enum-scrutinees"></a>
### 19.8 Inside enum scrutinees

When the scrutinee has an enum type, the enum prefix may be omitted in patterns. See [§10.6](#sec-case-matching) for details and examples. The same omission applies within a `case` over a choice scrutinee ([§35.5](#sec-choice-matching)): a case name resolves to a case pattern, never a type test.

---

<a id="sec-the-if-expression"></a>
## 20. The `if` Expression

The `if` expression selects between values, condition-first, as a parenthesized, self-delimiting atom (grammar A.7 `IfExpr`, the PrimaryAtom family):

```text
(if condition then trueValue else falseValue)
(if c1 then v1 elif c2 then v2 else fallback)
```

The parentheses are part of the form: in atom-start position, `(` followed by the reserved `if` — which begins no other expression — commits the reading at the second token, and the matching `)` closes the atom; there is no `end`. In call- and index-argument position the leading `(` is the argument list's own, so the atom supplies its pair — `f((if c then a else b))`. The reserved `then`, `elif`, and `else` separate the segments; the `else` branch is mandatory (an expression produces a value on every path); and each condition and branch is a **full expression** with no precedence restriction — in particular, a `throw` branch is admitted in *any* branch position.

Both branches must have a common type. **The common type:** the common type of branch types A and B is whichever of the two the other implicitly converts into — identical types trivially; [§5.1](#sec-implicit-conversions) widening (including constant narrowing); non-nullable `T` into `T?`; a subtype into its base class or implemented interface (a [§5.1](#sec-reference-conversions) reference conversion). If neither converts into the other, the expression is a compile error directing to an explicit conversion or upcast — there is **no** sibling-class least-upper-bound search (deliberately unlike the nearest-common-base rule of [§31.2.1](#sec-arm-patterns), which applies only to multi-type catch bindings). A `throw` branch is bottom-typed ([§17.12](#sec-the-throw-expression)) and imposes no constraint.

**Bare `null`.** A bare `null` branch likewise imposes no constraint of its own: it target-types to the **nullable form** of the other branches' common type — `(if c then s else null)` with `s: string` has type `string?`; its ownership is [§28.3](#sec-producers)'s null-arm absorption; an all-`null` arm set has no type and is a compile error.

**No branch-level target-typing** beyond the bare-`null` rule: a branch whose form requires a target type from context — a collection literal ([§15.4](#sec-collection-literals)), the `new()` shorthand ([§17.7](#sec-the-new-operator)), a bare case construction ([§35.3](#sec-choice-construction)) — is a compile error inside an `if` expression even when the whole expression occupies a target-typed position; write the statement form, or construct each arm through a typed expression. (Recorded decline, liftable — #3042.)

**Evaluation.** Conditions are evaluated in textual order; the first `true` condition selects its branch, the `else` branch is selected when none holds, and only the selected branch is evaluated.

**Ownership.** When the branches are class-typed, the expression's ownership is the arm-meet of [§28.3](#sec-producers)'s producers table: owned arms meet to owned, borrowed arms to borrowed with unioned source constraints, mixed arms are rejected; an *unmarked* read of a named owned binding written as a branch is a borrow arm, and the **marked** branch `move x` — `x` a local binding or `owned` parameter — transfers, consuming on the path where its branch is selected and leaving the binding per-path consumed after the construct ([§28.3](#sec-producers), [K7.4](#sec-kernel-k7)): `var best := (if fresh.Score() > cached.Score() then move fresh else move cached);`.

```bezel
var max := (if a > b then a else b);
var status := (if age >= 18 then "adult" else "minor");
```

Multi-way selection chains with `elif`, in the statement form's word order:

```bezel
var grade := (if score >= 90 then "A"
              elif score >= 80 then "B"
              elif score >= 70 then "C"
              else "F");
```

For many-way selection over one scrutinee, `case` is preferred ([§19](#sec-the-case-construct)).

The atom takes no precedence-table entry ([§17.1](#sec-precedence)): it is self-delimited and composes in any operand position without further parenthesization, exactly as the `case` atom does.

---

<a id="sec-statements"></a>
## 21. Statements

Every statement terminates with `;`. Control structures terminate with `end;`.

<a id="sec-variable-declarations"></a>
### 21.1 Variable declarations

```bezel
var balance: decimal;                 // explicit type, no initializer
var count: int := 0;                  // explicit type with initializer
var greeting := "Hello";              // type inferred
const Pi: double := 3.14159;          // const with explicit type
const MaxUsers := 1000;               // const with inferred type
```

A local of non-defaultable type must be assigned before it is read; a local of defaultable type declared without an initializer holds that type's default from its declaration — `var balance: decimal;` above is `0m` ([§7.9](#sec-definite-assignment-for-non-nullable-fields), [§17.11](#sec-the-default-operator)).

A local cannot be named `_`: the bare underscore is the reserved discard token ([§1.3](#sec-identifiers), [§17.13](#sec-the-discard-_)). `var _ := e;` is a compile error whose diagnostic names both sanctioned spellings — `_ := e;` to evaluate and release the value at end of statement, or `using var _ := e;` to hold it anonymously until scope end ([§17.13](#sec-the-discard-_), [§28.10](#sec-using-var)); `const _ := e;` is likewise rejected (a never-readable constant is useless by construction).

**Scope.** A local declared by `var`, `const`, `using var` or `await using var` is in scope from the end of its declaration to the end of the innermost enclosing statement block ([§21.6](#sec-do-end-blocks)); an inline `out` declaration's scope is [§22.4](#sec-inline-out-declarations)'s. The declaration's own initializer is not in that scope, as a binding atom's clause initializer is outside its binding's scope ([§17.15](#sec-the-binding-atom)): a name in the initializer resolves as it would if the declaration were absent. So in a body that declares no other local or parameter named `count`, the `count` read by `var count := count + 1;` resolves by [§2.7](#sec-name-resolution-order) to a member `count` where the enclosing type has one and is otherwise an undeclared name, and a lambda in a local's initializer cannot name that local.

**Local names.** A local may not take the name of another local declared directly in the same block, whether either is declared by `var`, `const`, `using var` or `await using var` ([§28.10](#sec-using-var)) or by an inline `out` declaration, whose scope is the enclosing block ([§22.4](#sec-inline-out-declarations)). A local declared directly in the body block of a method, constructor, operator, accessor or lambda may not take the name of one of that callable's parameters (an indexer's parameters included, [§23.4](#sec-indexers), and a setter's parameter `value`, [§23.3](#sec-block-form-properties)); the parameters themselves are distinct under [§22.1](#sec-method-declarations)'s *Parameter names*. The bindings of one pattern ([§19.3](#sec-patterns)) have distinct names, and so do the clauses of one binding atom ([§17.15](#sec-the-binding-atom)). Nor may a declaration take the name of a local or parameter that an enclosing scope has in scope at it. The rule reaches every binding form: a local, an inline `out` declaration, a `for` or `await for` variable, a `case`-arm or `catch`-arm binding ([§19.3](#sec-patterns), [§31.2.1](#sec-arm-patterns)), a binding-atom clause, and a lambda's parameter or destructuring slot ([§27.3](#sec-lambda-expressions), [§27.4](#sec-lambda-parameter-destructuring)). The names it reaches are those of the enclosing blocks' locals, of the enclosing loop variables and arm bindings, of the callable's parameters, of a primary-constructor parameter where that parameter is in scope ([§22.10](#sec-methods-and-constructors-primary-constructors)), and, inside a lambda, those of every body enclosing it. A loop variable is in scope in its loop's body ([§29.2](#sec-desugaring-of-for)), and an arm binding in its arm's guard and body, so a local of that body may not take its name either. A name not in scope at the declaration is outside the clause: sibling blocks, successive loops and the arms of one `case` reuse a name freely, as does a local declared after a nested block that declared the name, and the locals and parameters of a body are not in scope inside a local type it declares ([§21.10](#sec-local-type-declarations)). A repeated name is a compile error at the later declaration naming this rule. The ignore `_` binds nothing and is outside the rule. So are members and types: a local may share a field's, property's or method's name, the member staying reachable as `this.Name` or, for a static, by its type's name ([§2.7](#sec-name-resolution-order)), and a local type follows [§21.10](#sec-local-type-declarations). The two declarations would be live in one scope under one spelling, and a local or parameter has no qualified spelling, so the earlier binding, which can carry a different ownership obligation, would be unreachable for the rest of the later declaration's scope.

<a id="sec-runtime-const-locals"></a>
#### Runtime `const` locals

A local `const` declaration admits any initializer expression. The declaration is classified by the initializer's *form* and the declaration's type:

- **Compile-time constant** — the initializer is a constant expression by [§17.14](#sec-constant-expressions)'s inductive definition *and* the declared or inferred type is a primitive value type or `string`. Semantics unchanged: the name denotes a compile-time value, admissible in `case` patterns (A.8 `Constant`), in other constant expressions, in inline-array sizes, and in constant narrowing. An evaluation fault in a form-constant initializer remains a **compile error at the declaration** ([§17.14](#sec-constant-expressions)) — a faulting constant expression is never reclassified as a runtime const.
- **Runtime const** — every other admissible initializer. The declaration is a **single-assignment local binding**: initialized exactly once, at its declaration, by ordinary runtime evaluation. A reference to it is *not* a constant expression; a use in any compile-time position above is a compile error naming the declaration and its first non-constant subexpression.

A `const` local of either classification is not an assignable location: assignment, compound assignment, `++`/`--`, and binding to a `ref` or `out` parameter are compile errors naming the declaration. A lambda may capture a `const` local by read; the mutable-capture forms are excluded by the same rule. The initializer is mandatory (grammar A.6) — there is no declare-then-assign form. Class-level `const` (including `static const`, [§22.12](#sec-static-members)) is unchanged: member-level runtime single-assignment is `readonly`/`static readonly`.

**Ownership.** The initializer of a runtime `const` must not be an **owned production** ([§28.3](#sec-producers)): the binding never takes a disposal obligation and never holds an affine (consumable) value. Admitted: value-typed expressions (records included — a borrow-bearing record value carries [§9.7](#sec-records-and-disposal)'s ordinary source obligations), `string` and other runtime-managed values, `null` (the binding is then permanently null; [§28.3](#sec-local-variables-ownership-and-borrows)'s dead-null warning applies), and **borrows** — the binding is then a borrow carrying the initializer's source-liveness constraints, exactly as a plain unmarked `var` alias: the consume-site freeze ([K5](#sec-kernel-k5)) sees it as any other live local borrow, and its constraint on the source ends at its last use (it does **not** scope-pin the source; pinning remains [§28.10](#sec-using-var)'s job). Rejected, with a diagnostic naming this rule and the `using var` remedy: a fresh `new`, an `owned`-returning call, a `Task`-family or iterable-family call (`Drain()` and `ReceiveAll()` included — ordinary minting productions, [§28.3](#sec-producers); a lazy query likewise, its [§29.11](#sec-multiple-enumeration) single-consumption discipline riding the minted frame), a `move` (the marked transfer `const y := move x;` included — not a form), and a move-only value ([§15.3](#sec-move-only-value-types)). *(`const` bindings never change state — not by assignment, not by consumption, not by disposal; an owned, never-reassigned, scope-disposed local already exists: `using var`.)* In a generic body, an initializer whose ownership depends on the substitution is enforced per instantiation category ([§3.6](#sec-derived-type-properties) rule 2), with the diagnostic naming the instantiation; a body needing uniform admissibility across kinds writes `using var`.

```bezel
const n := items.Count + 1;          // runtime const: int
const name := user.Name;             // runtime const: string (runtime-managed)
const conn := pool.Primary;          // runtime const: a borrow, source pool

const cfg := LoadConfig();           // error: an owned production; bind owned
                                     //   values with `using var` (§28.10)
```

<a id="sec-the-if-statement"></a>
### 21.2 The `if` statement

```bezel
if amount > 0 then
  Balance := Balance + amount;
end;

if score >= 90 then
  grade := "A";
elif score >= 80 then
  grade := "B";
elif score >= 70 then
  grade := "C";
else
  grade := "F";
end;
```

The condition must be `bool`.

<a id="sec-the-while-statement"></a>
### 21.3 The `while` statement

A `while` statement may carry a loop label (`scan: while … do … end scan;`) — [§21.5](#sec-break-and-continue).

```bezel
while i < 10 do
  Console.WriteLine(i);
  i := i + 1;
end;
```

<a id="sec-the-for-statement"></a>
### 21.4 The `for` statement

A `for` (or `await for`) statement may carry a loop label — [§21.5](#sec-break-and-continue).

`for` iterates any iterable source. This includes values whose type implements `IEnumerable<T>` ([§29](#sec-iteration-2)), inline arrays `[N]T` (which do not implement `IEnumerable<T>` but support direct indexed iteration through a compiler intrinsic, [§15.1.2](#sec-inline-array-members)), and `Range<T>` values (which the compiler may optimize into counted loops):

```bezel
for var i in 1..10 do Console.WriteLine(i); end;
for var i in 0..<n step 2 do Process(i); end;
for var t in transactions do Process(t); end;

for var entry in dict do
  Console.WriteLine($"{entry.Key} -> {entry.Value}");
end;
```

`for` always declares its loop variable with `var`. An optional type annotation must match or be implicitly convertible from the source's element type:

```bezel
for var x: int in source do ... end;
```

The loop variable may be the ignore `_` ([§17.13](#sec-the-discard-_)): `for var _ in source do … end;` iterates for the body's effects with the element unbound — nothing is named, and the body cannot read the element. A type ascription on the ignore is rejected (`for var _: T in …` — a bare ignore takes its type from context, never an annotation, [§17.13](#sec-the-discard-_)). The iteration protocol's borrow/ownership semantics ([§29.2](#sec-desugaring-of-for)) are unchanged by the spelling; in an owning iteration ([§29.2](#sec-desugaring-of-for)'s owning path) the unbound element is disposed at each iteration's end exactly as a bound-but-unused iteration variable would be.

The loop variable is freshly bound on each iteration: a lambda captured inside the body sees the value of that specific iteration. Because the binding is fresh each iteration, assigning to the loop variable inside the body affects only that iteration — it does not alter how many iterations run, nor the next iteration's value, even when the source is a `Range<T>` the compiler has optimized into a counted loop.

If the source is empty, the body does not execute.

For async iteration, see `await for` ([§30.7](#sec-asynchronous-programming-async-iterators)).

<a id="sec-break-and-continue"></a>
### 21.5 `break` and `continue`

`break` exits a loop; `continue` skips the rest of the current iteration and advances to the next. The unlabeled forms target the immediately enclosing loop. Neither is legal outside a loop; doing so is a compile error.

**Loop labels.** A `while`, `for`, or `await for` statement may be prefixed with a *loop label* — an identifier followed by `:` ([§21.3](#sec-the-while-statement), [§21.4](#sec-the-for-statement), grammar A.6). Only loop statements take a loop label. The label names the loop: a labeled loop is a *named construct* in the sense of [§1.6](#sec-statements-and-termination), so its `end` may repeat the loop label (`end scan;`); because the construct now has a name, the introducing-keyword closer (`end for;`, `end while;`) applies only to unlabeled loops, and bare `end;` remains valid everywhere.

```bezel
scan: for var row in rows do
  for var cell in row do
    if cell.Bad then break scan; end;
  end;
end scan;
```

**Labeled forms.** `break name;` exits the enclosing loop labeled `name`; `continue name;` skips the rest of that loop's current iteration and advances it. `name` must be the loop label of a **lexically enclosing** loop statement in the **same callable body**; anything else is a compile error naming the labels in scope. The labeled forms are legal exactly where the unlabeled forms are — the label changes which loop is targeted, never where the statement may appear.

After `break name;`, execution continues at the first statement after the labeled loop. `continue name;` transfers control to the labeled loop's *advance point*: for `while`, the condition; for `for` and `await for`, the iteration-advance of the [§29.2](#sec-desugaring-of-for) desugaring — the next `MoveNext()`/`MoveNextAsync()` call on the enumerator paths, and the index/step increment (which then falls into the bound check) on the direct-indexed and counted forms. A `continue`, labeled or not, never re-runs the source expression or the enumerator acquisition, and never skips an advance.

On the way to its target, the jump exits every intervening scope — inner loop bodies, `do … end` blocks, `try` bodies — and each performs its ordinary exit obligations ([§28.3](#sec-local-variables-ownership-and-borrows), [§28.10](#sec-using-var), [§31.2](#sec-try-catch-finally)): `using var`/`await using var` disposals and pending `finally` blocks run in reverse order of establishment, and the jump is a body-exit edge of every loop body it exits, so each such body's iteration variable is subject to its own [§29.2](#sec-desugaring-of-for)/[§28.3](#sec-local-variables-ownership-and-borrows) discharge rule at the jump site. The labeled forms add or alter no disposal rule.

**Label scope, namespace, and duplicates.** A loop label is in scope throughout its loop statement and lives in a namespace of its own: it is never resolved against — and never collides with — variables, parameters, types, or members, and it is not an expression (a local `scan` and a label `scan` may coexist; `nameof` does not accept a label). A loop label that repeats a label already in scope at its declaration — the label of an enclosing labeled loop in the same callable body — is a compile error at the inner label: labels do not shadow. Loops that do not enclose one another may reuse a label freely; their labels are never simultaneously in scope. `_` is not a valid loop label: a label is a declaration, and `_` cannot be declared ([§1.3](#sec-identifiers), [§17.13](#sec-the-discard-_)).

**Callable boundary.** The enclosing-loop search — for the labeled and unlabeled forms alike — is confined to the callable ([§21.7](#sec-the-return-statement)'s list: method, constructor, destructor, lambda, property accessor, indexer accessor) whose body contains the statement. A `break` or `continue` inside a lambda cannot target a loop of the defining method, labeled or not; a compile error. A loop label is correspondingly visible only within its own callable body: a loop inside a lambda may reuse an enclosing method's label without conflict, since the outer label is not in scope there.

Neither may exit a `finally` block: inside a `finally`, a `break` or `continue` — labeled or unlabeled — whose target loop lies **outside** the `finally` is a compile error — the same rule as `return` in a `finally` ([§21.7](#sec-the-return-statement), [§31.2](#sec-try-catch-finally)). When the `finally` runs during exception propagation, such a jump would abandon the in-flight exception silently. Loops wholly inside the `finally`, and jumps among them, are unaffected.

<a id="sec-do-end-blocks"></a>
### 21.6 `do ... end` blocks

A `do ... end` block groups statements as a single statement and limits the lifetime of locals. Two purposes:

1. **Scoping.** Locals declared in a block are visible only until the matching `end`. `using var` resources ([§28.10](#sec-using-var)) are disposed when the block ends.
2. **Multi-statement bodies.** Anywhere a single statement is expected, `do ... end` containing several statements stands in.

```bezel
public method ProcessLargeFile(filename: string)
  var result := 0;

  do
    using var fs := new FileStream(filename, FileMode.Open);
    var data := fs.ReadAll();
    result := ProcessData(data);
  end;
  // fs has been disposed here

  Console.WriteLine($"Result = {result}");
end ProcessLargeFile;
```

When a `do ... end` block ends:
1. `using var` declarations within the block are disposed in reverse declaration order.
2. Local variables declared within the block go out of scope.

Loops use `do` as part of their syntax; `for ... do ... end` and `while ... do ... end` are not separate `do ... end` blocks.

<a id="sec-the-return-statement"></a>
### 21.7 The `return` statement

```bezel
return;                   // exit with no value
return expression;        // exit with a value
```

`return` exits the nearest enclosing **callable** — method, constructor, destructor, lambda, property accessor, or indexer accessor. It is unaffected by `do ... end`, loops, `case` arms, and `try`/`catch`/`finally`.

Form rules:

- A method or accessor with a return type must `return expression;` on every exit path.
- A method or accessor with no return type uses `return;` to exit early; falling off the end is implicit.
- Constructors and destructors use `return;` to exit early. `return expression;` is a compile error.
- Lambdas follow the same rule as methods.

The top-level operand of `return expression;` in a body with a declared return type is a **declared-result position**: when the declared type (for an `async` body, the declared `Task<T>`'s result type, [§30.1](#sec-async-methods)) is — nullability stripped — a choice with a case of the written name, a bare case construction target-types against it ([§35.3](#sec-choice-construction)).

**Statement-`case` totality.** A statement-position `case` ([§19.7](#sec-termination)) counts as exiting on every path — so a callable may end with it, with no trailing `return` — when both hold: **(i)** [§19.6](#sec-exhaustiveness) proves the match statically exhaustive, by any of its proofs, each a closed-value-space proof — a warning-only reading over an *open* value space (an open hierarchy) grants nothing; and **(ii)** every arm's body itself exits on every path (`return`, `throw`, or a nested total construct). Guarded arms must satisfy (ii) like any other arm but contribute nothing to (i) (the [§19.6](#sec-exhaustiveness) rule). For a `case` granted totality under this rule, the no-match edge is statically dead; an implementation lowers it as a defined trap (raising `MatchFailureException` or aborting) rather than fall-through, so that the grant's soundness never rests on the exhaustiveness computation alone (as-if: the trap is unreachable in a conforming implementation).

**Compound statements carry no special grant.** A callable may equally end with an `if`/`elif`/`else`, a `try`/`catch`/`finally`, or any other compound statement: a compound statement satisfies the every-exit-path rule by **ordinary reachability over its completion edges** — it counts as exiting on every path exactly when no path through it completes normally (an `if` chain exits when it has an `else` and every branch exits; a `try` exits when its `finally` block exits on every path — which only a `throw` or a non-terminating path can realize, `return` being rejected in a `finally` (below) — or when the `try` body and every `catch` arm do). The statement-`case` rule above is the sole grant keyed to an exhaustiveness proof.

`return` inside a `finally` block is a compile error.

`return` inside a lambda exits the lambda, not the method that defined it.

<a id="sec-throw"></a>
### 21.8 `throw`

`throw expression;` and the bare re-raise `throw;` (inside a catch arm's body) are the statement spellings of the `throw` expression, equivalent to the expression form followed by `;`; the operand rule, the bottom type, and the catch-context restriction are [§17.12](#sec-the-throw-expression)'s. Exception handling is [§31](#sec-exception-handling).

<a id="sec-statement-form-of-expressions"></a>
### 21.9 Statement form of expressions

A method call, an `await` expression, or any other expression whose result is `()` may appear as a statement on its own line, terminated with `;`. The statement form admits **any** expression whatever its result type — grammar A.6's `ExpressionStmt ::= Expression ";"` restricts the expression in no way — so a **bare accessor read** (`obj.SomeProperty;`, `obj[i];`) *is* an admissible expression statement: the getter runs ([§23](#sec-properties-and-indexers)) and its result is discarded under the next paragraph's rules, exactly as a call's result is. A `case` in statement position also stands alone as a statement; its value handling is **per arm**: an *expression*-bodied arm whose value is non-`()` gets this section's discard warning — and the non-trivial-dispose / interface / `Task` hard error — applied at that arm; statement-bodied and `do … end` arms have type `()` and are exempt.

An expression statement whose result is a non-`()` type is permitted but the compiler emits a warning: the result is silently discarded, which may indicate a bug (a return value the programmer forgot to use). **One exemption: the fluent-receiver discard.** A discarded **method-call** result draws no warning when it is a [§28.3](#sec-producers) **borrow** whose source set lies within the statement's receiver chain **and** whose static type equals the receiver's static type — the `return this` fluent shape (`sb.Append(x);`, stdlib §3.1, chained calls included): the caller still holds the receiver, so nothing computed is lost. Both conditions are load-bearing: dropping the type test would silence same-source *queries* (`FirstOrNull()`-class results are receiver-sourced too), and the exemption deliberately covers method calls only, **not accessor reads** — a clause with work to do, since a bare accessor read is itself an admissible statement (above): a property or indexer read whose static type equals the receiver's and whose result is the receiver-sourced borrow every storage read produces ([§28.3](#sec-producers)) — `node.Parent;` at a `Parent: Node` property — is exactly the shape the two conditions would otherwise exempt, and it stays diagnosed under this section's regime, keyed as that regime is on the result's static type. A fluent method whose declared return is a *base* of the receiver's type stays warned — conservative by design; `_ := …` remains available ([§17.13](#sec-the-discard-_)). Owned results and every other borrow keep this section's regime unchanged. To suppress the warning, use the discard form `_ := expression;` ([§17.13](#sec-the-discard-_)) — but only when the result type allows it. For non-trivial-dispose class types, for **interface types** — an interface's conformance set is open, so its implementations' trivial-dispose status cannot be proven across modules and an interface-typed result is treated as **possibly-non-trivial-dispose**, the same unknowability reasoning that makes interface-typed discards dispose the runtime type ([§17.13](#sec-the-discard-_)) — and for a `Task`-family value, the warning is replaced by a hard error directing the caller to the discard `_ := expression;` (immediate disposal, [§17.13](#sec-the-discard-_) — for an interface, disposal of the runtime type), `using var _ := expression;` (scope-end disposal) — neither available for a `Task`-family value, §17.13 — an explicit `.Dispose()`, or `Task.FireAndForget` as appropriate. The escalation is one rule over **three** kinds — it is not `Task`-specific — and it is keyed on the result's **static type**, not on its [§28.3](#sec-local-variables-ownership-and-borrows) ownership classification: a bare-statement call whose result type is a non-trivial-dispose class or an interface is the hard error whether the result is an owned production or a borrow, the fluent-receiver discard above being the sole exemption (`OpenLog();` — for [§17.13](#sec-the-discard-_)'s illustrative `OpenLog(): owned FileStream` — is rejected, and `_ := OpenLog();` is the remedy that section works). [§28.3](#sec-choosing-a-disposal-form)'s must-use **warning** is a different diagnostic at a different site — the implicit drop of a *bound*, undischarged owned local at scope end — and softens nothing here.

Method calls returning `()` and `await` expressions on `Task` (no result) are the common cases; no warning is emitted for these.

<a id="sec-local-type-declarations"></a>
### 21.10 Local type declarations

A `record` or `enum` may be declared as a **statement**, scoped to the enclosing body like a local variable (grammar A.6 `LocalTypeDecl ::= RecordDecl | EnumDecl`). The local type is an **ordinary nominal record or enum** — every §9 (records) and §10 (enums) rule applies unchanged; the sole relaxation is *where the declaration may appear*. The form lets a shape used once — a projection's result record, a small closed constant set scoped to one algorithm — live next to its single use instead of at module or class level.

```bezel
public static method Render(users: Array<User>): string
  record NameAge(Name: string, Age: int);   // local: visible only to end Render
  var rows := users.Select(lambda(u) => new NameAge(u.Name, u.Age)).ToArray();
  var sb := new StringBuilder();
  for var row in rows do
    sb.AppendLine($"{row.Name}: {row.Age}");
  end;
  return sb.ToString();
end Render;
```

**Grammar and admissible positions.** `record` and `enum` are reserved ([§1.4](#sec-keywords), Appendix B.1) and begin no other statement, so the statement reading commits at the first token and no existing program changes meaning. Two slots of the reused Appendix A.3 productions are restricted semantically: the `Visibility?` slot **must be empty** — a local type has no access surface (there is no "outside" holding a reference), so a visibility keyword is a compile error naming the rule; this deliberately contrasts with [§11.6](#sec-nested-types) nested types, where the keyword is *required* because a member has an access surface to declare. The `GenericParams?` slot **must be empty** (v1) — a local type declares no type parameters of its own. `LocalTypeDecl` is admitted wherever a `Statement` is: method, constructor, destructor, and accessor bodies, lambda `do`-bodies, `do … end` blocks, loop bodies, and statement-position arm bodies. "Method-local" reads throughout as *body-local*.

**Scope and name discipline.** A local type's name is in scope from its declaration statement to the end of the **innermost enclosing statement block** — a local variable's extent ([§21.1](#sec-variable-declarations), [§21.6](#sec-do-end-blocks)), except that a local type's scope also covers its own body (below). The declaration must precede first use; local types are therefore order-significant, and a local type's field types may name only types already in scope (module-visible types, the enclosing class's nested types, and *earlier* local types) — no forward references, hence no mutually recursive local types. Within its scope the name is an ordinary type reference in **body positions**: local-variable ascriptions, `new`, generic arguments (`Array<NameAge>`), `typeof`/`nameof`/`default`, casts and type patterns, and lambda-parameter ascriptions. The name may **not** appear in any **member signature of an enclosing or sibling declaration** — parameter, return, field/property/indexer, generic-constraint, or base/interface positions of the enclosing method itself, or of any member of any type declared outside the local type — which is a compile error naming that rule (*"a method-local type may not appear in a member signature"*); at those positions the name is not in scope, but the rule is stated so the diagnostic is the named one. The prohibition does **not** reach the local type's **own** members: the local type is an ordinary nominal record or enum whose members are declared by the §9/§10 rules unchanged — this section's sole relaxation being *where the declaration may appear*, and a restriction on which members it may declare would make a local record strictly weaker than a module-level one — and the name **is** in scope inside its own body, which is part of the declaration statement the scope runs from. `public method Twin(): Pair` and `public method Merge(other: Pair): Pair` inside a local `record Pair` are therefore admitted. The field-type rule above is untouched and governs **fields** on its own terms: a local type's field may name only a type already in scope by that rule's list — module-visible types, the enclosing class's nested types, and *earlier* local types — which never includes the type being declared, so a self-typed field stays a compile error (a record is a value kind, so such a field would have no finite size in any case). The declared name may **not shadow** any type name visible at the declaration point (a local `NameAge` silently shadowing a module-level `NameAge` is a trap, not a convenience — the collision is an error), nor collide with another declaration in the same body's declaration space (another local type or a local variable, the [§11.3](#sec-member-body)-style clash discipline applied to the body). Two *different* methods may each declare `record Row(…)`: the names never meet, and the types are distinct. Inside the local type's own member bodies, a bare name reaches the static members and nested types of the type whose body declares it, and of that type's enclosing types, by [§2.7](#sec-name-resolution-order)'s *Through nesting*; a bare instance member of that type, or a bare static member of a generic one, is that paragraph's compile error. The locals and parameters of the bodies enclosing the declaration, a primary-constructor parameter in scope there included ([§22.10](#sec-methods-and-constructors-primary-constructors)), are not in scope anywhere inside it: not in its member or accessor bodies, field and property initializers, parameter defaults, contract clauses or enum value initializers. A local type has no closure, and an instance of it can outlive the body that declared it (boxed through an interface, below). A bare name there in a position [§2.7](#sec-name-resolution-order) rule 1 resolves (a value read, an assignment target, a callee or a chain head) that the local type's own locals, parameters and members do not bind, and that is spelled like a local or parameter in scope at the declaration, is a compile error naming this rule, even where §2.7 would go on to find a member of a type enclosing the local type (*Through nesting*), a module declaration, an imported name, an alias or a module prefix; a compile-time `const` local is no exception. A type position, a named-argument label and a member name after `.` are not such lookups. A value the type needs reaches it as a field or an argument, and a constant as a static member of the local type or of a non-generic type enclosing it. Because those names are not in scope inside the local type, its own parameters and locals may reuse them ([§21.1](#sec-variable-declarations) *Local names*).

**Restrictions (v1).** A local type may not **reference an enclosing generic parameter** (an enclosing method's or class's `T`) — a compile error naming the rule; such a type would be implicitly generic, making its identity, [§9.2](#sec-body-records) equality synthesis, [§9.8](#sec-serialization-synthesis) serialization synthesis, and boxed conformances per-instantiation, a genuine design space disproportionate to the concrete-field motivating case, and a `forbid → allow` widening is compatible where the reverse would break. A welcome consequence of the restriction: a local type's identity is **instantiation-independent** — one nominal type per declaration even inside a generic body, so a public generic's carried body ([§2.8.2](#sec-artifact-interface)) carries it as ordinary body content with no per-instantiation identity questions. `choice` may **not** be declared locally (its payload-derived three-way classification, owning-match consume obligations, and coverage machinery are a heavier admission deserving its own study — recorded liftable with evidence); `class` and `interface` may not (a class carries ownership, destructors, and the §28 disposal machinery — body-scoped kernel surface for no recorded need; an interface is a contract for an outside a local has none of).

**Semantics — an ordinary nominal type.** Identity is **per-declaration**: two same-shaped local records in different methods are distinct types (nominal, deliberately — no structural unification, which is exactly the anonymous-types discipline the language declines). Auto-equality ([§9.2](#sec-body-records)), `with` ([§9.5](#sec-non-destructive-update-with)), auto-`ToString` ([§8.5](#sec-tostring)), serialization synthesis ([§9.8](#sec-serialization-synthesis) — eligibility by field types, conformance declared as usual), interface implementation ([§9.6](#sec-records-and-inheritance)), and the derived type properties ([§3.6](#sec-derived-type-properties) — auto-hashable, borrow-bearing per [§9.7](#sec-records-and-disposal), sendable per [§30.14](#sec-sendable-types), serialization-eligible) are all computed by their existing rules from the declaration. A local `enum` is a §10 enum wholesale: constants, explicit values, underlying types, methods, interface conformances, and `case` matching with prefix omission ([§10.6](#sec-case-matching)) and enum-scrutinee exhaustiveness ([§19.6](#sec-exhaustiveness)) inside the scope. Static members are admitted as on any record/enum (a local type's `static readonly` state is program-lived under [§22.13](#sec-static-initialization-order), like any other static).

**Boxing and escape — the one subtle rule, stated exactly as far as [§8.6](#sec-boxing) already goes.** A **non-borrow-bearing** local record ([§9.7](#sec-records-and-disposal) — no borrow-carrying fields; `string`/runtime-managed fields do not count) that implements an interface may be **returned boxed through that interface**: the type identity escapes *unnameably*, the precedent being a `private` nested type ([§11.6](#sec-nested-types)) escaping through a public interface today, and such a box is genuinely self-contained — records carry no disposal ([§9.7](#sec-records-and-disposal): records cannot implement `IDisposable`) and a non-borrow-bearing record holds no references whose sources it could outlive. A **borrow-bearing** local record boxes under [§8.6](#sec-boxing) *Boxing of borrow-bearing records* **unchanged**: a short-lived, call-bounded box is admitted, and storing such a box in a field, returning it from a method, or capturing it in a closure that escapes the source scope stays rejected by the same [§8.6](#sec-boxing)/[§9.7](#sec-records-and-disposal)/[§28.3](#sec-local-variables-ownership-and-borrows) rules as the unboxed form. The locality of the declaration adds **no new admission**: the case an unqualified admission would wrongly bless — `record View(Cell: Widget)` declared over a `using var` widget and returned boxed through an interface, the widget disposed at the method's end and the box left dangling — is exactly what §8.6's existing rejection stops, fully engaged for local records.

---

<a id="sec-methods-and-constructors"></a>
## 22. Methods and Constructors

<a id="sec-method-declarations"></a>
### 22.1 Method declarations

```bezel
public method Add(a: int, b: int): int
  return a + b;
end Add;

public method PrintGreeting(name: string)
  Console.WriteLine($"Hello, {name}!");
end PrintGreeting;
```

A method has a return type after `:`, or no `:` clause for a procedure (return type `()`).

**Parameter names.** The names one parameter list binds are distinct: those of a method, a constructor (a primary constructor's included, [§22.10](#sec-methods-and-constructors-primary-constructors)), an operator, an `extern` method ([§32](#sec-foreign-function-interface)) or a lambda ([§27.3](#sec-lambda-expressions)), a lambda's destructuring slots ([§27.4](#sec-lambda-parameter-destructuring)) counted with its parameters, and an indexer's parameters together with its setter's parameter `value` ([§23.3](#sec-block-form-properties), [§23.4](#sec-indexers)). A repeated name is a compile error at its second occurrence naming this rule; where the repeat is the setter's implicit `value`, which has no position of its own, the error is at the indexer parameter it repeats. A parameter is one name in the body's scope and, on a declared member, one address for a named argument ([§22.5](#sec-optional-parameters-and-named-arguments)); a repeated name would leave every parameter but one unreachable by either. The rule does not reach the ignore `_`, which a lambda may repeat because it binds nothing (Appendix A.7), nor a function type's parameter names, which are documentation only ([§27.1](#sec-function-types)).

A method body may be **empty** — grammar [A.4](#sec-members)'s `Statement*`, as for a `destructor` — and a procedure with an empty body completes immediately ([§21.7](#sec-the-return-statement)'s implicit fall-off). An empty body under a **declared return type** is a compile error on §21.7's ordinary ground: no path returns a value.

<a id="sec-expression-bodied-methods"></a>
### 22.2 Expression-bodied methods

When the body is a single expression, `=> expression` replaces the block. A method with **no declared return type** may also use a single *assignment* as its arrow body: `public method SetTotal(v: int) => _total := v;` — the same shape the accessor form `set => _x := value;` has always had; the asymmetry between the two identical declaration contexts was the one indefensible gap in the arrow-body family (the remaining per-context differences are recorded with reasons in the rationale). On a method with a declared return type the assignment form is an error (an assignment produces no value):

```bezel
public method Area(): decimal => Width * Height;
public method Max(a: int, b: int): int => (if a > b then a else b);
```

An expression body under a declared return type is a **declared-result position** ([§35.3](#sec-choice-construction)): a bare choice-case construction in it target-types against the declared type, exactly as a `return` operand does ([§21.7](#sec-the-return-statement)).

<a id="sec-parameter-modifiers"></a>
### 22.3 Parameter modifiers

- `ref` — pass by reference. The caller writes `ref` at the call site. The variable must be initialized before the call. Inside the callee the parameter is never flow-narrowed ([§7.4](#sec-narrowing-applies-to-locals-only)): its referent keeps the caller's other names for the whole call, so it is read at its declared type and narrowed through a local copy. A `ref` parameter whose declared type is a move-only value type ([§15.3](#sec-move-only-value-types); an owning choice's nullable wrapper `C?` among them, [§35.9](#sec-choice-nullable)), a function type's `ref` slot included, is a compile error at the declaration: no argument can bind it, since every location of that type is owned state at a `ref` argument ([*`ref` and `out` argument locations*](#sec-ref-and-out-argument-locations)). Take the value as a plain parameter and return it (`method Step(c: C): C`, called as `c := Step(c);`, [§15.3](#sec-move-only-value-types)'s *Parameter passing*), or produce it through `out`, which an `out var` recipient binds. A `ref` parameter whose declared type is or contains a type parameter is not rejected at its declaration; at a substitution that makes that type a move-only value type, no argument binds it, by the same bound.
- `out` — output parameter. The caller writes `out`. The variable need not be initialized before the call. The callee must assign every `out` parameter on every **normal-completion (return) path** (a path that exits by `throw` carries no assignment obligation); failing to do so is a compile error. `out` is **copy-out-on-normal-return**: within the callee the parameter denotes a callee-local slot, freely readable after assignment; on normal return the slot's value is copied to the caller's recipient; on an exception exit the recipient is untouched — an inline `out var` recipient stays unassigned ([§22.4](#sec-inline-out-declarations)) and a pre-existing recipient keeps its prior value. An implementation may pass a hidden reference, but only to storage that is the callee's for the call: no write to the recipient's location during the call — through a closure, another argument, the receiver, or static state — reaches the slot, no write to the slot reaches the recipient before normal return, and a partial write is never observable on the exception edge (an `extern` parameter's boundary `out` is [§32.5](#sec-boundary-out-ref)'s). For `out owned`, the callee-local slot is an owned slot: a value assigned to it before a later `throw` is discharged by the callee's ordinary exception-path discharge ([§28.3](#sec-local-variables-ownership-and-borrows)), its disposal established at the assignment ([§28.10](#sec-using-var)) — ownership reaches the caller only on normal return, so the value has exactly one owner at every instant (Appendix [C.3](#sec-appendix-c)).
- `owned` — ownership transfer. See [§28.8](#sec-ownership-transfer). **Call-site marker:** when the argument is a **named owned binding** — an owned local or an `owned` parameter, which the call leaves moved-from — the caller writes the transfer marker at the call site: `M(move x)` (an identifier-operand `move` expression, [§28.8.1](#sec-the-move-expression) — the marker is part of the argument expression, not an argument modifier; a **move-only value** argument is outside this marker rule at either parameter spelling and is written unmarked, [§15.3](#sec-move-only-value-types)'s *Parameter passing* bullet). A **fresh producer** — a `new` expression, a call returning `owned T`, an operator result, or a `move obj._field` — stays unmarked: no live binding is invalidated, so there is nothing to announce ([K3.13](#sec-kernel-k3)'s marker-economy rule). Omitting the marker on a named owned binding is a compile error naming the fix ("this call consumes `x`; write `M(move x)`"); writing it on a borrow, a fresh producer, or a non-`owned` parameter position is likewise an error (at a non-`owned` position the diagnostic names the borrow default — an owned expression may not feed a borrow slot). This is the visibility rule the other destructive modes already follow (`ref`/`out` at call sites), spelled with the same verb as the field take-out (`move x.f`, rationale §5.10). Where two same-name members differ only by ordinary `owned` — a declarable pair — the argument's ownership classification, for a named binding exactly this marker, completes overload applicability: `M(move x)` reaches the `owned` member, `M(x)` the plain one ([§22.6](#sec-owned-and-overload-resolution)).
- `out owned` — output parameter that produces an owned value. The callee assigns an owned value through the parameter; the caller receives ownership and must discharge it (typically with `out using var` at the call site, [§22.4](#sec-inline-out-declarations)). The combination `out owned` is the only modifier compound; the others are mutually exclusive.
- `scoped` — storage-bounded retention ([§28.14](#sec-scoped-callback-parameters)). On a *function-typed* parameter: the callee may store the callback, bounded by the storing object's lifetime; the caller's captures are checked against that bound. On a **class- or interface-typed** parameter (except one whose declared type, nullability stripped, is `Object`, [§28.14](#sec-scoped-callback-parameters)): the callee may store the *borrow* in a direct non-owned field of the bounding object; the caller's argument is checked against the same bound and **frozen** until the bound's scope exits, upgrading [§28.3](#sec-local-variables-ownership-and-borrows)'s residual-trust back-reference to a static guarantee. **Call-site marker:** a class- or interface-typed `scoped` argument is written `M(scoped x)` — the same mark-it-at-the-site discipline as the `move` marker above, though `scoped` remains an *argument modifier*: it marks a lending mode, not an action, and the asymmetry is deliberate; a fresh producer is rejected ([§9.7](#sec-records-and-disposal)'s no-temporary-source rule — bind it first). Function-typed arguments (lambda literals, method references) carry no call-site marker — their admission is capture-based. A function-typed parameter *without* `scoped` is **call-bounded**: the callee may invoke the callback during the call but may not retain it past the call ([§28.14](#sec-scoped-callback-parameters)). *(the transfer marker likewise appears in local binding and assignment positions — `var y := move x;`, `y := move x;` — [§28.3](#sec-local-variables-ownership-and-borrows).)*

<a id="sec-ref-and-out-argument-locations"></a>
#### `ref` and `out` argument locations
