A `ref` or `out` argument must be an **assignable storage location** — the [§17.6](#sec-the-increment-and-decrement-operators) lvalue categories: a mutable local variable, a **parameter** (the receiver `this` excepted — a store landing in the receiver's own storage is governed by [§9.4](#sec-value-receivers-are-borrows) and [§28.6](#sec-who-may-dispose)), a writable field, an indexer slot, or a property with an accessible setter — subject to: no `using var` binding ([§28.10](#sec-using-var)'s pin); no `readonly` field outside its per-instance assignable context ([§22.8](#sec-field-initializers)); and two recorded v1 bounds (liftable): no location of **owned state** — an owned local or `owned` parameter, an `owned` field, an owning-collection or owning-inline-array slot, or any location whose declared type is a move-only value type ([§15.3](#sec-move-only-value-types); an instance field of owning-choice or owning-inline-array type included, which takes [§28.7](#sec-reassigning-owned-fields)'s drop-on-overwrite as an `owned` field does; a location whose declared type is or contains a type parameter (`T`, `T?`, or a generic choice over it) is such a location at each instantiation at which that type is a move-only value type, the bound being a requirement of the declaration read at its instantiations under [§3.6](#sec-derived-type-properties) rule 2: `G(ref _v)` over `_v: T` in `class Box<T>` makes `Box<C>` a compile error wherever it is named, for a move-only `C`, and is admitted at every other substitution) — because a `ref` write is an assignment through an alias, invisible to the drop-on-overwrite and consume-site-freeze machinery that [§28.7](#sec-reassigning-owned-fields)/[§28.3](#sec-consume-site-freeze) key on syntactically visible stores (remedies: pass a borrow, use `owned` parameters/returns, or `move`); and no mutable static **field or auto-property** admitted by [§22.12](#sec-static-members) rule 2, whose store semantics are defined for direct assignment only. A **block-form** (accessor-bodied) static property is not such a static: it is an admitted property target, taken through the copy-in / copy-out bracket below like any other property with an accessible setter. A `ref` argument must additionally be definitely assigned before the call. For plain `out`, the same categories apply, plus the inline declarations `out var x` and the discard `out _` ([§22.6](#sec-overloading)); for `out owned`, exactly the recipient forms of [§22.4](#sec-inline-out-declarations), which admit no field, indexer slot, or property target.

**Exact referent type.** The argument's static type must be **exactly** the parameter's referent type. Because the parameter aliases the caller's location, no [§5.1](#sec-implicit-conversions) implicit conversion is admitted — not even a widening one that an ordinary by-value argument would take at the [§22.6](#sec-overloading) applicability check ([§14.5](#sec-type-argument-inference)'s exact-unification bullet is this rule's inference-time instance).

**A bare variable names its declared location.** A `ref` or `out` argument that is a bare local or parameter (`ref a`, `out a`) names that variable's storage, so its static type at the `ref`/`out` position (for this rule and for [§14.5](#sec-type-argument-inference)'s exact unification alike) is the variable's **declared** type. No flow narrowing applies to it, neither [§7.4](#sec-member-access-on-nullable-values)'s non-null narrowing nor [§12.7](#sec-type-tests-is-is-not-as)'s type narrowing. Inside `if a is Dog then … end;` over `a: Animal`, `ref a` matches a `ref x: Animal` parameter and not a `ref x: Dog` one, and at `M<T>(ref x: T)` it binds `T` to `Animal`; over `n: int?` narrowed non-null, `ref n` matches `ref x: int?` and not `ref x: int`. A `ref` callee's alias is live for the whole call, and §7.4 drops a mutably captured variable's narrowing only after the call, so a narrowed referent type would let a closure that captured `a` store an `Animal` that the callee then reads as a `Dog`. To pass the narrowed value, copy it out: `var d: Dog := a; G(ref d);`. This paragraph governs the bare variable only: a chain rooted at a narrowed variable (`ref a.Tag`, `ref o[0]`) reads its root, and the location it names is typed by its final hop, subject at a boxed location to §12.7's write rule and, inside a narrowed nullable value, to [§7.4](#sec-member-access-on-nullable-values)'s *Storage inside a narrowed nullable value*, which rejects `ref n.X` over `n: Pt?`.

**`ref` local and field targets alias; accessor targets bracket.** A `ref` argument naming a mutable local or writable field is a true alias: callee writes are visible through the caller's location immediately (the `Swap(ref a, ref b)` semantics [§14.1](#sec-generic-declarations) presupposes). An **indexer slot or property** target is instead **copy-in / copy-out** under [§17.6](#sec-increment-decrement-on-indexer-slots)'s evaluate-once discipline: the receiver and every index expression are evaluated exactly once, in [§22.5](#sec-optional-parameters-and-named-arguments)'s call-site textual order; for `ref`, the getter is called once to produce the callee's slot value (for `out` no getter call occurs); on **normal return** the setter is called once with the slot's final value. Write-backs for multiple accessor-mediated arguments run in argument textual order — `Swap(ref a[i], ref a[i])` is defined, the textually later write-back winning — and on an exception exit no write-back occurs, composing with the copy-out rule above. Accessor-mediated arguments are never aliases of each other or of anything else during the call.

<a id="sec-inline-out-declarations"></a>
### 22.4 Inline `out` declarations

```bezel
var success := parser.TryParse("42", out var num);
```

`out var name` declares a new variable inline. Its type is inferred from the method's `out` parameter declaration; an explicit type annotation is not permitted in the inline form. `out var _` is a compile error — it would declare nothing; write `out _`, which already means exactly this ([§17.13](#sec-the-discard-_)).

The variable's scope is the enclosing block, from the call onward. It is in scope in both branches of any surrounding `if` and after the call.

**Scope is not definite assignment.** The scope rule above says only where the name may appear; whether a read is *legal* follows the ordinary definite-assignment rules for locals ([§7.9](#sec-definite-assignment-for-non-nullable-fields), [§21.1](#sec-variable-declarations)), applied path-sensitively: an inline `out` variable counts as **assigned only on control-flow paths where the introducing call was actually evaluated**. Under short-circuit operators and conditional expressions the distinction is live. After `if flag and parser.TryParse(s, out var n) then ... end;`, the variable is definitely assigned *inside* the `then` branch — control reaches it only if the call ran (and returned `true`) — but not after the `if`, where a path exists on which `flag` was `false` and the call never executed. The analysis is required to honor the standard short-circuit facts (`A and Call(out var x)` assigns `x` when the whole expression is `true`; `A or Call(out var x)` assigns `x` when it is `false`), so the idiomatic guarded read stays accepted. On a path where the call may not have run, a read of a **non-nullable-reference-typed** out variable is a compile error, exactly as for any other unassigned non-nullable local; value-typed and nullable out variables follow [§7.9](#sec-default-initialization)'s default-initialization rules (the default value or `null` is what such a path observes). An `out using var` disposal obligation likewise attaches only on paths where the call executed **and completed normally**: under [§22.3](#sec-parameter-modifiers)'s copy-out rule a call that threw assigned nothing to the recipient — the assigned-but-unreturned value, if any, was discharged callee-side — so the throw edge carries neither the assignment fact nor the obligation.

For disposal-aware inline declarations, use `out using var`:

```bezel
if factory.TryCreate(config, out using var conn) then
  // conn is owned and non-null here; disposed at end of enclosing block
end;
```

When a method parameter is declared `out owned`, the callee produces an owned value through the output parameter, and the caller's recipient takes ownership of it. `out var x` declares a fresh local that **adopts** the classification the callee's declaration announces ([§28.3](#sec-local-variables-ownership-and-borrows)'s adoption clause): a borrow against a plain `out` parameter, whose sources are the call's ([§28.3](#sec-borrow-lifetime-rules)'s `ref`/`out` rule); against `out owned`, an **owned local** under the standard owned-local discharge rules, the must-use warning included. `out using var x` is the scope-bound owned form and is accepted only against `out owned`; `out _` is admitted against either kind ([§22.6](#sec-overloading)). A **pre-declared local** passed as plain `out x` is admitted against `out owned` exactly when it is in one of §28.3's two adoptable states — uninitialized (`var c: Connection?;`) or polymorphic-null — and adopts owned on every normal-return path of the call: the callee's declaration announces the production as owned, so a `null` assigned on the callee's `false` path leaves an owned local holding `null`, and [K7](#sec-kernel-k7) meets owned with owned at the join. The adoption happens **once**: from the call's normal return the local is state-matched by §28.3, so a second `out x` on the same local — including on a loop back edge — is rejected until the value is discharged (an owned-state location is not admitted at an `out` argument, [§22.3](#sec-ref-and-out-argument-locations)); the pre-declared form is therefore the single-use remedy of [§22.6](#sec-overloading), and the loop shape is written with the inline forms. No other lvalue category is admitted at `out owned` — a field, indexer slot, or property target is either an owned-state location §22.3 bars or a borrowing location the owned value would leak into ([§28.6](#sec-leak-prevention)). No use-site `owned` marker exists in this position: ownership is announced by the declaration alone ([§28.1](#sec-where-the-owned-modifier-can-appear), [K3.13](#sec-kernel-k3)). [§22.6](#sec-overloading) states how these recipient rules meet overload resolution: they are checked against the resolved signature and are not resolution signals.

<a id="sec-out-nullability-postcondition"></a>
#### Nullability postcondition on `out` parameters

*(this clause **is** a proven-tier contract clause — normatively, `out p: T? when true` on a `bool`-returning method carries `static ensures(not result or p <> null)`, discharged by this section's flow analysis; [§22.16](#sec-when-clause-unification). The `when` spelling remains the surface form; nothing here changes.)*

A `bool`-returning method may declare, on an `out` (or `out owned`) parameter of nullable type, the clause **`when true`** (or **`when false`**) after the parameter's type:

```bezel
public method TryGetCached(name: string, out conn: Connection? when true): bool;
```

The clause is a **compiler-checked postcondition**: on every path of the declaring body that returns the stated constant, the value assigned to the parameter must be provably non-null at the return ([§7](#sec-nullability-2)'s narrowing rules apply inside the callee); a violating path is a compile error in the declaring body. Paths returning the other constant carry no obligation (they typically assign `null`).

At the call site, the compiler narrows the `out` recipient exactly as if the caller had performed an explicit null test: in any region where the call's `bool` result is statically known to equal the stated constant — the controlled branch of `if TryX(…, out var c) then`, an `and`-conjunct, an early-exit guard — the recipient is treated as non-null, so [§22.6](#sec-practical-pattern)'s `c!` becomes plain `c`. The narrowing is invalidated by the standard rules of [§7.4](#sec-member-access-on-nullable-values). The clause is admitted **only** on `out`/`out owned` parameters of nullable type in `bool`-returning methods; anywhere else it is a compile error. It is part of the method's contract like the other parameter modifiers — an override must repeat it ([§12](#sec-inheritance-and-dispatch)'s modifier-match rule) — and it does not create a distinct overload.

This is the declared, checked form of the Try convention's flow narrowing ([§22.6](#sec-practical-pattern), stdlib §1). The design is a *declared, checked* contract, not a structural inference over every `bool`-plus-nullable-out method: an undeclared method keeps requiring the explicit `!`, so no signature silently gains a postcondition its body was never checked against. (Bezel deliberately has no attribute system; this is a compiler-recognized declaration clause in the sense of rationale [§18](Bezel_Design_Rationale.md#sec-things-deferred)'s narrow-modifier escape hatch, like `serialized`.)

<a id="sec-optional-parameters-and-named-arguments"></a>
### 22.5 Optional parameters and named arguments

```bezel
public method Log(message: string, level: string := "INFO", timestamp: bool := true)
  // ...
end Log;

Log("System started", timestamp := false);
Log(level := "ERROR", message := "Failed");
```

Named arguments may appear in any order after positional arguments. Each supplied argument binds **exactly one** parameter and each parameter is bound by **at most one** supplied argument: naming a parameter already bound positionally (`Log("Failed", message := "Retry")` against `Log(message: string, level: string := "INFO")`), or naming the same parameter twice, is a compile error at the call naming that parameter — not an applicability failure, so at an overloaded name it is diagnosed rather than resolved away ([§22.6](#sec-overloading)). **Every parameter that declares no default must be bound**, positionally or by name; leaving one unbound is the opposite disposition from binding one twice — it makes the candidate **inapplicable** ([§22.6](#sec-overloading)), so at an overloaded name an applicable sibling still resolves and the error is reported only where no candidate survives. The rule is stated here because the diagnostic cites this section and every construction site in the language reaches it through the same binding — a call, a `new` expression, and a record construction alike. Two positions admit none: an invocation through a function-typed value ([§27.1](#sec-function-types)), and an index position ([§23.5](#sec-properties-and-indexers-restrictions)). **A `ref`/`out`/`scoped` argument is positional-only:** those modifiers inhabit the `ArgModifiers` alternative of `Argument` (Appendix A.4), which has no named form — `M(out var result := n)` has no reading and does not parse, the `:=` of the binding form and the `:=` of the named form being the same token. The rule survives because those are **true argument modifiers** — grammar-level prefixes on the argument, not parts of its expression: for `out`'s binding forms (`out var x`, `out using var x`) a named spelling would put `:=` in two roles on one argument, and `scoped` shares the alternative and therefore the shape ([§22.3](#sec-parameter-modifiers)'s lending-mode line). A **transfer-marked** argument carries no modifier — the marker is part of the argument expression ([§22.3](#sec-parameter-modifiers), [§28.8.1](#sec-the-move-expression)) — so `M(item := move x)` is an ordinary named argument whose expression happens to be a `MoveExpr`, and is legal.

**Defaults and modifiers.** A default value is permitted only on parameters with **no modifier or `owned`** (an `owned` default is the owned-allocation form this section already blesses, e.g. a factory-call default); a default-value expression that **produces an owned value of non-trivial-dispose class type** ([§28.9](#sec-trivial-dispose-classes)) is admitted only when the parameter itself is declared `owned` — the parameter then receives ownership per [§22.3](#sec-parameter-modifiers)/[§28.8](#sec-ownership-transfer) and the callee discharges it — and is a **compile error on a plain (borrowing) parameter**, naming the undischargeable fresh instance (a trivial-dispose producer, e.g. a `new StringBuilder()` default, stays admissible on either form: on a plain parameter the materialized default is a compiler-introduced unbound owned temporary of the **calling statement** — owned by the call's full expression, freed at its [K8](#sec-kernel-k8) boundary ([§28.3](#sec-unbound-owned-temporaries)) — and the plain parameter borrows it call-bounded); `ref` and `out` parameters can never carry defaults — both require a caller-side location, which an omitted argument cannot supply. Every parameter after the first defaulted parameter must itself have a default.

**Evaluation order.** A call's **supplied** argument expressions are evaluated in **call-site textual order** — left to right as written, for positional and named arguments alike; naming an argument changes which parameter it binds to, never when it runs (`M(b := Next(), a := Next())` evaluates the `b` expression first). **Defaults for omitted parameters** are evaluated after all supplied arguments, in **parameter-list declaration order**; a default-value expression that reads an earlier parameter (below) observes that parameter's value for this call, whether supplied or itself just defaulted. The order is observable through side-effecting arguments and non-constant defaults (`DateTime.Now`, factory calls) and is normative; it matches C#'s treatment of supplied arguments.

<a id="sec-evaluation-timing"></a>
#### Evaluation timing

A default-value expression is evaluated **at each call site** where the default is used — not at the method's declaration site. The expression is re-evaluated every time a caller omits the parameter; the syntax `level: string := "INFO"` does not bind a single shared `"INFO"` instance to the parameter once and reuse it across calls.

This rule lets default-value expressions be non-constant:

```bezel
public method OpenAsync(path: string, timeout: TimeSpan := TimeSpan.FromSeconds(30))
public method LogAt(message: string, at: DateTime := DateTime.Now)
public method NewBuffer(size: int := 4096, fill: byte := 0)
```

`TimeSpan.FromSeconds(30)` and `DateTime.Now` evaluate per call. The first two examples produce a fresh value each time the default is taken; the third uses an integer literal whose evaluation is observably the same per call. There is no Python-style "default value is constructed once at definition and shared across calls" behavior: each call that omits a parameter materializes the default expression's value fresh, per call — the materialized value belongs to the **caller's side** of the call (the calling statement's full expression, [§28.3](#sec-unbound-owned-temporaries)), never to the callee's activation frame.

For default values whose expression has owned-allocation semantics (constructing a new class instance, returning an `owned` from a factory), the per-call evaluation produces a fresh owned instance per call. When the parameter is declared `owned` — which *Defaults and modifiers* above requires whenever the produced class is non-trivial-dispose ([§28.9](#sec-trivial-dispose-classes)) — the parameter receives ownership through the standard parameter-passing rules ([§22.3](#sec-parameter-modifiers), [§28.8](#sec-ownership-transfer)) and the callee discharges it. A trivial-dispose producer admitted on a **plain** parameter is owned on the **caller's side**: the materialized default is a compiler-introduced unbound owned temporary of the call's full expression, freed at that expression's [K8](#sec-kernel-k8) boundary ([§28.3](#sec-unbound-owned-temporaries)), with the plain parameter a call-bounded borrow of it — so the admission is derived from the ordinary temporary rules, not from an exemption, and a callee that stores its plain parameter carries exactly the recorded residual of any unbound owned temporary passed as a plain argument ([§28.3](#sec-unbound-owned-temporaries), [§28.11](#sec-borrowing-collections)), no new trust category. (Recorded as liftable, not adopted: nothing in this derivation is specific to trivial-dispose — a fresh plain-parameter default of any class type is equally call-boundable; that widening of the non-trivial rejection above is recorded for a future revision.) In every case the default-value expression must be type-valid in the parameter's position — the most natural pattern remains a factory method returning `owned T` bound to an `owned` parameter.

<a id="sec-permitted-default-value-expressions"></a>
#### Permitted default-value expressions

A default-value expression must be type-compatible with the parameter's declared type and must be free of side-effects on captured locals (the expression is a function-of-call-site, not a function-of-the-frame-containing-the-call). Specifically, a default-value expression may:

- be a literal, constant, or `default(T)`;
- call static methods, including factory methods that return owned instances;
- read other static state (with the usual static-initialization rules);
- read other parameters appearing **earlier** in the same parameter list (e.g. `M(a: int, b: int := a + 1)` is permitted; later-parameter forward references are not).

A default-value expression may not:

- reference instance state (`this`, instance fields, instance properties) — the default belongs to the method's signature, not to a particular receiver's frame;
- reference local variables (the call site's frame is not in scope);
- contain `await` (defaults are not async expressions; an async default would suspend an in-progress call before the body started, which has no clear semantics).

<a id="sec-where-a-default-is-evaluated"></a>
#### Where a default is evaluated

A default is part of the called method's signature, so recompiling against a new version of a library may pick up a changed default. It is evaluated by the callee, or by code generated at the call site against the callee's signature, at the implementation's choice (rationale [§9.16](Bezel_Design_Rationale.md#sec-member-comparisons-with-csharp)).

The evaluation-site freedom is mechanical only, never semantic: a default participates in the call per *Evaluation timing* above, and any owned value it produces is received and discharged by the `owned` parameter it initializes ([§22.5](#sec-optional-parameters-and-named-arguments) *Defaults and modifiers*) — so no observable disposal-point divergence between callee-evaluated and call-site-generated implementations exists.

<a id="sec-overloading"></a>
### 22.6 Overloading

Methods and constructors may be overloaded by parameter list. Overload resolution considers number, types, the `ref`/`out` modifiers, the presence of `owned` on an **ordinary parameter**, and the number of type parameters a method declares of its own — overloads differing in any of these are distinguishable (the ordinary-`owned` case under the declaration guard below; a generic method's parameter types compared as [§11.3](#sec-member-body) states). `owned` on an **`out` parameter** and `scoped` never distinguish overloads (below).

**Resolution pipeline (road-map).** Resolving a call spans several sections. The stages, in order, each defined in its own section:

1. Arity filtering and named-argument-to-parameter binding — [§22.5](#sec-optional-parameters-and-named-arguments); with an explicit type-argument list, filtering by type-parameter count — [§14.5](#sec-type-argument-inference).
2. Per-candidate type-argument inference for generic candidates — [§14.5](#sec-type-argument-inference).
3. Applicability over the (substituted) signatures: parameter types under the implicit conversions ([§5.1](#sec-implicit-conversions)) and the `ref`/`out` modifiers — this section.
4. Ownership-mode applicability, where a pair differs only by ordinary `owned` — *`owned` and overload resolution* below.
5. Exact-match ranking over the applicable candidates — *Implicit conversions and tie-breaking* below.
6. The defaulted-arity tie-break — *Implicit conversions and tie-breaking* below.
7. The non-generic preference, the last comparison — *Generic candidates* below.
8. Failing a unique winner: the ambiguity error (or, with no applicable candidate at all, the no-candidate error) — *Implicit conversions and tie-breaking* below.

The list is a road-map, not a restatement: each stage's rule lives only in its cited section. No stage reads a candidate's `where` constraints: they are checked on the selected candidate after resolution ([§14.5](#sec-type-argument-inference) *Constraints*). After resolution, the call's arguments evaluate in [§22.5](#sec-optional-parameters-and-named-arguments)'s stated order; a method *reference* to an overloaded name resolves by target type instead ([§27.6](#sec-method-references-to-overloaded-methods)).

**Generic candidates.** A generic method enters overload resolution only after per-candidate type-argument inference ([§14.5](#sec-type-argument-inference)): inference runs independently for each generic candidate, and a candidate whose inference fails is **inapplicable** — the call resolves among the remaining candidates without error from the failed one. Surviving candidates enter the ranking below with their substituted signatures. When a non-generic candidate and a generic candidate are both applicable, and neither the ranking below nor the defaulted-arity tie-break separates them, the **non-generic candidate is selected** — the specific declaration is the author's stated intent for that argument shape. The non-generic preference is the **last** comparison before ambiguity; in particular the defaulted-arity tie-break applies first: `M(n: int, m: int := 0)` and `M<T>(x: T)` on the call `M(5)` resolve to the *generic* candidate — it fills no default — preserving that tie-break's compatibility reasoning (adding an optional-parameter overload never re-routes existing calls), while `Show(x: int)` and `Show<T>(x: T)` on `Show(5)` resolve to the non-generic. Two generic candidates remain subject to the ordinary ambiguity rule.

<a id="sec-owned-and-overload-resolution"></a>
#### `owned` and overload resolution

`owned` on an **ordinary parameter** (without `out`) participates in overload resolution (the transfer marker of [§22.3](#sec-parameter-modifiers) makes the two forms visibly distinct at every call site). Two overloads may differ only by `owned` on an ordinary parameter — `Append(item: Widget)` beside `Append(owned item: Widget)` — subject to the declaration guard below. At an argument position where two applicable candidates differ only by ordinary `owned` — measured on the **substituted** signatures, after per-candidate inference ([§14.5](#sec-type-argument-inference)), so the mixed set `M(x: Widget)` / `M<T>(owned x: T)` engages this rule at `T = Widget` exactly as the same-shape non-generic pair would — the argument expression's ownership classification completes **applicability**, by four exhaustive clauses:

1. **An owned production is applicable only to the `owned` candidate:** a move-rooted argument (`move x` — [§22.3](#sec-parameter-modifiers)'s call-site marker; `move obj._f`; `move coll[i]`) or any other production the [§28.3](#sec-producers) producers table classifies owned — a fresh `new`, an `owned`-returning call, and kin; the producers table, not any list in this rule, is normative. (Its owned-local-read row is the one exception, **superseded at argument positions**: that row is position-classified — the read takes its clause from the position it appears in — and would be circular as a resolution key; at a pair position [§22.3](#sec-parameter-modifiers)'s marker discipline decides instead, an unmarked read falling to clause 2, a marked read to this clause.)
2. **A borrow is applicable only to the plain candidate:** an unmarked read of a named binding, a storage/property/indexer read, a plain-returning call.
3. **A context-typed production is applicable to both:** a `null` literal, a null-producing `default` form ([§17.11](#sec-the-default-operator)), or any other production the [§28.3](#sec-producers) producers table classifies context-typed is polymorphic null (no value to own, compatible with either), and the call falls to the ordinary ambiguity rule below. Because the pair's parameter types are identical, the explicit-cast remedy cannot select between the members, so the ambiguity diagnostic names the real remedies — bind first and pass the binding (a borrow: the plain member), or transfer a named owned binding (`M(move x)`: the owned member).
4. **An argument with no ownership classification is applicable to both** ([K1.6](#sec-kernel-k1) — an ordinary value, a `string`, a boxed value, a function value; reachable at a pair position through boxing or an implicit reference conversion), as is a **bottom-typed** argument — a `throw` expression ([§17.12](#sec-the-throw-expression)), which produces no value and carries no [K1](#sec-kernel-k1) ownership classification at all; both fall to the same ambiguity rule with the same remedy naming.

**The clause split is decidable from the argument alone:** for a named binding, [K3.13](#sec-kernel-k3)'s no-silent-consume rule and [§22.3](#sec-parameter-modifiers)'s marker make the marked/unmarked split total — an unmarked read never consumes, a marked read never borrows — so the argument's spelling, never the candidate under trial, decides its clause. The classification is consulted only where candidates differ by the marker; a single declared member keeps the ordinary compatibility rules unchanged.

**No ranking change, and conjunctive composition across positions:** the marker participates in applicability, never in the better-than relation — at most one member of a pair survives applicability at any argument carrying a classification, so the exact-match ranking, the defaulted-arity tie-break, and the non-generic preference operate on the surviving set exactly as written. The clauses apply per argument position and compose **conjunctively**: a candidate survives applicability only where it survives at every differing position, so a pair's `owned` member is reached only when *every* marked position receives an owned production; a call mixing an owned production at one differing position with a borrow at another leaves no surviving candidate and is a compile error whose diagnostic names the positions and their conflicting classifications — the remedy, where the mixture is intended, is a third member declaring exactly that mixture.

```bezel
public class Registry  // declaration sketch; method bodies elided
  public method Append(item: Widget);         // borrows; caller keeps ownership
  public method Append(owned item: Widget);   // takes; the caller's binding is consumed
end Registry;

r.Append(w);            // borrow — the plain overload; w untouched
r.Append(move w);       // transfer — the owned overload; w moved-from (§22.3)
r.Append(new Widget()); // fresh producer: an owned production — the owned overload
```

Routing a fresh production to the `owned` candidate is the useful reading: fresh productions *are* owned ([K1.5](#sec-kernel-k1)), and the alternative — a call-bounded borrow of an unbound temporary — would hand a storing callee a reference that dies at the statement boundary (the hazard shape [§15.4](#sec-collection-literals)'s fresh-store warning exists for). A caller who wants a fresh value *inspected* but not kept binds it first (`using var t := new Widget(); r.Append(t);`) — the standard remedy, unchanged. Where only one member is declared, today's rules — call-bounded borrows of fresh arguments at plain parameters included — are untouched. Constructors participate through the constructor sentence below: an owned-wrapping constructor pair — `new Wrapper(inner)` borrowing beside `new Wrapper(move inner)` taking — is declarable. An overloaded method reference to a pair resolves by target type under [§27.6](#sec-method-references-to-overloaded-methods)'s existing rules — `(owned T) -> ()` and `(T) -> ()` are distinct function types ([§27.1](#sec-function-types)). A pair whose marked position is defaulted on both sides makes an argument-omitting call fill defaults on both, and the existing two-defaults-filled ambiguity stance applies (stdlib pairs do not default the marked position, stdlib [§1](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-conventions)).

**Declaration guard (the erasure test).** A pair differing only by ordinary `owned` is declarable exactly when, at every differing position, the declared type — nullability stripped — is a **class type**, an **interface type**, or a **type parameter whose constraints exclude every substitution at which the pair collapses**: every substitution at which [§28.1](#sec-where-the-owned-modifier-can-appear) **erases** the marker — a value or runtime-managed substitution, where the substituted signatures become identical — and every **move-only value** substitution, where the marker is admitted-but-redundant ([§28.1](#sec-where-the-owned-modifier-can-appear), [§15.3](#sec-move-only-value-types) — the value transfers under either spelling, so the members collapse in behavior though not in spelling). Whether a constraint set qualifies is decided by [§14.2](#sec-constraints)'s conformance computation, at the declaration: a class bound (`where T: SomeClass`) qualifies — only class types satisfy it; an interface bound qualifies exactly when the interface's conforming set excludes every value-kind and runtime-managed type **as a matter of language rule**, not merely of the types visible at the declaration — `where T: IDisposable` qualifies, its closure guaranteed by [§8.7](#sec-dispose-is-not-on-object) (records, enums, choices, primitives, and inline arrays never implement `IDisposable`; [§28.2](#sec-the-idisposable-contract)) and inherited by every `IDisposable`-extending interface ([§14.2](#sec-interface-conformance) rule 3 — the conforming set is every class plus those interfaces, [§14.2](#sec-worked-example-where-t-idisposable)'s worked example), where `where T: IComparable<int>` does not (primitives and records conform, [§14.2](#sec-worked-example-where-t-icomparableint)'s worked example) and an **ordinary user-declared interface bound does not**: its conformance is open — a record, enum, or choice in any downstream module may list the interface ([§14.2](#sec-interface-conformance) rules 2, 4, 7; separate compilation, [§2.8](#sec-module-identity)) — so no declaration-site computation can exclude the erasing substitutions, and the pair clashes; and **`where T: class` does not qualify** — it admits `string` and function-type substitutions ([§14.2](#sec-constraints)), at which §28.1 erases the marker and the pair collapses to identical signatures. Where the pair are generic methods whose own type parameters correspond at the position ([§11.3](#sec-member-body) *Generic methods*), each member's constraints are decided **separately**, and the position qualifies only when both members' constraints qualify. Constraints do not make a candidate inapplicable ([§14.5](#sec-type-argument-inference) *Constraints*), so a substitution that only one member's constraints exclude still reaches both candidates, and the pair collapses there: `M<T>(x: T) where T: SomeClass` beside `M<T>(owned x: T)` clashes, since `M(5)` infers `T = int` for both, while `M<T>(x: T) where T: SomeClass` beside `M<T>(owned x: T) where T: IDisposable` is declarable, since every collapsing substitution violates both members' constraints. At any failing position the pair clashes: the declaration-site error of [§11.3](#sec-member-body), reported at the second declaration; per-instantiation collapse errors are not raised. Interface conformance needs no new rule: signature matching is already marker-aware ([§28.1](#sec-where-the-owned-modifier-can-appear)'s erasure paragraph, [§11.2](#sec-interface-declaration)/[§12.1](#sec-members-are-non-virtual-by-default)), so an interface may declare both members of a pair, a class implements each separately, an override repeats the modifier as always, and a generic interface pair falls under this guard like any other.

`scoped` does not participate in overload resolution: two overloads differing only in `scoped` on a parameter — `M(cb: () -> ())` and `M(scoped cb: () -> ())` — are a compile error. The criterion that admits ordinary `owned` above is not satisfiable here: a *function-typed* `scoped` argument carries no call-site marker at all (admission is capture-based, [§28.14](#sec-scoped-callback-parameters)), so the caller could not select between the pair — and lifting only the class- or interface-typed face, where the `M(scoped x)` marker ([§22.3](#sec-parameter-modifiers)) does exist, would make `scoped` resolution-significant for one operand kind and invisible for the other: a split inside one modifier. (`scoped` remains part of *function-type* identity, [§27.1](#sec-function-types): `(scoped () -> ()) -> ()` and `(() -> ()) -> ()` are distinct types. This rule is about selecting between same-name methods, not about type identity.)

`owned` on an **`out` parameter** stays outside the distinguishability list: **two methods differing only in the `owned` qualifier on an `out` parameter are a compile error.** The lifted half above keys on what the caller *passes* — an expression with an ownership classification; an `out` half would key on how the caller *binds* a result (`out var` vs `out using var`), making `out` the only position where resolution consults a binding form, and it would require a dedicated `out _` ambiguity remedy (the discard is compatible with both members of such a pair). And the distinction would misdescribe the surface it serves: the standard library never declares the same-name pair, because every shipped borrow/take `out` pair is **operation-distinct**, not merely ownership-distinct — `TryGetValue` leaves the entry where `TryPopValue` removes it; `TryPeek` leaves where `TryPop`/`TryDequeue` remove — so merging them would key a *mutation of the receiver* to how the caller binds an out-result. APIs expose borrowing and owning `out` forms under distinct method names.

The call-site form must still **match** the declaration under [§22.4](#sec-inline-out-declarations)'s recipient rules. A caller cannot write `out using var` against a plain `out` parameter (the result would have no owned source). These are compatibility checks against the *resolved* signature, not resolution signals. (An explicit type annotation on the inline `out` declaration is not permitted — the type is inferred from the callee's parameter, [§22.4](#sec-inline-out-declarations). Overloads that differ in the out parameter's *type* remain legal; when the inline form's inference is ambiguous between them, disambiguate by pre-declaring a typed local and passing plain `out x`.)

**`out _`.** The discard form applies to both parameter kinds: against `out T` the received value is dropped ([§17.13](#sec-the-discard-_)); against `out owned T` the discarded value is an unbound owned temporary disposed at the end of the full statement ([§28.3](#sec-unbound-owned-temporaries)). No ambiguity rule for `out _` against an out/out-owned pair is needed — the pair itself is not declarable.

The stance, restated: **ordinary-parameter `owned` distinguishes overloads under the declaration guard above; `owned` on an `out` parameter and `scoped` never do** — arity, a method's own type-parameter count, parameter types, the `ref`/`out` modifiers, and ordinary `owned` are the distinguishing facts. `ref` parameters do not admit `owned` (a `ref` location is borrowed by definition); `in` parameters do not exist as a separate modifier in Bezel.

<a id="sec-practical-pattern"></a>
#### Practical pattern

The common use is a pair of "try" methods exposing borrow and take forms under **distinct names** — the convention the standard library uses everywhere (`TryGetValue` vs `TryPopValue` on `OwningDictionary`, `TryPeek` vs `TryPop` on `OwningStack`):

```bezel
public class ConnectionPool  // declaration sketch; method bodies elided
  // Borrow a cached connection; the pool retains ownership.
  public method TryGetCached(name: string, out conn: Connection? when true): bool;

  // Take a cached connection out of the pool; the caller assumes ownership.
  public method TryPopCached(name: string, out owned conn: Connection? when true): bool;
end ConnectionPool;

// Caller A: borrows a cached connection (pool retains it)
if pool.TryGetCached("primary", out var c) then
  UseConnection(c);     // narrowed non-null by the `when true` postcondition (§22.4)
end;

// Caller B: takes ownership of a cached connection (pool no longer holds it)
if pool.TryPopCached("primary", out using var c) then
  UseConnection(c);     // owned, narrowed non-null; disposed at scope end
end;
```

Each name has one signature, and each call site's binding form matches its callee's declaration (the same-name pair differing only in `out` vs `out owned` is a compile error).

The implementation of the take-form (`TryPopCached`) uses [§28.8.1](#sec-the-move-expression)'s `move` expression on the pool's internal owned-element collection to transfer ownership from pool to caller. A typical body using a `OwningDictionary<string, Connection>` for the pool storage has the shape:

```bezel
private owned _cache: OwningDictionary<string, Connection>;

public method TryPopCached(name: string, out owned conn: Connection? when true): bool
  if not _cache.ContainsKey(name) then
    conn := null;
    return false;
  end;
  conn := _cache.PopValue(name);    // takes ownership, removes from dictionary
  return true;
end TryPopCached;
```

The out parameter is typed `Connection?` (nullable) so that the false-return path can write `null` — `default(Connection)` is a compile error for a non-nullable reference type ([§17.11](#sec-the-default-operator)), and the type system requires every `out` parameter to be assigned on every return path ([§22.3](#sec-parameter-modifiers) — throw paths carry no obligation, which is what lets a Try body open throwable resources before assigning). Callers consume with `out using var`; the `when true` clause narrows the recipient after the bool guard:

```bezel
if pool.TryPopCached("primary", out using var c) then
  // c is owned Connection? — narrowed non-null here by the `when true` postcondition
  UseConnection(c);
end;
```

The `when true` clause on the declaration is the documentation point: the API contract — "true return implies `conn` is non-null" — is stated in the signature, checked in the callee's body, and consumed by the caller's flow analysis ([§22.4](#sec-out-nullability-postcondition) — landing the flow-narrowing revision earlier versions deferred). Against a `Try` method *without* the clause, the explicit `!` remains required after the bool guard.

The `PopValue` method on `OwningDictionary<K, V>` ([§28.11](#sec-collections-do-not-own-elements), std lib [§4.9](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-owneddictionaryk-v)) removes the entry and returns ownership of the value. After the call, the pool no longer holds the connection; the `out owned` parameter `conn` carries the obligation to the caller.

For pool implementations that prefer index-based storage, `OwningArray<Connection>.PopAt(i)` provides the analogous take-and-remove operation. For the simplest case of a single-slot cache, an `owned Connection?` field with `move _slot!` followed by `_slot := null` (per [§28.8.1](#sec-the-move-expression)'s nullable-field detach pattern) is also valid — the choice between dictionary, array, and single-field forms is about how the pool indexes its connections, not about how ownership flows out.

<a id="sec-implicit-conversion-ranking"></a>
#### Implicit conversions and tie-breaking

The rules above (number, type, `ref`/`out`, the ownership-mode applicability clauses at ordinary-`owned` pairs, and the `owned`-on-`out` carve-out) determine which overloads are **applicable** to a call. When more than one overload remains applicable because an argument matches several candidates through different implicit conversions ([§5.1](#sec-implicit-conversions)), the compiler selects among them by the following precedence. This tie-breaking is applied only after arity and named-argument binding ([§22.5](#sec-optional-parameters-and-named-arguments)) have already filtered the set to the applicable candidates.

For a single argument position, one candidate is **better** than another when the better candidate requires *no* implicit conversion (the argument's static type matches the parameter type exactly) and the other requires an implicit conversion. An exact match is the only relation that distinguishes one applicable candidate from another at an argument position; two candidates that both require an implicit conversion at the same position are **equally ranked** there, regardless of which conversion each uses. Bezel does not rank one built-in implicit conversion above another: §5.1 admits a conversion only when no programmer-visible information is lost (or, for the wide-integer-to-float cases, when an explicit cast would be unjustified noise), so all admitted implicit conversions are treated as co-equal for resolution purposes. This includes the reference conversions of [§5.1](#sec-reference-conversions): `M(a: Animal)` versus `M(o: Object)` on a `Dog` argument is ambiguous — neither candidate is exact — and the caller upcasts explicitly.

**Lambda-literal arguments.** A lambda literal has no static type of its own; applicability and ranking at that argument position are decided by its **inferred return type**. The lambda's parameters take the candidate's (substituted) parameter types ([§27.4](#sec-parameter-type-inference)) and the body is typed ([§27.3](#sec-lambda-expressions)); the candidate is **applicable** at the position when the lambda's inferred return type equals the candidate's return slot, implicitly converts to it ([§5.1](#sec-implicit-conversions)), or binds it ([§14.5](#sec-type-argument-inference) phase 2 — a return slot containing a free type parameter); for a procedure slot (`-> ()`), [§27.3](#sec-lambda-expressions)'s value/procedure classification decides instead — an expression-bodied lambda whose body is not of type `()` is **applicable** at a procedure slot (`-> ()`) as [§27.3](#sec-lambda-expressions)'s result-discarding procedure lambda and ranks *converting* there, while a unit-typed body or a `: ()` ascription is exact and a block-bodied lambda that returns a value is inapplicable: `M(f: () -> ())` beside `M(f: () -> int)` on `M(lambda() => 42)` resolves to the second, exact where the first converts; for an `async` lambda at a `-> Task` slot [§30.6](#sec-async-lambdas)'s closed-slot conformance decides applicability instead — a valued body does not conform to `Task`. The candidate is **exact** at the position when the inferred return type equals the return slot after type-argument substitution, and *converting* otherwise — which is how `xs.Average(lambda(x) => x * 2)` over an `Array<int>` selects the `(T) -> int` overload of the stdlib `Average` family: the `int`-returning candidate is exact and the others convert. When no candidate is exact, the co-equal rule above applies unchanged: `bytes.Average(lambda(x) => x)` over an `Array<byte>` is ambiguous — every candidate converts the `byte` body result — remedied by widening in the body (`lambda(x) => int(x)`). A lambda whose body contributes no return binding ([§14.5](#sec-type-argument-inference) phase 2 — a collection-literal body) has no inferred return type: the candidate is **applicable** at the position when its substituted return slot is closed and admits the literal ([§15.4](#sec-collection-literals)), and the position ranks *converting*, never exact — so two candidates that differ only there (`M(f: (int) -> Array<int>)` beside `M(f: (int) -> Set<int>)`, called as `M(lambda(x) => [x])`) fall to the ambiguity below, remedied by a block body whose explicitly typed local names the collection.

**Method-reference arguments.** A method-reference argument ([§27.6](#sec-method-references)) likewise has no static type of its own until it is formed against a target; at an overloaded callee it is formed **per candidate** against that candidate's parameter type — the substituted type, for a generic candidate ([§14.5](#sec-type-argument-inference) phase 2, which binds the slot's free type parameters from the selected overload's signature); the declared type, for a non-generic one — and it ranks as a lambda literal does. The candidate is **applicable** at the position when formation succeeds under §27.6's criteria — signature equality, or an adapter the compiler synthesizes at the formation site for a [§5.1](#sec-implicit-conversions) conversion at a parameter or return slot (`Task<Todo?>` at a `Task` slot is the ordinary derived-to-base reference conversion), with modifier slots matching exactly and [§27.1.1](#sec-function-type-assignability)'s mint-announcing family boundary respected at the return slot. Where the referenced name is overloaded, [§27.6](#sec-method-references-to-overloaded-methods)'s exact-preferred ranking selects the reference's overload against the candidate's slot first; where that ranking finds no unique winner against a candidate's slot, **formation fails at that candidate** and the candidate is inapplicable at the position — the drop-out of an inference failure ([§14.5](#sec-type-argument-inference)'s *Interaction with overloading*), never an error reported at that candidate; §27.6's ambiguity is reported only where the reference has a single target. The candidate is **exact** at the position when the selected signature equals the slot, slot for slot, after type-argument substitution, and *converting* otherwise. So against `Get<A, R>(route: string, h: (A) -> Task<R>)` beside `Get<A>(route: string, h: (A) -> Task, status: int := 204)`, the reference `GetById: (int) -> Task<Todo?>` binds `A := int, R := Todo?` at the first and is exact there, binds `A := int` at the second and converts there (`Task<Todo?>` → `Task`), and the first is unambiguously better — the exact-match ranking decides before the defaulted-arity tie-break is reached. Where two candidates are exact at a method-reference position, the explicit-cast remedy below is inexpressible — a reference has no static type to cast — so the diagnostic names the reference remedies instead: an explicit type-argument list on the call, or a lambda that spells the intended overload ([§27.6](#sec-method-references-to-overloaded-methods)'s own disambiguation). §27.6's exact-preferred ranking is the mirror direction (which overload of the *reference* is selected against one target); this paragraph is the callee's direction.

**Parameter count at a function-typed position.** Whatever the argument's form — a function-typed value, a lambda literal, a method reference — a candidate whose function-typed slot has a different number of parameter slots from the argument's (a value's or reference's parameter slots; a lambda's parameter count) is **inapplicable** at that position, exactly as a candidate whose parameter type admits no conversion is, and never an error reported at that candidate ([§14.5](#sec-type-argument-inference)'s phase-1 bullet states it for a function-typed **value** at a generic candidate; a lambda literal and a method reference reach the slot at phase 2, where the same count prerequisite governs; [§27.1.1](#sec-function-type-assignability)'s rules are slot-wise over equal counts, so no conversion crosses a count difference).

A candidate is **unambiguously better** than another when it is better-or-equal on every argument position and strictly better (an exact match where the other converts) on at least one. The call resolves to a candidate that is unambiguously better than every other applicable candidate.

**Defaulted-arity tie-break.** When the applicable candidates differ in whether defaults must be filled for omitted optional parameters ([§22.5](#sec-optional-parameters-and-named-arguments)), one further comparison applies before declaring ambiguity: a candidate applicable **without filling any default** is preferred over a candidate that fills one or more, provided the no-defaults candidate is better-or-equal at every supplied-argument position under the ranking above. `M(5)` against `M(n: int)` and `M(n: int, m: int := 0)` resolves to `M(int)` — without this rule the call would be permanently ambiguous, and the explicit-cast remedy below cannot express "the fewer-parameter candidate". The tie-break distinguishes only all-arguments-supplied from some-defaults-filled; two candidates that both fill defaults remain subject to the ambiguity rule (the compiler declines to guess which omission the caller meant). This is C#'s rule, adopted with C#'s reasoning: adding an optional parameter to an overload set must not break existing calls that were exact against the shorter signature. The tie-break also separates generic from non-generic candidates, and does so **before** the non-generic-over-generic preference (the generic-candidates paragraph above): `M(5)` against `M(n: int, m: int := 0)` and `M<T>(x: T)` resolves to the generic — the candidate that fills no default — so this rule's compatibility reasoning holds for generic overload sets too.

If no candidate is unambiguously better — because each of two candidates is exact on a different argument, or because the remaining candidates all rely on implicit conversions that this rule treats as equally ranked — the call is **ambiguous** and is a compile error. The compiler reports the error and cites the candidate overloads; it never silently selects one. The caller resolves the ambiguity by adding an explicit cast ([§5.2](#sec-explicit-conversions)) to an argument so that exactly one candidate becomes an exact match (or so that all but one candidate become inapplicable). One exception: at an ambiguity between the two members of an ordinary-`owned` pair — clauses (3) and (4) of the ownership-mode applicability rule above — the explicit-cast remedy is inexpressible, the pair's parameter types being identical, so the diagnostic instead names the ownership-mode remedies: bind first and pass the binding (the plain member), or transfer a named owned binding with `M(move x)` (the owned member).

If no candidate is applicable at all — no candidate is reachable: a conversion §5.1 does not admit as implicit, a parameter-count difference at a function-typed slot, a method-reference formation that fails, or an inference that finds no binding — the call is a compile error with no candidates cited, because no overload was reachable.

This mirrors the resolution of overloaded method references ([§27.6](#sec-method-references-to-overloaded-methods)), where the absence of a unique winner is likewise a compile error citing the candidates, and it follows the same "explicit over implicit" stance that motivates Bezel's omission of user-defined conversion operators ([§25.4](#sec-no-user-defined-conversion-operators)): when two overloads serve a call equally well, the compiler declines to guess and requires the call site to be explicit.

**Example 1 — exact match preferred over a conversion.**

```bezel
public class Logger  // declaration sketch; method bodies elided
  public method Log(level: int);
  public method Log(level: long);
end Logger;

var lg := new Logger();
var n: int := 10;

lg.Log(n);            // n is int: exact match — calls Log(int), not the int→long widening
lg.Log(42);           // 42 is an int literal: exact match — calls Log(int)
lg.Log(42L);          // 42L is a long literal: exact match — calls Log(long)
```

**Example 2 — two equally-ranked conversions: ambiguous.**

```bezel
public class Converter
  public method Convert(n: long): string => "long";
  public method Convert(n: float): string => "float";
end Converter;

var cvt := new Converter();
var a: int := 10;

cvt.Convert(a);
// a is int. Neither candidate is an exact match.
//   Convert(long):  int→long  is implicit (§5.1).
//   Convert(float): int→float is implicit (§5.1).
// Both conversions are admitted by §5.1 and are equally ranked: neither
// candidate is better at the single argument position.
// Ambiguous call — compile error citing both candidates.
// Disambiguate with an explicit cast so exactly one is exact:
//   cvt.Convert(long(a));     // selects Convert(long)
//   cvt.Convert(float(a));    // selects Convert(float)
```

**Example 3 — exact on one argument, conversion on the other: unambiguously better.**

```bezel
public class Pair
  public method Apply(x: int, y: long): string => "int,long";
  public method Apply(x: int, y: int): string  => "int,int";
end Pair;

var p := new Pair();
var a: int := 5;
var b: int := 9;

p.Apply(a, b);
// arg x (int): exact in both — tie.
// arg y (int): exact in Apply(int,int); requires int→long in Apply(int,long).
// Apply(int,int) is better-or-equal on x and strictly better on y ⇒ unambiguously better.
// Resolves to Apply(int, int).
```

**Example 4 — each candidate exact on a different argument: ambiguous.**

```bezel
public class Calculator
  public method Compute(a: int, b: long): string => "int,long";
  public method Compute(a: long, b: int): string => "long,int";
end Calculator;

var calc := new Calculator();
var x: int := 5;
var y: int := 10;

calc.Compute(x, y);
// arg a (int): exact in Compute(int,long); int→long conversion in Compute(long,int).
// arg b (int): int→long conversion in Compute(int,long); exact in Compute(long,int).
// Each candidate is strictly better on a different argument; neither dominates.
// Ambiguous call — compile error citing both candidates.
// Disambiguate:
//   calc.Compute(x, long(y));    // makes Compute(int,long) exact on both ⇒ selects it
//   calc.Compute(long(x), y);    // makes Compute(long,int) exact on both ⇒ selects it
```

**Example 5 — no reachable candidate: error with no candidates cited.**

```bezel
public class Transformer  // declaration sketch; method bodies elided
  public method Transform(x: int);
  public method Transform(x: decimal);
end Transformer;

var t := new Transformer();
var n: float := 2.5f;

t.Transform(n);
// float→int is not implicit (§5.1: float's only implicit target is double).
// float→decimal is not implicit (§5.1: decimal and binary floats never mix implicitly).
// No candidate is applicable ⇒ compile error, no candidates cited (none reachable).
// The caller must convert explicitly, e.g. t.Transform(int(n)) or t.Transform(decimal(n)).
```

**Example 6 — applicability filtering removes a candidate, leaving one winner.**

```bezel
public class Handler
  public method Process(n: sbyte): string => "sbyte";
  public method Process(n: ushort): string => "ushort";
end Handler;

var h := new Handler();
var val: byte := 50;

h.Process(val);
// byte→sbyte is NOT implicit (§5.1: signed/unsigned same-or-narrower width never implicit).
//   ⇒ Process(sbyte) is not applicable.
// byte→ushort IS implicit (§5.1, byte row).
//   ⇒ Process(ushort) is the only applicable candidate.
// Resolves to Process(ushort). No ambiguity — only one candidate survived applicability.
```

The rule applies identically to constructor overload sets ([§22.7](#sec-constructors)): a `new T(...)` call is resolved among `T`'s constructors by the same exact-match-then-ambiguity precedence.

<a id="sec-constructors"></a>
### 22.7 Constructors

```bezel
public constructor(name: string, balance: decimal)
  _name := name;
  _balance := balance;
end constructor;
```

Constructors return no value. Multiple constructors are permitted; chaining uses `this(...)` or `base(...)` in the chaining position before the body ([§12.8](#sec-constructor-chaining)). When a class has a primary constructor ([§22.10](#sec-methods-and-constructors-primary-constructors)), an additional restriction applies: only the primary may chain to `base(...)`; convenience constructors must chain via `this(...)`.

**The implicit parameterless constructor.** A class that declares **no instance constructor** and no primary-constructor parameter list has an implicit parameterless constructor: `public`, no parameters, an empty body, chaining implicitly per [§12.8](#sec-constructor-chaining). It is what `new C()` reaches on such a class, and what [§12.8](#sec-constructor-chaining)'s inserted `base()` finds on a base class that declares none — the [§11.7](#sec-static-classes) `closed class Shape` / `sealed class Circle(radius: double): Shape` shape. Declaring **any** instance constructor suppresses it, a primary-constructor parameter list included; a `static constructor` does not (it is never a chaining or `new` target). A `static` class declares no constructors and is not instantiable ([§11.7](#sec-static-classes)), so it has none. The rule is stated for the **class** kind: a record's construction surface is [§9.1](#sec-positional-records)/[§9.2](#sec-body-records)'s. A **standard-library builtin** type is excepted: its constructor surface is closed by [§17.7](#sec-the-new-operator) and no implicit constructor is supplied.

A static constructor runs once before the type's first use. It carries no access modifier (the runtime is the only caller) and no parameters:

```bezel
class Utils
  static constructor()
    // ...
  end constructor;
end Utils;
```

A static constructor body may use `try`/`catch`. An exception caught inside the body does not transition the type to the failed state — the constructor completes normally and static initialization is considered successful. The failed state is entered only when an exception escapes the static initializer entirely. If the static initializer (the static field initializers, the static constructor body, or both) throws an *uncaught* exception, the type is left in a permanently failed state:

- Every subsequent access to a static member of the type — field read, field write, method call, property read or write, indexer — raises `TypeInitializationException` whose `InnerException` is the original exception (for the [§22.13](#sec-static-initialization-order) cycle backstop, the cached instance is the runtime-synthesized one and `InnerException` is `null`).
- The state is not recoverable: re-running static initialization is not attempted.
- Static fields whose initializers had not yet run remain at their default values, but those defaults are not observable: every access raises. For non-nullable reference fields, where no default value exists ([§7.9](#sec-definite-assignment-for-non-nullable-fields)), this rule is satisfied vacuously — every access to the type raises before any field read could occur, so the absence of a value is never observed. The compiler's definite-assignment analysis is not violated, because the failed-state machinery intercepts every access before any read of the field.
- Static fields whose initializers completed successfully before the failing initializer have their values; if any such field is `owned`, its value will be disposed at program exit per [§22.13](#sec-static-initialization-order). The runtime makes no guarantee about ordering of disposal across types when one of the types is in a failed state.

The `TypeInitializationException` is constructed at the moment the exception escapes the initializer, and **the access that triggered initialization observes it too**: the original exception never propagates raw out of static initialization; it is observable only as `InnerException`. The instance constructed on first failure is the one cached and rethrown; the triggering access and every subsequent access see the same cached `TypeInitializationException` instance. (When the escaping exception is itself the `TypeInitializationException` synthesized by [§22.13](#sec-static-initialization-order)'s cycle backstop, that instance is cached directly — no double wrapping.)

The rules above resolve into two scenarios:

| Scenario | Outcome |
|---|---|
| Static initializer (field initializer or static constructor body) throws an exception that escapes the initializer. | Type enters permanently failed state. Every subsequent access raises `TypeInitializationException` whose `InnerException` is the original (`null` for the [§22.13](#sec-static-initialization-order) cycle-backstop instance, which has no original). Owned static fields whose initializers had already completed are disposed at program exit. |
| Static initializer encounters an exception but catches it via `try`/`catch` inside the body. | Type initializes normally. The caught exception did not escape; subsequent member access proceeds without raising. Remaining initializers and the constructor body run as usual. |

<a id="sec-observing-this-during-construction"></a>
#### Observing `this` during construction

During construction, the object is built base-first ([§22.8](#sec-field-initializers)): when a class C's constructor body runs, C's own field initializers have run (step 2) but a *derived* class's have not — and C's body itself assigns C's remaining fields as it executes. Three rules keep [§7.9](#sec-definite-assignment-for-non-nullable-fields)'s guarantee true while `this` is under construction — rule 1 for every type kind whose constructors carry a §7.9 obligation, classes and records ([§9.4](#sec-value-receivers-are-borrows), *Constructor bodies are not receiver positions*) alike; rule 2 for classes only, a record having no dispatch to gate ([§9.6](#sec-records-and-inheritance)); rule 3 as stated, for both:

1. **The observation gate.** In a constructor body, a **synchronous observation
   of `this`** — an instance method, block-form accessor, or indexer invocation
   with receiver `this` (explicit or implicit); `this` as an argument; `this`
   stored anywhere; `this` as an `is`/`is not`/`as` operand or `case` scrutinee —
   is admitted only at points where **every field of the declaring type that
   [§7.9](#sec-definite-assignment-for-non-nullable-fields) requires to be
   explicitly initialized** is definitely assigned on every reaching path.
   Direct field assignments and reads, and **auto-property** assignments and
   reads (compiler-known storage, [§23.1](#sec-auto-properties) — each is the
   backing field's assignment or read, and the assignment counts toward the
   gate), are not observations — they keep their existing definite-assignment
   rules ([§28.8.1](#sec-the-move-expression), constructors paragraph). Fields
   with initializers count as assigned at body entry. In the **chaining
   position** (`base(...)`/`this(...)` arguments, a primary constructor's
   inheritance-clause base call) no field of the declaring type is yet
   assigned, so any observation of `this` there is a compile error — and, the
   carve-out above notwithstanding, a direct read of any field or auto-property
   of `this` is a compile error there too, whatever the field's type
   ([§12.8](#sec-constructor-chaining),
   [§22.10](#sec-methods-and-constructors-primary-constructors)): the only
   reads a chaining argument may make are of the constructor's own parameters,
   constants, and statics. A
   constructor chaining via `this(...)` enters its body with every such field
   assigned (the chained-to constructor's own [§7.9](#sec-definite-assignment-for-non-nullable-fields)
   obligation), so the gate is satisfied at entry.
2. **No virtual dispatch from constructor bodies of non-sealed classes.** A
   call from a constructor body to a `virtual`, `override`, or `abstract`
   member with receiver `this` — any dispatching call not through `base.` — is
   a compile error unless the declaring class is `sealed` and not `abstract`.
   During construction the runtime type may be a derived class whose field
   initializers have not yet run; dispatch would enter derived code over unset
   fields (the template-method-in-constructor problem). In a sealed,
   non-abstract class the dispatch target is statically bounded and the call is
   admitted under rule 1's gate; `base.M()` is non-dispatching and likewise
   needs only rule 1.
3. **Closures observe at invocation, not at capture.** Capturing `this` in a
   lambda or method reference is not a synchronous observation and is not gated
   by rule 1 — whether the capture is legal is [§28.14](#sec-scoped-callback-parameters)'s
   question, unchanged (form 3's owned-field subscription — stdlib
   [§6.5](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-events-ievent-eventsource) — stays the
   standard observer pattern). An admitted `this`-capturing closure
   that is nevertheless *invoked before construction completes* — possible only
   if the constructor itself, directly or transitively, causes the invocation
   (instance event sources are domain-serial, stdlib §6.5) — is a construction-time
   observation under the residual below.

**The recorded residual.** These checks reject every unsafe observation they can see and are **not a completeness guarantee** (the same bound as [§22.13](#sec-static-initialization-order)'s cycle approximation): a virtual call or derived-type downcast inside a non-virtual helper called after the gate, external code reached by an admitted `this`-escape that dispatches back, or a during-construction closure invocation can still enter a derived class's code before its initializers ran. The runtime bound is defined: before construction begins, every reference-typed field of the allocation is initialized to `null` and every **defaultable** ([§17.11](#sec-the-default-operator)) value-typed field to its [§7.9](#sec-default-initialization) default (normative); a read of a non-nullable reference field still at that null watermark raises `NullReferenceException` ([§31.4](#sec-standard-exception-types)) in **checked disposal mode** ([§28.2](#sec-checked-disposal)) and, unchecked, observes the watermark `null` with undefined behavior on any use requiring non-null — the same checked/unchecked split as use-after-dispose.

<a id="sec-field-initializers"></a>
### 22.8 Field initializers

A field declared in a class or record may include an initializer:

```bezel
class BankAccount
  private _balance: decimal := 0m;
  private owned _transactions: Array<Transaction> := new Array<Transaction>();
  private _createdAt: DateTime := DateTime.Now;
end BankAccount;
```

A field declared `readonly` may be assigned only in a field initializer or in a constructor body; assignment anywhere else is a compile error. **The context is per-instance, not per-type:** an *instance* `readonly` field is assignable only through an lvalue chain rooted at `this` — an explicit `this.F := e` or the bare in-scope spelling that resolves to `this`'s storage — so a constructor of the declaring type may **not** write another value's `readonly` storage held in a parameter, local, or field; a `static readonly` field is assignable only in its own static field initializer or in a constructor body of the declaring type, spelled as the bare name or `TypeName.F`. [§22.3](#sec-ref-and-out-argument-locations)'s `ref`/`out` rule and [§17.6](#sec-the-increment-and-decrement-operators)'s read-only-location rule inherit this context unchanged: binding another value's `readonly` storage to a `ref`/`out` parameter inside a constructor is the same store by other syntax. This is what [§7.4](#sec-member-access-on-nullable-values)'s narrowing licence assumes for an **instance** `readonly` field when it states that such a field has no writer on any path, through any alias, outside its construction window. The placement rule above admits an assignment to a `static readonly` field in an *instance* constructor of the declaring type, which makes a plain `new C()` a writer of the `TypeName._s` shape §7.4 also narrows; whether `readonly` should instead confine such a field to its static field initializer and static constructor — and so what once-ness would mean across the several instances such a constructor could build — is an open question ([#5577](https://github.com/s8lap/bezel-lang/issues/5577)). `readonly` on a field is analogous to `readonly` on an auto-property ([§23.1](#sec-auto-properties)).

**The single-assignment rule (instance and `static` `readonly` **fields**).** Placement is not the whole of `readonly`: the field is also assigned **at most once**. **Scope of this rule:** it governs `readonly` **fields**. It does not govern a `readonly` **auto-property** ([§23.1](#sec-auto-properties)): extending it there is declined, with its reasons recorded at `docs/proposals/DECLINED.md` (*Extending §22.8's single-assignment rule to `readonly` auto-properties*). For an *instance* `readonly` field the unit is one instance construction — on every path through the construction of a single instance, counting the field initializer (step 2 below) together with the bodies of every constructor that runs for that instance, the whole `this(...)` chain included, at most one assignment to the field executes. A field initializer and a constructor-body assignment are therefore **two** assignments wherever both run, which is wherever the constructor's chaining position holds `base(...)` or the implicit `base()` (the once-only rule below); and a `this(...)`-chaining constructor's body assignment is a second assignment when the chained-to constructor's own initializer or body already assigned the field. Assignments in **mutually exclusive** branches are one assignment per path and are admitted. For a `static readonly` field the unit is one type initialization: at most one assignment executes on any path through the static field initializer and the static constructor body ([§22.13](#sec-static-initialization-order)). *Assignment* here means every store form — `:=`, compound assignment, `++`/`--` ([§17.6](#sec-the-increment-and-decrement-operators)), and binding the field to a `ref` or `out` parameter, which is the same store by other syntax the paragraph above already names. The rule is **at most** once, not exactly once: a field of defaultable type ([§17.11](#sec-the-default-operator)) may go unassigned and take its default; [§7.9](#sec-definite-assignment-for-non-nullable-fields), not this rule, is what requires an assignment at all. This is the rule [§7.4](#sec-member-access-on-nullable-values)'s narrowing licence and [§21.1](#sec-variable-declarations)'s *member-level runtime single-assignment* both name: outside the assignment window the field holds its one assigned value and nothing can replace it.

**The checkable form.** So that conforming implementations agree on which programs compile — the posture [§7.4](#sec-member-access-on-nullable-values) takes for narrowing — the rule is checked as a compile-time approximation, and both of its rejections name it. An assignment to a `readonly` field is rejected when the field is **possibly already assigned** on some path reaching that point: the possibly-assigned set is unioned at every join (the dual of [§7.9](#sec-definite-assignment-for-non-nullable-fields)'s all-paths intersection), and it is seeded with the field's initializer wherever step 2 runs for the constructor being checked, and — so that the chain clause above has a checkable form rather than only an abstract one — a delegating `this(...)` call is treated as executing the target constructor's assignment window at the point of delegation, so a field assigned in the target is **possibly already assigned** on every path after it in the delegating body. An assignment lexically inside a **loop body** within the assignment window is rejected unconditionally: a loop could assign on more than one iteration, and this section's window is carved out of [§7.4](#sec-member-access-on-nullable-values)'s narrowing, so no flow fact bounds it. The loop rejection is a deliberate over-approximation — a guarded once-per-construction loop assignment is rejected — and is recorded liftable; write the assignment after the loop. Like the rule it approximates, the checkable form governs `readonly` **fields** (the scope statement above). It does not reach the open question above (an instance constructor's assignment to a `static readonly` field).

Field initializers run as part of construction in textual declaration order. The full sequence for a constructor:

0. Primary-constructor parameters ([§22.10](#sec-methods-and-constructors-primary-constructors)) that are referenced in body positions (method, property, constructor, or destructor bodies) are captured into their compiler-generated private fields; parameters referenced only in initializer positions are not captured ([§11.1](#sec-class-declaration)). This step is omitted for classes without a primary constructor.
1. The base or chained constructor call (`base(...)`, `this(...)`, or implicit `base()`). For a `this(...)` chain, the chained-to constructor runs to completion (its own steps of this sequence) before control returns here.
2. Field initializers, in declaration order — executed **only** by a constructor whose step 1 is `base(...)` or the implicit `base()` (see below).
3. The constructor body.

**Field initializers run exactly once per instance construction.** They execute as step 2 of the constructor whose chaining position holds `base(...)` or the implicit `base()` — the constructor at the end of any `this(...)` chain. A constructor that chains via `this(...)` **skips steps 0 and 2**: its effective sequence is the chained `this(...)` call, then its own body. (Step 0 is vacuous for such a constructor anyway: only non-primary constructors may chain via `this(...)` ([§22.7](#sec-constructors), [§22.10](#sec-methods-and-constructors-primary-constructors)), and primary-parameter capture happens inside the chained-to primary — which is why a `this(...)` argument may read neither a primary-constructor parameter nor any field of `this`, [§22.10](#sec-methods-and-constructors-primary-constructors).) Read without this rule, step 1's run-to-completion parenthetical plus an unconditional step 2 would run every field initializer twice under `this(...)` chaining — repeating allocations and initializer side effects, assigning `readonly` fields twice, and, for `owned` fields, disposing and recreating each initializer's value under [§28.7](#sec-reassigning-owned-fields)'s drop-on-overwrite. The once-only rule matches C# and the reference implementation.

Primary-constructor parameter capture occurs first so that the `base(...)`/`this(...)` argument expressions (step 1), field initializers (step 2), and the body (step 3) may reference the captured parameters by name. Step 0 is observable only through ordering: the captured fields are initialized before any user-written code runs.

Field initializers may reference: constants, literals, static members of any type ([§3.1](#sec-type-kinds)) — a record's, enum's, or choice's statics as much as a class's, which is why the example above reads `DateTime.Now`, a static of the record `DateTime` (stdlib [§2.5](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-datetime-timespan-dateonly-timeonly)) — enum constants and **choice case constructions** ([§10.1](#sec-basic-syntax), [§35.3](#sec-choice-construction)), `new` expressions, lambdas that capture only the above, primary-constructor parameters ([§22.10](#sec-methods-and-constructors-primary-constructors)), and `typeof` expressions.
