Case construction is named on its own because no other item reaches it: a case is not a static member of its choice ([§35.2](#sec-choice-members) enumerates what a choice body declares, and [§35.1](#sec-choice-declaration) counts cases as members only for the name-collision rule), it is not a `new` expression (a choice has no constructors — "a choice's construction *is* case selection", [§35.1](#sec-choice-declaration)), and it is not a constant expression in either form ([§17.14](#sec-constant-expressions), which admits an enum constant and no case). [§35.3](#sec-choice-construction) makes the qualified form the only spelling available here — the bare case reading does not extend to field initializers — so `Opt.Some(x)` and `Opt.None` are what one writes, and they are admitted. This list enumerates the **names** an initializer may reference; the expression forms that combine them are not restricted by it, so an initializer may apply operators, indexing, and calls to admitted references — subject to the prohibition in the next paragraph, which is not relaxed by this one as freely as `DateTime.Now` and `B._b + 1` do. The admission is kind-blind, and the list open in that way, because the prohibition below is what actually closes it: no static member of any kind, and no case of any choice, can observe `this`. (A static interface member is reachable only through a constrained type parameter, never on the interface name — [§11.8](#sec-static-interface-members) — and that rule is unchanged here.)

Field initializers may **not** reference: `this`, instance members, `base`, virtual methods, or any expression that would observe `this` indirectly.

The base-call-before-field-initializers ordering matches primary-constructor inheritance ([§22.10](#sec-methods-and-constructors-primary-constructors)) and C#, Java, and C++, and it keeps exception safety simple: when a derived field initializer throws, the base subobject is fully constructed and can be cleanly disposed by the runtime ([§22.9](#sec-owned-fields-and-exception-safety)).

<a id="sec-owned-fields-and-exception-safety"></a>
### 22.9 Owned fields and exception safety

When construction throws, the compiler unwinds the partially-constructed instance in **reverse declaration order** within the derived class (the **owned-field disposals** of [§28.4](#sec-the-destructor)'s generated `Dispose()` — that pass and nothing before it: never the destructor body, the explicit rule below — for primary-constructor capture fields, ordered after declared fields per [§22.10](#sec-capture-rule-and-layout-stability), this disposes captures first), then the base subobject's `Dispose()` ([§22.8](#sec-field-initializers)). The numbered steps in the cases below are [§22.8](#sec-field-initializers)'s construction sequence — step 0 capture, step 1 the base or chained call, step 2 field initializers, step 3 the body — not the generated `Dispose()`'s own numbering:

- An exception during the **base or chained constructor call** (step 1) leaves no derived state to clean up **beyond step 0's owned primary-constructor capture fields ([§22.8](#sec-field-initializers), [§22.10](#sec-capture-rule-and-layout-stability)), which are already populated and are disposed in reverse declaration order before the exception propagates** — the base ctor's own exception-safety logic disposes whatever it had constructed of the base subobject. The exception propagates to the derived ctor's caller; the derived instance is never observable.
- An exception during a **field initializer** (step 2) triggers disposal of any earlier derived owned fields whose initializers completed, in reverse declaration order, followed by the base subobject's `Dispose()` (which the runtime invokes because the base ctor completed successfully). The exception then propagates.
- An exception in the **constructor body** (step 3) triggers disposal of every owned field assigned during initialization (step 2) and the base subobject. Owned fields assigned imperatively in the body are also disposed if assigned successfully before the throwing statement.
- An exception in a **`this(...)`-chaining constructor** follows the same shape one level up (completing the [§22.8](#sec-field-initializers) once-only rule). A throw during the chained call itself is the first case above, with one precision for the `this(...)` reading: the chained-to constructor's unwinding has by then disposed everything its steps initialized — *including derived fields*, since field initializers ran as its step 2 — so there is nothing further to dispose. If the chaining constructor's **body** throws, the chained-to construction completed and the instance is at that point fully initialized: the runtime disposes it through the normal generated-`Dispose()` path ([§28.4](#sec-the-destructor)) before the exception propagates.

**The throwing class's destructor body does not run on construction unwind ([#3245](https://github.com/s8lap/bezel-lang/issues/3245)).** In every case above except the last's fully-initialized `this(...)`-chaining-body throw — where the instance is complete and is disposed through the normal generated-`Dispose()` path, destructor body included — the unwinding runs **only** the owned-field disposals (already-completed owned fields, captures included, in reverse declaration order) and — where the base construction completed — the base subobject's `Dispose()`; that base-chain `Dispose()` is the full [§28.4](#sec-the-destructor) sequence *for the base* — the base subobject completed construction, so its own destructor body legitimately runs — but the throwing class's `destructor` body is **never** executed on these edges. The ground is [§7.9](#sec-definite-assignment-for-non-nullable-fields): the never-observed-unset guarantee for non-nullable fields is issued only at constructor completion, and a destructor body running mid-unwind would be exactly the forbidden observer — it could read fields the failed construction never assigned. (This matches C++, where a throwing constructor's own destructor likewise does not run.) The consequence for raw resources — a native handle acquired in a constructor body and held in no owned field is *not* covered by this unwinding — is stated with the discipline that answers it where destructors are taught: [§28.4](#sec-the-destructor)'s one-resource-per-owning-wrapper rule.

Owned primary-constructor **capture fields**, populated at step 0, participate in every case above as owned fields whose initialization completed first: they are disposed in the same reverse-declaration-order pass (captures before declared fields, [§22.10](#sec-capture-rule-and-layout-stability)), and the capture **moves** the parameter, so no [§28.3](#sec-local-variables-ownership-and-borrows) parameter-level discharge ever also claims the value. An `owned` primary parameter that was *not* captured (referenced only in initializer positions) still holds its value on any construction throw before its consuming initializer ran — a step-1 throw, or a step-2 throw from an earlier initializer — and is discharged as an ordinary `owned` parameter by the exception-path discharge; once its consuming initializer has run, the owning field's disposal covers it. One owner at every instant, on every edge (Appendix [C.3](#sec-appendix-c)).

The unwinding's owned-field disposals are a [§28.4](#sec-the-destructor) multi-value cleanup pass run with the construction exception in flight: a disposer that throws during it **supersedes** that exception under [§28.4](#sec-the-destructor)'s rule, and the superseded exception is recorded into the superseding one's `SupersededChain` before the drop ([§31.2](#sec-try-catch-finally)'s record-before-drop rule).

The compiler generates the necessary `try`/`finally` around each phase. The base-first construction order ([§22.8](#sec-field-initializers)) is what makes this story clean: by the time any derived state exists, the base subobject is fully constructed and its destructor can run cleanly during unwinding.

<a id="sec-methods-and-constructors-primary-constructors"></a>
### 22.10 Primary constructors

A class may declare its primary constructor's parameters in the class header. A primary-constructor parameter list admits **plain, `owned`, and class- or interface-typed `scoped` parameters**; `ref` and `out` are rejected semantically (the grammar admits them through the shared Param production, the same over-admit-and-reject-semantically pattern Appendix A.4 uses elsewhere): a constructor's parameters initialize object state, and a by-reference alias or a caller-out slot has no meaning in that role. A **function-typed** `scoped` primary-constructor parameter is likewise rejected semantically (the capture rule below).

```bezel
public class BankAccount(name: string, initialBalance: decimal)
  private _name: string := name;
  private _balance: decimal := initialBalance;

  public method Deposit(amount: decimal)
    _balance := _balance + amount;
  end Deposit;
end BankAccount;
```

The parameters are in scope:

- Inside field initializers.
- Inside the inheritance clause's base call (see below).
- Inside the body of any method, property, constructor, or destructor of the class. The compiler captures them as private fields automatically.

They are **not** in scope in a convenience constructor's **chaining position** ([§12.8](#sec-constructor-chaining)): the arguments of a `this(...)` call run before the chained-to primary's capture step ([§22.8](#sec-field-initializers) step 0), so reading a primary-constructor parameter there is a compile error — as is reading any field or auto-property of the not-yet-constructed `this` from that position, for the same reason: a `this(...)`/`base(...)` argument runs before any field of the declaring type is assigned ([§22.7](#sec-observing-this-during-construction)). The only reads a chaining argument may make are of the constructor's own parameters, constants, and statics.

**A member parameter of the same name.** A member's parameter may be spelled like a primary-constructor parameter, as [§11.1](#sec-class-declaration)'s convenience constructor `constructor(name: string)` is: a member's parameter list is not among the positions above. The primary-constructor parameter is then not in scope anywhere in that member, whether in a chaining position, a contract clause or the body; where the parameter is a setter's `value`, the same holds throughout that setter. The name there is the member's parameter, and a reference to it does not capture the primary-constructor parameter. The capture field is not a member: `this.name` is member access ([§2.7](#sec-name-resolution-order)) and reaches a declared member only, never a primary-constructor parameter or its capture. Inside such a member the captured value therefore has no spelling. A member that needs both declares the field of remedy 1 below (`private _name: string := name;`) and reads it, or, outside a setter, renames its parameter. A member's parameter is the one binding that may take the name: a local, loop variable, arm binding, binding-atom clause or lambda parameter may not where the primary-constructor parameter is in scope ([§21.1](#sec-variable-declarations) *Local names*).

<a id="sec-capture-rule-and-layout-stability"></a>
#### Capture rule and layout stability

A primary-constructor parameter is captured as a compiler-generated private field **if and only if** it is referenced in a body position — inside the body of any method, property accessor, constructor, or destructor. Parameters used only in field initializers or in the inheritance clause's base call are *not* captured: their values flow directly into the field they initialize or the base argument they supply, and no separate parameter-named field exists.

```bezel
public class Greeter(name: string, prefix: string)
  // `prefix` flows into _label's initializer and is never used elsewhere — not captured.
  private _label: string := prefix + ": ";
  
  // `name` is referenced in Greet's body — captured as a private field.
  public method Greet(): string => _label + name;
end Greeter;
```

Here `Greeter` has two private fields after compilation: the explicit `_label`, and a compiler-generated capture field for `name`. There is no field for `prefix`.

**`owned` parameters and capture.** An `owned` primary-constructor parameter follows the same capture rule, with the ownership carried into the capture:

- Referenced **only in field initializers** (or the base call): not captured — the initializer consumes it (the [§11.1](#sec-class-declaration) `ResourceHolder` example; the explicit `owned` field takes the obligation).
- Referenced in a **body position**: captured as a compiler-generated **`owned` private field**, disposed by the generated `Dispose()` exactly like a declared owned field ([§28.4](#sec-the-destructor)). Capture fields are ordered **after** the class's declared fields, in parameter order; the reverse-declaration-order disposal pass therefore disposes captures *before* declared fields. A class that captures an `owned` parameter of non-trivial-dispose type is consequently **not trivial-dispose** ([§28.9](#sec-runtime-managed-types)) — the capture participates in the derived-property computation ([§3.6](#sec-derived-type-properties)) exactly like a declared owned field, including [§28.9](#sec-runtime-managed-types)'s disregard of `owned` fields whose type is itself trivial-dispose. Silently dropping the parameter would be a leak under [§11.1](#sec-class-declaration)'s ownership-transfer clause and Appendix C.3's disposed-exactly-once invariant.
- Referenced **both** in an owned-consuming initializer *and* in a body position: **compile error** — the body reference is a read of a moved-from value. Remedies: declare the field explicitly and reference the field in bodies, or drop the initializer consumption.
- A **class- or interface-typed `scoped`** primary-constructor parameter ([§28.14](#sec-scoped-callback-parameters)'s scoped construction) follows the same capture rule: referenced in a body position, it is captured as a compiler-generated **non-owned** private field — exactly the direct non-owned field of the bounding object that §28.14's callee side admits, the constructed object being the bounding object — and a reference in a field initializer or in the base call is the ordinary callee-side use of the parameter: a store into a non-owned field of the object being constructed, or an argument to the base constructor, admitted against a `scoped` base parameter (a forward whose bounding object is the same constructed object) and as an ordinary borrow argument against a plain one ([§28.14](#sec-scoped-callback-parameters)'s callee side). The capture field is not disposed and does not enter the trivial-dispose computation ([§28.9](#sec-runtime-managed-types)); a body reference to the parameter is a read of that field — a borrow sourced at `this` ([§28.3](#sec-producers)'s producers table), returned or passed on exactly as any back-reference field's read is. At the call site the argument carries the marker — `new Box(scoped src)` ([§22.3](#sec-parameter-modifiers)) — and is admitted under §28.14's bounding-object forms exactly as at a declared constructor: the holder is a `using var` local or `this`, the source is declared before the holder, a fresh producer is rejected, and the source is frozen until the holder's scope exits. The freeze is keyed on the signature, not on the capture: a `scoped` parameter referenced in no body and no initializer captures no field, and the call site freezes its source all the same, harmlessly. A **function-typed** `scoped` primary-constructor parameter is rejected: its capture field would be a `scoped` field, whose storage, never-read-out, and quiescence obligations §28.14 states over a declared field — use a regular constructor and a declared `scoped` field. (Recorded v1 bound; liftable.)
- A **plain function-typed** primary-constructor parameter (its declared type, nullability stripped, a function type) is call-bounded ([§28.14](#sec-scoped-callback-parameters)), and the call that bounds it is the construction. Field initializers and the base call run inside that call ([§22.8](#sec-field-initializers)), so there the parameter may be invoked or passed to a call-bounded parameter: `class Gauge(read: () -> int)` with `private _initial: int := read();` is admitted. A reference in a body position captures it into a compiler-generated field, which is a store of a call-bounded parameter in a field, so that reference is a compile error whatever the caller passes; a field initializer storing it in a declared field is the same rejection. The rule is the capture rule's: a reference in a method body is a capture even where that method runs only during construction, so a helper that an initializer calls takes the callback as an argument instead (`private _initial: int := Compute(read);`). The remedy for a callback the object keeps is a regular constructor with a `scoped` parameter and a declared `scoped` field.

This capture-iff-used rule keeps the generated field set small, but it has a **layout-stability consequence**: adding or removing a body-position reference to a primary-constructor parameter changes whether that parameter is captured as a field. Removing `Greet` from the example above removes the capture of `name`; adding a new method that references `prefix` adds a capture of `prefix`. The change is observable through any binary-metadata format keyed on the field set (binary serialization, native ABI). It is *not* observable through member-access reflection: Bezel has no field-enumeration or by-name member-access reflection, and that capability is declined rather than deferred (rationale [§18](Bezel_Design_Rationale.md#sec-things-deferred), [§5.18](Bezel_Design_Rationale.md#sec-type-identity-not-reflection)) — so the only programs that can observe a capture-set change are those reaching the field set through a binary format, not through runtime reflection.

Programs that need stable field layout across revisions — for binary serialization, framework-keyed reflection, or ABI guarantees with native code — should not rely on primary-constructor capture. The remedies, in order of preference:

1. Declare the field explicitly with an initializer that references the parameter (`private _name: string := name;`). The field's name is then under the programmer's control, and adding or removing body references doesn't change its existence.
2. Declare the parameter-derived value as a public property (`public readonly property Name: string := name;`). Public properties are part of the type's public surface and are therefore already stable.
3. Use a non-primary constructor with explicit field assignments. This is the most ceremony but the most stable.

Rationale [§9.16](Bezel_Design_Rationale.md#sec-member-comparisons-with-csharp) records why capture is keyed on use.

Primary-constructor parameters are **not** automatically promoted to public properties. To expose one, declare a property explicitly:

```bezel
public class BankAccount(name: string, initialBalance: decimal)
  public readonly property Name: string := name;
  private _balance: decimal := initialBalance;
end BankAccount;
```

When a class with a primary constructor has a base class, the base call appears in the inheritance clause:

```bezel
public class SavingsAccount(name: string, initialBalance: decimal, rate: decimal)
    : BankAccount(name, initialBalance)
  private _rate: decimal := rate;
end SavingsAccount;
```

This replaces an explicit `base(...)` call.

A class with a primary constructor may declare additional convenience constructors. Each must chain to another constructor via `this(...)`; only the primary may chain to `base(...)`. This is a **class** rule; a record's body constructor is not bound by it ([§9.3](#sec-combined-form)). The single-base-call rule keeps the base initialization logic and any captured-parameter side effects in one place: every instance of the class passes through the primary, regardless of which convenience entry point was used. Convenience constructors that need a different base call must be expressed as a different design — typically a derived class with its own primary, or a static factory method that constructs and post-configures.

<a id="sec-object-initializer-blocks"></a>
### 22.11 Object initializer blocks (retired)

Retired. The object-initializer block (`new T(args) with(...)` on a **class** type) does not exist: a `with` expression requires a record-typed source, and a class-typed source is a compile error ([§9.5](#sec-non-destructive-update-with)). In its place, use named/optional constructor arguments ([§22.5](#sec-optional-parameters-and-named-arguments)) — which run the constructor and respect its invariants — or bind the instance to a local and assign its members as ordinary statements, whose exception-path disposal is [§28.3](#sec-local-variables-ownership-and-borrows)'s general discharge of an owned local (no construct-specific rule remains). Record `with` on a freshly-constructed record (`new Point(1, 2) with(Y := 9)`) is unaffected ([§9.5](#sec-non-destructive-update-with)). The section number is retained so §22.12+ citations stay stable; the prior definition and the decision record are in the [changelog](Bezel_Changelog.md).

<a id="sec-static-members"></a>
### 22.12 Static members

**Statics and domains.** Static state is **process-global** — one instance across all domains — which makes unrestricted static mutability a side door through [§30.14](#sec-sendable-types)'s no-shared-mutable-state discipline. The rules:

1. **Lazy static initialization is runtime-synchronized**: a type's static initializer runs exactly once process-wide; a domain touching a type mid-initialization by another domain blocks until initialization completes (or observes the failed state, [§22.7](#sec-constructors)). Exit disposal order ([§22.13](#sec-static-initialization-order)) is therefore well-defined: the runtime records the single global initialization order.
2. **The verdict tables.** A static field or auto-property's admissibility is a function of its **mutability** — *mutable* (non-`readonly`, non-`const`), `static readonly` (the `owned` form included), or `const` — and of the **kind of its declared type**, with the type's statics-and-sharing facts (stdlib [§1](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-statics-and-sharing-facts)) consulted where a cell says so; the two tables below state rules 2–4. Columns: **mutable** is this rule — its admitted forms are the notes (i)–(iv) after the tables, then the store semantics that apply to every admitted mutable static; **`static readonly`** is rule 4, whose **ok** cells are rule 3's immutable content and rule 4's warning-suppression set; **`const`** is rule 3 within the `const` type requirement after rule 5 (a primitive value type or `string`), which every `—` there names. Verdicts: **ok** — admitted warning-free; **warn** — admitted with a **declaration-site warning** naming an obligation: confine every use of the storage to one domain, or take the synchronized spelling the cited note names — confinement discharges the obligation but is not compiler-observable and does not silence the warning; **error** — a compile error at the declaration site naming this rule. A declared type takes the first row that **names** it, and otherwise the first row that describes it (`string`, a reference type, [§3.1](#sec-type-kinds), has its own row in the first table, above the class-type row); the second table's last row is the residual. **†** is this rule's closing sentence: a mutable static admitted by none of (i)–(iv) is a compile error naming this rule — unsynchronized cross-domain mutation is exactly the race [§30.14](#sec-sendable-types) exists to exclude. **‡** is rule 3 where the type is a value type of sendable-value category, and otherwise rule 4's residual default (**warn**). The grounds behind these verdicts are recorded in rationale [§12.15](Bezel_Design_Rationale.md#sec-statics-verdict-grounds), keyed by the labels used here.

   *Reference-kinded declared types*

   | Declared type | mutable | `static readonly` | `const` |
   |---|---|---|---|
   | declares **synchronized**, not **displacement-unbounded** — the form-(i) set, (i) | ok (i) | ok — in the set | — |
   | `SharedEventSource<T>` — a form-(i) type; rule 5 | ok (i) | ok — rule 5's shape | — |
   | `Task?` / `Task<T>?` | ok (ii) | as a class type, below | — |
   | `OwningTask<T>?` | error — not (ii), † | as a class type, below | — |
   | `Channel<T>` — declares no facts | error — excluded from (i), † | warn — deliberately, 4(b) | — |
   | the four **displacement-unbounded** members of the warning-suppression set, 4(a) | error 4(a) | ok — in the set | — |
   | `string` / `string?` — a reference type ([§3.1](#sec-type-kinds)); rule 3 | error (iii)-closed | ok — rule 3 | `string`: ok; `string?`: — |
   | any other **class type** — `owned` or not; instance event sources included, rule 5 | error † | warn — rule 4 | — |
   | **interface type** | error † | warn — rule 4, 4(d) | — |
   | **function type** | error † | warn — 4(e) | — |

   *Value-kinded declared types, bare parameters, and the residual*

   | Declared type | mutable | `static readonly` | `const` |
   |---|---|---|---|
   | **primitive value type** ([§3.1](#sec-type-kinds)) or **enum type**, or nullable of either — (iii) | warn (iii) | ok — rule 3 | non-nullable primitive: ok; enum and both nullable forms: — |
   | **plain inline array** `[N]T` **field** with heap-free elements — (iii) | warn (iii) | ‡ | — |
   | **holds borrows** — a borrow-bearing record, a non-owning choice, a plain inline array | error (iii)-closed | [§9.7](#sec-records-and-disposal)'s static-field bullet, 4(f) | — |
   | **owning-classified choice** | error (iii)-closed | error — 4(g) | — |
   | **record** or compiler-known value builtin (`DateTime`, `Guid`, …), carrying no borrows | error (iii)-closed | ‡ | — |
   | **plain choice** carrying no borrows; **plain inline array** of any other element type | error (iii)-closed | ‡ | — |
   | any inline-array-typed **auto-property** | error (iii)-closed | ‡ | — |
   | **owning inline array** `[N owned]T?` / `[N owned]T` **field** | warn (iv) | warn — 4(h); disposed at exit | — |
   | **bare generic parameter** `T` / `T?` | error at the declaration, (v) | per instantiation, after substitution — 4(i) | — (under no substitution, 4(i)) |
   | any other declared type | error † | warn — rule 4's residual default | — |

   **(i) Internally-synchronized handle:** the field's type declares the **synchronized** fact and not the **displacement-unbounded** fact (stdlib [§1](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-statics-and-sharing-facts)'s statics-and-sharing facts — the formula is normative, and each grant's grounds live on the type's own fact line; derived membership (form-(i)), informative — currently `Mutex`, `Semaphore`, `Atomic<T>`, `AtomicInteger<T>`, `ChannelSender<T>`, and `SharedEventSource<T>` — stdlib §6.2–§6.5, §6.9; machine-checked, `scripts/check_docs.sh` 3b). `SharedEventSource<T>` is the set's one non-sendable member, safe to reach from every domain by static reachability rather than [§30.14](#sec-sendable-types) transfer (rule 5). `Channel<T>` declares no facts and is **excluded** (rationale §12.15): keep the `Channel<T>` domain-confined and publish a `ChannelSender<T>` static instead.

   **(ii) Lazy task cache:** a static whose declared type is `Task?` or `Task<T>?` — the admission is keyed to the declared type alone, so the check stays decidable at the declaration; the intended shape is [§22.13](#sec-static-initialization-order) pattern (b)'s once-set cache (Pattern A multi-await, [§30.5](#sec-result-lifetime-and-task-disposal)). `OwningTask<T>?` is *not* admitted here (rationale §12.15).

   **(iii) Warned value static:** a mutable static whose declared type is a **primitive value type** ([§3.1](#sec-type-kinds)) or an **enum type**, the nullable form of either, or — fields only — a **plain inline array** (`[N]T` without the `owned` slot marker, [§15.1](#sec-inline-arrays)) whose element type is itself, recursively, one of these. The warning is rule 4's posture applied to value statics: the storage is process-global and reachable from every domain, and the obligation it names is to confine every read and write of the field to one domain, or to move to a synchronized spelling — `AtomicInteger<T>`/`Atomic<T>` for the cell-sized primitives, `Atomic<int>` with a bit-cast for the floating-point types (stdlib §6.4's own note), a `Mutex` or `Locked<T>` cell for `decimal`, enums, and inline arrays, which no atomic admits. `static readonly`/`const` (rule 3) is the warning-free spelling where the value never changes after initialization. Form (iii) carries **none** of the store-semantics triple below: **post-initialization** stores are ordinary unsynchronized value stores with no atomicity, publication, or happens-before promise (the initializing store remains ordered by rule 1's initialization-completion edge; the [§30.13](#sec-runtime-model) admitted-static publication edge stays scoped to form (ii) and does not extend to form (iii)). Violating the obligation risks wrong or torn values, never memory unsafety (form (iii)'s violation class; rationale §12.15). No ownership interaction arises (nothing to discharge or dispose). The category set — primitives, enums, and plain heap-free inline arrays — **grows only by recorded ruling**; the tables' **error (iii)-closed** cells are compile errors under this rule's closing sentence, declined, not deferred (rationale §12.15).

   **(iv) Owning-inline-array static field:** a mutable static **field** of owning-inline-array type (`[N owned]T?` or `[N owned]T`, [§15.1.1](#sec-owning-inline-arrays)) is admitted — the admission [§22.13](#sec-static-initialization-order)'s *Disposal of static `owned` fields* and [§11.7](#sec-static-classes) name — with rule 4's **declaration-site warning**: the array's owned instances are reachable from every domain and its slots are mutable, so the obligation it names is to confine every slot read, slot write, `move arr[j]`, and whole-field reassignment to one domain, or to restructure behind a `Locked<T>` registry ([§30.12](#sec-data-owning-locks)). Obligation violation here is undefined behavior (a slot mutation racing another domain's slot read can dangle a borrow) — rule 4's violation class, not form (iii)'s. Of the store-semantics triple below, only **Atomicity** does not apply (a whole-array store is N pointer words, not one): slot stores, `move arr[j]`, and per-slot restoration follow [§15.1.1](#sec-owning-inline-arrays) unchanged. The **Ownership** and **Overwrite** bullets govern this form as they govern every admitted mutable static: whole-field reassignment is a **plain store that never auto-disposes displaced slots** ([§22.13](#sec-static-initialization-order)'s static-overwrite posture and ownership-discharge exemption — statics never take [§28.7](#sec-reassigning-owned-fields)'s drop-on-overwrite, which covers owning-inline-array locals and instance fields per slot, [§15.3](#sec-move-only-value-types)), and the compiler retains a reassignment warning at exactly this form: a whole-field reassignment reachable with provably non-moved-from slots warns, naming the slots at risk and the per-slot discharge mechanisms — the displaced slots persist undisposed until process exit (rationale §12.15). Disposal is [§22.13](#sec-static-initialization-order)'s program-exit pass — the type-level `owned` slot marker conveys the obligation, and no field-level `owned` modifier is written. `readonly` is not this form's alternative spelling (rationale §12.15).

   **(v) Bare generic parameter:** a mutable static field or auto-property whose declared type is a **bare generic parameter**, or its nullable form (`T`, `T?`), is admitted by no form above and is a **compile error at the declaration site**, whatever the parameter's constraints or eventual substitutions — and this holds wherever the declaration can appear: a generic class's statics, the statics of a type nested in a generic type, and a generic method's statics alike.

   **Store semantics.** Three apply to every admitted mutable static — all three to forms (i) and (ii), **Ownership** and **Overwrite** to form (iv), none to form (iii):

   - **Atomicity:** stores are single pointer-word writes the runtime performs atomically (no torn reference is ever observed), but a check-then-store sequence is **not** atomic across domains: racing first uses of a task cache may each start the work and store, last store winning — every stored task remains independently awaitable, so the race duplicates work without unsoundness; when exactly-once matters, use eager startup assignment ([§22.13](#sec-static-initialization-order) pattern (a)) or a `Mutex`.
   - **Ownership:** assigning a fresh owned value into an admitted mutable static discharges the producer — [§22.13](#sec-static-initialization-order)'s ownership-discharge exemption for non-`owned` statics extends to these fields; the referent becomes process-lived. An assignment through a settable static property of such a type discharges the producer in the same way, whatever the property's accessor form ([§28.3](#sec-borrow-lifetime-rules)'s *property stores of a borrow-carrying value*).
   - **Overwrite:** overwriting an admitted mutable static never disposes the displaced referent — deliberately *not* [§28.7](#sec-reassigning-owned-fields)'s drop-on-overwrite; the displaced referent remains alive until process exit (rationale §12.15).

3. `static readonly` of **immutable content** — value types of sendable-value category, `string`, enums — and `const` (a primitive value type or `string`, the requirement stated after rule 5) are unrestricted (shared-immutable).
4. A `static readonly` (including `owned`) field or auto-property of **class type** is admitted with a **declaration-site warning** unless the class is in this rule's **warning-suppression set**: the referenced instance is reachable from every domain, and confining its use to one domain — or ensuring its own internal synchronization — is the programmer's obligation (the checked-disposal backstop of [§28.2](#sec-the-idisposable-contract) applies; this is the singleton-with-resources pattern the warning text names). The **warning-suppression set** is derived, not curated: every type declaring the **synchronized** or the **immutable** fact (stdlib [§1](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-statics-and-sharing-facts)'s statics-and-sharing facts, each grant's grounds on the type's own fact line; derived membership (warning-suppression), informative — currently `Mutex`, `Semaphore`, `Atomic<T>`, `AtomicInteger<T>`, `ChannelSender<T>`, `SharedEventSource<T>`, `Locked<T>`, `RwLocked<T>`, `FrozenArray<T>`, and `CancellationTokenSource` — stdlib §4.19, and stdlib §6.1–§6.5, §6.9, §6.11; machine-checked, `scripts/check_docs.sh` 3b).

   **(a)** The four members outside rule 2's form (i) — the data-owning locks `Locked<T>`/`RwLocked<T>` ([§30.12](#sec-data-owning-locks); `static owned readonly` being the canonical process-global registry idiom), `FrozenArray<T>` (stdlib [§4.19](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-frozen-array)), and `CancellationTokenSource` (stdlib [§6.1](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-cancellationtoken-and-cancellationtokensource), the process-global shutdown source) — are outside it by their **displacement-unbounded** fact (rationale §12.15): no mutable statics of them.

   **(b)** A `static readonly Channel<T>` deliberately still warns (`Channel<T>` declares no facts) — the warning is the reminder that the channel is the single-consumer *receiving* end and must stay confined to one consuming domain ([§30.15](#sec-channels)).

   **(c)** This warning is independent of [§22.13](#sec-static-class-typed-fields-without-owned)'s non-trivial-`Dispose`-without-`owned` warning and the two may co-fire on one declaration: adding `owned` clears only the disposal warning — rule 4 applies to `owned` fields too — while this warning is silenced only by the type being in the warning-suppression set; confining the instance to one domain discharges the obligation the warning names. An implementation may present the co-firing pair as one combined diagnostic (Appendix [D](#appendix-d-conformance-levels)'s identity latitude).

   **The residual ([#3273](https://github.com/s8lap/bezel-lang/issues/3273)).** A `static readonly` field or auto-property whose declared type no row above names takes rule 4's declaration-site warning — the second table's last row: the storage is process-global, confining every use to one domain is the programmer's obligation, and the warning-suppression set is consulted against the **declared** type. Three kinds are excepted, (f)–(h); a bare generic parameter is (i)'s per-instantiation case.

   **(d)** **Interface type:** an interface-typed static's runtime referent is a class instance, so rule 4's obligation is unchanged, and no interface is in the warning-suppression set, so such a static always warns — [§22.13](#sec-static-class-typed-fields-without-owned)'s conservative non-trivial-`Dispose`-without-`owned` warning is the independent second diagnostic and the two co-fire, and [§28.5](#sec-owned-fields) admits the `owned` form.

   **(e)** **Function type:** a function-typed static warns (its **captured variables are a heap-allocated mutable cell**, [§27.5](#sec-closures), reachable from every domain through the field); the hazard class is form (iii)'s — wrong or torn values, never memory unsafety — and the warning does not discriminate capture-free function values from capturing ones (rationale §12.15).

   **(f)** A **borrow-bearing record**, a **non-owning choice that holds borrows** ([§35.4](#sec-choice-classification)'s holds-borrows property; an *owning* choice that also holds borrows takes (g)'s rejection, which this note does not displace), or a **plain inline array carrying borrows** ([§15.1.2](#sec-inline-array-members)) is governed by [§9.7](#sec-records-and-disposal)'s static-field bullet and **not** by this rule: admitted in the **null-source** form as that bullet defines it (every reference-typed field or payload, and every reference-typed slot of every inline-array field, `null`, through nested record and choice components — `CancellationToken.None` is the sanctioned shape) and rejected in every other, at that rule, whatever this one would otherwise say. A null-source value references nothing and draws no rule-4 warning.

   **(g)** An **owning-classified choice** ([§35.4](#sec-choice-classification) rule 1) is a **compile error at the declaration site** naming this rule, whether or not it also holds borrows: (f)'s null-source admission does not reach it, and nothing would dispose it — [§22.13](#sec-static-initialization-order)'s program-exit pass does not enrol it, and [§28.5](#sec-owned-fields) admits the `owned` field modifier only on class- and interface-typed fields (rationale §12.15). The spelling for a process-global singleton carrying one is a `static owned readonly` field of a **class** holding the choice ([§15.3](#sec-move-only-value-types)'s field-placement rule), whose destructor disposes it.

   **(h)** An **owning-inline-array-typed** `static readonly` field takes the default warning and *is* disposed at exit: [§22.13](#sec-static-initialization-order)'s owning-inline-array clause is not conditioned on the field's mutability, and form (iv)'s whole-field-reassignment warning cannot arise where the field cannot be reassigned.

   **(i)** A `static readonly` field or auto-property whose declared type is a **bare generic parameter**, or its nullable form (`T`, `T?`), is admitted at the declaration and classified **per instantiation, after substitution**: a substitution within rule 3's immutable content is unrestricted; a class-type substitution takes this rule's warning unless the substituted class is in the warning-suppression set; and any other substitution takes the **residual above**, applied at that instantiation: an interface or function-type substitution takes this rule's warning, the warning-suppression set consulted where applicable; a substitution that is borrow-bearing or holds borrows is [§9.7](#sec-records-and-disposal)'s null-source case, whose own rule already evaluates per instantiation ([§3.6](#sec-derived-type-properties) rule 2); and an owning-choice substitution is rejected on (g)'s disposal-site ground. A nullable substituted form classifies as its underlying type. The diagnostic lands **at the instantiation site** and names the offending type argument ([§3.6](#sec-derived-type-properties) rule 2's diagnostic pattern). A `const` of bare-parameter type is not admissible under any substitution: `const` requires a primitive value type or `string` (below), which no bare parameter ever is.
5. **Shared publication points are typed, not member-kinded** (the `event` member kind is retired, [§24](#sec-events)). A process-global publication point is an ordinary static field of type `SharedEventSource<T>` (stdlib [§6.5](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-events-ievent-eventsource)) — a form-(i) member, admitted warning-free in the recommended shape `private static owned readonly _e: SharedEventSource<T> := new();` with program-exit disposal ([§22.13](#sec-static-initialization-order)) — the tables' `SharedEventSource<T>` row. The guarantees are carried by the type and therefore hold at **every** subscription site, aliases included: the subscriber list is internally synchronized (subscribe, raise, and `Subscription.Dispose` may arrive from any domain), and every call resolving to a subscribe position **declared on** `ISharedEvent<T>`/`SharedEventSource<T>` — whatever the receiver's static spelling, a constrained generic parameter included — admits only **capture-free** handlers: a non-capturing lambda or a static method reference, the same admission as `Domain.Spawn` entries, as a stdlib-stated entry in [§28.14](#sec-scoped-callback-parameters)'s capture-free register; and method-reference formation over a register position is itself rejected ([§28.14](#sec-scoped-callback-parameters)), so no plain function-typed alias of `Subscribe`/`Add` can launder the admission. There is no static type through which a capture-admitting subscription to a shared source can be written (rationale [§13.6](Bezel_Design_Rationale.md#sec-retiring-the-event-member-kind)). No payload-sendability check is imposed: under capture-freedom plus raising-domain execution (stdlib §6.5), each payload is constructed and consumed within one domain. Instance sources (`EventSource<T>`/`AsyncEventSource<T>`) remain unsynchronized and capture-admitting — domain-serial per stdlib §6.5, captures per [§28.14](#sec-scoped-callback-parameters); a `static owned readonly` field of an instance-source type is admissible but draws rule 4's warning like any other unsynchronized class-typed static singleton, and confining it to one domain is the programmer's obligation the warning names.

Static methods, properties, fields, and constructors are declared with `static`. A class-level `const` is implicitly static; writing `static const` is redundant but permitted for clarity — both forms declare the same constant.

`const` declarations (with or without `static`) require a compile-time-constant expression ([§17.14](#sec-constant-expressions) — the referenced definition) and a primitive value type or `string`; local `const` declarations are classified by [§21.1](#sec-variable-declarations)'s split: the same two conditions make a compile-time constant, and any other initializer makes a runtime const. `static readonly` accepts any value but is read at runtime.

A static member of a *generic* class is accessed by supplying the type arguments on the type name in receiver position — `Registry<int>.Register()`, `Cache<string>.Default` — inside the class's own declaration as outside it: there `Registry<T>.Register()` names the current instantiation's member, as the bare `Register()` does ([§14.1](#sec-generic-declarations)). Each distinct instantiation has its own static state ([§22.13](#sec-static-initialization-order)). A static member declared on a base class is a member of every class derived from it ([§2.7](#sec-name-resolution-order)'s enclosing-type rule counts inherited statics; [§12.2](#sec-hiding-is-not-allowed)'s inherited members are visible at the derived declaration site) and may be named through a derived type: where `class D<T>: B<T>` declares no `_c` of its own, `D<string>._c` names the **declaring** type's cell at the substitution the base clause supplies — `B<string>._c` — and the two spellings are one cell. There is one cell per declaring instantiation, whatever type name reaches it. This is one form of the broader "generic arguments in an expression" family the grammar admits ([Appendix A.7](#sec-expressions)): generic type arguments on a name in receiver position (the static-member form here), and explicit method type arguments at a call site, `obj.Method<int>(args)`. Both supply generic arguments where an expression is expected, which raises the classic generics-vs-less-than ambiguity. The resolution is **normative and purely syntactic** (no name-resolution feedback):

> After an identifier in expression position, a `<` opens generic arguments **iff** scanning forward finds a balanced `<…>` group (respecting nesting) whose closing `>` is immediately followed by a token that can continue a primary expression — `.`, `?.`, `(`, or `[`. Otherwise the `<` is the relational operator.

Consequences worth stating: `f(a<b, c>(d))` parses as a generic call `f(a<b, c>(d))` — never as two relational arguments; to express the relational reading, parenthesize (`f((a<b), (c>(d)))`), consistent with the mandatory-parenthesization discipline of [§17.2](#sec-mandatory-parenthesization). The scan is bounded by the enclosing statement and commits no semantic judgment — a name that resolves to a non-generic entity after a syntactically-successful generic reading is an ordinary error at that name. Implementations and tooling may rely on this rule verbatim; it is the same rule stated in the Appendix A.7 `PrimaryAtom` commentary.

<a id="sec-static-initialization-order"></a>
### 22.13 Static initialization order

Within a single type, static fields are initialized in textual declaration order.

Across types, a type's static fields are initialized lazily on first use. Once initialization begins for a type, all of its static fields are initialized before any of its methods can run **on behalf of an outside observer**: the type's own static initialization — its static field initializers and the code they call, which execute while later fields may still be unassigned and are bounded by the forward-reference rule below rather than by this ordering sentence, and its static constructor and the code it calls, which run with every field initializer complete — is ordinary self-execution, not an outside observation. The static constructor, if any, runs after all static field initializers complete.

Forward references between `static readonly` fields of the same type are a compile error. Specifically: if the initializer expression for a `static readonly` field F reads a `static readonly` field G of the same type declared *after* F in the source — **directly, or transitively through the bodies of statically-resolvable calls** (the same call set as the cross-type dependency graph below — static methods and static property getters reached by direct name within the compilation unit, [§2.5](#sec-dependency-resolution); function values, virtual dispatch, and code outside the compilation unit contribute nothing) — the reference is rejected at compile time. Like the cross-type graph, the transitive check is a deliberate approximation, not a completeness guarantee: a same-type forward read routed through a function value, virtual dispatch, or a module boundary compiles, and at runtime observes the field's [§7.9](#sec-default-initialization) default — for a **non-nullable reference** static, the null watermark, which raises `NullReferenceException` at the read in checked disposal mode ([§22.7](#sec-observing-this-during-construction)'s residual bound, applied to static storage) and is undefined behavior to use unchecked. The error message names both fields and points to the textual ordering rule. A `static readonly` auto-property with an initializer ([§23.1](#sec-auto-properties)) stands under this rule exactly as a `static readonly` field, as F and as G alike: its backing storage is assigned in the same static initialization, in the same textual order.

The remedies are to reorder the declarations or, for a genuinely cyclic case, to move the logic into the static constructor, where ordering is explicit (rationale [§9.16](Bezel_Design_Rationale.md#sec-member-comparisons-with-csharp)).

A static constructor body may freely reference any of the type's static fields in any order; the constructor body runs after all field initializers have completed, so no forward-reference question arises there. Code that needs cyclic or order-independent static initialization should use the static constructor.

Forward references between `const` declarations are not subject to this rule: a `const` initializer must be a compile-time-constant expression ([§22.12](#sec-static-members)), so forward references between consts are either resolved at compile time (the textual order does not matter — consts have no temporal initialization) or are themselves a compile error for non-constant operands.

**Cycles across types.** Two rules, one compile-time and one runtime:

1. **Compile-time rejection over a defined approximation.** The compiler builds a static-initialization dependency graph over **distinct** types (edges require T ≠ U — a type's references to its own static members contribute no edges; the within-type ordering rule above governs those): type T depends on type U when T's static field initializers or static constructor body reference a static member of U — directly, or transitively through the bodies of **statically-resolvable calls** (static methods and static property getters reached by direct name within the compilation unit, [§2.5](#sec-dependency-resolution)). Calls through function values, virtual dispatch, and code outside the compilation unit contribute **no** edges. A cycle in this graph is a compile error naming the participating types. The check is a deliberate approximation: it rejects every cycle it can see and is **not a completeness guarantee** — a cycle routed through a function value, virtual dispatch, or a module boundary compiles.

2. **Runtime backstop — re-entrancy raises, never observes.** A touch of a type whose static initialization is **in progress on the same thread**, arriving from **outside that type's own initialization** (the runtime attributes each touch to the innermost static initialization in progress on the thread; a touch of T is *re-entrant* when that innermost initialization belongs to a different type — the T → U → T signature — and is *ordinary execution* when it is T's own, which is what lets a field initializer call the type's own static helpers and the static constructor read its own fields, above) — the signature of a cycle the approximation missed, since a cross-domain touch blocks instead ([§22.12](#sec-static-members) rule 1; the backstop is deliberately same-thread-only — an undetected cycle spanning two concurrently-initializing domains deadlocks in that blocking rather than raising, an accepted bound: no cross-domain waits-for detection is promised) — raises a runtime-synthesized `TypeInitializationException` whose message names the re-entrant type and whose `InnerException` is `null` (there is no original exception; [§31.4](#sec-standard-exception-types)). Partially-initialized statics are **never observable through a re-entrant touch**: silently proceeding on defaults would, for a non-nullable reference static, violate [§7.9](#sec-definite-assignment-for-non-nullable-fields)'s guarantee that no non-nullable field is ever observed unset. (A type's *own* initialization code observing its own later statics is governed by the forward-reference rule and its recorded residual above, not by this backstop.) The synthesized exception then escapes the in-progress initializer it interrupted, and the ordinary [§22.7](#sec-constructors) failed-state machinery takes over — with one adjustment stated there: an escaping exception that is itself a `TypeInitializationException` is cached directly, not wrapped again.

Enum constants are compile-time values and may be referenced freely from static initializers without triggering initialization.

`await` may not appear in static field initializers or static constructor bodies. Static initialization runs synchronously during type loading; suspending would leave the type in a partially-initialized state observable by other code. **Asynchronous values do not belong in static initializers** (a synchronous `task.Wait()` wrapper deadlocks when first-use occurs inside a domain continuation, which lazy initialization cannot rule out). Two sanctioned patterns:

**(a) Eager startup assignment of the task cache** — in an `async Main` (all four async forms are admitted, [§33.2](#sec-accepted-signatures)), assign the `Task<T>?` cache **before any spawn or other first use**; the check-then-store race of rule 2(ii) then never arises and the work runs exactly once. Every consumer awaits the cache, exactly as in pattern (b):

```bezel
public static class AppConfig                    // LoadConfigAsync(): Task<Config>
  private static _cfg: Task<Config>? := null;    // §22.12 rule 2(ii) task cache

  public static method Preload()                 // call from Main before any spawn
    _cfg := LoadConfigAsync();                   // plain sync assignment of the task
  end Preload;

  public static async method GetConfig(): Task<Config>   // pattern (b)'s accessor
    if _cfg = null then _cfg := LoadConfigAsync(); end;
    return await _cfg!;
  end GetConfig;
end AppConfig;

class Program
  public static async method Main(): Task<int>
    AppConfig.Preload();                         // eager: assigned before any spawn
    return Run(await AppConfig.GetConfig());     // Run(cfg: Config): int — first use; fail-fast at startup
  end Main;
end Program;
```

There is deliberately **no** synchronous-access, async-initialized, plain class-typed static: rule 2 admits no such form, and a write-once-before-first-use form would not be checkable at the declaration (rule 2's admission is keyed to the declared type so it stays decidable). Consumers pay one `await` against the cache and then hold borrows of the process-lived result.

**(b) Lazy async accessor** — for on-demand initialization, cache the *task*, not the value, and `await` it at every use site (Pattern A multi-await is exactly this fan-out shape, [§30.5](#sec-result-lifetime-and-task-disposal)):

```bezel
private static _cfg: Task<Config>? := null;
public static async method GetConfig(): Task<Config>
  if _cfg = null then _cfg := LoadConfigAsync(); end;
  return await _cfg!;
end GetConfig;
```

A non-`async` synchronous wrapper that blocks on the task is admitted **only** in code running outside any domain ([§30.3](#sec-the-task-and-taskt-types)) — startup code on the main thread — and never from a lazily-triggered initializer. *(The static cache in (b) is admitted by [§22.12](#sec-static-members) rule 2(ii), which also states the cross-domain first-use race and the exactly-once caveat; runtime enforcement of the statics-and-domains rules is implemented for lazy initialization — atomically guarded with cross-domain blocking (#1391), including the cross-artifact per-instantiation guard for imported generics (#1513); rule 5's shared-source subscriber-list synchronization is not yet implemented (the open half of #1728; the type itself is registered, type-checked, and allocated at HEAD). The `return await _cfg!;` line is [§30.5](#sec-result-lifetime-and-task-disposal)'s borrowed-source chain: each caller's task borrows through the process-lived cache, and no caller's teardown disposes it.)*

<a id="sec-disposal-of-static-owned-fields"></a>
#### Disposal of static `owned` fields

A static field may be marked `owned`. Static `owned` fields are disposed at program exit, after `Main` completes (normally, or by an uncaught exception — [§33.3](#sec-exit-code) defines the exit code for each), in **reverse order of static initialization** across all types — the type whose static initializer ran last is the first to have its static `owned` fields disposed. Within a single type, multiple static `owned` fields are disposed in reverse declaration order, mirroring the instance-field disposal rule ([§28.4](#sec-the-destructor)).

A static field of owning-inline-array type (`[N owned]T?` or `[N owned]T`, [§15.1.1](#sec-owning-inline-arrays)) participates in the same program-exit disposal pass even though it does not carry the `owned` field modifier — the type-level `owned` slot marker conveys the obligation. At program exit, each non-null slot's `Dispose()` is called in the same reverse-of-initialization order as for `static owned` fields, and the slots within each array are disposed in reverse slot order ([§15.1.1](#sec-owning-inline-arrays)). A static field of owning-inline-array type whose initializer threw is not disposed (the array's slots were never observable); a static field whose initializer completed successfully before a later failing initializer is disposed normally.

A static `owned` field whose initializer threw is not disposed (its value was never produced). A static `owned` field on a type left in a failed state ([§22.7](#sec-constructors)) whose initializer *did* complete successfully before the failing initializer is disposed normally.

The runtime guarantees disposal occurs on a single, dedicated **shutdown thread**, which — like the startup thread — runs **outside any domain** ([§30.13](#sec-runtime-model)): the blocking forms legal at startup ([§30.3](#sec-the-task-taskt-and-ownedtaskt-types), [§30.12](#sec-thread-synchronization)) are equally legal in exit-time destructors (the [§32.8](#sec-callbacks) registry teardown's blocking barrier depends on this). No other Bezel code runs concurrently during the shutdown sequence: continuations are not resumed and no new work is scheduled; the destructors the pass invokes — and any **lazy static initialization** their first touches trigger, which remains permitted under [§22.12](#sec-static-members) rule 1 unchanged — are the only Bezel code executing. Static `owned` fields initialized during the pass join it: the initialization appends to the recorded order, and the pass drains until no initialized-but-undisposed static `owned` field remains, taking late-initialized entries in reverse order of their own initialization; strict reverse-initialization order is guaranteed only among initializations completed before shutdown began (a mid-pass initialization cannot precede disposals already performed). Native libraries holding callbacks into Bezel code should withdraw or release them before disposal begins.

**A destructor that throws during this pass ([#3258](https://github.com/s8lap/bezel-lang/issues/3258)).** This exit pass **is** a [§28.4](#sec-the-destructor) multi-value cleanup pass — that section's list is illustrative, not exhaustive, as [§28.11](#sec-collection-element-ownership) already shows by running an owning collection's element cascade here and [§22.9](#sec-owned-fields-and-exception-safety)'s construction unwind shows by taking the discipline while absent from the list — so [§28.4](#sec-the-destructor)'s whole within-pass rule governs it unchanged: a throwing disposer does not skip the remaining values, every remaining static `owned` field and every remaining owning-inline-array slot is still disposed in the order above, the remaining steps of each generated `Dispose()` still run and physical reclamation still occurs, a later throw in the pass **supersedes** an earlier one, and [§31.2](#sec-try-catch-finally)'s record-before-drop rule appends the superseded exception's snapshot to the superseding one's `SupersededChain` before disposing it (the two owner-owned exemptions unchanged). The pass is entered with **no exception in flight** on both exit paths — a normal return has none, and an uncaught exception's handling is complete once [§33.3](#sec-exit-code) has emitted its report — so the pass supersedes nothing it did not itself raise, and [§28.4](#sec-the-destructor)'s no-exception-in-flight accounting is the one that applies: N throwing disposers leave the escaping exception carrying N−1 chronological entries. **What escapes the pass is reported, not propagated.** No Bezel code runs above the pass (the shutdown-sequence rule above) and `Main` has ended ([§33.3](#sec-exit-code)), so there is no handler and no propagation target: when the drain completes with an exception the pass raised and did not supersede, the runtime prints that exception's type, message, stack trace, `CauseChain`, and `SupersededChain` ([§31.4](#sec-standard-exception-types)) to standard error — the same content [§33.3](#sec-exit-code) prints for an uncaught exception, and identified as an exit-time disposal fault so the two reports are distinguishable — and then disposes it under [§31.1](#sec-exception-ownership)'s ordinary rule. A fault raised by that terminal disposal is not itself reported and does not recurse; the process exits. **The process exit code is not changed by this pass**: it is already determined on every one of [§33.3](#sec-exit-code)'s four determinations before the pass begins, and an exit-time disposal fault leaves it alone — the report is the signal, and a program whose success depends on a disposal-time effect needs the external mechanism the abnormal-termination text below already requires of it. A destructor's first touch of an as-yet-uninitialized type during the pass remains permitted ([§22.12](#sec-static-members) rule 1) and a failing initialization there behaves exactly as anywhere else ([§22.7](#sec-constructors)): the type enters its permanently failed state and the cached `TypeInitializationException` escapes into the pass, where it takes this paragraph's discipline like any other disposer throw — [§31.2](#sec-try-catch-finally)'s exemption intact, so being superseded drops it from the in-flight slot undisposed.

Disposal at program exit is largely cosmetic from the operating system's perspective — process termination reclaims process-private resources regardless. The motivation for the rule is consistency: the same `owned` mechanism that governs instance fields also governs static fields, so the same code patterns work in both places. Programs that rely on a particular shutdown ordering should organize their static state explicitly rather than depend on the program-exit ordering above.

<a id="sec-static-class-typed-fields-without-owned"></a>
#### Static class-typed fields without `owned`

A `static readonly` field of class type or interface type that is not marked `owned` is exempt from the [§28.8](#sec-ownership-transfer) ownership-discharge requirement, and the same exemption covers every store into a **mutable** static [§22.12](#sec-static-members) rule 2 admits: assigning a fresh owned value into such a field discharges the producer. The value lives for the duration of the program; the runtime reclaims its memory at process exit. The field is not disposed at program exit and must not hold resources that require explicit cleanup. Overwriting an admitted mutable static never disposes the displaced referent — deliberately *not* [§28.7](#sec-reassigning-owned-fields)'s drop-on-overwrite, because a racing first use may still hold and await a displaced task ([§22.12](#sec-static-members) rule 2(ii)); the displaced referent remains alive until process exit, an accepted bounded cost of the same kind as this exemption.

This exemption exists because many static fields hold long-lived, resource-free objects — caches, registries, singleton configuration — whose only "resource" is heap memory. Requiring `owned` on every such field would force program-exit disposal ordering for objects that have no meaningful cleanup.

If the static field holds a resource-bearing object, it must be marked `static owned readonly`, and the disposal-at-exit rules above apply. The compiler **warns** (not errors) when a `static readonly` field of a class type whose `Dispose()` is non-trivial — a class with a user-defined destructor, with `owned` fields of non-trivial-dispose type, or with owning-inline-array fields ([§28.9](#sec-runtime-managed-types)) — is declared without `owned`. For interface-typed static fields, the warning is conservative: the compiler emits it whenever the interface's set of permitted runtime types could include a class with a non-trivial `Dispose()`, which is the typical case. The warning text identifies the class (or the interface, with a note about its open implementation surface) and points at two remedies: (a) add the `owned` modifier to enroll the field in program-exit disposal, or (b) keep the field as-is if the singleton's lifetime is intentionally process-bound and its non-disposal at exit is acceptable. Remedy (a) addresses disposal only: a `static owned readonly` field of a class outside [§22.12](#sec-static-members) rule 4's warning-suppression set still draws rule 4's independent domain-reachability warning — the two warnings answer different questions (who disposes it; who may safely reach it across domains) and are cleared by different acts.

The diagnostic is a warning, not an error: such a field's lifetime contract is process-bound, and process termination ends it (rationale [§9.16](Bezel_Design_Rationale.md#sec-member-comparisons-with-csharp)).

##### Disposal under abnormal termination

The disposal-at-exit guarantees above apply only to **graceful shutdown** — `Main` returning normally, `Main` returning by an uncaught exception that the runtime intercepts, or an explicit `Environment.Exit()` call (std lib [§2.4](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-environment)) that runs through the standard shutdown sequence. Disposal does **not** run under any of these conditions:

- A `kill -9` / `TerminateProcess` external signal.
- A panic / fatal error in the runtime that bypasses orderly shutdown — including allocation failure ([§31.4](#sec-standard-exception-types)).
- An `abort()` from native code reached via FFI.
- A power loss or other unrecoverable hardware fault.

Programs whose correctness depends on disposal-time effects (writing a final log entry, releasing an external lock recorded outside the process) must not rely on `static owned` disposal alone — they need an external mechanism (a separate process holding the lock with a TTL, a write-ahead log, a watchdog) to recover when disposal does not run. This is the same caveat that applies to any cleanup mechanism that runs at process shutdown; Bezel's promise is "Dispose runs reliably during normal termination," not "Dispose runs in every case."

<a id="sec-no-params-no-ref-returns"></a>
### 22.14 No `params`, no ref returns

There is no `params` keyword. A variadic-style signature uses `Array<T>` with a collection literal at the call site:

```bezel
public method Log(messages: Array<string>) ...
Log(["hello", "world"]);
```

There are no ref returns. The compiler is expected to apply return-value optimization and copy elision for large value types.


---

<a id="sec-pure-members"></a>
### 22.15 Pure members

A member declared **`pure`** promises that evaluating a call to it — including every member it transitively calls — writes no storage outside the call's own frames, performs no I/O, runs no user code through disposal, and creates or touches no task, domain, channel, event, or synchronization object. A pure call may read any reachable state, may allocate runtime-managed values ([§28.9](#sec-runtime-managed-types)) and values of value, record, and enum type, and may fault by `throw` under the operand rule below. Purity is a declared, compiler-verified part of the member's signature — carried by the artifact interface ([§2.8.2](#sec-artifact-interface)) — not a derived type property ([§3.6](#sec-derived-type-properties)) and not a determinism or termination guarantee: a pure member may read *mutable* state, so two calls with identical arguments may return different values. The compiler rejects a `pure` member whose body violates the rules of this section, and rejects, inside a pure body, any call whose statically resolved declaration is not pure.

<a id="sec-pure-admissibility"></a>
#### Where `pure` may appear

`pure` is admitted on: instance and static methods; extension methods and expression-bodied extension properties; operator declarations; constructors; properties, indexers, and `get` accessors; interface methods, static interface members, interface properties and indexers; abstract and virtual members and overrides. `pure` occupies `async`'s slot in the modifier order ([§11.5](#sec-modifier-order)); the two are mutually exclusive.

`pure` is rejected on: **`async` members** and async lambdas (an `async` body interleaves with the domain's continuation queue and traffics in tasks; `pure` implies non-`async`, so `await` cannot appear in a pure body); **iterator methods** (`yield` — calling one executes none of its body, [§29.4](#sec-lazy-evaluation), and the produced enumerator's disposal runs cleanup at consumer-determined times; a pure-iterator form is deliberately left open, not designed); **destructors** (disposal is the effect context purity fences off); **`extern` declarations** ([§32](#sec-foreign-function-interface) — a foreign body cannot be checked, and no trust tier exists); **fields and auto-properties as declarations** (the auto-accessor classification is implicit, below; writing `pure` on an auto-property is rejected as redundant); **static constructors** ([§22.13](#sec-static-initialization-order) — no call site exists to consume the fact).

<a id="sec-pure-signature"></a>
#### Parameters and result

A pure member declares **no `ref`, `out`, `out owned`, `owned`, or `scoped` parameters**: `ref` is a writable alias of caller storage; `out` obliges a caller-visible assignment channel (the relaxation under the copy-out semantics is recorded liftable); `owned` brings a disposal obligation into the frame whose discharge runs `Dispose` — user code at disposal time; `scoped` grants a storage permission ([§28.14](#sec-scoped-callback-parameters)) a pure body can never exercise. A **move-only value parameter** ([§15.3](#sec-move-only-value-types) — an owning-choice instantiation, [§35.4](#sec-choice-classification) rule 1, or an owning inline array, [§15.1.1](#sec-owning-inline-arrays)) is likewise **rejected**: [§15.3](#sec-move-only-value-types) makes the plain spelling identical to the `owned` spelling for such a type, so the argument would arrive as a value-move carrying a real disposal obligation whose scope-end discharge runs user code — admitting it by its unmarked spelling would readmit exactly what the `owned`-parameter rejection excludes; for a generic parameter type the check is re-applied after substitution, at the instantiation site ([§35.11](#sec-choice-generics)). Plain parameters remain: **copyable** value types and records arrive as frame-local copies; class- and interface-typed parameters arrive as **borrows** (readable, never consumed); function-typed parameters arrive as values that may be held and returned but not invoked. (The borrow carve at [§25.2](#sec-operator-overloading-restrictions) reaches operator operands and `Equals(T)` only; this rule stands, recorded liftable — `DECLINED.md`.)

The return type is unrestricted except: an **`owned` class-typed return is rejected**, and so is a **move-only value return** ([§15.3](#sec-move-only-value-types) — an owning-choice instantiation, [§35.4](#sec-choice-classification) rule 1, or an owning inline array, [§15.1.1](#sec-owning-inline-arrays)) — no pure body can produce an owned class instance or a value that carries one, so either declaration would merely defer the error into the body; for a generic return type the check is re-applied after substitution, at the instantiation site ([§35.11](#sec-choice-generics)), as for the parameter rule above. Returning strings, values, records (including borrow-bearing records, subject to the ordinary [§9.7](#sec-records-and-disposal) lifetime rules), value-like and borrow-bearing choices (the latter under the same [§9.7](#sec-records-and-disposal) rules, [§35.4](#sec-choice-classification)), and function values is admitted.

<a id="sec-pure-body-rules"></a>
#### The pure body

A pure body may contain exactly the following; the list is closed, and everything outside it is rejected with a diagnostic naming the operation and this section.

1. **Reads of anything reachable.** Local and parameter reads; instance-field reads through `this` or any borrow; static field, `static readonly`, and `const` reads; enum constants; `typeof(T)` and `is`/`is not`/`as`; `nameof(…)`; `default(T)`; boxing a value (the box is runtime-managed). Reads are not effects — including reads of mutable state. Reads spelled as calls (property getters, indexers) are calls, governed by rule 6.
2. **Locals and frame-local mutation.** Variable declarations of every [§21.1](#sec-variable-declarations) form; assignment, compound assignment, and `++`/`--` where the target's **root is a local variable or by-value parameter of this body and the access path from that root traverses only value-typed storage** (record fields, inline-array slots). The first class-typed dereference on a path leaves the frame and makes the target prohibited. Mutating a record local, a record parameter copy, or an inline-array local is frame-private and admitted.
3. **Value, record, enum, choice, and string construction and operations.** All built-in operators on primitives, enums, and `string` (concatenation included); interpolated strings (each interpolated value's implied `ToString`/`Format` call is governed by rule 6); explicit and implicit conversions; range construction; record construction and `with` update, provided the invoked constructor is compiler-synthesized-pure or declared `pure`; choice construction — the payload-free case reference and the payload-case application ([§35.3](#sec-choice-construction); a choice has no user constructors, [§35.2](#sec-choice-members)) — provided every payload argument is itself admitted under these rules **and the constructed choice's classification is not owning** ([§35.4](#sec-choice-classification)): constructing an owning-classified choice is rejected whatever case is selected — even its payload-free and value-payload cases mint an owned move-only value ([§35.3](#sec-choice-construction)) that no admitted operation of this fragment can discharge (the move-only return is rejected above; `move`, `owned` arguments, and the other consuming positions are prohibited by this list), so the error lands at the construction site rather than deferring into the scope-end disposal machinery the fragment fences off; for a generic choice the classification is per-instantiation and the check is enforced at the instantiation or use site ([§35.11](#sec-choice-generics)); inline-array construction and literals of value/record element type.
4. **Defining lambdas and forming method references.** Closure allocation is runtime-managed ([§28.9](#sec-runtime-managed-types)) — permitted like string concatenation. A lambda *body* defined inside a pure body is **not** checked under these rules: it is a separate function that provably cannot run during the pure call (invoking function-typed values is prohibited, rule 6's contrapositive), and its later invocation happens at the caller's effect discipline. Captures follow [§28.3](#sec-local-variables-ownership-and-borrows)/[§28.9](#sec-runtime-managed-types) unchanged. (Forming a method reference *from* a pure method loses the purity fact at the formation boundary — function types carry no purity in this revision.)
5. **All control flow.** `if`/`elif`/`else`, `case`, `while`, `for`, `do … end`, `break`/`continue`/`return`, `try`/`catch`/`finally`, and `throw` — including the bare re-raise; a caught exception binding is a borrow ([§31.1](#sec-the-throw-operand)) and is readable under rule 1. A `for` loop is admitted when its desugaring does not construct an enumerator: over `Range<T>` of primitive steppable type, the direct counted-loop form ([§16.5](#sec-iteration), [§29.2](#sec-desugaring-of-for)) — elsewhere an admitted elision — is **the normative semantics inside a pure body**; over inline arrays, spans, `ReadOnlyStringSpan`, and value-typed `OwningBuffer<T>` the desugaring is already the direct indexed loop; and over a source whose **static type at this body's own check site** is concretely **`Array<T>`, `OwningArray<T>`, class-typed `OwningBuffer<T>`, or `string`**, [§29.2](#sec-desugaring-of-for)'s admitted protocol elision is likewise **the normative semantics inside a pure body**: the compiler emits the direct indexed loop — a bounds read and per-element reads, rule-1 material — and constructs no enumerator. (The bound is read as an intrinsic length fact of the concrete layout, exactly as the counted loop's endpoints are. `string.Length` and the `string` indexer (stdlib [§9.6](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-string)) and the `Count` properties of `Array<T>`/`OwningArray<T>` (stdlib [§4](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-system-collections-generic)) are `pure`-declared, so for those reads either lowering satisfies the fragment; where they are not — the element indexers — the intrinsic-layout reading is the only admissible lowering. The marker follows the stored extent and stops there: `OwningBuffer<T>.Length` (stdlib [§4.14](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-owned-buffers-and-spans)) is `pure`-declared as an immutable-once-allocated extent read, while an element indexer — which at a class element type lends a borrow of an owned slot — is not, and the [§4.14](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-owned-buffers-and-spans)/[§4.15](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-arrayspant-readonlyarrayspant) span families carry no purity markers at all.) The iteration variable's type and state are [§29.2](#sec-desugaring-of-for)'s for the elided form (a value copy for value elements and `string`; a borrow of the element for class-typed elements — default iteration over `OwningArray<T>` remains borrowing). A source whose static type is an **interface** (`IEnumerable<T>` included) or a **generic type parameter** — even one instantiated at a concrete sequence type — remains **rejected**: the remedy is declaring the source at a concrete sequence type (a concretely-typed parameter, or a concretely-typed binding before the loop). No index-loop spelling is available inside a pure body at such a source either: `IEnumerable<T>` declares no `Count` or indexer; `IReadOnlyList<T>`'s indexer is not `pure`-declared (stdlib [§4.1](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-borrowing-collection-interfaces)), so rule 6 rejects the element read; and a type-parameter source has only its constraint interfaces' members — the same wall.
