The structural-modification fault of [§29.12](#sec-mutation-during-iteration) is preserved by the elision as everywhere; inside a pure region no admitted operation can structurally modify a collection (stores through class-typed paths and non-pure calls are both prohibited), so the fault path is statically unreachable there and an implementation may omit its check in pure bodies with no observable difference.
6. **Calls to pure members.** A call — method, operator, accessor read, or constructor in the admitted positions — is permitted iff the member **declared on the receiver's static type** (or the statically resolved member, for statics and extensions) is `pure`-declared or pure-classified (below). Every entry point of the task, domain, channel, event, synchronization, and I/O surfaces is excluded by this one rule — none is or can be `pure`-declared — with no per-API enumeration.
7. **`throw`, with the construction carve-out below.**

Prohibited, as the closed list's contrapositive: any store whose target root is an instance field, a static field, an indexer slot of a class instance, or whose access path dereferences a class-typed reference (stores to `this`'s fields outside pure constructors' birth stores included); every owned-consuming or disposal-running operation (`Dispose()`, `move`, `owned` arguments, `set(owned)` stores, the consuming discard); **class construction** — `new C(…)`, collection literals of class collection types, calls returning `owned` class instances — except the throw operand below (constructors and destructors run arbitrary user code, and an owned instance drags in the discharge machinery); **invoking function-typed values** (the value's type carries no effect information); `await`; `yield`; `extern` calls.

<a id="sec-pure-throw"></a>
#### The throw carve-out

Inside a pure body, `new E(args)` is admitted **only** as the immediate operand of a `throw` statement or `throw` expression, and only when **(a)** the invoked constructor of `E` is `pure`-declared — covering, transitively, its chained constructors and `E`'s field initializers — and **(b)** `E` is a **trivial-dispose** class ([§28.9](#sec-runtime-managed-types); the diagnostic names the property). Condition (a) fences the constructor's code; for the destructor, ownership of the operand transfers to the exception machinery at the throw ([§31.1](#sec-the-throw-operand)) and disposal runs after the matching catch arm — condition (b) makes every dispose-after-arm reachable inside a pure region provably run no user code — for a trivial-dispose operand the after-arm disposal is the compiler-inserted flag-setting free ([§28.9](#sec-runtime-managed-types), [§28.2](#sec-checked-disposal)) — since every exception in flight within the region is either a carve-out throw from the region's own call subtree or a runtime-raised built-in ([§31.4](#sec-standard-exception-types) — all trivial-dispose). The carve-out follows §31.1's operand rule otherwise (`E` must, like every throwable, be `Exception`-derived — [§31.1](#sec-the-throw-operand); `Exception` itself and every built-in are trivial-dispose, so the requirement subtracts nothing from the carve-out's reachable set). Without it a pure method could fault only through provoked built-in exceptions — the validation idiom (`throw new ArgumentException(…)`) would be unwritable in the entire pure fragment. The trace capture the exception machinery performs at the throw ([§31.1](#sec-the-throw-operand)) is the runtime's own bookkeeping, not a store the body performs; it does not violate this section's rules.

**Intrinsic purity (the stdlib contract).** A standard-library member whose body is runtime-provided may carry `pure` — including on intrinsic auto-properties and indexer getters, where an authored body would be required otherwise. For a **compiler-intrinsic record**, the declared auto-property surface that [§9.2](#sec-body-records) fixes for the generated members does not by itself decide purity: a declared property whose value the intrinsic **recomputes** takes the marker under this paragraph, since the classification rule below reaches only a body that reads a stored slot; a declared property that does read one is classified and the marker on it is the redundant spelling rejected above. The marker is the library's *stated contract*, normative for the implementation (the runtime body must satisfy this section's rules — the [§32.10](#sec-boundary-contract)-style documented-contract posture) and trusted by the checker rather than verified from source. An exception raised by a pure intrinsic must be a **trivial-dispose** class ([§28.9](#sec-runtime-managed-types)) — extending the enumeration above, so that every exception in flight within a pure region remains disposal-inert. Every built-in exception type's `()` and `(message)`-form constructors (and `ArgumentException`/`ArgumentOutOfRangeException`'s `(message, paramName)` forms) are `pure` ([§31.4](#sec-standard-exception-types)); user-authored `extern` declarations remain outside `pure` entirely.

```bezel
public static pure method Checked(x: int, low: int, high: int): int
  if low > high then
    throw new ArgumentException("low must not exceed high", nameof(low));
  end;
  return (if x < low then low else (if x > high then high else x));
end Checked;
```

<a id="sec-pure-constructors"></a>
#### Pure constructors

A constructor may be declared `pure`. Its body is checked under the pure-body rules with one addition, the **birth-store rule**: assignments whose target root is a field of `this` (including `readonly` auto-property backing stores) are permitted — the instance under construction is unreachable from any other holder until the constructor returns, so its initialization is not an observable effect. The rule extends to the class's **field initializers** ([§22.8](#sec-field-initializers) — they execute as part of construction): a class with a pure constructor must have field initializers satisfying the pure-body rules. A pure constructor's `base(…)`/`this(…)` chain target must itself be pure. A record's compiler-synthesized positional constructor is pure-classified (below); an authored record constructor may be declared `pure` under the same rules, and record construction inside a pure body requires a synthesized-pure or `pure`-declared constructor. In this revision, pure *class* constructors are consumable only at the throw operand; they are specified generally because the stdlib exception constructors need them now and future widenings reuse them unchanged.

<a id="sec-pure-classification"></a>
#### Members classified by rule (synthesized bodies)

Compiler-synthesized member bodies have no author to make a promise; the compiler classifies them by checking its generated code under the pure-body rules: an **auto-property getter** is pure (a backing-field read); an **auto-property setter** is never pure; a **record's synthesized members** — positional constructor, `Equals`/`GetHashCode` ([§9.2](#sec-body-records)), `ToString`, `with`-copy — are pure iff every constituent operation is pure under the ordinary rules (for equality and hash: iff every field's equality dispatch target is pure — primitives, `string`, enums, and qualifying records; a class-typed field's virtual `Equals` disqualifies). The classified body is language-authored — its content changes only when the declaration's form changes, which is already a visible contract event ([§3.6](#sec-derived-type-properties) rule 3's discipline). Authored bodies always require the explicit keyword.

<a id="sec-pure-dispatch"></a>
#### Checking and dispatch

Each pure body is checked in isolation against the rules above; every call site is admitted by the *declaration* of the statically named member, never by inspecting its body — no inference, no interprocedural fixpoint, and recursion needs no special case (the declarations are the induction hypothesis). Cross-module, the imported declaration carries the modifier ([§2.8.2](#sec-artifact-interface)). Virtual and interface dispatch is sound by three matching rules ([§12.1](#sec-members-are-non-virtual-by-default), [§11.2](#sec-interface-declaration)):

1. **Purity is never dropped.** An `override` of a pure member must itself be declared `pure`, and a class member implementing a pure interface member must be declared `pure`; omission is a compile error at the override or implementation.
2. **Purity may be strengthened.** An override or implementation *may* declare `pure` where the overridden or interface member is not; the strengthened fact is usable only through the derived or concrete static type — dispatch admission keys on the static type's declaration, so a non-pure base slot admits nothing, whatever the runtime type.
3. **Monotone down the chain.** An override matches against the nearest overridden declaration: once a chain member is pure, every further override is pure.

Admission therefore implies that every dynamic target of the dispatched call is a checked pure body. `pure` is not an overload discriminator ([§22.6](#sec-overloading)): like `async`, it constrains the body and the contract, not selection. A generic pure member is checked once, at its declaration, under its constraints; calls on constraint-typed values resolve to the constraint interface's declared members — none pure in this revision — so generic pure bodies handle type-parameter-typed values opaquely (copy, hold, return). Nothing purity-relevant depends on the substitution.

<a id="sec-pure-accessors"></a>
#### Properties, indexers, accessors

Purity attaches to the *getter*; `pure` on `set` is always rejected. Expression-bodied and read-only block-form properties take property-level `pure`, marking the single getter; read-write block-form properties mark per accessor (`pure get => …; set => …;`) — the property stays read-write, only the getter joins the pure surface; indexers follow the same forms; interfaces declare `pure readonly property P: T;`, `pure method …;`, and `pure get;` accessor forms, with implementations restating purity per dispatch rule 1.

```bezel
public class Account
  private _balance: decimal := 0m;

  public property Balance: decimal
    pure get => _balance;
    set => _balance := value;
  end Balance;

  public pure property IsOverdrawn: bool => _balance < 0m;
end Account;
```

Default-value expressions of a pure member's parameters are checked under the pure-body rules (they evaluate at call sites, [§22.5](#sec-optional-parameters-and-named-arguments)). Purity is deliberately **not determinism**: the stronger tiers (result-depends-only-on-arguments; provable termination) are separate promises with separate machinery, and `pure` permanently means effect-free. Every [§17.14](#sec-constant-expressions) constant expression is valid pure-body material; the converse does not hold — a call to a pure method is not a constant expression, and pure calls are not compile-time evaluated.

<a id="sec-contract-clauses"></a>
### 22.16 Contract clauses

A method or constructor declaration may carry **contract clauses** between its signature and its body — precondition clauses **`requires(E)`** and postcondition clauses **`ensures(E)`** — and a class body may declare **invariant members** (**`invariant(E);`**). A clause's parentheses are structural — part of the clause syntax, not of its expression — so a clause is self-delimiting and carries no terminator; the `invariant` member, being a member, keeps the member-terminating `;`. Each clause's expression is of type `bool`, is admitted under the pure-body discipline of [§22.15](#sec-pure-members) with the amendments of this section, and can neither write state, consume or dispose a value, nor suspend. A `requires` clause is evaluated on every invocation, after argument binding and before any execution of the member; a clause evaluating `false` raises `ContractViolationException` ([§31.4](#sec-standard-exception-types)), in every build mode. An `ensures` clause is evaluated on every normal-completion path, after the return value and every `out` slot are bound and before the frame's scope-end disposals; within it the contextual keyword `result` denotes the returned value, read as a borrow, and `old(E)` denotes the value `E` had at entry; a path that exits by `throw` evaluates no `ensures` clause. The class invariant — the conjunction of a class's and its base classes' invariant members — is evaluated at the boundaries this section fixes: construction exit and the public entry and exit points, with `this`-receiver calls exempt. Every clause occupies exactly one recorded enforcement tier — **proven**, **checked**, or **assumed** — and the `static` clause qualifier demands the proven tier: a `static` clause the implementation cannot discharge statically is a compile error. Clauses bind overrides and implementations ([§12.1](#sec-members-are-non-virtual-by-default), [§11.2](#sec-interface-declaration)): they are inherited, never restated; an override or implementation may add `ensures` clauses and may not declare `requires` clauses. Contract clauses are part of the member's contract, carried by the artifact interface ([§2.8.2](#sec-artifact-interface)); they never distinguish overloads ([§22.6](#sec-overloading)).

```bezel
public class Account
  private _balance: decimal := 0m;
  private _limit: decimal := 0m;

  invariant(_balance + _limit >= 0m);

  public constructor(limit: decimal)
    requires(limit >= 0m)

    _limit := limit;
  end constructor;

  public method Withdraw(amount: decimal)
    requires(amount > 0m)
    requires(amount <= _balance + _limit)
    ensures(_balance = old(_balance) - amount)

    _balance := _balance - amount;
  end Withdraw;
end Account;
```

<a id="sec-clause-typing"></a>
#### Clause typing: `bool`, pure, borrow-only

A contract clause's expression — and each operand of `old` within it — is type-checked in the context of the declaring member: the member's parameters (all modifiers), `this` where the member has one, and the enclosing scopes' static and type members are in scope; the member's body locals are not. A **binding atom** ([§17.15](#sec-the-binding-atom)) is admitted — its bindings are clause-internal names, letting a clause name a subresult instead of recomputing it (`ensures(var n := result.Count; n >= 0 and n <= _capacity)`); its initializers and body are checked under this section's rules expression-wise; owned productions cannot arise in them (the pure fragment's records-only allocation), so clause atoms never carry disposals; and an atom clause spelled as a marked transfer (`var y := move x;` — a [K3.4](#sec-kernel-k3) consuming position elsewhere, [§17.15](#sec-the-binding-atom)) is **rejected** in a contract clause, preserving the borrow-only guarantee below. The expression must be of type `bool` ([§4.1](#sec-bool) — no truthiness), and is admitted under the **pure-body rules of [§22.15](#sec-pure-body-rules)**, applied expression-wise, with three clause-specific amendments: **`throw` is rejected** (a clause states a proposition; the mechanism, message, and blame of a violation belong to this section's machinery — the pure fragment's throw carve-out remains available to *callees* of the clause); **`await` is rejected**, on every member including `async` ones (a clause is not part of an async body's statement sequence and has no suspension semantics); **`old` and `result`** are admitted only as this section defines, and anywhere else each is an ordinary identifier ([Appendix B.2](#sec-contextual-keywords)).

The borrow-only guarantee — a clause may not consume, dispose, move, or reassign — is the sum of existing classifications, not a new checker: assignment, compound assignment, and `++`/`--` are *statements* and cannot be spelled in an expression; stores reachable through calls are excluded because callees must be pure; no owned-consuming position can arise (pure callees declare no `owned` parameters, `move` is prohibited by purity, the `throw` operand is rejected above, the discard is a statement, the marked-transfer atom is inadmissible in clause position — A.7's positional admission — and `set(owned)` stores are stores) — a read of a named owned binding in a clause is always [§28.3](#sec-local-variables-ownership-and-borrows)'s unmarked borrow read; and `Dispose()` is never pure-declared. An `ensures` clause reading an `owned` parameter is checked against §28.3's per-path ownership state at each return edge: on a path where the binding was moved out, the read is a moved-from read and a compile error naming the consuming site — the idiom for contracts over consumed inputs is `old(…)` over a copyable projection of the input — a whole-value `old` of a move-only input is rejected by the capture taxonomy below. Flow narrowing works inside clauses unchanged (`requires(x <> null and x.Count > 0)` narrows per [§7.4](#sec-member-access-on-nullable-values)).

Purity is what makes the tier system coherent: because a clause has no effects, evaluating it, eliding it, or proving it are indistinguishable to every non-violating program.

<a id="sec-clause-evaluation"></a>
#### Evaluation semantics

| Point | Order of operations |
|---|---|
| Member entry | bind arguments ([§22.5](#sec-optional-parameters-and-named-arguments)'s order) → `requires` clauses, declaration order, stop at first `false` → `old` operands, textual order → *constructors:* `base(...)`/`this(...)` chain → field initializers ([§22.8](#sec-field-initializers)) → body |
| Normal return edge | compute and bind the return value; every `out` callee-local slot holds its final value ([§22.3](#sec-parameter-modifiers)) → `ensures` clauses, declaration order → the class invariant, at instrumented boundaries → scope-end disposals and auto-drops ([§28.3](#sec-local-variables-ownership-and-borrows)) → `out` copy-out and return |
| Throw exit | no clause evaluation of any kind; the ordinary exception-path discharge unwinds the frame |

**`requires`** clauses evaluate on every invocation, after argument binding completes and before any of the member's own execution — before a constructor's `base(...)`/`this(...)` chain, before field initializers, before the first body statement — in declaration order, stopping at the first clause producing `false`, which faults with `ContractViolationException` raised from the member (parameters bound; no body effect has occurred; the object and all arguments are exactly as the caller left them, clauses being pure). A `requires` clause of an instance method may observe `this` (a borrow) and its fields; a **constructor's** `requires` may not observe `this` in any of [§22.7](#sec-observing-this-during-construction)'s senses (no field of the declaring type is assigned at clause time) — it reads parameters and statics only. An `out` parameter is unassigned at entry and unreadable in `requires` clauses. On a `this(...)`-chaining constructor, the chained-to constructor's own `requires` clauses evaluate when the chain invokes it. The boundary with *expected failure* is Guide 2's rule, unchanged and load-bearing: input whose invalidity is a normal outcome at a trust boundary is handled with Try shapes, nullable returns, or `choice` returns, never with `requires`; a `requires` states what a correct caller already guarantees, and its violation is a bug report, not a result. The standard library's conventions state the full library-side decision procedure — the failure-signal rule, classifying every declared fault condition across `requires`, the value shapes, `choice` returns, typed exceptions, and termination (stdlib [§1](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-failure-signal-rule)).

**`ensures`** clauses evaluate on every **normal-completion path** — a `return`, a unit-typed method falling off its end, an arrow body's completion, a constructor body's completion — and never on a path that exits by `throw`. The evaluation point is precisely: after the return value is computed and bound and after every `out` parameter's callee-local slot holds its final value, and **before** the frame's scope-end work (`using var` disposals, owned-local auto-drops, `out` copy-out) — so every borrow the frame holds is still live for the clause. Within an `ensures` clause of a member with a declared return type, **`result`** denotes the value being returned, typed as the declared return type, in a **read-only borrow position**: for a class- or interface-typed return — `owned` or plain — the clause observes the referent without consuming, disposing, or extending it, and the ownership transfer the return performs completes after the clause. `result` is a compile error in a unit-typed member's clauses, in a constructor's clauses, and in any `requires` or `invariant` clause. An `ensures` clause may read `out` parameters (the callee-local slot of §22.3's copy-out model, definitely assigned on every normal path), and `this`, fields, statics, and plain parameters as borrows; on a constructor, `ensures` evaluates at body completion, where every [§7.9](#sec-definite-assignment-for-non-nullable-fields)-required field is assigned.

**`old(E)`** — within an `ensures` clause of a **method**, `old(E)` denotes the value `E` had at the member's entry, defined by desugaring: for each `old` operand across the member's `ensures` clauses, in textual order, the compiler introduces a hidden entry binding equivalent to `var __oldN := E;` — the hidden binding a **copy** (or, in the reference arm below, [§28.3](#sec-local-variables-ownership-and-borrows)'s unmarked borrow), never a consume — evaluated exactly once per invocation, immediately after the last `requires` clause passes (a rejected call evaluates none), and each `old(E)` reads its binding at the return edge. Textually identical operands may share one binding (unobservable, operands being pure). Every rule that governs a user-written binding governs the hidden one — `old` adds **no new ownership machinery**. The capture is by operand kind:

- **Copyable operands are captured by copy:** value, record, enum, inline-array (without the `owned` marker), `string`, and function-typed operands — for the runtime-managed reference kinds ([§28.9](#sec-runtime-managed-types)) the copy is of the reference, and no ownership machinery arises. A borrow-bearing record or inline-array operand, or a choice operand that holds borrows ([§9.7](#sec-records-and-disposal), [§15.1.2](#sec-inline-array-members), [§35.4](#sec-choice-classification)'s holds-borrows property), is admitted with its carried borrows under [§9.7](#sec-records-and-disposal)'s ordinary rules — an inline array's under the one source set [§15.1.2](#sec-inline-array-members) gives the array value.
- **Class- and interface-typed operands are captured as a frame-resident borrow** whose source is whatever sourced `E` at entry: the consume-site freeze rejects a marked transfer of a local or parameter source while the capture is live, an explicit `Dispose()` of the source is the site-announced kill with the checked-mode backstop, and a field-path source is in the same residual-trust regime as every field-held borrow.
- **A move-only value operand is a compile error at the contract clause** ([#3113](https://github.com/s8lap/bezel-lang/issues/3113)). Such an operand ([§15.3](#sec-move-only-value-types) — an owning inline array, [§15.1.1](#sec-owning-inline-arrays), an owning-classified choice, [§35.4](#sec-choice-classification), or the nullable wrapper `C?` of one, [§35.9](#sec-choice-nullable)) admits no sound capture: a copy is the operation move-only-ness forbids, and the literal desugaring would not copy but *consume* — every store of a move-only value into an owning location is a move ([K3.12](#sec-kernel-k3)), a contract clause mutating the state it exists to observe. The diagnostic names the **copyable-projection** remedy: capture a copyable fact of the pre-state instead — an element- or payload-derived copyable value (`old(pool[i] <> null)` over an owning inline array's nullable slots, a `pure` member's value read through a borrowed element) or, for an owning choice, a `pure` choice method's result over the borrowed receiver ([§35.2](#sec-choice-members); clause calls to pure members per [§22.15](#sec-pure-members)) — or a borrowing-match projection over the operand, `old((case c of …))`, which consumes nothing ([§35.5](#sec-choice-matching)) and needs no member on the choice. Where the operand's type is move-only only at some instantiations — a choice instantiation whose classification is owning per type argument ([§35.11](#sec-choice-generics)), or a bare type parameter — the clause type-checks once at the declaration as this section's [Scope](#sec-contract-scope) requires, and the rejection is re-applied after substitution at the instantiation site, under [§3.6](#sec-derived-type-properties) rule 2, exactly as [§22.15](#sec-pure-members)'s move-only parameter and return rules are.

**`old` is shallow:** a class-typed capture holds the entry *reference*, so member reads through it observe the referent's **post-state** — `old(_items).Count` reads the count *now*; `old(_items.Count)` captures the entry count. The recommended idiom is value-typed projections; implementations should warn on a class-typed `old` capture dereferenced for a member in the clause. `old` is a compile error in `requires` clauses, in `invariant` members, in constructor clauses (fields sit at §22.7's null watermark — no prestate exists), and outside clauses entirely; `old(old(E))` is a compile error.

**Faults during clause evaluation.** A clause expression may fault (an indexer's `IndexOutOfRangeException`, arithmetic overflow, a pure callee's own validation throw). The fault propagates from the clause's evaluation point **as itself** — never converted to `ContractViolationException`, because the clause did not evaluate to `false`; it failed to evaluate, which is a defect in the *contract*, and the original exception is its diagnosis. At an `ensures` point the fault turns the completion exceptional; the ordinary exception-path machinery unwinds the frame.

**No nested-check suppression.** Clause evaluation calls pure members; those members' own clauses check normally during the outer clause's evaluation — checks compose as ordinary calls. A genuinely cyclic `requires` chain manifests as `StackOverflowException`, like any unbounded recursion.

**Clause granularity is semantic.** `requires(a) requires(b)` is not a style variant of `requires(a and b)`: the clause is the unit of tier, blame, evaluation order (stop at first failure), and interface identity. Recommended style, non-normative: one condition per clause, each clause on its own line and, where a member's clause region is followed by a body, a blank line between the last clause and the first body statement — the promises above the gap, the doing below it. Both recommendations are style only: neither is part of the grammar, no implementation consults the layout, and a member written without them means exactly what the same member written with them means.

<a id="sec-contract-violation"></a>
#### Failure semantics and the enforcement modes

**`ContractViolationException`** joins the built-in hierarchy ([§31.4](#sec-standard-exception-types)), deriving directly from `Exception` — clause evaluation is a language operation, like the indexer's `IndexOutOfRangeException`. It is catchable; its `Message` carries the clause kind, the member, and the clause's source text. Programs must not use it for control flow — it reports a bug (a caller bug for `requires`, an implementation bug for `ensures`/`invariant`), not an outcome.

**`requires` violations are always-on**: an unproven `requires` clause is compiled as a runtime check in every build mode; it is never elided. (A proven clause is discharged statically and compiles to nothing — elision-by-proof is the only elision. An implementation may additionally elide the check at a particular call site it can statically discharge — unobservable by purity — but the clause's recorded tier stays checked.) This is the always-on posture of the `throw new ArgumentException(…)` prologue the clause replaces; the remedy for hot paths is the proven ratchet, not a knob.

**`ensures` and `invariant` run under checked-contracts mode** — a per-build choice between two conformance modes, independent of [§28.2](#sec-checked-disposal)'s disposal-checking mode: in **unchecked (release) mode** — the default — unproven `ensures` and `invariant` clauses are not evaluated; in **checked-contracts mode** they are evaluated at this section's points, a `false` clause raising `ContractViolationException`. The two modes give identical observable behavior for every program whose checked clauses never evaluate `false` and never fault: clauses are pure, so non-evaluation is unobservable by construction — the deliberate contrast with §28.2, whose release relaxation is undefined behavior. `requires` clauses are outside the mode entirely.

<a id="sec-contract-tiers"></a>
#### The tier system: proven / checked / assumed

Every contract clause occupies exactly one **tier**, determined statically per clause: **proven** — discharged statically at the clause's discharge site, never evaluated at runtime, zero cost in every mode (prover soundness is a conformance obligation); **checked** — compiled to a runtime evaluation at this section's points, under the mode rules above; **assumed** — stated and carried, neither proven nor evaluated (unpopulated in this revision; reserved for contract clauses on `extern` declarations, to be designed jointly with the extern-purity question).

**Discharge sites differ by clause kind.** An `ensures` or `invariant` clause is discharged at the **declaring body**: the prover shows every normal-completion path establishes it — `static ensures`/`static invariant` makes an unprovable body a compile error at the declaration ([§22.4](#sec-out-nullability-postcondition)'s existing rule) — **the behaviour the prover fragment brings**, not this revision's: until it lands a `static invariant` is inert and warns at the clause (*Out of scope in this revision*, below). A `requires` clause is the body's assumption; its discharge site is **every call site**: the caller's compiler substitutes the actual arguments into the clause and discharges the instance — `static requires` makes an undischargeable call a compile error at that call, and the callee compiles no runtime check because every admitted call carries a proof. A **`static requires` clause may mention only state its call sites can see** (the member's parameters, and members visible to every caller); a `static requires` over non-public state is a compile error at the declaration. Checked `requires` clauses are unrestricted.

**The current prover floor** — exactly two things inhabit the proven tier: a clause whose expression (after call-site substitution, for `requires`) is a **constant expression** ([§17.14](#sec-constant-expressions)) folding to `true` (folding to `false` is a compile error at the clause — a statically violated contract; a faulting constant folding is a compile error per §17.14's own rule); and the `when true`/`when false` postconditions of [§22.4](#sec-out-nullability-postcondition) — which this section defines as `static ensures` clauses, proven by the existing [§7](#sec-nullability-2) nullability flow analysis over the declaring body. Apart from those, every authored clause is therefore **checked**: the runtime tier stands alone, and the prover grows under a fixed meaning. The **Contract proving** conformance feature (Appendix [D.2](#sec-extended-features)) fixes the extended prover fragment now, so the `static` qualifier's meaning never drifts: linear integer arithmetic over parameters, fields, `result`, and `old` captures (under [§6.1](#sec-integer-arithmetic)'s checked semantics); null tests composed with §7's flow narrowing; and case analysis over enums, closed hierarchies ([§19.6](#sec-exhaustiveness)), and choice cases ([§35](#sec-choices)). Everything outside the fragment stays checked; `static` on an out-of-fragment clause is an error, never a silent downgrade to a runtime check.

<a id="sec-contract-inheritance"></a>
#### Inheritance, interfaces, and dispatch

Contracts are **slot-bound**: a clause declared on a virtual or abstract member, or on an interface member, is part of that slot's contract and binds every override and implementation.

1. **Clauses are inherited verbatim, never restated.** An override or implementing member does not repeat the base or interface clauses; its invocations are checked against them wherever the member is reached, directly or by dispatch.
2. **An override or implementation may add `ensures` clauses**, conjoined with the inherited ones at its return edges — strengthening the postcondition, always sound for callers. A caller through the base static type cannot name the added guarantee; every execution honors it.
3. **An override or implementation may not declare `requires` clauses.** Strengthening a precondition breaks every caller dispatching through the base contract, and no weakening syntax exists in this revision: the override's effective precondition is the inherited one, verbatim.
4. **Multiple contract roots combine soundly.** A member reachable through several contract-bearing declarations has: effective `requires` = the **disjunction over roots** of each root's clause conjunction (a caller reached the member through *some* static type and established that root's precondition); effective `ensures` = the **conjunction of all roots'** clauses plus the member's own additions. Roots evaluate in inheritance-declaration order, clauses in declaration order within a root; `requires` evaluation short-circuits at the first satisfied root; if none is satisfied the violation names every root's failed clause set.
5. **Monotone down the chain**: an override inherits from its nearest overridden declaration transitively; `ensures` additions accumulate and nothing is dropped mid-chain.
6. **Clause context is the declaring type**: an inherited clause evaluates as declaring-type code (it may read the base's `private` fields), and `result` in an inherited `ensures` binds to the actual invocation's returned value (type-identical by §12.1's exact-return-match rule).
7. **Abstract members carry clauses** — the intended home: the slot's contract written where the slot is declared, every concrete subclass bound.

Clauses never distinguish overloads and are not part of [§22.6](#sec-overloading) resolution; two members differing only in clauses are the same signature and clash.

<a id="sec-class-invariants"></a>
#### Class invariants

An **invariant member** (`invariant(E);`) declares a predicate over the instance's state, checked under this section's clause rules in the context of the declaring class (its `private` fields readable; `old` and `result` rejected). The **class invariant** of C is the conjunction of every invariant member of C and of every base class, evaluated base-first, declaration order within each class. The invariant is an *observable-boundary* property: it must hold whenever the instance is observable from outside itself, and it may be freely false while the instance is operating on itself.

**The instrumentation set** — the invariant is evaluated at exactly these points, in checked-contracts mode:

- **Construction exit**: the normal completion of the **most-derived constructor** of a construction, of any visibility, after its body and its `ensures` clauses. A base constructor completing as part of a derived construction is *not* an instrumentation point (the [§22.8](#sec-field-initializers) sequence is interior — derived initializers have not run), nor is a `this(...)`-chained-to constructor completing mid-chain. Every fresh instance satisfies its full dynamic class invariant before it is observable; a violation raises `ContractViolationException` and the partially-constructed instance unwinds under [§22.9](#sec-owned-fields-and-exception-safety)'s ordinary machinery.
- **Entry and normal exit** of every `public` instance **method**. Order at entry: `requires` clauses, then the invariant; at exit: `ensures` clauses, then the invariant.
- **Entry and normal exit** of every `public` **setter** — block-form, auto-property, indexer, `set(owned)` alike. (Auto-property assignments inside constructors are backing-field stores, not accessor invocations, so construction does not double-check.)
- **Getters are exempt**, with the residual recorded: a mutating block-form getter escapes invariant checking; the recommended getter is a [§22.15](#sec-pure-members) pure one, which cannot mutate.
- **Never instrumented:** non-public methods and setters, static members, destructors, and `Dispose` (disposal legitimately tears the state down); throw exits check nothing.

**The visibility boundary and the `this`-reentrancy exemption.** Public-only is the boundary: non-public calls are the implementation's interior, where an algorithm may pass through broken intermediate states (`internal` is interior — module-mates are co-implementors, not clients). A call whose receiver is `this` — explicit or implicit — from inside any instance member of the class or a subclass enters the member's **unchecked face**: no invariant evaluation at that call's entry or exit. Every instrumented public member compiles to a checked face (entry checks → unchecked face → exit checks) and an unchecked face (the body); call sites with syntactic receiver `this` bind to the unchecked face — statically decidable, including for virtual dispatch (a `this`-receiver dispatching call reaches the dynamic target's unchecked face). Calls on *other* instances of the same class check normally. Invariant evaluation itself runs as interior code, so a clause may call a `pure` public method of the same instance without recursion. **Dispatch checks the dynamic class's invariant**: an external call through a base-typed reference evaluates the full dynamic class invariant — base and derived conjunction — at the dynamic target's checked face.

Construction composes with [§22.7](#sec-observing-this-during-construction) exactly: at the most-derived constructor's normal completion every §7.9-required field of every class in the chain is definitely assigned, so evaluating the invariant is admitted by the observation gate by construction. The recorded residual is inherited, not enlarged: a during-construction `this`-escape re-entering a public method from outside the instance hits a checked face over fields still at the null watermark, faulting per §22.7's stated bound. Invariant evaluation is a boundary-time read of instance state in the calling domain — no new cross-domain access arises, and no rule of [§30.13](#sec-runtime-model)/[§30.14](#sec-sendable-types) changes.

**Out of scope in this revision**, each recorded: record invariants (constructor-exit plus a `with`-update instrumentation point — a later design); interface-declared invariants (need interface carriage to transport); static-class and static-state invariants (an `invariant` in a static class is a compile error — no instance boundary exists); `static invariant` parses from day one and is useful when the prover fragment lands — and because it is **inert** until then, the compiler **must** emit a warning at the clause naming that fact. The clause is a prove-time obligation with no prover to discharge it and no run-time instrumentation standing in, so `static invariant(false);` compiles and does nothing; nothing else in the program distinguishes that from a checked predicate, and a contract a reader believes is enforced is worse than no contract. The warning changes no verdict — every program that compiled before compiles still — and it is withdrawn, not merely silenced, when the prover fragment lands.

<a id="sec-contract-scope"></a>
#### Scope

In scope: instance, static, and extension methods (the receiver is a borrow, [§26.7](#sec-ownership-in-extensions), readable in clauses); constructors; abstract methods; interface methods and static interface members; record and enum methods (`old` over receiver fields captures by the value rules; the *invariant* member is class-only); generic members (clauses type-check once at the declaration under constraints — constraint-typed receivers offer no pure members in this revision, so clauses over bare-`T` values are near-inexpressible, recorded honestly); `Main`.

**Async methods: `requires` only.** A `requires` on an `async` method evaluates in the **synchronous prefix** — after argument binding, before any body statement and therefore before the first suspension ([§30.1](#sec-async-methods)) — so a violation surfaces synchronously at the call expression, on the caller's own stack, not through the task. `ensures` on an `async` method is rejected in this revision (the settlement-time design — evaluation in the completing frame before delivery, faulting the task, `old` captures living in the state-machine frame — is recorded in proposal 0043 §10.1 and staged for its own verification pass). Clauses on **iterator methods** are rejected (calling one executes none of its body, so no coherent evaluation point exists; eager `requires`-at-call is the recorded revisit). No clauses on **accessors**, **operators**, or **lambdas** in this revision (each recorded liftable; a lambda's contract belongs to its function type — the same abstracted-position bucket as function-type purity). No clauses on **`extern` declarations** (the assumed tier's intended client, designed jointly with extern purity), **destructors**, or **static constructors**.

<a id="sec-when-clause-unification"></a>
#### The `when`-clause identity

[§22.4](#sec-out-nullability-postcondition)'s nullability postcondition **is** a proven-tier contract clause. Normatively, for a `bool`-returning method, `method M(…, out p: T? when true, …): bool` is `method M(…, out p: T?, …): bool` carrying the clause `static ensures(not result or p <> null)` (and `when false` correspondingly `static ensures(result or p <> null)`). Everything §22.4 mandates falls out of this section's rules: the declaring-body obligation is the §7 flow prover discharging a `static ensures` at its discharge site; the evaluation point is this section's; the call-site narrowing is caller-side **consumption of a proven ensures** — the first shipped instance of the consumption pattern the prover fragment generalizes. The `when true`/`when false` clause is the postcondition's **only source spelling**: the `static ensures` reading above states what the clause *means* — what the proven tier discharges and what a call site consumes — and is not a second way to write it. A hand-written `static ensures(not result or p <> null)` is an ordinary static postcondition: proven or rejected like any other, and it narrows nothing at the call site — [§22.4](#sec-out-nullability-postcondition)'s narrowing is keyed on the clause. Across a module boundary the clause is carried by the parameter's postcondition modifier ([§2.8.6](#sec-interface-delta-classification)'s modifier row), not by a contract record: a hand-written clause of the same canonical text produces the same [§2.8.2](#sec-artifact-interface) contract record and still grants no call-site narrowing — the modifier is the only carrier of that grant. One rule is deliberately retained rather than generalized: [§12.1](#sec-members-are-non-virtual-by-default) requires an override to repeat the `when` clause exactly; a postcondition is never weakened.

<a id="sec-properties-and-indexers"></a>
## 23. Properties and Indexers

A property is a member that looks like a field on access. An indexer is a property whose name is replaced by a parameter list in square brackets.

<a id="sec-auto-properties"></a>
### 23.1 Auto-properties

```bezel
public property Name: string;                         // read-write
public property Id: int private set;                  // read-write with private setter
public readonly property AccountNumber: string;       // read-only
public readonly property Pi: double := 3.141592653589793;  // read-only with initializer
```

The compiler generates the backing field, and every assignment to an auto-property stores into it; at a function type that store is one of [§28.3](#sec-borrow-lifetime-rules)'s *property and indexer stores*, which admit only a capture-free value. A `readonly` auto-property may be assigned only in a field initializer or in a constructor, under [§22.8](#sec-field-initializers)'s **per-instance** assignable context; that section's *single-assignment* rule governs fields and does not extend here (its scope statement). The assignment is a store to the backing field (no setter exists to invoke, [§22.7](#sec-observing-this-during-construction) rule 1), and it is admitted only through `this` for an instance auto-property, or in the declaring type's own static initialization for a `static readonly` one.

<a id="sec-expression-bodied-read-only-properties"></a>
### 23.2 Expression-bodied read-only properties

**`readonly` has one meaning: it is written exactly where shape cannot express read-onlyness** — auto-properties ([§23.1](#sec-auto-properties)) and interface properties, whose accessor sets are declared, not shaped. On every body-bearing form — an expression-bodied property or indexer, a get-only block form, and the expression-bodied properties of choices, enums, and extensions — read-onlyness is already expressed by the shape, and writing `readonly` there is a compile error (the grammar's `readonly?` slots on those productions are over-admissions, rejected semantically per the shared-production policy); on a block form declaring a setter it is contradictory and likewise an error.

```bezel
public property Area: decimal => Width * Height;
public property IsEmpty: bool => _count = 0;
public property FullName: string => $"{FirstName} {LastName}";
```

An expression-bodied property's (or indexer's) body is checked against the declared type and is a **declared-result position** for choice-case constructions ([§35.3](#sec-choice-construction)); a **getter's** expression body under the property's declared type ([§23.3](#sec-block-form-properties)) is the same position (a setter's body is checked against no result type and is not).

<a id="sec-block-form-properties"></a>
### 23.3 Block-form properties

```bezel
public property Balance: decimal
  get => _balance;
  set => do
    if value < 0m then throw new ArgumentException("Balance cannot be negative"); end;
    _balance := value;
  end;
end Balance;
```

The implicit setter parameter is `value`. It is a parameter of the setter, and [§21.1](#sec-variable-declarations)'s *Local names* applies to it as to any other parameter. Each accessor uses `=> expression` or `=> do ... end`. A read-only property in block form omits `set`; a write-only property omits `get`.

Accessor visibility ([§13.6](#sec-accessor-visibility)) may make a getter or setter more restrictive than the property as a whole.

**Explicit setter parameter modifier.** The setter's implicit `value` parameter has no modifier by default and takes a borrow of the property's declared type. At a function type it carries the empty source set, because every assignment that reaches a setter admits only a capture-free value ([§28.3](#sec-borrow-lifetime-rules)'s *property and indexer stores*); it is therefore not a call-bounded parameter ([§28.14](#sec-scoped-callback-parameters)), and the setter may store it. An assignment of a value that can carry a borrow through an instance property of a class or interface, other than through `set(owned)`, is judged at the site as a store of that value into a non-`owned` field of the receiver, and one through a static property as a store into a non-`owned` static field of the property's declared type, whatever the setter's body does with `value` ([§28.3](#sec-borrow-lifetime-rules)'s *property stores of a borrow-carrying value*). For owning collections (like `OwningArray<T>`'s indexer setter) the setter needs to take ownership of the new value (and dispose the previous slot value). Write an explicit `set(owned)` parameter spec to declare an owned-taking setter:

```bezel
public class OwningArray<T> where T: class
  public property [i: int]: T
    get;                     // implicit value: T, borrow-returning
    set(owned);              // explicit owned: takes owned T;
                             //   disposes previous slot value
  end;
end OwningArray;
```

The spelling `set(owned)` takes the value owned. The parameter is `value` in every setter, and its type is always the property's declared type, so neither is written. The form is admitted on block-form properties and indexers; abstract/interface accessor bodies (`;`-terminated) carry the spec the same way (`set(owned);`). The standard-library owning collection types (`OwningArray<T>`, `OwningDictionary<K, V>`) use this form for their indexer setters; the owning-collection interfaces (`IOwningList<T>`) declare it on their abstract indexer setters. Assignment through a `set(owned)` property or indexer is a marker-free owned-consuming position — the declared slot announces the consume: a named owned binding on the right-hand side is consumed with no call-site transfer marker — and writing one is an error naming the announcement ([§28.3](#sec-move-semantics-for-owned-locals)).

<a id="sec-indexers"></a>
### 23.4 Indexers

An indexer is a property whose name is replaced by `[parameters]`:

```bezel
public property [i: int]: string => _items[i];        // expression-bodied

public property [row: int, col: int]: double => _grid[row * _width + col];

public property [key: string]: int
  get => _values[key];
  set => do
    if value < 0 then throw new ArgumentException("must be non-negative"); end;
    _values[key] := value;
  end;
end;
```

A block-form indexer's `end` clause has no name to reference; it is plain `end;`.

Inside a member of a class with its own indexer, `this[i]` is required (the brackets need a left-hand side).

Indexers may be declared in interfaces with the body-less form (write `readonly` before `property` to expose only a getter):

```bezel
interface IList<T>: IReadOnlyList<T>, ICollection<T>
  property [i: int]: T;
end IList;
```

Indexers may be overloaded by parameter type list. They participate in `virtual`/`override`/`sealed`/`abstract` like methods.

Records may declare read-only indexers. A record may declare a read-write indexer whose setter does not store the receiver — every store landing beyond a class- or interface-typed hop, [§9.4](#sec-value-receivers-are-borrows)'s mediating shape (stdlib [§4.14](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-owned-buffers-and-spans)/[§4.15](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-arrayspant-readonlyarrayspant)'s span records, combined-form records with no mutable properties, are the canonical case); a setter body storing the receiver's own storage cannot be declared ([§9.4](#sec-value-receivers-are-borrows)). Positional-only records have no body to declare an indexer in.

<a id="sec-properties-and-indexers-restrictions"></a>
### 23.5 Restrictions

- Enums may not declare indexers.
- Static indexers are not supported.
- `ref` and `out` parameters are not allowed in indexer parameter lists.
- Index arguments are **positional-only**. The named-argument form (`Identifier :=`, [§22.5](#sec-optional-parameters-and-named-arguments)) is not admitted at an index position — a compile error naming this rule. Indexer parameters may not declare default values, so [§22.5](#sec-optional-parameters-and-named-arguments)'s optional-parameter and named-binding machinery is never reached from an index position; an indexer's parameter names are declaration-internal, not caller-bindable API surface (consistent with [§23.4](#sec-indexers)'s overloading by parameter *type* list).
- Assigning to a member of a value-typed indexer result is a compile error: `g[0].X := 5` would modify a discarded copy. Read, modify, write back through the setter. (When the container is itself a **record**, the write-back setter exists only in [§9.4](#sec-value-receivers-are-borrows)'s mediating form ([§23.4](#sec-indexers)) — where the write-back would need to land in the record's own storage, the update is a `with` over the whole containing value, [§9.5](#sec-non-destructive-update-with).)
- Properties and indexers whose declared type is a move-only value type (an owning inline array or an owning-classified choice, [§15.3](#sec-move-only-value-types)) are not admitted. A getter would need to either copy the move-only value (forbidden by move-only semantics) or move it out of the backing storage (which would leave the storage in moved-from state, conflicting with the property abstraction). Programs that need to expose an owning inline-array field interactively use a regular public field (with the inline array's `owned` slot marker conveying the ownership) or, for transfer-out semantics, an explicit method that returns the owned value. This is a general principle, named here: **accessor read faces are lend-only; transfer-out is a method** — a getter never transfers ownership out, while `set(owned)` remains the marker-free write face (axiom [A4](#sec-axiom-register); [§29.1](#sec-iterator-protocol)'s `TakeCurrent()` is the standard library's instance of the method half).

<a id="sec-the-type-of-an-event-member"></a>

<a id="sec-events-on-interfaces"></a>
## 24. Events (retired member kind)

Retired. The `event` member kind does not exist: an event is the two-declaration library pattern documented normatively in stdlib [§6.5](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-events-ievent-eventsource) — a `private owned readonly` source field and a public borrowing property of the interface face — with identical subscriber-side call sites and semantics (rationale §13.6). The `+=`/`-=` subscription desugaring remains language-defined at [§17.2](#sec-notes-on-operators); shared (cross-domain) publication points use the `ISharedEvent<T>`/`SharedEventSource<T>` pair under [§22.12](#sec-static-members) rule 5. The word `event` remains reserved (Appendix B.3): an `event` declaration is a reserved-word error, and the migration spelling is stdlib §6.5's pattern. The section anchors are retained for citation stability; the prior definition and the decision record are in the [changelog](Bezel_Changelog.md).

<a id="sec-operator-overloading"></a>
## 25. Operator Overloading

Records, enums, choices ([§35.2](#sec-choice-members) admits of a choice body exactly what an enum body admits, operator overloads included), and classes may overload operators. Operators are declared as `public static` methods using the `operator` keyword — **`public` is required**: an operator invoked through `a + b` syntax has no call-site spelling that could name a restricted member, so any other visibility is a compile error (Appendix A.4's OperatorDecl admits only `public static`).

<a id="sec-overloadable-operators"></a>
### 25.1 Overloadable operators

- Unary: `+`, `-`, `~`
- Binary: `+`, `-`, `*`, `/`, `mod`, `&`, `|`, `^`, `<<`, `>>`
- Comparison: `<`, `>`, `<=`, `>=`, `=`, `<>`

`not` is **not** user-overloadable. It is the boolean-negation operator and applies only to `bool` ([§6.5](#sec-bitwise-operations)); types wanting a domain-specific inversion provide a named method (`.Negate()`, `.Inverted()`) or overload `~` if a bitwise reading applies. This is the one place where Bezel explicitly excludes a unary operator from the overload set in favor of a named method, so that the boolean reading of `not` is preserved at every call site.

The following operators are also not overloadable, for various reasons:

- The null-forgiving `!`, the null-coalescing `??`, and the type-test operators `is`, `is not`, `as` — these have null-aware or type-system semantics fixed by the language; user types do not customize them.
- Range operators `..` and `..<` — these construct values of the language-built-in `Range<T>` type ([§16](#sec-range-expressions)); user types do not customize them.
- The `in` operator — customization is via the structural `Contains` lookup ([§17.5](#sec-the-in-operator)).
- The increment and decrement statements `++` and `--` — statements, not operators of the expression grammar ([§17.6](#sec-the-increment-and-decrement-operators)): a declared `operator ++`/`operator --` is a **compile error at the operator token**, its diagnostic naming this exclusion, and a type spells advancement as `x := x + 1` under its own `operator +`, or as a named method (the shape the standard library's `ISteppable<T>.Step` already takes).
- Assignment and compound-assignment operators (`:=`, `+=`, `-=`, `*=`, `/=`, `mod=`, `&=`, `|=`, `^=`, `<<=`, `>>=`, `??=`) — Bezel has no compound-operator overload mechanism; the compound forms desugar mechanically to read-modify-write using the underlying binary operator's overload, with the evaluation counts and result typing of [§6.6](#sec-compound-assignments).
- The `+=` and `-=` event-subscription forms ([§17.2](#sec-notes-on-operators)) — a fixed, language-defined desugaring available only on `EventSource<T>`, `AsyncEventSource<T>`, and `SharedEventSource<T>`; they are not operator overloads and are not part of the user-overloadable surface.
- The short-circuit boolean operators `and` and `or` — like `not`, they are fixed on `bool`; their short-circuit evaluation cannot be expressed by a user method's eager parameters, so they are not overloadable. Element access `[ ]` is customized through indexers ([§23.4](#sec-indexers)), not through operator overloads.

<a id="sec-operator-overloading-restrictions"></a>
### 25.2 Restrictions and resolution

**Declaring-type operand.** At least one parameter of an operator overload must be the declaring type; a binary overload may pair the declaring type with any other type in either position (as `DateTime.operator +(t: TimeSpan, d: DateTime)` does). An operator whose parameters never mention the declaring type would be unreachable by the resolution rule below.

**Resolution.** For `a <op> b` on non-primitive operands, the candidate set is the union of the `operator <op>` overloads declared on the **static types of both operands, including declarations inherited from their base classes** (a derived-typed operand reaches its base's operators, as in C#: no user-facing upcast exists that could reach them otherwise, and [§12.2](#sec-hiding-is-not-allowed)'s no-hiding rule — which covers operator declarations per token, stated explicitly there — prevents a derived class from redeclaring an operator token its base declares, so one chain contributes no duplicate candidates). A derived-typed operand satisfies a base-typed parameter by the ordinary argument rules. Parameters match operands **in order** — there is no automatic commutation (`4 - v` is not matched against `operator -(v: V, n: int)`). If distinct applicable overloads are found on both operand types, the expression is a compile error citing the candidates (mirroring [§22.6](#sec-overloading)'s the-compiler-declines-to-guess stance). A unary operator consults the operand's type and its base classes, likewise.

**Type-parameter operands (connecting this section to [§11.8](#sec-static-interface-members)).** A generic type parameter declares no operators of its own; for an operand whose static type is a type parameter `T`, the candidate set is drawn from the **static-interface constraints** on `T` ([§11.8](#sec-static-interface-members)): the `static operator` members those interfaces declare, matched in order as above and bound at instantiation to the conforming type's own declarations. The complete-group rule below does double duty here: because every concrete type that declares one of `<`, `>`, `<=`, `>=` must declare all four, a constraint interface that declares any one of them (the stdlib `INumber<T>`/`ISteppable<T>` declare `<` alone) entitles the generic body to **all four** — each use still resolves at instantiation to the conforming type's *own* declaration of that operator, never by synthesizing `a > b` from `b < a`. The same holds for the `=`/`<>` pair. Primitive substitutions satisfy the entitlement through their intrinsic operator set ([§11.8](#sec-static-interface-members)'s compiler-provided conformances, §3.5).

- `=` and `<>` may **not** be overloaded on classes or on inline arrays. For classes, `=` always invokes `Equals`. For inline arrays, the language-defined structural equality of [§8.3](#sec-equals-and-gethashcode) is the only `=` available; inline arrays cannot be extended ([§26.2](#sec-what-can-be-extended)), so the overload mechanism does not reach them. Records, enums, and choices may overload `=` and `<>` ([§35.2](#sec-choice-members)).
- Comparison operators must be overloaded as a complete group: `<`, `>`, `<=`, `>=` together; `=` and `<>` together.
- **Operator parameters admit no parameter modifiers.** `ref`, `out`, `owned`, and `scoped` on an operator's parameter list are rejected semantically — the grammar admits them through the shared `Param` production, the same over-admit-and-reject pattern as [§22.10](#sec-methods-and-constructors-primary-constructors)'s primary constructors. Operands are received as plain borrows (or value copies) under their type kinds; the return slot's optional `owned` (grammar A.4) is the sole ownership annotation on operators. Operator operand positions therefore never consume a named owned binding — the transfer marker is not admitted in operator-operand position (axiom [A7](#sec-axiom-register)), and under this rule none is needed. **For a move-only operand type** — an owning choice ([§35.4](#sec-choice-classification)), the one move-only kind with an operator surface ([§15.3](#sec-move-only-value-types), [§9.4](#sec-value-receivers-are-borrows)) — operand positions bind **borrows** of the operand values: [§15.3](#sec-move-only-value-types)'s by-value-move rule governs plain *parameters*, not operator operands, and the borrow is the reading the intrinsic move-only comparison already uses (§15.3's borrowing comparison) and that [§19.3](#sec-patterns)/[§35.5](#sec-choice-matching) already give the receiver, the scrutinee, and payload bindings. The [§19.3](#sec-patterns) discipline governs through the borrow — reads and non-destructive matches admitted, consuming operations rejected — and both operands are live after the operation. The accepted limit: an operator body cannot transfer an operand's payload into its result; it constructs the result from fresh or copied parts. (The marker-free operands that consume by keyword — `throw x` ([§31.1](#sec-the-throw-operand)), a Pattern B `await x`, an owning-iterator `yield return x` — are separate, non-operator positions, enumerated in [§28.3](#sec-consume-table).)

When a record overloads `=` and `<>`, the overloaded operators are invoked for `a = b` and `a <> b` directly, once [§8.4](#sec-=-and)'s null-safe wrapper has decided any absent operand — they do not delegate to `Equals`. The auto-generated or user-supplied `Equals(Object?)` and `Equals(T)` methods continue to exist; they are reachable via `.Equals(...)` call syntax and are what collections and pattern matching use. The disjunction is a two-case split: a **heterogeneous** overload leaves the record auto-hashable, so both are the auto-generated ones; a **homogeneous** one strips the property ([§9.2](#sec-body-records)), so both are user-supplied — of which the co-declaration rule below obliges only `Equals(T)`, and a record that wants a meaningful `Equals(Object?)` declares it too — undeclared, that member is not callable on a record-typed receiver ([§9.2](#sec-body-records)'s per-member use-site error) and the inherited box-identity `Equals` is reached only through an `Object`-typed receiver, per [§9.2](#sec-body-records)'s three-member remedy.

**Co-declaration rule (compiler-enforced).** A record, enum, or choice that overloads `=`/`<>` with **both operands of the declaring type** must also declare `Equals(T)` and `GetHashCode` — on a record, an enum, or a choice alike (a record's `override GetHashCode`; an enum's or choice's `override` or plain spelling, [§10.5](#sec-restrictions), [§35.2](#sec-choice-members)) — the same discipline, and the same diagnostic style, as [§8.3](#sec-equals-and-gethashcode)'s Equals→GetHashCode pairing. The three surfaces (`=`, `Equals`, hashing) can otherwise silently diverge exactly where it hurts: `a = b` true while a `Set<T>` treats them as distinct. The rule does not force delegation (operator overloads admit heterogeneous operand types, so "the operator is the body of Equals" is ill-defined in general); it forces the author to *state* all three, so a divergence is a visible choice rather than an accident. Heterogeneous-operand overloads (`T = U`) carry no such obligation. On a **move-only** `T`, the declared `Equals(other: T): bool` parameter binds a **borrow** exactly as the operator operands above do — keyed on the member shape (the [§10.5](#sec-restrictions)-family comparison surface), not on co-declaration, so a lone `Equals(T)` on an owning choice takes the same reading — and `a.Equals(b)` consumes neither value. An **elective** method parameter of the declaring type (`Merge(other: C)`, say) is outside the carve and remains [§15.3](#sec-move-only-value-types)'s by-value-move. (There is no exemption for compiler-intrinsic types. The pointer records of stdlib [§10.0](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-intptr-and-uintptr) and [§10.5](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-system-interop-ptr) — `IntPtr`, `UIntPtr`, `Ptr<T>` — declare `Equals(T)` and `override GetHashCode` beside their operators like any other record: the homogeneous overload these types declare strips them of **auto-hashable** ([§9.2](#sec-body-records)'s third disqualifier), so without the co-declared pair the two types whose purpose is comparison by address would carry an overloaded `=` with no `Equals`/`GetHashCode` beside it — outside **hashable** ([§3.6](#sec-derived-type-properties)'s hashable row, whose *declares user equality* arm is this very rule) and unusable as a `Dictionary`/`Set` key, this rule's own divergence reached from the other side.)

**No applicable operator.** A use of one of [§25.1](#sec-overloadable-operators)'s operators, binary or unary, to which neither a [§3.5](#sec-operators-on-primitive-types) intrinsic nor an overload from the candidate set above applies is a compile error at the expression: `Color + 1` over an enum that declares no `operator +`, or `-r` over a record that declares no unary `-`. `string` is covered by those two sources, its comparison operators being §3.5 intrinsics and its `+` a declared overload. The one fallback is equality: `=` and `<>` with no applicable overload are [§8.4](#sec-=-and)'s equality, which governs them.

<a id="sec-examples"></a>
### 25.3 Examples

```bezel
record Vector2(X: double, Y: double)
  public static method operator +(left: Vector2, right: Vector2): Vector2 =>
    new Vector2(left.X + right.X, left.Y + right.Y);

  public static method operator *(v: Vector2, scalar: double): Vector2 =>
    new Vector2(v.X * scalar, v.Y * scalar);
end Vector2;
```

Bitwise complement is overloadable for types with a natural bit-pattern or set-complement reading:

```bezel
record BitMask(Bits: ulong)
  public static method operator ~(m: BitMask): BitMask =>
    new BitMask(~m.Bits);
end BitMask;
```

For domain-specific inversion that does not match a bitwise reading, define a named method instead:

```bezel
record TriBool(Value: int)
  public method Negate(): TriBool => (case Value of
    0 => new TriBool(1),
    1 => new TriBool(0),
    _ => this);
end TriBool;
```

The named method form makes the inversion explicit at the call site (`t.Negate()` rather than `not t`), which is preferable when the operation departs from the boolean reading of `not` ([§14.4](Bezel_Design_Rationale.md#sec-not-is-not-user-overloadable) of the design rationale).

When an operator overload is block-bodied (statements followed by `end`, rather than the expression form `=> ...`), the optional name in the closing `end` is written as `end operator OpToken;` — e.g. `end operator ~;` or `end operator +;`. The named-end form is recommended for non-trivial operator bodies.

<a id="sec-no-user-defined-conversion-operators"></a>
### 25.4 No user-defined conversion operators

User-defined types — records and classes — cannot declare implicit or explicit conversion operators. There is no syntactic form for declaring "convert from S to T" on a user type; the explicit-cast expression `T(value)` ([§5.2](#sec-explicit-conversions)) and the implicit-conversion rules ([§5.1](#sec-implicit-conversions)) apply only to the built-in conversions enumerated in [§5](#sec-type-conversions) and to the compiler-intrinsic conversions on `IntPtr`/`UIntPtr` ([§32.7](#sec-pointers-and-intptr)).

To express a conversion between user types, define a named factory or instance method:

```bezel
// Construction-style conversion: factory method on the destination type.
record Money(Amount: decimal, Currency: string)
  public static method FromDecimal(amount: decimal, currency: string): Money =>
    new Money(amount, currency);
end Money;

// Projection-style conversion: instance method on the source type.
record User(Id: int, Name: string, Email: string);

record UserDto(Id: int, Name: string, Email: string)
  public method ToUser(): User => new User(Id, Name, Email);
end UserDto;
```

Rationale [§14.5](Bezel_Design_Rationale.md#sec-no-implicit-conversion-operators) records why conversions between user types are named methods.

The compiler-intrinsic conversions on `IntPtr` and `UIntPtr` ([§32.7](#sec-pointers-and-intptr)) — explicit casts to and from `long` and `ulong` — are not user-defined and are not covered by this rule. They exist because `IntPtr`/`UIntPtr` are intrinsic FFI-boundary types whose explicit-cast forms are part of the compiler's pointer-handling surface, not a user-overridable mechanism.

---

<a id="sec-extension-blocks"></a>
## 26. Extension Blocks

An extension block adds methods and computed read-only properties to a type without modifying the type's source.

<a id="sec-extension-blocks-declaration"></a>
### 26.1 Declaration

*(Extension methods and expression-bodied extension properties may be declared `pure` — [§22.15](#sec-pure-members); the receiver borrow composes with the read rules.)*

```bezel
extension string
  public property IsBlank: bool => this.Length = 0 or this.Trim().Length = 0;
  public method Words(): owned Array<string> => this.Split(' ');
end;
```

An extension block is declared at module level. It may be `public` or `internal` (default `internal`). The block ends with `end;` or `end extension;` ([§1.6](#sec-statements-and-termination)).

Inside the block, methods and computed properties are written as if they were instance members. `this` refers to the receiver.

<a id="sec-what-can-be-extended"></a>
### 26.2 What can be extended

- Classes (including `Object`).
- Interfaces.
- Records.
- Enums.
- Built-in primitive types.

What cannot be extended:

- Type parameters (`extension T` is meaningless).
- Nullable types directly (`extension int?`). Extend the non-nullable form; callers handle nullability at the call site with `?.` ([§7.5](#sec-null-conditional-access)).
- Function types.
- Choices. The extendable list above is closed against the choice kind — no [§14.2](#sec-constraints) constraint names the value-like classification bound a payload-generic extension surface would need, and the value-payload combinator surface of stdlib `Result<T, E>` is **compiler-provided** ([§35.2](#sec-choice-members)), not an extension block.
- Inline-array types (`extension [N]T`). Inline arrays are value-typed but their identity is per-size — `[3]int` and `[4]int` are distinct types — so an extension declaration would have to fix N, making the form rarely useful. Operations that should work across multiple inline-array sizes are typically written as static methods that take a specific inline-array type per overload, or that take a heap-array view (`Array<T>`) that the caller constructs from the inline array's contents.

<a id="sec-extension-blocks-restrictions"></a>
### 26.3 Restrictions

- Only methods and computed read-only properties. An extension property is **expression-bodied only** (`property Name: Type => expr;`) — the block-accessor form is not admitted; multi-statement logic goes in a method.
- No fields, auto-properties, constructors, destructors, or `owned` fields.
- No operator overloads.
- No indexers.
- No `static` members: a `static` modifier inside an extension block is a compile error. An extension block adds receiver-directed members only; statics resolve against the extended type's own declarations ([§22.12](#sec-static-members)), and admitting extension statics would need its own resolution, merging, and ambiguity story for no recorded need. Write a static method on a static class instead.
- No `virtual`, `override`, `abstract`, or `sealed` — extensions are statically dispatched.
- Extension members must be declared `public` or `internal`; `protected` and `private` are compile errors — an extension block has no declaring class and no inheritance, so [§13.1](#sec-levels)'s definitions for those levels do not apply. The member's effective visibility is the more restrictive of the block's reach and the member's own declaration (mirroring [§11.6](#sec-nested-types)'s nested-type rule).
- Extension members see only the extended type's public API. From the same module, `internal` members are also visible.

<a id="sec-generic-extensions"></a>
### 26.4 Generic extensions

**Type-parameter binding.** In the extended type's argument positions, each **bare single-segment non-nullable identifier** introduces a fresh block-level type parameter — *always*, shadowing any same-named type in scope (the compiler warns on such shadowing). This is the only implicit type-parameter binding in the language, so the rule is stated exactly: multiple parameters are permitted (`extension Dictionary<K, V>`), and each binds a distinct name: an identifier introduced at two argument positions (`extension Dictionary<K, K>`, `extension IEnumerable<Pair<T, T>>`) is a compile error at its second occurrence naming this rule, since the head binds names and states no equality between positions; a **concrete** instantiation is written with keyword/primitive types, qualified names, or generic instantiations (`extension IEnumerable<int>`, `extension IEnumerable<Array<byte>>`), none of which are bare single-segment identifiers. The alternative — resolving the identifier against scope and only binding when unresolved — is declined: it would let an unrelated type declaration elsewhere silently re-mean an extension block (action at a distance). The binding rule applies at **any nesting depth** of the extended type's argument positions: `extension IEnumerable<Array<T>>` binds `T`, and `extension Dictionary<K, Array<V>>` binds `K` and `V`. "Argument positions" are a **constructed generic type's** argument positions and nothing else: a **function type's parameter and return slots are not among them**, so `extension Array<(T) -> T>` binds no `T`, and the bare identifier there is a compile error naming this rule rather than an unresolved-name error. The nesting clause composes only through generic arguments — `extension IEnumerable<Array<(T) -> T>>` binds nothing either. A **nullable-marked** identifier in an argument position (`extension Array<T?>`) binds nothing and is a compile error naming this rule — only the bare non-nullable identifier introduces a parameter. Nothing is lost by the rejection: a bare `T` already unifies with nullable arguments (`extension Array<T>` applies to `Array<int?>` with `T = int?`); the only capability a `T?` head would add — constraining a block to *only* nullable instantiations — is deferred until a need is recorded.

```bezel
extension IEnumerable<T> where T: IComparable<T>
  public method Sort(): owned Array<T>
    var items := this.ToArray();
    // ...
    return items;
  end Sort;
end;
```

The block-level type parameter is in scope throughout the block. Methods may introduce their own type parameters, named apart from the block's ([§14.1](#sec-generic-declarations)):

```bezel
extension IEnumerable<T>
  public method Map<U>(transform: (T) -> U): owned Array<U>
    var result := new Array<U>();
    for var item in this do
      result.Add(transform(item));
    end;
    return result;
  end Map;
end;
```

A `where` clause on the block constrains which instantiations of the extended type the extension applies to. The head names the extended type at the block-level parameters, and the extended type's declared constraints are decided there as at an instantiation site ([§14.2](#sec-constraints) *A type parameter as the type argument*), by the parameters' constraints, which are the block's `where` clause and nothing else: `extension OwningArray<T>` is a compile error naming the constraint and `T`, `extension OwningArray<T> where T: class` is admitted, and `extension Counter<K>` likewise states `where K: hashable`. No requirement of [§3.6](#sec-derived-type-properties) rule 2 is carried from the head: each receiver the block applies to is an instantiation formed, and checked, where its type is named.

<a id="sec-resolution"></a>
### 26.5 Resolution

When the compiler encounters `x.Foo(args)`:

1. **Instance members win — by name.** If `x`'s declared type (or any base type) *declares* any instance member named `Foo` — of any arity, applicability, or accessibility — instance resolution is committed and extension blocks are **never consulted** for that name on that receiver. If the committed instance lookup then fails (no applicable overload, [§22.5](#sec-optional-parameters-and-named-arguments)/[§22.6](#sec-overloading), or the member is inaccessible, [§13.1](#sec-levels)), the call is a compile error citing the instance member(s); it does not fall back to an extension (the diagnostic should note a same-named extension where one exists). Blocking by *name* rather than by applicability or accessibility keeps resolution predictable: whether a call reaches an instance member or an extension never depends on argument types or the caller's access level, so changing an overload's signature or a member's visibility cannot silently re-route a call across the instance/extension boundary.
2. **Extension members.** If the receiver's type declares no instance member of that name, the compiler searches the current module and all imported modules — which always includes the standard library's extension modules over always-available types ([§2.3](#sec-always-available-names)'s invariant) — for extension blocks on `x`'s type, base types, or implemented interfaces, considering only extension members visible at the call site ([§26.3](#sec-extension-blocks-restrictions)'s effective-visibility rule). When an extension block is declared on a generic type (e.g. `extension IEnumerable<T>`), the block-level type parameter is inferred from the receiver's type: if `x` has type `Array<int>` and `Array<int>` implements `IEnumerable<int>`, then `T` is inferred as `int`. The receiver-driven inference is the unification of [§14.5](#sec-type-argument-inference) applied to the extension head: the receiver's static type is unified against the declared head, exactly and structurally, binding the block-level parameters.
3. **Most specific type wins.** Extensions on the most specific type are preferred per the subtype ordering below.
4. **Ambiguity.** If two equally-specific extensions match, the call is a compile error.
