Because extension blocks are nameless, the diagnostic must identify each candidate by what it *has*: its **defining module**, its **declared head including any `where` clause**, and its **declaration site**. The remedies are the mechanisms that exist: remove or narrow a conflicting import; hoist the intended behavior into a helper static method (taking the receiver as a parameter) on a static class and call that; or, when the colliding blocks are under the author's control, give the members **distinct names**, or merge the blocks into one member that dispatches internally (rationale [§17.10](Bezel_Design_Rationale.md#sec-auto-ranked-extension-specificity)). No call-site syntax qualifies an extension's defining type, because extension blocks are nameless and extensions have no static-invocation form; a first-class extension-disambiguation spelling is deferred, not designed here (rationale [§18](Bezel_Design_Rationale.md#sec-things-deferred)).

Adding a real method to a type silently takes priority over an extension with the same name — by design.

Extensions are resolved on the **compile-time** type of the receiver, not the runtime type. Polymorphism requires `virtual`, not extensions.

<a id="sec-specificity-ordering"></a>
#### 26.5.1 Specificity ordering

For receiver type R, specificity ranks the **applicable** candidates: extension members of the called name that match the call's arity and argument types, from blocks whose head matches R (step 2 of [§26.5](#sec-resolution)), with block-level `where` clauses satisfied by the arguments inferred from the receiver. A `where` clause is an *applicability* filter, never a ranking signal.

An extension on E1 is **more specific** than one on E2 when E1 is a subtype of E2 and E2 is not a subtype of E1. The subtype test is evaluated on the **receiver-substituted heads**: each candidate's declared extension head has its block-level type parameters replaced by the arguments inferred from the receiver (step 2 of [§26.5](#sec-resolution)) before the test runs. Derived class beats base class; class beats interface implemented by that class; derived interface beats extended interface. So for a receiver of type `Array<int>`: `extension Array<T>` (substituted head `Array<int>`) is more specific than `extension IEnumerable<T>` (substituted head `IEnumerable<int>`), because `Array<int>` is a subtype of `IEnumerable<int>`.

If neither candidate's substituted head is a proper subtype of the other's, the candidates are equally specific and rule 4 of [§26.5](#sec-resolution) produces an ambiguity error. In particular, candidates with **identical substituted heads** never auto-rank: neither a more-concrete-looking declared head (`extension IEnumerable<int>` and `extension IEnumerable<T>` are indistinguishable after substitution for an `Array<int>` receiver) nor a stronger `where` clause on the same head makes one candidate more specific than the other. Auto-ranked specialization is declined, with a recorded re-addition condition (rationale [§17.10](Bezel_Design_Rationale.md#sec-auto-ranked-extension-specificity)).

```bezel
extension IEnumerable<T> where T: value
  // where T: value — the for-based body returns the iteration variable, which
  // at a class or interface substitution would be an enumerator-sourced borrow
  // that may not escape the loop (§28.3, §29.2); at value substitutions
  // the return copies the value and the admission is vacuous.
  public method First(): T
    for var item in this do return item; end;
    throw new InvalidOperationException("empty sequence");
  end First;
end;

extension Array<T>
  public method First(): T
    if this.Count = 0 then throw new InvalidOperationException("empty array"); end;
    return this[0];
  end First;
end;

var xs: Array<int> := [1, 2, 3];
var f := xs.First();     // selects the Array<T> member — substituted head Array<int>
                         // is a subtype of substituted head IEnumerable<int>
```

By contrast, two candidates whose substituted heads are identical are equally specific. If both of the following blocks are visible at the call site, the call is a compile error:

```bezel
extension IEnumerable<T> where T: value
  public method First(): T
    for var item in this do return item; end;
    throw new InvalidOperationException("empty sequence");
  end First;
end;

extension IEnumerable<int>
  public method First(): int
    // a hand-specialized int form
    for var item in this do return item; end;
    throw new InvalidOperationException("empty sequence");
  end First;
end;

var xs: Array<int> := [1, 2, 3];
var f := xs.First();     // ERROR: ambiguous — both substituted heads are IEnumerable<int>
```

The diagnostic names both candidates, and the remedies are rule 4's ([§26.5](#sec-resolution)).

<a id="sec-multiple-blocks-for-the-same-type"></a>
### 26.6 Multiple blocks for the same type

Multiple `extension` blocks targeting the same type may appear across files in the same module. The compiler merges them. Duplicate signatures are a compile error.

<a id="sec-ownership-in-extensions"></a>
### 26.7 Ownership in extensions

The receiver is always a borrow; extensions cannot store `this`, return it as `owned`, or dispose it. For a **value-kind** receiver, [§9.4](#sec-value-receivers-are-borrows)'s value-receiver rule applies in the extension body exactly as in a declared member body: a store landing in the receiver's own storage is a compile error (a store beyond a class- or interface-typed hop leaves the receiver and is legal — §9.4's mediating shape), and the receiver is fixed at the call as §9.4 states (*The receiver value is fixed at the call*); no extension member reaches a move-only receiver (§9.4 *Move-only receivers*). Other parameters may be `owned`, following normal method rules. Extensions may return `owned` values.

---

<a id="sec-lambdas-and-function-types"></a>
## 27. Lambdas and Function Types

Functions are first-class values: stored, passed, returned, held in fields.

<a id="sec-function-types"></a>
### 27.1 Function types

A function type is written `(params) -> returnType`:

```bezel
var add: (int, int) -> int;
var isPositive: (int) -> bool;
var log: (string) -> ();              // procedure
var noop: () -> ();
var now: () -> DateTime;
```

The parallel with method declarations:

| Method | Function type |
|---|---|
| `method Foo(x: int): bool` | `(int) -> bool` |
| `method Foo(x: int)` | `(int) -> ()` |
| `method Foo(): int` | `() -> int` |
| `method Foo()` | `() -> ()` |
| `method Foo(owned t: T)` | `(owned T) -> ()` |
| `method Foo(ref n: int)` | `(ref int) -> ()` |
| `method Foo(out r: int)` | `(out int) -> ()` |
| `method Foo(out owned r: T)` | `(out owned T) -> ()` |

A method without a return type has function type returning `()`.

Function types may include the parameter modifiers `owned`, `ref`, `out`, `scoped`, and the combination `out owned`. The modifier is part of the type — `(T) -> ()` and `(owned T) -> ()` are distinct function types, and the same applies to the other modifier forms. Function-type compatibility requires modifiers to match exactly; there is no implicit conversion between modified and unmodified parameter slots. The available modifier combinations match those of method declarations ([§22.3](#sec-parameter-modifiers) and grammar A.4). A `scoped` parameter position is likewise part of a function signature's identity, like `ref`/`out` ([§28.14](#sec-scoped-callback-parameters)): `(scoped () -> Task) -> ()` and `(() -> Task) -> ()` are distinct types with no conversion between them.

Function types may include parameter names. Names are documentation only; they do not affect type identity:

```bezel
var handler: (itemId: int, quantity: int, priority: int) -> bool;
```

`(int, int, int) -> bool` and the named form are the same type. Calls are positional.

**A call through a function-typed value admits no named argument ([#4085](https://github.com/s8lap/bezel-lang/issues/4085)).** The named form (`Identifier :=`, [§22.5](#sec-optional-parameters-and-named-arguments)) at an invocation whose callee is a function-typed value — a parameter, local, field, or property of function type, or any expression of one — is a compile error naming this rule, at the plain invocation form and at the null-conditional form `e?(…)` over a nullable function type ([§27.2](#sec-nullable-function-types), [§27.7](#sec-calling-function-values)) alike: the treatment [§23.5](#sec-properties-and-indexers-restrictions) gives an index position, for the same reason — the names a function type may declare are documentation, not caller-bindable surface, and a function type declares no defaults, so §22.5's optional-parameter and named-binding machinery is never reached. The form is *rejected*, not bound by position: a name accepted and then ignored could spell one binding and perform another (`caller(b := 2, a := 100)` against `(a: int, b: int) -> int` read as a swap and ran as `caller(2, 100)`). Binding by name and an order-checked label are both declined (rationale [§3.16](Bezel_Design_Rationale.md#sec-function-value-calls-are-positional)).

<a id="sec-function-type-assignability"></a>
#### 27.1.1 Function-type assignability

A function-typed **value** may be used where a different function type is expected under one narrow variance rule; everything else requires an exact match — and every rule below is slot-wise over **equal parameter counts**: a value is never usable at a function type with a different number of parameter slots, whatever the slots' types (at an overloaded call [§22.6](#sec-implicit-conversion-ranking)'s *Parameter count at a function-typed position* makes such a candidate inapplicable at the position):

- **Parameter slots** of class or interface type are **contravariant**: the target's parameter type must implicitly *reference*-convert to the value's ([§5.1](#sec-implicit-conversions), reference conversions only) — a `(Animal) -> ()` value is usable where `(Dog) -> ()` is expected. A slot whose type in the target is a function type is not such a slot, whatever the value's slot type: a `(Object) -> ()` value is not usable where `(() -> int) -> ()` is expected.
- The **return slot**, when of class or interface type, is **covariant**: the value's return type must implicitly reference-convert to the target's — a `() -> Dog` value is usable as `() -> Animal`. A return slot whose type in the value is a function type is not such a slot, whatever the target's: a `() -> (() -> int)` value is not usable where `() -> Object` is expected.
- **Value-typed, record-typed, and primitive slots are invariant.** No numeric widening, boxing, or other representation-changing conversion applies to a slot of an already-constructed function value: there is no adapter object to perform it.
- **Modifier slots** (`owned`/`ref`/`out`/`out owned`/`scoped`) must match **exactly** ([§27.1](#sec-function-types)); per-slot nullability follows the standard [§7](#sec-nullability-2) rules.
- **Mint-announcing return slots are announcement-bearing** (the slot's declared family is **type-announced**, [K6.2](#sec-kernel-k6); unified)**:** a function-typed value whose return slot (nullability stripped) is a mint-announcing type — a `Task`-family type, or one of the eight [§29.3](#sec-iterator-methods)/[§30.7](#sec-asynchronous-programming-async-iterators) iterable and enumerator interface heads (`IEnumerable<T>`, `IEnumerator<T>`, `IAsyncEnumerable<T>`, `IAsyncEnumerator<T>`, `IOwningEnumerable<T>`, `IOwningEnumerator<T>`, `IOwningAsyncEnumerable<T>`, `IOwningAsyncEnumerator<T>`; a declared slot type is all this rule can key on, so a lazy query needs no separate mention: a lazy query's declared type is ordinarily a head already, and where it is not ([§28.3](#sec-producers)'s derived-interface case) [§27.6](#sec-method-references) keeps it off every formed slot) — is usable only where the target's return slot (nullability stripped) is also a type of the **same family** — covariance applies *within* a family (`() -> Task<int>` is usable as `() -> Task`; `() -> IEnumerable<Dog>` as `() -> IEnumerable<Animal>` under the ordinary reference-conversion rule: `IEnumerable<out T>`, stdlib §4.12) and never across a family boundary (`() -> Task<int>` is not usable as `() -> Object`, nor `() -> IEnumerable<int>` as `() -> Object`, nor either family's slot as the other's). Nor can within-family covariance launder the **drain contract**: the owning heads extend `IDisposable`/`IAsyncDisposable`, not the non-owning heads (stdlib §4.13), so no reference conversion exists from `() -> IOwningEnumerable<T>` to `() -> IEnumerable<T>` — a consuming face never retypes to a lending one. The rule is a **use-site admission, not a conversion**: it engages even where no conversion is required. The **target's return slot is read from its declared, pre-substitution type**: a bare-type-parameter slot is not announcement-bearing, so a mint-announcing value may not inhabit it even at an instantiation whose substitution makes the two types coincide — the inhabitant-side closure of the bare-parameter seam ([§28.3](#sec-bare-type-parameter-returns); for the `Task` family the member's parameter-position instantiation is itself already excluded there). The unmarked mint-announcing return is container-ownership-transferring ([§28.3](#sec-producers)) — the same announcement-by-declared-type logic as an `owned` return — so it takes the modifier slots' exact-match discipline rather than the concrete-class covariance rule: retyping it to a non-family slot would erase the calls-mint announcement, and an invocation through the retyped face would classify the minted frame as a borrow — a leak. Stdlib §5's derived interfaces (`IOrderedEnumerable<T>`, `IGrouping<TKey, T>`) extend `IEnumerable<T>` but are outside the family: a value whose return slot is one of them is not announcement-bearing and takes the ordinary covariance rule — sound, including covariantly *into* a head-typed target slot, because no derived-interface slot can conceal a minting face ([§28.3](#sec-factory-methods-and-sourceless-returns)'s static-announcement rule leaves no unmarked derived-interface factory to form over, [§28.3](#sec-bare-type-parameter-returns)'s *Concrete-slot function bodies* admission rejects a minting lambda inhabitant, and [§27.6](#sec-method-references) bars a lazy-query-kinded callee from being formed at a derived-interface slot at all). The same boundary governs **method-reference formation** ([§27.6](#sec-method-references)): formation over a callee whose declared return type is mint-announcing — any callee kind — may bridge only to a target slot in the same family (and a property reference over a mint-announcing-typed property is rejected outright — [§27.6](#sec-method-references)); once formed, a value obeys this bullet whatever its origin.

Assignability under this rule preserves **identity**: the value is the same function object viewed at a compatible function type (like interface variance, [§12.9](#sec-variance)), so function-value equality ([§27.7.1](#sec-equality-of-function-values)) is unaffected by the retyping. This *value*-assignability rule is distinct from **method-reference formation** ([§27.6](#sec-method-references)): forming a reference from a *named method* against a target type may bridge any [§5.1](#sec-implicit-conversions) implicit conversion, because the compiler synthesizes the adapter at the formation site; once formed, the value obeys the narrower rule above. This subsection is the single normative statement of these criteria; [§27.6](#sec-method-references) defers to it, and the admission of a **lambda literal** at a target-typed non-call position ([§27.3](#sec-lambda-expressions)) is the one other site-typed bridge — the literal, like a formed reference, is typed at the site.

<a id="sec-lambda-parameter-modifiers"></a>
#### Lambda parameter modifiers

Lambda parameters may carry the same modifiers when the target function type expects them:

```bezel
// _pool is a field of the enclosing class: private owned _pool: OwningArray<Connection>;
var adopt: (owned Connection) -> () := lambda(owned c) => _pool.Add(move c);
```

When the target type is known from context, the lambda's parameter modifiers may be omitted in source — the compiler infers them from the target. When inferring is not possible (a `var` introduction with no target context), the modifier must be written explicitly to produce a function value of the modified type.

<a id="sec-nullable-function-types"></a>
### 27.2 Nullable function types

```bezel
var callback: ((int) -> bool)?;       // nullable function returning bool
var nullableReturn: (int) -> bool?;   // non-null function returning a nullable bool
```

The parentheses around the function type are required before `?`. Without them, the `?` would attach to the return type.

<a id="sec-lambda-expressions"></a>
### 27.3 Lambda expressions

A lambda expression is **keyword-led** (grammar A.7 `LambdaExpr`): the reserved word `lambda` — preceded by `async` for the asynchronous form ([§30.6](#sec-async-lambdas)) — then a parenthesized parameter list (the empty pair for zero parameters; there is no paren-free form), an optional **return-type ascription**, `=>`, and the body. The keyword commits the parse at its first token — `lambda` begins no other expression or statement — the same committed-reading property the paren atoms have ([§17.1](#sec-precedence) note); in particular, a parenthesized construct followed by `=>` (a `when`-guard arm, a grouped expression) can never be read as a lambda prefix.

Expression body:
```bezel
var twice := lambda(x: int) => x * 2;
var greet := lambda(name: string) => $"Hello, {name}!";
```

Block body:
```bezel
var processItem := lambda(item: Item) => do
  var normalized := Normalize(item);
  var enriched := Enrich(normalized);
  return enriched;
end;
```

Inside a value-returning block-bodied lambda, `return` is required on every exit path.

**Ignored parameters.** A parameter slot may be the ignore `_` ([§17.13](#sec-the-discard-_)): it is accepted, binds nothing, and contributes its slot to the lambda's function type as normal — under a target type `(T, U) -> U`, `lambda(_, x) => x` ignores its first argument. Because nothing is named, several ignores may coexist: `lambda(_, _) => 0` is legal. No parameter modifier and no type annotation compose with the bare ignore — `FuncParamMods` with `_` is rejected (a `ref` parameter reads and writes through its operand, which an ignore cannot supply, and a `scoped` parameter that binds nothing stores nothing), and a typed ignore slot is spelled by the target type, exactly the [§27.4](#sec-parameter-type-inference) inference story. The destructure-slot `_` ([§27.4](#sec-lambda-parameter-destructuring)) is the same nothing-is-bound reading per slot. A slot whose type is the **unit type** ([§4.7](#sec-the-unit-type)) may equally be *named*: under a target type `(()) -> ()` — the no-payload event handler of stdlib [§6.5](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-events-ievent-eventsource) — `lambda(u) => …` binds `u` to that type's single value as an ordinary value-typed parameter, so the ignore is a style preference at such a slot and not a requirement.

**Which block-bodied lambdas return a value.** A block-bodied lambda is a **procedure lambda** — its type is `(…) -> ()` — exactly when no path through its body executes a value-carrying `return e;`: its exits are bare `return;` and falling off the end. A body where one path returns a value and another exits without one is a compile error, the same totality rule as for methods. A target type, when present, is checked against this classification — a procedure-bodied lambda does not convert to a value-returning function type, nor the reverse.

**The return-type ascription.** Between the parameter list and `=>`, a lambda may ascribe its return type: `lambda(x: int): long => x * 2`. The ascription is **optional everywhere inference succeeds** — it is never a new obligation — and when present it behaves exactly as a method's declared return type: each `return e;` (and an expression body) is checked against it under [§5.1](#sec-implicit-conversions), including implicit widening (`return dog;` under `: Animal`); the ascription is a written integer target for [§4.2](#sec-integer-types)'s target-typed integer constant (`lambda(): long => 3_000_000_000`, admitted by [§5.1](#sec-implicit-conversions)'s constant narrowing); and a declared nullable return is the target that admits `null`-producing arms ([§20](#sec-the-if-expression)). A unit ascription (`: ()`) declares a procedure lambda. When both a target type and an ascription are present, they must agree under [§27.1.1](#sec-function-type-assignability)'s return rule — the ascription never bridges a conversion the value itself could not. An ascribed lambda's `return` operands and expression body are **declared-result positions** for choice-case constructions ([§35.3](#sec-choice-construction)) — the ascription is a written declared result type, exactly as a method's.

**Return-type inference without a target.** In a context with no target type, a value-returning block-bodied lambda's return type is inferred only when **every** `return e;` expression in the body has the *same* type; otherwise the lambda is a compile error asking for a target type, a return-type ascription (this section), or an ascribed variable type. The compiler does not unify divergent return types to a common supertype — an inference that silently computed `Animal` from `return dog;` and `return cat;` would make the lambda's type sensitive to distant hierarchy edits; the programmer states the intended type instead (the explicit-over-implicit stance of [§22.6](#sec-implicit-conversion-ranking)). The ascription is the on-site spelling of that statement:

```bezel
var classify := lambda(score: int): string? => do
  if score < 0 then return null; end;
  if score >= 90 then return "A"; end;
  return "pass";
end;
```

Expression-bodied lambdas need no inference rule: the body expression's type is the return type, and a body of type `()` makes a procedure lambda.

**Admission at a target-typed non-call position.** A lambda literal at a position that supplies a function-typed target other than a call argument — the initializer of a declared function-typed local or field, an assignment to a function-typed location, a `return` against a declared function-typed return type — is admitted under the argument-position rule of [§14.5](#sec-type-argument-inference) phase 2 and [§22.6](#sec-overloading) (*Lambda-literal arguments*): its parameters take the target's parameter types ([§27.4](#sec-parameter-type-inference)), the body is typed, and its inferred return type must equal the target's return slot or implicitly convert to it ([§5.1](#sec-implicit-conversions)); otherwise the lambda is a compile error at the position (`var f: (int) -> long := lambda(x) => x * 2;` is admitted, the `int` body widening to `long`). The conversion is admitted for the reason [§27.1.1](#sec-function-type-assignability) gives for method-reference formation — the compiler types the body at the site and can bridge it; a function-typed **value** at the same position is not a literal and takes §27.1.1's narrower rule unchanged. An ascribed lambda's ascription is its written return type and must agree with the target as the ascription paragraph above states — judged as a value's return type under §27.1.1 — so an ascription narrows what the position admits: `var g: (int) -> long := lambda(x): int => x * 2;` is rejected where the unascribed form is admitted.

For procedure lambdas, the body may also be a single expression whose result is discarded — a target-driven classification: at an overloaded call such a lambda is applicable at a procedure slot (`-> ()`) and ranks *converting* there ([§22.6](#sec-overloading) *Lambda-literal arguments*); the discarded result is under [§21.9](#sec-statement-form-of-expressions)'s expression-statement regime — a warning for a copyable, `string`, runtime-managed or trivial-dispose result, and for a non-trivial-dispose class, an interface-typed or a `Task`-family result the hard error directing to `_ := …` or `using var _ := …` ([§17.13](#sec-the-discard-_)) in a block body:
```bezel
var log := lambda(msg: string) => Console.WriteLine(msg);
```

<a id="sec-parameter-type-inference"></a>
### 27.4 Parameter type inference

When the lambda's target type is known from context, parameter type annotations may be omitted:

```bezel
var doubled := numbers.Select(lambda(x) => x * 2);
var positives := numbers.Where(lambda(x) => x > 0);
```

In top-level contexts with no target type (`var f := lambda(x) => x * 2;`), parameter types must be specified.

<a id="sec-lambda-parameter-destructuring"></a>
#### Lambda-parameter record destructuring

A lambda parameter may be a positional record **destructuring** in place of an identifier:

```bezel
var labels := entries.Select(lambda(Entry(k, v)) => $"{k}: {v}");
var positives := points.Where(lambda(Point(x, _)) => x > 0);
```

The form reuses [§19.3](#sec-patterns)'s positional-destructuring spelling with parameter-position restrictions. A destructuring parameter is a **binding form, not a test**, so only irrefutable elements are admitted:

- The head must name a **positional record type**, and it must be *exactly* the parameter's type: when a target type supplies the parameter type, a head naming any other type is a compile error (no subtype test, nothing to fail at runtime); when no target type is available, the head *is* the annotation — `lambda(Entry(k, v)) => …` alone types the parameter as `Entry`.
- Each slot is a naked identifier binding, a discard `_`, or a nested destructuring meeting the same rules; the slot count must equal the record's positional-field count. Constants, ranges, relationals, type tests, `var`-form bindings, and alternatives are compile errors in parameter position — they are refutable, and a parameter list is not a `case`.
- The destructuring parameter admits no modifiers (`ref`, `scoped`) and no separate type annotation — the head carries the type.

Semantics are by desugaring: `lambda(Entry(k, v)) => body` behaves exactly as `lambda(p: Entry) => do var k := p.«first field»; var v := p.«second field»; …body… end` — each binding is an ordinary read of the corresponding positional field at body entry, with the standard ownership meaning ([§28.3](#sec-local-variables-ownership-and-borrows)): a copy for value-typed fields, a **borrow** of the argument's field for class-typed fields, a shared reference for runtime-managed fields. Nothing is consumed: the record argument is untouched, the bindings own nothing, and the lambda's function type is unchanged by the spelling (`(Entry) -> R`).

<a id="sec-closures"></a>
### 27.5 Closures

A lambda may reference variables from its enclosing scope. Captured variables are heap-allocated in a closure object, a `ref` or `out` parameter excepted (below). Modifications to a captured variable inside the lambda are visible outside, and vice versa. (For a captured **owned** binding the sharing is read-only in the ownership sense: the lambda may not assign to it, transfer from it, or dispose it — [§28.3](#sec-captured-owned-bindings).)

```bezel
public method MakeCounter(): () -> int
  var count := 0;
  return lambda() => do
    count := count + 1;
    return count;
  end;
end MakeCounter;
```

A lambda's parameters, destructuring slots and locals do not take the name of a local or parameter in scope where the lambda appears ([§21.1](#sec-variable-declarations) *Local names*), so each variable the lambda can capture has inside it the one spelling it has outside.

For `for` loop variables, each iteration produces a fresh binding. A lambda captured inside the body sees that iteration's value.

**Capturing a `ref` or `out` parameter.** A lambda may capture a `ref` or `out` parameter of an enclosing method, constructor or lambda ([§22.3](#sec-parameter-modifiers)). The capture names the parameter's own location, not a copy: a `ref` parameter aliases the caller's location, so a write through the closure is a write to it, and an `out` parameter is the callee's slot for the call, copied out on normal return. Neither location exists for the closure past the call, so the capture contributes the declaring body's scope to the closure's source set, whatever the parameter's type, as a captured owned local contributes its enclosing scope ([§28.3](#sec-borrow-lifetime-rules)'s closure bullet). The closure may be invoked, bound to a local, captured by another closure and passed as an argument within the call, under the rules for each; it may not be returned (in a deferred-activation frame included), stored in a field or collection, written through an `out` or `ref` parameter, or passed to a set-erasing position. The bound rides the source set, so it reaches every function value whose set carries such a capture — a closure that captures the closure, and a function value an invocation of it returns — by the closure bullet's provenance rule. A deferred-activation frame that carries such a value inherits the same bound: one minted by invoking it (the task an `async` lambda returns, an iterator or query frame), as a frame minted by invoking a call-bounded callback does ([§28.14](#sec-scoped-callback-parameters)'s *Call-bounded × deferred activation*, shape (2)), and one that holds it by frame residence, minted by a call that receives it at a plain function-typed parameter (shape (1)). Such a frame is consumed to its [K6.1](#sec-kernel-k6) bound within the call, an iterator or query frame by enumerating or disposing it. A task cannot be: a body that declares a `ref` or `out` parameter is never `async` ([§30.1](#sec-async-methods)), and disposing an unsettled task does not stop its frame ([§30.5](#sec-result-lifetime-and-task-disposal)). So in a synchronous body a task-returning invocation of such a value, and a task-returning call that receives it at a plain function-typed parameter, are compile errors; the abandonment residual [§30.1](#sec-async-methods) carries for a frame-held object borrow has no backstop at a stack location. A write to a captured `out` parameter inside the closure is not on the declaring body's paths: it does not discharge [§22.3](#sec-parameter-modifiers)'s must-assign obligation. A method reference formed over such a parameter's value (`a.M`) reads the parameter at formation ([§27.6](#sec-method-references)) and captures no location. To keep the value past the call, capture a copy: `var snap := x; return lambda() => snap;`.

**Definite assignment across a closure.** A lambda body's definite assignment ([§7.9](#sec-definite-assignment-for-non-nullable-fields)) starts from the enclosing body's state at the lambda's **formation**, the point at which the lambda expression is evaluated. A captured variable the enclosing body has definitely assigned there is assigned throughout the body. One it has not — a local of non-defaultable type, or an `out` parameter of any type, whose slot is unassigned until the callee writes it ([§22.3](#sec-parameter-modifiers)) — is unassigned at the body's entry, so a read of it in the body is a compile error unless the body assigns it first on every path to the read. One formation counts the variable assigned: where the lambda expression is the whole right-hand side of a plain assignment to a captured local or `out` parameter (`f := lambda …`), that variable is assigned in the lambda's body, since the store follows the right-hand side's evaluation, forming a lambda invokes nothing, and so no invocation precedes the store. This is how a recursive closure is written: `var fact: (int) -> int; fact := lambda(n: int) => (if n <= 1 then 1 else n * fact(n - 1));`. The analysis does not follow invocations: a write in the body is not on the enclosing body's paths, so it assigns the variable nowhere outside the body, for a local as for an `out` parameter (above). Given `out x: int` not yet assigned, `var f := lambda() => x + 1; x := 5; return f();` is rejected, although `f` runs after the assignment; assign `x` before forming the lambda. A lambda formed inside a lambda body starts from that body's state at its own formation.

<a id="sec-method-references"></a>
### 27.6 Method references

When a lambda's body is just a call to an existing method, the method reference may be used directly:

```bezel
var parsed := strings.Select(int.Parse);
var lengths := names.Select(string.Length);       // property reference
var sorted := numbers.OrderBy(Math.Abs);          // static method
var greetings := names.Select(greeter.Greet);    // bound instance method
```

Method references work for static methods, instance methods (the instance is captured at formation — by reference for class-typed receivers, **by copy** for value-shaped (record) receivers, which is what denies record receivers identity in [§27.7.1](#sec-equality-of-function-values)), properties, and extension methods. A property reference produces the getter; its type is `(Receiver) -> PropertyType` for instance properties and `() -> PropertyType` for static properties. Whether the property also has a setter is irrelevant; setter references are not supported. The reference's signature must be compatible with the target function type: its parameter and return types unify with the target's under the standard implicit-conversion rules ([§5.1](#sec-implicit-conversions)) — the same criterion applied to an overloaded reference (below) — while modifier slots (`owned`/`ref`/`out`/`scoped`) must match exactly. (Formation may bridge representation-changing conversions by synthesizing an adapter at the reference site; assignability between two already-formed function-typed *values* is the narrower variance rule of [§27.1.1](#sec-function-type-assignability). Return-slot bridging respects the mint-announcing family boundary of [§27.1.1](#sec-function-type-assignability).) A parameter slot of function type is not formed over a callee parameter declared `Object`, or at a type parameter the formation substitutes with a function type ([§28.14](#sec-scoped-callback-parameters)'s *method-reference formation bar*).

A property reference over a property whose declared type (nullability stripped) is a **mint-announcing type** — `Task`-family or iterable-family — is rejected at the formation site: the reference's function type would carry a mint-announcing return slot, whose invocation the rule classifies as an owned mint ([§28.3](#sec-producers), *Calls mint for the mint-announcing families*), while the underlying getter lends its storage ([§30.11](#sec-taskcompletionsourcet-and-ownedtaskcompletionsourcet)'s source-owns-task rule; the stored-view property face, whose lend-only guarantee is axiom [A4](#sec-axiom-register)'s) — formation would pair two owners over one stored frame. Read the property directly — consume a task through [§30.5](#sec-result-lifetime-and-task-disposal)'s admitted borrow positions, iterate a stored view as storage — or wrap a genuine *producer* (a method reference over a `Task`- or iterable-returning method remains the ordinary, admissible spelling). The same mint/lend boundary governs return-slot bridging at formation generally ([§27.1.1](#sec-function-type-assignability)'s family rule).

A method reference over a callee — **any callee kind** — whose declared return type (nullability stripped) is one of the [§29.3](#sec-iterator-methods)/[§30.7](#sec-asynchronous-programming-async-iterators) iterable or enumerator interfaces or a lazy query — the calls-mint rule's frame-minting producers ([§28.3](#sec-producers) *Calls mint for the mint-announcing families*: "the caller … hold[s] the container obligation") — may be formed only against a target slot whose return (nullability stripped) is also such an interface, or left at the callee's own type — the own-type spelling takes **precedence** over the rejection list that follows: a reference formed at exactly the callee's declared signature bridges nothing, and the list governs *retyping*, which is the only place it applies (its one carve is the lazy-query-kind bar below): bridging the reference to any other return slot (`() -> Object`, a concrete class or interface type, a bare-type-parameter slot) is rejected at the formation site — the retyped face would erase the frame-mint announcement (type-announced, [K6.2](#sec-kernel-k6)), and an invocation through it would classify under the producers row as a borrow: a leaked caller-owned frame. Where the callee is minting **by its lazy-query kind** and its declared return type is outside the eight heads (a stdlib §5 derived interface — `OrderBy`/`ThenBy`'s `IOrderedEnumerable<T>`; [§28.3](#sec-producers) *Calls mint for the mint-announcing families*), the own-type spelling is **not available**: formation must bridge to a head-typed slot, the adapter being the ordinary reference conversion `IOrderedEnumerable<T>` → `IEnumerable<T>` that formation already synthesizes (the adapter clause above). No formed value therefore ever carries a derived-interface return slot over a minting callee — which is what keeps [§27.1.1](#sec-function-type-assignability)'s derived-interface admission sound. The `Task`-family boundary is the same rule at the other family; a *formed* value's retyping obeys [§27.1.1](#sec-function-type-assignability)'s announcement-bearing rule whatever the value's origin.

For an extension method, the reference uses the extended type's name as qualifier; the resulting function has the receiver as its first parameter:

```bezel
var counter: (IEnumerable<int>) -> int := IEnumerable<int>.Count;
```

Indexers cannot be used as method references; the parameter list makes the natural function type ambiguous.

<a id="sec-method-references-to-overloaded-methods"></a>
#### Method references to overloaded methods

When the named method (or property) is overloaded, the reference is resolved using the **target function type** at the use site. The compiler selects the overload whose parameter types and return type unify with the target's parameter and return types under the standard implicit-conversion rules ([§5.1](#sec-implicit-conversions)):

```bezel
var sortedByAbs := numbers.OrderBy(Math.Abs);     // double or int? Resolved
                                                  //   from numbers.ElementType
                                                  //   and OrderBy's target type.
```

If `numbers` has type `Array<int>`, `OrderBy<TKey>` expects a `(int) -> TKey`; the reference `Math.Abs` resolves to the `Math.Abs(int): int` overload. If `numbers` is `Array<double>`, the same reference resolves to `Math.Abs(double): double`.

**Selection among several unifying candidates: exact-preferred.** More than one overload may unify with the target — against `(int) -> TKey`, `Math.Abs(long): long` also unifies, the target's `int` parameter converting to `long`. Among unifying candidates, one whose parameter types — and return type, where the target's return position is closed — match the target's **exactly** is preferred; candidates that unify only through conversion are co-equal (the [§22.6](#sec-implicit-conversion-ranking) posture applied to the reference's signature), so absent an exact candidate the reference is ambiguous and the compiler reports the candidates. This is the **exact-preferred ranking** that [§14.5](#sec-type-argument-inference) phase 2 cites: `numbers.OrderBy(Math.Abs)` over `Array<int>` selects `Abs(int): int` — exact at the closed parameter position, binding `TKey := int` — and the converting overloads lose to it. The mirror direction — how a formed reference ranks among the *callee's* overloads when it is an argument to an overloaded call — is [§22.6](#sec-implicit-conversion-ranking)'s *Method-reference arguments*: exact where the selected overload's signature equals the substituted slot, converting where formation bridges a conversion; a candidate against whose slot this ranking finds no unique winner is inapplicable there, and the ambiguity above is reported only at a single target.

When no target type is available (e.g., `var f := Math.Abs;` with no annotation), the reference is ambiguous and the compiler reports an error pointing to the candidate overloads. The user disambiguates by adding a type annotation: `var f: (int) -> int := Math.Abs;`.

When a name `T.M` could resolve to either a *static* member of `T` or an *instance method reference* of `T` (a method requiring a receiver), the static member wins. The instance form has no separate syntax in this version — if both interpretations apply and the programmer wants the instance form, the disambiguation is to use a lambda: `lambda(t: T) => t.M(...)`. This case is rare in practice; it arises only when `T` declares an instance method named `M` and a static member also named `M`, which is unusual style.

<a id="sec-calling-function-values"></a>
### 27.7 Calling function values

```bezel
var sum := add(2, 3);

var maybeHandler: ((int) -> ())? := null;
maybeHandler?(42);                      // null-conditional call; no-op when null
```

The null-conditional call result is nullable. Both forms are positional: the named-argument form is not admitted at a call through a function-typed value ([§27.1](#sec-function-types)).

<a id="sec-equality-of-function-values"></a>
#### 27.7.1 Equality of function values

Function-typed values compare with `=` and `<>` by the following rule (normative):

- A **lambda** (closure) value equals only itself — reference equality on the closure instance. Two separately-constructed lambdas with identical source text are *not* equal, even if they capture the same variables.
- A **method reference** equals another method reference **iff** both denote the **same method** and, for instance references, are bound to the **same receiver** — receiver sameness being reference identity for class-typed receivers. A static (or extension-method) reference to `M` equals every other reference to `M`. Repeated evaluations of `obj.Method` on the same class-typed `obj` are therefore **guaranteed equal**: equality is defined on the (method, receiver) pair, so whether the implementation caches or re-allocates the underlying function object is unobservable.
- A method reference whose receiver is **value-shaped** (a record — [§27.6](#sec-method-references) captures the instance by copy) has no receiver identity: two separate evaluations compare **unequal** (each holds a distinct copy); only the same function object equals itself — and since every store-once spelling (a function-typed local or field passed to `+=`) is rejected at the scoped `Add` position by [§28.14](#sec-scoped-callback-parameters)'s admission bound 3, deterministic `-=` unsubscription for record receivers is not expressible in v1 (recorded below); use `Subscribe` and the owned `Subscription` (stdlib [§6.5](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-events-ievent-eventsource)). *(Alternative declined: defining receiver sameness by the record's own `Equals` would drag user equality dispatch into function-value comparison and make `-=` matching sensitive to value mutation between subscribe and unsubscribe; recorded in the changelog entry.)*
- A lambda never equals a method reference, and property references follow the method-reference rule (the getter is the method).

The practical consequence: function values should still not be used as dictionary keys or set elements, but event unsubscription is deterministic for named methods: `EventSource<T>.Remove` — and the `-=` desugaring ([§17.2](#sec-notes-on-operators)) — matches handlers by the function-value equality above, so `+=`/`-=` with a named method reference on a class-typed receiver reliably unsubscribes (same method, same receiver). `+=`/`-=` with separately-constructed lambdas does not match (each lambda is a fresh closure object).

The reliable pattern for `+=` followed by later `-=` is a **named method reference**: same method + same class-typed receiver compare equal (the rule above), so re-evaluated references match — and a method reference is one of the verified argument forms that [§28.14](#sec-scoped-callback-parameters)'s v1 admission bound 3 admits at the scoped `Add` position. (The `+=`/`-=` forms require a source-typed operand ([§17.2](#sec-notes-on-operators)), which under the stdlib §6.5 event pattern is the publisher's private field; the examples below are publisher-side code, where `_clicked += OnButtonClicked` is [§28.14](#sec-scoped-callback-parameters)'s form-4 self-capture admission (chain root `this`). A method reference passed at *another* publisher instance's `+=` additionally faces the form-4 declared-before test.)

```bezel
_clicked += OnButtonClicked;
// later:
_clicked -= OnButtonClicked;   // same method, same receiver: matches and unsubscribes
```

For a **lambda** handler, deterministic unsubscription goes through `Subscribe` and the owned `Subscription` (stdlib [§6.5](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-events-ievent-eventsource)). A lambda equals only itself, and the store-once spelling that would preserve the single closure instance — a function-typed field or local passed to `+=` — is **not admissible** at the subscription site: `Add` is a `scoped` (storing) position, and [§28.14](#sec-scoped-callback-parameters)'s admission bound 3 rejects function-typed locals and field reads as unverifiable argument forms (the verified forms are lambda literals and method references). The anti-pattern below therefore also silently fails to unsubscribe — each lambda is a fresh closure object:

```bezel
_clicked += lambda(e) => UpdateStatus(e.X, e.Y);
// later:
_clicked -= lambda(e) => UpdateStatus(e.X, e.Y);   // a different lambda, no match
```

```bezel
// The lambda form with deterministic teardown — and the form that also works
// anywhere, since Subscribe is on the IEvent<T> face:
using var sub := button.Clicked.Subscribe(lambda(e) => UpdateStatus(e.X, e.Y));
// disposing sub severs the registration (stdlib §6.5)
```

For named methods bound to **record** (value-shaped) receivers, deterministic `-=` unsubscription is **not expressible in v1** (recorded): the equality rule requires the very same function object, and every store-once spelling — a function-typed local or field — is rejected at the `Add` site by [§28.14](#sec-scoped-callback-parameters) bound 3. The remedy is `Subscribe` plus the owned `Subscription`, which needs no equality match at all. (Bound 3 is marked *liftable*; a future revision admitting provably-single-assignment private fields at scoped call sites would make the store-once form expressible again.)

<a id="sec-type-aliases"></a>
### 27.8 Type aliases

A `type` declaration introduces an alias for any existing type, binding with `:=` like every other binding in the language:

```bezel
type UserId := int;
type ConnectionPool := Dictionary<string, Array<Connection>>;

/// <summary>Handles an HTTP response.</summary>
/// <param name="status">The HTTP status code.</param>
/// <returns>True if handled successfully.</returns>
type ResponseHandler := (status: int, body: string, elapsed: TimeSpan) -> bool;
```

A type alias is a pure synonym — it does not create a new type. `UserId` and `int` are interchangeable. An alias may not reference itself, directly or through other aliases, in its aliased type or in its `where` clause: `type A := Array<A>;`, `type P := Q; type Q := P;` and `type Sorted<T> := Array<T> where T: Sorted<T>;` are compile errors, a synonym naming an existing type and a cycle naming none. A self-reference in the `where` clause is not [§11.8](#sec-static-interface-members)'s recurrence constraint, which names a declared interface whose identity does not depend on the constraint.

For genuinely distinct types (`UserId` and `OrderId` should not be interchangeable despite both being `int`), use a single-field record — in the positional form below where the type carries no validating condition, or in [§9.2](#sec-body-records)'s body form where it does ([§9.9](#sec-constructor-only-records)):

```bezel
record UserId(Value: int);
record OrderId(Value: int);
```

Type aliases may be declared at module level. A module-level alias is always **module-internal**: `TypeAliasDecl` admits no visibility keyword (Appendix [A.2](#sec-source-file)), the alias is never among the public names an `import` makes visible ([§2.2](#sec-imports)), and it is not part of the public surface the module's interface describes ([§2.8.2](#sec-artifact-interface)) — an importing module that wants the same shorthand declares its own alias (aliases are free; they create no type). Exportable aliases are deferred (rationale [§18](Bezel_Design_Rationale.md#sec-things-deferred)).

<a id="sec-generic-type-aliases"></a>
#### Generic type aliases

A type alias may declare type parameters:

```bezel
type Handler<T> := (T, string?) -> bool;
type Lookup<K, V> := Dictionary<K, Array<V>>;
type Predicate<T> := (T) -> bool;
type Reducer<T, TAccum> := (TAccum, T) -> TAccum;
```

Each instantiation of the alias is interchangeable with the corresponding instantiation of the aliased type. `Lookup<string, int>` and `Dictionary<string, Array<int>>` are the same type.

Generic aliases may carry constraints, written exactly as on generic methods:

```bezel
type Sorted<T> := IOrderedEnumerable<T> where T: IComparable<T>;
```

The constraint applies to the alias's parameter; uses of the alias must satisfy it.

A generic alias is subject to the self-reference rule above and must resolve to a concrete type after substitution. Aliases of aliases are permitted:

```bezel
type IntPredicate := Predicate<int>;       // Predicate<int>, which is (int) -> bool
```

Type aliases — generic or not — see through to the aliased type for identity, equality, method dispatch, and overload resolution. They are a naming convenience, not a separate type kind.

---

<a id="sec-resource-management"></a>
## 28. Resource Management

Bezel has no garbage collector. Class instances are heap-allocated by `new` and must be disposed exactly once; the compiler tracks every instance's ownership ([§28.3](#sec-local-variables-ownership-and-borrows)) and the disposal happens at a statically-known point. Records, enums, and primitives need no disposal — their memory is reclaimed when their containing scope exits.

**Reading this chapter.** Most readers are API *consumers* — code that uses classes and calls methods — and need only a small subset: the two local declaration forms and the disposal spellings ([§28.3](#sec-local-variables-ownership-and-borrows); [§28.10](#sec-using-var); *Choosing a disposal form*, [§28.3](#sec-choosing-a-disposal-form)); borrow-source liveness ([§28.3](#sec-borrow-lifetime-rules)); owned fields ([§28.5](#sec-owned-fields)); the `owned` return and the transfer marker ([§28.8](#sec-ownership-transfer), [§28.8.1](#sec-the-move-expression)); the join rule ([K7](#sec-kernel-k7)); drain-and-adopt over owning collections ([§28.11](#sec-collection-element-ownership)); and the no-capture-consume rule for closures (*Captured owned bindings*, [§28.3](#sec-captured-owned-bindings)) — the subset Guide 01 teaches by example. The remainder is API-*author* surface, needed when declaring signatures and callback-taking abstractions: the call-classification machinery of [§28.3](#sec-local-variables-ownership-and-borrows) — the kernel with its consume and announcement tables — and the storage-bounded callback admission of [§28.14](#sec-scoped-callback-parameters). This paragraph locates rules; it states none.

**Nullability in type keying.** Every rule of this chapter and of [§30.5](#sec-result-lifetime-and-task-disposal) that is keyed on a type a declaration writes — a declared type, or a slot or component of one at any depth — reads it with nullability stripped: `C?` qualifies as `C`, `T?` as `T`, `(() -> T)?` as `() -> T`. A rule that distinguishes a nullable type names it (`null` admissible under a nullable declared type; `[N owned]T?` beside `[N owned]T`). Whether a rule reads a declared type before or after generic substitution is not a chapter convention: each rule states its own keying.

A small set of types are **runtime-managed** and exempt from manual disposal: `string`, `Type`, boxed value types, and function values ([§28.9](#sec-runtime-managed-types)). **Trivial-dispose** class instances — instances of classes whose disposal provably runs no user code and releases only memory — are exempt from the disposal *ceremony* only, never from lifetime tracking: ownership is tracked exactly as for any other class, and the compiler frees each instance at its holder's release point ([§28.9](#sec-trivial-dispose-classes), [§28.2](#sec-checked-disposal)).

The discard form `_ := expr;` ([§17.13](#sec-the-discard-_)) disposes the value at the end of the discard statement for any class or interface type (an unbound owned temporary, [§28.3](#sec-unbound-owned-temporaries)); it is rejected at compile time only for a `Task`-family value ([§17.13](#sec-the-discard-_), axiom [A6](#sec-axiom-register)), whose disposal would abandon a running operation. For supervised fire-and-forget on tasks, use `Task.FireAndForget` ([§30.10](#sec-standard-library-task-helpers)).

<a id="sec-summary-of-disposal-obligations-by-type-kind"></a>
#### Summary of disposal obligations by type kind

| Type kind | Disposal required? | Mechanism |
|---|---|---|
| Classes | Yes — exactly once | `using var` ([§28.10](#sec-using-var)), `owned` fields ([§28.5](#sec-owned-fields)), explicit `.Dispose()`, discard `_ := …` ([§17.13](#sec-the-discard-_)), or auto-drop at scope end ([§28.3](#sec-owned-local-discharge-requirement)) |
| Interface-typed locations | Yes — treated as class | `using var` or `owned` field; discard via `_ := …` is **permitted** — it disposes via runtime dispatch at end of statement ([§17.13](#sec-the-discard-_)), so a future non-trivial implementation poses no cross-module hazard |
| Records | No | Stack-allocated or inline; no heap block to release |
| Enums | No | Value type; no heap block |
| Primitives | No | Value type; no heap block |
| `string` | No — runtime-managed | `Dispose()` is a no-op ([§28.9](#sec-runtime-managed-types)) |
| Boxed value types | No — runtime-managed | `Dispose()` is a no-op ([§28.9](#sec-runtime-managed-types)) |
| Function values | No — runtime-managed | `Dispose()` is a no-op ([§28.9](#sec-runtime-managed-types)) |
| Inline arrays `[N]T` (without `owned` slots) | No | Value type; stored inline in enclosing context; no separate allocation to dispose ([§15.1](#sec-inline-arrays)) |
| Inline arrays `[N owned]T?` or `[N owned]T` (with `owned` slots) | No, indirectly | Move-only value type; the array's host (class field, local) discharges by disposing each (non-null) slot ([§15.3](#sec-move-only-value-types)) |
| `Array<T>` and other borrowing collections | No — trivial-dispose ([§28.9](#sec-runtime-managed-types)) | The instance is compiler-freed at its holder's release point; the backing storage is part of the instance's single allocation, released by that one free (a layout fact, not a lifetime mechanism); `Dispose()` runs no user code. Elements are borrows and are never disposed — nor disposable through the collection (owning-family collections own and cascade, [§28.11](#sec-collections-do-not-own-elements)) |
| `OwningArray<T>` and other owning collections | Yes — class types | Dispose cascades through owned elements ([§28.11](#sec-collections-do-not-own-elements)) |

<a id="sec-where-the-owned-modifier-can-appear"></a>
### 28.1 Where the `owned` modifier can appear

The `owned` modifier appears in specific declaration positions. It is **admissible** in the following positions:

- **Method parameter declarations.** `method M(owned p: T)` — the parameter takes ownership of the value at the call site; the method body is responsible for discharging it before returning.
- **Return type declarations.** `method Acquire(): owned Connection` — the return value is an owned reference; the caller assumes responsibility for its disposal.
- **Field declarations on classes.** `private owned _resource: Connection` — the field stores an owned reference; the containing class's destructor disposes it.
- **Local variables via `using var`.** `using var c := Connect()` — the local is owned and is disposed at scope exit.
- **`out` parameter declarations.** `out owned p: T` — the parameter is an out-position that produces an owned reference for the caller to take.
- **Function-type parameter slots.** `(owned T) -> ()` — the parameter slot of a function type may carry `owned`. The modifier is part of the function type's identity (see [§27.1](#sec-function-types)); `(T) -> ()` and `(owned T) -> ()` are distinct types.
- **Function-type return slots.** `() -> owned Connection` — the return slot of a function type may carry `owned`. The same identity rule applies.
- **Lambda parameters.** `lambda(owned x) => ...` or `lambda(owned x: T) => ...` — a lambda's parameter list carries the same modifiers as the target function type expects.
- **Choice payload fields.** `Fetched(owned response: Response)` — the payload slot takes ownership at construction and the active case's owned payloads are disposed with the value ([§35.1](#sec-choice-declaration), [§35.4](#sec-choice-classification)); admissibility and the bare-type-parameter erasure follow the type requirement below.
- **Inline-array slot marker.** `[N owned]T` and `[N owned]T?` — the `owned` keyword placed between the size and the closing bracket marks the inline array's slots as owned (see [§15.1.1](#sec-owning-inline-arrays)). The array becomes a move-only value type ([§15.3](#sec-move-only-value-types)). This is the type-level position for owning inline arrays; an owning-inline-array field on a class does **not** additionally carry the `owned` field modifier (the slot marker already conveys the obligation).

The modifier is **not admissible** in the following positions:

- **Record fields.** Records cannot have owned fields per [§28.5](#sec-owned-fields).
- **Inline-array element types.** Writing `[N](owned T)` is not a well-formed syntax — `owned` on inline arrays appears in the slot-marker position `[N owned]T`, not on the element type. To hold owned elements in a resizable collection, use `OwningArray<T>`.
- **Generic type arguments.** This version does not admit `owned` on generic type arguments ([§14.4](#sec-owned-as-a-generic-argument)). Use named owning collection types (stdlib [§4](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-system-collections-generic)) or `OwningTask<T>` (stdlib [§6](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-system-threading)) when the use case requires an owning generic.

**Type requirement.** In the method-parameter, return-type, `out`-parameter, lambda-parameter, choice-payload ([§35.1](#sec-choice-declaration)), and function-type parameter/return slot positions above, `owned` requires the declared type to be a **class type other than `Type`** ([§28.9](#sec-runtime-managed-types): the process-interned type-identity token is runtime-managed and carries no obligation to transfer), **an interface type, or a bare type parameter**. The clauses:

1. **Move-only value types** ([§15.3](#sec-move-only-value-types)): the modifier is admitted-but-redundant — the type's own move semantics already transfer the obligation.
2. **Any other type** — a primitive, `string`, `Type`, a function type, an ordinary record, an enum, a non-owning inline array, or the unit type: `owned` is a **compile error**. Such values carry no disposal obligation to transfer ([§28.9](#sec-runtime-managed-types)) — the same reasoning as [§28.5](#sec-owned-fields)'s field restriction and [§30.5](#sec-result-lifetime-and-task-disposal)'s rejection of `OwningTask<T>` at non-class T.
3. **Bare type parameters**: the marker's meaning is fixed **per instantiation** — the [§3.6](#sec-derived-type-properties) rule 2 pattern, the same pre-substitution-keying / per-instantiation-enforcement split as [§28.3](#sec-bare-type-parameter-returns)'s bare-type-parameter rule. The generic body type-checks under the class-or-interface assumption (a function value reaches a bare-type-parameter position only capture-free, [§28.3](#sec-borrow-lifetime-rules)'s set-erasing positions, so what the assumption admits stays sound at a function-type substitution). At a **class or interface** substitution the marker has its ordinary transfer meaning; at a **move-only value** substitution it is admitted-but-redundant, as for the concrete type (clause 1); and at every **other value or runtime-managed** substitution it is **erased by the substitution** — the substituted signature is the unmarked one. Erased means: no obligation exists to transfer ([§28.9](#sec-runtime-managed-types)); parameters and returns pass by value; an `out owned` slot delivers a plain value; marker-keyed call-site and binding forms written under the class assumption remain admissible with no-op effect ([§28.10](#sec-using-var)'s uniform admissibility); the marker does not survive into a substituted function type's identity (`(owned T) -> ()` at `T = int` *is* `(int) -> ()`, [§27.1](#sec-function-types)); and every rule keyed on the marker — [§11.2](#sec-interface-declaration)/[§12.1](#sec-members-are-non-virtual-by-default) signature matching, [§22.3](#sec-parameter-modifiers)'s call-site marker — reads the erased substituted form.
4. **Erasure changes substituted signatures, never classification keys**: a declared `owned T` return remains outside [§28.3](#sec-bare-type-parameter-returns)'s bare-type-parameter rule at every instantiation. Rejecting these instantiations instead would make the `owned` spelling unusable for any fresh-producing generic whose domain admits value substitutions — precisely the signatures the static-return rule directs at the spelling ([§28.3](#sec-factory-methods-and-sourceless-returns)) and the static-interface producer members of stdlib §2.19.
5. **Two rejections remain.** A declaration whose constraints exclude class and interface substitutions outright (`where T: value`) rejects the marker **at the declaration** — it could never be more than redundant, clause 2's reasoning applied at the only point it is decidable. And [§28.5](#sec-owned-fields)'s generic **field** rule is deliberately unchanged — an `owned` field at an inadmissible substitution stays an instantiation-site error, because a field marker commits the containing type's shape (destructor synthesis, the [§3.6](#sec-derived-type-properties) derived properties) in a way a call-boundary marker does not; the asymmetry is recorded, liftable if a mixed-domain owning-slot case arrives.
6. Authors who intend the marker to be meaningful at every instantiation still constrain the domain (`where T: IDisposable` excludes the runtime-managed reference types at the declaration, [§14.2](#sec-constraints)).

The rules for how `owned` interacts with method bodies, control flow, and disposal are in the subsections that follow.

<a id="sec-the-idisposable-contract"></a>
### 28.2 The `IDisposable` contract

Every class implicitly implements `IDisposable` via a compiler-generated `Dispose()`:

```bezel
interface IDisposable
  method Dispose();
end IDisposable;
```

`Dispose()` on any class instance is idempotent: the first call performs the disposal; subsequent calls are no-ops. The compiler-generated `Dispose()` is thread-safe with respect to idempotency: concurrent calls from multiple threads will execute the disposal logic exactly once; all other concurrent callers observe the no-op path. (Within a single execution domain concurrent calls cannot arise — [§30.13](#sec-runtime-model) — and they cannot arise across domains either, since domains share no mutable state ([§30.14](#sec-multiple-domains)); the thread-safety guarantee matters where disposal is reachable from foreign threads through the FFI.) This machinery — the idempotent, flag-setting disposal together with the checked-disposal mode below — is the runtime backstop the ownership kernel records as [K4.1](#sec-kernel-k4) ([§28.3](#sec-ownership-kernel)).

<a id="sec-checked-disposal"></a>
#### Use after disposal; checked disposal mode

Use of an instance after its first `Dispose()` is a program error. How the error manifests depends on the *disposal-checking mode*, a per-build choice between two conformance modes:

- **Checked mode** — any instance member access on a logically-disposed instance — an instance method call (including interface and virtual dispatch), a property or indexer accessor invocation, or a field access through the reference — raises `DisposedAccessException` ([§31.4](#sec-standard-exception-types)). This is the default: a build that selects neither mode is a checked build.
- **Unchecked (release) mode** — use of a disposed instance is undefined behavior; a build selects it explicitly. A further `Dispose()` call remains a no-op, not an error, in both modes.

The two modes give identical observable behavior for every program that never uses a disposed instance. A program that would raise `DisposedAccessException` in checked mode has undefined behavior in unchecked mode: unchecked mode is the release-build relaxation of the default checked semantics — selected per build, never implied — not a different language.

Checked mode is implementable with state the language already requires: idempotent disposal implies a per-instance disposed flag, and the split between logical disposal and physical reclamation ([§28.12](#sec-asynchronous-disposal)) gives the implementation latitude to defer reclaiming a disposed instance's memory in checked mode (quarantine, delayed free) so that the flag remains readable after disposal. The check itself is a flag test on member entry; implementations are expected to omit it entirely in unchecked builds, so unchecked builds pay no cost for the mode's existence.

**The compiler-inserted free.** For a **trivial-dispose** instance ([§28.9](#sec-trivial-dispose-classes)) the compiler inserts a **free** at the holder's release point: **logical disposal followed by reclamation** — it sets the per-instance disposed flag and runs no user code (the class has none to run). Riding the flag is what makes checked mode's backstop uniform across the language: a member access through a surviving borrow of a freed trivial-dispose instance — a store-rule residual, a retained fresh `Add` argument ([§15.4](#sec-collection-literals), [§28.11](#sec-borrowing-collections)) — raises `DisposedAccessException` deterministically, exactly as for a non-trivial class; no class in the language dangles without this backstop. The costs are stated and checked-mode-only: trivial-dispose instances carry the per-instance flag word, member access through a borrow is a live flag test in checked mode, and [§28.12](#sec-asynchronous-disposal)'s logical/physical split may quarantine their physical reclamation; unchecked builds pay nothing, per this section's existing posture.

The compiler additionally **must** emit a compile-time warning when a local variable is used (read, borrowed from, or consumed) after an explicit `Dispose()` call — or a discard of the binding ([§17.13](#sec-the-discard-_)) — on the same variable that dominates the use site on every path: the straight-line subset of use-after-dispose (derives: [K4.2](#sec-kernel-k4) + [K7.4](#sec-kernel-k7)). A second `Dispose()` on the same binding is such a use and draws this warning ([K3.9](#sec-kernel-k3)'s **explicitly-disposed** post-state): the no-op carve-out above states the **runtime** contract of a repeated call and suppresses no diagnostic. The warning-free spelling of idempotence is one explicit disposal — the auto-drop and a `using var`'s scope-end disposal are not repeat calls, the binding having reached a discharge point ([§28.3](#sec-owned-local-discharge-requirement)). A *conditional* kill is treated more strictly: at a join of an explicitly-disposed path with a still-owned path the variable is **maybe-consumed** and a later use is a compile error ([§28.3](#sec-ownership-state-of-locals)). **The split is between the two kills, never between the use forms**: under a *dominating* kill every use in the list above draws this warning — a **consume** exactly as a read does, `move x` and an `owned` argument position included — and under a *conditional* kill every one of them is [§28.3](#sec-ownership-state-of-locals)'s error. A diagnostic that varies with the syntactic position of the use rather than with the kill is not this rule: the two spellings describe one program state, and the checked-disposal backstop (this section's `DisposedAccessException`) is what stands behind both.

`Dispose()` is not on `Object`; it is class-only. Records, enums, primitives, and inline arrays do not implement `IDisposable`.

User code does not implement `Dispose()` directly. The customization points are:

- A `destructor` for cleanup logic.
- `owned` fields for fields that should be disposed with the containing object.

Declaring a member named `Dispose` on a **class** or a **record** is a **compile error** at that declaration, whatever its parameter list; the diagnostic names the two customization points above — the [§9.3](#sec-combined-form) posture for a body member colliding with a compiler-generated one, keyed on the name as [§12.2](#sec-hiding-is-not-allowed) is. On a class the name is the compiler's: the generated `Dispose()` is what `using var` ([§28.10](#sec-using-var)), the owned-field cascade ([§28.4](#sec-the-destructor)), the discard ([§17.13](#sec-the-discard-_)), and an explicit call ([§28.6](#sec-who-may-dispose)) all reach, and it cannot be overridden ([§28.4](#sec-the-destructor)) — so a user member of that name is never run, and at an optional-parameter declaration (`Dispose(mode: int := 0)`, [§22.5](#sec-optional-parameters-and-named-arguments)) it is additionally ambiguous at every zero-argument call. On a record the name promises a disposal contract the kind does not have ([§9.7](#sec-records-and-disposal)). **Interfaces are unaffected** — the rule reaches **classes and records only**, and an interface may itself declare `method Dispose();`: an interface member declares no body, so the name displaces no compiler-generated member and traps no one, and the rule above is keyed on "class or record" with no clause reaching interfaces. `IDisposable` declares it (stdlib [§2.10](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-idisposable-and-iasyncdisposable)) and interfaces extend it; a user interface declaring it directly is admitted on the same ground — as is a class's `DisposeAsync` implementation ([§28.12](#sec-asynchronous-disposal)).

**Scoped-callback backstop.** In checked disposal mode, invoking a callback stored under a `scoped` parameter ([§28.14](#sec-scoped-callback-parameters)) after its bounding object's disposal has completed — a violation of the callee's quiescence obligation — faults deterministically as `DisposedAccessException`, exactly like any other member access through a logically-disposed instance.

<a id="sec-local-variables-ownership-and-borrows"></a>
### 28.3 Local variables, ownership, and borrows

Bezel tracks two kinds of class-typed reference at compile time:

- **Owned** — the holder is responsible for disposing the referenced object exactly once.
- **Borrowed** — the holder is not responsible for disposal; the reference is valid only for as long as some other holder (the *source*) keeps the object alive.

The `owned` keyword ([§28.5](#sec-owned-fields), [§28.8](#sec-ownership-transfer)) marks fields, parameters, and return types as owned. Local variables are not annotated; their ownership state is inferred from how they are introduced. Throughout this chapter, *owned*/*borrowed* name the classification and **holder** names the role: the binding, slot, or frame that carries an obligation or a borrow at a given point.

**Glossary.** Terms of art used throughout this chapter and its satellites, each defined at the cited clause:

- ***Owned* / *borrowed*** — the two ownership **classifications** of a class- or interface-typed value ([K1](#sec-kernel-k1) below); a ***holder*** is the **role**: the binding, slot, or frame that carries the obligation or borrow at a given point (this section's opening paragraph). Where prose speaks of a value's *owner*, it means the holder of the value's disposal obligation.
- ***Drop*** — a discard that carries **disposal**: the implicit scope-end drop ([K3.14](#sec-kernel-k3), [§28.3](#sec-owned-local-discharge-requirement)) and drop-on-overwrite ([K3.11](#sec-consume-table), [§28.7](#sec-reassigning-owned-fields)). A removal that disposes nothing — a borrowing collection's `Remove`/`Clear` — is said to ***remove*** ([§28.11](#sec-collection-element-ownership)'s operation table), never to drop.
- ***Borrowing position*** — an operand position where the read of an owned binding borrows rather than consumes; the enumeration follows the *Producers* table ([§28.3](#sec-producers)).
- ***Marker-free position*** — an owned-consuming position at which the target or keyword already announces the consume, so no transfer marker is written and writing one is rejected as redundant ([K3.13](#sec-kernel-k3); the [consume table](#sec-consume-table)'s Spelling column).
- ***Site-announced*** — a kill that is both keyword-visible at the kill site and flag-backstopped ([K4.2](#sec-kernel-k4)); the closed set is the consume table's three rows tagged K4.2.
- ***Type-announced*** — a classification read off the callee's declared, pre-substitution type ([K2.4](#sec-kernel-k2), [K6.2](#sec-kernel-k6); the [announcement table](#sec-announcement-table) is the per-callee-kind matrix).
- ***Mint-announcing*** — a declared return type — `Task`-family, iterable-family, or a lazy query — at which every call mints a fresh owned frame ([K6.3](#sec-kernel-k6)).

<a id="sec-ownership-kernel"></a>
#### The ownership kernel (K1–K9)

Every rule of this chapter and of [§30.5](#sec-result-lifetime-and-task-disposal) is one of: a kernel principle below, a derivation from them, or a recorded axiom (register at the end of this subsection; reasons in the rationale). Derivation and axiom tags — *derives: K…* / *axiom A…* — mark the classification at each rule. A future revision that adds an ownership rule states which kind it is.

<a id="sec-kernel-k1"></a>
**K1 — Value classification.** At every program point, every expression and binding of class or interface type (K1.6 exempts the runtime-managed remainder) has exactly one ownership classification — the two reference kinds of this section's opening, completed by the transfer and analysis states:

1. **owned** — the holder carries the disposal obligation: dispose exactly once, on every path.
2. **borrowed** — no obligation; validity is bounded by the borrow's source set (K2).
3. **moved-from** — the obligation has transferred out; the binding or slot is unreadable until reassigned, and discharge machinery skips it ([§28.8.1](#sec-the-move-expression)).
4. **maybe-consumed** — the K7 join of owned with moved-from or explicitly-disposed; unreadable; scope-end disposal is per-path.

   Three auxiliary bookkeeping states complete the analysis:

   - **uninitialized** — declared, unassigned; unreadable ([§7.9](#sec-definite-assignment-for-non-nullable-fields)). The local adopts the state of the first assignment that reaches it ([§28.3](#sec-ownership-state-of-locals)'s adoption clause).
   - **polymorphic-null** — `var x: T? := null;` before the first non-null assignment; adopts the state of that assignment, by the same clause. A null arm or RHS is compatible with either target, having no value to own.
   - **explicitly-disposed** — the binding after a site-announced kill that moves no obligation ([K4.2](#sec-kernel-k4)'s `Dispose()` and discard, the [consume table](#sec-consume-table)'s row K3.9). Scope-end machinery skips it, and a straight-line read falls under [§28.2](#sec-checked-disposal)'s use-after-dispose warning regime rather than the moved-from error.

5. **Atoms.** Fresh productions are owned: `new`, reference-typed collection literals, `owned`-returning calls, `move` results, owned operator results. Reads of storage lend: a field, property, indexer, or slot read is a borrow whose source is the storage's holder. Reads of named bindings lend unless the position consumes (K3): an unmarked read of an owned binding is a borrow of the binding. Calls lend by default: an instance method's plain (non-`owned`) class-typed return is a borrow whose source is the receiver — sound jointly with the callee-side admission rules (K2.4). A static callee's plain class- or interface-typed return is admissible only where the declared type announces the classification (**type-announced**, K2.4/K6.2), and is otherwise rejected at the declaration (the static-return rule, *Factory methods* below). (The *Producers* table below is the worked enumeration; the [announcement table](#sec-announcement-table) beside it is the per-callee-kind matrix for calls.)
6. **The runtime-managed exemption; the trivial-dispose ceremony exemption.** Values of runtime-managed type (`string`, `Type`, boxed value types, function values) and of ordinary value type carry no classification and no obligation; `owned` markers over them are inadmissible or erased per instantiation ([§28.1](#sec-where-the-owned-modifier-can-appear)). Trivial-dispose class instances ([§28.9](#sec-runtime-managed-types)) carry the classification **and the free obligation**, but the obligation's *user-visible* content is empty and its discharge is never demanded *of the program*: any undischarged trivial-dispose value is freed silently by the compiler at its owner's release point — no warning (the ceremony exemption), no user code (the class has none to run; the free sets the disposed flag, [§28.2](#sec-checked-disposal)). The exemption is ceremony-only: the borrow half of the machinery — source sets, escape checks, the freeze — is demanded over trivial-sourced references everywhere, and every rule of this chapter reads them by its letter.
7. **One holder.** An obligation has exactly one holder at a time; every transfer moves it, never copies it. Copy-semantics holders (record fields) therefore cannot hold obligations ([§28.5](#sec-owned-fields)).

<a id="sec-kernel-k2"></a>
**K2 — The source algebra.** Every borrow carries a **source set**. A source is one of:

- a **named location**: a local binding, a parameter, `this`, a field path rooted at a live object, or static storage — the one distinguished *always-live* source (process-lived, disposed only at exit, [§22.13](#sec-static-initialization-order));
- a **frame** (K6): a task, iterator/enumerator frame, or lazy query value, itself an ordinarily-classified value;
- a **full-expression temporary**: an unbound owned temporary ([§28.3](#sec-unbound-owned-temporaries)), live exactly to its K8 boundary.

The taxonomy defines what a source *is* and how it bounds a borrow; which source kinds a particular operand position accepts — [§30.5](#sec-result-lifetime-and-task-disposal)'s awaited-task positions are the worked case — remains that construct's own enumeration.

1. **Weakest source bounds.** A borrow is valid only where *every* source in its set is live; equivalently, it is bounded by its weakest source.
2. **Union under composition.** Joins, `??` and arm meets, transitive re-borrows, and frame carriage combine borrows by taking the union of their source sets.
3. **Escape must be bounded.** A borrow may not reach a holder — a binding of wider scope, a field, a collection, a frame, a return — whose lifetime the checker cannot bound by the borrow's source set. Where scopes are statically comparable (locals, temporaries, loop back edges), violation is rejected.
