an **iteration-variable** borrow is admissible only where its derived source chain reaches the receiver under [§29.2](#sec-desugaring-of-for)'s desugaring and [§29.1](#sec-current-semantics-on-borrowing-and-owning-enumerators)'s `Current` semantics at the loop source's static type — a collection-backed source re-borrows (the chain runs element slot → collection → receiver), an enumerator-owned yield does not, and at an interface-typed enumeration source the backing is unprovable, so the variable's source is conservatively the loop's implicit enumerator, a scope-bound local, and returning it is rejected; the index-based spelling `this[i]`, on a receiver that declares an indexer, is receiver-sourced and admissible — **a plain source parameter** — directly, a borrow reached through it, or the result of invoking a function-typed source parameter, itself classified by this rule, so that each plain argument of the invocation is a source of the result and must be admissible here in turn (`static method Map<A, B>(a: A, f: (A) -> B): B => f(a);` is rejected at every instantiation whose `B` this check reaches, `Map<int, Item>` as well as `Map<Item, Item>`: `a` is no source parameter, and an argument typed by a type parameter counts under the weakest assumption its constraints establish, item 4 of [*The sources an argument contributes*](#sec-argument-contributions); `Map` is admitted where `B` is a value type that carries no borrow) — or **static storage**: a bare read of a `static` class- or interface-typed field, `owned` or non-`owned` in the admissible forms — process-lived, [§22.13](#sec-static-initialization-order); admitted from these method bodies even though the concrete-typed admission below is property-getter-only, because this rule's non-empty-set caller side classifies the result as a borrow, never as owned — no second owner can arise.
3. The declared bare-type-parameter return is the signature-level type announcement of the argument-sourced classification ([K2.4](#sec-kernel-k2)), exactly as the deferred-activation kinds announce theirs ([*Returning a deferred-activation frame*](#sec-returning-a-deferred-activation-frame)); the parameter-sourced prohibition of the borrow-lifetime rules — unchanged for concrete-typed static returns, whose `static method Pick(a: Res, b: Res): Res return a;` remains rejected — is lifted here **because every caller re-establishes the borrow against its own receiver and arguments**.
4. A fresh owned value, or a borrow of an owned local, a `using var`, an `owned` parameter, or a temporary, is rejected at the return site — the value would die with the callee or escape unowned; a generic body that produces fresh values declares `owned T` and transfers.
5. With an **empty** potential source set the factory regime governs the body instead: return paths supply fresh or owned values; parameter-sourced borrows remain rejected exactly as for concrete types; and a **static-storage-sourced borrow return is likewise rejected** under an empty-set bare-type-parameter signature: this rule's caller side classifies the empty-set result as owned, so a static-storage borrow would acquire a second owner — the two-owners defect this rule exists to close. Expose a cached instance through a **static property** instead; the *Static property access `T.P`* producers row is that shape's sound caller-side classification, the same property-face resolution as the calls-mint rule's stored-view remedy and the concrete-typed static-method rejection in the borrow-lifetime bullet below. (The concrete-typed case is treated identically: the static-storage admission below is property-getter-only, so a concrete-typed static method returning static storage is rejected callee-side and factory-classified caller-side exactly as here.)
6. (The accumulator shape of [§11.8](#sec-static-interface-members)'s `Sum<T>` — an empty-set factory call combined with operator results through `INumber<T>` — is well-formed at every substitution: stdlib §2.19's producer members and `Sum`'s own return are spelled `owned T`, admissible over the mixed numeric domain under [§28.1](#sec-where-the-owned-modifier-can-appear)'s per-instantiation erasure — the results transfer at class and interface substitutions and are plain values elsewhere.)

**`Task`-family substitutions are excluded from bare-parameter function slots (derives: [K1](#sec-kernel-k1) + [K2.4](#sec-kernel-k2) + [K6.3](#sec-kernel-k6)).** The pre-substitution keying that makes this rule and the calls-mint rule sound cannot see through a function slot, and post-substitution keying remains the recorded decline. The seam is closed instead by admissibility, completing the marker fence (`owned`-return function slots are already type-excluded from bare-parameter slots — [§28.1](#sec-where-the-owned-modifier-can-appear), [§27.1.1](#sec-function-type-assignability)): a member whose declared type or signature contains, anywhere within a parameter's declared type, a function type whose **return slot is a bare type parameter** is **inadmissible at an instantiation substituting a `Task`-family type** (`Task`/`Task<T>`/`OwningTask<T>`) for that parameter. The use is rejected at the instantiation under [§3.6](#sec-derived-type-properties) rules 2/4's per-instantiation pattern, the diagnostic naming the instantiation and the sound spellings: declare the slot with a `Task`-family return (`f: () -> Task<T>` — pre-substitution mint-classified) or a concrete function type, or build the task collection by statement (`tasks.Add(FetchAsync(x))`). Every non-mint substitution is untouched; a bare parameter in a function type's *parameter* slots, or as a plain parameter type (`Pick<T>(a: T, b: T): T` at `T = Task<int>` — a sound argument-sourced lend), is outside this rule. With this exclusion, [§27.1.1](#sec-function-type-assignability)'s family boundary, and the concrete-slot callee-side admission on lambda and body return paths ([§28.3](#sec-producers) *Concrete-slot function bodies* — the fence that catches a minting lambda inhabitant the first two cannot see: `Wrap<Object>(lambda() => Work())` substitutes no family type and retypes no formed value), no **`Task`-family** value whose invocations mint can inhabit a slot whose invocations this rule classifies as lends. **The iterable family needs no per-substitution exclusion:** under the unified calls-mint rule every iterable-family-returning callee and formed function value announces its mint in its declared type, so the mint-laundering inhabitants are rejected **inhabitant-side** — formation and retyping at [§27.6](#sec-method-references)/[§27.1.1](#sec-function-type-assignability)'s announcement boundary, which is read against the target slot's declared, pre-substitution type, and a minting lambda on its return path (a fresh frame is an owned production, rejected by this rule's callee-side admission and by *Concrete-slot function bodies* below) — while borrow-returning and value-typed callbacks stay admissible. An iterable-head substitution at such a member is therefore ordinary — `xs.Select(lambda(x) => x.Items)` over a property-face `Items` is legal at `U = IEnumerable<Item>`.

**Function-type substitutions are excluded from type parameters in nested parameter slots (derives: [K1.6](#sec-kernel-k1) + [K2.4](#sec-kernel-k2)).** A member is inadmissible at an instantiation substituting a function type for a type parameter `T` when, within some parameter's declared, pre-substitution type, `T` occurs anywhere within a parameter slot of a function type that itself occupies a parameter slot of that type: `reg: ((T) -> ()) -> ()`, `reg: ((() -> T) -> ()) -> ()`. A function value of the caller's supplies the arguments of that inner slot by invoking it, so no source set the caller reads covers them, while the generic body may store them under the class-or-interface assumption ([§28.1](#sec-where-the-owned-modifier-can-appear)). The use is rejected at the instantiation, capture-free arguments included, under [§3.6](#sec-derived-type-properties) rules 2/4's per-instantiation pattern; the diagnostic names the instantiation and the sound spellings: a concrete function type for the slot, or a type for `T` that is not a function type. A `T` directly at a parameter, or in a return slot reached through return slots only, is the closure bullet's set-erasing check ([§28.3](#sec-borrow-lifetime-rules)); a `T` in a parameter slot one level down (`visit: (T) -> ()`) carries values from the body to the caller, which that check makes capture-free.

**Concrete-slot function bodies (derives: [K2.4](#sec-kernel-k2) — the row's type announcement has a callee side, as every type-announced classification in this section does).** A lambda checked against a function-type target whose return slot — read from the target's declared, pre-substitution slot type ([K2.4](#sec-kernel-k2); the calls-mint rule's pre-substitution keying) — is a **concrete class or interface type** (not `owned`; not mint-announcing — a `Task`-family or iterable-family slot's callee side is the calls-mint rule above) admits on each return path exactly the sources the producers row's callers re-establish: `null` (for a nullable slot), a capture-sourced borrow, a plain-parameter-sourced borrow, or static storage — the bare-T non-empty-set admission read against the target's own slots. A **fresh owned value** — a constructor result, a `move` result, a factory-call result, a `Task`-family or iterable-family call result, or any other owned production — is rejected at the return path ([§28.6](#sec-leak-prevention): the row classifies every invocation as a borrow, so no caller would ever dispose it); spell the slot's return `owned` to transfer (the stdlib's own generic-factory convention, `init: (int) -> owned T`, stdlib §4.14). At value and runtime-managed check-site types the admission is vacuous ([§3.6](#sec-derived-type-properties) rule 2's per-instantiation-category pattern, exactly as the bare-T callee side; the lazy-operator selector rules' stricter per-element treatment of runtime-managed mints in lazy positions is unaffected). A lambda checked against a slot whose declared return is a bare type parameter takes the bare-T admission above at every substitution, inferred or explicit. Method references need no new clause: a method's own body is already checked against its declared signature, and [§27.1.1](#sec-function-type-assignability)/[§27.6](#sec-method-references) admit only compatible faces into the slot.

**Iterator and iterable returns (derives: [K6.2](#sec-kernel-k6) + [K6.3](#sec-kernel-k6) — an instance of the calls-mint rule).** A method whose body uses `yield return` or `yield break` (synchronous or async, returning one of the eight iterable/enumerator heads per [§29.3](#sec-iterator-methods)) is a factory by construction — its return is the freshly-constructed state machine — and the natural return type is the iterable interface, unmarked, at **every callee kind** (the [announcement table](#sec-announcement-table)'s row 2): requiring `owned` on every iterator return type would be redundant noise over a type-announced transfer — the recorded reason the type-announced set exists — and an explicit `owned` remains admissible emphasis with identical semantics. A composed-frame non-iterator body (`static method Evens(xs: Array<int>): IEnumerable<int> => xs.Where(IsEven);`) is admitted by the same clause, *Returning a deferred-activation frame* below governing its carried sources. Callers discharge the ownership obligation under the standard rules (typically via the for-loop's implicit `using var __source` binding). The standard library follows the convention: the `IEnumerable<T>` extensions (`Where`, `Select`, etc.) return **lazy queries** under [§29.11](#sec-multiple-enumeration)'s enumeration-right discipline, layered over the container obligation the standard rules discharge, and the owning-collection `Drain()` methods returning `IOwningEnumerable<T>` (stdlib §4.5) and the async twin `ReceiveAll()` (stdlib §6.9) are ordinary minting members — instance members, each minting a fresh drain-view frame per call.
<a id="sec-move-semantics-for-owned-locals"></a>
#### Move semantics for owned locals

Reading an owned local `x` in one of the [consume table](#sec-consume-table)'s positions **transfers ownership out of `x`**: afterward `x` is in the table's post-state — **moved-from** at the transfer rows (it may not be read again until reassigned, and it has no disposal obligation), **explicitly-disposed** at row K3.9. Reading an owned local in a borrowing position leaves `x` unchanged, and an **unmarked** read of a named owned binding in a local binding/assignment position is a **borrow** — the aliasing idiom `var b := a;` never silently consumes `a` ([K3.13](#sec-kernel-k3)).

Where the transfer is spelled and where it is marker-free is the table's Spelling column, stated once there: the marker at the call site — `M(move x)` ([§22.3](#sec-parameter-modifiers)) — and in **local binding and assignment positions** — `var y := move x;`, `y := move x;`, `using var y := move x;` ([§28.10](#sec-using-var) adoption); no marker at the marker-free positions — an **`owned` field or owning-collection slot**, `return` under an `owned` return type or an unmarked mint-announcing return type ([K3.2](#sec-kernel-k3)), or a user-declared `set(owned)` property or indexer ([§23.3](#sec-block-form-properties): `cache.Current := c;` consumes without a call-site marker, exactly as at the stdlib owning-collection indexer-set, whose setters are themselves declared `set(owned)`) — and none anywhere for a fresh producer (no live binding is invalidated).

Three spelling errors follow, mirroring the call-site marker's rules: the marker on a **borrow or fresh-producer right-hand side**; a marked reassignment into a **borrowed-state** LHS (the state-match rule above); and the marker **at a marker-free position** — `return move x;` under an `owned` return, `throw move x`, `_ := move x;`, an owned-field or `set(owned)` store spelled `sink._f := move x;`, a Pattern B `await move t` ([§30.5](#sec-result-lifetime-and-task-disposal)), an owning iterator's `yield return move x;` — **one spelling per site**: the announcement is the spelling there, and the diagnostic names it.

A fresh declaration (`var y := move x;`, `using var y := move x;`), an **uninitialized** LHS (`var y: Res; … y := move x;`), or a **polymorphic-null** LHS (`var best: Res? := null; … best := move cur;` — the null-literal producers row) adopts owned state from the marked transfer, exactly as it would from a fresh producer — the last two by the adoption clause of *Ownership state of locals*.

The marked assignment form is what makes the loop-accumulator pattern expressible — keep the best, dispose the rest:

```bezel
var best: Res? := null;
for var i in 0..<count do
    var cur := new Res(i);
    if best = null or cur.Score() > best!.Score() then
        best := move cur;          // transfer; the displaced best is disposed (§28.7)
    else
        cur.Dispose();             // or let cur auto-drop with the must-use warning
    end;
    // after the if: cur is moved-from on the taken path, disposed on the other —
    // the §28.3 join rules (maybe-consumed) forbid reading it; scope-end disposal is per-path.
end;
// best: owned; discharge or auto-drop per the standard rules.
```

```bezel
// Wrapper's constructor takes `owned inner: Buffer`; CloneBuffer(): owned Buffer.
public method Wrap(s: Buffer): owned Wrapper
  using var copy := s.CloneBuffer();   // copy is owned + scope-bound
  return new Wrapper(move copy);       // ERROR: cannot move out of a `using var`
end Wrap;

public method Wrap2(owned s: Buffer): owned Wrapper
  return new Wrapper(move s);          // OK: s is moved into Wrapper's constructor
                                       // s is now in moved-from state
end Wrap2;
```

A `using var` is owned but is additionally bound to its scope: it cannot be moved out of, only borrowed from (axiom [A5](#sec-axiom-register)). A value that must be transferred out is introduced as a non-`using var` owned local instead.

<a id="sec-captured-owned-bindings"></a>
**Captured owned bindings (derives: [K2](#sec-kernel-k2) + [K5.5](#sec-kernel-k5)).** Inside a closure, a captured owned binding — an owned local or `owned` parameter of the enclosing body — is uniformly in **borrow state**: reads borrow (the producers rows above), and assignment to it, a marked transfer from it, an explicit `Dispose()` or discard of it, and every other owned-consuming use of it are compile errors — a closure cannot consume, reassign, or dispose a captured owned binding (a closure-side consume would be a kill no body-local liveness can see — K5.5's decidability bound; the move-only closure rule of [§28.9](#sec-runtime-managed-types), "the closure does not own the array", is the same principle). Mutation of captured **plain** (borrowed- or value-state) locals is unaffected ([§27.5](#sec-closures)). A callback that must genuinely consume a value takes an `owned` parameter and is invoked with the value transferred from outside ([§28.9](#sec-runtime-managed-types)).

<a id="sec-borrow-lifetime-rules"></a>
#### Borrow lifetime rules

A borrowed value's lifetime is the lifetime of its *source* ([K2.1](#sec-kernel-k2)). The compiler enforces, as instances of [K2.3](#sec-kernel-k2)'s bounded-escape rule:

- A borrowed local may not be returned from a method whose return type is `owned`.
- A borrowed local may not be returned from a method at all unless the return is a borrow with a well-defined source that outlives the call (derives: [K2.4](#sec-kernel-k2) — only sources every caller can re-establish against its own actuals; the sourceless static case is rejected at the declaration). In this version the admitted sources are:
  1. a **receiver-sourced** borrow from an instance method — a bare owned-field read (not of a mint-announcing-typed field, `Task`-family or iterable-family, [§28.6](#sec-leak-prevention)), `this`, or a borrow reached through the receiver's fields and indexers ([§28.6](#sec-leak-prevention)) — or the receiver-parameter borrow of an extension method ([§26.7](#sec-ownership-in-extensions));
  2. a **static-storage-sourced** borrow, from a **static property getter** only, returned through a non-`owned` return type: a bare read of a `static` **class- or interface-typed field** — `owned`, `readonly` without `owned` ([§22.13](#sec-static-class-typed-fields-without-owned)'s exemption: the referent is process-lived and never disposed), or a [§22.12](#sec-static-members) rule 2 admitted mutable static (whose stores never dispose a displaced referent, so every referent it has ever held stays alive to process exit). Its source is the declaring type's static storage, [K2](#sec-kernel-k2)'s always-live source ([§22.13](#sec-static-initialization-order)): every admissible static field form keeps its referents alive to process exit. This is the callee-side form of the *Static property access `T.P`* and *Static field access `T.f`* producers rows above (the stdlib §6.5 event pattern's static idiom and the stdlib §3.2 `Encoding` singletons are the motivating cases).
  3. A static **method** may not return such a read: nothing signature-visible distinguishes a storage-returning static method from a factory, so the signature itself is rejected as the sourceless-factory case (*Factory methods* above); were it admitted, every caller would mint a second owner for the borrowed-out storage — the two-owners pairing the empty-set carve closes for bare-type-parameter signatures, closed here for concrete ones. Re-expose the field through a static property (whose `T.P` read is the sound caller-side dual) or transfer with an `owned` return.
  4. A borrowed *local or parameter* with **no** source that outlives the call — e.g. a static method returning one of its parameters, `static method Pick(a: Res, b: Res): Res return a;` — may **not** be returned; this callee-side prohibition and the declaration-site static-return rule (*Factory methods* above) are one boundary seen from two sides.
  5. (Value-typed and runtime-managed returns are not borrows and are outside this rule — a returned function value's **carried** borrows are judged by the closure bullet below; the mint-announcing and bare-type-parameter declared return kinds are the [announcement table](#sec-announcement-table)'s rows 2–3 and 5–6 — a returned frame's carried borrows under *Returning a deferred-activation frame* ([§28.3](#sec-returning-a-deferred-activation-frame)), the bare-parameter admissions under *Bare-type-parameter returns* ([§28.3](#sec-bare-type-parameter-returns)).)
- A method's return type that names an **owning-collection or owning-wrapper type** (`OwningArray<T>`, `OwningDictionary<K, V>`, `OwningSet<T>`, `OwningStack<T>`, `OwningQueue<T>`, `OwningLinkedList<T>`, `Shared<T>`, `Weak<T>`, and the other owning collection and wrapper types — **not** `OwningTask<T>` and not the iterable-family interfaces: mint-announcing returns are governed by *Calls mint for the mint-announcing families* above, a call minting a caller-owned frame, a stored frame re-exposed only through property/field/slot borrows) follows the *same* owned-vs-borrow rule as any other reference return (the *Producers* table above): declared `owned`, the caller takes ownership; declared **without** `owned`, the result is a **borrow** with a documented source (the `Owning*` type name denotes *element* ownership, orthogonal to the container ownership the `owned` qualifier governs — [§5.11](Bezel_Design_Rationale.md#sec-owning-collections)). The borrow-return restrictions then apply unchanged: a bare owning-collection *field* read may be returned (its source is the receiver, [§28.6](#sec-leak-prevention)); a borrowed *local* or *parameter* with no source that outlives the call may **not** be returned; a `move`d field or a freshly-produced owning value must be returned through an `owned` return type. A borrow returned this way carries the capability restriction of [§28.6](#sec-borrowed-owning-collections) — the caller may not `Dispose` it (the owner does); it may otherwise be read and mutated like any borrowed collection.
- A borrow may be stored in a field of an object only if the borrow's source provably outlives that object. In clauses:
  1. **The admission.** A borrowed scope-bound *local* never satisfies the rule — it is disposed at the end of its scope, which a field of the object outlives — so a borrowed local may not be assigned to any field. A borrow whose source *does* outlive the object **is** admissible: the idiomatic form binds it through a constructor parameter into a non-owned class-typed field (the `_owner: Customer` back-reference of [§28.5](#sec-owned-fields)), where the caller-side source outlives the constructed object. Such a **borrowing class-typed field** — a non-owning class-typed field whose target is owned elsewhere — is the back-edge that serialization synthesis treats specially ([§9.8](#sec-serialization-synthesis)). The field stores a plain reference.
  2. **The check.** The assignment-site check is structural and decidable — borrows sourced from a parameter that is **not `owned`** — a plain or `scoped` parameter — or from the receiver are admissible; scope-bound locals and temporaries are rejected — and an **`owned` parameter is scope-bound**: the method disposes its undischarged value at its own end (*Auto-drop (affine)* below), so a borrow of it is rejected here exactly as a borrow of a scope-bound local is. A borrow returned by **invoking a function value** whose declared return slot is a plain concrete class or interface type (the [announcement table](#sec-announcement-table)'s row 4, function-value invocation column) is sourced from the invoked value and from the invocation's plain arguments. The invoked value contributes its source set (the closure bullet below), read here in one way: a function-typed parameter in it, plain or `scoped`, contributes **itself**, a parameter source, whether the invoked value is that parameter, a local the flow analysis traces to it, or the function-typed result of invoking it. Each plain argument contributes its sources by kind ([§28.3](#sec-argument-contributions)). Whatever inhabits a function-typed parameter returns only `null`, static storage, a borrow of what it captures (a method reference's bound receiver included), or a borrow of its own parameters, the result of invoking a function-typed one among them (*Concrete-slot function bodies* above). The captures are sources the caller holds at the call, and the parameters are bound to the invocation's arguments. The call bound the closure bullet places on a plain function-typed parameter therefore bounds the function value and its function-typed results, not an object borrow its invocation returns. So `_v := make()` with `make: () -> Item` is admitted under clause 3's residual. Where `x` is a scope-bound local, `_v := pick(x)` with `pick: (Item) -> Item` and `_v := wrap(lambda() => x)` with `wrap: (() -> Item) -> Item` are rejected, and so is `_v := f()` where `f` traces both to `make` and to a lambda capturing `x`, and `_v := get(r)` with `get: (Ref) -> Item` and `r := new Ref(x)` for `record Ref(Item: Item)`. A generic body's `V := g()` with `g: () -> T` is checked the same way under the class-or-interface assumption ([§28.1](#sec-where-the-owned-modifier-can-appear)), with the same residual at a class or interface substitution.
  3. **The residual.** The residual is a [K4.3](#sec-kernel-k4)-recorded trust clause: whether the caller-side source actually outlives the object is the programmer's obligation, not a compile-time guarantee, with [K4.1](#sec-kernel-k4)'s backstop as the named safety net. In the default build that backstop is live — a member access through the stored borrow after the source's disposal raises `DisposedAccessException` ([§28.2](#sec-checked-disposal)), undefined behavior only in an explicitly selected unchecked build — the trust-admission report ([§28.3](#sec-diagnostics)) names every such store, and a `scoped` parameter ([§28.14](#sec-scoped-callback-parameters)) makes the bound static. The caller-side source is whatever the caller passed, and the caller's check reads only the callee's signature (derives: [K2.3](#sec-kernel-k2) + [K4.3](#sec-kernel-k4) + [K8.1](#sec-kernel-k8)). An unbound owned temporary or a borrow of a scope-bound local, passed to a plain parameter that the callee stores — directly, through a field path rooted at it (`this.keep := x.child`), or as a borrow a call on it returns (`this.keep := x.Self()`) — is admitted at the call, for a local, virtual, interface or imported callee alike. Neither source is lifetime-extended: the temporary is disposed at its [K8](#sec-kernel-k8) boundary and the local at its scope's end, and a member access through the stored borrow after that point is the backstop's fault. A temporary meets the obligation only when the object dies within the same full expression. The remedies are to bind the source to a holder that outlives the object, to declare the parameter `scoped` (which rejects a fresh producer and bounds a local statically), to declare it `owned` (which takes the value), or to declare an `owned` overload beside it, to which a fresh argument routes ([§22.6](#sec-overloading)).
  4. **The domain clause.** The caller-side obligation includes **not transferring the source's object to another domain** — and, its extension, **not consuming it into a construction that makes it reachable from other domains**: `FrozenArray<T>.From(move …)` (stdlib §4.19), a `Shared<T>`/`Locked<T>`/`RwLocked<T>` constructor whose result is then shared across domains ([§28.13](#sec-shared-ownership), [§30.12](#sec-data-owning-locks)), or a store into an admitted static ([§22.12](#sec-static-members)); such a consume is not itself a domain transfer, but it creates or publishes an object other domains may reach while the pre-consume borrow still aliases its storage, and every statement of this clause applies to it verbatim. A field-stored borrow of an object later moved across a domain boundary — directly, or through a different binding such as `move box.f` into a spawn argument or channel send — is *not* rejected by the consume-site freeze below (the freeze sees only local borrows of the consumed binding — [K5.6](#sec-kernel-k5)) and is **not** caught by checked disposal mode (the object stays alive in the receiving domain, so no disposed flag is ever set); it is a data race.
  5. **Reach.** The same domain clause attaches to **every** residual-trust borrow admission: collection-held borrows ([§28.11](#sec-borrowing-collections)'s store rule) and borrows held by a **pending async frame** ([§30.1](#sec-async-methods) — an unsettled task's receiver and plain reference-typed arguments, and the capture-set contribution of its plain function-typed arguments (*Deferred-activation callees* below: the sources of the borrows a callback captures, and a forwarded plain function-typed parameter as itself), live in the state machine, in no local borrow binding the freeze can see; §30.1's settlement obligation carries the clause explicitly). These residuals are the honest limit of the static rule ([§30.14](#sec-multiple-domains)). A class- or interface-typed `scoped` parameter ([§28.14](#sec-scoped-callback-parameters)) upgrades this residual-trust admission to a fully static bound at participating call sites.
- A borrow may not be assigned to a local whose scope strictly encloses the borrow's source's scope — including flowing into a loop-carried binding along a back edge when the source is declared inside the loop body (`prev := cur;` where `cur` is per-iteration). The scope comparison is structural and decidable; the diagnostic is the standard *"Borrow held by `x` would outlive its source `y`."*
- A borrowed local may not be captured by a closure that may outlive the borrow's source. A **closure is a borrow-carrying value** ([#4154](https://github.com/s8lap/bezel-lang/issues/4154)), and whether it may outlive a source is decided by its **source set**, read off the value's provenance ([K2.2](#sec-kernel-k2)'s union under composition, bounded by [K2.1](#sec-kernel-k2)'s weakest source) — the tracking [§28.9](#sec-runtime-managed-types) describes as separate from the function value's own runtime-managed lifetime: a lambda literal or method reference contributes the sources of the borrows it captures — a captured borrowed local or parameter that binding's source, a captured owned local its enclosing scope (the producers row *Captured owned local inside a closure* above), a captured `ref` or `out` parameter, whatever its type, the declaring body's scope as well ([§27.5](#sec-closures)), a captured function value its own set transitively, and a method reference's bound receiver as a capture (the next bullet) — where a lambda's captures include the free bindings of every lambda nested in its body that resolve outside that body; a local or parameter contributes the union of the sets of the forms the flow analysis traces it to, a plain function-typed **parameter** carrying a set its signature does not announce ([K2.4](#sec-kernel-k2)) and so bounded by the call, [§28.14](#sec-scoped-callback-parameters)'s call-bounded tier; **invoking** a function value yields a value carrying the invoked value's set (a lambda's body can return a closure only over what the lambda itself captures, its own locals being scope-bound; a method's function-typed return is borrow-free by construction under the sink rule below, so a method call's result carries the empty set); a function value read from a field, a collection, a property or an indexer carries the empty set — those holders admit only capture-free function values, by the same sink rule (the capture-set contribution of *Deferred-activation callees* below rests on exactly this), and a `scoped` field's value is never read out as a value at all ([§28.14](#sec-scoped-callback-parameters)); and a function value whose provenance this body cannot otherwise trace carries an **unannounced** source, which satisfies no sink rule and is bounded by the call. Every rule in this list then applies to the function value **by that set**, with no closure-specific list: it may be bound to a local — plain `var` or `using var` alike, the `using var` adding only non-reassignability ([§28.9](#sec-runtime-managed-types)) — whose scope does not strictly enclose any source's scope (the local-scope bullet above, loop back edges included; a declaration's own block never strictly encloses a source that is in scope at it, so an initializer is admitted by construction and only assignment to an already-declared local can cross scopes — each assignment checked on its own, a later read of the local carrying the union of the sets the analysis traces it to); it may be immediately invoked; it may be captured by another closure, whose set then includes its own; and it may **not** be stored in a field, in any collection, or through an `out`/`ref` parameter, and may not be returned from the enclosing method (by `return`, or by `yield return` in an iterator, whose element type announces no source set either), **while its source set is non-empty** — a function type announces no source set ([K2.4](#sec-kernel-k2)), so no holder outside this body can re-establish it and no caller could bound it, the ground [§28.14](#sec-scoped-callback-parameters) states for a received callback (a plain signature carries no capture set), read at every position that erases the set; a capture-free function value is admitted at each of those sinks (a property or indexer assignment included — the *property and indexer stores* below), and a capture-bearing one is stored only through a `scoped` parameter under §28.14's storage-bounded admission. A **set-erasing position** is a position whose declared type, nullability stripped, is not a function type and to which a function value converts: a position declared `Object` (the one such type a function value converts to, [§3.1](#sec-type-kinds)), and a parameter, return slot, `ref` or `out` location, record component, choice payload or inline-array slot whose declared, pre-substitution type, nullability stripped (the element type, for an inline array), is a bare type parameter, at an instantiation substituting a function type for it. A function value reaches such a position by implicit conversion — at an argument, an initializer, an assignment, a `return` (a lambda's included), a pattern binding, a collection-literal element or a `with` assignment — and, when it is the argument of a function-typed parameter whose declared return slot, reached through return slots only at any depth (`() -> T`, `() -> () -> T`), is a bare type parameter so substituted, through the result of every invocation of that parameter, which carries the argument's set. A function value as the receiver of a member `Object` declares (`f.ToString()`, `f.GetHashCode()`, an interpolation hole) is not at a set-erasing position. At every set-erasing position **a function value with a non-empty source set is rejected, and a capture-free one is admitted**: the declared type announces no source set, so no holder reached through it could re-establish one ([K2.4](#sec-kernel-k2)), and no rule reading the position — the field-store bullet's residual, [§28.11](#sec-borrowing-collections)'s store rule, the [announcement table](#sec-announcement-table)'s row 5 — sees a borrow to bound ([K2.3](#sec-kernel-k2)). The check is the caller's, over its own flow analysis and the callee's declared signature, enforced per instantiation category ([§3.6](#sec-derived-type-properties) rule 2); the generic body is not re-checked and stays under [§28.1](#sec-where-the-owned-modifier-can-appear)'s class-or-interface assumption. A `scoped` parameter is never a set-erasing position: it is declared at a function type, or at a class or interface type other than `Object` ([§28.14](#sec-scoped-callback-parameters)). The remedies are a capture-free function value; a parameter declared at a function type and invoked within the call ([§28.14](#sec-scoped-callback-parameters)); a `scoped` one where the callee must retain the callback; and, for a selector, the expression form `(if c then f else g)`, whose arms keep their sets. Two routes reach a set-erasing position with no conversion at a caller, and each has its own rule: a method reference formed over one ([§28.14](#sec-scoped-callback-parameters)'s *method-reference formation bar*), and a type parameter in a parameter slot of a parameter slot (*Function-type substitutions are excluded from type parameters in nested parameter slots*, after the `Task`-family exclusion above). A `return` inside a lambda body leaves only that lambda: a closure returned there over a binding declared *outside* the body carries only sources the enclosing lambda's own value already carries (its captures include the nested lambda's outward-resolving free bindings), so that return escapes nothing the enclosing value's binding was not checked for, while one over a binding declared *inside* the body is the scope-bound rejection at that return. Immediate invocation, `using var` binding, and argument passing are consequences of this rule, not a closed list. And it may be passed as an argument to a function-typed parameter — where the callee's use is bounded by its signature: a plain parameter is **call-bounded** (the callee may not retain the callback past the call — for a deferred-activation callee, past the returned frame's life ([§28.14](#sec-scoped-callback-parameters), *Call-bounded × deferred activation*); compiler-verified for user-authored callees, [§28.14](#sec-scoped-callback-parameters)), and a `scoped` parameter stores under [§28.14](#sec-scoped-callback-parameters)'s storage-bounded admission, which checks the captures against the bounding object. *(An extension method's parameter is an ordinary plain parameter — every plain function-typed parameter admits capture-bearing arguments on the caller side, except through the return-slot arm of the set-erasing positions above. The standard library's lazy query operators, whose returned query values retain the callback until enumeration, are the normative instance of the deferred-activation frame-residence rule ([§28.14](#sec-scoped-callback-parameters)): the retention is bounded by the query value, whose carried sources include the callback's captures ([§28.3](#sec-unbound-owned-temporaries)) — no `scoped` marking and no certification are involved (stdlib §5).)*
- The same capture-and-escape rule applies to **method references** ([§27.6](#sec-method-references)) that bind an instance receiver: `obj.Method` produces a function value whose captured environment includes `obj`. If `obj` is a borrow, the resulting function value is subject to the closure-escape rules above as if `obj` had been captured by an explicit lambda — its source set is `obj`'s. The function value's runtime-managed status ([§28.9](#sec-runtime-managed-types)) governs the *function value's own* lifetime; it does not relax the lifetime constraints on borrows captured by the function value.
- **Property stores of a borrow-carrying value (derives: [K2.3](#sec-kernel-k2)).** An assignment to an instance property of a class or interface (`obj.P := e`, or a bare `P := e` naming the property) whose setter is not declared `set(owned)`, of a value whose type can carry a borrow (a class or interface type that is not runtime-managed ([§28.9](#sec-runtime-managed-types)), or a borrow-bearing record, choice or inline array ([§3.6](#sec-derived-type-properties))), is judged at the site as a store of that value into a non-`owned` field of the receiver, whatever form the property is declared in: by the field-store bullet above, [§9.7](#sec-records-and-disposal)'s instance-field bullet and [§28.6](#sec-leak-prevention)'s fresh-store rule. It is admitted exactly where that store would be. A borrow of a scope-bound local or of an `owned` parameter, and a freshly-produced owned value, are rejected at the assignment; a class- or interface-typed borrow that the field-store bullet admits (one sourced at a plain parameter or at the receiver, among others) is admitted under that bullet's residual; and a borrow-bearing record or choice value is admitted only in the null-source form. An auto-property's assignment is a store to its backing field ([§23.1](#sec-auto-properties)), and a site that reaches the property through an interface or a `virtual` or `abstract` member cannot tell which form the dispatch reaches, so the verdict reads the assignment, as the next bullet's does for a function value. A block-form setter's `value` is a plain parameter of the setter's body ([§23.3](#sec-block-form-properties)); the field-store bullet's clause 3, for a temporary or local passed to a plain parameter that the callee stores, is not reached through a property assignment. A `set(owned)` setter is an owned-consuming position (K3.1). An indexer assignment of such a value is not reached by this bullet: it is a call of the indexer's setter, or a [§28.11](#sec-borrowing-collections) slot store. An assignment to a **static** property ([§22.12](#sec-static-members); `T.P := e`, or a bare `P := e` naming it) of such a value, not through `set(owned)`, is judged in the same way as a store of that value into a non-`owned` static field declared as the property is (of its declared type, and `readonly` for a `static readonly` auto-property), whatever form the property is declared in. A `static readonly` auto-property is assigned only in its declaring type's own static initialization ([§23.1](#sec-auto-properties)), where a freshly-produced owned value is discharged as into a `static readonly` field ([§22.13](#sec-static-class-typed-fields-without-owned)). At a settable static property a freshly-produced owned value is admitted only where [§22.12](#sec-static-members) rule 2 admits a mutable static of that type (forms (i) and (ii)): the producer is discharged and the referent is process-lived ([§22.13](#sec-static-class-typed-fields-without-owned)'s exemption), whatever the setter does with `value`, a setter that does not store it included. At any other declared type, where a settable static property can only be block-form (rule 2 rejects the auto-property), it is [§28.6](#sec-leak-prevention)'s fresh-store error. A borrow of a scope-bound local or of an `owned` parameter is rejected; a class- or interface-typed borrow is admitted where the field-store bullet admits it, under its residual and domain clause; and a borrow-bearing record or choice value is admitted only in the null-source form ([§9.7](#sec-records-and-disposal)'s static-field bullet).
- **Function-typed holders (derives: [K2.4](#sec-kernel-k2)).** A **function-typed holder** is a field (a `scoped` field excepted), a record component, a choice case's payload field, an inline-array slot, a location reached through a `ref` or `out` parameter, or the enclosing method's return or `yield return` slot (a property or indexer getter's included), whose declared type — for an inline array, its declared element type — is a function type; a property or indexer slot assigned a function value, whatever its declared type (clause 1 keys on the assigned value's static type); and any collection slot. At every function-typed holder the closure bullet's sink rule holds: a store of a function value **admits a capture-free value and rejects one whose source set is non-empty** (a capture-bearing closure, a plain function-typed parameter, a local carrying either), judged at the site, whatever form the member is declared in. Two exclusions are load-bearing: a **lambda's** `return` is not a holder (the closure bullet's lambda-`return` clause), and a `scoped` field or parameter stores under [§28.14](#sec-scoped-callback-parameters)'s storage-bounded admission instead. A record component, choice payload or inline-array slot declared at a type parameter is not a function-typed holder; at a function-type substitution it is a set-erasing position (the closure bullet above). The stores, by holder:
  1. ***Property and indexer stores of a function value.*** A property or indexer assignment of a value whose static type, nullability stripped, is a function type (`obj.P := f`, a bare `P := f` inside the declaring type, `r[i] := f`) is a store. An auto-property's assignment is a store to its compiler-generated backing field ([§23.1](#sec-auto-properties)). A site that reaches the member through an interface or a `virtual` or `abstract` member cannot tell an auto-property from a block-form setter, and an auto-property implements an interface property ([§11.2](#sec-interface-declaration)), so the rule reads the assignment, not the accessor form. A block-form setter's implicit `value` of function type therefore carries the empty set ([§23.3](#sec-block-form-properties)) and is not a call-bounded parameter ([§28.14](#sec-scoped-callback-parameters)), so its body may store it. A property or indexer **read** of function type carries the empty set (the closure bullet's provenance list): an auto-property's read is a read of the backing field its assignments store to, and any other getter's result leaves through the getter's return slot, a function-typed holder above. The remedy for a capture-bearing callback is a method with a `scoped` parameter of function type ([§28.14](#sec-scoped-callback-parameters)).
  2. ***Record components of function type.*** A record component (a positional field, a body auto-property or a public field: the [§9.5](#sec-non-destructive-update-with) `with` targets) is a holder at its declared type. An argument for such a component at every call of the record's auto-generated primary constructor ([§9.1](#sec-positional-records); a `new` expression or a body constructor's `this(...)` chain) and a `with` assignment to it (`r with(F := f)`) are stores. The generated constructor's parameter for such a component therefore carries the empty set, as a block-form setter's `value` does, and is not a call-bounded parameter ([§28.14](#sec-scoped-callback-parameters)). A record's declared constructor is checked like any other body: its plain function-typed parameter is call-bounded, so storing it in a component is rejected there. The record's [§9.7](#sec-records-and-disposal) classification is unchanged, a function type being runtime-managed, and a function value read from such a component carries the empty set, as one read from a field does. The remedy for a capture-bearing callback is a class with a `scoped` field behind a `scoped` constructor parameter ([§28.14](#sec-scoped-callback-parameters)).
  3. ***Choice payloads and inline-array slots of function type.*** A choice case's payload field, and each slot of an inline array (the array a local, a parameter, a field, a record component or a payload alike), is a holder at its declared type. A payload argument for such a field at a case construction ([§35.3](#sec-choice-construction), the declared-result form included), each element of a collection literal whose target is such an inline array ([§15.4](#sec-collection-literals)), wherever the literal stands (an initializer, an assignment, an argument, a `return`, a component or payload argument), and an element assignment to such a slot (`fs[i] := f`) are stores. A local inline array is no exception: the array is a value that copies into returns, fields, components and plain arguments, none of which announces a source set. A function value bound out of such a payload by a pattern ([§35.5](#sec-choice-matching)), or read from such a slot, carries the empty set. The choice's classification and holds-borrows property ([§35.4](#sec-choice-classification)) and the inline array's borrow-bearing property ([§3.6](#sec-derived-type-properties)) are unchanged, a function type being runtime-managed. The remedy for a capture-bearing callback is a function-typed local of its own, or a class with a `scoped` field behind a `scoped` constructor parameter ([§28.14](#sec-scoped-callback-parameters)).

A borrowed value may be passed as a non-`owned` argument to another call: the callee further borrows for the duration of the call, and retains the borrow past the call only where its declaration announces the retention (a deferred-activation frame, a `scoped` parameter, a `ref` or `out` location) or under a recorded trust clause ([K4.3](#sec-kernel-k4)), as a store into a field or a borrowing collection is (the field-store bullet above, [§28.11](#sec-borrowing-collections)).

**A `ref` or plain `out` location outlives the call** (derives: [K2.3](#sec-kernel-k2) + [K2.4](#sec-kernel-k2), with [K2.2](#sec-kernel-k2)'s union). A `ref` or plain `out` argument location ([§22.3](#sec-ref-and-out-argument-locations)) whose type, after substitution, can carry a borrow — a class or interface type, a function type, or a borrow-bearing record, choice or inline array ([§3.6](#sec-derived-type-properties); an inline array of class or interface elements among them) — is caller storage: the callee may store into it a borrow sourced at its receiver, a plain parameter, or static storage, and a borrow of its own scope-bound locals, temporaries or `owned` parameters is rejected there as at a field. Where the location's declared type is a function type it is also a function-typed holder (*Function-typed holders* above), so a function value stored there is admitted only capture-free. A borrow sourced at a `scoped` parameter is not a plain-parameter source and is rejected there: its own value, which [§28.14](#sec-scoped-callback-parameters) admits only into the bounding object's fields, a borrow reached through it, and the result of invoking it. The caller therefore treats each such location as receiving any borrow the call carries: the sources the receiver and every plain (non-`owned`, non-`scoped`) argument contribute, each counted by kind as [*The sources an argument contributes*](#sec-argument-contributions) states (the receiver as an argument of its type), and the current value of every such `ref` argument. At the call, each of those borrows must be admissible into each such location exactly as the direct assignment of it would be — the local bullet's scope comparison at a local or parameter, the field rule above at a field, the assignment through the accessor at an accessor target (the *property stores of a borrow-carrying value* and *property and indexer stores* bullets above) — and a violation is rejected at the call site; after the call the location's source set is their union. An `out _` discard names no location and takes no part. The rule reads only the callee's signature: a callee that stores nothing is checked as one that stores everything.

<a id="sec-consume-site-freeze"></a>
#### The consume-site freeze

Consuming an owned **binding** — a local or an `owned` parameter — while a **live local borrow of its current value** exists is a compile error, unless the kill is unfrozen: [K5](#sec-kernel-k5)'s criterion, stated once there and read off the [consume table](#sec-consume-table)'s Frozen column. The consume sites are the table's eleven rows — including an `owned` argument's `Domain.Spawn` and channel `Send` instances ([§30.14](#sec-multiple-domains)/[§30.15](#sec-channels)) and **reassignment** of the binding itself (the displacement row: drop-on-overwrite is a consume of the displaced value, [§28.7](#sec-reassigning-owned-fields)).

A borrow is *live* at a consume site when some path from the site reaches a later use of it — [K5.5](#sec-kernel-k5)'s body-local backward dataflow, traced directly, through a `using var` pin ([§28.10](#sec-using-var)), or through a closure value that is itself still live. A live local of **borrow-bearing record** type ([§9.7](#sec-records-and-disposal)) — a span is the canonical case —, of **borrow-bearing inline-array** type (its held borrows' sources being its one source set, [§15.1.2](#sec-inline-array-members)), or of a **choice type that holds borrows** ([§35.4](#sec-choice-classification)'s holds-borrows property, whatever the choice's classification) counts as a live local borrow of every held borrow's source (stated explicitly, because stdlib §4.19's construction-time soundness is load-bearing on it): `var s := buf.AsSpan();` freezes `buf` against `FrozenArray<T>.From(move buf)` — and every other consume — for as long as `s` is live. The check is decidable and local to the method body ([K5.5](#sec-kernel-k5)); the diagnostic names the consumed binding, the borrow, and the borrow's surviving use.

**Unborrowed reassignment stays legal** — only the silent kill under a live borrow is rejected, and the site-announced kills stay unfrozen under their flag backstop ([K5.3](#sec-kernel-k5); [K5.7](#sec-kernel-k5)/[K5.8](#sec-kernel-k5)'s two recorded shapes excepted, each stated at its home). The one idiom the freeze rejects — borrow, transfer the source into a longer-lived owner, keep using the pre-transfer borrow — has a mechanical rewrite: transfer first, then re-borrow from the new owner (`pool.Add(move item); var b := pool[pool.Count - 1]; b.Configure();`).

**Scope.** Fields and collection slots are **not** frozen ([K5.6](#sec-kernel-k5)): a borrow of `obj.f`'s or `coll[i]`'s current value is invalidated by an overwrite or mutation of the slot under the runtime-checked posture ([§28.7](#sec-reassigning-owned-fields), [§28.11](#sec-element-slot-policy)); a slot kill *by move* — `move box.f` into a transfer, a spawn argument, or one of the domain-reachable constructions of the domain clause — disposes nothing and sets no flag, and is governed by the borrow lifetime rules' domain clause above ([K4.3](#sec-kernel-k4)), a recorded obligation, not by this exemption. An owning inline array's **whole-value** reassignment at a **local binding** is a binding consume under [K5.2](#sec-kernel-k5), not a slot overwrite: the exemption covers a store into `arr[i]`, not a store into `arr` ([§15.3](#sec-move-only-value-types)'s *Whole-value reassignment* rule); at an owning-inline-array **field**, the whole-value overwrite stays under this exemption's runtime-checked posture, like every owned-field overwrite ([§28.7](#sec-reassigning-owned-fields)). The [§28.14](#sec-scoped-callback-parameters) admission freeze on captured sources is the storage-bounded form of this rule, covering the site-announced kills as well — [K5.7](#sec-kernel-k5)'s derivation from the criterion's conjunct (ii), stated at [§28.14](#sec-scoped-callback-parameters). A value-kind receiver's source is **not** frozen either: a copyable receiver's member runs over the call's fixed receiver value ([§9.4](#sec-value-receivers-are-borrows)), so overwriting the source during the call — a mutably captured local, a field through an alias — changes nothing the member reads; a move-only receiver's member borrows the source in place under this exemption's runtime-checked posture, with [§19.3](#sec-patterns)'s write-point rule closing the one read the flag cannot backstop.
<a id="sec-owned-local-discharge-requirement"></a>
#### Owned-local discharge requirement

An owned local is disposed exactly once on every control-flow path. The program may *discharge* the obligation explicitly — transferring it elsewhere or disposing it by hand — at any of the [consume table](#sec-consume-table)'s positions (an **unmarked** binding `var y := x;` is a borrow of `x` and discharges nothing, [K3.13](#sec-kernel-k3); the post-discharge binding state is the table's column). If it does not, the compiler disposes the value at the end of its scope:

**Auto-drop (affine)** (derives: [K3.14](#sec-kernel-k3)). When an owned local — or an `owned` parameter — reaches a *normal-exit* scope end without having reached a discharge point, and is not in moved-from state, it is **disposed implicitly at that scope end** (for an `owned` parameter, at the end of the method) — the same implicit disposal that the *Exception-path discharge* below performs on the unwinding edge, now applied to the normal-exit edge as well. Bezel is therefore **affine**: every owned value is disposed exactly once on every path — explicitly where the program discharges it, implicitly at scope end otherwise — and the move analysis ([§28.8.1](#sec-the-move-expression)) leaves a transferred value in moved-from state so the scope-end disposal skips it; nothing is disposed twice. On a path that never moves it out, a plain `var` owned local (or undischarged `owned` parameter) thus behaves like a `using var`: reclaimed when its scope ends.

**Must-use warning ([K3.14](#sec-kernel-k3)'s lint).** Because a plain `var` (or an undischarged `owned` parameter) that is implicitly dropped is indistinguishable in *effect* from a `using var`, the compiler emits a **warning** (not an error) at the implicit-drop site of a plain-`var` owned local or `owned` parameter that is not trivial-dispose under [§28.9](#sec-trivial-dispose-classes)'s ceremony exemption (which states the key the classification is read from, and which is over the obligation, so it covers every holder form this warning attaches to), to surface a drop that may have been unintended. The warning names the local and lists the explicit alternatives: declare it `using var` (scope-bound disposal — the value may not then be moved out), `move`/return it (transfer the obligation), or dispose it explicitly with `.Dispose()` or discard it with `_ := …` ([§17.13](#sec-the-discard-_)). The warning is **suppressed** when the local is declared `using var` (the scope-bound intent is then explicit), when it is explicitly disposed or discarded — including through the null-conditional and null-forgiving spellings `x?.Dispose()` / `x!.Dispose()`, required for nullable owned locals — when it is moved or returned (no implicit drop occurs), and — for a **bound lazy query** — when the binding's **enumeration right is spent** at one of [§29.11](#sec-multiple-enumeration)'s statically visible consumption points. **This sentence is the closed set of suppressions**, shared with §29.11: every condition but the last either declares the drop's intent or leaves no drop to announce, while the spent-enumeration-right condition does neither — the frame is still auto-dropped at scope end — and suppresses on the lint's own ground, since what the lint announces is a value produced and never used and a spent right is the use. No other use of an owned binding suppresses the warning: a mere read is not a discharge. The warning is a lint over a sound program — it changes no semantics, only flags the implicit drop — so a project may tune or silence it; the auto-drop runs regardless. The rule is uniform across body kinds: for an `owned` parameter of an **iterator or async method**, whose undischarged value is disposed by the frame at teardown ([§29.8](#sec-iterators-with-owned-parameters), [§30.1](#sec-async-methods)) rather than at a lexical scope end, the warning attaches at the parameter's declaration; the adoption idiom `using var r := move reader;` suppresses it exactly as `using var` suppresses the local form.

The obligation is always satisfied — by the program or by the compiler — and the lint, not an error, marks the implicit case.

**Exception-path discharge** (derives: [K3.15](#sec-kernel-k3) — edge parity). Owned locals and owned parameters that are live when an exception propagates out of their enclosing block are disposed implicitly during stack unwinding: the compiler treats every owned local and owned parameter as if it were wrapped in an implicit `try`/`finally` whose `finally` disposes the value if it is still owned (not already moved-from and not already explicitly disposed). Exceptions therefore do not produce leaks even under a plain `var` or an unre-bound `owned` parameter; the only difference between the edges is the lint — a plain-`var` implicit drop on the *normal-exit* edge carries the must-use warning above, while the (non-local) exception edge does not. This is what makes plain `var` owned locals safely usable as accumulators that are eventually moved out by `return` or by an `owned` argument: the intent of a plain `var` is "I will discharge this explicitly somewhere"; the intent of a `using var` is "auto-dispose at scope end, never move out."

The implicit cleanup ordering follows reverse declaration order across multiple owned locals in the same scope, mirroring the destructor's field-disposal rule ([§28.4](#sec-the-destructor)). When the exception passes through nested scopes, the inner scope's locals are disposed before the outer scope's, in the same way `using var` cleanups nest.

The implicit cleanup does **not** apply to:
- Locals that are already in moved-from state at the point the exception unwinds past them.
- Locals that were already explicitly disposed before the throwing operation.
- Borrows (locals not in the owned state); these have no disposal obligation.
- Value-typed and runtime-managed-typed locals; these have no `Dispose` to call.

A user who wants to perform additional cleanup on the exception path (logging the partial result, performing a partial-state recovery) writes an explicit `try`/`finally` or `try`/`catch`/`throw` around the relevant operations. The implicit auto-dispose composes with explicit `finally` blocks on the single establishment-ordered cleanup stack of [§28.10](#sec-using-var): an owned local's implicit disposal is established at its declaration — exactly as if it were a `using var` — so a `finally` established *after* the declaration runs before the disposal (with the local still in scope), and one established *before* it runs after. Undischarged `owned` parameters' implicit disposals are established at entry to the body, and an expression's unbound owned temporaries at their production (see *Unbound owned temporaries* below).

<a id="sec-unbound-owned-temporaries"></a>
#### Unbound owned temporaries

The discharge requirement above governs *named* owned values — locals, fields, and parameters. An owned value may also be produced as an **unbound temporary**: the result of an `owned`-returning call (or other owned producer) that is not bound to any name, not `move`d, and not returned, but used only by *borrowing* operations within the expression — as the receiver of a further call, as a non-`owned` argument, as an operator operand, as a member or index access, or as the scrutinee of a `case` (whose boundary extension is defined below). Such a temporary is disposed at the **end of the full expression** in which it is produced, after every use of it within that expression has completed (derives: [K1](#sec-kernel-k1) + [K3.15](#sec-kernel-k3) + [K8](#sec-kernel-k8)). A **trivial-dispose** temporary is freed at the same K8 boundary as a non-trivial one is disposed — the compiler-inserted, flag-setting free of [§28.9](#sec-runtime-managed-types)/[§28.2](#sec-checked-disposal), identical timing, no user code. The borrowing uses include serving as the operand of a Pattern A `await` or `.Result` read whose borrowed result is itself confined to the same full expression ([§30.5](#sec-result-lifetime-and-task-disposal), [§30.3](#sec-the-task-taskt-and-ownedtaskt-types)) — for such an operand the disposal is deferred to the end of the full expression rather than performed at the await, so the borrowed result outlives its uses.

**The scoped-bind pinned slot ([§30.5](#sec-the-scoped-await-bind)).** A fresh `Task<T>` (class T) producer expression that is the exact initializer of a fresh local `var`/`const` declaration under the scoped await-bind is **not left** an unbound temporary of this section: the compiler binds it — establishing a hidden, unnameable `using var` slot ([§28.10](#sec-using-var)) at the declaration, pinned to the innermost enclosing block — and the ordinary named-location machinery governs from there. The classification (which expressions are unbound owned temporaries of task type) is this section's, unchanged; the re-pointing of its consequence at that one declaration form — bind-to-slot instead of dispose-at-boundary — is stated at [§30.5](#sec-the-scoped-await-bind).

**The full expression boundary.** The disposal boundary above — and the boundary wherever this specification uses the term for value lifetime — is [K8](#sec-kernel-k8)'s **full expression**, which includes desugared bindings such as [§29.2](#sec-desugaring-of-for)'s `__source` (in an expression statement, "end of the full expression" and "end of the statement" coincide, [§21.9](#sec-statement-form-of-expressions)); [K8.2](#sec-kernel-k8) makes each **evaluation** of a condition or pattern guard its own boundary, so condition temporaries never accumulate across iterations. (Distinguish the grammar-level use of the phrase — "the scrutinee is a full Expression", [§19.1](#sec-forms) — which is about parse precedence, not this lifetime boundary.)

**`case` scrutinees extend the boundary.** For a `case` whose scrutinee produces an unbound owned temporary, the boundary is [K8.3](#sec-kernel-k8)'s: the **whole `case` construct**, in statement position exactly as in expression position, which is what keeps [§19.3](#sec-patterns)'s pattern bindings — borrows whose source is the scrutinee — alive through the arm body: in `case pool.PopFirst() of var f: FastConnection => f.Warm(), _ => () end;` the binding `f` reads a temporary that is disposed after the selected arm finishes, never before it (the declined reject-instead alternative is recorded at rationale [§5.24](Bezel_Design_Rationale.md#sec-the-full-expression-boundary)).

**Binding-atom bindings are named temporaries.** A binding atom's clause whose initializer is an owned production ([§17.15](#sec-the-binding-atom)) produces a **named** unbound owned temporary: within the atom the binding is an ordinary named owned binding — the consume table's positions discharge it, and a consumed binding is not disposed by the boundary pass — but its boundary is the **atom itself** ([K8.5](#sec-kernel-k8)), tighter than the enclosing full expression: undischarged at the atom's completion, it is disposed there, after the body's evaluation, in reverse clause order, before the enclosing expression continues; the exception edge discharges it during unwinding on the same establishment-ordered cleanup stack. No must-use warning attaches (the binding names a temporary; its disposal is the language's job). The escape rule is [K8.4](#sec-kernel-k8) applied at the atom boundary: a borrow or frame whose source set includes an atom binding may not leave the atom — not in the body's value, not by store, not by capture in an escaping closure — and is rejected, never lifetime-extended; the remedy is a statement-level `using var` ([§28.10](#sec-using-var)).

When the full expression is instead exited by an **exception** — an operand or argument evaluated later throws before the temporary's transfer or consumption point — every already-produced, not-yet-consumed unbound owned temporary is disposed during unwinding by the same implicit `try`/`finally` mechanism as named locals (*Exception-path discharge* above; [K3.15](#sec-kernel-k3)/[K8.1](#sec-kernel-k8)): each temporary's disposal is established at its production, so the pass runs in reverse order of production on the establishment-ordered cleanup stack ([§28.10](#sec-using-var)), under [§28.4](#sec-the-destructor)'s multi-value supersession discipline. A temporary that had already transferred — into an `owned` parameter, a binding, an owned slot, or a return — is not disposed by this pass (its new owner's rules govern), and a temporary whose producing subexpression never ran was never produced. Exceptions therefore do not leak mid-expression producers: in `Combine(new Connection("a"), Fail())` where `Fail()` throws, the already-produced `Connection` — evaluated first under [§22.5](#sec-optional-parameters-and-named-arguments)'s call-site textual order, and not yet transferred because the call to `Combine` never began — is disposed during the unwind.

This is the unnamed-temporary counterpart of the discard contract ([§17.13](#sec-the-discard-_)) and the discharge requirement above: a *named* owned value reaches a discharge point or is auto-dropped at scope end with the must-use warning; an *unnamed* owned temporary — which no named form can reach — is reclaimed automatically once the expression that produced it is finished with it. A temporary that is instead bound (to a `var`/`using var`), `move`d, returned, or transferred into an owning location is governed by the corresponding transfer or discharge rule and is **not** disposed under this rule (it would otherwise be disposed twice).

For example, in `Folded(src).Sorted()` where `Folded(src): owned Array<T>` and `Sorted` borrows its receiver, the `Folded(src)` temporary is borrowed by `Sorted`, then disposed once the statement completes — exactly once, with no leak and no double-free. Disposal runs *after* the borrowing use, so the receiver is live for the duration of the call.

**A callee that stores a plain argument.** A non-`owned` argument position is a borrowing use whatever the callee's body does with the parameter, and the temporary's disposal at its boundary does not depend on that body. Where the callee stores the parameter, the store is the borrowed-field rule's caller-side residual (*Borrow lifetime rules* above) or the borrowing-collection store rule's ([§28.11](#sec-borrowing-collections)): the stored borrow dangles from the boundary on, and the temporary is not lifetime-extended ([K8.4](#sec-kernel-k8)). In `holder.Hold(new Item());`, where `Hold(x: Item)` assigns `x` to a field, the `Item` is disposed at the end of the statement. A retention a declaration announces is rejected instead: the deferred-activation callees below, a borrow-bearing record's or choice's construction ([§9.7](#sec-records-and-disposal)), a `scoped` parameter ([§28.14](#sec-scoped-callback-parameters)), and an assignment through an instance property of a class or interface, which is a store, not a call (*property stores of a borrow-carrying value* above): `holder.Item := new Item();` is rejected unless `Item`'s setter is declared `set(owned)`.

The rule is uniform across the source of the temporary: a user method declared `owned` and the standard-library materializers — themselves declared `owned`: `ToArray(): owned Array<T>`, `Sorted()`, `Reversed()`, `ToSet(): owned Set<T>`, `ToDictionary(...): owned Dictionary<K, V>` ([§5.11](Bezel_Design_Rationale.md#sec-owning-collections); these own the *container*, borrowing the elements) — are treated identically, so an unbound materializer result in a chain (`items.Where(p).ToArray().Length`, `xs.ToSet().Count()`) is reclaimed at end-of-statement by the same rule. The `owned` return qualifier is the single signal that drives the reclaim; there is no special-cased list of method names.

**Deferred-activation callees (derives: [K2.4](#sec-kernel-k2) + [K6](#sec-kernel-k6)).** A call can defer its use of a borrowed argument past the full expression: an iterator or async-iterator factory ([§29.3](#sec-iterator-methods), [§30.7](#sec-asynchronous-programming-async-iterators)) captures its plain reference-typed arguments into a state machine that runs later, and a lazy query operator ([§29.11](#sec-multiple-enumeration)) retains its source until enumeration. The returned **deferred-activation frame carries its arguments' borrows**: it is treated as a borrow-carrying value whose sources are the call's receiver and the sources its plain arguments contribute ([§28.3](#sec-argument-contributions)), a plain function-typed argument counting by its **capture-set contribution** (below) and a `CancellationToken` excepted (its source obligation is [§30.8](#sec-cancellation)'s); the ordinary rule that a borrow may not outlive its source applies to it. **The capture-set contribution.** A function value is runtime-managed ([§28.9](#sec-runtime-managed-types)) and is itself no borrow — but the borrows its closure captures are, and they ride the frame exactly as long as the callback does ([§28.14](#sec-scoped-callback-parameters)'s frame residence): a plain function-typed argument contributes its captured borrows' **sources** to the frame's source set, **transitively** — a captured value that is itself a function value or a deferred-activation frame contributes *its* sources by this same rule. The contribution is computed from the argument's statically-known value provenance: a lambda literal — or a local the flow analysis traces to lambda literals, method references, plain function-typed parameters of the enclosing body, or the results of invoking such traced values (an invocation yields a value carrying the invoked value's set — the closure bullet's provenance rule above), in any mix (a join contributes the union of the traced forms' contributions per this table) — contributes its captured borrows' sources (a value-typed capture contributes nothing, living in its heap capture cell — a `ref` or `out` parameter, which has none, contributes the declaring body's scope, [§27.5](#sec-closures); a runtime-managed capture contributes only what this rule assigns it — a `string` nothing, a function value or frame its sources); a method reference contributes its receiver's source (a static method reference, nothing); a plain function-typed **parameter** of the enclosing body — the one statically opaque form that can carry borrow captures — contributes **itself** as a carried source, and every caller re-establishes the contribution against its own actual argument by this same rule, the signature-level re-establishment this classification already uses for receivers and arguments. A function value read from anywhere else — a field, a collection element, a property or indexer read, a method call's result — contributes nothing, and soundly so: the closure-escape rules (the *Borrow lifetime rules* above) admit a borrow-capturing closure into none of those locations, so such values are borrow-free by construction. The one storing location that does hold capture-bearing callbacks — a `scoped` field ([§28.14](#sec-scoped-callback-parameters)) — is no counterexample, because its value cannot reach this position at all: passing a `scoped` field's value to a deferred-activation callee's plain function-typed parameter would let the stored callback ride a frame beyond the bounding object's control, and is rejected as exactly the escaping read-out [§28.14](#sec-scoped-callback-parameters) bars (frame residence type-announces retention for call-site arguments; it opens no read-out for stored callbacks). And a `scoped` parameter has no admitted path into a plain function-typed argument position either ([§28.14](#sec-scoped-callback-parameters)'s callee-side rights — `scoped`-field store, same-bound `scoped` forwarding, invocation — include none). In particular, an unbound owned temporary passed as a plain argument to such a callee — or reached through a plain function-typed argument's capture-set contribution (a method reference over a fresh receiver) — is admissible only when the returned frame is itself fully consumed **within the same full expression**; where the frame outlives the expression — bound to a name, returned, stored, or used as a `for`/`await for` source (whose desugaring binds it, [§29.2](#sec-desugaring-of-for)) — the program is rejected, the same reject-not-extend posture as [§9.7](#sec-records-and-disposal)'s no-temporary-source rule for records. The remedy names the source first: `var src := Source(3); await for var line in Shout(src) do … end;`. The callee classification is signature-level and decidable: a callee whose return type is one of the [§29.3](#sec-iterator-methods)/[§30.7](#sec-asynchronous-programming-async-iterators) iterable or enumerator interfaces, or a lazy query — or a **`Task`-family type** (`Task`, `Task<T>`, `OwningTask<T>`): an async callee's state-machine frame holds its plain reference-typed arguments' borrows until *settlement* ([§30.1](#sec-async-methods)), so an unbound owned temporary argument is admissible only when the returned task is consumed to settlement within the same full expression — awaited there, or blocked on outside a domain ([§30.3](#sec-the-task-taskt-and-ownedtaskt-types)). A task that instead escapes the full expression (bound — `using var t := SumAsync(Nums(3));` — returned, stored, or passed to `Task.FireAndForget`) is rejected: the temporary dies at the full expression's end, so the violation of [§30.1](#sec-async-methods)'s source-outlives-settlement obligation is statically certain, and the reject posture — not [§30.1](#sec-async-methods)'s trust posture, which covers only sources whose lifetimes the checker cannot compare — applies. The classification is deliberately conservative: it is by declared return type, so a callee returning an already-materialized collection typed as `IEnumerable<T>`, or an async callee that happens to complete before returning, is treated as borrow-carrying/escaping all the same; the remedy is always the same one line — bind the source first.

<a id="sec-returning-a-deferred-activation-frame"></a>
**Returning a deferred-activation frame (derives: [K6.2](#sec-kernel-k6) + [K2.4](#sec-kernel-k2)).** The callee-side borrow-return prohibition (*Borrow lifetime rules* above) does not apply to a return whose declared type is one of the deferred-activation kinds — the [§29.3](#sec-iterator-methods)/[§30.7](#sec-asynchronous-programming-async-iterators) iterable and enumerator interfaces, a lazy query, or a `Task`-family type (the [announcement table](#sec-announcement-table)'s rows 2–3): the declared return type itself announces the borrow-carrying classification (**type-announced**, [K6.2](#sec-kernel-k6)), and every caller re-establishes the returned frame's constraints against **its own** receiver and arguments by the signature-level rule above. A non-iterator method may therefore compose and return such a frame — `public static method Evens(xs: Array<int>): IEnumerable<int> => xs.Where(IsEven);` (an instance or extension callee states the same contract in the same unmarked spelling — the container half, *Calls mint for the mint-announcing families* above; `owned` remains admissible emphasis) — provided every borrow the returned frame carries is sourced from the method's own parameters or receiver (directly or through the receiver's fields, the receiver-sourced notion of [§28.6](#sec-leak-prevention)); an iterator method is the canonical instance, its returned state machine carrying exactly its parameters' borrows ([§29.4](#sec-lazy-evaluation)). A returned frame carrying a borrow of anything else — a scope-bound local, a `using var`, a temporary — is rejected at the return site, since the frame would outlive the source; the remedy is to materialize instead (return an `owned` collection — the materializers above). The callee-side check is structural over the returned expression's construction: the frame's carried sources are what the deferred-activation calls that built it put in it (*Deferred-activation callees* above) — each call's receiver and the sources its plain arguments contribute ([§28.3](#sec-argument-contributions)), a plain function-typed argument counting by its capture-set contribution and a `CancellationToken` excepted — followed transitively through intermediate frames. In a generic body an argument whose type is a type parameter, or whose borrow-bearing or holds-borrows classification turns on one, therefore counts what it contributes at every substitution its constraints admit.
