A returned frame whose capture-set contribution reaches a scope-bound local, a `using var`, or a temporary is rejected at the return site exactly as a directly-carried borrow of one is — `return Doubled(nums, lambda(x) => scale.Apply(x));` over a `using var scale` is the canonical reject: the consumer would enumerate into a closure over a disposed object. A contribution that is the method's own plain function-typed parameter, or a capture sourced from its parameters or receiver, is admitted under the same parameter-/receiver-sourced admission as any other carried borrow. The classification stays deliberately by declared return type: a method returning an already-materialized collection typed as `IEnumerable<T>` is treated as borrow-carrying all the same — sound and conservative (the caller over-constrains its own arguments); declare the return `owned Array<T>` to advertise the stronger contract. This exception lifts only the borrow-return prohibition, and it governs the *carried* borrows only: the container itself transfers under *Calls mint for the mint-announcing families* above — fresh or owned on every return path, a borrowed container rejected — for the `Task`-family, iterable, and lazy-query kinds alike. The owned-escape rules of [§28.6](#sec-leak-prevention) are unaffected for values *outside* the families: a freshly-produced owned value at a concrete non-family type (a materialized collection returned as `Array<T>`, a `move` result) still requires an `owned` return type.

<a id="sec-diagnostics"></a>
#### Diagnostics

The compiler must produce error messages that name the variable, its current ownership state, and the rule violated. Recommended wordings for the commonest — an owned local going out of scope undisposed ([K3.14](#sec-kernel-k3)), an escaping borrow ([K2.1](#sec-kernel-k2)/[K2.3](#sec-kernel-k2)), a read of a moved-from local ([K1](#sec-kernel-k1)), a move of a `using var` (axiom [A5](#sec-axiom-register)) and the consume-site freeze ([K5](#sec-kernel-k5)) — are teaching text in the code-generation reference ([§4.6](Bezel_For_Code_Generation.md#sec-recommended-diagnostic-wordings)), not part of this specification.

**The trust-admission report.** A conforming implementation offers a per-build **trust-admission report mode**. In that mode, at every site where the compiler makes an admission that rests on a [K4.3](#sec-kernel-k4)-recorded trust clause — a parameter-, receiver- or field-path-sourced borrow stored into a non-`owned` class- or interface-typed field (the borrowed-field store rule above, and its restatements at [§28.6](#sec-leak-prevention), [§31.1](#sec-the-throw-operand) and [§22.16](#sec-contract-clauses)); such a borrow stored into a borrowing-family collection or the key slot of an `OwningDictionary<K, V>` ([§28.11](#sec-borrowing-collections)'s store rule), including a store whose receiver the structural check leaves unclassified; a borrow held by a pending frame past the call that minted it — a task passed to `Task.FireAndForget`, stored, or bound and not awaited on every path before a held source's scope exits, a Pattern A `await` of a borrowed task operand, and a `return await` over a borrowed source that is not process-lived static storage ([§30.1](#sec-async-methods), [§30.5](#sec-result-lifetime-and-task-disposal)); and a [§28.14](#sec-scoped-callback-parameters) admission carrying the registration-lifetime residual (bounding forms 3 and 4) or the quiescence obligation (a user-declared `scoped` field) — the compiler **emits a warning** naming the rule and its clause, the borrow and its source, the holder, the obligation (the source outlives the holder's use of it, and is neither transferred to another domain nor consumed into a domain-reachable construction while held), and the static remedies available at that site: `scoped` ([§28.14](#sec-scoped-callback-parameters)), a `SlotHandle` key in place of the borrow (stdlib [§4.21](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-owning-slot-map)), a `Shared<T>` handle ([§28.13](#sec-shared-ownership)), an owning-family holder ([§28.11](#sec-collection-element-ownership)), or awaiting the frame to settlement ([§30.1](#sec-async-methods)). The report is informative: it changes no verdict and no generated code, and outside the mode it is not emitted. **A compilation unit that emits no report under the mode carries no recorded trust clause**: every borrow it holds in a field, a collection slot or a pending frame is statically bounded ([K2.3](#sec-kernel-k2)) or absent. The claim reaches exactly the register above — not the site-announced kills ([K4.2](#sec-kernel-k4), runtime-checked under [§28.2](#sec-checked-disposal)), not [§22.12](#sec-static-members)'s statics obligations (their own declaration-site warnings), not the documented trust of the foreign-function boundary ([§32.10](#sec-boundary-contract)), and not the certification grants of axiom [A10](#sec-axiom-register) — and it is per compilation unit: a program-wide claim needs every artifact in the build's closure compiled under the mode.

These rules ensure that every owned class instance is disposed **exactly once** at runtime and that no owned reference is silently leaked (drop-on-overwrite, [§28.7](#sec-reassigning-owned-fields), covers every overwrite — the move-only inline array's whole-value reassignment included, per slot, [§15.3](#sec-move-only-value-types)). Borrow **liveness** is enforced statically for locals, returns, and captures *up to explicit disposal*: the consume-site freeze rejects a move, transfer, or reassignment of a borrowed-from binding, and the scope rules reject every escape past the source's scope — but an **explicit `Dispose()`** of a borrowed-from source is deliberately not statically tracked (rationale [§5.1](Bezel_Design_Rationale.md#sec-owned-not-borrows)'s recorded trade-off; the one exception is a source frozen by a [§28.14](#sec-scoped-callback-parameters) storage admission, whose disposal *is* statically rejected for the bound's extent): use through a surviving borrow raises `DisposedAccessException` in checked disposal mode ([§28.2](#sec-the-idisposable-contract)) and is undefined behavior unchecked. For *field-held* and *collection-held* borrows ([§28.11](#sec-borrowing-collections)'s store rule), liveness holds up to the caller-side lifetime obligations of the bullets above, backstopped by checked disposal mode.

<a id="sec-choosing-a-disposal-form"></a>
#### Choosing a disposal form (recap)

One mechanism, two specializations, one lint. Every owned local (and undischarged `owned` parameter) is disposed exactly once on every path by the affine auto-drop above — the exception-path discharge being the same mechanism on the unwinding edge. `using var` and an explicit `Dispose()` therefore never add *safety*; they add **declared intent** and **timing**:

| Form | Disposes at | Movable out? | Diagnostic | Exception edge |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `using var x := …` | scope end, every exit path | no — scope pin ([§28.10](#sec-using-var)) | none (intent declared) | same disposal, same point |
| plain `var x := …`, undischarged | scope end (auto-drop) | yes | **must-use warning** at the implicit drop (none at a trivial-dispose type, [§28.9](#sec-trivial-dispose-classes)) | disposed silently during unwinding |
| plain `var` + explicit `x.Dispose();` | at the call; the scope-end pass skips the disposed value | yes, until disposed | none | a throw *before* the call is covered by the unwind — the pattern is exception-safe |
| `_ := expr;` (discard, [§17.13](#sec-the-discard-_)) | end of the discard statement | — (unnamed) | none (the discard is the announcement, [K3.13](#sec-kernel-k3)) | unbound-temporary rules above |
| `_ := x;` on a named owned binding | end of the discard statement; `x` left explicitly-disposed | — | none | as explicit dispose |
| unbound owned temporary | end of the full expression; during unwinding if the expression is exited by an exception | — | none | disposed during unwinding, reverse order of production |

*(One carve-out lives outside this table: a `Task`-family value — nullability stripped — may not be discarded; `_ := …;` is rejected, use `Task.FireAndForget` ([§17.13](#sec-the-discard-_)).)*

Doctrine (non-normative): reach for **`using var`** when the value lives and dies here — the default. Use **plain `var`** when ownership will move on (factory results being returned, accumulators, the loop-carried best) — the must-use warning then marks any path where it silently does not. Use an **explicit `.Dispose()`** only for an *early or conditional* release point inside a scope — and prefer a `do … end` block around a `using var` where the release point is really a scope. Use **`_ := expr;`** to dispose an unwanted owned result immediately. **Auto-drop is the safety net, not a style.** Unlike in C#, a trailing `x.Dispose();` is *not* an exception-safety bug — the unwinding edge always discharges live owned locals (Exception-path discharge above; rationale [§5.23](Bezel_Design_Rationale.md#sec-the-affine-model)) — so an explicit `Dispose()` in Bezel signals only an early release point, never `try`/`finally` plumbing.

<a id="sec-the-destructor"></a>
### 28.4 The `destructor`

A class may declare at most one destructor. Its body runs exactly once, the first time `Dispose()` is called.

```bezel
class FileStream
  private _handle: IntPtr;

  public constructor(path: string)
    using var cpath := CString.From(path);
    _handle := NativeOpen(cpath);
  end constructor;

  destructor
    if _handle <> IntPtr.Zero then
      NativeClose(_handle);
      _handle := IntPtr.Zero;
    end;
  end destructor;
end FileStream;
```

The compiler generates a public, idempotent `Dispose()` that:

1. Runs the destructor body, if any.
2. Disposes all owned-bearing fields in reverse declaration order. This covers fields marked `owned` (class- or interface-typed; the field's value's `Dispose()` is called) and fields of owning-inline-array type (`[N owned]T?` or `[N owned]T`; each non-null slot's `Dispose()` is called per [§15.1.1](#sec-owning-inline-arrays)). Inline-array fields without `owned` slots, value-typed fields, and runtime-managed fields require no disposal.
3. Chains to the base class's `Dispose()`.

After step 3 has propagated to the root of the hierarchy, the object's memory is reclaimed — immediately, or deferred under checked disposal mode's quarantine latitude ([§28.2](#sec-checked-disposal), [§28.12](#sec-asynchronous-disposal)). Memory reclamation is not part of the user-observable `Dispose()` contract — programs cannot rely on the precise moment at which an object's storage becomes available for reuse.

Destructors run in subclass-to-base order. `Dispose()` cannot be overridden; the customization point is `destructor`.

There is no `disposing` parameter, no manual `_disposed` flag, no `base.Dispose()` call.

**The destructor body runs on disposal, never on construction unwind — hold one raw resource per owning wrapper.** The generated `Dispose()` above disposes a *completed* instance. A constructor that throws unwinds under [§22.9](#sec-owned-fields-and-exception-safety) instead: already-completed owned fields and the base chain are disposed, and the throwing class's own destructor body is **not** run (the [§7.9](#sec-definite-assignment-for-non-nullable-fields) ground is stated there). A raw resource that only the destructor knows how to release — a native handle in an `IntPtr` field, foreign memory — is therefore protected only from the moment its constructor *completes*: a resource acquired in a constructor body and orphaned by a later throw in that body leaks. Three actions still run after a constructor body's last statement, and each can throw into that unwind: the constructor's `ensures` clauses and the construction-exit invariant check ([§22.16](#sec-contract-clauses)), and the scope-end disposals of the body's `using var` locals. A class that releases a raw resource in its destructor therefore holds exactly that one resource and acquires it as its constructor's final act, declaring no `invariant` member and no constructor `ensures` and arranging its `using var` locals so that their scope-end disposals precede the acquisition. The `FileStream` example above acquires as its final act and declares neither; its `cpath`, the acquisition's own argument and so live at the `NativeOpen` call, is the one disposal left between acquisition and completion — the residual that the rule below, that destructors should not throw, covers. A class needing two raw resources — or fallible work after an acquisition — wraps each resource in its own such class and composes the wrappers as `owned` fields ([§28.5](#sec-owned-fields)): owned fields assigned before the throwing statement are disposed on every unwind edge ([§22.9](#sec-owned-fields-and-exception-safety)), and the composite then needs no destructor at all ([§28.5](#sec-owned-fields); rationale [§5.29](Bezel_Design_Rationale.md#sec-destructor-body-not-on-ctor-unwind)).

**Destructors should not throw; behavior is defined when one does.** A destructor body (and hence the disposal it customizes) is expected not to throw. When one does:

- The exception propagates from the **disposal point** — the explicit `Dispose()` call, the `using var`/auto-drop scope-end site, the drop-on-overwrite site ([§28.7](#sec-reassigning-owned-fields)), the owning container's cascade, or an unbound owned temporary's end-of-full-expression (or unwind) disposal ([§28.3](#sec-unbound-owned-temporaries)).
- Before it propagates, the **remaining steps of the generated `Dispose()` still run**: the remaining owned-field disposals (reverse declaration order) and the base-class chain complete, and physical reclamation still occurs — a cleanup fault never leaks the object ([§28.12](#sec-asynchronous-disposal)'s posture, [§28.2](#sec-the-idisposable-contract)'s exactly-once invariant).
- In a **multi-value cleanup pass** — the enumeration is illustrative, not exhaustive: scope-end disposal of several locals, an owning collection's element cascade, an owning inline array's per-slot drop-on-overwrite pass ([§28.7](#sec-reassigning-owned-fields)), the exception-path discharge (including the unwind disposal of an expression's produced temporaries, [§28.3](#sec-unbound-owned-temporaries)), [§22.9](#sec-owned-fields-and-exception-safety)'s construction unwind, and [§22.13](#sec-static-initialization-order)'s program-exit static-disposal pass — a throwing disposer does not skip the remaining values: every remaining disposal still runs. If a later disposal in the same pass also throws, the later exception **supersedes** the earlier one — the [§31.2](#sec-try-catch-finally) `finally`-supersession discipline, its record-before-drop rule included — and the superseded exception is disposed (the two owner-owned instances excepted, [§31.2](#sec-try-catch-finally)). The accounting follows from the record-before-drop rule: a pass entered with **no exception in flight** whose N disposers all throw leaves the escaping exception carrying N−1 chronological entries; a pass entered **on an exception edge** — the exception-path discharge, and [§22.9](#sec-owned-fields-and-exception-safety)'s construction unwind — carries that exception's own entry as well, ahead of them.

<a id="sec-owned-fields"></a>
### 28.5 Owned fields

A field marked `owned` belongs to the containing object exclusively:

```bezel
class BankAccount
  private owned _transactions: Array<Transaction>;       // non-nullable, owned
  private owned _cache: TransactionCache?;               // nullable, owned
  private _owner: Customer;                              // back-reference, not owned
end BankAccount;
```

The `owned` modifier:

1. **Auto-disposes** the field when the containing object is disposed (after the destructor body runs, in reverse declaration order; a nullable field is null-checked before disposal, and a null field disposes nothing).
2. **Prevents leaks** by rejecting code that would let an owned reference escape the containing object.

Restrictions (derives: [K1.6](#sec-kernel-k1) + [K1.7](#sec-kernel-k1); the generic-argument position's absence is axiom [A14](#sec-axiom-register)):

- Only fields whose type is a **class type or an interface type** may be `owned`. Interface-typed owned fields are admitted because runtime dispatch resolves disposal to the underlying class's `Dispose()`; an `owned IConnection` field disposes whichever class implementation it currently holds.
- `string` fields may not be `owned`. String memory is runtime-managed.
- `Type` fields may not be `owned`. The type-identity token is process-interned and runtime-managed ([§28.9](#sec-runtime-managed-types)).
- Function-typed fields may not be `owned`. Function values are runtime-managed ([§28.9](#sec-runtime-managed-types)).
- Inline-array fields (`[N]T`, `[N]T?`) without the `owned` slot marker may not be `owned`. The array's slots hold borrows (or value-typed copies); there is no per-slot ownership to manage.
- Inline-array fields with the `owned` slot marker (`[N owned]T`, `[N owned]T?`) are move-only value types that carry owned slots ([§15.3](#sec-move-only-value-types)). They are admissible as class fields *without* a separate `owned` modifier on the field; the inline array's own `owned` slot marker already signals that the class's generated `Dispose()` disposes each non-null slot ([§28.4](#sec-the-destructor) step 2). Writing `private owned slots: [16 owned]Connection?;` is rejected as a double-marking error — the field modifier is omitted because the type-level marker already conveys the obligation.
- Local variables are not marked `owned`; use `using var`.
- Records may not have `owned` fields, and may not have inline-array fields with the `owned` slot marker (records support only copy semantics, not move semantics; see [§15.3](#sec-move-only-value-types)).

**Generic class fields** (derives: [K1.6](#sec-kernel-k1), checked per instantiation). When a generic class declares `private owned _slot: T` (where T is a type parameter), the restriction "only fields of class or interface types may be `owned`" is checked at *instantiation*. A `where T: class` constraint admits classes, interfaces, `string`, and function types ([§14.2](#sec-constraints)) — broader than what `owned` fields admit. Instantiating the generic with a type that satisfies `where T: class` but is neither a class nor an interface (`string`, function types) is a compile error at the instantiation site, with a message naming the rejected type. The generic body itself type-checks under the assumption that T is a class-or-interface type; programmers writing such generics should use `where T: class` and document that runtime-managed reference types are not admitted, or use a more specific constraint like `where T: IDisposable` (which automatically excludes records and runtime-managed types per [§14.2](#sec-constraints)'s interface-conformance rule).

A class with only owned-bearing fields (`owned` class/interface fields and/or owning-inline-array fields) and no native resources needs no destructor — the compiler-generated cleanup is sufficient.

<a id="sec-leak-prevention"></a>
### 28.6 Leak prevention

The compiler enforces:

- A *bare read* of an owned field **lends** ([K9.1](#sec-kernel-k9)) and may be returned through a **non-`owned`** return type as a **borrow** of the field — its source is the receiver, exactly as for `return this` (*Methods returning `this`* below); uniformly so for a class-typed owned field and for an owning-collection field (`owned _items: OwningArray<T>`). The caller's borrow carries the ordinary [K2.3](#sec-kernel-k2) obligations — no disposal (the receiver rule below, [Who may call `Dispose()`](#sec-who-may-dispose)), no `owned` store, no use past the receiver's lifetime; the field's holder (the receiver's destructor) still disposes it. Two edges are ruled by [§28.3](#sec-local-variables-ownership-and-borrows). A **static** field read — `owned`, or non-`owned` in either admissible form ([§22.13](#sec-static-class-typed-fields-without-owned), [§22.12](#sec-static-members) rule 2) — is returnable only from a **static property getter**, whose source is the declaring type's process-lived static storage ([§22.13](#sec-static-initialization-order); the callee-side form of [§28.3](#sec-local-variables-ownership-and-borrows)'s static-property and static-field producers rows); a static **method** returning such a read is [§28.3](#sec-factory-methods-and-sourceless-returns)'s sourceless-factory rejection whatever the field's form — its callers would mint a second owner; re-expose the field through a static property or transfer with an `owned` return. And a **mint-announcing-typed** field — `Task`-family or iterable-family — is not returnable through an unmarked mint-announcing *method* return, that return type being container-ownership-transferring ([§28.3](#sec-producers), *Calls mint for the mint-announcing families*): a stored frame — a stored task, a stored collection view — is instead re-exposed through a **property, field, or collection slot** (`public property Items: IEnumerable<Item> => _items;` is the stored-view face; the static-property face above stands for statics), or at the **concrete collection type**, whose non-`owned` return is this bullet's ordinary receiver-sourced borrow.
- **Transferring** an owned field's value out — a `move` expression ([§28.8.1](#sec-the-move-expression)), the only owned read ([K9.1](#sec-kernel-k9)) — is the only way to hand ownership onward: to a *callee* when consumed in place by an `owned` parameter, and to the *caller* only through an `owned` return type — and, because [§28.8.1](#sec-the-move-expression) admits no terminal-move dispensation, only in the take-restore-return shape (`TakeTransactions` below; a terminal `return move _f;` is rejected on its own return edge, [§28.8.1](#sec-the-field-restoration-rule)). A `move`d owned field returned through a non-`owned` return is an **error** (derives: [K1.7](#sec-kernel-k1) + [K2.3](#sec-kernel-k2) — the moved value would escape with no owner), and a freshly-produced owning value (`return new OwningArray<T>(...)`) returned through a non-`owned` return is likewise an error. (For the mint-announcing families — `Task` and iterable — the unmarked return type itself announces the transfer — type-announced, [K6.2](#sec-kernel-k6) — so a fresh **or owned** frame, a `move`d owned field of such a type included, is returnable, indeed required, through an unmarked mint-announcing return; [§28.3](#sec-producers).)
- An owned field's value reaches a non-owned class-typed field of another object only as a **borrow**, under [§28.3](#sec-local-variables-ownership-and-borrows)'s borrowed-field store rule (derives: [K1.5](#sec-kernel-k1)/[K9.1](#sec-kernel-k9) + [K2.3](#sec-kernel-k2); receiver- and parameter-rooted holders admissible, scope-bound-local- and temporary-rooted rejected; each admissible store carries the [K4.3](#sec-kernel-k4)-recorded trust clause and [K4.1](#sec-kernel-k4) backstop of every field-held borrow). The recorded obligation is precise: the storing side vouches for the field's **current value** — which [§28.7](#sec-reassigning-owned-fields) drop-on-overwrite or a [§28.8.1](#sec-the-move-expression) `move` may end before the holder's own life ends — not merely for the holder. It never reaches such a field as an owned value: a bare read cannot transfer ([K9.1](#sec-kernel-k9)), and a freshly-produced or `move`d owned value stored into a non-owned field is the fresh-store error below.
- A **freshly-produced owned value** — a `new` expression, a call returning `owned T`, a `move` expression, or an owned operator result — stored into a non-`owned` (borrow) field is an **error** (derives: K1.7 + K2.3): the field does not own its referent, so the fresh value would be left with no owner and leak. Declare the field `owned` (the containing object then disposes it, [§28.5](#sec-owned-fields)), or hand the value to a method that takes it `owned`. This is the storing-side counterpart of the non-`owned`-return rule above.
- A **property or indexer getter** may not return a freshly-produced owned value (axiom [A4](#sec-axiom-register)). A getter is a borrow-producing position — properties and indexers do not carry `owned` ([§23](#sec-properties-and-indexers); the `owned` modifier applies only to fields), so its return is always a borrow — and a fresh owned value returned through it would escape with no owner and leak. Expose the factory as a **method returning `owned T`** instead, which can hand the caller ownership.

These rules apply to **trivial-dispose** class types unchanged ([§28.9](#sec-runtime-managed-types) — the ceremony exemption waives warnings, never escape checks): a fresh trivial-dispose value stored into a non-`owned` field is the fresh-store error above (declare the field `owned` — which, at a trivial-dispose field type, does not flip the containing class's classification, [§28.9](#sec-trivial-dispose-classes)); a getter returning one (`get => new Random();`) is the A4 error above — the fresh value's owner would be a call-bounded temporary the caller's borrow outlives; and a fresh trivial-dispose value through a non-`owned` **instance** return is rejected exactly as any fresh value is (static signatures are already type-announced, [§28.3](#sec-factory-methods-and-sourceless-returns)).

```bezel
public method GetTransactions(): OwningArray<Transaction>
  return _transactions;     // OK: borrows the field — the caller may
                            //   read/iterate/mutate/drain it but not dispose it.
end GetTransactions;

public method TakeTransactions(): owned OwningArray<Transaction>
  var fresh := new OwningArray<Transaction>();  // build the replacement first (§28.8.1)
  var taken := move _transactions;              // take: the field is now moved-from
  _transactions := fresh;                       // restore — required on every exit path (§28.8.1)
  return taken;                                 // transfer: the caller owns the taken array
end TakeTransactions;

public method LeakTransactions(): OwningArray<Transaction>
  return new OwningArray<Transaction>();  // ERROR: a freshly-produced owning
                                          //   value through a non-`owned`
                                          //   return escapes with no owner.
end LeakTransactions;
```

The same no-escape principle governs storing into a field and returning from a getter:

```bezel
class Handle
  private _c: Cell;            // borrow field (no `owned`)
  public constructor()
    _c := new Cell();          // ERROR: a fresh owned value stored into a
  end constructor;             //   non-`owned` field has no owner — declare `owned _c`.

  public property Item: Cell
    get => new Cell();         // ERROR: a getter may not return a fresh owned
  end Item;                    //   value — use `method MakeItem(): owned Cell`.
end Handle;
```

Passing an owned field as a plain argument is permitted; the callee receives a parameter-sourced borrow under [§28.3](#sec-local-variables-ownership-and-borrows)'s ordinary rules — the callee further borrows for the duration of the call, and may store the borrow into a non-owned class-typed field only where the borrowed-field store rule admits it (the [§28.5](#sec-owned-fields) back-reference idiom), in which case the [K4.3](#sec-kernel-k4) trust obligation rests on the caller's choice of argument exactly as it rests on the constructor caller in that idiom. Handing the callee *ownership* takes the explicit [§28.8](#sec-ownership-transfer) forms: an `owned` parameter fed by a `move` of the field.

<a id="sec-who-may-dispose"></a>
#### Who may call `Dispose()`

Explicit disposal — `x.Dispose()`, the `x?.Dispose()` / `x!.Dispose()` spellings, and the discard of a named owned binding ([§17.13](#sec-the-discard-_)) — requires a receiver the disposer **owns** (derives: [K3.9](#sec-kernel-k3)): an owned local or `owned` parameter, a `using var`, an unbound owned temporary ([§28.3](#sec-unbound-owned-temporaries)), a `move` result, or an `owned` field / owning-collection slot / `static owned` field read by code of the owning object's declaring type. The field admission covers the [§28.7](#sec-reassigning-owned-fields) dispose-then-assign legacy and the destructor idioms of [§28.4](#sec-the-destructor)/[§28.8.1](#sec-the-move-expression) unchanged, and it is by **declaring type**, matching [§13.1](#sec-levels)'s class-level privacy: code of class C may dispose an `owned` field of any C instance it can reach — the same access symmetry as any private-member touch. (A receiver-instance-only restriction would introduce an access category the language does not otherwise draw.) The call and the discard are one consume-table row ([K3.9](#sec-kernel-k3)): the same site-announced kill, the same explicitly-disposed post-state, the disposal at the disposing statement.

**After an explicit `Dispose()` of an owned field or owning-collection slot, nothing further is required.** The call is an **early release point**, not a discharge of the slot's obligation: the slot keeps its reference and its [K9](#sec-kernel-k9) obligation, and the containing object's teardown still runs the cascade over it ([§28.4](#sec-the-destructor) step 2), where the second call is [§28.2](#sec-the-idisposable-contract)'s no-op — and, at a **trivial-dispose** slot type, the compiler's single free stays at the holder's release point, which [§28.9](#sec-trivial-dispose-classes) already fixes as the containing object's teardown, the explicit call having performed logical disposal only. No restoration obligation arises: [K9.2](#sec-kernel-k9)'s rule is scoped to a `move` of the slot and grounded in the hole a moved-from slot leaves for the destructor to observe, and a disposal leaves no hole — which is why a non-nullable `owned` field, for which no restoring value exists short of acquiring a fresh resource, is admitted here as readily as a nullable one. A method may therefore dispose an owned field and return (the early-close shape), reassign it ([§28.7](#sec-reassigning-owned-fields)'s dispose-then-assign), or assign `null` to a nullable one. A later **read** of the slot is not statically diagnosed — [§28.2](#sec-checked-disposal)'s use-after-dispose warning is a straight-line rule over a **local**, while a field's value is readable and reassignable from every method of its declaring type and this section's admission is by declaring type, not by receiver instance — so the reader is [K4.1](#sec-kernel-k4)'s backstop: a member access through it raises `DisposedAccessException` in checked disposal mode and is undefined unchecked, the posture [§28.7](#sec-reassigning-owned-fields) states for an overwritten field and [§28.3](#sec-diagnostics) states for disposal of a borrowed-from source.

`Dispose()` through a **borrow** is a compile error. The borrow receivers: a borrowed local or parameter — including `this`: an object may not dispose itself out from under its owner, so a Close()-style method that wants disposal semantics lets the owner dispose, or puts the work in the class's `destructor` — a non-`owned` field read, an owned-field read outside the declaring class, a getter or other non-`owned` call result (a `Task`-family call result is an owned temporary — [§28.3](#sec-producers) — and is not in this list), a `catch`-arm binding ([§31.1](#sec-exception-ownership)), a pattern binding ([§19.3](#sec-patterns)), a captured owned binding inside a closure ([§28.3](#sec-captured-owned-bindings), [§28.9](#sec-runtime-managed-types)), and an element borrow of an **owning** collection (`pool[i].Dispose()` — use `Remove`/`RemoveAt`, the indexer-set, or `move coll[i]`, whose forms keep the slot state coherent, [§28.11](#sec-collections-do-not-own-elements)). The check is structural and decidable — it reads the receiver expression's ownership classification, which [§28.3](#sec-local-variables-ownership-and-borrows) already computes at every call site.

**No element-borrow disposal.** An element borrow obtained from a **borrowing-family** collection — an indexer-get, a default-iteration variable, the entry fields of dictionary iteration — is a borrow like any other: disposing it is a compile error, with no exception. The owned-receiver rule is exception-free: **only owners dispose** — the retired element-borrow carve is recorded at the axiom register's A8 tombstone ([§28.3](#sec-axiom-register)). Elements a holder semantically owns belong in owning locations — an owning-family collection ([§28.11](#sec-element-slot-policy)), whose `Dispose()` cascades; selective or interleaved cleanup takes the elements *out* first (`Drain()`, `move coll[i]`, the `Pop*` family) into owned bindings and disposes those. The same rule was always in force for `IEnumerable<T>`-, enumerator-, and lazy-query-typed sources (tracked borrows; an iterator's yields are enumerator-owned, [§29.2](#sec-desugaring-of-for)): `for var x in xs.Where(p) do x.Dispose(); end;` is rejected.

This rule states who may *invoke* disposal; it changes nothing about what disposal does. [§28.2](#sec-the-idisposable-contract)'s idempotence stands (the dispose-then-scope-end-no-op shapes of [§30.5](#sec-result-lifetime-and-task-disposal) have owned receivers and are unaffected), and it is distinct from the consume-site freeze's recorded boundary ([§28.3](#sec-consume-site-freeze)): that boundary governs disposing an **owned** binding while borrows *of it* are live (legal — the site-announced kill with a runtime backstop); this rule governs whether the receiver expression is owned at all.

<a id="sec-borrowed-owning-collections"></a>
#### Borrowed owning collections

A borrow of an owning collection — produced by returning a bare owning-collection field (above), or by any borrow-producing read of one — may not be **disposed**: the borrower does not own the container, and the actual owner (the `using var`, the owned local, or the object whose field this is) disposes the container and cascades to its elements at scope/destructor end. This is the general receiver rule above ([Who may call `Dispose()`](#sec-who-may-dispose)) at its most consequential instance, since the container's `Dispose()` cascades through every element. The restriction is owner-liveness, not memory safety: under [§28.2](#sec-the-idisposable-contract)'s idempotence the owner's later disposal would no-op — but the owner and every other borrower still treat the container and its elements as live, and a borrower's `Dispose()` would destroy value the owner relies on (every later use then faults in checked disposal mode).

Every *other* operation remains available, exactly as on any borrowed collection — deliberately narrower than a full read-only restriction, since Bezel's borrowed collections are already mutable: the idiomatic *pass-and-fill* pattern `method Fill(a: OwningArray<T>) a.Add(…)` takes a borrowed `OwningArray<T>` and adds to it ([§28.8](#sec-ownership-transfer)). The mutation and ownership-transfer operations — the owning `Add` / `Insert`, the ownership-taking indexer-set, `Remove*`, `Clear`, `Drain`, `Pop*` / `Dequeue` — are **memory-safe on a borrow**: each preserves the dispose-exactly-once invariant (an element transferred out is owned by its new holder; the owner then disposes a smaller or empty container). The read operations (indexer-get, `Count` / `Length`, `Contains`, iteration, the borrowing LINQ queries) are likewise available. The owning collection types deliberately declare **no** value-copy materializers (`ToArray` / `Sorted` / `Reversed` / `ToSet` / `ToDictionary`) — uniquely-owned elements cannot be copied out of the container without double-owning or draining them (stdlib [§4.5](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-ownedarrayt), which also states the reachable-by-extension forms and their lifetime obligation). Only `Dispose` is restricted; an *owned* owning collection (a `using var`, an owned field accessed by its owner, a `move`d value) additionally admits it.

<a id="sec-methods-returning-this"></a>
#### Methods returning `this`

A method that returns `this` returns a borrow of the receiver ([K1.5](#sec-kernel-k1)'s calls-lend default) — the return type is the class type, not `owned`. The caller receives a reference whose lifetime is bounded by the receiver's lifetime. This enables method chaining:

```bezel
using var sb := new StringBuilder();
sb.Append("hello").Append(" ").Append("world");    // each Append returns a borrow of sb
```

The chained calls all operate on the same object. The returned borrow may not be assigned to an `owned` field or returned as `owned` — it is the receiver under a different name. The compiler infers the borrow from the method's non-`owned` return type.

When a chain originates from a `new` expression — `new StringBuilder().Append("a").Append("b")` — the owned value produced by `new` is the root of the chain. The compiler treats the overall chain expression as owned (its root is a `new`). The borrow-returning intermediate calls do not lose the root's ownership; the chain as a whole must reach an owned location or `using var`, just as any other `new` expression must.

<a id="sec-reassigning-owned-fields"></a>
### 28.7 Reassigning owned fields and locals — drop-on-overwrite

**Assignment to an owned field or owned local disposes the displaced value (derives: [K3.11](#sec-kernel-k3)).** The right-hand side is evaluated first; then, if the previous value is live (non-null and not moved-from — the per-slot tracking [§28.11](#sec-collection-element-ownership)'s indexer-set rule already defines), it is disposed; then the new value is stored. The disposal is **null-guarded and dynamically dispatched**, exactly the machinery scope-end disposal already uses. A moved-from or null location therefore stores without disposal — which is precisely how the field-restoration rule's `move`-then-reassign idiom ([§28.8.1](#sec-the-move-expression)) stays single-disposal — and with overwrite covered, the [§28.3](#sec-local-variables-ownership-and-borrows) claim — *every owned value is disposed exactly once on every path* — holds without qualification. Both move-only value kinds ([§15.3](#sec-move-only-value-types)) take this rule at whole-value reassignment: an owning-classified **choice** as a single value ([§35.4](#sec-choice-classification) — it has no partial states), and an owning **inline array** per live slot, in reverse slot order — [§15.3](#sec-move-only-value-types)'s *Whole-value reassignment* rule is the definition site for the per-slot details, the moved-from-slot accounting and the self-assignment no-op included. The one overwrite location outside this rule is unchanged in kind, not a carve on it: **static** fields never take drop-on-overwrite for *any* type — [§22.13](#sec-static-initialization-order)'s static-overwrite posture, which governs the [§22.12](#sec-static-members) form-(iv) owning-inline-array static exactly as it governs a displaced class-typed admitted static. Scope: `owned` fields, plain-`var` owned locals, and — for whole-value reassignment — move-only value locals and instance fields; `using var` locals are not reassignable at all ([§28.10](#sec-using-var)).

```bezel
public method Resize(newSize: int)
  _buffer := new Array<byte>(newSize, 0);   // sized ctor (stdlib §4.4); previous _buffer disposed here, implicitly
end Resize;
```

An explicit `field.Dispose();` before the assignment remains legal and behavior-preserving — `Dispose` is idempotent ([§28.2](#sec-the-idisposable-contract)), so the implicit disposal of an already-disposed value is a no-op.

**Overwrite while borrowed.** Reassigning a plain-`var` owned **local** while a live local borrow of its current value exists is rejected by the consume-site freeze ([K5.2](#sec-kernel-k5); [§28.3](#sec-consume-site-freeze)) — the implicit disposal would silently invalidate the borrow. Reassigning an owned **field or collection slot** is not statically frozen ([K5.6](#sec-kernel-k5); the consume table's frozen column, [§28.3](#sec-consume-table)); a borrow of the displaced value is invalidated at the overwrite, caught as `DisposedAccessException` in checked disposal mode and undefined unchecked — the same runtime-checked posture as explicit `Dispose()` (rationale [§5.1](Bezel_Design_Rationale.md#sec-owned-not-borrows)).

**Ordering and exceptions.** A throwing RHS leaves the field/local untouched and still-owned ([K9.5](#sec-kernel-k9); it is disposed later by the normal unwinding rules): the implicit path has no exception-unsafe window, unlike the manual dispose-then-assign pattern's hazard of a disposed field holding a dangling reference while the constructor throws. Disposers themselves are still expected not to throw ([§28.4](#sec-the-destructor)); a throwing disposer during overwrite propagates after the store is abandoned, leaving the new value an unbound owned temporary disposed by [§28.3](#sec-unbound-owned-temporaries)'s unbound-temporary rule — on this exception edge, during the unwind. For the owning inline array the composition is stated rather than derived: the per-slot pass is a **multi-value cleanup** in [§28.4](#sec-the-destructor)'s sense — a slot disposer that throws does not stop the pass, the remaining live slots are still disposed, and a later throw supersedes an earlier one under [§31.2](#sec-try-catch-finally)'s ordinary rule — after which the store is abandoned exactly as above: the RHS value (its own slots intact) is the unbound owned temporary the unwind disposes. Every slot the pass disposed is left empty — an unobservable state, reached only on the abandoned store's unwind, where the displaced value's only remaining reader is the unwinding discharge itself (which is how the emptiness coexists with [§15.1.1](#sec-owning-inline-arrays)'s non-nullable slot invariant) — and that discharge observes only empty slots: exactly-once per slot object on the exception edge, as on the normal one.

<a id="sec-ownership-transfer"></a>
### 28.8 Ownership transfer

`owned` may appear on a parameter or return type to mark ownership transfer across method boundaries. When a parameter is `owned`, the caller relinquishes ownership and may not use the argument after the call ([K3.3](#sec-kernel-k3)); when a return type is `owned`, the caller receives ownership and is responsible for disposal ([K3.2](#sec-kernel-k3)).

```bezel
public method TakeOwnership(owned resource: Stream)
  _resource := resource;     // moves into owned field; the previous
                             // _resource is disposed by the assignment (§28.7)
end TakeOwnership;

public static method NewBuffer(size: int): owned Array<byte>
  return new Array<byte>(size, 0);   // sized ctor (stdlib §4.4); owned by virtue of new, returned as owned
end NewBuffer;
```

The owned-field assignment in `TakeOwnership` drop-on-overwrites the displaced value ([§28.7](#sec-reassigning-owned-fields)): a replacement method needs no explicit dispose-first step — the assignment alone suffices:

```bezel
public method ReplaceResource(owned resource: Stream)
  _resource := resource;   // previous _resource disposed here, implicitly (§28.7)
end ReplaceResource;
```

Moving an owned field's contents *out* of the field uses the `move` expression form ([§28.8.1](#sec-the-move-expression); [K9.1](#sec-kernel-k9)–[K9.2](#sec-kernel-k9): the field is left *moved-from* and must be reassigned on every path to the method's exit). The pattern for "atomically take this field's contents and return them as owned" is:

```bezel
public method ReplaceAndReturn(): owned Stream
  var fresh := new FileStream(_path, FileMode.Open);   // build replacement first
  var old := move _resource;          // take from field
  _resource := fresh;                  // restore field
  return old;                          // return the taken value
end ReplaceAndReturn;
```

A `new` expression produces an owned value ([K1.5](#sec-kernel-k1)). Its result either reaches an owned location (`owned` field, `using var`, `owned` parameter, `owned` return) or is explicitly disposed within the same method, or — if bound to a plain `var` that is neither moved nor disposed — is **auto-dropped at the end of its scope** with the plain-`var` must-use warning ([K3.14](#sec-kernel-k3); [§28.3](#sec-owned-local-discharge-requirement)). The obligation is satisfied on every path; the warning, not a hard error, marks an implicit drop.

Implicit boxing ([§8.6](#sec-boxing)) is **not** subject to this rule. When a value type is boxed to be used where `Object` or an interface is expected, the boxed wrapper is a runtime-managed value ([§28.9](#sec-runtime-managed-types); [K1.6](#sec-kernel-k1)), not an owned `new`-result. The boxing itself is not a `new` expression and produces no disposal obligation; `Console.WriteLine(42)` does not need to discharge anything.

<a id="sec-the-move-expression"></a>
### 28.8.1 The `move` expression

`move x.f` is the one owned read of an owned field ([K9.1](#sec-kernel-k9)): it transfers ownership to the read site and leaves the field in *moved-from* state. `move coll[i]` is the analogous form for an owned-element collection slot ([§28.11](#sec-collections-do-not-own-elements)); the rules below are written for the field case and apply to the collection-slot case with "field" read as "slot." The identifier-operand form `move x` — `x` a named local binding, an `owned` parameter, or the bare in-scope spelling of an `owned` field of the enclosing instance (`move _resource`, which is `move this._resource`; the field forms carry this section's restoration obligation, the named-binding forms do not) — is the same verb at a named operand: [K3.4](#sec-kernel-k3)'s marked transfer (*Move semantics for owned locals*, [§28.3](#sec-move-semantics-for-owned-locals)). Its admitted positions — with each consume position's marker spelling and freeze status — are the consume table's rows ([§28.3](#sec-consume-table)); elsewhere it is rejected (axiom [A7](#sec-axiom-register)), as it is at **marker-free positions** (positions whose target or keyword already announces the consume, [§28.3](#sec-move-semantics-for-owned-locals)). The restoration machinery below is specific to fields and slots: a moved-from *binding* is unreadable until reassigned, with no restoration obligation. Static fields are not eligible ([K9.4](#sec-kernel-k9)).

The `move` expression's static type is the slot's element type (the `T` in `owned T`); the result is owned and is subject to the standard [§28.3](#sec-local-variables-ownership-and-borrows) discharge rules like any other owned value.

<a id="sec-the-field-restoration-rule"></a>
#### The field-restoration rule

The rule is [K9.2](#sec-kernel-k9)'s restoration rule: every control-flow path from the move site to the method's exit must execute an assignment `x.f := value;` between the move and the exit, statically enforced — failure is a compile error. The exit paths considered include normal return, fall-through (for `()`-returning methods), `throw`, `yield break` (in iterator methods), and any other transfer of control that leaves the method body. The rule applies to every reachable exit; an unreachable exit (one the compiler proves cannot occur) does not contribute an obligation. In particular there is no terminal-move dispensation: a **terminal move** — `return move x.f;`, or any return whose operand evaluation performs the move with no restoring assignment before the exit — is rejected, the return edge being itself an unrestored exit. Restoration precedes the return (*build before take* — the `ReplaceAndReturn` shape of [§28.8](#sec-ownership-transfer)), or the field is declared nullable and restored to `null` (*Detaching via a nullable field*, below); only a destructor body is exempt ([K9.3](#sec-kernel-k9)).

The error message identifies the move site, the unrestored exit path, and the three standard remedies: assign a value on the offending path; move the move into the branch where reassignment is reachable; or, if the field should sometimes hold no value, declare it nullable and assign `null` after the move.

```bezel
// ERROR: field _resource was moved at line 2 and not reassigned
//        on the path through the false branch of `if replace` (line 3).
public method Wrong(replace: bool): owned Stream
  var old := move _resource;
  if replace then
    _resource := new FileStream(_path, FileMode.Open);
  end;
  return old;
end Wrong;
```

The fix is to reassign on every path:

```bezel
public method Right(replace: bool): owned Stream
  var fresh := new FileStream(_path, FileMode.Open);
  var old := move _resource;
  _resource := fresh;
  return old;
end Right;
```

Or to scope the move to the branch where reassignment is mandatory:

```bezel
public method Right2(replace: bool): owned Stream?
  if not replace then return null; end;
  var fresh := new FileStream(_path, FileMode.Open);
  var old := move _resource;
  _resource := fresh;
  return old;
end Right2;
```

<a id="sec-exception-paths-are-not-exempt"></a>
#### Exception paths are not exempt

[K9.2](#sec-kernel-k9)'s path set includes exception edges: a throwable expression between the move and the reassignment introduces an exit path on which the reassignment has not run, and if the destructor on `this` is reached via that path, it would observe the field in moved-from state — the hole a destructor must never observe:

```bezel
// ERROR: if DangerousFactory throws, _resource is moved but never reassigned;
//        the exception edge is an unrestored exit.
public method WrongOrder(): owned Stream
  var old := move _resource;
  var fresh := DangerousFactory();
  _resource := fresh;
  return old;
end WrongOrder;
```

The fix is to perform any throwable construction *before* the move, leaving only non-throwable assignments and the return between the move and the exits:

```bezel
public method RightOrder(): owned Stream
  var fresh := DangerousFactory();   // may throw — but no move yet
  var old := move _resource;          // cannot throw
  _resource := fresh;                  // cannot throw (the slot is moved-from:
                                       //   no drop-on-overwrite runs)
  return old;                          // cannot throw
end RightOrder;
```

The general rule — *build before take* — is the resource-management discipline this rule encodes. It is the same discipline that motivates strong exception-safety guarantees in C++ RAII code and that drives the "build a complete replacement, then commit it" pattern in transactional code.

For the purpose of the analysis (derives: [K9.2](#sec-kernel-k9) + [K3.11](#sec-kernel-k3)), the following expressions are non-throwable:

- assignments where neither the LHS nor the RHS is a throwable expression **and** the assignment performs no drop-on-overwrite of a possibly-live value: a store into an `owned` field, a plain-`var` owned local, or an owning-collection slot that may hold a live (non-null, not moved-from) value is **throwable** — the implicit [§28.7](#sec-reassigning-owned-fields) disposal runs the displaced value's destructor, which may throw with defined behavior ([§28.4](#sec-the-destructor)), propagating from the drop-on-overwrite site. Stores into provably moved-from or null locations, and stores into borrow-state or value-typed locations, remain non-throwable — which is why this section's restoration idioms are unaffected (`_resource := fresh;` after a `move` targets a moved-from slot). A **compound assignment** (and `++`/`--`) carries no classification of its own: it is throwable **exactly when its desugared form is** ([§6.6](#sec-compound-assignments)/[§17.6](#sec-the-increment-and-decrement-operators) — alike spellings classify alike): `x /= d` and `n mod= d` are throwable because the division and modulo they desugar to are (below), `x += y` on an overflow-checked type is throwable because checked arithmetic is, and a compound spelling whose desugaring contains no throwable constituent — with this bullet's drop-on-overwrite condition applied to the write-back — is non-throwable exactly as its plain spelling is.
- field reads
- local-variable reads
- literals
- `move x.f` itself (the move is a state transition, not a runtime check)
- `null`-coalescing where neither operand is throwable

Method calls; indexer accesses (on inline arrays `[N]T`, on resizable collection classes such as `Array<T>` whose indexer can throw `IndexOutOfRangeException` or `KeyNotFoundException`, and on any user-declared indexer); division and modulo (which can throw `DivideByZeroException`); arithmetic on overflow-checked types; explicit casts in function-call form (e.g., `short(x)` and `int(d)`, which can throw `OverflowException` for numeric narrowing per [§5.2](#sec-explicit-conversions) or `NullReferenceException` for nullable-to-non-nullable casts per [§5.3](#sec-nullable-casts)); explicit enum casts from integer values (which throw `OverflowException` for values equal to no declared constant per [§5.4](#sec-enum-casts)); shifts whose count is not a compile-time constant (an out-of-domain count raises `OverflowException` per [§6.5](#sec-bitwise-operations)); a range expression with a computed step ([§16.4](#sec-stride)); and `await` are throwable. The `!` null-forgiving operator is throwable when the target is null.

The `as` operator is **not** throwable: a failed `as` cast returns `null` rather than raising ([§12.7](#sec-type-tests-is-is-not-as), [§17.4](#sec-the-is-is-not-and-as-operators)). Code that uses `as` between a move and the field-restoration point does not introduce an unrestored exception edge.

A `new T(...)` expression is likewise **not** in the throwable inventory. This section already separates *can raise* from *analysis-throwable* — `!` is throwable only when the target is null, `as` not at all — and `new` joins that stated family: a constructor body is ordinary code and may throw, but a constructor that throws completes no object, so there is no restored-with value the analysis loses on that edge — and the hazard the throw does create, the partially-constructed object's owned state, is the constructor's own exception-safety territory ([§22.9](#sec-owned-fields-and-exception-safety); [§28.3](#sec-local-variables-ownership-and-borrows)/[§28.6](#sec-leak-prevention)), not the field-restoration analysis's. The common restoration idiom is therefore legal: `var old := move _r; _r := new Res();` restores on every path this rule counts — the reading the `Wrong` example above encodes, whose stated error names only the false branch of `if replace` because the true branch's in-branch `new` restoration is valid. (The hoisted `new`s in the compiling examples above are the uniform build-before-take spelling, kept for stylistic uniformity.) The exclusion covers the construction only: a `new` expression's **argument** expressions classify on their own, so `_r := new Res(Fetch());` still puts `Fetch()`'s exception edge between the move and the restoration.

<a id="sec-loops-and-conditional-control-flow"></a>
#### Loops and conditional control flow

Loops that may execute zero times do not satisfy the rule:

```bezel
// ERROR: the while loop may run zero times, leaving _resource moved
//        but unreassigned.
public method WrongLoop(): owned Stream
  var old := move _resource;
  while SomeCondition() do
    _resource := MakeStream();
    break;
  end;
  return old;
end WrongLoop;
```

The fix is the same as the conditional case: ensure the reassignment is unconditional. Restructure so the reassignment dominates the exits:

```bezel
public method RightLoop(): owned Stream
  var fresh := MakeStream();
  while SomeCondition() do
    fresh := MakeStream();   // refine fresh in the loop
  end;
  var old := move _resource;
  _resource := fresh;
  return old;
end RightLoop;
```

The analysis reuses the control-flow graph and dominance frontiers that the existing definite-assignment analysis builds for non-defaultable locals ([§7.9](#sec-definite-assignment-for-non-nullable-fields)); no new machinery is required.

<a id="sec-constructors-and-destructors"></a>
#### Constructors and destructors

Both bodies are [K9.3](#sec-kernel-k9)'s cases. Inside a constructor body, the field has no value to move until it has been assigned: a `move x.f` before the field's first assignment is a definite-assignment violation, the same rule as for any other read of an unassigned non-nullable slot ([§7.9](#sec-definite-assignment-for-non-nullable-fields)). After the first assignment, `move` is permitted, with the same field-restoration rule applying to constructor exit paths.

Inside a destructor body, the field is being read for final disposal. `move x.f` inside a destructor takes the field's value out, which causes the compiler-generated auto-dispose pass for that field to skip it (the field is in moved-from state and has nothing to dispose). The taken value must still be discharged through one of the standard mechanisms — assigned to a local with `using var`, passed as `owned` to a helper, or explicitly disposed. The destructor's exit obligation is satisfied if the moved value reaches a discharge point; the field-restoration rule does *not* require reassignment inside a destructor (K9.3 — teardown, no future read).

<a id="sec-interaction-with-using-var"></a>
#### Interaction with `using var`

`using var u := move x.f;` is the canonical pattern for "take the field's value out and consume it scope-bound." The `using var` discharges the moved value at scope end; the field-restoration rule still applies at the surrounding method's exits.

```bezel
public method ProcessAndReplace()
  var fresh := new FileStream(_path, FileMode.Open);
  using var old := move _resource;        // moved into using var; disposed at scope end
  _resource := fresh;                      // restore
  // ... use old ...
  // at scope end: old.Dispose()
end ProcessAndReplace;
```

The using-var consumes the moved value; the explicit reassignment satisfies the field-restoration rule. No swap helper is needed.

<a id="sec-detaching-via-a-nullable-field"></a>
#### Detaching via a nullable field

A class that wants "take the resource away and leave the field empty" declares the field nullable and assigns `null` after the move:

```bezel
private owned _resource: Stream?;        // nullable

public method Detach(): owned Stream?
  if _resource = null then return null; end;
  var taken := move _resource!;          // move out the non-null contents
  _resource := null;                      // restore (to null)
  return taken;
end Detach;
```

The reassignment to `null` satisfies the field-restoration rule; the destructor's auto-dispose pass treats the null field correctly per [§28.5](#sec-owned-fields).

For non-nullable owned fields, "leave the field empty" is not expressible — by design, a non-nullable field's type contract says a value is always present. Code that needs sometimes-empty semantics declares the field nullable.

<a id="sec-interaction-with-overload-resolution-and-parameter-passing"></a>
#### Interaction with overload resolution and parameter passing

`move x.f` produces an owned value and is type-suitable as the argument to an `owned` parameter — but the exception-edge rule above applies with full force: a method call is throwable, so an argument-position move whose restoration follows the call is rejected on the call's exception edge (the compiling form is `TransferToHelperSafe` below):

```bezel
// ERROR: TakeOwnership may throw (method calls are throwable, above) — on that
//        edge _resource is moved but never reassigned: the WrongOrder shape.
public method TransferToHelper()
  var fresh := new FileStream(_path, FileMode.Open);
  TakeOwnership(move _resource);          // owned argument; helper consumes
  _resource := fresh;                      // restores the normal edge only
end TransferToHelper;
```

The argument expression `move _resource` runs as part of argument evaluation, so the field is moved-from from the moment of the move expression's evaluation, and the reassignment after the call satisfies the rule on the **normal** edge only — the exception edge is an unrestored exit, and the shape above is a **compile error** exactly as `WrongOrder` is. As with all exception-path concerns, the fix is to construct the replacement and reassign before the call:

```bezel
public method TransferToHelperSafe()
  var fresh := new FileStream(_path, FileMode.Open);
  var taken := move _resource;
  _resource := fresh;                      // restore before the call that may throw
  TakeOwnership(move taken);               // owned argument (call-site marker, §22.3), no field state at risk
end TransferToHelperSafe;
```

This is the same "build then take then restore" discipline, with the call moved to after the restore.

**A raise from the consuming call does not hand the obligation back.** The transfer of an `owned` argument completes when the call is **entered**: the argument expression's evaluation leaves a named operand moved-from ([K1](#sec-kernel-k1)'s state 3, this section's identifier-operand form), and the callee's `owned` parameter is the value's new holder ([§28.3](#sec-consume-table)'s row K3.3 — post-state *moved-from*, disposal moment “the callee's”). If the call then raises — from the callee's body, or from a constructor's field initializers or body ([§22.9](#sec-owned-fields-and-exception-safety)) — the caller's binding is moved-from on the exception edge exactly as on the normal one, and the value is discharged on the callee's side: as an undischarged `owned` parameter by [§28.3](#sec-owned-local-discharge-requirement)'s exception-path discharge, or, once it has reached an `owned` field, by [§22.9](#sec-owned-fields-and-exception-safety)'s construction unwinding. Nothing leaks, and a `catch` arm may not dispose the argument a second time — the binding is unreadable there, as after any move. The boundary's other side is [§28.3](#sec-unbound-owned-temporaries)'s unbound-temporary rule: where the raise happens **before** the call is entered — a later argument's evaluation throwing — the already-produced temporary has not transferred and is disposed by the caller's unwinding pass. One owner at every instant, on both edges (Appendix [C.3](#sec-appendix-c)). A callee that must not take ownership on its failing paths announces that in its signature — a plain (borrowing) parameter, or a verdict-returning shape — rather than leaving the caller to recover a value the raise has not returned.

<a id="sec-runtime-managed-types"></a>
### 28.9 Runtime-managed types

The following types are exempt from manual disposal ([K1.6](#sec-kernel-k1)'s runtime-managed exemption). Their `Dispose()` is a no-op (or, for types that are not classes and therefore have no `Dispose()` at all, the type's lifetime is managed by the runtime without user involvement). How the runtime manages their lifecycle (reference counting, region allocation, or other) is not part of this specification.

- `string` — pervasive; created by literals, interpolation, concatenation, and library methods.
- `Type` — the type-identity token (stdlib [§2.13](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-the-type-class)). The runtime holds exactly one instance per type for the life of the process and user code never allocates one: `typeof(T)` ([§17.10](#sec-the-typeof-operator)) and `value.GetType()` ([§8.2](#sec-gettype)) read the interned instance, which is never reclaimed. No `Type` expression is an owned production, none lends a borrow, and no holder carries an obligation for one; `owned` over `Type` is inadmissible ([§28.1](#sec-where-the-owned-modifier-can-appear), [§28.5](#sec-owned-fields)). The instance is not compiler-freed at any holder's release point — the trivial-dispose free below would set the disposed flag on a token every other holder still reads.
- Boxed value types — created implicitly when a value type is used where `Object` (or an interface) is expected; a box's payload is fixed at boxing and no operation writes it ([§8.6](#sec-boxing); the shapes that could appear to are compile errors at their own sites — [§12.7](#sec-type-tests-is-is-not-as)'s narrowed writes, [§9.4](#sec-value-receivers-are-borrows)'s receiver-storing member bodies and its settable-member conformance rejection), so a boxed value is an immutable shared reference.
- **Function-typed values** — values of any function type `(T1, ..., Tn) -> R`, regardless of whether they capture. This includes lambda closures (capturing or not), method references (`obj.Method` and `Type.StaticMethod`), and any value whose static type is a function type. Function-typed fields, parameters, and locals are not subject to `owned` annotations and carry no disposal obligation; a `using var` local of function type is nonetheless permitted (disposal at scope end is a no-op) and serves only the non-reassignability role ([§28.10](#sec-using-var)) — a plain `var` of function type scopes its captures identically ([§28.3](#sec-borrow-lifetime-rules), the closure bullet).

  Runtime management governs the *function value itself* — the heap-allocated closure object that backs it — and relaxes nothing about the values the closure captures: a captured borrowed class reference is subject to [§28.3](#sec-local-variables-ownership-and-borrows)'s borrow-escape rules, so a function value that outlives the captured borrow's source is rejected; the compiler tracks captured borrows separately from the function value's own lifetime.

  Capturing an *owned* class-typed local does **not** transfer ownership into the closure: the capture is a borrow whose source is the local's enclosing scope, borrow-state throughout — the closure may not assign to, transfer from, or dispose the captured binding, and may not outlive that scope ([§28.3](#sec-captured-owned-bindings)) — and the original `using var` (or other owned location) retains the disposal obligation. This is what makes function-typed values runtime-managed without contradicting the no-GC promise: a closure cannot extend the lifetime of an owned class instance, so reclaiming the closure never leaves a destructor un-run. Programs that genuinely need to extend an owned class's lifetime past a closure boundary restructure to keep the owned location in scope (for example, an owned field of a longer-lived object) or use `Task.FireAndForget` for the specific case of fire-and-forget tasks.

  Capturing a *move-only* local (an owning inline array, [§15.3](#sec-move-only-value-types)) follows the same rule: the closure captures a borrow whose source is the local's enclosing scope, and may not outlive it. The borrow form is the only consistent option — a move-only capture cannot be a copy (copying is forbidden) and cannot be a move (the local is still in scope under its name; moving into the closure would leave it moved-from in surprising ways). Reads of slots through the captured borrow are admitted; `move arr[i]` through it is not (the closure does not own the array) — a closure that must consume slot contents takes an owned-parameter argument and is invoked with `move`d slots from outside.

This tier is exhaustive: **no runtime lifetime mechanism exists for user-defined classes at all** — no reference counts, no regions, no heap scanning, no pauses. Every class the user can write — trivial-dispose or not — is freed by compiler-inserted code at a statically-known point, so the no-garbage-collector claim is unconditional for class instances.

Note that **inline arrays** `[N]T` (see [§15.1](#sec-inline-arrays)) are not on this list. Inline arrays are value types, stored inline in their enclosing context; they have no separate allocation to reclaim and no disposal contract independent of their host. Inline arrays with owned slots (`[N owned]T?`) are move-only value types ([§15.3](#sec-move-only-value-types)) that participate in the ownership system as part of their host's lifecycle. There is no separate runtime-managed fixed-size-array form; fixed-size arrays are inline arrays ([§15.1](#sec-inline-arrays)) and the heap arrays `Array<T>` / `OwningArray<T>` ([§15.2](#sec-heap-arrays)).

The compiler does not warn about undisposed runtime-managed values and does not require them to appear in `using var` or `owned` declarations.

**Accessor faces are uniform across type kinds.** A property or indexer **read** is a lend for every declared type — the [A4](#sec-axiom-register)/[§28.6](#sec-leak-prevention) rule for class and interface types, and the same face for runtime-managed types: a getter never transfers a reclamation obligation to its reader, and the two accessor body spellings of [§23.3](#sec-block-form-properties) (`get => e` and `get => do … end`) are semantically indistinguishable at every read site. A getter body whose result is a fresh runtime-managed production (an interpolation, a concatenation, a library call) remains admissible — runtime-managed values are exempt from the ceremony — and the implementation reclaims the production; **how** is not specified, per the lifecycle carve above.

<a id="sec-trivial-dispose-classes"></a>
#### Trivial-dispose classes

A class whose disposal **provably runs no user code and releases only memory** — it has no destructor, no `owned` fields of non-trivial-dispose type, no fields of owning-inline-array type (`[N owned]T?` or `[N owned]T`, [§15.1.1](#sec-owning-inline-arrays)), and its base class (if any, other than `Object`) is itself trivial-dispose — is a **trivial-dispose class** — a property of a **declared class**, computed from that declaration's own structure and carried as such in the artifact interface ([§3.6](#sec-derived-type-properties) rule 3, [§2.8.2](#sec-artifact-interface)). It is therefore not defined for a **compiler-synthesized frame** — an iterator or async state machine, or a lazy query value ([K2](#sec-kernel-k2)'s *frame* source, [K6](#sec-kernel-k6)) — which declares nothing for the check to read: the ceremony exemption does not reach a frame, and the must-use lint applies to a frame-typed owned local on [§28.3](#sec-owned-local-discharge-requirement)'s ordinary terms ([§29.11](#sec-multiple-enumeration) states the bound-query case) (derives: [K1.6](#sec-kernel-k1) — empty *user-visible* obligation content). The check is recursive and, for generics, per-instantiation ([§3.6](#sec-derived-type-properties) rule 2; the next subsection): an `owned` field whose declared type is itself trivial-dispose does **not** disqualify the holder — the synthesized disposal cascade over such fields frees memory and runs no user code, which is exactly what the property asserts. Mutually-recursive `owned` trivial-dispose references are admitted; the property is evaluated coinductively (assume the types under test trivial-dispose, then check the rules) — the same convention sendability states for its own recursive `owned` references ([§30.14](#sec-sendable-types)). *Provably runs no user code and releases only memory* means the generated `Dispose()` performs no user-authored work: it releases the instance's own allocation (including the intrinsic backing storage of the compiler-known borrowing collections, part of the instance's single allocation — [§28.11](#sec-borrowing-collections)) and the trivial-dispose trees under its `owned` trivial-dispose fields; storage released by a declared destructor is not in that category (`OwningBuffer<T>`, below). Trivial-dispose classes are tracked like every other class — references to them are classified, source-bounded, and escape-checked by the letter of this chapter's rules. The exemption's principle: the ceremony announces observable disposal *effects*, and a trivial-dispose class's disposal has none to announce — which is why the exemption's boundary is exactly this section's runs-no-user-code line, and why it extends no further (Design Rationale [§5.28](Bezel_Design_Rationale.md#sec-silent-tracking)). They are exempt from the **ceremony** only:

- No **must-use / auto-drop diagnostic** attaches to a trivial-dispose value. The [§28.3](#sec-owned-local-discharge-requirement) must-use warning is not emitted at the implicit-drop site of a plain-`var` owned local, of an undischarged `owned` parameter — a method's, an iterator's ([§29.8](#sec-iterators-with-owned-parameters)), or an async method's ([§30.1](#sec-async-methods)) — or of an owning iteration variable ([§29.2](#sec-desugaring-of-for)) whose type is trivial-dispose; nor at a `new` expression of a trivial-dispose class type whose result reaches no `owned` location or `using var`. The exemption is over the **obligation**, not over the expression that produced the value: the obligation's user-visible content is empty, and the compiler frees the undischarged value at its holder's release point ([K1.6](#sec-kernel-k1)). **This exemption's** classification is read from the **produced type** where the drop site's value has a statically-known producer (a `new` expression, an `owned`-returning call), and from the **declared type** otherwise ([§3.6](#sec-derived-type-properties) rule 1's declared-types posture); *statically-known producer* is [§28.3](#sec-producers)'s own notion, whose producers table already classifies every initializer, so the key asks for no analysis the compiler does not already run at every binding. The produced-type arm is what keeps the exemption **value**-keyed, as [K1.6](#sec-kernel-k1) states it: a trivial-dispose *declared* type standing over a destructor-bearing production — `var b: Base := new Derived();` at a trivial-dispose `Base` — is not exempt. The **interface** clause sits inside that key rather than beside it: an interface type is never trivial-dispose, its conformance set being open across modules ([§21.9](#sec-statement-form-of-expressions)'s possibly-non-trivial-dispose reading), so a drop site is unexempt wherever the key selects an interface type — every site with no statically-known producer whose declared type is an interface, and every producer whose *produced* type is itself an interface (an `owned IThing`-returning call). Where a producer is present, its produced type decides in both directions whatever the declared type is: `var b: Base := new Derived();` above is not exempt, and `var t: IThing := new TrivialThing();` at a trivial-dispose `TrivialThing` is — an open conformance set says nothing about a value whose class the producer already fixes, which is what value-keying means. The one adjacent diagnostic is [§15.4](#sec-collection-literals)'s store-position lint — a distinct warning with its own trigger, not this exemption's; [§21.9](#sec-statement-form-of-expressions)'s discarded-result warning is likewise unaffected.
- The discard statement `_ := expr;` ([§17.13](#sec-the-discard-_)) is legal for a trivial-dispose class: the value is freed at end of statement, no user code running — the same timing as for a non-trivial-dispose class ([§17.13](#sec-the-discard-_)); the difference is only whether the discard does cleanup work.
- Every trivial-dispose instance has exactly one statically-known holder at every point — the [K1](#sec-kernel-k1) classification it carries ([§28.3](#sec-local-variables-ownership-and-borrows)) — and the compiler inserts a **free** ([§28.2](#sec-checked-disposal): logical disposal followed by reclamation — the per-instance disposed flag is set, no user code runs, and checked disposal mode backstops a surviving borrow exactly as for any other class) at that holder's release point: scope end for locals and `using var` ([§28.3](#sec-owned-local-discharge-requirement)); the K8 boundary for unbound temporaries ([§28.3](#sec-unbound-owned-temporaries)); drop-on-overwrite for reassignment ([§28.7](#sec-reassigning-owned-fields)); the containing object's teardown for `owned` fields ([§28.5](#sec-owned-fields)); process exit for statics ([§22.13](#sec-static-initialization-order)); after the matching catch arm for throw operands ([§31.1](#sec-the-throw-operand)); frame teardown for frame-held values ([§29.8](#sec-iterators-with-owned-parameters), [§30.1](#sec-async-methods)); and the aggregate owner's release point for literal-tree nodes ([§15.4](#sec-collection-literals)).

`using var` on a trivial-dispose class is permitted; it names the holder explicitly and has no observable effect other than scope limitation (the free at scope end runs no user code).

Standard library classes that are trivial-dispose include `Random` ([§2.7](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-random) of the standard library), `StringBuilder` ([§3.1](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-stringbuilder) of the standard library — it declares no destructor and no `owned` fields, and its intrinsic backing storage is released by the instance's own free, exactly as a borrowing collection's is), and the singleton `Encoding` subclass instances ([§3.2](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-encoding) of the standard library). User-defined classes with no destructor, no owned fields of non-trivial-dispose type, and no owning-inline-array fields are automatically trivial-dispose.

<a id="sec-trivial-dispose-for-generic-class-instantiations"></a>
#### Trivial-dispose for generic class instantiations

For a generic class `C<T>` (or `C<T1, T2, ...>`), the trivial-dispose check is performed on the **instantiation** rather than on the generic declaration (derives: [K1.6](#sec-kernel-k1), computed per instantiation). The compiler substitutes the actual type arguments and applies the rules above to the resulting concrete class.

```bezel
public class Box<T>(value: T)
  public Value: T := value;
  // No destructor, no owned fields. Box<T> is trivial-dispose for any T.
end Box;

public class OwningBox<T>(owned value: T) where T: class
  public owned Value: T := value;
  // Has an owned field of T. OwningBox<T> is trivial-dispose exactly when the
  // substituted T is (§3.6 rule 2): the synthesized cascade over an owned
  // trivial-dispose field runs no user code.
end OwningBox;

using var m := new MyClass();
_ := new Box<int>(0);                          // OK (trivial-dispose)
_ := new Box<MyClass>(m);                      // OK (trivial-dispose; Box doesn't own its T — it borrows m)
_ := new OwningBox<MyClass>(new MyClass());    // OK (disposes the owned T field at end of statement, §17.13)
```

Per-instantiation analysis means trivial-dispose status is computed *after* type substitution — for an `owned` field of a substituted type, from whether the substituted type is itself trivial-dispose (the recursive clause of the definition above). The standard collection types — `Array<T>`, `Dictionary<K, V>`, `Set<T>`, `LinkedList<T>`, `Stack<T>`, `Queue<T>` — are trivial-dispose for every non-owned choice of type argument because they do not own their elements ([§28.11](#sec-collections-do-not-own-elements)). A program that holds `Array<MyClass>` may discard the array (the elements remain owned by their original sources, unaffected by the array's free, which releases the array's own allocation only); a program that holds `OwningBox<MyClass>` may also discard it, but the discard *disposes* the box — its `owned` T field is disposed at end of statement ([§17.13](#sec-the-discard-_)) — rather than merely releasing an empty shell.

The owned-element variants of the standard collection types — `OwningArray<T>`, `OwningDictionary<K, V>`, `OwningSet<T>`, `OwningSlotMap<T>`, etc. — are **not** trivial-dispose at any instantiation: they own their elements, disposal cascades through to the elements, and their storage primitive declares a destructor.
