A program that holds `OwningArray<MyClass>` carries the ordinary discharge obligations — the ceremony exemption does not apply, because element disposal needs to run. `OwningBuffer<T>` is non-trivial-dispose for **both** element kinds: for class-typed T its destructor cascades through every non-null slot; for value-typed T the cascade is empty, but the type still declares a destructor over its manually-managed backing allocation (stdlib [§4.14](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-owned-buffers-and-spans)) — it is the user-expressible storage primitive, and destructor-released storage is exactly what the trivial-dispose definition excludes. The resizable owning collections compose over it through `owned` fields of that non-trivial type ([§28.11](#sec-collection-element-ownership)), which is what keeps the owning family non-trivial at every instantiation. The contrast with `Array<T>` is the defining line: a borrowing collection's backing storage is an intrinsic part of the instance's single allocation, released by the instance's one compiler-inserted free with no user code running, so its `Dispose()` provably runs no user code and releases only memory.

The rule does not require the type arguments to be *themselves* trivial-dispose: `Array<MyClass>` is trivial-dispose even if `MyClass` is not — the elements are owned elsewhere and the array's free does not dispose them. The key question is **does the generic class itself need to do disposal work**; a type argument's own status enters the computation only where the class holds it through an `owned` field (the recursive clause above), which is how per-instantiation status arises in practice — `OwningBox<T>` above is trivial-dispose at trivial-dispose substitutions and non-trivial-dispose elsewhere, [§3.6](#sec-derived-type-properties) rule 2's instantiation-site machinery carrying the verdict. What the language does not admit is *conditionally-declared structure* — an `OwnedIfClass<T>` with an `owned T` field only when T is a class type cannot be written (the `owned` modifier's field-type requirement is expressed at declaration time, not conditionally on the substitution).

<a id="sec-trivial-dispose-classification-is-part-of-the-api-surface"></a>
#### Trivial-dispose classification is part of the API surface

Adding a destructor, an `owned` field of non-trivial-dispose type, or an owning-inline-array field to a class promotes it from trivial-dispose to non-trivial-dispose — as does an existing `owned` field's declared type itself flipping non-trivial-dispose (the recursive clause above: the flip propagates through owned-field types, across modules). The flip changes **ceremony, never tracking** — both sides are tracked, and the free-or-dispose point is the holder's release point either way — but it can still be **source-affecting**: a `_ := new ThatClass();` discard that ran no user code now runs the destructor at end of statement ([§17.13](#sec-the-discard-_)); an unused instance that was freed silently now draws the must-use auto-drop warning ([§28.3](#sec-owned-local-discharge-requirement)); and a fresh instance admitted as a literal-tree node ([§15.4](#sec-collection-literals)) or as a plain-parameter default ([§22.5](#sec-optional-parameters-and-named-arguments)) is rejected there after the upgrade, so code relying on those admissions may fail to compile.

API authors should:

- Treat the trivial-dispose status of public classes as part of their published contract.
- Document trivial-dispose status in the class's API documentation.
- Avoid adding a destructor to a previously-trivial class without bumping the major version of the containing module.

When the addition is necessary (the class genuinely now owns a resource), the standard migration-guide pattern applies: list the affected discard sites and direct callers to `using var _ := …`, an explicit `.Dispose()`, or `Task.FireAndForget` (for tasks).

<a id="sec-using-var"></a>
### 28.10 `using var`

*(The non-owned single-assignment counterpart is the runtime `const` local, [§21.1](#sec-variable-declarations): `using var` binds owned values with declared scope-end disposal; `const` binds values and borrows that carry no obligation.)*

`using var` declares a local that is disposed when the enclosing block ends:

```bezel
public method ProcessFile(filename: string)
  using var fs := new FileStream(filename, FileMode.Open);
  using var buffer := new Array<byte>(4096, 0);   // sized ctor (stdlib §4.4)
  var data := fs.ReadAll();
  // fs and buffer disposed here in reverse order
end ProcessFile;
```

Disposal happens on every exit path: normal completion, `break`, `return`, or exception. **Cleanup ordering is uniform across exit edges:** `using var` compiles to `try`/`finally` ([§29.6](#sec-restrictions-inside-try-catch-finally)), so `using var` disposals and explicit `finally` clauses form one establishment-ordered stack — on *every* exit edge (normal, `return`, `break`/`continue`, exception, and an iterator's early disposal, [§29.7](#sec-disposal-of-partially-consumed-iterators)), pending cleanups run in reverse order of establishment. No edge runs the two kinds in separate category-ordered phases. A `try` statement's own `finally` is **established at entry to the protected block** — before any establishment the block itself performs. Consequently, on every exit edge, an owned local or `using var` declared **inside** the protected block (established later) is disposed **before** the `finally` runs, exactly as the desugared nested `try`/`finally` of this section and [§29.6](#sec-restrictions-inside-try-catch-finally) would dispose it; cleanups established **before** the `try` run after the `finally`, as before ([§31.2](#sec-try-catch-finally)).

An expression whose arm-meet is **owned** — a `??`, an `if` expression, or an expression-position `case` over owned producers (the [K7](#sec-kernel-k7) meet; [§28.3](#sec-producers)) — is an owned producer for this section's admission: `using var x := (if useFresh then new Buffer() else source.CloneBuffer());` — where `CloneBuffer` is declared `CloneBuffer(): owned Buffer`, making both arms fresh producers — binds `x` owned and disposes it at scope end. (An arm that is an *unmarked* read of a named owned binding is a borrow arm per the producers table — the whole expression is then a borrow and the `using var` a borrow-pin; a **marked** arm `move cached` is an owned arm.)

`using var` is a scope pin (axiom [A5](#sec-axiom-register)): it is implicitly non-reassignable, and reassigning a `using var` variable is a compile error. To use a different resource later in the method, introduce a new `do ... end` block.

**Adopting a named owned binding (derives: [K3.4](#sec-kernel-k3)).** `using var y := move x;` transfers a named owned local or `owned` parameter into a scope-bound binding: `y` takes over the disposal obligation and `x` is left moved-from — the binding-position form of the [§22.3](#sec-parameter-modifiers) transfer marker ([§28.3](#sec-local-variables-ownership-and-borrows)). An **unmarked** `using var y := x;` is a **compile error** when its right-hand side is a named owned binding whose declared type, nullability stripped, is a class or interface type. This includes the null-forgiving read `x!` (classified as the bare `x` is, [§17.8](#sec-the-null-forgiving-operator)), a parenthesized `(x)` (parentheses group and introduce no expression of their own, [§4.2](#sec-integer-types)), the anonymous `using var _ := x;` and `await using var y := x;` ([§28.12](#sec-asynchronous-disposal)). A *named owned binding* here means:

- a local whose ownership state at the `using var` declaration is owned ([§28.3](#sec-ownership-state-of-locals)) — a `var` or `using var` local (one that adopted the owned state by assignment included), an owned iteration variable ([§29.2](#sec-desugaring-of-for)), an `out owned` recipient, an owning-match arm binding ([§35.5](#sec-owning-match)); or
- an `owned` parameter.

Two shapes are **not** covered. A captured owned binding inside a closure is in borrow state ([§28.3](#sec-captured-owned-bindings) *Captured owned bindings*). A bare identifier that resolves to a field — an implicit-`this` read, or the bare spelling of the declaring type's own static field — is a field read. Over both, the unmarked form is the borrow-pin of *`using var` initialized from a borrow* below.

The covered spelling does not say whether `y` adopts `x` or views it, and the compiler does not choose. The diagnostic names the remedies the source admits: `move x` to adopt — except over a `using var` source, which is never movable out (axiom [A5](#sec-axiom-register)) — or a `var` or `const` binding ([§21.1](#sec-variable-declarations)), a view that leaves the obligation with `x`. The anonymous form has no view to offer (`var _` and `const _` are rejected, [§21.1](#sec-variable-declarations)): besides `move x`, its remedy is deleting the declaration. Over a `Task`-family source the anonymous form is reported under [§17.13](#sec-the-discard-_)'s rejection (axiom [A6](#sec-axiom-register)) first, and `using var _ := move x;` is never offered as its remedy.

A **bare type parameter** whose constraints do not exclude class and interface substitutions ([§28.1](#sec-where-the-owned-modifier-can-appear) clause 5) is a class or interface type for this rule: the generic body type-checks under the class-or-interface assumption ([§28.1](#sec-where-the-owned-modifier-can-appear) clause 3), so `using var y := x;` over an `owned x: T` is rejected once, in the body, before substitution, and `move x` adopts at every instantiation — redundant at a move-only substitution and erased at an erasing one, as for the declaration marker (clauses 3–4).

Where `x` is a local of **move-only value type** ([§15.3](#sec-move-only-value-types)) the unmarked form **adopts**: a move-only binding has no borrow reading to disambiguate, so the plain read moves ([K3.12](#sec-kernel-k3); [§15.3](#sec-move-only-value-types)'s *Local-to-local assignment*, and the [announcement table](#sec-announcement-table)'s row 8 for the call form), `y` carries the value's owned slots to the end of *its* block and `x` is left moved-from.

**The anonymous binding.** `using var _ := expression;` (and `await using var _ := …;`, [§28.12](#sec-asynchronous-disposal)) is the **anonymous owning binding** ([§17.13](#sec-the-discard-_)): the same scope-end disposal, non-reassignability, admission rules, and borrow-pin case as a named `using var` — with no name bound. `_` is not in scope after the declaration, and nothing can read the value; the form is the sanctioned spelling for holding a value to scope end without naming it (`using var _ := mutex.Acquire();`). Adoption composes: `using var _ := move x;` consumes `x` into the anonymous binding exactly as the named form would. A `Task`-family value may not be bound this way ([§17.13](#sec-the-discard-_), axiom [A6](#sec-axiom-register)); the **named** `using var t := call();` remains the unsupervised idiom ([§30.10](#sec-standard-library-task-helpers)).

**The compiler-introduced slot.** The scoped await-bind ([§30.5](#sec-the-scoped-await-bind)) establishes a compiler-introduced, unnameable slot of exactly this section's kind on the same establishment-ordered cleanup stack — established at the declaration statement, disposed at the innermost enclosing block's end on every exit edge, ordered against neighbouring cleanups exactly as a hand-written `using var` at the same line would be.

`using var` accepts a value-type or runtime-managed right-hand side. For ordinary value types and runtime-managed types, the disposal at scope end is a no-op (these types do not require disposal per [§28.9](#sec-runtime-managed-types)), and the only effect is the reassignability restriction. For move-only inline arrays (`[N owned]…`, [§15.3](#sec-move-only-value-types)), the local's owned slots are auto-disposed at scope end regardless of whether `using var` is used; the only additional effect of `using var` on a move-only local is the reassignability restriction. The uniform admissibility of `using var` across value-typed, runtime-managed, and move-only RHSes makes it safe to use uniformly in generic code or in compiler-generated desugarings (such as the for-loop body of [§29.2](#sec-desugaring-of-for)) without inspecting the underlying type kind.

To dispose before the enclosing method returns, nest in a `do ... end`:

```bezel
public method Process()
  var result := 0;
  do
    using var fs := new FileStream("data.txt", FileMode.Open);
    using var buffer := new Array<byte>(4096, 0);   // sized ctor (stdlib §4.4)
    result := fs.Read(buffer, 0, buffer.Count);     // bytes read (stdlib §7.1)
  end;     // fs and buffer disposed here
  Console.WriteLine($"count = {result}");
end Process;
```

<a id="sec-using-var-initialized-from-a-borrow"></a>
#### `using var` initialized from a borrow

When the right-hand side of a `using var` declaration is a borrow rather than an owned value (a method call without an `owned` return — unless its declared return type is a `Task`-family type, an owned production per [§28.3](#sec-producers) — an indexer access, a field read, or an unmarked read of a **borrow-state** named binding (a plain parameter, a borrowing alias or loop variable, a captured owned binding inside a closure) — an unmarked read of a class- or interface-typed named **owned** binding is rejected (*Adopting a named owned binding* above), and an unmarked read of a **move-only value** binding moves instead and is an owned right-hand side, [§15.3](#sec-move-only-value-types)), the `using var` does **not** assume a disposal obligation (derives: [K2](#sec-kernel-k2) — no obligation can be assumed from a borrow): at scope end, no `Dispose()` is called, because the value is not owned by this scope. The `using var` still **pins** the borrow's source for the duration of the scope — meaning the borrow lifetime rules of [§28.3](#sec-local-variables-ownership-and-borrows) treat the source as in-scope for the using-var's entire lexical extent. Concretely: the borrow stays **live** until the using-var's scope ends, exactly as if it were used at every point up to that end, and the [consume-site freeze](#sec-consume-site-freeze) then governs every consume of the source in that range — the frozen kills (a move, a transfer, a reassignment of the binding) are compile errors, and the **site-announced** kills stay unfrozen under their flag backstop ([K4.2](#sec-kernel-k4), [K5.3](#sec-kernel-k5)): an explicit `Dispose()` of the source is permitted, and a read through the pinned binding afterwards raises `DisposedAccessException` in checked disposal mode ([§28.2](#sec-checked-disposal)). The pin adds no exception to [K5](#sec-kernel-k5)'s two recorded shapes; the [§28.14](#sec-scoped-callback-parameters) storage admission remains the one admission whose captured sources are frozen against explicit disposal as well ([§28.3](#sec-diagnostics)). Pinning is a compile-time constraint, not a runtime mechanism; the compiler enforces it by extending the borrow's required-liveness range to cover the using-var's scope.

This case is what allows the for-loop desugaring ([§29.2](#sec-desugaring-of-for)) to wrap an arbitrary source in `using var __source := source` without taking ownership when `source` is borrowed; programmers also encounter it directly when using `using var` for scope-pinning of a borrowed iterable.

<a id="sec-collections-do-not-own-elements"></a>
<a id="sec-collection-element-ownership"></a>
### 28.11 Collection element ownership

Bezel has two families of collection types (axiom [A9](#sec-axiom-register)):

- **Borrowing collections** (`Array<T>`, `LinkedList<T>`, `Dictionary<K, V>`, `Set<T>`, `Stack<T>`, `Queue<T>`) store references whose holders continue to own the elements. Element disposal is the arrangement of whoever owns the elements — owned bindings, owned fields, or an owning-family collection; it never happens through the borrowing collection ([§28.6](#sec-who-may-dispose)).

- **Owning collections** (`OwningArray<T>`, `OwningLinkedList<T>`, `OwningDictionary<K, V>`, `OwningSet<T>`, `OwningStack<T>`, `OwningQueue<T>`, `OwningSlotMap<T>`) own their elements: every ingress member takes ownership, and the collection's `Dispose()` cascades through every element. Owning collections require `where T: class` (and, for `OwningDictionary<K, V>`, `where V: class`) — owning makes sense only for class-typed values.

The two families are declared separately in the standard library ([§4](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-system-collections-generic)). A program chooses the form that matches the intended ownership semantics. There is no implicit conversion between the two families; an `OwningArray<Connection>` is not an `Array<Connection>` and vice versa. What every element operation does, for both families, is the element slot policy below.

<a id="sec-element-slot-policy"></a>
#### The element slot policy

Every standard collection's element semantics follow from one classification, not from per-collection rules (derives: [K1](#sec-kernel-k1) per slot + [K2.3](#sec-kernel-k2)/[K4.3](#sec-kernel-k4) for stored borrows). A collection's slots are classified by the collection's family and the element type's *element category* — a derived type property ([§3.6](#sec-derived-type-properties)):

| Element category | Borrowing family slots | Owning family slots |
|---|---|---|
| value type (non-move-only) | copies | *(rejected at instantiation)* |
| runtime-managed reference (`string`, function types, `Type`; [§28.9](#sec-runtime-managed-types) — no *declared* element type is a boxed value type, [§9.7](#sec-records-and-disposal), so an `Object` or interface element type is classified by the row below) | shared references | *(rejected at instantiation)* |
| class / interface type | borrows | owned |
| move-only value type ([§15.3](#sec-move-only-value-types) — owning inline arrays and owning-classified choices, [§35.4](#sec-choice-classification)) | *(rejected at instantiation)* | *(rejected at instantiation)* |

(The owning family admits only class/interface element types; see the instantiation-site restriction in [§14.4](#sec-owned-as-a-generic-argument). Move-only element types are deferred for both families — see stdlib [§4.14](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-owned-buffers-and-spans) and the rationale.) For dictionaries the classification applies independently to the key slots and the value slots: an owning dictionary owns its *values*; its keys are value-like and classified per the borrowing column (stdlib [§4.9](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-owneddictionaryk-v)).

The slot kind alone determines what every element operation does:

| Operation | copy slots | shared-reference slots | borrow slots | owned slots |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| store (`Add`, `Insert`, indexer-set) | copies the value in (a **borrow-bearing record** value carries [§9.7](#sec-records-and-disposal)'s lifetime obligation: every carried source must provably outlive the collection — statically checked) | stores the reference | stores the borrow; the element's source must outlive the collection's use of it (enforced per the store rule under *Borrowing collections* below) | takes `owned`; indexer-set disposes the previous value first (skipped for a moved-from slot) |
| `Remove` / `RemoveAt` | removes the copy | removes the reference | removes the borrow; the caller's ownership is unaffected | **disposes** the removed element |
| `Clear()` | removes all | removes all | removes all | **disposes** every element, in the order the `Dispose()` row below gives |
| `Dispose()` of the collection | no user-visible work (the backing storage is part of the instance's allocation, released with it — [§28.9](#sec-runtime-managed-types)) | no user-visible work (as previous column) | no user-visible work; elements untouched | **disposes** every live element — reverse storage order for ordered collections (below), implementation-defined order for unordered — then releases storage |
| indexer-get / default iteration | copy out | reference out | borrow out (source: the element's original holder; the collection is a transit point) | borrow out (source: the collection) |
| ownership out | *(none — nothing owned)* | *(none)* | *(none)* | `move coll[i]`, the `Pop*` family, `Drain()` |

The per-collection clauses in the remainder of this section and in the standard library document ([§4](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-system-collections-generic)) are presentations of this table for each concrete type; they do not introduce element semantics of their own, and a per-collection statement that diverges from the table is a defect in this specification. The storage embodiment of the owning column is `OwningBuffer<T>` (stdlib [§4.14](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-owned-buffers-and-spans)), the primitive over which the resizable owning collections compose; the borrowing family's storage remains a compiler intrinsic — a user-expressible borrow-storing primitive is deferred, recorded in the rationale ([§5.20](Bezel_Design_Rationale.md#sec-one-element-policy)).

<a id="sec-borrowing-collections"></a>
#### Borrowing collections

For a borrowing collection, the slot policy's copy, shared-reference, and borrow columns are the entire element story, and the member signatures are the standard library's ([§4](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-system-collections-generic)): `Dispose()` is a no-op — the family is trivial-dispose ([§28.9](#sec-runtime-managed-types)), its intrinsic backing storage part of the instance's single allocation and released with it by the instance's free — `Clear()`, `Remove`, and `RemoveAt` remove without disposing (the element's holder, if any, keeps its obligation), and an indexer-get produces a borrowed reference whose source is whichever holder the borrow originally came from: the collection is a transit point, not a source.

**Storing a borrow (derives: [K2.3](#sec-kernel-k2)).** Storing a class-typed borrow into a borrowing collection follows the same shape as [§28.3](#sec-local-variables-ownership-and-borrows)'s borrowed-field rule. The store-site check is structural and decidable: parameter-sourced (a parameter that is not `owned`), receiver-sourced, and field-sourced borrows are admitted — the same check reaches the key slot of `OwningDictionary<K, V>`, a borrowing position ([§15.4](#sec-collection-literals)); a borrow of a **scope-bound binding** — an `owned` parameter included, its value being disposed at the method's end ([§28.3](#sec-owned-local-discharge-requirement)) — stored into a collection that provably outlives that scope — the collection is a field, is reachable from one, escapes the method, or is a local of strictly wider scope — is **rejected** at the store site. The residual is a [K4.3](#sec-kernel-k4)-recorded trust clause: whether each admitted element's source actually outlives the collection's use of it is the programmer's obligation, with [K4.1](#sec-kernel-k4)'s backstop as the named safety net; the obligation carries the borrowed-field rule's **domain clause** ([§28.3](#sec-borrow-lifetime-rules), clause 4) for each admitted element's source object while the collection retains the borrow. A **fresh unbound owned temporary** of class type passed to `Add`/`Insert`/indexer-set is not a borrow of any named source but a temporary that dies at its K8 boundary ([§28.3](#sec-unbound-owned-temporaries)): the store is admitted under [§15.4](#sec-collection-literals)'s recorded literal-only-rejection asymmetry and draws that section's fresh-store warning (the hazard is stated per argument family there — the retained reference dangles at the K8 boundary, backstopped by checked disposal mode, [§28.2](#sec-checked-disposal)).

A holding class that semantically owns its elements declares an owning-family collection — the type states the intent and `Dispose()` cascades.

The recommended pattern when a class semantically owns a collection-of-resources:

```bezel
class BankAccount
  private owned _transactions: OwningArray<Transaction>;

  public constructor()
    _transactions := new OwningArray<Transaction>();
  end constructor;
end BankAccount;
```

`owned` on the field handles container disposal, and the owning collection's cascade disposes every element — no destructor is needed. A class wanting *selective or interleaved* cleanup takes elements out first — `Drain()` in a loop, `move _transactions[i]`, or the `Pop*` family — into owned bindings whose disposal it controls.

A dictionary whose holder owns the **values** is `OwningDictionary<K, V>`'s shape by construction — it owns its values, its keys are ordinarily value-like — a class-typed key is held as a borrow, and [§15.4](#sec-collection-literals)'s fresh-store warning reaches that position — and `Dispose()` cascades over the values ([stdlib §4.9](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-owneddictionaryk-v)). The reverse asymmetry (owned keys, borrowed values) has no collection form and no recorded client; a holder with that shape keeps the keys in an owning collection of their own.

<a id="sec-owning-collections"></a>
#### Owning collections

An owning collection's element behavior is the slot policy's owned column, and its member surface — which types declare `Add`/`Insert` and the indexer, the order-disciplined pair's `Push`/`Pop`/`Enqueue`/`Dequeue` egress, the `PopAt`/`PopFirst`/`PopLast` and `Try*` forms — is declared in the standard library ([§4.2](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-owning-collection-interfaces), §4.5–§4.12): ingress members take `owned` arguments, `Remove`/`RemoveAt`/`Clear` dispose what they remove, `Dispose()` disposes every element and then frees the backing storage, and reads — the indexer-get and default iteration — produce borrows whose source is the collection (`move coll[i]` is the explicit-take form, below).

**The element-borrow use-after-removal warning.** A read that produces such a borrow — the indexer-get `coll[i]`, the iteration variable of default iteration over the collection, and a stdlib §5 class-element terminal accessor whose receiver's statically-traced provenance ([§29.11](#sec-multiple-enumeration)) roots at the collection — names the collection binding as the borrow's source. The compiler **must warn** when a local holding such a borrow is used (read, borrowed from, or passed) after a call on the **same collection binding** that **disposes the borrowed element** and **dominates the use on every path** — the dominating-kill shape of [§28.2](#sec-checked-disposal)'s use-after-dispose warning, with the kill on the collection rather than on the binding (derives: [K4.2](#sec-kernel-k4) + [K7.4](#sec-kernel-k7), the source per [K2.1](#sec-kernel-k2)): `Clear()`, which disposes every element; `Remove(b)` — the element-removal member of the sequence and set families — where the argument is the borrow itself; and `RemoveAt(i)` where the borrow was taken as `coll[i]` with the same index expression — a constant, or a local read not reassigned between — the per-slot precision the moved-from tracking below uses, and no structural operation of [§29.12](#sec-mutation-during-iteration)'s list on the same collection binding between the borrow and the kill: a reposition or removal ahead of the slot would change which element the index names. An element-level write — an indexer-set — does not draw this warning: it is not a [§29.12](#sec-mutation-during-iteration) structural operation, and the two warnings share one operation vocabulary (a chosen silence, liftable; the checked-mode backstop stands behind it). A keyed removal — `OwningDictionary<K, V>`'s `Remove(k)` after a borrow taken as `od[k]` — is likewise outside the kill set in this revision: the set is keyed on the ordered collections' slot index, and a keyed leg would restate it over key equality ([§8.3](#sec-equals-and-gethashcode)) (a chosen silence, liftable; the backstop stands behind it). A borrow re-taken after the mutation is clean, and a use before the mutation, or on a path the kill does not dominate, draws nothing. The warning names the disposing call and the remedies: re-take the borrow after the mutation; take the element out first through `PopAt`/`Pop`/`PopValue`, which leave no borrow behind; or mutate after the last use. Where the element type overrides `Equals`, `Remove(b)` may dispose an equal element other than the borrowed one; the warning is stated as certain there regardless — an over-warn, recorded, with re-taking the borrow as its remedy. The program stays accepted; no per-site suppression exists (rationale [§5.28](Bezel_Design_Rationale.md#sec-silent-tracking)).

The indexer-set disposes the displaced value per [§28.7](#sec-reassigning-owned-fields)'s drop-on-overwrite ([K3.11](#sec-kernel-k3)) — no explicit `Dispose()` at the assignment site — and a slot already in moved-from state takes the new value with nothing to dispose (*Indexer setter on a moved-from slot*, below). A user-written `set(owned)` accessor over an owned field behaves identically through the ordinary owned-field assignment in its body ([§23.3](#sec-block-form-properties), [§28.7](#sec-reassigning-owned-fields)); the compiler-synthesized owning indexer setter uses the same discipline.

Ownership leaves an owning collection through the egress members and through `move coll[i]` (below). A `Pop`-family member removes the element and returns it as `owned` in a single step, closing the slot (subsequent indices shift down for sequence types; the dictionary entry is removed for `OwningDictionary`). **`Drain(): IOwningEnumerable<T>`** returns an iterable that drains the source as it is iterated: after full iteration the source collection is empty; partial iteration drains only the elements yielded, and the rest remain. The user iterates with `for var item in coll.Drain() do ... end;`, where `item` is owned; the [§28.3](#sec-owned-local-discharge-requirement) discharge rules apply in the loop body (`using var u := move item;` is the typical form — marker; an undischarged item auto-drops at body end with the must-use warning).

Owning collections need no explicit element pass: disposing the collection already disposes the elements — the cascade is the type's contract.

Default iteration `for var item in coll do ... end` produces *borrows* of each element via the collection's `IEnumerable<T>` conformance — the collection still owns its elements after iteration. To consume, iterate over `coll.Drain()`, whose static type `IOwningEnumerable<T>` selects [§29.2](#sec-desugaring-of-for)'s owning path and yields owned values.

```bezel
public method UseEach()
  using var pool := new OwningArray<Connection>();
  pool.Add(Connect("primary"));      // ownership transfers in
  pool.Add(Connect("secondary"));     // ownership transfers in

  // Default iteration: each conn is a borrow
  for var conn in pool do
    conn.Ping();                      // pool still owns conn afterward
  end;

  // Drain iteration: each conn is owned
  for var conn in pool.Drain() do
    using var c := move conn;         // discharge each owned element
    c.SendShutdown();
  end;
  // pool is now empty; using var on pool disposes the (empty) array
end UseEach;
```

Disposal of the collection itself — at the end of a `using var` scope, in a destructor's auto-dispose pass, or at static-program-exit for a `static owned` field — disposes every element it still holds, then frees the backing storage, in the table's order: **reverse storage order** for the ordered collections — descending index for `OwningArray`, tail-to-head for `OwningLinkedList`, pop order for `OwningStack`, the reverse of dequeue order for `OwningQueue`, descending slot index for `OwningSlotMap` (stdlib [§4.21](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-owning-slot-map)) — and implementation-defined for the unordered (`OwningDictionary`, `OwningSet`). `Clear()` disposes the elements it holds in that same order and keeps the emptied collection.

The order is stated over **storage** rather than over insertion. The two coincide for a collection built by appending alone, and diverge as soon as a positional ingress has been used — `OwningArray.Insert(0, x)` makes the newest element the first index, and `OwningLinkedList.AddFirst`/`AddBefore` do the same for the chain. After `OwningArray.Sort` or `Reverse` insertion order is not merely different from storage order but **not recoverable from the collection at all**: these types store elements, not arrival order, so an insertion-keyed rule would name an order no conforming implementation can produce. Storage order is observable, computable at every point in a collection's life, and equal to the older term wherever the older term was well defined.

<a id="sec-move-on-a-collection-slot"></a>
#### `move` on a collection slot

The `move` expression form ([§28.8.1](#sec-the-move-expression)) extends to owning-collection slots. `move coll[i]` reads the i-th element of an owning collection as an owned value, leaving the slot in moved-from state.

`move coll[i]` is admitted on exactly these receivers, each of whose indexer names an **owned slot** (the owned column of the element slot policy above): an `OwningArray<T>` or `OwningDictionary<K, V>` slot; an `OwningBuffer<T>` slot for class-typed `T` (the dynamic-size owning storage primitive, stdlib [§4.14](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-owned-buffers-and-spans)); a `Span<T>` slot for class-typed `T`, a view whose slot is its underlying buffer's; and a slot of either owning inline-array form, `[N owned]T?` or `[N owned]T` ([§15.1.1](#sec-owning-inline-arrays)). No other receiver admits it; an interface-typed receiver, `IOwningList<T>` included, is not among these. A copy, shared-reference or borrow slot, and a read-only view, admit none: a value-typed `OwningBuffer<T>` or `Span<T>` (a value has no ownership to transfer; the plain indexer-get suffices), the borrowing collections, `ArraySpan<T>` and `ReadOnlyArraySpan<T>` (stdlib [§4.15](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-arrayspant-readonlyarrayspant)), `ReadOnlySpan<T>` for any `T`, and `ReadOnlyStringSpan` (stdlib [§3.3](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-readonlystringspan)) reject `move coll[i]` at compile time. `move span[i]` is `move span.Buffer[span.Start + i]` after a bounds check against `span.Length`: it leaves the slot moved-from in the *underlying buffer* (the span carries no slot state), throws `IndexOutOfRangeException` with no slot moved-from when `i` is out of range, and is restored in the usual way (`span[i] := null`). `OwningStack<T>`, `OwningQueue<T>`, `OwningLinkedList<T>`, `OwningSet<T>`, and `OwningSlotMap<T>` declare no indexer, so `stack[i]` names no member and `move stack[i]` has no slot to apply to; their ownership-out methods (`Pop`, `Dequeue`, etc.) perform the equivalent take-and-discharge in a single call.

The field-restoration rule applies ([K9.2](#sec-kernel-k9), with per-slot tracking): the slot must be reassigned before the surrounding method exits. For nullable element types (`OwningArray<T>` internally storing `T?`, `OwningDictionary<K, V>`, `[N owned]T?`, `OwningBuffer<T>` for class-typed T which stores `T?`), assigning `null` to a moved-from slot satisfies the rule. For non-nullable element types (`[N owned]T`), restoration requires assigning a fresh owned T value — a constructor call, another moved value, or a borrow promoted to ownership. Code that needs "leave the slot empty after take" must use the nullable form. (For value-typed `OwningBuffer<T>` the rule is moot — `move buf[i]` is not admitted, so no restoration obligation arises.)

**Indexer setter on a moved-from slot.** When the slot is in moved-from state, assigning to it through the indexer setter does *not* trigger the owned-setter's "dispose previous value" semantics — the previous value was already taken out by `move`, so there is no previous value to dispose. The slot transitions directly from moved-from to holding the new value. This matches owned-field/local reassignment ([§28.7](#sec-reassigning-owned-fields)): a moved-from location accepts the new value with nothing to dispose. The compiler's per-slot moved-from tracking is what makes this distinguishable from a non-moved-from slot, where the setter does dispose the previous value.

The compiler tracks moved-from state per slot when the index is a compile-time constant or a local read. For variable indices that the compiler cannot prove are constant within the method, the analysis is conservative: after `move coll[i]` with a non-constant `i`, the *entire collection* is treated as having one or more slots in moved-from state. The admissible restoration operations depend on the collection kind:

- For heap owning collections (`OwningArray<T>`, `OwningDictionary<K, V>`, and class-typed `OwningBuffer<T>`): `coll[j] := value` for any `j` (treated as restoration of one slot if `j` matches the moved index, or as unrelated reassignment otherwise), `coll.Clear()` for those that provide it, or `coll.Dispose()` (which dispose the entire collection, satisfying the obligation by destruction). `OwningBuffer<T>` does not provide `Clear()` directly; the equivalent is a loop assigning `null` to every slot or disposing the buffer.
- For inline owning arrays (`[N owned]T?` or `[N owned]T`): `arr[j] := value` for any `j` (for nullable forms, `arr[j] := null` is also a valid restoration that marks slots empty). Inline arrays have no `Clear()` or `Dispose()` method (they are value types, not classes); restoration is per-slot assignment only.

The `PopAt` family of methods covers the common case where the user wants to take an element out and let the collection close the gap; `move coll[i]` is the building block for advanced cases where the slot is taken and immediately reassigned to a new value:

```bezel
public method ReplaceAt(index: int, owned newValue: T)
  var old := move pool[index];      // take from slot
  pool[index] := newValue;           // restore slot with new value
  old.Dispose();                     // dispose the old value
  // (or `using var taken := move pool[index];` for scope-bound disposal)
end ReplaceAt;
```

The same exception-safety rules apply: any throwable expression between the move and the reassignment must be an exit path on which the slot has been restored. The "build before take" discipline from [§28.8.1](#sec-the-move-expression) carries over directly.

<a id="sec-compatibility-between-borrowing-and-owning-forms"></a>
#### Compatibility between borrowing and owning forms

`Array<T>` and `OwningArray<T>` are distinct, unrelated types (axiom [A9](#sec-axiom-register)), with no implicit conversion between them in either direction. Exposing an owning array's elements as an `Array<T>` means draining it and rebuilding a borrowing array, and no shorthand is provided: the operation hands each element's ownership to the caller. A consumer that only reads declares one of the read-only iteration interfaces — `IEnumerable<T>`, `IReadOnlyCollection<T>`, `IReadOnlyList<T>` — which both types implement, and accepts either source:

```bezel
public method ReportEach(items: IEnumerable<Connection>)
  for var c in items do Console.WriteLine(c.Name); end;
end ReportEach;

public method UseOwnedPool()
  using var pool := new OwningArray<Connection>();
  pool.Add(Connect("a"));
  pool.Add(Connect("b"));
  ReportEach(pool);     // OK: OwningArray<Connection> implements IEnumerable<Connection>
                        //     iteration yields borrows
end UseOwnedPool;
```

A generic helper works the same way:

```bezel
public method ReportEachGeneric<T>(items: IEnumerable<T>) where T: class
  for var c in items do Console.WriteLine(c.ToString()); end;   // Object's surface only under `where T: class` (§14.2)
end ReportEachGeneric;

// Call with Array<Connection>: T inferred as Connection.
// Call with OwningArray<Connection>: T inferred as Connection.
// Same generic instantiation for both source forms.
```

The borrowing-iteration interfaces (`IEnumerable<T>`, `IReadOnlyList<T>`, `IReadOnlyCollection<T>`) are the shared abstractions between the two collection families. The mutating interfaces (`ICollection<T>`/`IList<T>` for borrowing; `IOwningCollection<T>`/`IOwningList<T>` for owning) are separate hierarchies, intentionally so — `Add` has different semantics in each (borrow-taking vs. owned-taking). Code that abstracts over mutation must pick one hierarchy.

<a id="sec-asynchronous-disposal"></a>
### 28.12 Asynchronous disposal

For resources requiring asynchronous cleanup, classes may implement `IAsyncDisposable`:

```bezel
interface IAsyncDisposable
  method DisposeAsync(): Task;
end IAsyncDisposable;
```

`DisposeAsync` is declared without an `async` modifier on the interface; `async` is an implementation-side modifier and never appears on interface method declarations. Implementations add `async` to the matching method and use `await` freely.

A class that implements `IAsyncDisposable` also has its compiler-generated synchronous `Dispose`. The two are distinct phases of the disposal lifecycle:

1. **Logical disposal** runs once. For `await using`, the awaited `DisposeAsync()` performs whatever asynchronous cleanup the class defines; the destructor body (if any) is **not** also run, because `DisposeAsync` supersedes it — per class, along the reclamation chain (step 2). For plain `using` (or a synchronous `Dispose()` call) on a class that implements both, the destructor body runs synchronously and `DisposeAsync` is **not** invoked — the class's two cleanup paths are alternatives, not a sequence. A user-written `DisposeAsync` should not call `Dispose` itself.
2. **Physical reclamation** runs once, after logical disposal has completed: owned fields are disposed in reverse declaration order, the base class's reclamation chains, and the heap block is released. This phase is the same regardless of which logical-disposal path ran. For `await using`, the runtime invokes physical reclamation as the second step of the implicit `Dispose()` it issues after `DisposeAsync` returns; the destructor bodies at the levels named next are skipped. Across a hierarchy, `DisposeAsync` supersedes a destructor body **per class**: at each level of the reclamation chain the destructor body is skipped if that level declares or overrides `DisposeAsync`, and runs if that level does not — a base class whose only cleanup is its destructor is cleaned up exactly as on the synchronous path. Physical reclamation of owned fields and the heap block is unaffected. So for `class Der: Base, IAsyncDisposable` where `Base` declares no `DisposeAsync`, `await using` runs `Der.DisposeAsync`, skips `Der`'s destructor, and runs `Base`'s destructor. Where a base level does declare `DisposeAsync`, chaining to `base.DisposeAsync()` is the override's obligation, as a destructor's chain is unconditional on the synchronous path: an override that does not chain forgoes that level's asynchronous cleanup, and its destructor body is skipped all the same. The rule is object-central: physical reclamation runs **exactly once, immediately after whichever logical-disposal path completes** — a synchronous `Dispose()`, `await using`'s implicit sequence, or a **direct `DisposeAsync()` call** awaited outside `await using` (legal; the awaited task's completion is logical-disposal completion, and reclamation follows exactly as if `await using` had issued it). This includes the fault edge: when `DisposeAsync` completes **by throwing**, logical disposal is over — the runtime performs physical reclamation, then the exception propagates from the await. A `DisposeAsync()` task that is itself abandoned without an await (e.g. `using var t := obj.DisposeAsync();` with no await) still runs to its terminal state ([§30.5](#sec-result-lifetime-and-task-disposal)); logical disposal completes at that terminal state and reclamation follows there — abandonment delays reclamation, it never skips it. Cleanup faults never leak the object ([§28.2](#sec-the-idisposable-contract)'s exactly-once invariant; the §22.9 exception-safety posture).

**Implicit discharge is synchronous.** The implicit disposal paths — auto-drop of a plain-`var` owned local or undischarged `owned` parameter at scope end, the exception-path cleanup, drop-on-overwrite, container cascades, and frame teardown ([§28.3](#sec-owned-local-discharge-requirement), [§28.7](#sec-reassigning-owned-fields), [§28.11](#sec-collections-do-not-own-elements), [§29.8](#sec-iterators-with-owned-parameters), [§30.1](#sec-async-methods)) — always take the synchronous `Dispose()` path, on every edge and in every context including `async` bodies: an implicit disposal point never awaits. Asynchronous cleanup runs only where the program wrote `await using` (whose implicit `finally` awaits `DisposeAsync` on both the normal and exception edges of an async body, with [§29.7](#sec-disposal-of-partially-consumed-iterators)'s synchronous fallback on early iterator abandonment) or awaited a direct `DisposeAsync()` call. A class whose async cleanup must run therefore needs an `await using var` binding — the [§28.3](#sec-owned-local-discharge-requirement) must-use warning on an implicitly-dropped value is the nudge — and the no-destructor warning below covers the class side.

A class that implements `IAsyncDisposable` and has resources requiring cleanup **should** also declare a `destructor` that performs the synchronous fallback of the same cleanup. If a class implements `IAsyncDisposable` but has no destructor, synchronous `Dispose()` performs only physical reclamation (owned-field disposal and base chaining) — any cleanup that `DisposeAsync` would have performed is skipped. The compiler emits a warning when a class implements `IAsyncDisposable` without a destructor: *"Class implements IAsyncDisposable but has no destructor; synchronous Dispose() will skip async cleanup."*

A second call to `Dispose()` or `DisposeAsync()` after either has run is a no-op ([§28.2](#sec-the-idisposable-contract)'s idempotence rule). The runtime tracks completion at the granularity of the object, not per-method.

The compiler-inserted free of a **trivial-dispose** instance ([§28.9](#sec-runtime-managed-types)) is this same two-phase lifecycle in degenerate form: logical disposal sets the per-instance flag and runs no user code, and physical reclamation follows — immediately in unchecked builds, deferrable under checked mode's quarantine latitude ([§28.2](#sec-checked-disposal)) so the flag stays readable behind surviving borrows.

`await using` is the async counterpart of `using var`:

```bezel
public async method ProcessAsync(): Task
  // ConnectAsync and SendAsync are illustrative: the standard library's
  // System.Net module is deferred to a future revision (std lib §11).
  await using var connection := await ConnectAsync(url);
  await connection.SendAsync(data);
  // connection.DisposeAsync() awaited at scope end
end ProcessAsync;
```

`await using` is valid only inside an async method or async lambda.

When a class implements both `IDisposable` and `IAsyncDisposable`, prefer `await using` in async contexts.

<a id="sec-shared-ownership"></a>
### 28.13 Shared ownership: `Shared<T>` and `Weak<T>`

The ownership model gives every disposal obligation exactly one holder ([K1.7](#sec-kernel-k1)). `Shared<T>` (stdlib [§2.16](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-shared-and-weak)) is the scoped exception — a compiler-known class whose instances (*handles*) jointly own one underlying value; the value is disposed exactly once, when the last handle is disposed. Shared ownership is opt-in, visible at every site (`Clone()` is an explicit call), and **domain-local except for synchronized `T`** (see the sendability rule below; [§30.14](#sec-sendable-types)).

```bezel
using var primary := new Shared<Connection>(Connect("db"));   // consumes the owned Connection; count = 1
using var second  := primary.Clone();                          // count = 2; an independent owned handle
second.Get().Ping();                                           // borrow of the underlying Connection
// scope end: second disposed (count 1), then primary disposed (count 0) → Connection disposed
```

The semantics, stated against the existing model:

- **Handles are ordinary owned class instances.** Every rule of this chapter applies to a handle unchanged: it is produced owned (by `new Shared<T>(...)` or `Clone()`), discharged by `using var`, an `owned` field, an `owned` parameter or return, `move`, or explicit `Dispose()`; branch joins, exception-path discharge, and the leak-prevention rules of [§28.6](#sec-leak-prevention) see nothing new. A handle may be stored in owning collections (`OwningArray<Shared<T>>`) like any class instance. The *only* novel behavior is inside the compiler-known type: the shared count, and last-one-disposes.
- **`new Shared<T>(owned value: T)`** consumes an owned T — the constructor is an owned-consuming position like any other ([§28.3](#sec-local-variables-ownership-and-borrows)); after construction the handle's disposal obligation *is* the value's. `T` must be a proper class type; runtime-managed and value types are rejected at instantiation ([§14.4](#sec-owned-as-a-generic-argument) pattern — they have no disposal obligation to share).
- **`Clone(): owned Shared<T>`** produces a new handle and increments the count. Cost and intent are visible at the call site; there is no implicit handle duplication anywhere in the language (assigning a handle moves or borrows it per the ordinary rules — it never silently clones).
- **`Get(): T`** produces a *borrow of the underlying value whose source is the handle*, valid while that handle lives — the same shape as the owning-collection indexer-get ([§28.11](#sec-element-slot-policy) owned column: borrow out, source: the collection). The borrow does not extend the value's lifetime; the handle does. [§28.6](#sec-leak-prevention)'s owned-field-return rule is not violated: `Get()` is the compiler-known accessor dispensation that owning-collection reads already have.
- **Disposal.** Disposing a handle decrements the count; disposing the last live handle disposes the underlying value (running its destructor cascade normally). Handle disposal is idempotent per [§28.2](#sec-the-idisposable-contract). The exactly-once invariant of [Appendix C](#sec-appendix-c) is preserved: the value's `Dispose()` runs once, from the last handle.
- **Cycles leak.** A value that (transitively, through owned fields) holds a `Shared<T>` handle participating in its own ownership keeps its count above zero forever — the standard reference-counting hazard. The compiler does not detect ownership cycles through `Shared<T>`. Break cycles with `Weak<T>`.
- **`Weak<T>`** (stdlib [§2.16](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-shared-and-weak)) is a non-owning observer minted from a handle (`shared.Downgrade(): owned Weak<T>`). A weak handle does not keep the underlying value alive; **`TryUpgrade(): owned Shared<T>?`** atomically produces a new strong handle if the value is still alive, and `null` otherwise (Try shape (b), stdlib §1 — the handle is a proper class type at every instantiation, so null alone carries the signal; `using var` + null test at the call site, the `Mutex.TryAcquire` idiom). Weak handles are themselves ordinary owned class instances and are disposed like any other.
- **Aliasing.** Multiple handles give multiple borrows of one mutable value within a domain. This is serial-execution-safe ([§30.13](#sec-runtime-model)) and carries the same *logical* aliasing hazards as any other long-lived borrow; nothing about `Shared<T>` relaxes use-after-dispose ([§28.2](#sec-checked-disposal)) for borrows taken from a handle that is then disposed.
- **Sendability.** `Shared<T>` is sendable **iff `T` is in the `Shared`-payload synchronized set**: the derived set of every type declaring the **synchronized** or the **immutable** fact and not the **self-distributing** fact (stdlib [§1](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-statics-and-sharing-facts)'s statics-and-sharing facts — the formula is normative, each grant's grounds live on the type's own fact line, and the set grows only by a fact ruling under stdlib §1's discipline; derived membership (shared-payload), informative — currently `Mutex`, `Atomic<T>`, `AtomicInteger<T>`, `Semaphore`, `Locked<T>`, `RwLocked<T>`, `FrozenArray<T>`, and `CancellationTokenSource` — stdlib §4.19, and stdlib §6.1–§6.4, §6.11; machine-checked, `scripts/check_docs.sh` 3b). For such `T`, a cloned handle may move to another domain (as a spawn argument or through a channel), the handle count is maintained with synchronized operations, and the underlying value is still disposed exactly once, by whichever domain drops the last handle; for an **immutable**-fact `T` the reclamation synchronization that sharing needs is carried by `Shared<T>`'s own synchronized handle count together with the string-precedent storage tolerance ([§30.14](#sec-sendable-types)). For every other `T`, `Shared<T>` remains domain-local and not sendable — the count synchronization alone would not make an unsynchronized `T` safe to reach from two domains. This realizes §6.2's "reached by multiple domains simultaneously" for mutexes: `Shared<Mutex>` is the cross-domain sharing idiom (clone, move the clone, both domains `Get().AcquireAsync()` — the blocking `Acquire()` is barred inside domain continuations, [§30.12](#sec-thread-synchronization)).

---

<a id="sec-scoped-callback-parameters"></a>
### 28.14 Scoped callback parameters: storage-bounded capture

The closure-capture rule ([§28.3](#sec-borrow-lifetime-rules)) admits a function value wherever its source set — the union of its captures' sources — admits a borrow: bound to a local whose scope does not strictly enclose a source's, immediately invoked, or passed as an argument to a function-typed parameter, among the rest (a parameter declared `Object`, or at a bare type parameter that the call substitutes with a function type, is instead a set-erasing position, [§28.3](#sec-borrow-lifetime-rules)'s closure bullet) (this section's own *v1 admission bounds*, item 3 below, keeps its narrower list of argument forms whose capture set is verifiable at a `scoped` call site). This section defines the argument form's two variants, whose bound is carried by the parameter's signature: a plain parameter is **call-bounded** (the callback is scoped to the call), and a `scoped` parameter is **storage-bounded** — **a stored callback whose lifetime is bounded by the object that stores it** (derives: [K2.3](#sec-kernel-k2) + [K5.7](#sec-kernel-k5), under axiom [A11](#sec-axiom-register)'s forms).

**The `scoped` modifier.** A function-typed parameter may be declared `scoped`: `method Spawn(scoped body: () -> Task)`. The declaration is a two-sided contract:

- **The callee may store the callback**, but only in `scoped` fields **of the bounding object itself** (below), or forward it to another `scoped` parameter whose bounding object is the same object; it may invoke it. It may not return it, move it into non-`scoped` storage, or store it in any other object. A `scoped` **field** holds such a callback: it may be invoked, overwritten, or cleared, but never read out as an escaping value — including into a deferred-activation call: passing a `scoped` field's value to a plain function-typed parameter whose call mints a deferred-activation frame (below) is such an escaping read-out and is rejected, since the frame would retain the stored callback independently of the bounding object and beyond severance's reach; the capture-set contribution ([§28.3](#sec-unbound-owned-temporaries)) soundly assigns storage reads nothing only because this read-out is barred. *(Liftable: a future revision may instead admit the read with the field's containing object as the contributed source, bounding the frame by the bounding object.)* These obligations are compiler-verified for user-authored callees. *(v1 deliberately excludes storage reached through owned fields of the bounding object: an owned child holding the callback could be moved out (§28.8.1), extending the callback past its bound. Direct fields only.)* A `scoped` parameter on a **static** method is admitted only when the method's return is `owned`, so that a call site can resolve bounding form 2 or 3; declaring `scoped` on a static method with no `owned` return is a compile error — there is no receiver, no constructed object, and no instance to hold the stored value, so nothing could ever bound the storage.
- **The caller's captures are storage-bounded.** At the call site the compiler resolves the **bounding object** (axiom [A11](#sec-axiom-register)):
  1. a constructor call → the constructed object;
  2. a call whose return is `owned` **and** is the initializer of a `using var`/`await using var` local → the returned object;
  3. a call whose return is `owned` **and** is directly assigned to (or initializes) an **`owned` field of `this`** → `this`;
  4. a call whose receiver is a **member chain** rooted at `this` or a local binding in which every hop is an **`owned` field** — → the **chain head**: `this` for `this._clicked.Add(h)` (and the bare `_clicked += h` spelling — the stdlib §6.5 event pattern), the local `pub` for `pub._clicked.Add(h)` (cross-instance `private` access is class-keyed, [§13.1](#sec-levels)). A chain containing a non-owned (borrow) field hop, an indexer, a getter, or an intervening call resolves **no** bounding object (capture-free callbacks only): across a borrow hop the storing object is externally owned and may outlive the chain head, so the head's teardown would not sever the registration (*liftable*: a future revision may admit *transparent getters* — an expression-bodied getter whose body is a bare read of an `owned` field of its receiver, exactly the stdlib §6.5 event pattern's property — restoring chain-hop resolution through such properties; recorded, not shipped);
  5. otherwise → the receiver.

  The forms are tested **in order; the first that resolves determines the bounding object** — `using var sub := pub.Clicked.Subscribe(h)` bounds by `sub` (form 2, the tightest bound; `Clicked` being the stdlib §6.5 pattern's getter-faced property, no later form would resolve a bound at all — an off-idiom discharge of the `Subscription` admits capture-free handlers only, with the `using var`/owned-field discharges of forms 2/3 as the admitted capture-bearing spellings).

  A closure argument capturing locals or parameters is admitted **iff** the bounding object resolves to one of:
  - a `using var`/`await using var` local `L` (directly, through the initializer resolution of forms 1/2, or as the chain head / receiver of forms 4/5), where every captured **local** source is declared **before** `L` in the same or an enclosing scope (`this` and the enclosing method's parameters count as declared before every local), **or is `L` itself, or is a value whose borrow provably originates from `L`** (self-capture: `scope.Spawn(lambda() => Work(scope.Token))` and the bound intermediate `var tok := scope.Token;` are both admitted; `L` outlives every invocation of what it stores, and the quiescence rule below plus [§28.12](#sec-asynchronous-disposal)'s logical-before-physical ordering guarantee no stored callback observes a reclaimed `L`); or
  - **`this`** (per forms 3/4), where every captured source is `this` itself or a value whose borrow provably originates from `this` — the only things the stored callback can dangle on are then the very object whose teardown bounds the storage. *Captured source* is [§28.3](#sec-borrow-lifetime-rules)'s notion here as everywhere: a capture that contributes no source — a value-typed local or parameter, or a `string` — is not a captured source and does not bar the admission (*v1 admission bounds* item 1 below).

  Until `L`'s scope exits, the captured local sources are **frozen** (derives: [K5.7](#sec-kernel-k5)): they may not be moved from, reassigned, or disposed — the consume-site freeze ([§28.3](#sec-consume-site-freeze)) **plus explicit disposal**. The bound is exact in both directions: **after** `L`'s scope exits the sources are unfrozen, because `L` is disposed at that scope end ([§28.10](#sec-using-var)) and *Quiescence* below admits no invocation after disposal completes — bounding `L` in a `do … end` block ([§21.6](#sec-do-end-blocks)) is therefore the sanctioned way to transfer a captured source out afterwards (the *v1 admission bounds* item 2(a) below states the one loop-carried residual). The storage freeze covers the site-announced kills the consume-site rule exempts — [K5.7](#sec-kernel-k5), a derivation from the criterion's conjunct (ii), an instance rather than an exception: a stored callback's later invocation is invisible at a `Dispose()` site, and this admission promises a fully static bound, so a runtime flag is not an admissible backstop for the admitted captures and [§28.3](#sec-consume-site-freeze)'s site-announced-kill carve-out does not apply to them. A bounding object that is none of the admitted resolutions — a plain expression, a parameter, a returned value that reaches no admitted slot — admits **no** capture-bearing arguments (capture-free callbacks are always admitted).

  **The registration-lifetime residual.** Forms 3 and 4 bound invocations by an object whose teardown must sever the storage: for form 4 the storing member is reached through the bounding instance's **owned** fields (the chain-hop restriction above) and is therefore disposed with it; for form 3 the returned handle (e.g. a `Subscription`, stdlib [§6.5](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-events-ievent-eventsource)) held in the `owned` field severs the registration when `this` is disposed — logical disposal precedes physical reclamation ([§28.12](#sec-asynchronous-disposal)), so severance completes before any capture dangles. The admission therefore carries one obligation the checker does not close: **the registration must not be extended past the bounding object** — `move`-ing the handle-holding `owned` field (or a storing owned child) out into longer-lived storage re-opens the invocation window. This is deliberately the same recorded residual-trust shape as the quiescence rule ([K2.3](#sec-kernel-k2) + [K4.1](#sec-kernel-k4)) below — structural checks decidable, the temporal guarantee the programmer's, `DisposedAccessException` in checked disposal mode the deterministic backstop — and it deliberately re-opens a corner of the owned-field-extraction closure recorded here: the alternative (freezing such fields against `move`) would require flow-marking fields by what initialized them, a per-value property a field declaration does not carry. Recorded, not silent.

**Quiescence.** Disposal of the bounding object must guarantee that no stored callback is invoked after disposal completes (by draining in-flight work or severing registrations before teardown). For compiler-known types the guarantee is stated normatively in the standard library (`TaskScope`, the stdlib §6.5 event types, the task-completion sources). For user-authored types the obligation is the recorded residual of [K2.3](#sec-kernel-k2)'s admission posture: the storage-site checks are structural and decidable; the temporal guarantee is the author's, with [K4.1](#sec-kernel-k4)'s backstop as the named safety net ([§28.2](#sec-checked-disposal)). A callback that runs *during* the drain may touch the bounding object soundly: logical disposal precedes physical reclamation ([§28.12](#sec-asynchronous-disposal)).

**The call-bounded default (derives: [K2.4](#sec-kernel-k2) — a plain signature carries no capture set, so no retention can be type-announced).** A function-typed parameter declared *without* `scoped` is **call-bounded** (a setter's `value` excepted, and a record's generated-constructor parameter for a component whose declared type is a function type, which carry the empty source set, [§23.3](#sec-block-form-properties), [§28.3](#sec-borrow-lifetime-rules)'s *record components of function type*): the callee receives the callback for the duration of the call only — or, when the call mints a deferred-activation frame, for the duration of that frame's life (*Call-bounded × deferred activation* below). Within the callee the callback may be invoked, bound to locals, and passed on as an argument to another call-bounded parameter (a deferred-activation callee's included — the retention that creates rides the returned frame, judged below); it may **not** be stored in a field of any object (a property or indexer assignment is such a store, and so is a store into a function-typed record component, choice payload or inline-array slot, a local array's included, [§28.3](#sec-borrow-lifetime-rules)'s *function-typed holders*; so is a body reference to a primary-constructor parameter, which captures it into a field, [§22.10](#sec-capture-rule-and-layout-stability)), stored into any collection, a local one included (a function value read from a collection carries the empty set, [§28.3](#sec-borrow-lifetime-rules)'s closure bullet; a deferred-activation frame carrying the callback, or a task minted by invoking it, may be held in a *purely local* collection, one that is not a parameter, a borrow or a field nor reached through one, as in a local binding: *Call-bounded × deferred activation* below), returned, captured by a closure that itself escapes the callee (judged by these same rules, applied transitively), or forwarded into a `scoped` parameter position. The last restriction is load-bearing: the callee cannot see its argument's capture set, so it cannot vouch for the [§28.14 admission](#sec-scoped-callback-parameters); a callee that needs to register a callback it received must itself declare the parameter `scoped` (the forwarding rule above then requires the same bounding object). These obligations are compiler-verified for user-authored callees — structural and decidable, the same sink checks [§28.3](#sec-local-variables-ownership-and-borrows) applies to frame-bounded borrows.

The caller side is correspondingly unrestricted: **any** closure — capture-bearing or not — may be passed to a call-bounded parameter (one whose declared return slot is a bare type parameter at a function-type substitution excepted: that is a set-erasing position's return-slot arm, [§28.3](#sec-borrow-lifetime-rules)'s closure bullet), since every captured source trivially outlives the call (for a deferred-activation callee the admission is re-keyed to the returned frame — *Call-bounded × deferred activation* below). (The default completes the lattice: plain = call-bounded, `scoped` = storage-bounded.)

**The stdlib retention register.** Standard-library callees state their retention in their signatures — `scoped` where they store — and the per-position roster is the standard library's, not this section's: the stdlib §6.5 subscribe positions and stdlib §6.10's `Spawn` declare `scoped`; the shared-event subscribe positions admit **capture-free** handlers only, a non-capturing lambda or a static method reference (stated at stdlib §6.5, keyed on the resolved callee; user implementations of `ISharedEvent<T>` gain no retention right and are verified under the ordinary call-bounded regime above); the lazy query operators' retention is the frame residence of *Call-bounded × deferred activation* below — a normative consequence of their deferred-activation signatures, not a certification (stdlib §5); the asynchronous spawn positions of [§30.14](#sec-multiple-domains) (`Domain.Spawn`, the `Parallel` combinator bodies — stdlib §6.12) sit under §30's capture and sendability rules rather than this section's; and the [§30.11](#sec-taskcompletionsourcet-and-ownedtaskcompletionsourcet) task-completion-source admission is a named carve of its own, axiom [A10](#sec-axiom-register)'s (*Relation to §30.11* below).

**The method-reference formation bar (protects the position-keyed register admissions — axioms [A10](#sec-axiom-register)/[A11](#sec-axiom-register) — and the set-erasing positions of [§28.3](#sec-borrow-lifetime-rules)'s closure bullet).** Register positions are stated at the callee, not marked in the parameter's function type, so — to keep the admission alias-proof — **forming a method reference over a capture-free-register position is a compile error** (covering every register entry: `Domain.Spawn`'s and the shared-event positions): the formed value's plain function type would erase the admission, and a call through it would reach the trusted storing implementation under the call-bounded default's caller side above, which admits any closure. (`scoped`-marked positions need no such bar: `scoped` is part of function-type identity, [§27.1](#sec-function-types), and survives formation.) Forming a method reference is likewise a compile error when a parameter slot of the formed function type is, nullability stripped, a function type and binds to a callee parameter that is a set-erasing position — one declared `Object`, or at a bare type parameter that the formation's substitution makes a function type (`var add := xs.Add;` at `xs: Array<() -> int>`; `var keep: (() -> int) -> () := k.Keep;` over `Keep(o: Object)`): a call through the formed value passes its argument to a plain function-typed parameter, which the call-bounded default's caller side admits whatever its set, and the callee would receive it at a position that announces none. The bar holds for capture-free uses too; the remedy is a lambda, `lambda(g) => xs.Add(g)`, whose body the closure bullet checks.

**Call-bounded × deferred activation (unified across the deferred-activation kinds).** Two shapes are defined. (1) **Frame residence** (derives: [K6.1](#sec-kernel-k6) + [K6.2](#sec-kernel-k6)). A callee whose call mints a deferred-activation frame (the kinds of [§28.3](#sec-unbound-owned-temporaries) *Deferred-activation callees*: an `async` callee — the returned task; an iterator or async-iterator callee — the returned enumerable or enumerator frame ([§29.3](#sec-iterator-methods), [§30.7](#sec-asynchronous-programming-async-iterators)); a lazy query operator — the returned query value, stdlib §5) holds a plain function-typed parameter in that frame: the callback runs after the constructing call has returned, and frame residence is **not** an escape sink — the deferred-activation return type is the signature-level type announcement of the retention ([K6.2](#sec-kernel-k6)), exactly as it announces the frame's carried borrows ([§28.3](#sec-returning-a-deferred-activation-frame)). The bound is the **frame's life** (K6.1): a task's settlement ([§30.1](#sec-async-methods)); an iterator frame's completion or disposal ([§29.4](#sec-lazy-evaluation), [§29.7](#sec-disposal-of-partially-consumed-iterators) — the `for` desugaring's `using var` bounds both, [§29.2](#sec-desugaring-of-for); `await for`'s, [§30.7](#sec-asynchronous-programming-async-iterators)); a lazy query's single-consumption point ([§29.11](#sec-multiple-enumeration); the retention transfers into the consuming frames by the transitive rule of [§28.3](#sec-unbound-owned-temporaries)). The caller-side admission above ("every captured source trivially outlives the call") is correspondingly re-keyed to the returned frame: the callback's captured borrows' sources are **carried sources of the frame** ([§28.3](#sec-unbound-owned-temporaries)'s capture-set contribution), bounded by the ordinary borrow machinery — the scope and store rules and the frame-return check — and, for a task, by [§30.1](#sec-async-methods)'s source-outlives-settlement obligation where lifetimes cannot be statically compared, discharged by awaiting before the captured sources' scopes exit; the abandonment idioms carry the residual exactly as they do for object borrows ([§30.1](#sec-async-methods)). Callee-side, the sink checks above still govern the body's own uses of the parameter, and they extend transitively to the frame: a call-bounded callback **forwarded** to a plain function-typed parameter of another deferred-activation call rides that call's frame — admitted when the frame is consumed within the callee or returned under a deferred-activation return type (the announcement composes: the outer caller re-establishes against its own arguments); a frame that carries the callback and escapes any other way — stored in a field or in a collection that is not purely local (*The call-bounded default* above), captured by an escaping closure — is an escape of the callback itself, rejected by these same rules applied transitively. No `scoped` spelling is involved: `scoped` states open-ended storage in an object under the storage-bounded admission above, while frame residence is bounded by a value the caller's own flow analysis tracks — the lazy query operators' plain signatures are this shape's normative instance (stdlib §5), and an iterator callee that needs owned state alongside a callback declares an `owned` parameter beside it ([§29.8](#sec-iterators-with-owned-parameters)). (2) A callee — synchronous or async — that **invokes** a call-bounded callback whose invocation **mints a deferred-activation frame** must treat the minted frame as inheriting the call bound: it must consume the frame to its [K6.1](#sec-kernel-k6) bound before returning — a task awaited to settlement, an iterator or query frame enumerated or disposed — and may not store it, return it, or otherwise let it escape the call. For the task instance: returning it, storing it, passing it to `Task.FireAndForget`, or binding it and dropping it undisposed-to-settlement (`using var t := cb();` with no await) lets the callback's caller-sourced environment outlive the call through the still-running frame ([§30.5](#sec-result-lifetime-and-task-disposal)) and is an **escape sink**, rejected by the same structural verification as the other sinks above — as is storing or returning a minted iterator or query frame, which carries the callback the same way. In a **synchronous** callee a task-returning invocation is itself rejected (derives: [K6.3](#sec-kernel-k6) + [K3](#sec-kernel-k3) — the minted task inherits the call bound, and a non-`async` body has no consuming position for it): a non-`async` body cannot await the returned task at all (and blocking on it is barred inside continuations, [§30.3](#sec-the-task-taskt-and-ownedtaskt-types)), so invoking a plain function-typed parameter whose invocation yields a `Task`-family value is a compile error there — declare the parameter `scoped` (shifting the admission to the caller under the storage-bounded rules above) or, for the task case, make the callee `async`. An iterable- or query-minting invocation carries no such rejection: a synchronous body consumes the frame to its bound by enumerating or disposing it. The await-to-settlement requirement is per-path and admits **fan-out**: the returned tasks may be accumulated in a purely local collection (*The call-bounded default* above) provided every one of them is awaited to settlement before the callee returns on every path — awaiting an aggregation helper over that collection (`await Task.WhenAll(pending)`, [§30.10](#sec-standard-library-task-helpers)) discharges all of its inputs, since the aggregate completes only after every input settles.

**Class- and interface-typed `scoped` parameters: scoped construction.** The `scoped` modifier extends beyond function types: a class- or interface-typed parameter may be declared `scoped` — `constructor(scoped stream: Stream)` — applying the same two-sided contract to a **passive borrow** instead of a callback:

- **Callee side:** the callee may store the borrow in a direct non-owned field of the bounding object — the ordinary back-reference field of [§28.5](#sec-owned-fields)/[§28.3](#sec-local-variables-ownership-and-borrows) (a primary-constructor parameter's compiler-generated capture field is such a field, [§22.10](#sec-capture-rule-and-layout-stability)) — and may forward it only to another `scoped` parameter with the same bounding object. It may not return it or store it anywhere else; passing it as a plain (non-`scoped`) argument is an ordinary borrow argument, and a store the receiving callee makes is that callee's own §28.3 admission with its residual. No new field kind is introduced: `scoped` on the *parameter* **upgrades** [§28.3](#sec-local-variables-ownership-and-borrows)'s residual-trust back-reference admission to a static bound at the participating call sites; a plain (non-`scoped`) borrow parameter stored per §28.3 remains legal with the trust residual.
- **Caller side:** the argument carries the call-site marker — `new StreamReader(scoped stream)` ([§22.3](#sec-parameter-modifiers)) — and is admitted under the bounding-object forms above with *the argument's borrow source* in place of a closure's capture set: the source must satisfy the same declared-before/self/`this`-derived tests, and it is **frozen** until the bound's scope exits. A **fresh producer** argument is rejected (`new StreamReader(scoped new FileStream(...))` — the unbound owned temporary dies at the end of the full expression; [§9.7](#sec-records-and-disposal)'s no-temporary-source rule, identical remedy: bind the source first). A **value-typed argument** at an interface-typed `scoped` parameter, which reaches it by boxing ([§8.6](#sec-boxing)) and carries the same marker, meets this bound exactly where [§9.7](#sec-records-and-disposal)'s instance-field bullet admits storing the value in an instance field of a class: a value that is not borrow-bearing, or one in that bullet's null-source form. A move-only value does not box ([§8.6](#sec-boxing)); any other admitted value's box carries no borrow, so the argument has no borrow source: it is admitted under every bounding object and freezes nothing, its own location included, since the box holds a copy fixed at boxing. A borrow-bearing value is rejected there: the callee may keep the box in a field of the bounding object, which §9.7 and §8.6 reject for a record-carried borrow whatever the field's lifetime; the remedy is a class implementing the interface. At an argument whose type is a type parameter the condition is read at each instantiation ([§3.6](#sec-derived-type-properties) rule 2).
- **No quiescence obligation arises:** a stored borrow is passive data — it never fires. With declared-before admission, the freeze, and reverse-declaration-order disposal ([§28.10](#sec-using-var)), the source provably outlives the bounding object *including its destructor*; the guarantee is fully static with **no residual trust** — strictly stronger than the callback case. The [§28.2](#sec-checked-disposal) backstop remains defense-in-depth only.
- **Not at `Object`:** a parameter whose declared type, nullability stripped, is `Object` may not be declared `scoped`; the declaration is a compile error. `Object` is the one class to which a function value also converts ([§3.1](#sec-type-kinds)), so such a parameter would receive a callback and a borrow under one declaration, while this section's two contracts differ in the argument's call-site marker and in the field that may hold it — a `scoped` field, never read out, for a callback; a readable non-owned field for a borrow. A position declared `Object` is set-erasing in any case ([§28.3](#sec-borrow-lifetime-rules)'s closure bullet), so the callback half could admit only a capture-free argument. Declare the parameter at the class or interface type the callee stores.
