**Borrow-bearing parameters and results are forbidden (derives: [K2.1](#sec-kernel-k2) + [K6.1](#sec-kernel-k6) — a frame outlives the synchronous call; stack slots cannot enter it).** An `async` method, `async` lambda, or async iterator may not declare a parameter whose type is a borrow-bearing record ([§9.7](#sec-records-and-disposal)) — a span (stdlib §4.14, §4.15) or any record carrying a non-runtime-managed borrow — or a borrow-bearing inline array ([§15.1](#sec-inline-arrays), [§3.6](#sec-derived-type-properties)'s borrow-bearing row: `[2]Item` for a class `Item`, `[2]Pair` for a borrow-bearing record `Pair`), or a choice that **holds borrows** ([§35.4](#sec-choice-classification)'s holds-borrows property: whatever its classification, an *owning* choice that holds borrows included — [#3110](https://github.com/s8lap/bezel-lang/issues/3110)), nor a result/element type that is such a record, inline array or choice; for a generic async method the check is re-applied after substitution, so an instantiation whose type argument makes a parameter borrow-carrying is rejected at the instantiation site. The reason is structural: an ordinary borrow is bounded by the synchronous call frame that receives it and is unwound at return ([§28.3](#sec-local-variables-ownership-and-borrows), [§8.6](#sec-boxing)), but an async method captures its parameters into a heap-allocated state-machine frame that outlives the synchronous call and lives until the task settles — a moment the caller does not lexically bound, since the task is an ordinary heap value that may be stored, moved, awaited elsewhere, or fire-and-forgotten ([§30.10](#sec-standard-library-task-helpers)). A borrow captured into that frame from a caller-side source therefore has no stack frame whose unwinding bounds it, and [§28.3](#sec-local-variables-ownership-and-borrows)'s frame-local borrow-lifetime rules cannot establish that the source outlives the frame. The **one exception** is a borrow-bearing record the standard library certifies with a normatively-stated source-outlives-task obligation backstopped by checked disposal mode ([§28.2](#sec-the-idisposable-contract)): currently only `CancellationToken` ([§30.8](#sec-cancellation); axiom [A10](#sec-axiom-register)), whose borrowed source is a disposal-tracked `CancellationTokenSource` and whose default argument is the null-source sentinel `CancellationToken.None` ([§9.7](#sec-records-and-disposal)) — the [K4.3](#sec-kernel-k4) residual-trust shape, on the same stdlib-certified footing as [§30.11](#sec-taskcompletionsourcet-and-ownedtaskcompletionsourcet). Records whose only borrows are of **declared** runtime-managed types (`string`-backed spans such as `ReadOnlyStringSpan`, function types) are not borrow-bearing ([§9.7](#sec-records-and-disposal)) and are unaffected — no declared field type is a boxed value type, that being a category of runtime *value* ([§28.9](#sec-runtime-managed-types), [§8.6](#sec-boxing)). Where a buffer must cross an `await`, pass a heap-owned window — an `Array<T>` with explicit `offset`/`count`, or an owned result type. This rule keys on the **`async` modifier**, which is what makes a declaration's frame this section's business; a standard-library position whose declared signature carries none — `async` being implementation-side and invisible in signatures ([§28.12](#sec-asynchronous-disposal)) — but whose implementation nevertheless holds its parameter in a frame until settlement is outside the rule's scope and states its own retention and obligation where it is declared. There is exactly one such position: `AsyncEventSource<T>.RaiseAsync` (stdlib [§6.5](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-events-ievent-eventsource)), whose `T` this section therefore does not restrict.

**`ref` and `out` parameters are forbidden (derives: [K2.1](#sec-kernel-k2) + [K6.1](#sec-kernel-k6)).** An `async` method, `async` lambda, or iterator method — synchronous or async ([§29.3](#sec-iterator-methods)) — may not declare a `ref` or `out` parameter; a compile error at the declaration. The grammar admits the modifiers through the shared `Param` production and the rejection is semantic — the same over-admit-and-reject pattern as [§22.10](#sec-methods-and-constructors-primary-constructors)'s primary constructors and [§23.4](#sec-indexers)'s indexer parameter lists. The reason is the same structural one as the borrow-bearing rule above: a `ref`/`out` argument is a reference to a caller stack slot, bounded by the synchronous call — but these bodies capture their parameters into a heap-allocated state-machine frame that outlives the synchronous call, so the captured slot reference dangles the moment the method returns its task or enumerable at the first suspension; and [§22.3](#sec-parameter-modifiers)'s `out` contract ("must assign every `out` parameter on every exit path") has no coherent exit for a body whose synchronous exit *is* that early return. The rule extends to conversions: an `async` lambda may not be assigned to a function type ([§27.1](#sec-function-types)) whose parameter list carries a `ref`/`out` slot. Non-`async` methods that merely *return* `Task`-family types are unaffected (a user-written such body has no state machine — the out-contract completes synchronously; the standard-library exception noted above is a `Task`-returning *payload* position, not a `ref`/`out` one, so it does not qualify this sentence), as are `owned` parameters ([§29.8](#sec-iterators-with-owned-parameters), above); other parameter modifiers' admissibility is governed by their own sections ([§28.14](#sec-scoped-callback-parameters) for `scoped`). (The alternative — requiring every `out` assigned before the first suspension point — was considered and declined: it is coherent for `out` only and unsound for `ref` (the callee can *read* the dead slot after resumption, not just write it), fragile (inserting an `await` above the assignment breaks callers), and has no known use case; C# rejects both, for both method kinds.)

**Borrow-bearing record locals across suspension (derives: [K2.1](#sec-kernel-k2) + [K6.1](#sec-kernel-k6) — frame-resident sources).** A local of borrow-bearing record or borrow-bearing inline-array type — or of a choice type that holds borrows ([§35.4](#sec-choice-classification)'s holds-borrows property, whatever the choice's classification) — whose live range crosses a suspension point (`await`, `await using`, `await for`, or — in an async iterator — `yield return`, which suspends the frame while the consumer runs arbitrary code between `MoveNextAsync` calls, [§29.3](#sec-iterator-methods), [§30.7](#sec-asynchronous-programming-async-iterators)) is captured into the state-machine frame together with the borrows it carries. It is admitted across the suspension **iff every borrow it carries has a frame-resident source**: an owned local, a `using var`/`await using var`, or an `owned` parameter of the same async body — locations the frame itself owns (below), which therefore provably survive every suspension. A borrow whose source is caller-side — a plain parameter, `this`, a field reached through `this`, or a capture from an enclosing scope — does not qualify: the source's owner may dispose it while the frame is suspended, and, as with the parameter rule above, a raw span window has no disposal-tracked object through which checked mode could catch the dangle. The program is rejected at the suspension point, naming the local, the non-resident source, and the remedy: re-derive the record after the `await`, or copy the borrowed data into frame-owned storage before it. Values of a stdlib-certified borrow-bearing record (currently only `CancellationToken`) are exempt however obtained — they carry the certified source-outlives-settlement obligation of [§30.8](#sec-cancellation) instead. (A **synchronous** iterator's `yield return` is subject to the same rule — its heap frame has the same shape; see [§29.4](#sec-lazy-evaluation).)

**`owned` parameters transfer into the frame (derives: [K3](#sec-kernel-k3) with the frame as scope).** An async method's `owned` parameters transfer into the state-machine frame at call time, exactly as an iterator's do ([§29.8](#sec-iterators-with-owned-parameters)). The body may move them out under the ordinary rules — chaining one with `return await <param>` moves it into the outer task's chained slot ([§30.5](#sec-result-lifetime-and-task-disposal)) and counts as such a move-out, so the outer task's teardown, not this rule, disposes it; any `owned` parameter never moved out is disposed by the frame when the task reaches its terminal state — on every completion path (success, fault, and cancellation), after the body's `using var` cleanups and `finally` clauses, in reverse declaration order ([§28.4](#sec-the-destructor)'s ordering). Parameters of move-only value type ([§15.3](#sec-move-only-value-types)) carrying no borrows ride the same machinery — an owning choice that holds borrows is rejected by the borrow-bearing rule above ([§35.4](#sec-choice-classification)'s holds-borrows property), never reaching this one. An `owned` parameter never discharged by the body carries the [§28.3](#sec-owned-local-discharge-requirement) must-use warning at its declaration; `using var c := move conn;` on entry is the warning-free way to declare frame-lifetime intent. Disposing a not-yet-settled task does not cut this short: the underlying operation runs to its terminal state ([§30.5](#sec-result-lifetime-and-task-disposal)), and the frame's parameters are disposed then.

**Borrowed parameters, `this`, and captures are held until settlement (derives: [K6.4](#sec-kernel-k6) + [K4.3](#sec-kernel-k4)).** An async method's plain (non-`owned`) parameters of class or interface type ([§28.3](#sec-local-variables-ownership-and-borrows)'s borrow vocabulary), its `this` receiver, and an `async` lambda's captures are borrows captured into the state-machine frame, as is the capture-set contribution of a call's plain function-typed arguments ([§28.3](#sec-unbound-owned-temporaries)) — all held not for the duration of the synchronous call but until the task **settles**. The call-site admission is unchanged (any borrow admissible as an argument remains admissible, [§28.3](#sec-local-variables-ownership-and-borrows), with the statically-certain exceptions of [§28.3](#sec-unbound-owned-temporaries)'s deferred-activation rules: an unbound owned temporary may not source a borrow into a frame — iterator or task — that escapes the full expression, and a callback argument's capture-set contribution is rejected by the ordinary scope, store, and frame-return rules where the frame provably escapes a contributed source's lifetime); what the frame adds is a temporal obligation on the **caller**: *every borrow source reaching an async call must outlive the settlement of the returned task, and the borrowed object must not be transferred to another domain — nor consumed into a domain-reachable construction ([§28.3](#sec-local-variables-ownership-and-borrows)'s domain-clause extension) — before that settlement.* The domain clause ([§28.3](#sec-borrow-lifetime-rules)'s field-store bullet, clause 4) is stated here because a frame-held borrow is invisible to the consume-site freeze ([§28.3](#sec-consume-site-freeze) — it lives in the state machine, in no local borrow binding); as everywhere, its violation has no runtime backstop. The obligation is a [K4.3](#sec-kernel-k4)-recorded trust clause: the structural checks are decidable, the temporal guarantee is the programmer's, with [K4.1](#sec-kernel-k4)'s backstop as the named safety net — a violation is a deterministic `DisposedAccessException` in checked disposal mode ([§28.2](#sec-the-idisposable-contract)) and undefined behavior in unchecked mode. The obligation is discharged trivially by the dominant shape — awaiting the task before any source's scope exits — and structurally by `TaskScope` ([§30.10](#sec-standard-library-task-helpers); stdlib [§6.10](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-taskscope)), whose disposal quiesces its children before the enclosing scope unwinds. The shapes that carry a live residual are the abandonment idioms — `using var t := call();` dropped without an await, and `Task.FireAndForget(call())` — where an argument's or the receiver's owner can dispose it while the frame is suspended ([§30.10](#sec-standard-library-task-helpers) names the hazard). Abandon only tasks whose inputs are owned (transferred in), sendable-copied, `string`/value-typed, or otherwise guaranteed to outlive the operation; supervise everything else to settlement.

An async method's `return expression;` completes the task with the value. `return;` (in `Task`-returning forms) completes the task with no value. Falling off the end of a `Task`-returning async method is equivalent to `return;`. A `Task<T>`-returning async method must `return` a value on every path.

<a id="sec-await"></a>
### 30.2 `await`

`await` suspends the current async method until a task completes:

```bezel
var result := await someTask;
```

The shape above is the simple case — appropriate when `someTask` returns a value type, `string`, or `Task` (no value). When the task's result type is a class, one of the patterns in [§30.5](#sec-result-lifetime-and-task-disposal) applies; the bare assignment shown here is rejected.

Behavior:

- If the task is already completed, `await` returns the result synchronously.
- If the task is faulted, `await` re-raises the exception.
- If the task was cancelled, `await` raises `OperationCanceledException`.
- If the task is running, the async method suspends; when the task completes, the continuation is queued to its domain ([§30.13](#sec-runtime-model)).

`await` is valid only inside an `async` method or `async` lambda.

<a id="sec-the-task-and-taskt-types"></a>
<a id="sec-the-task-taskt-and-ownedtaskt-types"></a>
### 30.3 The `Task`, `Task<T>`, and `OwningTask<T>` types

```bezel
public class Task
  public readonly property IsCompleted: bool;
  public readonly property IsFaulted: bool;
  public readonly property IsCancelled: bool;

  public method Wait();

  destructor;       // runs continuation cleanup and disposes any
                    //   unconsumed `owned` result. Disposing a task
                    //   abandons a running operation, which is why
                    //   `_ := someAsyncCall();` is rejected
                    //   ([§17.13](#sec-the-discard-_), A6).
end Task;

public class Task<T>: Task
  public readonly property Result: T;
end Task;

public class OwningTask<T>: Task where T: class
  // Owning task: result transfers ownership to the awaiter (Pattern B).
  // Single-consumer by type.
  public readonly property Result: T;
                    // reading Result on a COMPLETED OwningTask
                    // in an owned-consuming position transfers ownership
                    // exactly like `await` (the result buffer is consumed;
                    // a second read/await raises InvalidOperationException).
                    // Subject to the same §30.3 blocking rules as Task<T>.Result:
                    // legal on an incomplete task only outside domains.
end OwningTask;
```

`Wait()` and `Result` are synchronous escape hatches for **code running outside any domain** — in practice, the synchronous portion of program startup: a non-`async` `Main`, and code it calls directly on the main thread. There, they block the calling thread until the task completes; the pool's workers drain the task's domain concurrently, so completion makes progress (this is the same mechanism by which the runtime itself drives an `async Main`, [§33.2](#sec-accepted-signatures)).

**Inside a domain continuation — equivalently, anywhere `await` is available or the caller was reached from one — a blocking wait on an incomplete task is an error.** A domain executes its continuations serially to completion ([§30.13](#sec-runtime-model)); a continuation blocked in `Wait()`/`Result` freezes its domain, and any awaited chain whose completion routes through that domain can never finish: a deterministic deadlock, not a hazard. The compiler rejects `Wait()` and `Result` lexically inside `async` methods and `async` lambdas (there, `await` is strictly superior and always available). Where static rejection cannot see the call (a non-`async` helper invoked from a continuation), the runtime raises `InvalidOperationException` at the call site instead of parking: *"blocking wait inside a domain continuation; the domain can never advance — await the task, or query IsCompleted."* Reading `Result` on a **completed** task is always legal and non-blocking: on a faulted task it re-raises the exception; on a cancelled task it raises `OperationCanceledException`.

Reading `Result` on a completed `Task<T>` whose `T` is a **class** type (Pattern A) is additionally subject to the same owning-source rule as `await` ([§30.5](#sec-result-lifetime-and-task-disposal) consumer-side rules; unified with [§28.3](#sec-unbound-owned-temporaries)'s temporary machinery in): the read produces a **borrow whose source is the task expression's location** — a named owning position bounds the borrow by that location's lifetime, and an unbound owned temporary (`SomeProducer().Result`) is admitted when the borrow is confined to the same full expression, the temporary being disposed at the expression's end exactly as for the corresponding `await`. A form whose borrow escapes a temporary read's full expression remains a compile error, exactly as the corresponding `await` is — and the one desugared exception holds in lockstep too: a fresh `var`/`const` declaration whose initializer is exactly such a completed-task `.Result` read is the scoped await-bind ([§30.5](#sec-the-scoped-await-bind)), binding the producer to the same hidden scope-pinned slot.

`OwningTask<T>` exposes `Result`: reading it on a **completed** task in an owned-consuming position transfers ownership of the result to the reader exactly as `await` does — the result buffer is consumed, and a second read or `await` raises `InvalidOperationException`. The same blocking-wait rules as `Task<T>.Result` apply (legal on an incomplete task only outside a domain). Awaiting an `OwningTask<T>` in an owned-consuming position remains the normal way to obtain the result (see [§30.5](#sec-result-lifetime-and-task-disposal) Pattern B).

`Task`, `Task<T>`, and `OwningTask<T>` are classes — they require disposal, with the patterns described in [§30.5](#sec-result-lifetime-and-task-disposal). Listing `IDisposable` explicitly in the inheritance clause would be redundant since every class implicitly implements it ([§28.2](#sec-the-idisposable-contract)). The `destructor;` form above follows the standard library documentation-shorthand convention (stdlib [§1](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-conventions)); the actual destructor body is provided by the runtime and runs the continuation-cleanup logic described in [§30.10](#sec-standard-library-task-helpers) (the `FireAndForget` and `using var`-disposal-without-await cases).

<a id="sec-multiple-awaiters"></a>
### 30.4 Multiple awaiters

A `Task` or `Task<T>` may be awaited from multiple places, sequentially or concurrently. Every awaiter sees the same eventual state. The underlying computation runs once. Continuations resume in unspecified order, but never concurrently with one another within a domain ([§30.13](#sec-runtime-model)).

<a id="sec-multiple-awaits-on-ownedtaskt"></a>
`OwningTask<T>` is single-consumer by type — the Pattern B container of [§30.5](#sec-result-lifetime-and-task-disposal) (derives: [K2](#sec-kernel-k2) fan-out vs. [K1.7](#sec-kernel-k1) — one obligation moves once; `InvalidOperationException` is its dynamic dual): **the first await spends the task regardless of outcome** (success, fault, or cancellation), and a second await raises `InvalidOperationException`, even after a successful first await — the result has already been moved out. (The "awaiting a faulted task re-raises" rule of [§30.9](#sec-exception-handling-in-async-methods) applies to `Task`/`Task<T>` and to the *first* await of an `OwningTask<T>` only.) Sharing an `OwningTask<T>` across multiple potential awaiters is not the intended pattern. For fan-out with a class-typed result, use `Task<T>` (Pattern A); for single-consumer ownership-transferring resource production, use `OwningTask<T>` (Pattern B).

<a id="sec-result-lifetime-and-task-disposal"></a>
### 30.5 Result lifetime and task disposal

The task owns any class-typed result it produces; the task *itself* is owned by the caller of the call that produced it ([§28.3](#sec-producers)'s `Task`-family production rule — the patterns below govern the *result*; the container obligation is the caller's from the call site on). The pattern by which a result is consumed is selected by the producer's return type — there is no syntactic peeking at `await`'s context.

<a id="sec-producer-side-return-type-rules"></a>
#### Producer-side return-type rules

(axiom [A3](#sec-axiom-register) — the two-container design: `Task<T>` for class T carries shared borrows, `OwningTask<T>` a single owned transfer; the kernel checks both patterns' flows, forces neither.)

- `Task` and `Task<T>` for **copyable** value type ([§15.3](#sec-move-only-value-types)), `string`, or runtime-managed T: produced as today; no ownership obligation crosses the await boundary.
- `Task<T>` for **class** T: the task may be awaited from multiple places. Every awaiter receives a borrow of the same underlying result. The result's lifetime is tied to the task — disposing the task disposes the result. This is **Pattern A**.

  **Pattern A result slots are of three kinds (scope-bound chaining; borrowed-source chains).** What the outer task's result slot records — and what its teardown disposes — is determined by what the async body produced:

  1. **A fresh owned value** (a `return` of an owned expression): the task **owns the result** and its destructor disposes it directly (derives: [K1](#sec-kernel-k1)).

  2. **`return await` over an owned Pattern A source — the chained slot** (derives: [K2](#sec-kernel-k2) + [K6](#sec-kernel-k6) — the task cannot own what it borrowed, so the container moves into a chained slot; exactly-once transitively). The result is a *borrow through the source task*: ownership of the **source task** transfers into the outer task's state (a **chained** slot), and the outer destructor disposes the chained source task, never the borrowed result directly. "Disposing the task disposes the result" thereby holds *transitively*, and every Pattern A borrow has a defined owner at every link of the chain. **Chaining from a scope-bound source.** When the source of `return await <source>` is an `owned` parameter of the enclosing async method, the transfer into the chained slot is an ordinary [§28.3](#sec-local-variables-ownership-and-borrows) **move-out** of the parameter: it is thereby moved out, so [§30.1](#sec-async-methods)'s dispose-at-terminal-state rule for not-moved-out `owned` parameters does not apply to it — the outer task's teardown disposes the chained task instead. When the source is a `using var`/`await using var` local — which [§28.3](#sec-local-variables-ownership-and-borrows) forbids moving — no move occurs: the source's slot already lives in the enclosing state-machine frame, and the chained-slot arrangement **defers its disposal** from the frame's scope end to the outer task's teardown; a disposal-*timing* dispensation of the same kind as the await-consumes-operand rule below, not an exception to the `using var` no-move rule (axiom [A12](#sec-axiom-register)). On both paths the source task is disposed exactly once — by the outer task's destructor, transitively.

  3. **`return await` over a borrowed source** (derives: [K2](#sec-kernel-k2) + [K4.3](#sec-kernel-k4) — no transfer possible; teardown disposes nothing; the residual discharges trivially for process-lived statics)**.** When the source is a **borrow** — an admitted static task field or property ([§22.13](#sec-static-initialization-order)(b)'s cache is the canonical case), an `owned` field of `this` read without `move`, an owning-collection slot, a borrowing-iteration variable, or any other admitted borrowed operand — no ownership transfers: the outer task's result slot records a **borrow through the source task**, and the outer task's teardown disposes **nothing** on that link. Transfer is impossible for a borrowed source and would be unsound (a static cache disposed at some caller's teardown while every other caller still awaits it; an owned field moved without `move`); the borrowed-source chain is the only coherent third kind.

  Soundness of the borrowed-source chain (kind 3) rides on the source outliving the outer task's result uses — a caller-side residual of [K4.3](#sec-kernel-k4)'s recorded family, backstopped per [K4.1](#sec-kernel-k4) (the task and its result are disposal-tracked, so a violated bound faults as `DisposedAccessException`, [§28.2](#sec-checked-disposal)) — and it is discharged **trivially for process-lived static storage**: an admitted static task field lives for the duration of the program and is never disposed before exit ([§22.13](#sec-static-initialization-order)), and even overwriting the mutable cache never disposes the displaced referent (same section), so a chained borrow of it cannot dangle. The chained move-out of an **owned** source (an `owned` parameter or a plain owned local — kind 2 above; a `using var` source is not moved, only disposal-deferred) is keyword-visible in the Pattern A `return await` form itself and joins no consume-site freeze list — unfrozen under [K5](#sec-kernel-k5)'s criterion ([K5.4](#sec-kernel-k5)): (i) holds at the form, and (ii) holds because its new owner is the outer task, which cannot dispose the chained task before this body — including its `finally` blocks — completes, so every borrow that survives the kill finds its referent intact and disposal-tracked ([§28.3](#sec-consume-site-freeze)).
- `OwningTask<T>` for **class** T: the task produces a single owned result. Awaiting transfers ownership to the awaiter. The task may be awaited at most once for a successful (non-faulted, non-cancelled) result. This is **Pattern B**.
- `OwningTask<T>` for **copyable** value type, `string`, or runtime-managed T: a compile error. `owned` on such a result is meaningless.
- A **move-only value T** ([§15.3](#sec-move-only-value-types) — an owning-classified choice instantiation ([§35.4](#sec-choice-classification) rule 1) or an owning inline array ([§15.1.1](#sec-owning-inline-arrays))) is admitted by **no row**: declaring `Task<T>` or `OwningTask<T>` over such a T is a **compile error at the declaration** — [§30.4](#sec-multiple-awaiters)'s multi-award rule would hand the same must-move-exactly-once value to every awaiter, and `OwningTask<T>` admits class T only. For a generic declaration whose result classification depends on a type parameter (`Task<Result<T, E>>`), the check is re-applied after substitution — an instantiation whose type arguments make the result move-only is rejected at the instantiation site, as for the borrow-bearing rejection ([§30.1](#sec-async-methods)) and per [§35.11](#sec-choice-generics)'s instantiation-site enforcement.

`OwningTask<T>` is the right choice for resource acquisition — operations whose entire purpose is to produce a fresh, single-consumer resource (a connection, a lock token, a parsed document). `Task<T>` is the right choice for fan-out: multiple subscribers reading the same eventual result.

<a id="sec-consumer-side-rules"></a>
#### Consumer-side rules

For `await someTask`, the consumer's obligations are determined by the task's static return type:

**Copyable value type, `string`, or runtime-managed result:** any form is permitted. The result is a value or shared-immutable reference.

```bezel
var n := await CountBytesAsync(url);     // result is int
var s := await FetchStringAsync(url);    // result is string
```

For these forms, the awaited task expression may be a bare producer call (as above); the await operator is **owned-consuming with respect to its operand** when the operand is an **unbound owned temporary** ([§28.3](#sec-unbound-owned-temporaries)) — a bare producer call or other unnamed owned task expression. The implicit task-disposal performed by the runtime as part of the await satisfies the discharge requirement on the temporary — the user does not write a separate `using var` for the task. A **named** operand — a `using var` or plain owned local, an `owned` parameter, an `owned` field — is **borrow-awaited**: the await neither consumes nor disposes it, multiple awaits are permitted per [§30.4](#sec-multiple-awaiters), and an owned local operand keeps its ordinary [§28.3](#sec-local-variables-ownership-and-borrows) discharge (auto-drop at scope end). Named-operand consumption is the **Pattern B (`OwningTask<T>`) rule only** (below); it does not apply to `Task`/`Task<T>`.

**`Task<T>` for class T (Pattern A)** (derives: [K2](#sec-kernel-k2) — the admission is [§28.3](#sec-local-variables-ownership-and-borrows)'s ordinary borrow machinery applied to the awaited operand)**:** the borrow produced by the await must have a source whose lifetime the compiler can bound, and that source is the awaited task expression's **own location** — the operand kinds are [K2](#sec-kernel-k2)'s. A *reference to* a **named location** whose lifetime is visible at the await site bounds the borrow by that location's scope ([K2.1](#sec-kernel-k2)); for a plain borrowed operand, the binding's own borrow chain carries the true-task-outlives-the-use residual ([K2.2](#sec-kernel-k2) + [K4.3](#sec-kernel-k4)), and a borrowed alias of an admitted operand inherits the admission. The everyday helper — `public async method Report(t: Task<Data>): Task` awaiting its plain parameter — is admitted on exactly this ground: the caller's own obligations ([§30.1](#sec-async-methods)'s settlement, [§30.4](#sec-multiple-awaiters)'s fan-out) keep the underlying task alive around the callee's use, and ownership of the location was never the admission's real criterion (the field-path and static-storage positions are themselves borrow reads). An **unbound owned temporary** ([§28.3](#sec-unbound-owned-temporaries)) — a bare producer call or other unnamed owned task expression — bounds the borrow by its [K8](#sec-kernel-k8) full-expression boundary, *provided the borrowed result is used only within that expression*: the temporary is then disposed at the expression's end, after every use of the borrow, and disposing the task disposes the borrowed result with it. A producer call whose result is directly consumed by a Pattern A return in the enclosing async method is the **chained slot** (kind 2 above; [K6](#sec-kernel-k6)) — a task *move*, not a borrow escape. A borrow that would **escape** the full expression of an unbound-temporary await — a store, a non-chained return, a binding other than the scoped await-bind's — has no source that survives the expression, and the await is a compile error ([K8.4](#sec-kernel-k8): rejected, never lifetime-extended); bind the task to a `using var` first. The one admitted escape shape is a **desugaring, not an extension**: a fresh `var`/`const` declaration whose initializer is exactly such an await is the **scoped await-bind** ([below](#sec-the-scoped-await-bind)) — the compiler binds the producer to a hidden `using var` slot at the same line, so the operand is a named location and no unbound temporary remains.

The admitted positions are [K2](#sec-kernel-k2)'s source kinds, and the closure is K2's named-location taxonomy — this paragraph, not any list, is the rule: a task-typed storage read through any field path rooted at a live object — or of admitted static task storage ([§22.12](#sec-static-members) rule 2(ii)'s lazy cache, read as `_cfg!`, or a `static readonly` task field: [K2](#sec-kernel-k2)'s always-live source, so the borrow is valid everywhere) — and a borrowed alias of any admitted operand, are admitted with the source set the path derives, a plain task-typed **borrow** field's held chain joining the derived set ([K2.2](#sec-kernel-k2)); the frame case is the chained slot the principle paragraph above already states. Worked instances (an illustration, not a closed set):

- **A reference to a `using var` or `await using var`-bound local** of static type `Task<T>`. The canonical form. The await produces a borrow whose source is the local; the borrow is valid within the local's scope.
- **A reference to an `owned` parameter** of the enclosing method, of static type `Task<T>`. The parameter's lifetime spans the method body; the borrow is valid within the body.
- **An indexer access on an owning collection** whose static type is `OwningArray<Task<T>>` (or analogous), where the collection itself occupies an owning location. The await produces a borrow whose source is the collection; the borrow is valid within the collection's lifetime. The same applies to dictionary indexer access into `OwningDictionary<K, Task<T>>`.
- **An iteration variable** in `for var task in tasks do ... end` where `tasks` is `Array<Task<T>>` or `OwningArray<Task<T>>` (borrowing iteration, not Drain). Each `task` is a borrow whose source is `tasks`; the await within the loop body produces a borrow valid for the loop body.

Two notes ride particular instances rather than the admission itself. A **plain owned local** operand is a named location like any other — consuming or reassigning the binding while the borrow lives is rejected by the consume-site freeze ([§28.3](#sec-consume-site-freeze)), an explicit `Dispose()` remains the site-announced kill with the checked-mode backstop, and `using var` stays the canonical form (the pin makes the bound obvious). And at an **admitted static task field**, the class-typed result reached through the chain is process-shared across every domain that awaits the cached task; [§22.12](#sec-static-members) rule 4's confine-or-synchronize obligation applies to it unchanged.

`Process(await Producer())` is therefore **admitted**: the producer's task is an unbound owned temporary, its borrowed result is consumed by `Process` within the same full expression, and the task — and with it the result — is disposed at the end of the statement ([§28.3](#sec-unbound-owned-temporaries)); the disposal runs after the borrowing use, so the result is live for the call, exactly as in the `Folded(src).Sorted()` example there. What the principle rejects is a borrow that **outlives** an unbound temporary. For one such shape the compiler writes the remedy itself: `var x := await Producer();` — a fresh local `var`/`const` declaration whose initializer is exactly the await — is the **scoped await-bind** ([below](#sec-the-scoped-await-bind)), desugared to a hidden pinned slot so the task is bound, not temporary. Every other escaping shape — a `using var` bind, an assignment to an existing local, a composition binding a class-typed member, a store, a non-chained return — remains rejected: the borrow would survive the expression while the task that sources it dies with it. There the fix is still to bind the producer's result to a `using var` first:

```bezel
using var task := Producer();
Process(await task);
```

The borrow produced by `await task` (where `task` occupies one of the admitted positions) may flow to:

- A `var` binding: `var r := await task;` — `r` is a non-owned local with the same source as `task`.
- A non-owned argument: `Process(await task);`.
- A `return` expression whose return type accepts a borrow with the same source (e.g., `return await task;` from an async method returning Pattern A `Task<T>`).

The borrow may **not** flow to (derives: [K1](#sec-kernel-k1) state-match — a borrow cannot assume an obligation — for the owning readings; the `using var` bullet's pin reading additionally rests on the task-bounded result lifetime above):

- A `using var` binding: `using var r := await task;` is rejected — a **position-specific rule about the await result**, not a general requirement that `using var` take an owned right-hand side (elsewhere a borrow right-hand side is admitted as a **borrow-pin** with no disposal obligation: [§28.3](#sec-local-variables-ownership-and-borrows)'s binding rules, [§28.10](#sec-using-var-initialized-from-a-borrow)'s pin case — [#3085](https://github.com/s8lap/bezel-lang/issues/3085)). For the await result specifically, this list's own ground decides both readings: the owning reading founders on the K1 state-match above — a borrow cannot assume the disposal obligation the spelling would announce — and the pin reading announces a scope the result cannot carry independently, its lifetime being the task's own ("disposing the task disposes the result", above), so the location worth pinning is the task's: `using var task := Producer(); var r := await task;`.
- An assignment to an `owned` field or owned-element collection slot — would manufacture ownership the source did not grant.
- An `owned` parameter argument.
- A `return` expression whose return type is `owned T` or carries ownership.

```bezel
using var task := FetchAsync(url);
var response := await task;              // borrowed reference, OK
ProcessResponse(response);
// At end of scope: task is disposed; response disposed with it.
```

For an operand in no admitted position the await remains a compile error, and the message identifies it and references the principle above.

<a id="sec-the-scoped-await-bind"></a>
**The scoped await-bind** (derives: [K2.1](#sec-kernel-k2) + [§28.10](#sec-using-var)'s cleanup stack — the admission is a desugaring into today's language, not a new borrow rule)**:** in a local declaration `var x := await E;` or `const x := await E;` whose initializer full expression is **exactly** the await, where `E` is an expression [§28.3](#sec-unbound-owned-temporaries) would otherwise classify as an **unbound owned temporary of static type `Task<T>` for class T** (a bare producer call or any other unnamed owned task expression), no unbound temporary arises at all: the compiler binds it to a **hidden scope-pinned slot** — established on the [§28.10](#sec-using-var) establishment-ordered cleanup stack at the declaration statement, disposed at the end of the **innermost enclosing block** on every exit edge, exactly as a hand-written `using var` at the same line would be — and `x` is an ordinary **borrowed** local whose source is that slot. The slot is unnameable: no program text can read, move, re-await, or dispose it. The desugaring is literal:

```bezel
var cfg := await FetchAsync(url);        // the scoped bind…

using var task2 := FetchAsync(url);      // …desugars to exactly this pair,
var cfg2 := await task2;                 //    the slot fresh and inexpressible
```

Disposal timing, exception behavior, and borrow bounds are **identical to the hand-written form** — the rule adds no lifetime the programmer could not have written, only removes the demand that they write it.

**Which producer expressions qualify** — exactly [§28.3](#sec-unbound-owned-temporaries)'s unbound-owned-temporary classification at static type `Task<T>` (class T), a classification the compiler already computes at every await site; the rule introduces no new enumeration, only re-points an existing one:

- **A direct producer call** — bare, instance, interface-dispatched, or through a function value — qualifies: calls mint ([§28.3](#sec-producers)), and the result is a fresh unbound owned task.
- **A conditional producer** — `var x := await (if useAlt then FetchAltAsync() else FetchAsync(url));` — qualifies: the arm-meet of two mints is owned ([K7.1](#sec-kernel-k7)), and the whole parenthesized form is one unbound owned temporary. The qualification test is the classification, not the syntax.
- **A producer call carrying an unbound owned temporary source** — `var x := await SumAsync(Nums(3));` — does **not** qualify: the desugared slot's frame escapes the temporary's boundary ([§28.3](#sec-unbound-owned-temporaries) *Deferred-activation callees*, [K6.1](#sec-kernel-k6) + [K6.5](#sec-kernel-k6)), exactly as the hand-written `using var t := SumAsync(Nums(3));` is rejected. Bind the argument first.
- **A named operand** — `await t` for any admitted named position above — does **not** engage the rule: those binds are already governed by the admitted positions. The rule fires only at declarations no other rule admits; no otherwise-accepted program changes meaning or timing.
- **A composition** — `var y := (await E).Name;` binding a class-typed member, `var z := await E ?? fallback;` — does **not** qualify: the initializer must be exactly the await. (A `string`/value member read through `(await E).Name` already compiles under expression confinement.)

**Which binding forms qualify:** `var` and `const` alike — a runtime `const` binds values and borrows that carry no obligation ([§21.1](#sec-variable-declarations)), which the await's borrow is; the `const` adds non-reassignability of `x` only. (A [§17.15](#sec-the-binding-atom) binding-atom clause is not a local declaration and does not engage the rule; [K8.5](#sec-kernel-k8)'s atom boundary governs it verbatim.) The near-miss forms stay rejected, and their diagnostics must teach: each message names the rejecting rule and the admitted spelling (recommended wordings: the code-generation reference, [§4.6](Bezel_For_Code_Generation.md#sec-recommended-diagnostic-wordings)):

- `using var x := await FetchAsync(url);` — rejected, as above (the await produces a borrow, which the may-not-flow list above bars from a `using var` binding). The message names the may-not-flow list and offers `var x := await …;` (the compiler pins the task) or the explicit two-line form.
- `x := await FetchAsync(url);` (assignment to an existing local) — rejected: the existing binding's scope may strictly enclose this statement's block, and honoring it would hoist the hidden slot beyond the two-liner the desugaring writes. The message names the scoped await-bind's fresh-declaration condition and offers the two-line form, `using var task := …; x := await task;`.
- `return await FetchAsync(url);`, field stores, `owned` arguments — untouched: the chained-slot rule (kind 2 above) and the may-not-flow list govern as today.

**The slot's semantics, worked.** Its position on the cleanup stack is the declaration's: a `using var` declared *after* the bind disposes *before* the slot, one declared *before* disposes after — identical to the two-line form. On an early `return`, the slot's disposal runs during that return's scope exit, after `x`'s last use. If `E`'s production or the await faults, the already-produced task is disposed during unwinding by the same establishment-ordered pass that covers a hand-written `using var` ([K3.15](#sec-kernel-k3) edge parity), and the binding never comes into being; a later statement's throw unwinds the slot in stack order. Two scoped binds in one scope create two slots, disposed in reverse order at scope end. A bind inside a loop body pins to the loop *body*: per-iteration disposal, no accumulation across iterations. **No second await is expressible** — the slot is unnameable and the single await already ran, so [§30.4](#sec-multiple-awaiters)'s multi-await surface never opens (name the task with the two-line form to award twice); the slot holds a **settled** task, so [§30.1](#sec-async-methods)'s source-outlives-settlement obligation is discharged before any code can observe the slot. The consume-site freeze has **no surface**: no user-visible binding exists to consume, reassign, or dispose ([K5](#sec-kernel-k5) has nothing to guard); reassigning `x` itself merely ends its interest — the slot's disposal stays at scope end, as re-purposing `cfg` in the two-line form never moves `task`'s disposal either. `x` is an ordinary borrow: every [§28.3](#sec-local-variables-ownership-and-borrows) borrow rule applies to it unchanged (returns, stores, captures past the scope: rejected by the ordinary machinery — the slot is a scope-bound source). The checked-mode backstop is unchanged: task and result remain disposal-tracked, and any path the static rules cannot see faults as `DisposedAccessException` ([§28.2](#sec-checked-disposal)).

**`.Result` in lockstep.** The admission applies identically to the completed-task `.Result` read, as [§30.3](#sec-the-task-taskt-and-ownedtaskt-types) states: `var x := P().Result;` (legal outside domains) desugars to the same hidden slot.

**Error participation:** wherever the hidden slot participates in a later diagnostic, the message names it — e.g. *"the result borrowed by `cfg` is owned by the awaited task pinned at line N, disposed at the end of that block."* An informational surface at the admitted bind itself (inlay hints and the like) remains non-normative tooling.

**`OwningTask<T>` for class T (Pattern B)** (derives: [K1](#sec-kernel-k1) + [K3](#sec-kernel-k3) — the await mints an owned result, which must reach a discharging position)**:** the await must appear in an **owned-consuming context** — the consume table's positions ([§28.3](#sec-consume-table)), not re-listed here. The Pattern-B-specific instances: the announcing `return` type may be one that *wraps* `owned T` (such as `OwningTask<T>`); the owned binding forms are `using var x := await ...` (the canonical form; `await using var x := await ...` for an asynchronously-disposable result) and `var x := await ...`, which introduces an owned local of class type T under [§28.3](#sec-local-variables-ownership-and-borrows)'s standard discharge rules from the binding point forward; and the discard statement `_ := await ...;` ([§17.13](#sec-the-discard-_), [K3.9](#sec-kernel-k3)) disposes the awaited result at the end of the statement as an unbound owned temporary ([§28.3](#sec-unbound-owned-temporaries)): the end-of-statement counterpart of `using var _ := await ...;`.

The task is disposed implicitly without disposing its result; it cannot be awaited again, and a second await raises `InvalidOperationException`.

The await operator on a `OwningTask<T>` for class T is itself **owned-consuming with respect to its operand** (derives: [K3.5](#sec-kernel-k3) + [K4.2](#sec-kernel-k4)): when the awaited expression is an owned task value (a plain owned local of `OwningTask<T>` — not a `using var` binding: a `using var` cannot be moved out of ([§28.3](#sec-local-variables-ownership-and-borrows)), so a read of it is a borrow and such an await is the borrowed-operand case below — an iteration variable from draining an `OwningArray<OwningTask<T>>`, an `owned` parameter, or any other owned-typed expression of `OwningTask<T>`), the await consumes the task as part of the operation and satisfies the discharge requirement on the operand — **on all outgoing edges of the await, including the fault/cancel (exception) edge**: after a faulted first await, an owned operand is moved-from per [§28.3](#sec-local-variables-ownership-and-borrows), and a retry requires binding a fresh task. The implicit task-disposal that the runtime performs is the same operation that satisfies the type system's discharge rule; one is the runtime view, the other is the static-analysis view of the same event.

Like `throw x` ([§31.1](#sec-the-throw-operand)) and the discard `_ := x;` ([§17.13](#sec-the-discard-_)), this consume is a [K4.2](#sec-kernel-k4) **site-announced kill** with a runtime backstop: the `await` keyword plus the single-consumer operand type are the site announcement — keyword-visible at the kill site — and the await's implicit task disposal sets the disposed flag, so a stale borrow of the operand faults deterministically as `DisposedAccessException` in checked disposal mode ([§28.2](#sec-checked-disposal)). Pattern B await therefore deliberately joins no consume-site freeze list; and the position is **marker-free** ([K3.13](#sec-kernel-k3)'s set), so it takes no operand marker — the transfer marker is not admitted where the target already announces the consume ([§28.3](#sec-move-semantics-for-owned-locals)); it is [K3.5](#sec-kernel-k3) in the kernel's owned-consuming enumeration.

In practice this means the natural patterns work without explicit task disposal:

```bezel
// Iteration variable from draining: task is owned, await consumes it
for var task in taskArray.Drain() do
  results.Add(await task);     // task discharged by the await; no further obligation
end;

// Local variable of owned task type
var theTask := SomeFactory();   // theTask: owned OwningTask<T>
using var result := await theTask;  // theTask discharged by the await
```

In neither case does the user need a separate `using var` to discharge the task itself — the await's implicit disposal *is* the discharge.

Pattern B tasks are single-consumer by type — once awaited they are spent, and sharing a `OwningTask<T>` across multiple potential awaiters is not the intended pattern. In the typical case the operand is owned (an owned local, an owned parameter, or an iteration variable from draining an array of tasks), and the discharge rule applies as described above. When the operand is borrowed, the await still disposes the task implicitly per the runtime semantics, but no discharge is owed for it. The `using var task := SomeFactory(); var x := await task;` shape, where `task` is `using var`-bound and then awaited, is one common form; the await's implicit disposal happens first, and the using-var's disposal at scope end is a no-op per the idempotency rule ([§28.2](#sec-the-idisposable-contract)).

```bezel
// Canonical form: using-var binding
using var token := await semaphore.AcquireAsync();
DoCriticalWork();
// At end of scope: token disposed, releasing the semaphore.

// Plain var binding — token is an owned local subject to standard discharge rules
var token := await semaphore.AcquireAsync();
TransferToHelper(move token);     // owned local consumed by owned parameter

// Direct ownership transfer to a method call accepting owned
results.Add(await loadTask);     // results: OwningArray<T>; Add takes owned

// Direct return
public async method Acquire(): OwningTask<Connection>
  return await ConnectAsync(url);     // owned T flows to owned T return
end Acquire;
```

A bare `var x := await someTask;` compiles: `x` is an owned local under the standard [§28.3](#sec-local-variables-ownership-and-borrows) discharge rules; an `x` never discharged auto-drops at scope exit with the must-use warning. (`var x := <owned producer>` is an owned-consuming binding and a Pattern B await is such a producer — [§28.3](#sec-producers)'s binding rules govern: an unmarked read of a named owned binding stays a borrow, and the transfer spelling is `var y := move x;` ([K3.4](#sec-kernel-k3)).)

For an asynchronously-disposable owned result, use `await using var`:

```bezel
// ConnectAsync is illustrative; see §28.12 note.
await using var connection := await ConnectAsync(url);
await connection.SendAsync(data);
// At end of scope: connection.DisposeAsync() awaited.
```

For a `OwningTask<T>` not awaited in an owned-consuming context — a bare expression-statement `await t;`, whose minted result would be dropped silently, or an await in a non-owned-consuming expression position (a non-`owned` argument, an operand of a larger expression) — the await is a compile error. The explicit discard `_ := await t;` is **not** such a case: the discard is itself an owned-consuming position (this section's list; [§17.13](#sec-the-discard-_)) and disposes the result. The error message names the owned-consuming positions admitted by the rule above and points to the `using var` form as the canonical choice.

<a id="sec-disposing-an-unconsumed-ownedtaskt"></a>
#### Disposing an unconsumed `OwningTask<T>`

If a `OwningTask<T>` is dropped or disposed before its result has been transferred — for example, by `using var` on the task itself with no await — disposing the task disposes the result if one was produced (derives: [K1](#sec-kernel-k1) cascade + [§30.13](#sec-runtime-model)'s non-blocking discipline — the container owns the result until transfer). This makes "fire and forget then drop" safe for owned-result tasks.

```bezel
do
  using var t := semaphore.AcquireAsync();
  // No await; nothing transferred. If t completes before we leave the block,
  // its produced token is disposed (the semaphore is released).
end;
```

When the task has not completed at the point of disposal, the `Dispose()` call attaches a continuation that disposes the produced result whenever it appears, then returns immediately. The dispose call does not block waiting for completion. The underlying operation continues to run; any side effects of the operation still occur, and the result, when produced, is disposed by the continuation. The task transitions to its terminal disposed state immediately for the purposes of any further awaits — any await of an already-disposed task raises `InvalidOperationException`, a never-awaited-then-disposed task's first await included.

A task that has been awaited and faulted, or awaited and cancelled, has no owned result to dispose; disposal is a no-op for the result.

Dropping a not-yet-settled task this way leaves the running frame holding whatever borrows entered it — the receiver and any borrowed arguments — so [§30.1](#sec-async-methods)'s source-outlives-settlement obligation rests on the caller (in the example above: `semaphore` must outlive the abandoned acquisition's settlement).

<a id="sec-constructing-a-completed-task-with-a-class-typed-result"></a>
#### Constructing a completed task with a class-typed result

The factory `Task.FromResult<T>(value: T)` produces a completed task whose result is `value`. It is restricted to non-class T (value types, `string`, runtime-managed reference types); calling it with a class-typed T is a compile error.

For class T, use `Task.FromOwnedResult<T>(owned value: T): OwningTask<T>` instead (derives: axiom [A3](#sec-axiom-register) + [K1](#sec-kernel-k1) — an externally-supplied owned value transfers into the single-consumer container). The caller transfers ownership of `value` to the task; the produced task is Pattern B (single-consumer, owned result), and consumers await it under the `using var x := await ...` shape:

```bezel
class TaskFactoryDemo
  async method Consume(): Task
    var i := await Task.FromResult(42);                                // T = int, value-typed
    var s := await Task.FromResult("done");                            // T = string, runtime-managed
    using var m := await Task.FromOwnedResult<MyClass>(new MyClass());  // T = MyClass → OwningTask<MyClass>
  end Consume;
end TaskFactoryDemo;
```

The same split applies to `TaskCompletionSource<T>`: the standard form is for non-class T (copyable value, string, runtime-managed) and produces `Task<T>`; `OwningTaskCompletionSource<T> where T: class` is the form for class T and produces `OwningTask<T>`. See [§30.10](#sec-standard-library-task-helpers) and [§30.11](#sec-taskcompletionsourcet-and-ownedtaskcompletionsourcet).

There is no factory for producing a Pattern A `Task<T>` of class T from an externally-supplied owned value; Pattern A class-typed tasks arise from async methods whose body returns a value (the compiler inserts the appropriate ownership transfer into the task's slot) and from awaiting other Pattern A sources. Imperative completion of a Pattern A class-typed task is a future-revision question; the cases that motivate it are uncommon, and the available patterns (writing an async wrapper that awaits an `OwningTaskCompletionSource` and re-publishes the result) cover the practical needs.

<a id="sec-idiom-async-resource-acquisition"></a>
#### Idiom: async resource acquisition

The combination of `OwningTask<T>` and Pattern B is what makes resource-acquisition APIs natural:

```bezel
// Abbreviated from stdlib §6.3: the declared parameter list also carries
//   `token: CancellationToken := CancellationToken.None`.
public class Semaphore
  public async method AcquireAsync(): OwningTask<SemaphoreToken>;
end Semaphore;

// Caller:
using var token := await sem.AcquireAsync();
DoWork();
// token disposed at scope end -> semaphore released.
```

The owned-result task expresses the intent directly; no separate synchronous allocation step is needed.

<a id="sec-async-lambdas"></a>
### 30.6 Async lambdas

```bezel
var reader: (string) -> Task<string> := async lambda(path) => do
  using var task := File.ReadAllTextAsync(path);   // stdlib §7.3
  return await task;
end;

var quick: (string) -> Task<int> := async lambda(url) => await CountBytesAsync(url);

var loader: (string) -> OwningTask<Resource> := async lambda(path) => do
  return await LoadResourceAsync(path);     // Pattern B return; the lambda's
                                             //   state machine forwards the
                                             //   owned Resource through.
end;
```

The function type of an async lambda has a `Task`, `Task<T>`, or `OwningTask<T>` return type. The choice follows the same rules as for async methods ([§30.1](#sec-async-methods)): `Task` for void, `Task<T>` for borrowing or value-typed results, `OwningTask<T>` for class-typed results that transfer ownership to the awaiter (Pattern B; see [§30.5](#sec-result-lifetime-and-task-disposal)).

**Which wrapper, and from where.** An `async` method writes its wrapper; an `async` lambda's is fixed by the first of three sources that applies. (1) A **return-type ascription** ([§27.3](#sec-lambda-expressions)) names it. (2) Otherwise a **closed target return slot** names it — any position supplying a closed function-typed target ([§27.3](#sec-lambda-expressions)'s non-call positions; a call candidate's parameter type once [§14.5](#sec-type-argument-inference)'s bindings are substituted, [§22.6](#sec-overloading)) whose return slot contains no free type parameter — and the body must conform to the named type exactly as an `async` method's body conforms to its declared type under [§30.1](#sec-async-methods) and [§30.5](#sec-result-lifetime-and-task-disposal): a fresh owned class result is admitted under either `Task<C>` (Pattern A, kind 1 — the task owns the result) or `OwningTask<C>` (Pattern B), so the target decides between them, and a valued body does not conform to a plain `Task`; a closed head binds nothing, so reading it is reading a declared type, not an inference. At an overloaded call, two closed candidates that differ only in the wrapper are both exact for a fresh-owned-class body and fall to [§22.6](#sec-overloading)'s ambiguity, remedied by an ascription. (3) Otherwise — no target, or a target return slot that still contains a **free type parameter** — the wrapper follows from the **body alone**, by the sentence above. That inferred type then unifies against the slot as any lambda's inferred return type does ([§14.5](#sec-type-argument-inference) phase 2): `async lambda(x: int) => 42` at an `(int) -> Task<R>` slot binds `R := int`; `async lambda(req: HttpRequest) => Http.Text("ok")`, whose body is a fresh owned class result, infers `(HttpRequest) -> OwningTask<HttpResponse>`, which reaches no instantiation of `Task<T>` ([§30.3](#sec-the-task-taskt-and-ownedtaskt-types): `Task<T>` and `OwningTask<T>` are siblings under `Task`) — that candidate is **inapplicable**, and a sibling candidate whose slot is `(A) -> OwningTask<HttpResponse>` is the one that applies. The head of a free slot is never read as the wrapper: a written `Task<R>` names no declared type for the body until `R` is bound, and binding `R` from the head would be a target-directed inference §14.5 does not have. A fresh-owned-class body meant for a `Task<R>` slot says so with an ascription (`async lambda(req: HttpRequest): Task<HttpResponse> => …` — source (1), binding `R := HttpResponse`) or with an explicit type-argument list. The parameter slots of an async lambda's function type are plain, `owned`, or `scoped` only: a target type carrying a `ref` or `out` slot is rejected for an `async` lambda ([§30.1](#sec-async-methods)).

<a id="sec-asynchronous-programming-async-iterators"></a>
### 30.7 Async iterators

An async iterator combines `yield` and `await`. The method is `async` and returns `IAsyncEnumerable<T>` — unmarked at any callee kind, the declared type announcing the caller-owned frame ([§29.3](#sec-iterator-methods); an explicit `owned`, as below, is admissible emphasis):

```bezel
public async method ReadLinesAsync(path: string): owned IAsyncEnumerable<string>
  // OpenAsync, ReadLineAsync, and AtEnd are illustrative; the example shows
  // the async-iterator shape, not a stream API in the standard library.
  // OpenAsync's result is a concrete class declaring a destructor, so `fs` may
  // be live across the `yield return` (the yield-liveness rule below).
  await using var fs := await OpenAsync(path);
  while not fs.AtEnd do
    yield return await fs.ReadLineAsync();
  end;
end ReadLinesAsync;
```

```bezel
interface IAsyncEnumerable<out T>
  method GetAsyncEnumerator(token: CancellationToken := CancellationToken.None): owned IAsyncEnumerator<T>;
end IAsyncEnumerable;

interface IAsyncEnumerator<out T>: IAsyncDisposable
  method MoveNextAsync(): Task<bool>;
  readonly property Current: T;
end IAsyncEnumerator;
```

Consume with `await for`:

```bezel
public async method ProcessFileAsync(path: string): Task
  await for var line in ReadLinesAsync(path) do
    Process(line);
  end;
end ProcessFileAsync;
```

`await for` is valid only inside an async method or async lambda. It desugars analogously to `for`: it acquires an async enumerator with `await using`, calls `MoveNextAsync()` with `await` in a loop.

<a id="sec-cancellation-in-await-for"></a>
#### Cancellation in `await for`

`await for` accepts an optional `with` clause to pass a `CancellationToken` to the async enumerator:

```bezel
await for var line in ReadLinesAsync(path) with token do
  Process(line);
end;
```

The `with token` clause passes `token` as the argument to `GetAsyncEnumerator(token)`. When omitted, `CancellationToken.None` is passed. The `with` clause is syntactically distinct from the record `with(...)` suffix — it appears after the `in` source expression and before `do`, its content is a single expression of type `CancellationToken`, and it carries no parenthesized assignment list ([§9.5](#sec-non-destructive-update-with)'s header rule: `with` followed by `(` `Identifier` `:=` is the record-update suffix on the source; any other `with` opens this clause).

**Token routing in generated async iterators.** For a compiler-generated async iterator, the enumerator returned by the generated `GetAsyncEnumerator(token)` captures the token, and every `MoveNextAsync()` performs an implicit `token.ThrowIfCancellationRequested()` — on entry, and at each resume from suspension within the advance — so a requested cancellation faults the in-flight `MoveNextAsync` task with `OperationCanceledException` at the next suspension boundary. The iterator body cannot otherwise observe the enumerator's token: there is no implicit binding of it to a body name (a C#-`[EnumeratorCancellation]`-style parameter binding is declined as implicit binding). A body that needs to observe cancellation mid-operation declares its own `CancellationToken` parameter, and the caller passes the same token both ways.

<a id="sec-async-iteration-with-owned-yields"></a>
#### Async iteration with owned yields

For async iterators that produce owned values, declare the return type as `IOwningAsyncEnumerable<T>` (where `T: class`; unmarked at any callee kind, [§29.3](#sec-iterator-methods) — the `owned` below is admissible emphasis) and `await for` over the result:

```bezel
public async method OpenFilesAsync(paths: IEnumerable<string>): owned IOwningAsyncEnumerable<FileStream>
  for var path in paths do
    yield return await OpenAsync(path);    // each yielded FileStream is owned
  end;
end OpenFilesAsync;

public async method ProcessAllAsync(paths: IEnumerable<string>): Task
  await for var fs in OpenFilesAsync(paths) do
    using var f := move fs;                 // discharge owned iteration variable
    await ProcessOneAsync(f);
  end;
end ProcessAllAsync;
```

The `await for` desugaring picks `GetOwningAsyncEnumerator()` (and `TakeCurrent()`) when the source has static type `IOwningAsyncEnumerable<T>`. Each iteration variable is owned; the §28.3 discharge rules apply on every exit edge of the loop body — the same rule as for synchronous `for` over `IOwningEnumerable<T>` ([§29.2](#sec-desugaring-of-for) "Iterator yield ownership"). When the source implements both `IAsyncEnumerable<T>` and `IOwningAsyncEnumerable<T>`, the static type of the source expression selects the desugaring; default iteration uses `IAsyncEnumerable<T>` (borrowing), and the owning path requires the source to be typed `IOwningAsyncEnumerable<T>` explicitly.

The `with token` clause works the same way for owning async iterators — `await for var fs in OpenFilesAsync(paths) with token do ...` passes the token to `GetOwningAsyncEnumerator(token)`.

**`await` inside `finally`.** Inside an async iterator, `await` may not appear in a `finally` block — a compile error. The `yield` placement restrictions of [§29.6](#sec-restrictions-inside-try-catch-finally) apply unchanged; this rule additionally restricts `await`, and only inside async *iterators* (an ordinary `async` method may await in its `finally`, [§30.9](#sec-exception-handling-in-async-methods)). The reason is disposal: when a consumer abandons iteration early, the iterator's pending `finally` blocks run synchronously inside `Dispose` ([§29.7](#sec-disposal-of-partially-consumed-iterators)) — there is no async driver at that point, so a suspension inside the `finally` would have nowhere to resume; the continuation would be silently discarded, which is precisely the defined-fault philosophy's forbidden outcome. A `finally` that needs asynchronous cleanup awaits *before* yielding (hoisting the resource acquisition), or the type implements the cleanup in its `Dispose` path. This mirrors the catch-guard rule of [§30.9](#sec-exception-handling-in-async-methods): positions evaluated during synchronous unwinding or dispatch are synchronous.

The rule governs **source-written** `finally` blocks only. The implicit finally of an `await using var` in an async iterator is exempt on the normal path: at scope end the generated code awaits `DisposeAsync()` under the ordinary async driver — which is why this section's own `ReadLinesAsync` example is well-formed. On **early abandonment** — the consumer disposes a suspended iterator — [§29.7](#sec-disposal-of-partially-consumed-iterators)'s synchronous disposal pass takes [§28.12](#sec-asynchronous-disposal)'s synchronous-fallback path for every `await using var` active at the suspension point: the destructor runs and `DisposeAsync` is skipped ([§28.12](#sec-asynchronous-disposal)'s no-destructor warning covers types whose async cleanup has no synchronous fallback). For a class that implements `IAsyncDisposable` and declares **no destructor** — no synchronous fallback at all, by design (`TaskScope`, stdlib [§6.10](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-taskscope), is the standard instance) — that silent skip would void cleanup the type states normatively. An `await using var` whose static type is such a class (or is of **interface** static type — `IAsyncDisposable` or any interface deriving from it: an interface cannot promise a destructor, so the runtime type's fallback posture is statically unknowable and interface-typed bindings are conservatively included; a recorded liftable bound) therefore **may not be live across a `yield return`** in an async iterator: a compile error at the yield, naming the binding and the remedies — dispose before the yield, or hoist the work into a non-iterator `async` helper called between yields. The check is static and local: the class-level fact is the one [§28.12](#sec-asynchronous-disposal)'s declaration-site warning already keys on, and across-suspension liveness is the analysis [§30.1](#sec-async-methods)'s borrow-bearing-record rule already runs. For types **with** a destructor, the synchronous-fallback path above remains the defined degraded behavior, unchanged. (Driving `DisposeAsync` from the abandonment pass via an async unwind driver would lift this restriction wholesale; that driver is deferred future work, not foreclosed.)
<a id="sec-cancellation"></a>
### 30.8 Cancellation

Cancellation is cooperative via `CancellationToken`. The standard library defines the surface (the full declaration is in std lib [§6.1](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-cancellationtoken-and-cancellationtokensource); the members referenced by the language rules are shown here). Sources compose: a **linked** source — `CancellationTokenSource.CreateLinked(a, b)` / `CreateLinkedAll(parents)` — cancels when any parent token cancels, with the parent sources outliving the linked source per the ordinary source-outlives-token rule; a linked source may take a parent token borrowed through a `Shared<CancellationTokenSource>` handle, the sharing form of [§28.13](#sec-shared-ownership) — the child is then published and signal-only like its parent (stdlib §6.1); where no source is published, cross-domain cancellation remains a channel message, rationale §12.6. Cancel-on-dispose makes `using var` scopes double as cancellation scopes (stdlib §6.1).

```bezel
public record CancellationToken
  public static readonly property None: CancellationToken;
  public readonly property IsCancellationRequested: bool;
  public method ThrowIfCancellationRequested();
  public method Register(scoped callback: () -> ()): owned Subscription;
end CancellationToken;

public class CancellationTokenSource
  public constructor();
  public readonly property Token: CancellationToken;
  public readonly property IsCancellationRequested: bool;
  public method Cancel();
  public method CancelAfter(delay: TimeSpan);
  public static method CreateLinked(a: CancellationToken, b: CancellationToken): owned CancellationTokenSource;
  public static method CreateLinkedAll(parents: Array<CancellationToken>): owned CancellationTokenSource;
  destructor;       // cancel-on-dispose: signals cancellation to observing tokens
end CancellationTokenSource;
```

`CancellationToken` is a record holding a borrowed reference to its source. The token observes the source's state; when `Cancel()` is called on the source, all tokens derived from it report `IsCancellationRequested == true`. Per the record-disposal rules ([§9.7](#sec-records-and-disposal)), the token does not own the source; the source must outlive any tokens that observe it. For typical short-lived uses (token passed as a parameter to async calls that complete before the source is disposed), this is automatic.

That conditional is load-bearing: passing a token to an `async` method captures it into a state-machine frame that lives until the task settles, and `CancellationToken` is the **single stdlib-certified exception** to [§30.1](#sec-async-methods)'s borrow-bearing-parameter prohibition. The certification is this normative obligation: **the `CancellationTokenSource` must outlive the settlement of every task observing one of its tokens.** Where the source is shared across domains ([§28.13](#sec-shared-ownership); stdlib §6.1), the obligation binds each observing domain and is discharged by that domain holding a live handle for the settlement's duration — the handle keeps the source alive, the borrow does not. Awaiting the call inside the source's `using var` scope discharges the obligation; abandoning such a task ([§30.10](#sec-standard-library-task-helpers)) transfers it to whatever outlives the task. A token read after its source's disposal raises `DisposedAccessException` in checked disposal mode ([§28.2](#sec-the-idisposable-contract)) and is undefined behavior in unchecked mode — the same residual-trust shape as [§28.3](#sec-local-variables-ownership-and-borrows)'s borrowed-field rule.

Reading `IsCancellationRequested` on a `CancellationToken` involves reading through the borrowed reference to the `CancellationTokenSource`. This read is guaranteed to be atomic and to observe the effect of a `Cancel()` call from another thread without additional synchronization — the runtime ensures the necessary memory ordering. The `ThrowIfCancellationRequested()` method is similarly thread-safe.

`CancellationToken` is auto-imported as a language primitive ([§2.3](#sec-always-available-names)). `CancellationTokenSource` and the other threading types live in `System.Threading` and require explicit `import System.Threading;`.

`CancellationToken.None` (a token whose source never cancels) is provided for callers that do not want cancellation.

By convention, async methods that should be cancellable accept a `CancellationToken` parameter and pass it to inner async calls. Cancellation typically happens at `await` points: the inner call observes the request and completes with `OperationCanceledException`.

<a id="sec-exception-handling-in-async-methods"></a>
### 30.9 Exception handling in async methods

- An exception thrown in the synchronous prefix of an async method (before any `await`) faults the returned task, not the immediate caller.
- An exception thrown after an `await` faults the task.
- Awaiting a faulted task re-raises the exception with the original stack trace preserved.
- `try`/`catch` inside an async method catches exceptions normally, including those raised by `await`.

**Fault ownership.** A faulted task **owns its fault exception**. Awaiting a faulted task (or reading a faulted `Result`, [§30.3](#sec-the-task-taskt-and-ownedtaskt-types)) re-raises the task-owned instance; the catching arm's binding is a **borrow** of it, exactly as [§31.1](#sec-throwing-and-catching) frames every caught exception — but the instance is **exempt from [§31.1](#sec-throwing-and-catching)'s dispose-after-arm rule** (the [§31.4](#sec-standard-exception-types) `TypeInitializationException` pattern): handling completes without disposing it, which is what makes re-raising the same instance to every awaiter of a multi-awaited `Task`/`Task<T>` ([§30.4](#sec-multiple-awaiters)) sound. The exception is disposed **exactly once, by the task that owns it, when the task is disposed** — with two timing refinements: a task disposed while its own fault exception is in flight defers that disposal until the exception's handling completes (so a `using var`-bound task unwound by its own fault never destroys the exception mid-dispatch), and an await that consumed its operand task ([§30.5](#sec-result-lifetime-and-task-disposal)) performs the deferred task disposal as its terminal act, after handling completes. Imperative fault paths transfer ownership **in**: `SetException`/`TrySetException` on the task-completion sources and `Task.FromException` take the exception as an `owned` parameter ([§30.11](#sec-taskcompletionsourcet-and-ownedtaskcompletionsourcet), stdlib §6.6/§6.7); a caller holding only a caught *borrow* constructs a fresh exception chaining the cause (`new Exception(ex.Message, ex)`, [§31.4](#sec-standard-exception-types) snapshot chaining) — consistent with [§31.1](#sec-throwing-and-catching)'s rule that caught instances do not escape their arm. The **aggregation helpers are the one exception to the first sentence** ([§30.10](#sec-standard-library-task-helpers) aggregation contracts): a non-successful `WhenAll` aggregate — borrowing and owning input forms alike — owns no fault instance of its own — when the first non-successful input is faulted, awaiting the aggregate re-raises, *as a borrow*, the fault owned by that **input** task (a cancelled first input raises a fresh `OperationCanceledException`, [§30.3](#sec-the-task-taskt-and-ownedtaskt-types)), which keeps every fault single-owned; the input-lifetime consequences are stated with the contracts.

`await` has no syntactic restrictions on its placement inside `try`/`catch`/`finally` *bodies*. The state machine handles suspension across exception-handling boundaries correctly.

Catch **guards** are the one exception: a `when` guard on a catch arm ([§19.4](#sec-guards)) is evaluated synchronously during exception dispatch and may not contain `await` (a compile error, in async and sync methods alike). Exception dispatch — deciding *which* arm handles a raised exception — runs to completion without suspension; permitting a suspension point inside dispatch would leave the exception neither caught nor propagating across the suspension. A guard that needs asynchronous information awaits it *before* the `try`, or catches unconditionally and re-raises (`throw;`, [§21.8](#sec-throw)) after an awaited check in the arm body.

```bezel
public async method WithCleanupAsync(): Task
  try
    await DoWorkAsync();
  catch
    var ex: Exception => do
      await LogErrorAsync(ex);
      throw;
    end
  finally
    await ReleaseResourcesAsync();
  end;
end WithCleanupAsync;
```

The `do ... end` block is required here because the arm body has multiple statements. When the body is just a re-raise, the bare `throw` expression makes the arm a one-liner:

```bezel
catch
  var ex: TransientException => Retry(ex),
  var ex: Exception => throw          // re-raise unrecognized exceptions
end;
```

<a id="sec-standard-library-task-helpers"></a>
### 30.10 Standard library task helpers

The standard library provides the following, a subset (stdlib §6.7 declares the full set, `Task.WhenEach` included):

- `Task.FromResult<T>(value: T): Task<T>` — completed task with a value. Restricted to non-class T (value types, `string`, runtime-managed reference types). For class T, see `Task.FromOwnedResult` below; calling `FromResult` with a class-typed T is a compile error pointing to the owned variant.
- `Task.FromOwnedResult<T>(owned value: T): OwningTask<T> where T: class` — completed Pattern B task whose owned result is `value`. The caller transfers ownership of `value` to the task. Awaiters consume the task under Pattern B ([§30.5](#sec-result-lifetime-and-task-disposal)): the await must appear in an owned-consuming context (`using var`, an `owned` parameter, an `owned` return, etc.), and ownership transfers to that context. Use this when constructing a completed task from a freshly-acquired or freshly-constructed class instance that the awaiter should own.
- `Task.FromException<T>(owned exception: Exception): Task<T>` and the non-generic `Task` form. The exception parameter is `owned`: the produced task owns its fault exception per [§30.9](#sec-exception-handling-in-async-methods).
- `Task.FromCancelled<T>(): Task<T>` and the non-generic form.
- `Task.Delay(milliseconds: int, token: CancellationToken := CancellationToken.None): Task` and `Task.Delay(duration: TimeSpan, token: CancellationToken := CancellationToken.None): Task` — one signature per duration shape, the cancellation argument a `:=` default rather than a second overload (stdlib [§1](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-conventions)'s optional-trailing-argument rule; the declarations are stdlib [§6.7](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-task-static-helpers)'s).
- `Task.WhenAll(tasks: Array<Task>): Task` — completes when all tasks complete.
- `Task.WhenAll<T>(tasks: Array<Task<T>>): Task<Array<T>>` — homogeneous result type for non-class T.
- `Task.WhenAll<T>(owned tasks: OwningArray<OwningTask<T>>): OwningTask<OwningArray<T>> where T: class` — the **owning `WhenAll` overload**: the Pattern B aggregator, distinguished from the borrowing forms by its parameter type and spelled at the call site by the transfer marker (`await Task.WhenAll(move tasks)`, [§22.3](#sec-parameter-modifiers)).
