- For storage whose address an in-flight extern call holds (a `ref`/`out` argument, an inline-array argument, a passed `Pointer`/`DangerousPointer()` result): remaining valid until that call returns. A [§32.8](#sec-callbacks) callback that disposes or overwrites such storage mid-call — e.g. by reassigning an owned field of a captured receiver whose buffer address is the call's own argument (drop-on-overwrite disposes the displaced value, [§28.7](#sec-reassigning-owned-fields)) — is a use-after-free no compile-time rule can see.
- For addresses of Bezel-owned mutable storage (`RawBytes.Pointer`, `CString`/`WString.Pointer`, `OwningBuffer<T>.DangerousPointer()` — stdlib §10, §4.14): native retention of such an address past the synchronous call is a use-after-free hazard no rule in this chapter can track — validity ends at a disposal the native side is never told about. The recorded mitigation is structural: one wrapper class owns both the buffer and the native registration, so its destructor severs the registration before the buffer's disposal ([§32.13](#sec-c-compatible-records)'s wrapper posture).
- For a `Ptr<T>` that has crossed a domain boundary ([§30.14](#sec-sendable-types) computes `Ptr<T>` sendable; ratified): foreign memory reached through a crossed pointer is outside domain isolation; unsynchronized cross-domain `Load`/`Store` on the same address is a data race and undefined behavior — synchronization ([§30.12](#sec-thread-synchronization)) is the programmer's obligation.

When the contract is violated, the consequences are unspecified.

<a id="sec-symbol-binding"></a>
### 32.11 Symbol binding: names, aliases, and C-variadic imports

**The name rule, stated.** An extern method's identifier **is** the imported symbol name unless an alias clause says otherwise. The alias clause `:= symbol "name"`, written after the return clause (grammar A.3), binds the declaration to the named symbol instead — delivering rationale §16.1's hand-written declarations "with the names they want". Several declarations, of any mix of shapes, may bind one symbol.

**Resolution and failure timing.** The bare-name file derivation of [§32.3](#sec-library-specification) is normative, not illustrative: the runtime derives the platform file name from the bare library name exactly per §32.3's stated per-platform convention (Linux: `.so` with the platform's shared-library version resolution; macOS: `.dylib`; Windows: `.dll`) and resolves it through the platform loader's standard search path; a full-path library string bypasses derivation and loads the named file directly (§32.3). Every extern symbol of a program resolves during **startup, before `Main` runs**; a missing library or missing symbol aborts startup with a diagnostic naming both. Build-time resolution (static linking of a stub) satisfies the bound a fortiori. An implementation may bind lazily as an internal strategy **only if it preserves the observable failure point** — every resolution failure still surfaces before `Main` (e.g. by probing all declared symbols at startup); deferring a resolution failure to first call is non-conforming. *Recorded cost, deliberate:* with no conditional compilation (proposal 0034) and no runtime library loading ([§32.14](#sec-deferred-ffi-surface)), a module declaring any symbol absent on the current platform makes every program linking that module fail at startup there, even when the call is never reached. Fail-fast is chosen: extern declarations are per-platform artifacts already ([§32.13](#sec-c-compatible-records)'s platform-honesty note), and a probe-for-availability binding needs conditional compilation, not late failure — reopen alongside 0034 (rationale §16.7).

**`variadic(N)`** on the symbol clause declares: *the named symbol is a C-variadic function whose fixed parameters are the first N declared parameters; the remaining declared parameters pass in the symbol's variadic slots.* The Bezel method stays fixed-arity (ordinary overloading, ordinary calls); the compiler emits the **variadic calling sequence** (on SysV x86-64: `%al` set correctly). `N` ≤ the declared arity; `N` equal to the arity is legal and load-bearing ("call this variadic symbol with zero variadic arguments" — the only sound minimum-arity binding of a variadic symbol). Not combinable with the `env` pairing ([§32.8](#sec-callbacks)).

**No silent promotions.** C applies default argument promotions to variadic arguments; Bezel refuses to do this implicitly: a variadic-position parameter must already have a promoted type — `int`, `uint`, `long`, `ulong`, `double`, `IntPtr`, `UIntPtr`, `CString`, `WString`, `Ptr<T>`, an FFI function type, or a single-integer/pointer-field record ([§32.13](#sec-c-compatible-records), marshalling as its promoted scalar field — a recorded step past accepted proposal 0033's list; rationale §16.6). Declaring `float`, `bool`, `byte`, `sbyte`, `short`, or `ushort` in a variadic position is a compile error naming the type to write ("C promotes `float` variadic arguments to `double`; declare the parameter as `double`"). `RawBytes` is excluded from variadic positions: its two-slot marshalling ([§32.5](#sec-ffi-compatible-types)) does not fit the one-slot-per-parameter promotion accounting the `%al`/stack contract depends on — pass `Ptr<byte>`/`IntPtr` plus an explicit length.

**The documented trap.** Binding a variadic C symbol with a plain fixed-arity extern declaration — no `variadic(N)` — is **undefined behavior** on ABIs whose variadic callees consult a caller-set register (SysV x86-64's `%al`); it may appear to work on one target and fail on another. The compiler cannot detect it (the symbol's C-side arity is not visible); the sound spelling is `variadic(N)` with `N` equal to the declared arity.

Worked — the two load-bearing shapes:

```bezel
// curl_easy_setopt(CURL*, CURLoption, ...) — one trailing arg, type keyed by option:
extern "libcurl"
  public method SetOptLong(h: IntPtr, opt: int, value: long): int
      := symbol "curl_easy_setopt" variadic(2);
  public method SetOptStr(h: IntPtr, opt: int, value: CString): int
      := symbol "curl_easy_setopt" variadic(2);
  public method SetOptPtr(h: IntPtr, opt: int, value: IntPtr): int
      := symbol "curl_easy_setopt" variadic(2);
  public method SetOptWriteFn(h: IntPtr, opt: int,
      cb: (Ptr<byte>, UIntPtr, UIntPtr, IntPtr) -> UIntPtr): int
      := symbol "curl_easy_setopt" variadic(2);   // a static callback plugs in here (§32.8)
end;

// open(2) with O_CREAT — open is ITSELF variadic (int open(const char*, int, ...)),
// so BOTH arities go through the clause; a bare 2-ary `method open(...)` declaration
// would be exactly the %al trap above:
extern "libc"
  public method Open2(path: CString, flags: int): int
      := symbol "open" variadic(2);          // N = declared arity: a variadic call with
                                             //   ZERO variadic args — the SOUND spelling
                                             //   of the fixed-arity workaround
  public method OpenCreate(path: CString, flags: int, mode: uint): int
      := symbol "open" variadic(2);
end;
```

This is also the general recipe for `fcntl`/`ioctl` (aliases per request shape). **True call-site varargs** (`printf(fmt, args...)`-style trailing arguments typed per call site) are declined for v1 — they need a new call-arity rule and per-call-site promotion checking, and the measured corpus is fully served by aliases ([§32.14](#sec-deferred-ffi-surface); rationale §16.6).

<a id="sec-foreign-memory"></a>
### 32.12 Foreign memory: `Ptr<T>`

`Ptr<T>` is a typed foreign address: a compiler-intrinsic value record in the explicitly-imported `System.Interop` module (declaration surface: stdlib [§10.5](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-system-interop-ptr)), with representation identical to `IntPtr`. The two types partition the roles ([§32.7](#sec-pointers-and-intptr)): `IntPtr` is *placement* — an opaque address flowing through signatures and pointer arrays — and `Ptr<T>` is *access*.

1. **The pointee gate** (per-instantiation, [§3.6](#sec-derived-type-properties)-style diagnostics): `T` is drawn from the **FFI-pointee set** — integer types, `float`, `double`, `bool`, `IntPtr`, `UIntPtr`, and C-compatible records ([§32.13](#sec-c-compatible-records)). `Ptr<Ptr<U>>` is **not** admitted (v1 decline; `Ptr<IntPtr>` plus explicit `FromIntPtr` re-typing expresses every `T**` shape — one visible step per indirection; rationale §16.3 records the decline and the sanctioned single-field-record reconstruction). The pointee set is an enumerated closed set plus one derived property; it is deliberately not a second §3.6 table row — enumerations are not structural classification. The pointee set is deliberately **not** [§32.5](#sec-ffi-compatible-types)'s FFI-compatible scalars: `Ptr<T>` is an FFI-compatible scalar — C may point at one, and `ref p: Ptr<T>` is an admitted extern parameter whose C type is `T**` ([§32.5](#sec-boundary-out-ref)) — but it is **not** a member here, which is exactly what makes `Ptr<Ptr<U>>` inadmissible. C-compatible records are members here and are not scalars. Neither set contains the other.
2. **Trust posture, inherited verbatim**: every `Load`/`Store`/`LoadAt`/`StoreAt`/`Add`/`CopyToArray`/`CopyFromArray` is trusted but unverified — the address's validity, alignment, and pointee type are the programmer's declaration; a wrong one is undefined behavior. No bounds, no lifetimes, no partially-verified tier (rationale §16.3 records the declined checked-memory shape).
3. **Element-scaled, named, never operatored arithmetic**: `LoadAt(i)`/`StoreAt(i, v)`/`Add(count)` scale by `T`'s target-ABI stride; there is no `p + 1`, no `-`, no ordering comparisons (ordering over unrelated allocations is undefined behavior in C; nothing in the binding corpus needs them). Byte-granular work is `Ptr<byte>`.
4. **`Ptr<bool>`**: 1-byte slots; loads read any non-zero byte as `true` ([§32.5](#sec-ffi-compatible-types)'s receive rule); stores write 0 or 1.
5. **Record pointees** ([§32.13](#sec-c-compatible-records)): `Load`/`Store` copy whole structs between foreign memory and Bezel record values; `LoadAt`/`Add` stride by the struct's ABI size. A record load is not bitwise — `bool` fields are normalized field-wise on load and written as 0/1 on store.
6. **Reading pointers from memory** (the `char**` shape): `Ptr<IntPtr>` — `LoadAt(i)` yields an `IntPtr` to re-type via `Ptr<U>.FromIntPtr` or hand to `string.FromCStringPointer`.
7. **No pinning exists or is needed**: Bezel has no moving collector ([§28](#sec-resource-management)); every address the language exposes is stable until its owner's disposal. Stated once, normatively, here.
8. **Sendability, ratified**: [§30.14](#sec-sendable-types)'s value-type rule computes `Ptr<T>` sendable; this section ratifies the outcome — a non-sendable carve-out would be laundered in one line through `ToIntPtr`/`FromIntPtr` and protect nothing — and attaches the cross-domain trust bullet of [§32.10](#sec-boundary-contract).
9. **The no-object-address invariant, stated**: no Bezel class reference converts to an address. The only addresses in the language are buffer interiors (the stdlib accessors: `RawBytes.Pointer`, `CString`/`WString.Pointer`, `OwningBuffer<T>.DangerousPointer()`), foreign values (`Ptr<T>`/`IntPtr` received from native code), and code (`Interop.CodeAddress`). Object identity stays outside the address space — load-bearing for [§30.14](#sec-sendable-types) (no laundering an object across domains through an integer) and for the unforgeability of [§28](#sec-resource-management)'s dispose-through-borrow rules (rationale §16.7's `ForeignHandle` deferral).
10. **Address accessors and bulk transfer** — the stdlib surface this section governs: `RawBytes.FromForeign(p, length, freeOnDispose)` (stdlib [§10.3](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-rawbytes)) wraps `[p, p + length)` without copying — a view, or `free(3)`-on-dispose; `CString.Pointer`/`WString.Pointer` (stdlib §10.1–§10.2) and `OwningBuffer<T>.DangerousPointer()` (stdlib [§4.14](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-owned-buffers-and-spans)) expose Bezel-owned addresses under the retention obligation of [§32.10](#sec-boundary-contract).

Worked — the sqlite3 blob read (the gate, `Zero`, and the one-explicit-copy principle):

```bezel
import System.Interop;

extern "sqlite3"
  public method sqlite3_column_blob(stmt: IntPtr, col: int): Ptr<byte>;   // borrowed; valid
  public method sqlite3_column_bytes(stmt: IntPtr, col: int): int;        //   until next step
end;

public static class Blobs
  public static method ReadBlob(stmt: IntPtr, col: int): owned Array<byte>
    var n := sqlite3_column_bytes(stmt, col);
    var p := sqlite3_column_blob(stmt, col);
    if n = 0 or p = Ptr<byte>.Zero then          // SQLite returns NULL for the empty blob
      return new Array<byte>(0, 0);              // sized ctor (count, fill), stdlib §4.4
    end;
    return p.CopyToArray(n);                     // ONE explicit copy; result is Bezel-owned
  end ReadBlob;
end Blobs;
```

<a id="sec-c-compatible-records"></a>
### 32.13 C-compatible records

1. **The derived property** ([§3.6](#sec-derived-type-properties) table row): a record is **C-compatible** iff every field's type is an FFI-compatible scalar (integer types, `float`, `double`, `bool`, `IntPtr`, `UIntPtr`, `Ptr<T>`), an inline array `[N]T` of such a scalar ([§32.5](#sec-ffi-compatible-types)'s element set; inline arrays of record elements are a recorded liftable bound, [§32.14](#sec-deferred-ffi-surface)), or another C-compatible record (nesting; recursion is impossible — records are value types). Everything else disqualifies: `string`, `char`, `decimal`, nullable types, enums, class/interface/function-typed fields — a C-compatible record is by construction not borrow-bearing and has no disposal obligations ([§9.7](#sec-records-and-disposal)). Per §3.6's common rules the property is computed never declared, evaluated per-instantiation for generic records, part of the public contract, and named in diagnostics.
2. **The layout promise** — the language's first normative representation guarantee, scoped exactly here: *a C-compatible record's in-memory representation is the target C ABI's layout for the corresponding C struct — fields in declaration order (positional parameters in positional order; body fields in declaration order), each at its C-equivalent type's ABI alignment, with the ABI's intra-struct and trailing padding.* Field reordering and packing optimizations are forbidden for classified records; all other records keep unspecified layout. What the promise does **not** include is platform-independence: sizes and layouts vary exactly as C's do, and *which* C struct matches which platform remains the programmer's trusted declaration — glibc's and macOS's `struct addrinfo` order fields differently; each platform gets its own declaration, exactly as a hand-written C binding would. The [§3.6](#sec-derived-type-properties) reservation-clause exception is ratified together with this promise; neither stands without the other (rationale §16.5).
3. **Admission — by address** ([§32.5](#sec-ffi-compatible-types)): as `ref`/`out` extern parameters (C sees `R*`; [§32.5](#sec-boundary-out-ref)'s rules) and as `Ptr<R>` pointees ([§32.12](#sec-foreign-memory)). **By value is not admitted**, except the single-field form below; by-value parameters/returns and struct-receiving callbacks are deferred with reasons ([§32.14](#sec-deferred-ffi-surface)).
4. **Typed handles: the single-field admission.** A C-compatible record with exactly one field, of *integer or pointer* scalar type (integer types, `IntPtr`, `UIntPtr`, `Ptr<T>` — not `float`/`double`, not `bool`), is FFI-compatible **directly** — parameter, return, `ref`/`out`, and callback positions — marshalling exactly as its field. The restriction is ABI-driven, not aesthetic: for an integer-class single-eightbyte aggregate, "as the scalar itself" holds on both vouched target families (SysV x86-64 classes it INTEGER; Win64 passes 8-byte aggregates in the integer slots), while `struct { double }` diverges (SysV: XMM; Win64: integer slot, where a bare `double` rides XMM) — admitting it would mandate a wrong-register miscompile on a vouched target. Float/double single-field records join Stage D ([§32.14](#sec-deferred-ffi-surface)); `bool` is excluded to avoid pinning an aggregate-normalization rule nothing needs. Other targets must implement the equivalent integer-slot check before enabling the admission.
5. **Lifetime: wrapper classes are the answer** — recorded guidance, normative in the way [§32.6](#sec-string-marshalling)'s ownership patterns are: foreign-handle lifetime lives in an ordinary class whose destructor calls the foreign release function and whose body owns every dependent registration and buffer, making the teardown order structural. A declaration-bound destructor (a `closes fn` clause) is declined with reasons (rationale §16.7).
6. **Unions and bitfields — declined** (no structural spelling survives §3.6's computed-never-declared discipline; bitfield layout is ABI-quirky). Recorded workarounds: a widest-member or `[N]byte` slot plus `Ptr<byte>` reinterpretation; bitfield words as their containing integer plus masks (rationale §16.5).

Worked — `clock_gettime` (a two-`long` record, boundary `out`, the errno window):

```bezel
import System.Interop;
import System.IO;                    // IOException (§31.4; stdlib §7.5)

// C (POSIX, Linux x86-64): struct timespec { time_t tv_sec; long tv_nsec; };
public record TimeSpec(Sec: long, Nsec: long);          // C-compatible: two longs

extern "libc"
  public method clock_gettime(clockId: int, out ts: TimeSpec): int;
end;

public static class Clock
  public static method MonotonicNanos(): long
    var rc := clock_gettime(1, out var ts);               // CLOCK_MONOTONIC
    if rc <> 0 then
      var e := Interop.LastErrno();                       // read FIRST (§32.9)
      throw new IOException($"clock_gettime failed: errno={e}");
    end;
    return ts.Sec * 1000000000L + ts.Nsec;
  end MonotonicNanos;
end Clock;
```

Worked — typed handles (the type-confusion half of the handle problem):

```bezel
public record Sqlite3Db(Raw: IntPtr);
public record Sqlite3Stmt(Raw: IntPtr);

extern "sqlite3"
  public method sqlite3_open(filename: CString, out db: Sqlite3Db): int;
  public method sqlite3_prepare_v2(db: Sqlite3Db, sql: CString, nByte: int,
      out stmt: Sqlite3Stmt, out tail: IntPtr): int;
  public method sqlite3_step(stmt: Sqlite3Stmt): int;
  public method sqlite3_finalize(stmt: Sqlite3Stmt): int;
  public method sqlite3_close(db: Sqlite3Db): int;
end;
```

Passing a statement where a database belongs is a compile error (rationale §16.2), at zero runtime cost and with no new declaration form (ordinary positional records; `db.Raw = IntPtr.Zero` is the null test). The lifetime half is the wrapper pattern:

```bezel
public class Database(handle: Sqlite3Db)
  private _handle: Sqlite3Db := handle;

  public property Raw: Sqlite3Db => _handle;

  destructor
    _ := sqlite3_close(_handle);           // policy lives HERE: this binding chooses to
                                           //   ignore SQLITE_BUSY (leak-on-misuse beats
                                           //   crash); another may verify or log
  end;
end Database;
```

The `sigaction` shape shows the declaration honesty and the one function-field rule: `Handler` is an `IntPtr`, not a function-typed field — function-typed fields are deliberately **not** C-compatible, because loading such a field back from foreign memory would materialize a callable Bezel function value from an arbitrary address (the call-through-pointer capability [§32.14](#sec-deferred-ffi-surface) keeps deferred). Installing a Bezel handler goes through `Interop.CodeAddress` ([§32.8](#sec-callbacks)); whether *running* a handler in a raw signal context is async-signal-safe is [§32.10](#sec-boundary-contract)'s flagged narrower obligation.

```bezel
// glibc x86-64 layout — the raw kernel struct orders fields differently (per-platform declaration):
public record SigAction(
  Handler: IntPtr,          // sa_handler / sa_sigaction (union head — see the unions decline)
  Mask: [16]ulong,          // glibc sigset_t: 1024 bits
  Flags: int,
  Restorer: IntPtr);        // glibc-internal; set to IntPtr.Zero

extern "libc"
  public method sigaction(signum: int, ref act: SigAction, out old: SigAction): int;
end;
```

<a id="sec-reserved-for-future-revisions"></a>
<a id="sec-deferred-ffi-surface"></a>
### 32.14 Deferred FFI surface

*(What remains deferred is recorded with its blockers, not as bare names — rationale §16.7.)*

1. **Exporting Bezel methods to native callers.** Blockers: (a) symbol-export/C-ABI entry generation belongs to the module/build layer (proposal 0034); (b) runtime initialization for a foreign process entering a Bezel `.so` on an unregistered thread ("runtime not yet started" is open — [§32.10](#sec-boundary-contract)'s foreign-thread obligations presuppose a started runtime); (c) no consumer in the binding corpus. Re-defer until an embedding use case exists.
2. **Calling function pointers received from native** (`dlsym` results): the recorded shape is an `FnPtr<F>` intrinsic (`FromIntPtr`, `Invoke`) — the highest-risk primitive in this space (it executes, not merely corrupts). `Interop.CodeAddress` is one-way precisely so this stays independently deferred; it takes its own proposal once a plugin/loader case sets the evidence bar.
3. **By-value structs, struct-receiving callbacks, and float/double single-field records** (Stage D): requires frontend ABI *classification* (eightbyte splitting, INTEGER/SSE classing, hidden `sret`) atop [§32.13](#sec-c-compatible-records)'s layout engine, per target, in both call directions — large, with real miscompile risk; the only corpus casualty is `div_t`-style small-struct returns. Ships only behind a dedicated review cycle with per-target ABI-classification tests.
4. **`ForeignHandle<T>`** (object↔`IntPtr` handles, the `GCHandle` analog) — deferred with recorded reasons (rationale §16.7), including [§32.12](#sec-foreign-memory)'s no-object-address invariant; the registry idiom ([§32.8](#sec-callbacks)) covers the retained-callback shape with strictly better failure behavior (graceful miss, not silent use-after-free). Reopening condition recorded: a measured registry cost that matters, or a native API that requires the user pointer to be the object itself.
5. **True call-site varargs** — declined for v1 ([§32.11](#sec-symbol-binding)); the v2 candidate if per-arity aliases proliferate in real bindings.
6. **Foreign-thread registration** for long-lived embedder threads — deferred with item 1's blocker (b).
7. **Inline arrays of C-compatible records** (`[N]R`) as record fields and extern parameters — a recorded liftable v1 bound ([§32.5](#sec-ffi-compatible-types), [§32.13](#sec-c-compatible-records)): C struct-array fields exist in the wild; lifting is layout work plus tests on §32.13's engine, no new mechanism.
8. **First-class runtime library loading** (program-controlled `dlopen`-style loading and binding of extern blocks, deferring [§32.11](#sec-symbol-binding)'s startup resolution): subsumed by items 1–2's runtime questions. (Binding `dlopen`/`dlsym` themselves through the FFI as opaque `IntPtr` handles remains expressible, [§32.7](#sec-pointers-and-intptr); what is deferred is calling the resolved pointers — item 2.)

<a id="sec-program-entry-point"></a>
## 33. Program Entry Point

<a id="sec-the-main-method"></a>
### 33.1 The `Main` method

Every Bezel executable has exactly one entry point: a `public static method Main` declared on a class in the **root compilation** ([§2.8.4](#sec-program-assembly)) — with several qualifying candidates permitted only under [§33.5](#sec-program-entry-point-resolution)'s explicit disambiguation. The **main module** is the module containing the selected entry point (when the root compilation is an import SCC of several modules ([§2.5](#sec-dependency-resolution)), every member module's classes are searched — the build-target rule; several candidates across members are the ordinary [§33.5](#sec-program-entry-point-resolution) conflict). A qualifying signature in a dependency artifact is **inert** ([§2.8.4](#sec-program-assembly) rule 3): never selected, never a conflict, an ordinary method. The runtime locates the entry point and invokes it to start the program.

<a id="sec-accepted-signatures"></a>
### 33.2 Accepted signatures

```bezel
public static method Main()
public static method Main(args: Array<string>)
public static method Main(): int
public static method Main(args: Array<string>): int
public static async method Main(): Task
public static async method Main(args: Array<string>): Task
public static async method Main(): Task<int>
public static async method Main(args: Array<string>): Task<int>
```

A signature outside this set does not qualify as an entry point; a method named `Main` with a non-qualifying signature is an ordinary method.

For the `async` forms, the runtime drives `Main`'s task as the main domain's first continuation and blocks the **startup thread** — which runs outside any domain ([§30.13](#sec-runtime-model)) — until the task settles; the pool's workers drain the main domain meanwhile. This is the mechanism [§30.3](#sec-the-task-taskt-and-ownedtaskt-types) cites: the one legitimate blocking wait, at the process edge.

`Main` must be `public` and `static`. An instance method named `Main` does not qualify.

<a id="sec-exit-code"></a>
### 33.3 Exit code and termination

When `Main` returns `int` or `Task<int>`, the returned value becomes the process exit code. Otherwise, normal completion produces an exit code of 0.

**Uncaught exception:** an exception escaping `Main` (or the awaited `Main` task faulting) produces exit code **70** (the conventional software-error code, matching `EX_SOFTWARE`), after the runtime prints the exception's type, message, stack trace, `CauseChain`, and `SupersededChain` ([§31.4](#sec-standard-exception-types)) to standard error. The report's content is the list just given; it is not defined as a call to `ToString()` ([§31.4](#sec-standard-exception-types)), which renders no stack trace. The [§22.13](#sec-static-initialization-order) shutdown sequence (static `owned` disposal) still runs, and it runs with this exception's handling already complete — nothing is in flight when the pass begins, so a disposer that throws inside it supersedes nothing and is reported separately under [§22.13](#sec-static-initialization-order)'s exit-time rule.

**Live domains at exit:** when `Main` completes, spawned domains that have not completed are **abandoned**: the runtime signals no cancellation, runs no further continuations of theirs, and proceeds to the shutdown sequence — their owned state is reclaimed by the process exit, not by disposal, and their pending effects are lost. A program that needs a spawned domain's work must join it (await its completion task) before returning; the abandonment rule makes `Main`'s return the single authoritative end of computation rather than introducing an implicit barrier. In-flight continuations of the **main** domain queued behind `Main`'s completion are likewise not run.

**`Environment.Exit(code)`:** callable from any domain; it initiates the same shutdown sequence (no further continuations anywhere, static `owned` disposal on the dedicated shutdown thread, then process exit with `code`). It never returns. Like abandonment above, it is a statement that remaining work is deliberately discarded.

**Exit-time disposal faults.** Every determination above fixes the exit code **before** [§22.13](#sec-static-initialization-order)'s shutdown pass begins — `Main`'s `int` return and normal completion's 0 because the pass runs after `Main` completes, an uncaught exception's 70 and `Environment.Exit`'s argument because both are stated above as fixed ahead of the sequence — and no event inside the pass changes it. A destructor that throws during the pass is therefore reported to standard error under [§22.13](#sec-static-initialization-order)'s exit-time rule and mints no exit code of its own; this section has no row for it by decision, not by omission.

<a id="sec-command-line-arguments"></a>
### 33.4 Command-line arguments

The `args` parameter, when present, contains the command-line arguments. The program's own executable path is not included; `args[0]` is the first user-supplied argument.

`args` is typed `Array<string>` (the heap-allocated form, [§15.2](#sec-heap-arrays)). This matches the rest of the standard library, where collection-typed parameters are uniformly `Array<T>` or an `IList<T>`/`IEnumerable<T>` interface. The runtime constructs `args` once at program entry and does not mutate it; users who want fixed-size discipline do not call resize methods on it.

Programs that want to forward args to a method expecting `IEnumerable<string>` or `IList<string>` can pass `args` directly. Programs that need a specifically-sized inline buffer (for FFI marshalling, for example) construct a fresh inline array from the args' contents.

<a id="sec-program-entry-point-resolution"></a>
### 33.5 Resolution

A program is ill-formed if more than one method qualifies as the entry point. This applies both across classes (multiple classes each declaring a qualifying `Main`) and within a single class (one class declaring more than one of the eight signature shapes from [§33.2](#sec-accepted-signatures)). The search space is the root compilation only ([§2.8.4](#sec-program-assembly)): a qualifying `Main` in a dependency artifact is inert and never conflicts.

For the cross-class case, the build tool must accept a disambiguation naming the class whose `Main` is the entry point (spelled `--main-class FullyQualifiedName` in this specification's examples); the named class is selected as the entry point and a successful build ensues. Without disambiguation, the compiler produces an error listing every qualifying `Main` it found.

For the within-class case, no flag-based disambiguation is provided: a class may declare at most one qualifying `Main`. A class that overloads `Main` with multiple qualifying signatures is rejected at compile time with a clear error pointing to the ambiguous overloads. (A class may still declare a non-qualifying `Main` alongside a qualifying one — for example, an instance method named `Main` does not qualify, so it does not conflict.)

The exact CLI surface is implementation-defined — different tools may use `--main`, `--entry-point`, project-file properties, or other surfaces — but every conforming implementation must expose a mechanism semantically equivalent to "name the fully-qualified class whose `Main` to use." The mechanism's spelling is part of [§2.6](#sec-build-phases)'s implementation-defined build-tool surface, as every build request's is ([§2.8.4](#sec-program-assembly) rule 1); `--main-class FullyQualifiedName` is the spelling this specification uses in examples.

<a id="sec-example"></a>
### 33.6 Example

```bezel
module HelloWorld;

class Program
  public static method Main(args: Array<string>)
    if args.Count > 0 then
      Console.WriteLine($"Hello, {args[0]}!");
    else
      Console.WriteLine("Hello, Bezel!");
    end;
  end Main;
end Program;
```

A library build has no entry point ([§2.8.4](#sec-program-assembly)); a qualifying `Main` in a library compilation is an ordinary method.

---

<a id="sec-comments-and-documentation"></a>
## 34. Comments and Documentation

Three comment forms ([§1.5](#sec-comments)):

- `// ...` line comment.
- `/* ... */` block comment, does not nest.
- `/// ...` documentation comment.

Documentation comments use XML element syntax. Recognized tags include `<summary>`, `<param>`, `<paramref>`, `<typeparam>`, `<typeparamref>`, `<returns>`, `<exception>`, `<remarks>`, `<example>`, `<see>`, `<seealso>` (`<typeparam>`, `<typeparamref>`, and `<paramref>` — generic declarations are documented like any other). The compiler preserves them in output metadata for documentation generators; it does not interpret tag content beyond preservation. Unrecognized tags are preserved verbatim in the same metadata: recognition affects only how documentation tooling may render a tag, never compilation.

Documentation comments are meaningful only immediately before a declaration.

```bezel
/// <summary>
/// Represents a bank account with deposit and withdrawal functionality.
/// </summary>
public class BankAccount: IBankAccount
  /// <summary>The current balance.</summary>
  public property Balance: decimal;

  /// <summary>
  /// Deposits the specified amount into the account.
  /// </summary>
  /// <param name="amount">The amount to deposit. Must be positive.</param>
  /// <exception cref="ArgumentException">Thrown when amount is non-positive.</exception>
  public method Deposit(amount: decimal)
    if amount <= 0m then
      throw new ArgumentException("Amount must be positive.", nameof(amount));
    end;
    Balance := Balance + amount;
  end Deposit;
end BankAccount;
```


---

<a id="sec-choices"></a>
## 35. Choices

A **choice** is a closed nominal sum: a value type whose values are drawn from a fixed, named set of **cases**, where each case may carry a positional payload. Conceptually it sits between enums (closed, named, no payloads) and records (field products, no case discrimination). Construction is qualified (`FetchOutcome.Failed(504, "upstream timeout")`) — or bare in a declared-result position ([§35.3](#sec-choice-construction)); consumption is `case` with positional destructuring and full static exhaustiveness ([§19.6](#sec-exhaustiveness) — no `_` arm needed when every case is covered). *(the section is numbered here to preserve every existing section number and anchor — its conceptual home in the [§3.1](#sec-type-kinds) kind ordering is between enums and classes.)*

```bezel
public choice FetchOutcome
  Fetched(owned response: Response),      // owned class payload
  NotModified,                            // payload-free case
  Failed(status: int, message: string);   // value payloads

  public method IsSuccess(): bool => (case this of
    Fetched(_)   => true,
    NotModified  => true,
    Failed(_, _) => false);
end FetchOutcome;
```

<a id="sec-choice-declaration"></a>
### 35.1 Declaration

Each value of a choice type has exactly one **active case** at a time; the active case determines which payload components the value carries. A case declares zero or more positional **payload fields**, each `Identifier ":" Type` with an optional leading `owned` marker; a case with no payload list is **payload-free**. Case names are PascalCase by convention and must be distinct within the choice; a case name may not collide with any member name of the choice (the [§11.3](#sec-member-body) member rules apply with cases counted as members), and **`Equals`, `GetHashCode` and `ToString` are reserved against case names on every classification** — not only on the choices where [§35.7](#sec-choice-equality) synthesizes them. The ground is §35.7's own remedy rather than uniformity: outside the auto-hashable set those members are not generated and a use draws the section's use-site compile error, which the author removes **by declaring the member** ([§35.2](#sec-choice-members)) — so a case holding one of those names would put the stated remedy out of reach for exactly the choices that need it. Keying the reservation on classification would also make [§3.6](#sec-derived-type-properties)'s auto-hashable flip legalize or outlaw a case name as a side effect, a consequence its recorded flip list does not carry. A choice declares at least one case. Choices are implicitly sealed and cannot derive from any type; a choice may implement interfaces ([§35.8](#sec-choice-boxing)). Choices cannot have destructors, constructors, instance fields, block-form or storage-backed properties, indexers, or nested types — the same restriction set as enums ([§10.5](#sec-restrictions)), for the same reasons, plus one: a choice's instance storage *is* its cases' payloads, declared in the case list and reachable only through matching.

A choice payload field may not, directly or transitively through value-typed components (record fields, inline-array elements, other choices' payloads), have the declaring choice's own type: a value type cannot contain itself. Recursive sums are expressed with a class node in the cycle (an `owned` class payload whose class holds the nested choice), exactly as recursive records are.

The `owned` payload marker's admissibility follows [§28.1](#sec-where-the-owned-modifier-can-appear)'s type requirement verbatim: admissible on class types, interface types, and bare type parameters; admitted-but-redundant on move-only value types; a compile error on any other type. For a **bare type parameter** payload the marker follows §28.1's per-instantiation erasure — the payload slot is owned at class and interface substitutions and the marker is erased at value and runtime-managed substitutions. Case-payload position is among §28.1's admissible positions.

<a id="sec-choice-members"></a>
### 35.2 Members

A choice body may declare, after the case list, exactly what an enum body may ([§10.4](#sec-methods-properties-static-members)'s exhaustive list; the grammar admits A.4's full `Member` on a choice body and this list rejects the rest): instance methods, expression-bodied read-only instance properties, static methods, `static readonly` fields (including `static owned readonly`), `const` members, and operator overloads. `this` in a choice instance method is a **borrow** of the receiver value — [§9.4](#sec-value-receivers-are-borrows)'s general value-receiver rule, which choices satisfy by construction: no assignable instance storage exists, so its store rejection is vacuous here; owned-consuming operations through `this` are rejected — the same reasoning as [§19.3](#sec-patterns)'s move-only scrutinee rule (a method invocation must not silently consume its receiver), and for a generic choice this keeps method-body checking independent of the instantiation's classification ([§35.11](#sec-choice-generics)). Choice members take the value kinds' dispatch-modifier rule ([§9.2](#sec-record-dispatch-modifiers), *Dispatch modifiers on value kinds*) — statically dispatched, `override` admitted exactly where [§10.5](#sec-restrictions) admits it on an enum, the `Object`-virtual surface spelled `override` or plain — and §10.5's `Equals`/`GetHashCode`/`ToString` replacement rule carries over for the boxable classifications. **That clause scopes replacement, not declarability:** a choice of any classification — owning and borrow-bearing included — may declare plain `Equals(other: C): bool` and `GetHashCode(): int` members, statically dispatched like every choice method; on a non-boxable classification they replace nothing, no box existing to dispatch `Object`'s virtuals through, and are reachable by static dispatch only. [§25.2](#sec-operator-overloading-restrictions)'s co-declaration obligation is therefore *declarable* on every classification; the operand and `Equals(T)`-parameter positions of a **move-only** choice bind **borrows** ([§25.2](#sec-operator-overloading-restrictions)). At an **owning** classification `this` borrows the receiver's storage in place, and an `async` or iterator member is not callable on the receiver ([§9.4](#sec-value-receivers-are-borrows) *Move-only receivers*); a borrowing match over `this` binds a move-only payload under [§19.3](#sec-patterns)'s write-point rule.

A choice has no user constructors, instance fields, or storage-backed properties by design: a choice's construction *is* case selection — a user constructor would have to pick a case, which the qualified case form already spells — and independent instance storage alongside the payload union would make every value part-product-part-sum, destroying the one-active-case invariant that exhaustiveness and disposal both lean on.

**Compiler-provided per-instantiation members.** The standard library's `Result<T, E>` (stdlib [§2.20](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-result)) carries four **conditionally-admitted members** ([§14.2](#sec-conditionally-admitted-members)) — the value-payload combinators `Map`, `MapError`, `AndThen`, `UnwrapOr` — declared in its own listing and admissible **only where the receiver instantiation and the member's result instantiation are both value-like** ([§35.4](#sec-choice-classification) rule 3) — for `Map<U>`/`AndThen<U>` the result is `Result<U, E>`, for `MapError<F>` it is `Result<T, F>`, so a call whose inferred `U` or `F` would make the result instantiation borrow-bearing or owning is rejected exactly as a call on such a receiver is; the rejection lands at the use site under [§3.6](#sec-derived-type-properties) rule 2, the diagnostic naming the classification, the deciding payload, and the owning-match remedy ([§35.5](#sec-choice-matching)). These members stand outside [§35.11](#sec-choice-generics)'s once-and-classification-independent body discipline — their bodies are compiler-provided and exist only where the members are admissible — under [§14.2](#sec-conditionally-admitted-members) rule 1, whose compiler-known-standard-library footing is [§3.6](#sec-derived-type-properties)'s behavior-dispatch reservation together with the compiler-provided-conformance precedent of [§11.8](#sec-static-interface-members); a user-declared choice method cannot be conditioned on the instantiation's classification. A call to one of these members is an **ordinary call**: [§22.5](#sec-optional-parameters-and-named-arguments)'s argument-evaluation order governs it unchanged — every supplied argument expression is evaluated at the call site before the call, whichever case the receiver holds — and being compiler-provided grants no evaluation-order exemption.

<a id="sec-choice-construction"></a>
### 35.3 Construction and payload ownership

Construction is qualified, resolving exactly as enum constants do ([§10.1](#sec-basic-syntax)): `FetchOutcome.NotModified` for a payload-free case (a value expression, not a call), `FetchOutcome.Failed(504, "upstream timeout")` for a payload case. Within a `case` over a choice scrutinee the prefix may be omitted in patterns ([§35.5](#sec-choice-matching)); in expression position outside a **declared-result position** (below) the qualified form is required, exactly as for enum constants outside their scrutinee. For a **generic** choice the type arguments are written at the construction (`Result<int, string>.Ok(value)`): [§14.5](#sec-type-argument-inference)'s posture — type-level arguments are never inferred from constructor arguments — extends to case construction unchanged.

**Declared-result target-typing.** In a **declared-result position** — the top-level operand of a `return e;` statement in a body with a declared return type ([§21.7](#sec-the-return-statement)); the expression body of a member or accessor checked against a declared type ([§22.2](#sec-expression-bodied-methods), [§23.2](#sec-expression-bodied-read-only-properties), [§23.3](#sec-block-form-properties), indexers per [§23.4](#sec-indexers)); or a `return e;` statement or expression body checked against a lambda's **return-type ascription** ([§27.3](#sec-lambda-expressions)) — where the declared type — for an `async` body, the declared `Task<T>`'s result type, per [§30.1](#sec-async-methods)'s completion rule — nullability stripped, is a **choice instantiation** `C<…>` (or non-generic choice `C`) that declares a case named `N`: the form `N(args)` is a **case construction** of `C<…>.N(args)`, and the bare identifier `N` is the payload-free case value `C<…>.N`. The declared type supplies the choice type and all its type arguments whole; nothing is inferred from the construction's arguments ([§14.5](#sec-type-argument-inference)'s posture above is untouched), and partial qualification does not join the family — `Result.Ok(v)`, the generic type with no arguments, remains an error; the admitted spellings are the fully qualified form and the bare case name. Payload-argument binding and ownership are exactly the qualified form's (below): the form is resolved to a case construction before classification or any ownership rule runs. A declared nullable `C<…>?` target-types through the stripped form and the result converts by [§5.1](#sec-implicit-conversions)'s `T → T?` wrapping. The rule reads the declared type **as written**, with the enclosing declaration's type parameters rigid: it does not fire on a bare type parameter (`method M<R>(): R` declares no choice), while a written choice instantiation inside a generic body (`method M<T>(): Result<T, string>`) fires normally; a non-`async` method declared over a `Task`-family type returns a task, not a choice, so the case reading never fires in its body. When the declared type is not a choice, or is a choice without a case of the written name, the form is an ordinary expression under ordinary resolution — nothing changes. Within a declared-result position whose type *is* such a choice, the case reading is **authoritative**: it wins over any same-named local, parameter, member, or type in scope, and the compiler warns on such shadowing — naming the case and the shadowed declaration, with the remedy (qualify the intended member call, bind its result to a differently-named local first, or rename the shadowed binding — a local or parameter cannot be qualified). A payload case written bare, or a payload-free case written with an argument list, is the arity error [§35.5](#sec-choice-matching) names on the pattern side. The qualified construction remains valid everywhere.

The case reading takes exactly the **declared-result** group — group (v) — of the [written-declared-type positions](#sec-written-declared-type-positions) ([§17.7](#sec-the-new-operator)) and does not extend beyond it: not to lambdas whose return type arrives only by target inference (no ascription written), not to argument position (the [§17.7](#sec-the-new-operator) `new()` shorthand draws the same line), not to `var` initialization, typed local declarations, field initializers, default parameter values, or typed assignment targets (the family's other groups — the `new()` shorthand takes three of them, this rule none), and not to subexpression positions within a return operand — in `return (if c then Ok(v) else Error(e));` the branches are operands of the `(if …)` atom ([§20](#sec-the-if-expression)) and resolve ordinarily; write two `return` statements, or the qualified form. (A redundant parenthesized grouping around the whole operand — `return (Ok(v));` — is transparent for this purpose.) Outside the family a bare case-named form keeps its ordinary resolution (or its ordinary-resolution error); when that error arises in a body whose declared result type is a choice with the written case name, the diagnostic carries a note naming the two remedies (move the construction to a declared-result position, or qualify it).

```bezel
// Declared-result positions: the declared type supplies Result<int, string> whole.
public method ParsePercent(text: string): Result<int, string>
  if not int.TryParse(text, out var value) then
    return Error($"not a number: {text}");   // = Result<int, string>.Error(…)
  end;
  if value < 0 or value > 100 then
    return Error($"out of range: {value}");
  end;
  return Ok(value);                          // = Result<int, string>.Ok(…)
end ParsePercent;

public method CachedOutcome(): FetchOutcome => NotModified;   // bare payload-free case value
```

Payload arguments bind to the case's payload fields as to a parameter list, and the `owned` payload marker has exactly an `owned` parameter's call-site semantics ([§22.3](#sec-parameter-modifiers), [§28.3](#sec-local-variables-ownership-and-borrows)):

```bezel
var resp := new Response(headers, stream);
return FetchOutcome.Fetched(move resp);       // call-site marker; resp is moved-from after
```

- An argument to an **owned payload slot** is an owned-consuming position (the [K3.3](#sec-kernel-k3) `owned`-argument position): a fresh producer or unbound owned temporary transfers with no marker (no live binding is invalidated); a named owned binding requires the [§22.3](#sec-parameter-modifiers) call-site marker (`move resp`) and is left moved-from; the consume-site freeze ([K5](#sec-kernel-k5)) rejects the transfer while a live local borrow of the binding exists.
- An argument to a **plain class- or interface-typed payload slot** is a borrow, and [§9.7](#sec-records-and-disposal)'s **no-temporary-source rule** applies verbatim: constructing a choice that holds borrows ([§35.4](#sec-choice-classification)'s holds-borrows property — borrow-bearing or owning alike) from a temporary bound to a borrow-carrying payload is rejected (bind the source to a named local first).
- **Copyable value**, `string`, and runtime-managed payload arguments copy or share per their type kinds; an argument for a payload declared at a function type is a store that admits only a capture-free function value ([§28.3](#sec-borrow-lifetime-rules)'s *choice payloads and inline-array slots of function type*); a **move-only value** payload argument transfers by value-move ([§15.3](#sec-move-only-value-types), [K3.12](#sec-kernel-k3)), the argument expression moved-from after the construction.

The constructed value's own ownership follows its classification ([§35.4](#sec-choice-classification)): a value-like construction is an ordinary value; a borrow-bearing construction is a borrow-carrying value under §9.7's rules; an owning construction is an **owned move-only value** — [§28.3](#sec-producers)'s producers rows for move-only values cover it (the caller takes ownership and discharges by binding, storing, returning, or consuming it), and a construction not bound to any name is an unbound owned temporary under [K8](#sec-kernel-k8)'s full-expression machinery. Orthogonally, a construction of any choice that holds borrows ([§35.4](#sec-choice-classification)'s holds-borrows property) is *additionally* a borrow-carrying value under §9.7's rules — for an owning choice the two regimes compose.

A method returning an owning choice writes the plain type (`method Fetch(url: string): FetchOutcome`); `owned` on the return is admitted-but-redundant per [§28.1](#sec-where-the-owned-modifier-can-appear)'s move-only clause, exactly as for owning inline arrays.

<a id="sec-choice-classification"></a>
### 35.4 The classification

Two derived type properties ([§3.6](#sec-derived-type-properties)) are computed from the payload fields of *all* a choice's cases. The first is the input to the second.

**Holds-borrows ([#3110](https://github.com/s8lap/bezel-lang/issues/3110)).** A choice **holds borrows** — a derived type property in its own right — iff any case has a *borrow-carrying* payload field, under [§9.7](#sec-records-and-disposal)'s field-level definition with its transitivity clause reading **this property** at a nested choice payload. For a generic choice the property is evaluated per instantiation under [§3.6](#sec-derived-type-properties)'s rule 2, a declaration change that flips it is breaking under rule 3, and diagnostics name it under rule 4.

The **choice classification** is then:

1. A choice is **owning** if any case has a payload field marked `owned` (a class, interface, or — at a class or interface instantiation — bare-type-parameter payload), or a payload field of a move-only value type ([§15.3](#sec-move-only-value-types) — an owning inline array or another owning choice, transitively).
2. Otherwise, a choice is **borrow-bearing** if it holds borrows.
3. Otherwise the choice is **value-like**: every payload is a value, a `string`, a runtime-managed type, or (transitively) a value-like record or choice. A value-like choice is an ordinary copyable value type.

Payloads whose **declared** types are runtime-managed reference types (`string`, function types) are classification-neutral — and neutral for holds-borrows — exactly as in [§9.7](#sec-records-and-disposal): such values have unbounded lifetime by construction. And exactly as there, it is the payload's *declared* type that is read: a payload declared `Object` or an interface type is borrow-carrying, so a choice with such a payload **holds borrows** and is borrow-bearing by rule 2 above — it never reaches rule 3, whose enumeration does not admit it in any case ([#3281](https://github.com/s8lap/bezel-lang/issues/3281)).

The two properties are orthogonal by construction: the classification drives copy/move/dispose semantics, holds-borrows drives borrow obligations — it adds obligations, never subtracts semantics. A **borrow-bearing** choice always holds borrows (rule 2); an **owning** choice *can* — `Loaded(owned response: Response, log: Logger)` is owning by rule 1 with `log` a held borrow; a **value-like** choice never does (rule 3's construction). Every choice that holds borrows — whatever its classification — is subject to [§28.3](#sec-local-variables-ownership-and-borrows)'s borrow-lifetime rules through [§9.7](#sec-records-and-disposal)'s bullet list, applied verbatim with "record" read as "record or choice": such a value may not outlive any held borrow's source; may not be constructed from a temporary source; may not be stored in a class instance field or (outside the null-source form) a static field; is constrained in returns, closures, and collection copies; and is forbidden as an `async` method's parameter or result ([§30.1](#sec-async-methods)). A live local of a choice type that holds borrows counts as a live local borrow of every held borrow's source for the consume-site freeze ([K5.5](#sec-kernel-k5)), exactly as for records.

**Owning choices are move-only value types** ([§15.3](#sec-move-only-value-types)). Every §15.3 rule applies as written: local-to-local assignment moves (unmarked — copies are impossible, so there is nothing for a marker to disambiguate); parameter passing is by value-move; return transfers; a move-only value carrying no borrows may be a class field (the class's destructor disposes it) — an **owning choice that holds borrows** may not be a class field ([§15.3](#sec-move-only-value-types), the holds-borrows property above: it is the only move-only kind that can hold borrows, an owning inline array's slots being `owned`, and the store would let the borrows outlive their sources) — and no move-only value may be a record field; an owning choice may not be a **static** field either — a compile error at the declaration site ([§22.12](#sec-static-members) rule 4's note (g)), since [§22.13](#sec-static-initialization-order)'s program-exit pass does not enrol it and [§28.5](#sec-owned-fields) admits the `owned` field modifier only on class- and interface-typed fields, so nothing would dispose it (the spelling for a process-global singleton carrying one is a `static owned readonly` field of a **class** holding the choice, whose destructor disposes it); locals are auto-disposed at scope end with the must-use warning ([K3.14](#sec-kernel-k3)); exception edges discharge implicitly ([K3.15](#sec-kernel-k3)); `using var` is admitted — it locks reassignment and suppresses that warning ([§28.3](#sec-owned-local-discharge-requirement)), the auto-dispose running either way, and an unmarked move-only initializer is adopted, not pinned ([§28.10](#sec-using-var)). And the async seam is closed on the owning side as on the borrow-bearing side: no [§30.5](#sec-result-lifetime-and-task-disposal) producer row admits a move-only value result, so a `Task<T>` or `OwningTask<T>` declared over an owning choice is a compile error at the declaration — for generic declarations, re-checked after substitution at the instantiation site ([§30.5](#sec-result-lifetime-and-task-disposal), [§35.11](#sec-choice-generics)). Two owning-choice rules are *stronger* than the owning-inline-array precedent, deliberately:

- **Disposal is defined by the active case.** Disposing an owning choice value disposes the active case's `owned` payloads (in payload declaration order) and, recursively, any move-only payloads; payload-free and value-payload cases dispose nothing. There is no per-slot moved-from state to consider: payloads are reachable only through matching, never as assignable slots — the value is always wholly owned or wholly moved-from. (This is a statement about the *storage* model — no payload is an assignable slot with a persistent moved-from state demanding restoration. The owning match's within-construct window — some payloads transferred at selection, the remainder disposed at construct completion, [§35.5](#sec-owning-match), positional slots, marked named slots, and the payloads reached recursively through a nested destructuring alike — routes inside one consume, at every level it reaches, and leaves this rule untouched.)
- **Drop-on-overwrite is defined and automatic** (derives: [K3.11](#sec-kernel-k3)). Whole-value reassignment of an owning-choice local or field *disposes the displaced value* per [§28.7](#sec-reassigning-owned-fields), like an owned class binding. A choice has no partial states, so the single-value form of that rule applies as written; the owning inline array — whose slots *can* be individually moved-from — takes the same rule per slot ([§15.3](#sec-move-only-value-types)). Reassignment is a consume of the displaced value and is frozen while borrows of it live ([K5.2](#sec-kernel-k5)). `x := null;` on an owned `C?` location likewise disposes the displaced value's payloads ([§35.9](#sec-choice-nullable)).

<a id="sec-choice-matching"></a>
### 35.5 Matching

<a id="sec-choice-borrowing-match"></a>
#### The borrowing match (the default)

Matching a choice value **non-destructively** is the default everywhere, and [§19.3](#sec-patterns)'s rules apply verbatim: a pattern binding is a borrow whose source is the scrutinee's source; the scrutinee retains its ownership state; the construct never moves from the scrutinee. For a value-like choice, payload bindings are copies (value payloads) or shared references (`string`/runtime-managed payloads); for borrow-bearing and owning choices, class-typed payload bindings are borrows, and a binding of a payload of **move-only value type** ([§15.3](#sec-move-only-value-types) — an owning inline array, or a nested owning choice) is likewise a **borrow** ([#3094](https://github.com/s8lap/bezel-lang/issues/3094)) — [§19.3](#sec-patterns)'s move-only scrutinee rule applied at the slot: a copy is forbidden and a borrowing match transfers nothing, so the borrow is the only consistent reading; reads through the binding are admitted, and consuming operations through it (`move b[i]`) are rejected — the binding does not own. Because the borrow is in place, it may not be live at a write point of the construct, and a use of it as a receiver or operand, or of a closure that captured it at a call that invokes it or takes it as an argument, is live across that call, unless the scrutinee's source is provably unwritten — [§19.3](#sec-patterns) *Move-only payload bindings across a write point*. A local that is not mutably captured and not named by a `ref` or `out` argument in the construct is such a source, and so is a `readonly` field outside its construction window and a binding over either; `this`, a mutable field, an element and a `ref` parameter are not. An **unmarked read of a named owned binding in scrutinee position stays a borrowing match** — [§19.3](#sec-patterns)'s move-only scrutinee rule, now load-bearing: it is what makes *peeking* at an owned outcome legal and non-consuming.

```bezel
var outcome := client.Fetch(url);       // owned move-only local
case outcome of                          // borrowing match; outcome unchanged
  Failed(var s, _) when s >= 500 => ScheduleRetry(),
  _                              => ()
end;
// outcome is still owned here; discharge or auto-drop per §28.3.
```

<a id="sec-owning-match"></a>
#### The owning match

An **owning match** transfers the selected case's `owned` and move-only value payloads into the arm's bindings and consumes the scrutinee value. It is triggered in exactly two scrutinee forms — each announcing the consume at the site, in the [K3.13](#sec-kernel-k3) sense that something at the site tells the reader the value is consumed:

1. **An unbound owned temporary** of owning-choice classification — a fresh construction, an owning-choice-returning call, a `move` result. This is the dominant shape and needs no marker, as fresh producers never do:

   ```bezel
   case client.Fetch(url) of                 // owning match over the temporary
     Fetched(var r)       => RenderOwned(move r),    // r: owned Response in the arm
     NotModified          => RenderCached(),
     Failed(var s, var m) => ShowError(s, m)
   end;
   ```

   The scrutinee temporary's full expression is the **whole `case` construct** — [K8.3](#sec-kernel-k8), applied unchanged — so payloads not transferred into bindings (discarded slots like `Fetched(_)`, and the payloads of the value when a `_` arm, or a non-destructuring arm on a path on which it does not consume its binding, is selected) are disposed when the construct completes, by the same unbound-temporary pass that disposes the container. An exception out of an arm disposes the not-yet-consumed remainder during unwinding ([K3.15](#sec-kernel-k3)).

2. **A named owned binding under an explicit scrutinee transfer marker** — `case move outcome of …`, the scrutinee an identifier-operand `move` expression ([§28.8.1](#sec-the-move-expression); derives: [K3.4](#sec-kernel-k3)'s marked-transfer family; frozen per [K5.1](#sec-kernel-k5)). This is the marker discipline ([§28.3](#sec-local-variables-ownership-and-borrows) *Move semantics for owned locals*) extended to scrutinee position, with its exact rules: the marker is required because the unmarked read is a borrow (above), an unmarked read never silently consumes, the marker on a borrowed or fresh-producer scrutinee is an error, and the consumed binding is left **moved-from** when the construct completes. Because the transfer hands payloads **alive** to the arm's bindings — no disposed flag is set, nothing faults — the consume is frozen while a live local borrow of the binding's value exists, precisely the reasoning that froze the owning-iterator `yield return` ([§29.2](#sec-iterator-yield-ownership)) and left Pattern B `await` unfrozen ([§30.5](#sec-result-lifetime-and-task-disposal) sets the disposed flag; this construct does not). *(The scrutinee marker is not redundant here, though move-only values move unmarked into owning stores ([§15.3](#sec-move-only-value-types); [K3.12](#sec-kernel-k3)): scrutinee position has an unmarked borrow reading to disambiguate, so the marker carries meaning.)*

   ```bezel
   var outcome := client.Fetch(url);
   case move outcome of                      // marked consume; outcome moved-from after `end`
     Fetched(var r) => do
       using var resp := move r;             // adopt: scope-bound disposal (§28.10)
       Render(resp);
     end,
     NotModified          => RenderCached(),
     Failed(var s, var m) => ShowError(s, m)
   end;
   ```

In an owning match, an `owned`-payload binding (`var r` above) is an **owned local of the arm body's scope**, and [§28.3](#sec-local-variables-ownership-and-borrows)'s standard rules apply to it on every arm-exit edge — the [§29.2](#sec-iterator-yield-ownership) owning-iteration-variable model: falling off the arm still owning the value auto-drops it with the must-use warning naming the binding and the standard remedies (`using var u := move r;` adoption in a `do … end` arm, an owned-consuming call, an explicit `r.Dispose()`, `_ := r;`); exception edges discharge implicitly. In *expression-position* arms (which cannot contain statements, [§19.2](#sec-arms)), the warning-free discharges are an owned-consuming call (`RenderOwned(move r)`) or §19.2's helper-method extraction. A **non-destructuring** arm's binding (`var y => …`) names the consumed value itself, which the construct holds until it completes — in either scrutinee form, the whole construct its boundary ([K8.3](#sec-kernel-k8)'s boundary; its borrow reading holds during trial, as *Guards: borrow during trial, transfer on selection* states; the named-temporary shape [K8.5](#sec-kernel-k8) states for a binding atom): a consume of the binding in the arm body — a plain store (`var z := y`), an owned-consuming argument, the arm's result flowing into an owning location — **receives** the value, moving it as [K3.12](#sec-kernel-k3) moves a move-only value into any owning location, and the construct's completion pass then has nothing to dispose; on a path that leaves the arm without consuming it, the value is disposed at construct completion, as above, with no must-use warning. **Copyable** value payloads bind as copies. A payload of **move-only value type** ([§15.3](#sec-move-only-value-types) — an owning inline array, or a nested owning choice) **transfers into its binding at arm selection exactly as an `owned` payload does** ([#3094](https://github.com/s8lap/bezel-lang/issues/3094)): [K3.12](#sec-kernel-k3) already moves a move-only value into every owning location it flows to, and [§28.1](#sec-where-the-owned-modifier-can-appear)'s marker is admitted-but-redundant on such a field, so the marked and unmarked field spellings behave identically; the binding is then a move-only owned local of the arm body's scope under §15.3's standard rules — auto-disposed at scope end with the must-use warning ([K3.14](#sec-kernel-k3)), moved unmarked into owning stores, exception edges discharging implicitly ([K3.15](#sec-kernel-k3)). Discarded owned and move-only value slots (`Fetched(_)`), like unlisted ones, are disposed at construct completion as above — [§35.4](#sec-choice-classification)'s recursive active-case disposal. Nested destructuring of a **class- or interface-typed** owned payload arises only in the **named** form, and only with a class head — classes have no positional pattern surface, and an interface-typed pattern head is not admitted in v1 ([§19.3](#sec-patterns)) — and it routes nothing: each nested named slot is a property getter read, a borrow that can mint no obligation ([§28.6](#sec-leak-prevention)), so the payload itself is never transferred and is disposed at construct completion exactly as a discarded slot. Through a **move-only choice payload** — the one nested move-only shape with a pattern surface (inline arrays have none) — nested destructuring **routes recursively** in an owning match, and the recursion runs exactly through the slots that **transfer**: a positional slot, and any pattern nested within one. A nested pattern beneath an **unmarked named slot** routes nothing at any depth: the payload and everything inside it stay with the consumed value, disposed at construct completion, and every binding beneath that slot is a borrow ([§19.3](#sec-patterns)). A **marked named slot** cannot carry a nested pattern at all — its right-hand side is a binding, by admission condition (iii) ([§19.3](#sec-patterns)). Where the recursion runs, inner bindings receive their payloads at selection, and the un-bound remainder at every level is disposed at construct completion. (In a borrowing match, nested destructuring binds borrows at every level — the default above, unchanged.)

```bezel
public choice AcquireOutcome
  Ready(conns: [4 owned]Connection?),          // move-only value payload — owning (§35.4)
  Empty;
end AcquireOutcome;

case pool.Acquire() of                         // owning match over the temporary
  Ready(var b) => Dispatch(b),                 // b transfers at selection (§15.3 local);
                                               //   the call consumes it by value-move
  Empty        => ()
end;
// A Ready(_) arm, or an unmatched Ready under a `_` arm, would instead dispose
// the array's slots at construct completion — trace (b) below, unchanged.
```

A **marked named slot** (`Fetched(move response = var r)`, [§19.3](#sec-patterns)) rides this machinery unchanged: during pattern matching and guard evaluation its binding is a borrow like every other pattern binding (*Guards* below — a guard-declined arm transfers nothing, and two arms marking the same payload are two candidate recipients, not two owners); ownership transfers into the binding at arm selection exactly as the corresponding positional slot's would; and the binding is then the same owned local of the arm body's scope as above, on every arm-exit edge. The un-transferred remainder — unlisted fields, unmarked named slots, discarded siblings — is disposed at construct completion, or during unwinding, by the disposal traces below, which cover marked named slots with no new path: the marker changes routing within the already-consumed value, never whether or when the value is consumed.

**What does not trigger an owning match:** an unmarked named-binding scrutinee (borrowing, above); a borrowed scrutinee of any provenance (field read, parameter, `this`); and the position of the *construct's result* — whether the `case`'s value flows into an owned slot is the [§28.3](#sec-producers) arm-meet row's business and has no bearing on how the scrutinee is consumed.

<a id="sec-owning-match-guards"></a>
#### Guards: borrow during trial, transfer on selection

In an owning match, pattern bindings are **borrows of the scrutinee's payloads** — at every level a nested pattern reaches — **during pattern matching and guard evaluation**; ownership transfers into the selected arm's bindings **when an arm is selected** (its pattern matched and its guard, if any, evaluated true). A guard therefore observes borrows and cannot consume a binding (owned-consuming positions reject a borrow); after selection, the arm body sees the bindings in their owning-match states.

If **no arm** of an owning match selects: in statement position the construct completes with no action and the consumed value's payloads are disposed at construct completion (the value was consumed by the announcing scrutinee form; its contents have nowhere to go); in expression position `MatchFailureException` is raised ([§19.6](#sec-exhaustiveness)) and the payloads are disposed during unwinding by the standard exception-path machinery. Exhaustive matches — the normal case — never reach either.

<a id="sec-case-patterns"></a>
#### Case patterns

- A **payload-free case** is matched by its bare name (`NotModified`) — a constant-style pattern resolving through the scrutinee-type prefix-omission rule, extended from enums ([§10.6](#sec-case-matching), [§19.8](#sec-inside-enum-scrutinees)): within a `case` whose scrutinee is a choice, the choice prefix may be omitted. A name resolving to a case is a case pattern, never a type test.
- A **payload case** is matched by a positional destructuring pattern `CaseName(slot, …)` with the case's exact payload arity — grammar A.7's existing destructuring production. All [§19.3](#sec-patterns) slot rules carry over: naked identifiers bind, `var x` binds explicitly, `_` discards per slot, per-slot `|` alternatives among binding-free members, nested patterns recurse.
- A payload case's slots may equivalently be matched **by name** — `Fetched(response = var r)` — resolving the case's payload field names ([§19.3](#sec-patterns) *Named destructuring*, [§35.1](#sec-choice-declaration)); the slot list is positional or named, never mixed. All the same slot rules carry over. The borrowing match binds payload borrows. In an owning match a named slot transfers exactly when it is **marked**: `Fetched(move response = var r)` transfers the payload into `r` at arm selection, per slot, exactly as the corresponding positional slot would ([§19.3](#sec-patterns) — owning match, `owned`-marked or move-only value payload, binding RHS); an **unmarked** named slot does not transfer — an unmarked-named-matched owned or move-only value payload is borrowed during the arm and disposed at construct completion ([§19.3](#sec-patterns)). A program wanting the payload transferred writes the positional destructure, or the marked named slot.
- A payload case may **not** be matched bare: `Fetched` without parentheses is a compile error naming the arity — matching a payload while ignoring it is spelled visibly as `Fetched(_)`, the same explicitness §19.3 demands of record destructuring arity.
- Payload-free case names are admissible members of `|` **alternative lists** (and count toward exhaustiveness, [§19.6](#sec-exhaustiveness)); payload-carrying case patterns are not, even in the all-discard form — they are destructurings, not constants ([§19.3](#sec-patterns)).

<a id="sec-owning-match-traces"></a>
#### Disposal traces (the four paths of an owning match)

All four paths ride existing machinery; none introduces a new disposal-site kind.

**(a) Normal path, payload bound and adopted.**

```bezel
case client.Fetch(url) of
  Fetched(var r) => do
    using var resp := move r;    // r moved into resp; resp disposed at arm-body end
    Render(resp);
  end,
  NotModified          => RenderCached(),
  Failed(var s, var m) => ShowError(s, m)
end;
```

The scrutinee temporary is produced owned; arm selection transfers the payload's ownership into `r`; the adopt idiom moves it into `resp`, disposed at the `do … end` block's close; the container value, now payload-empty, is reclaimed at construct completion with nothing left to dispose. Exactly one disposal of the payload, at a statically known site.

**(b) Normal path, payload discarded.**

```bezel
case client.Fetch(url) of
  Fetched(_)  => Count("hit"),     // owned payload never bound
  _           => Count("other")
end;
```

The `Fetched(_)` discard binds nothing; the payload stays with the consumed scrutinee value and is disposed at construct completion by the unbound-temporary pass — the "disposal runs after every use within the expression" ordering [K8.1](#sec-kernel-k8) defines. The `_` arm on a `NotModified`/`Failed` value disposes nothing (those cases carry no owned payloads).

**(c) Guard-declined path.**

```bezel
case move outcome of
  Fetched(var r) when r.IsStale() => do _ := r; RefetchLater(); end,
  Fetched(var r)                  => do using var resp := move r; Render(resp); end,
  _                               => ()
end;
```

During the first arm's guard, `r` is a **borrow** — `r.IsStale()` is an ordinary borrowing call, and a consuming use in the guard would be rejected. If the guard declines, no transfer has happened; the second arm's selection performs it. Two arms binding the same payload are two candidate *recipients*, not two owners: transfer happens once, at selection.

**(d) Exception path.**

```bezel
case move outcome of
  Fetched(var r)       => do Validate(r); Publish(move r); end,    // Validate may throw
  NotModified          => (),
  Failed(var s, var m) => throw new UpstreamException(m)
end;
```

If `Validate(r)` throws, `r` — an owned local of the arm-body scope — is disposed by the exception-path discharge ([K3.15](#sec-kernel-k3)) exactly as any owned local is; the consumed scrutinee (already payload-transferred) has nothing further to dispose. If the `Failed` arm's `throw` runs, that case's payloads are values and need no disposal; an owned payload in a throwing arm is covered by the same unwind pass. The moved-from `outcome` binding is skipped by every pass, as always.

<a id="sec-choice-diagnostics"></a>
#### Diagnostics

Per [§3.6](#sec-derived-type-properties) rule 4, the new errors name the classification and the rule. Each property-keyed rejection of an owning choice (boxing, sendability, `new()`) names the payload that decides the classification; the consume-site freeze reuses [§28.3](#sec-local-variables-ownership-and-borrows)'s diagnostic; and the must-use warning at an owning-match binding's implicit drop names the binding and the arm-position remedies. Recommended wordings — for these, for a payload case written without a payload pattern, for a misplaced `case move`, and for an arm whose refutable slot pattern leaves a case uncovered under [§19.6](#sec-exhaustiveness)'s one-level rule — are teaching text in the code-generation reference ([§4.6](Bezel_For_Code_Generation.md#sec-recommended-diagnostic-wordings)).

<a id="sec-choice-exhaustiveness"></a>
### 35.6 Exhaustiveness

The static-proof rule for choice scrutinees is [§19.6](#sec-exhaustiveness)'s choice bullet: coverage is counted **per case name, one level deep** — a payload-free case by a constant-style pattern naming it (directly or in a `|` list), a payload case by a destructuring whose every slot is irrefutable. Guarded arms and refutable-slot arms contribute nothing to the static proof. Because the case set is closed by the declaration, exhaustiveness holds across module boundaries, and adding a case to a published choice is a source-breaking change for consumers exactly as adding a sealed leaf is.

Generic choices need no per-instantiation machinery: for `case r of Ok(var v) => …, Error(var e) => … end` over a `Result<int, ParseError>` scrutinee, coverage is by case *name* — the bindings take the substituted payload types. Class-hierarchy sums put the discriminant in the runtime *type*, which is why generic-leaf coverage over a closed hierarchy is not statically proven and requires an irrefutable arm ([§19.6](#sec-exhaustiveness-generic-leaves)); a choice's discriminant is a name, and the problem does not arise — for a value-shaped generic sum a choice is the steered spelling, and none of §19.6's generic-hierarchy limitation applies to it. Nested refutable patterns (`Ok(0)`) are admitted syntactically and contribute nothing statically; a program wanting nested totality writes nested `case` constructs, which are proven exhaustive level by level.

<a id="sec-choice-equality"></a>
### 35.7 Equality, hashing, `ToString`

A **value-like** choice is **auto-hashable** ([§3.6](#sec-derived-type-properties), the [§9.2](#sec-body-records) property) when every payload field of every case is a [§9.2](#sec-body-records) admissible component type, with one addition to the recursive rule: another auto-hashable choice is admissible. The generated `=` is true exactly when both operands have the same active case and every corresponding payload compares equal by its type's `=`; the generated `GetHashCode` combines the case discriminant with the per-payload hashes (order-sensitive, [§8.3](#sec-equals-and-gethashcode)); the generated `ToString` produces `"TypeName.CaseName(field1: value1, …)"`, and `"TypeName.CaseName"` for a payload-free case. Methods, computed properties, statics, and operators other than a homogeneous `=`/`<>` neither qualify nor disqualify, per §9.2's membership list; a homogeneous `=`/`<>` overload disqualifies the choice exactly as it disqualifies a record, and [§25.2](#sec-operator-overloading-restrictions)'s co-declaration rule then supplies the equality surface. A payload field marked **`equality skip`** ([§9.2](#sec-equality-skip); grammar A.3 `CaseField`) reads per [§9.2](#sec-equality-skip)'s skip-model table — excluded from its case's payload comparison and hash, exempt from admissibility — under one gate the record form lacks: the clause never changes classification ([§35.4](#sec-choice-classification)), so the rescue holds only while the choice remains **value-like** — an `owned` or class-typed payload keeps its classification and such a choice is non-auto-hashable whatever the clause says (next paragraph); a skipped class-typed payload never rescues a choice, where a skipped class-typed field can leave a borrow-bearing record hashable ([§9.2](#sec-equality-skip)).
