- A primary-constructor parameter is plain, `owned`, or class- or interface-typed `scoped`; `ref`, `out`, and a function-typed `scoped` parameter are rejected semantically, and a body-referenced `scoped` parameter is captured as a non-owned field of the constructed object under [§28.14](#sec-scoped-callback-parameters)'s scoped construction ([§22.10](#sec-capture-rule-and-layout-stability)).
- A plain function-typed primary-constructor parameter is not referenced in a body position: its capture would store a call-bounded parameter in a field ([§22.10](#sec-capture-rule-and-layout-stability); K2.4).
- A static constructor takes no parameters and no access modifier.
- At a call, each supplied argument binds exactly one parameter, each parameter is bound by at most one supplied argument, and every parameter declaring no default is bound by some argument; naming a parameter already bound positionally, or naming one twice, is a compile error, while leaving a required parameter unbound makes the candidate inapplicable ([§22.5](#sec-optional-parameters-and-named-arguments), [§22.6](#sec-overloading)).
- The names one parameter list binds are distinct — a method's, constructor's, operator's, `extern` method's or lambda's (a lambda's destructuring slots counted, `_` exempt), and an indexer's together with its setter's parameter; a function type's parameter names are outside the rule ([§22.1](#sec-method-declarations)).
- A method declared `async` returns `Task`, `Task<T>`, `OwningTask<T>`, `IAsyncEnumerable<T>`, `IAsyncEnumerator<T>`, `IOwningAsyncEnumerable<T>`, or `IOwningAsyncEnumerator<T>`.
- A method using `yield return`/`yield break` does not also use plain `return`.
- An `async` method, `async` lambda, or iterator method (sync or async) declares no `ref` or `out` parameter; an `async` lambda's target function type carries no `ref`/`out` slot ([§30.1](#sec-async-methods), [§29.3](#sec-iterator-methods)).
- `yield` does not appear in lambdas, in `try` blocks whose surrounding statement has a `catch`, or in catch arm bodies or `finally` blocks.
- `return` does not appear in `finally` blocks.
- `break` and `continue` appear only inside loops of the same callable body; a labeled form names the loop label of a lexically enclosing loop statement of that body; neither exits a `finally` block (the target loop — labeled or unlabeled — must not enclose the `finally`; [§21.5](#sec-break-and-continue), [§31.2](#sec-try-catch-finally)).
- A loop label appears only on `while`/`for`/`await for` statements, duplicates no loop label in scope at its declaration, and — when the loop's `end` carries a closer label — matches it per [§1.6](#sec-statements-and-termination): the loop label if the loop has one, the introducing keyword otherwise.
- A local does not take the name of another local declared directly in its block, nor, declared directly in a callable's body block, that of one of the callable's parameters; the bindings of one pattern and the clauses of one binding atom have distinct names; no local, loop variable, arm binding, binding-atom clause, or lambda parameter or destructuring slot takes the name of a local or parameter in scope at its declaration, a setter's implicit `value` included; `_` is exempt ([§21.1](#sec-variable-declarations)).
- `++` and `--` appear only as statements.
- A compound assignment evaluates its target once — each LHS constituent once, getter and setter each once ([§6.6](#sec-compound-assignments), [§17.6](#sec-increment-decrement-on-indexer-slots)); its result stores back directly, or through the checked narrow-integer write-back where [§6.6](#sec-compound-assignments) admits it — any other type mismatch is a compile error.
- Bare `throw` (the expression form without an operand, and equivalently the statement form `throw;`) appears only inside a catch arm body.
- The operand of `throw expr` is an owned expression whose static type is `Exception` or a class deriving from it; primitive, `string`, record, enum, inline-array, unit, function-typed, `Object`-typed, and interface-typed operands are rejected, as are borrowed class references ([§31.1](#sec-throwing)).
- A field initializer does not reference `this`, instance members, or virtual methods.
- A `readonly` field is assigned at most once on any path through one instance construction (initializer and every constructor body in the `this(...)` chain counted together) or, for a `static readonly` one, through one type initialization; an assignment lexically inside a loop body in that window is rejected unconditionally ([§22.8](#sec-field-initializers); whether the rule extends to `readonly` auto-properties is that section's open question).
- A synchronous observation of `this` in a constructor body (instance call, argument, store, type test) occurs only after every [§7.9](#sec-definite-assignment-for-non-nullable-fields)-strict field of the declaring type is definitely assigned; in the `base(...)`/`this(...)` argument position it is always rejected ([§22.7](#sec-observing-this-during-construction)).
- A `virtual`/`override`/`abstract` member is not called on `this` from a constructor body unless the class is `sealed` and not `abstract`; `base.M()` is exempt ([§22.7](#sec-observing-this-during-construction)).
- Reference-typed fields are null-initialized before construction begins; a checked-mode read of a non-nullable reference field still at the watermark raises `NullReferenceException` ([§22.7](#sec-observing-this-during-construction)).
- A `bool`-returning method's `when true`/`when false` nullability postcondition is admitted only on an `out`/`out owned` parameter of nullable type; every path of the declaring body that returns the stated constant must leave the parameter provably non-null, and an override must repeat the clause exactly ([§22.4](#sec-out-nullability-postcondition)).
- In a value-kind instance member body `this` is a borrow of the receiver value, a store landing in the receiver's own storage is a compile error at the member body in each of [§9.4](#sec-value-receivers-are-borrows)'s producing spellings (a chain hopping through a class- or interface-typed member instead lands legally in the borrowed heap object — the mediating shape), and no value kind conforms to an interface declaring a settable property or indexer ([§9.4](#sec-value-receivers-are-borrows)).
- A member call on a copyable value-kind receiver runs over the value its receiver expression denoted at evaluation, a full-expression temporary bounded by the call; no store during the call changes what `this` denotes ([§9.4](#sec-value-receivers-are-borrows); K8.4). A member call on a move-only receiver borrows the receiver's storage in place, bounded by the call. A move-only value disposed in place with no replacement is left in a disposed state that checked mode tests on every read through `this` or a borrowing binding. No `async` or iterator member is called on a move-only receiver ([§9.4](#sec-value-receivers-are-borrows), [§15.3](#sec-move-only-value-types)).
- A record declaring positional fields does not declare a constructor carrying a contract clause ([§9.9](#sec-constructor-only-records)): the auto-generated primary constructor can carry none, so the combination is a compile error at the record declaration, the diagnostic naming the body-record and static-factory remedies.

<a id="sec-async"></a>
### C.6 Async

- `async` does not combine with `abstract` on a method.
- `await` appears only inside `async` methods, `async` lambdas, and the synchronous prefix of `await for`.
- `await` does not appear in static field initializers or static constructor bodies.
- `await using` appears only inside async contexts.
- The `with` clause in `await for ... with token` must be of type `CancellationToken`.
- Awaiting a `Task<T>` for class T (Pattern A — axiom [A3](#sec-axiom-register)) requires the awaited expression to be an admitted borrow source under [§30.5](#sec-result-lifetime-and-task-disposal)'s closure — [K2](#sec-kernel-k2)'s named-location taxonomy, an unbound owned temporary whose borrowed result is confined to its full expression, the chained Pattern A return, or the scoped await-bind desugaring ([§30.5](#sec-the-scoped-await-bind), `.Result` in lockstep) — every other escape of the borrow rejected.
- `await` on a `OwningTask<T>` (Pattern B — A3's owned-transfer container) must appear in an owned-consuming context ([K3](#sec-kernel-k3)'s positions), an owned operand consumed on all edges as a site-announced kill (the [consume table](#sec-consume-table)'s [K3.5](#sec-kernel-k3) row — no marker, no freeze, disposed-flag backstop; K4.2), a second await a compile-time moved-from read on an owned operand and `InvalidOperationException` on a borrowed one ([§30.5](#sec-result-lifetime-and-task-disposal)).
- `OwningTask<T>` is a compile error when T's underlying (nullability-stripped) type is neither a class nor an interface type ([§14.4](#sec-owned-as-a-generic-argument)). The argument-type check is performed during type checking; the diagnostic identifies the rejected argument and points at [§14.4](#sec-owned-as-a-generic-argument).
- An `async` method, `async` lambda, or async iterator declares no parameter, result, or element type that is a borrow-bearing record, a borrow-bearing inline array ([§15.1](#sec-inline-arrays)), or a choice that holds borrows ([§30.1](#sec-async-methods), [§35.4](#sec-choice-classification)'s holds-borrows property; [K2.1](#sec-kernel-k2) + [K6.1](#sec-kernel-k6)); `CancellationToken` is the single stdlib-certified exception (axiom [A10](#sec-axiom-register)); for generic async methods the check re-applies after substitution.
- No `ref`/`out` parameters on async methods, async lambdas, or iterators; no async lambda targets a function type with `ref`/`out` slots ([§30.1](#sec-async-methods); K2.1 + K6.1).
- An `await using var` of a class implementing `IAsyncDisposable` without a destructor (or of interface static type) is not live across a `yield return` in an async iterator ([§30.7](#sec-asynchronous-programming-async-iterators)).
- A local of borrow-bearing record or inline-array type, or of a choice type that holds borrows ([§35.4](#sec-choice-classification)'s holds-borrows property), does not cross a suspension point (`await`, `await using`, `await for`, or `yield return` in an iterator or async iterator — [§29.4](#sec-lazy-evaluation)) unless every borrow it carries has a frame-resident source ([§30.1](#sec-async-methods); K2.1 + K6.1).
- A blocking wait or blocking acquisition never parks a thread inside a domain continuation — the blocking forms rejected at compile time in `async` bodies, `InvalidOperationException` where a continuation would actually park at runtime ([§30.3](#sec-the-task-taskt-and-ownedtaskt-types), [§30.12](#sec-thread-synchronization)).
- The task returned by invoking a call-bounded callback is awaited to settlement on every path before the callee returns — abandonment an escape sink, the invocation itself rejected in a synchronous callee ([§28.14](#sec-scoped-callback-parameters); K6.1/[K6.4](#sec-kernel-k6), K6.3 + K3).
- A deferred-activation callee's plain function-typed parameter is retained only through frame residence — in the frame its call mints, bounded by that frame's life — every other retention past the call an escape sink ([§28.14](#sec-scoped-callback-parameters); K6.1 + K6.2).
- An unbound owned temporary is not passed as a plain argument to a deferred-activation or `Task`-family callee whose returned frame (or task) escapes the full expression ([§28.3](#sec-unbound-owned-temporaries); [K6.5](#sec-kernel-k6) + K8.4).
- A `Task`-family call result is an owned production at the call site ([§28.3](#sec-producers)): `using var text := File.ReadAllTextAsync(path);` binds an owned task — an obligation-assuming binding, not a [§28.10](#sec-using-var-initialized-from-a-borrow) pin — and [§30.5](#sec-result-lifetime-and-task-disposal)'s named-owning-location admissions read accordingly. (K6.3 — no axiom; the iterable family mints identically.)

<a id="sec-patterns-and-case"></a>
### C.7 Patterns and `case`

- A `_` arm appears at most once and is the last arm.
- A type-pattern `T` does not bind; a `var name: T` pattern binds.
- A type-pattern matches only non-null values; `null` matches only the `null` literal pattern, the `var` pattern, and `_`.
- `step` is not used in patterns; it is a range modifier only.
- A relational pattern requires a scrutinee type with an intrinsic ordering, and a range pattern one [§16.3](#sec-the-ranget-type) admits as a range's `T`, the integer types and `char`; over any other type, including one that declares an `operator <` group and a type parameter whatever its constraints, either pattern is a compile error ([§19.3](#sec-patterns), [§16.6](#sec-empty-ranges-and-equal-bound-ranges)).
- A record-destructuring pattern's positional-binding count matches the record's positional-field count; the same arity rule applies to choice-case destructuring, and a payload-carrying case may not be matched bare ([§35.5](#sec-choice-matching)).
- A destructuring pattern's slot list is **positional or named, never mixed**, a named slot's identifier resolving under [§19.3](#sec-patterns)'s per-kind rule, with an unmarked named-slot binding a borrow and a constant slot an `=` test, exactly as positionally ([§19.3](#sec-patterns)).
- A **marked named slot** (`move N = var x`) is admitted exactly in an owning match, naming an `owned`-marked or move-only payload field of the matched case with a top-level binding RHS, transferring per slot at arm selection — unmarked named slots never transfer ([§19.3](#sec-patterns), [§35.5](#sec-owning-match)).
- A borrowing-match binding of a payload of move-only value type, at any depth, or of the whole of a scrutinee that is such a binding, is not live at a write point of the construct — a non-`pure` call, implicit ones and those made during matching included; a store of a move-only value to, or a `move` out of, non-local storage; a disposing store; an `await`; a `yield return` — and a use of it as a receiver or operand, or of a closure that captured it at a call that invokes it or takes it as an argument, is live across that call, unless the scrutinee's source is provably unwritten. The provably unwritten sources are: a stable local of the body over the construct ([§7.4](#sec-stable-locals)) other than a borrowing-match binding; storage inside its value; a `readonly` field outside construction; or a binding over such a source ([§19.3](#sec-patterns), [§35.5](#sec-choice-borrowing-match)).
- A choice `case` with every declared case covered by an unguarded, irrefutable-slot arm is statically exhaustive with no `_` arm ([§19.6](#sec-exhaustiveness)); the marked owning-match scrutinee (`case move x of`) is a consume subject to the freeze ([K5](#sec-kernel-k5)), and guard evaluation in an owning match observes borrows, with transfer at arm selection ([§35.5](#sec-owning-match-guards)).
- A `case` over a **non-nullable record** scrutinee — non-nullable by its static type after [§7.4](#sec-member-access-on-nullable-values) narrowing at the `case` ([§19.1](#sec-forms)) — is statically exhaustive with no `_` arm when some unguarded arm is an all-slots-irrefutable destructure for that record type, or an exact-type pattern for it ([§19.6](#sec-exhaustiveness)); coverage is one level deep and a refutable slot contributes nothing.
- Static exhaustiveness counts only **unguarded** arms; a `when`-guarded arm contributes nothing to the proof ([§19.6](#sec-exhaustiveness)).
- A `case` over a closed hierarchy whose root or any leaf is generic is **not proven** statically exhaustive by leaf coverage; it is completable only by an irrefutable arm — an unguarded `_` or an unguarded untyped `var` — and draws the non-exhaustiveness warning without one ([§19.6](#sec-exhaustiveness-generic-leaves)).
- A statically exhaustive enum `case` cannot raise `MatchFailureException`: every producer of an enum value yields a declared value ([§5.4](#sec-enum-casts), [§9.8](#sec-serialization-synthesis), [§17.11](#sec-the-default-operator)), and the enum constants-coverage proof feeds [§21.7](#sec-the-return-statement)'s statement-`case` totality grant.
- Every class type named in a catch-arm pattern — bare, binding, or listed in a multi-type alternative — is `Exception` or a class deriving from it; an arm naming any other class type (`Object` included) is a compile error ([§31.2.1](#sec-arm-patterns)).
- A multi-type catch alternative in **binding** form types the binding as the listed types' **nearest common base** — with every listed type `Exception`-derived, always `Exception` or a class deriving from it ([§31.2.1](#sec-arm-patterns)).
- A generic type parameter used as a catch-arm type must carry an **`Exception`-derived class bound** (`where TEx: Exception`, or a class deriving from it); an unconstrained, value-constrained, or `where TEx: class`-only parameter, or one bounded by a class outside the `Exception` family, is a compile error, checked at the generic declaration ([§31.2.1](#sec-arm-patterns)).

<a id="sec-appendix-c-serialization"></a>
<a id="sec-appendix-c-serialization-synthesis"></a>
### C.8 Serialization synthesis

- A type declaring `ISerializable`/`IDeserializable` ([§9.8](#sec-serialization-synthesis)) that is not serialization-eligible is a compile error **at the conformance declaration**, naming the first offending member.
- A record's serialized components are value-shaped only (primitive/`string`/enum/eligible record/value-like eligible choice/`T?`/non-owning inline array — [§9.8](#sec-serialization-synthesis)'s record-admissibility); a class-, interface-, `Shared<T>`-, `Weak<T>`-, or heap-collection-typed serialized component makes a record ineligible (compile error at the conformance declaration). Positional and body records agree.
- A class enters serialization synthesis by declaring `ISerializable`/`IDeserializable`; its serialized shape is read from the field types (`owned`/value → owning edge, `Shared<T>` → identity participant, `Weak<T>` and plain borrow → back-edge), with no header shape clause.
- A derived class's serialized components include its base chain's, base-first; each class in the chain declaring a component of its own declares `ISerializable` or `IDeserializable` itself and hand-writes neither member, otherwise a compile error at the derived class's conformance declaration; and constructor selection binds inherited owning-tree and plain borrowing components by name as it binds own ones. The derived class's synthesized `Serialize` and `Deserialize` are not [§12.2](#sec-hiding-is-not-allowed) hiding declarations; a `Serialize` or `Deserialize` it hand-writes where a base's member of that name is synthesized is one ([§9.8](#sec-serialization-synthesis)).
- The synthesized `Serialize` of a class with no `polymorphic` registry of its own raises `SerializationException` when the receiver's run-time type is a derived class, however the member is reached (a component's `Serialize`, a base-typed receiver, a member a derived class inherits); a `Weak<T>` or plain borrowing back-edge, written as a `$ref`, does not reach it. A class is a synthesized class, admissible as a component, only for a serialization interface its own inheritance clause lists. No component is rejected because its static type is not `sealed` ([§9.8](#sec-serialization-synthesis)).
- An `abstract` or `closed` class with no `polymorphic` registry of its own and a synthesized `Serialize`, as a serialized component's type (directly, or under `T?`, `Shared<T>`, or a collection's element, key or value type; a `Weak<T>` or plain borrowing back-edge is admitted), is a compile error at the conformance declaration, as is such a class's `IDeserializable` with no hand-written `Deserialize` ([§9.8](#sec-serialization-synthesis)).
- `Shared<T>`/`Weak<T>` are admissible as serialized components when `T` is a serialization-eligible class; a `Shared<T>` serializes by identity (the tag keyed on the underlying value `Get()` borrows, reconstructed by `Clone()`), a `Weak<T>` as a back-reference (reconstructed by `Downgrade()`). A cycle closes through a nullable `Weak<T>?` back-edge on a `Shared<T>` spine — ordinary ownership-valid construction, no two-phase window.
- Identity is preserved on deserialization (a `$ref` binds to the already-reconstructed object, never duplicated). A `Weak<T>` reference whose target is never strongly reached anywhere in the graph raises `SerializationException` at deserialization.
- A `polymorphic` registry (a class-body member) is closed: each discriminator is a unique non-empty string literal, each registered type must be assignable to the declaring class and itself type-driven serialization-eligible (compile error at the registry otherwise); an unregistered discriminator (read) or unregistered run-time type (write) raises `SerializationException`. No reflective subtype discovery.
- A `serialized optional` component whose type is not defaultable ([§17.11](#sec-the-default-operator)) is a compile error at the conformance declaration, as a `serialized skip` component of non-defaultable type already is ([§9.8](#sec-serialization-synthesis)).
- `serialized` and its in-clause words `skip`, `optional` are contextual (the field-name clause); `polymorphic` is contextual in the class-member registry position ([Appendix B.2](#sec-contextual-keywords)).

<a id="sec-appendix-c-ffi"></a>
### C.9 FFI

- `extern` methods appear only inside `extern` blocks.
- `extern` declarations have no body.
- `extern` method signatures use only FFI-compatible types ([§32.5](#sec-ffi-compatible-types)).
- Empty `extern` blocks are rejected.
- `ref`/`out` on extern parameters are admitted only for FFI-compatible scalars and C-compatible records ([§32.5](#sec-boundary-out-ref)); `owned`, `out owned`, and `scoped` extern parameters are rejected.
- Nullable extern forms are exactly `CString?`/`WString?`/`RawBytes?` and nullable FFI function types; nullable value types are rejected at the boundary ([§32.5](#sec-ffi-compatible-types)).
- An inline-array extern argument is an assignable storage location; `[N]T` extern returns are rejected ([§32.5](#sec-ffi-compatible-types)).
- `RawBytes` occupies two C slots in parameter positions; `RawBytes` extern returns are rejected ([§32.5](#sec-ffi-compatible-types)).
- A callback argument of an extern call may not capture a binding that is an `out` argument of the same call ([§32.5](#sec-boundary-out-ref)).
- `Ptr<T>`'s pointee is gated per-instantiation to the FFI-pointee set; `Ptr<Ptr<U>>` is rejected ([§32.12](#sec-foreign-memory)). The C-compatible property is computed per [§3.6](#sec-derived-type-properties) and named in diagnostics ([§32.13](#sec-c-compatible-records)); the single-field direct admission requires exactly one integer-or-pointer scalar field.
- `env` pairing is well-formed: at most one `env` marker per extern declaration, paired with exactly one function-typed parameter containing exactly one `env` position; `env` does not combine with `variadic(N)`; capture-bearing callback arguments are admitted only at the paired parameter ([§32.8](#sec-callbacks)).
- `variadic(N)` requires N ≤ the declared arity and rides the `symbol` clause; variadic-position parameter types are drawn from the promoted set, and the diagnostic for a non-promoted type names the type to declare ([§32.11](#sec-symbol-binding)).
- `Interop.CodeAddress<F>`'s argument satisfies the static callback admission; `F` is gated per-instantiation to FFI-compatible function types ([§32.8](#sec-callbacks)).

<a id="sec-operators"></a>
### C.10 Operators

- `=` and `<>` are not overloaded on classes.
- An operator overload is `public static` and at least one parameter is the declaring type ([§25.2](#sec-operator-overloading-restrictions)).
- Operator parameters carry no parameter modifiers (`ref`/`out`/`owned`/`scoped` are rejected semantically); `owned` may appear only on an operator's return type ([§25.2](#sec-operator-overloading-restrictions)).
- A record/enum/choice overloading homogeneous `=`/`<>` also declares `Equals(T)` and `GetHashCode` — on a record, `override GetHashCode`; on an enum or choice, `override` or plain (the [§25.2](#sec-operator-overloading-restrictions) co-declaration rule; [§10.5](#sec-restrictions)).
- A body record or value-like choice carrying a **homogeneous** `=`/`<>` overload is **not auto-hashable**; a heterogeneous-operand one (`T = U`) neither qualifies nor disqualifies ([§9.2](#sec-body-records)'s membership list and third disqualifier, [§35.7](#sec-choice-equality); ruled).
- Comparison operators are overloaded as a complete group (`<`, `>`, `<=`, `>=` together; `=` and `<>` together).
- An enum has no intrinsic ordering: `<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=` on enum operands resolve only to declared `operator` overloads, and are a compile error where none applies; an order is written `int(a) < int(b)`, as a declared group, or through `IComparable<E>` ([§10.5](#sec-restrictions), [§3.5](#sec-operators-on-primitive-types)).
- The bitwise complement operator is `~`; the boolean negation operator is `not`. They are not interchangeable. `~` is user-overloadable; `not` is not.
- `++` and `--` are not user-overloadable: `operator ++`/`operator --` is not an `OpToken` (Appendix A.4), and such a declaration is a **compile error at the operator token** whose diagnostic names that rule ([§25.1](#sec-overloadable-operators) states it and its reason; [§17.6](#sec-the-increment-and-decrement-operators) reads it at the use site). `x++`/`x--` is admitted only on an operand of a type [§6.6](#sec-compound-assignments)'s compound form admits — an integer type, a floating-point type, `decimal`, or `char` ([§17.6](#sec-the-increment-and-decrement-operators)).
- Assignment and compound-assignment operators (`:=`, `+=`, `-=`, `*=`, `/=`, `mod=`, `&=`, `|=`, `^=`, `<<=`, `>>=`, `??=`) are not user-overloadable. The `+=` and `-=` event-subscription forms on `EventSource<T>`, `AsyncEventSource<T>`, and `SharedEventSource<T>` are a fixed compiler desugaring ([§17.2](#sec-notes-on-operators)), not operator overloads.

<a id="sec-static-initialization"></a>
### C.11 Static initialization

- Cyclic static initialization across distinct types is rejected at compile time where visible to [§22.13](#sec-static-initialization-order)'s dependency approximation, a missed cycle raising the runtime-synthesized `TypeInitializationException` at the same-thread re-entrant touch with partially-initialized statics never observed; within-type forward reads are rejected through the same call set, the residual routes recorded with the checked-mode watermark bound ([§22.13](#sec-static-initialization-order)).
- A type's static initializer runs exactly once process-wide; a cross-domain touch of a type mid-initialization blocks until initialization completes or observes the failed state ([§22.12](#sec-static-members) rule 1).
- A mutable (non-`readonly`, non-`const`) static field or auto-property has one of [§22.12](#sec-static-members) rule 2's admitted forms — an internally-synchronized handle type (a type declaring the **synchronized** and not the **displacement-unbounded** fact (stdlib §1)), a `Task?`/`Task<T>?` lazy cache, or the warned form-(iii)/(iv) value and owning-inline-array statics — anything else rejected.
- `static readonly` of immutable content, and `const` (a primitive value type or `string`), are unrestricted; a `static readonly` field of class or interface type outside rule 4's warning-suppression set — the types declaring the **synchronized** or the **immutable** fact (stdlib §1): the six form-(i) types (`SharedEventSource<T>` included), `Locked<T>`, `RwLocked<T>`, `FrozenArray<T>`, and `CancellationTokenSource` — draws the [§22.12](#sec-static-members) rule 4 declaration-site warning; every other `static readonly` field or auto-property takes that rule's residual — the warning by default (function types included), [§9.7](#sec-records-and-disposal)'s null-source rule for borrow-carrying value kinds, and rejection — taking precedence where a choice is both — for an owning-classified choice, which [§22.13](#sec-static-initialization-order)'s exit pass would not dispose.
- A handler argument at any call resolving to a subscribe position declared on `ISharedEvent<T>`/`SharedEventSource<T>` is compiler-checked capture-free, method-reference formation over such a position rejected so the admission holds at every site ([§28.14](#sec-scoped-callback-parameters), [§22.12](#sec-static-members) rule 5; stdlib §6.5).
- The access that triggers a failing static initialization, and every subsequent access, observe the same cached `TypeInitializationException`; the original exception is observable only as its `InnerException` ([§22.7](#sec-constructors)).
- A `const` declaration's initializer is a constant expression ([§17.14](#sec-constant-expressions)); an initializer whose compile-time evaluation faults (overflow, division by zero) is rejected at the declaration, never deferred to runtime.

<a id="sec-entry-point"></a>
### C.12 Entry point

- An executable build's root compilation ([§2.8.4](#sec-program-assembly)) defines exactly one qualifying `Main` method, or `--main-class` ([§33.5](#sec-program-entry-point-resolution)) selects one when several classes qualify; a qualifying `Main` in a dependency artifact is inert — an ordinary method, never a candidate, never a conflict ([§33.1](#sec-the-main-method)).
- A class declares at most one qualifying `Main`; multiple qualifying overloads in the same class are rejected at compile time without flag-based override.
- `Main` is `public static`. If `async`, its return type is `Task`, `Task<int>`, or one of the parameterized forms; otherwise it returns `()` or `int`.

<a id="sec-appendix-c-modules"></a>
### C.13 Module identity and program assembly

- Every module in a program is the product of exactly one compilation; no source file joins a module by declaring its name, and `internal` access is closed by the declaring module's compilation — including between co-members of an SCC unit ([§2.8.1](#sec-module-identity-and-closure)).
- A build whose artifact set contains two distinct artifacts declaring the same module name — or an artifact declaring a module name the implementation provides — is rejected, naming both origins; bit-identical duplicate presentations are deduplicated, not diagnosed ([§2.8.1](#sec-module-identity-and-closure) rules 3/5).
- An `import` naming the enclosing file's own module is a compile error ([§2.8.1](#sec-module-identity-and-closure) rule 4).
- A build missing a member of the dependency closure — including modules referenced only from declaration bodies carried in an interface — is an error naming the missing module ([§2.8.3](#sec-transitive-closure-and-type-identity) rule 1).
- Naming a transitively-reachable type in source requires importing its declaring module; using its values does not ([§2.8.3](#sec-transitive-closure-and-type-identity) rule 2).
- Disagreeing descriptions of one type in a build's closure (a stale artifact) are a build error naming the artifacts ([§2.8.3](#sec-transitive-closure-and-type-identity) rule 3).
- Presenting an executable artifact as a dependency is a build error naming the artifact and its kind ([§2.8.4](#sec-program-assembly) rule 4).
- A member's contract records — clause kind, `static` qualifier, canonical text, recorded tier — and a class's `invariant` records agree across all descriptions of a type in a build's closure; disagreement is the rule-3 staleness error ([§2.8.2](#sec-artifact-interface), [§2.8.3](#sec-transitive-closure-and-type-identity)).
- A contract record's recorded tier is the clause's [§22.16](#sec-contract-tiers) tier, a declaration fact (the `static` qualifier; the constant-fold prover floor), never what a particular compilation opportunistically discharged at a body or call site ([§2.8.2](#sec-artifact-interface)).

---

### C.14 Purity

- `pure` combines with neither `async` nor `yield`; destructors, static constructors, `extern` declarations, and auto-properties carry no `pure`.
- A pure member declares no `ref`/`out`/`out owned`/`owned`/`scoped` parameter, no move-only value parameter or return ([§15.3](#sec-move-only-value-types)), and no `owned` class-typed return.
- A pure body contains no store whose target root leaves the frame, no disposal-running or owned-consuming operation, no class construction outside the throw carve-out, no invocation of a function-typed value, no enumerator-constructing `for`, and no call to a member not pure-declared or pure-classified ([§22.15](#sec-pure-body-rules)).
- The throw-carve-out operand's class is trivial-dispose and its invoked constructor pure ([§22.15](#sec-pure-throw)); the dispose-after-arm on such an operand is the compiler-inserted flag-setting free, running no user code ([§28.9](#sec-runtime-managed-types), [§28.2](#sec-checked-disposal)).
- Overrides and implementations of pure members restate `pure`; purity never narrows down an override chain ([§22.15](#sec-pure-dispatch)).
- Field initializers of a pure-constructed class and default-value expressions of pure members' parameters satisfy the pure-body rules.

### C.15 Contract clauses

- A contract clause's expression is `bool`, satisfies the [§22.15](#sec-pure-members) pure-body rules, and contains no `throw`, no `await`, no store, and no owned-consuming or disposal-running operation.
- `requires` evaluates after argument binding and before the chain/initializers/body, in declaration order, and is never elided unless proven; `ensures` evaluates on every normal-completion path after result and `out`-slot binding and before scope-end disposals, and never on a throw path.
- `result` appears only in `ensures` of a member with a declared return type and is a borrow position, and each `old` operand evaluates exactly once at entry under [§22.16](#sec-contract-clauses)'s capture rules — copyable kinds by copy, class/interface operands as frame-resident borrows, move-only operands rejected with the copyable-projection remedy ([§28.3](#sec-local-variables-ownership-and-borrows)'s binding rules).
- An override or implementation declares no `requires` and may add `ensures`; inherited clauses are never restated; multi-root `requires` combines by disjunction, `ensures` by conjunction.
- A `static`-qualified clause the active prover cannot discharge at its discharge site (declaring body for `ensures`/`invariant`; each call site for `requires`) is a compile error; a `static requires` mentions only caller-visible state; a constant clause folding `false` is a compile error.
- The class invariant is evaluated at most-derived-construction exit, public-method entry/exit, and public-setter entry/exit — never on non-public members, destructors, `Dispose`, throw paths, or `this`-receiver calls.
- Clauses never distinguish overloads; `invariant` members appear only in classes; `old`/`result` appear only where the rules above admit them.

<a id="appendix-d-conformance-levels"></a>
## Appendix D: Conformance Levels

**Diagnostic identity.** This specification mandates *when* a diagnostic is produced (accept / warn / reject) and, in places, what it should name; it deliberately defines **no error-code registry or message taxonomy**. Diagnostic identity — codes, exact wording, formatting — is implementation-defined, and conformance claims about diagnostics classify outcomes only (a mandated rejection is satisfied by any error at the mandated site; a mandated warning by any warning). A future revision may introduce a code registry if multiple implementations materialize; until then, requiring exact messages would freeze prose this document revises freely.

This specification defines two conformance levels. The partition exists so that an implementation can be *complete and sound for a well-defined inner language* before the outer features are attempted, and so that the test-suite and teaching material can follow the same boundary.

<a id="sec-the-levels"></a>
### D.1 The levels

- **Core conformance.** An implementation conforms at the Core level when it implements every normative rule of this specification *except* the Extended features listed in D.2, and *rejects* — with a diagnostic naming the construct and the feature — any program that uses an Extended feature it does not implement. Silent misbehavior on Extended input is non-conforming; clean rejection is the Core-conforming response.
- **Full conformance.** An implementation conforms at the Full level when it implements the entire specification: Core plus every Extended feature.

An implementation may also conform at "Core plus named features" (e.g., *Core + Events + FFI*), implementing some Extended features and rejecting the rest; a conformance claim of this form names the features implemented.

<a id="sec-extended-features"></a>
### D.2 The Extended features

| Feature | Specification sections | Standard-library sections |
|---|---|---|
| **Events** | the event-subscription desugaring of [§17.2](#sec-notes-on-operators) | stdlib [§6.5](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-events-ievent-eventsource) entire — `EventSource<T>`, `IEvent<T>`, `AsyncEventSource<T>`, `IAsyncEvent<T>`, `ISharedEvent<T>`, `SharedEventSource<T>` — plus `Subscription` (stdlib [§2.11](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-subscription)) |
| **Asynchronous programming** | [§30](#sec-asynchronous-programming) entire — including domains, spawning, and channels ([§30.13](#sec-runtime-model)–[§30.15](#sec-channels)); [§28.12](#sec-asynchronous-disposal) (`await using`, `IAsyncDisposable`); the async-iterator forms of [§29](#sec-iteration-2) (`IAsyncEnumerable<T>`, `IAsyncEnumerator<T>`, `IOwningAsyncEnumerable<T>`, `IOwningAsyncEnumerator<T>`) | `Task`, `Task<T>`, `OwningTask<T>`, completion sources, `CancellationToken`/`CancellationTokenSource`, `Mutex`/`Semaphore`/`Atomic<T>`, `Domain`, `Channel<T>`/`ChannelSender<T>`, the async forms of IO and sequence operations |
| **Serialization synthesis** | [§9.8](#sec-serialization-synthesis) | stdlib §2.14–2.15 |
| **Foreign Function Interface** | [§32](#sec-foreign-function-interface); the FFI clauses of [§15.1.3](#sec-inline-array-ffi); the C-compatible row and reservation-clause exception of [§3.6](#sec-derived-type-properties) | `Ptr<T>`, `Interop` (stdlib §10.5–§10.6); `RawBytes.FromForeign`, `CString`/`WString.Pointer` (stdlib §10.1–§10.3); `OwningBuffer<T>.DangerousPointer` (stdlib §4.14) |
| **Buffers and spans** | the buffer/span clauses of [§28.11](#sec-collection-element-ownership) (`move` on `OwningBuffer`/`Span` slots) | stdlib §3.3, §4.14–4.16 |
| **Contract proving** | the extended prover fragment of [§22.16](#sec-contract-tiers) (linear integer arithmetic, null-test flow, closed-set case analysis) — what gives the `static` clause qualifier reach beyond the constant-and-`when`-clause floor; a Core implementation **rejects** a `static` clause it cannot discharge (D.1's clean rejection), never downgrading a demanded proof to a runtime check | — |
| **Sequence operations (LINQ-style)** | — | stdlib §5 entire |
| **Shared ownership** | [§28.13](#sec-shared-ownership) | `Shared<T>`, `Weak<T>` (stdlib §2.16) |
| **Move-only value types (owning inline arrays, owning choices)** | [§15.1.1](#sec-owning-inline-arrays) and the `owned` slot marker of Appendix A.5's `InlineArrayType`; [§15.3](#sec-move-only-value-types); the owning choice classification and its clauses — the `owned` payload marker's owning reading, the owning match ([§35.4](#sec-choice-classification)–[§35.5](#sec-owning-match)), the drop-on-overwrite rule, and the transfer-closure field clause of [§35.12](#sec-choice-sendability); the move-only discard clause of [§17.13](#sec-the-discard-_); the owning-inline-array field clauses of [§28.5](#sec-owned-fields) (including the double-marking rejection) and [§22.13](#sec-static-initialization-order); the `old`-operand rejection of [§22.16](#sec-contract-clauses); the move-only clause of [§28.7](#sec-reassigning-owned-fields); the move-only row of [§28.11](#sec-element-slot-policy)'s element-category table; the owned-slot clauses of [§29.2](#sec-desugaring-of-for)'s inline-array desugaring and the move-only paragraph of [§29.8](#sec-iterators-with-owned-parameters); the move-only instantiation checks of [§7.10](#sec-generics-and-nullability) and [§14.2](#sec-constraints) (`where T: value`) | — |

Everything not listed is **Core**: lexical structure through generics, records, enums, classes, interfaces, inheritance, nullability, patterns and `case`, expressions and statements, operators and overloading, properties and indexers, the entire ownership system of [§28](#sec-resource-management) (except §28.12, §28.13, and the move-only value-type clauses of §28.5, §28.7, and §28.11 carved to the **Move-only value types** row above), synchronous iteration ([§29](#sec-iteration-2)'s non-async forms, including iterator methods and `IOwningEnumerable<T>`), exceptions ([§31](#sec-exception-handling)), the entry point, and the corresponding standard-library sections.

<a id="sec-feature-dependencies"></a>
### D.3 Dependencies and closure

- Extended features depend on Core; Core depends on no Extended feature. The Core sections' references *into* Extended sections (e.g., [§28.3](#sec-local-variables-ownership-and-borrows)'s notes on async lambdas, [§9.7](#sec-records-and-disposal)'s span examples) are normative only for implementations of the referenced feature.
- The async-iterator forms belong to **Asynchronous programming** and additionally require synchronous iteration (Core). **Buffers and spans**, **Sequence operations**, and **Shared ownership** depend only on Core. **Events**' async event source requires **Asynchronous programming**; the synchronous `EventSource<T>` does not, and neither do `ISharedEvent<T>`/`SharedEventSource<T>`: their capture-free admission is ordinary [§28.14](#sec-scoped-callback-parameters) typing, and in a single-domain build the synchronization guarantee is satisfied vacuously; the deferred shared-async twin, if ever shipped, requires Asynchronous programming like `AsyncEventSource<T>`.
- **Move-only value types** depend only on Core (value-like and borrow-bearing choices are Core; only the owning classification is this row's), and no other Extended feature depends on them: **Buffers and spans** does not (`OwningBuffer<T>`, `Span<T>`, and `ReadOnlySpan<T>` reject move-only element types, [§14.4](#sec-owned-as-a-generic-argument)); **Asynchronous programming** *references* them — [§30.14](#sec-sendable-types)'s transfer-closure rule 2 admits an owning-inline-array field, and [§30.1](#sec-async-methods)'s frame rule covers move-only parameters — but does not depend on them: an Extended section's references into another Extended feature's clauses are normative only for implementations of both features, the first bullet's rule for Core-section references into Extended sections generalized to Extended-to-Extended references.
- A Core implementation's standard library omits the types of unimplemented Extended features entirely (they are absent, not stubbed); programs referencing them fail name resolution with the feature-naming diagnostic of D.1.

<a id="sec-conformance-and-the-runtime-model"></a>
### D.4 Conformance and the runtime model

The execution-domain guarantees of [§30.13](#sec-runtime-model) are stated within the Asynchronous-programming feature, but their soundness consequences for [§28](#sec-resource-management) hold trivially in a Core implementation: with no `async`/`await`, every program is a single continuation in a single domain. A Core implementation therefore satisfies the domain guarantees by construction.
